sections.text:

Arterial Supply: Plantar and dorsal metatarsal arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:

- body, which appears in utero at third month;

- head, which appears during the third to fourth years.

These ossification centers fuse with each other during the 17th and 20th years (Standring, 2016).

18137.name: Proximal Articular Facet of Third Metatarsal Bone
18137.latin: Facies articularis proximalis ossis tertii metatarsi

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The proximal articular facet of third metatarsal bone is the triangular, posterior area of its base. It articulates with the third metatarsal articular facet of the lateral cuneiform bone, contributing to the formation of the tarsometatarsal joints.

18277.name: Distal Articular Facet of Third Metatarsal Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The distal articular facet of third metatarsal bone is the convex, anterior area of its head. It articulates with the proximal articular facet found on the proximal phalanx of the third toe, forming the third metatarsophalangeal joint.

sections.text:
Location: Foot.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Key Features: Head, body, base, tuberosity, and articular facet.

Articulates With: Middle phalanx of third toe.

Arterial Supply: Proper plantar digital arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The distal phalanx of third toe is one of the fourteen phalangeal bones of the foot. It is classified as a long bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: head, body, and base;

- landmarks: tuberosity and articular facet.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The distal phalanx is located distal to the middle phalanx and articulates with it at the distal interphalangeal joint.

sections.title: Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the distal phalanx occurs at two ossification centers, these are found in the:

- body, which appears in utero during the third month;

- base, which appears within the second to eighth years.

These ossification centers fuse with each other by the 18th year (Standring, 2016).

sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the head, body, and base of the distal phalanx can be easily palpated.

22099.name: Cuboid Articular Facet of Navicular Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The cuboid articular facet is the small area found on the lateral surface of the navicular bone. It articulates with the navicular articular facet of the cuboid bone, forming the cuboideonavicular joint.

20737.name: Distal Articular Surface of Navicular Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The distal articular surface (anterior surface) of navicular is the convex, anterior area of the bone. It’s one of the six surfaces of the navicular bone, the other five being the plantar, dorsal, medial and lateral surfaces, and the proximal articular surface.

The distal articular surface of navicular bone contains the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiform articular facets.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Foot.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Tuberosity, plantar process, proximal and distal articular surfaces, and cuboid articular facet.

Articulates With: Talus, cuboid bone, medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiform bones.

Arterial Supply: Dorsalis pedis and medial plantar arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the navicular bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the third year (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the tuberosity of navicular bone is subcutaneous and can be palpated as a large bony prominence that is located anteroinferior to the medial malleolus.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of navicular bone

- Köhler’s disease

- Calcaneonavicular coalition

- Talonavicular coalition

- Naviculocuneiform coalition

- Cuboideonavicular coalition

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

23738.name: Proximal Articular Surface of Navicular Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The proximal articular surface (posterior surface) of navicular bone is the oval, concave, posterior area of the bone. It’s one of the six surfaces of the navicular bone, the other five being the plantar, dorsal, medial and lateral surfaces, and the distal articular surface.

The proximal articular surface of navicular bone articulates with the navicular articular surface of the talus, contributing to the formation of the talocalcaneonavicular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior talar articular facet (posterior facet for talus, or posterior talar articular surface) is the large, oval area found along the dorsal surface of the calcaneus. It’s one of the three facets on the calcaneus that articulates with the talus, the other two being the anterior and middle talar articular facets.

The posterior talar articular facet articulates with the posterior calcaneal articular facet of the talus, contributing to the formation of the talocalcaneonavicular joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Foot.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Calcaneal tuberosity, sustentaculum tali, calcaneal sulcus, and anterior, medial and lateral processes of calcaneal tuberosity.

Articulates With: Talus, cuboid bone.

Arterial Supply: Calcaneal anastomosis; medial and lateral plantar arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the calcaneus occurs at two ossification centers:

- a large center, which forms the majority of the bone and appears in utero during the third month;

- a small center, which is found along the posterior surface of the bone and appears within the sixth to eighth years.

These two ossification centers fuse during the 14th to 16th years (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text:
The following bony features of the calcaneus are relevant to surface anatomy.

- The sustentaculum tali may be palpated as a small prominence located inferior to the medial malleolus.

- The medial process of calcaneal tuberosity may sometimes be deeply palpated along the posteromedial aspect of the foot.

- The lateral surface of the calcaneus is easily palpated as it’s mostly subcutaneous.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of calcaneus

- Talocalcaneal coalition

- Calcaneonavicular coalition

- Calcaneocuboid coalition

- Haglund’s heel/syndrome

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The middle talar articular surface (middle facet for talus, or middle talar articular facet) is the oval, concave area found along the dorsal surface of the sustentaculum tali of calcaneus. It’s one of the three facets on the calcaneus that articulates with the talus, the other two being the anterior and posterior talar articular facets.

The middle talar articular facet articulates with the middle calcaneal articular facet of the talus, contributing to the formation of the talocalcaneonavicular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The cuboid articular surface (anterior surface) of calcaneus is the saddle-shaped, articular area on the anterior aspect of the anterior process of calcaneus. It’s one of the six surfaces of the calcaneus, the other five being the posterior, dorsal, plantar, medial and lateral surfaces.

The cuboid articular surface of calcaneus articulates with the proximal articular surface of cuboid bone, forming the calcaneocuboid joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior talar articular surface (anterior facet for talus, or anterior talar articular facet) is the small, flat area found along the dorsal surface of the anterior process of calcaneus. It’s one of the three facets on the calcaneus that articulates with the talus, the other two being the middle and posterior talar articular facets.

The anterior talar articular facet articulates with the anterior calcaneal articular facet of the talus, contributing to the formation of the talocalcaneonavicular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior calcaneal articular facet (posterior facet for calcaneus, or posterior calcaneal articular surface) is the large, oval, concave area found along the inferior aspect of the body of the talus. It’s one of the three facets on the talus that articular with the calcaneus, the other two being the anterior and middle calcaneal articular facets.

The posterior calcaneal articular facet articulates with the posterior talar articular facet of the calcaneus, forming the subtalar joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The middle facet for calcaneus (middle calcaneal articular facet, or middle calcaneal articular surface) is the oval, convex area found along the inferior aspect of the head of talus. It is one of the three facets on the talus that articular with the calcaneus, the other two being the anterior and posterior calcaneal articular facets.

The middle facet for calcaneus articulates with the middle talar articular facet of the calcaneus, contributing to the formation of the talocalcaneonavicular joint.

sections.text:
The proximal articular surface (posterior surface) is the triangular, posterior area of the lateral cuneiform bone. It’s one of the six surfaces of the lateral cuneiform bone, the other five being the plantar, dorsal, medial and lateral surfaces, and the distal articular surface.

The proximal articular surface articulates with the lateral cuneiform articular facet of the navicular bone, contributing to the formation of the cuneonavicular joint.

sections.text:
Location: Foot.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Proximal and distal articular surfaces, and second, third and fourth metatarsal articular facets.

Articulates With: Cuboid bone, navicular bone, intermediate cuneiform bone, second, third, and fourth metatarsal bones.

Arterial Supply: Dorsalis pedis artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the lateral cuneiform bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the first year after birth (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
sections.text: In some individuals, the fourth metatarsal articular facet of lateral cuneiform bone is absent (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the dorsal surface of lateral cuneiform bone can be palpated proximal to the base of the third metatarsal bone.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of lateral cuneiform bone

- Intercuneiform coalition

- Naviculocuneiform coalition

- Cuboideocuneiform/cubocuneiform coalition

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

23969.name: Distal Articular Surface of Lateral Cuneiform Bone
23969.latin: Facies articularis distalis ossis cuneiformis lateralis
alternate: Anterior Surface of Lateral Cuneiform Bone
Anterior Surface of Third Cuneiform Bone
Distal Articular Surface of Third Cuneiform Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The distal articular surface (anterior surface) is the triangular, anterior area of the lateral cuneiform bone. It’s one of the six surfaces of the lateral cuneiform bone, the other five being the plantar, dorsal, medial and lateral surfaces, and the proximal articular surface.

The distal articular surface contains the third and fourth metatarsal articular facets.

17865.name: Cuboid Articular Facet of Lateral Cuneiform Bone
17865.latin: Facies articularis cuboidea ossis cuneiformis lateralis
alternate: Cuboid Articular Facet of Third Cuneiform Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The cuboid articular facet is the large, oval, posteriorly located area on the lateral surface of the lateral cuneiform bone. It articulates with the lateral cuneiform articular facet of the cuboid bone, forming the cuneocuboid joint.

16935.name: Proximolateral Articular Area of Medial Cuneiform Bone
16935.latin: Area articularis proximolateralis ossis cuneiformis medialis

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The proximolateral articular area of medial cuneiform bone consists of the proximal and lateral aspects of the bone that articulate with adjacent bones. It includes the proximal articular surface and intermediate cuneiform articular facet of medial cuneiform bone.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Foot.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Proximal and distal articular surfaces, dorsal and plantar surfaces, second metatarsal articular facet, and intermediate cuneiform articular facet.

Articulates With: Navicular bone, first and second metatarsal bones, intermediate cuneiform bone.

Arterial Supply: Dorsalis pedis artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the medial cuneiform bone may occur at two ossification centers, which appear within the second year (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the medial surface of medial cuneiform bone can be palpated on the medial aspect of the foot, between the tuberosity of navicular bone and the base of first metatarsal bone.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of medial cuneiform bone

- Intercuneiform coalition

- Naviculocuneiform coalition

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

16730.name: Second Metatarsal Articular Facet of Medial Cuneiform Bone
16730.latin: Facies articularis metatarsi secundi ossis cuneiformis medialis
alternate: Second Metatarsal Articular Facet of First Cuneiform Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The second metatarsal articular facet is the small, rounded, anteriorly located area on the lateral surface of the medial cuneiform bone. It is one of the two articular facets found on the lateral surface of the medial cuneiform bone, the other being the intermediate cuneiform articular facet.

It articulates with the medial cuneiform articular facet of the second metatarsal bone, contributing to the formation of the tarsometatarsal joints.

24356.name: Distal Articular Surface of Medial Cuneiform Bone
24356.latin: Facies articularis distalis ossis cuneiformis medialis
alternate: Anterior Surface of First Cuneiform Bone
Anterior Surface of Medial Cuneiform Bone
Distal Articular Surface of First Cuneiform Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The distal articular surface (anterior surface) is the kidney-shaped, anterior area of the medial cuneiform bone. It’s one of the six surfaces of the medial cuneiform bone, the other five being the plantar, dorsal, medial and lateral surfaces, and the proximal articular surface.

The distal articular surface articulates with the proximal articular facet of the first metatarsal bone, contributing to the formation of the tarsometatarsal joints.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Foot.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Proximal and distal articular surfaces, plantar and dorsal surfaces, and medial and lateral cuneiform articular facets.

Articulates With: Navicular bone, lateral and medial cuneiform bones, second metatarsal bone.

Arterial Supply: Dorsalis pedis artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the intermediate cuneiform bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the third year (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
sections.text: In some individuals, an accessory ossicle may be associated with the intermediate cuneiform bone (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the intermediate cuneiform bone is difficult to palpate, as it’s more proximally positioned than the medial and lateral cuneiform bones.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of intermediate cuneiform bone

- Intercuneiform coalition

- Naviculocuneiform coalition

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

19366.name: Articular Area of Intermediate Cuneiform Bone
alternate: Articular Area of Middle Cuneiform Bone
Articular Area of Second Cuneiform Bone

sections.title: Description

24235.name: Proximal Articular Surface of Cuboid Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The proximal articular surface (posterior articular surface) is the triangular, posterior area of the cuboid bone. It’s one of the six surfaces of the cuboid bone, the other five being the plantar, dorsal, medial and lateral surfaces, and the distal articular surface.

The proximal articular surface of cuboid bone articulates with the articular surface for cuboid bone on the calcaneus, forming the calcaneocuboid joint.

19573.name: Navicular Articular Facet of Cuboid Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The navicular articular facet is the small, oval, posteriorly located area on the medial surface of the cuboid bone. It articulates with the cuboid articular facet of the navicular bone, forming the cuboideonavicular joint.

22123.name: Distal Articular Surface of Cuboid Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The distal articular surface (anterior surface) is the oval, anterior area of the cuboid bone. It’s one of the six surfaces of the cuboid bone, the other five being the plantar, dorsal, medial and lateral surfaces, and the proximal articular surface.

The distal articular surface of cuboid bone contains the fourth and fifth metatarsal articular facets.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Foot.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Tuberosity, calcaneal process, proximal and distal articular surfaces, and navicular articular facet.

Articulates With: Calcaneus, navicular bone, lateral cuneiform bone, fourth and fifth metatarsal bones.

Arterial Supply: Medial and lateral plantar arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the cuboid bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears just before birth (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the cuboid bone can be located by first identifying the tuberosity of fifth metatarsal bone, which can be palpated on the lateral aspect of the foot. The lateral surface of cuboid bone is then found in the depression located immediately proximal to this landmark.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of cuboid bone

- Calcaneocuboid coalition

- Cuboideonavicular coalition

- Cuboideocuneiform/cubocuneiform coalition

- Cuboid syndrome

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

22594.name: Lateral Cuneiform Articular Facet of Cuboid Bone
22594.latin: Facies articularis cuneiformia lateralia ossis cuboidei
alternate: Third Cuneiform Articular Facet of Cuboid Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lateral (third) cuneiform articular facet is the large, oval, anteriorly located area on the medial surface of the cuboid bone. It articulates with the cuboid articular facet of the lateral cuneiform bone, forming the cuneocuboid joint.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The sesamoid bones of the foot are the pair of small, oval, nodule-like bones found along the plantar aspect of the great toe. The two distal tendons of the flexor hallucis brevis muscle each contain one of these sesamoid bones.

In some individuals, other sesamoid bones within the foot may be found at the metatarsophalangeal joints of the second and third toes.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The sesamoid bones of the foot are located inferior to the first metatarsophalangeal joint, within the tendons of the flexor hallucis brevis muscle. The tendon of the flexor hallucis longus muscle travels between the sesamoid bones.

sections.title: Function
Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Knee region.

Bone Type: Sesamoid bone.

Key Features: Apex, base, articular and anterior surfaces, vertical ridge, and medial and lateral articular facets.

Articulates With: Femur.

Arterial Supply: Genicular anastomosis.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The patella (or kneecap) is a bone found in the knee region. It’s somewhat triangular and is classified as the largest sesamoid bone. It contains the following bony features:

- surfaces: articular and anterior surfaces, medial and lateral borders, apex, and base;

- landmarks: vertical ridge and medial and lateral facets.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Surfaces and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The patella is located anterior to the knee joint, within the quadriceps tendon. The patellar tendon extends inferiorly from the apex of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. The patella articulates with the femur at the patellofemoral joint, which contributes to the formation of the knee joint.

The patella’s functions are to strengthen the quadriceps tendon for knee extension and to reduce friction between the quadriceps tendon and adjacent bones at the knee joint.

sections.title: Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the patella occurs at several ossification centers, which appear within the third to sixth years. Complete ossification occurs during early adolescence (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
sections.text: In some individuals, the patella may be present in a bipartite or tripartite condition (i.e., divided into two or three parts, respectively). This usually results from failure of the ossification centers to fuse (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the anterior surface of patella is subcutaneous and therefore easily palpated.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Patellar fracture

- Patellar tracking and dislocation

- Patellofemoral pain syndrome

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The articular (posterior) surface of the patella is the smooth, concave area on the inner aspect of the bone. It consists of a vertical ridge, which divides it into unequal medial and lateral articular facets.

The articular surface of the patella articulates with the distal end of the femur, forming the patellofemoral joint. Overall, the patellofemoral, medial femorotibial, and lateral femorotibial joints collectively form the knee joint.

23272.name: Articular Area of Distal Part of Tibia

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of distal part of tibia is the smooth, inferior end of the bone. It includes the fibular notch, inferior articular surface of the tibia, and articular facet of the medial malleolus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Leg.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Key Features: Body, medial and lateral condyles, tibial tuberosity, soleal line, and fibular notch.

Articulates With: Femur, fibula, talus.

Arterial Supply: Genicular anastomosis, anterior and posterior tibial arteries, medial malleolar network.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
Variations
sections.text:
In some individuals:

- the proximal part may present an additional intercondylar tubercle;

- an accessory ossicle, known as the os subtibiale, may be present between the distal part of tibia and the talus (Standring, 2016).

The tibia also displays sexual dimorphism, where the mean tibial length is greater in males than in females (Standring, 2016). Additionally, the female tibia is more slender, with a straighter body and smaller and narrower condyles and malleoli (Brzobohatá et al., 2016)

sections.title: Surface Anatomy
List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of tibia

- Osgood-Schlatter disease

- Medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints)

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Brzobohatá, H., Krajíček, V., Horák, Z. and Velemínská, J. (2016) 'Sexual Dimorphism of the Human Tibia through Time: Insights into Shape Variation Using a Surface-Based Approach', PLoS One, 11(11), pp. e0166461.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The fibular articular facet is the small, smooth, circular area found on the posteroinferior aspect of the lateral condyle of the tibia. It articulates with the articular facet of the head of the fibula, forming the superior tibiofibular joint.

21158.name: Articular Area of Proximal Part of Tibia

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of proximal part of tibia is the somewhat flat, superior end of the bone. It includes the articular facets of the medial and lateral condyles of the tibia.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular facet of lateral malleolus is the flat, triangular area found along the medial aspect of the lateral malleolus of the fibula. It’s located anterior to the malleolar fossa of the fibula and articulates with the lateral malleolar facet of the talus, contributing to the formation of the ankle joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Leg.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Key Features: Head, neck, body, lateral malleolus, malleolar groove and malleolar fossa.

Articulates With: Tibia, talus.

Arterial Supply: Genicular anastomosis, anterior and posterior tibial arteries, lateral malleolar network.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
Variations
Surface Anatomy
List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of fibula
- Free vascularized fibular grafting (FVFG)

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

24833.name: Articular Facet of Head of Fibula

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular facet of the head of the fibula is the flat, circular area found along the superomedial aspect of the head of the fibula. It articulates with the fibular articular facet of the tibia, forming the superior tibiofibular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The head of the femur (femoral head) is the smooth, spherical-like, proximal end of the bone. It's orientated in the superomedial direction and is continuous inferolaterally with the neck of the femur. It contains the fovea of the head of the femur.

The head of femur is covered with articular cartilage, and articulates with the acetabulum of the hip bone, forming the hip joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Thigh.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Key Features: Head, neck, body, greater and lesser trochanters, and medial and lateral condyles.

Articulates With: Hip bone, tibia, and patella.

Arterial Supply: Medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, superior and inferior gluteal arteries, perforating branches of deep femoral artery, genicular anastomosis.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
Variations
Surface Anatomy
List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of femur (e.g. femoral neck, trochanteric, mid-shaft, and distal fractures)

- Coxa vara/valga

- Osteoarthritis of hip joint

- Total hip arthroplasty

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

21538.name: Articular Area of Distal Part of Femur

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of distal part of femur is the convex, inferior end of the bone. It includes the patellar surface of the femur and the articular facets of the medial and lateral condyles of the femur.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Pelvic girdle.

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Body, superior and inferior pubic rami, pubic crest, pecten pubis, and pubic tubercle.

Articulates With: Ilium, ischium, and femur.

Arterial Supply: Obturator, inferior epigastric, and medial circumflex femoral arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the pubis occurs at two ossification centers, these are found in the:

- superior pubic ramus, which appears in utero during the fourth to fifth months;

- body of pubis, which appears during early to middle adolescence.

These ossification centers fuse with each other during middle adolescence to early adulthood. Fusion between the body of ilium, body of ischium, and superior pubic ramus occurs at the acetabulum during middle to late adolescence, forming the fused hip bone. Fusion between the ramus of ischium and inferior pubic ramus occurs within the seventh to eighth years, forming the fused ischiopubic ramus (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of superior pubic ramus

- Fracture of inferior pubic ramus

- Diastasis of pubic symphysis

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lunate surface of the ilium is the peripherally located, smooth, articular portion of the acetabulum. It’s horseshoe-shaped and is covered with hyaline cartilage for the articulation with the head of the femur, forming the hip joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The auricular surface of the ilium is the ear-shaped, articular area of the sacropelvic surface of ilium. It's located inferior to the iliac tuberosity and articulates with the auricular surface of the sacrum, forming the sacroiliac joint. Located immediately anterior to the auricular surface is a groove, the preauricular sulcus, which provides an attachment site for the anterior sacroiliac ligament.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Pelvic girdle.

Bone Type: Flat bone.

Key Features: Body, ala, iliac crest, iliac fossa, and anterior superior iliac spine.

Articulates With: Ischium, pubis, sacrum, and femur.

Arterial Supply: Iliolumbar, obturator, superficial circumflex iliac, and superior gluteal arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the ilium occurs at three ossification centers, these are found in the:

- body of ilium, which appears in utero at the ninth week;

- iliac crest, two centers are located here and appear within early to middle adolescence.

These ossification centers fuse with each other during middle adolescence to early adulthood. Fusion between the body of ilium, body of ischium, and superior pubic ramus occurs at the acetabulum during middle to late adolescence, forming the fused hip bone (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of ilium

- Iliac bone graft harvesting

- Iliac horn syndrome

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Pelvic girdle.

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Body, ramus, ischial tuberosity, ischial spine, and greater and lesser sciatic notches.

Articulates With: Ilium, pubis, and femur.

Arterial Supply: Inferior gluteal, obturator, and medial circumflex femoral arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the ischium occurs at two ossification centers, these are found in the:

- body of ischium, which appears in utero during the fourth month;

- ischial tuberosity, which appears during early to middle adolescence.

These ossification centers fuse with each other during middle adolescence to early adulthood. Fusion between the body of ilium, body of ischium, and superior pubic ramus occurs at the acetabulum during middle to late adolescence, forming the fused hip bone. Fusion between the ramus of ischium and inferior pubic ramus occurs within the seventh to eighth years, forming the fused ischiopubic ramus (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the ischial tuberosity can be palpated in the inferior portion of the gluteal region, during flexion of the thigh at the hip joint.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of ischium

- Avulsion fracture of ischial tuberosity

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

19471.name: First Metacarpal Articular Facet of Trapezium Bone
19471.latin: Facies articularis metacarpi primi ossis trapezii

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The first metacarpal articular facet is the saddle-shaped area found on the distal aspect of the trapezium bone. It articulates with the proximal articular facet of the first metacarpal bone, contributing to the formation of the carpometacarpal joints.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Tubercle, palmar and dorsal surfaces, and scaphoid and trapezoid articular facets.

Articulates With: Scaphoid, trapezoid, first and second metacarpal bones.

Arterial Supply: Radial artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the trapezium bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the fourth to fifth years (Standring, 2016). Complete ossification occurs during early to middle adolescence.

sections.title: Variations
sections.text: In some individuals, the trapezium bone may be present in a bipartite condition (i.e., divided into two parts) (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the trapezium bone can be palpated proximal to the base of first metacarpal bone during opposition of the thumb.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Fracture of trapezium bone

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

17956.name: Proximomedial Articular Area of Trapezium Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The proximomedial articular area of trapezium bone consists of the proximal and medial aspects of the bone that articulate with adjacent bones. It includes the scaphoid and trapezoid articular facets, and the second metacarpal articular facet.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Tubercle, palmar, and dorsal surfaces; radial, capitate, and trapezium articular facets.

Articulates With: Radius, lunate, capitate, trapezoid, and trapezium.

Arterial Supply: Superficial palmar branch of radial artery and dorsal carpal branch of radial artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the scaphoid bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the fourth to fifth years (Standring, 2016). Complete ossification occurs during early adolescence.

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text:
The following bony features of the scaphoid bone are relevant to surface anatomy:

- The dorsal surface of scaphoid bone can be palpated in the anatomical snuffbox, distal to the radial styloid process.

- The tubercle of scaphoid bone can be palpated proximal to the thenar eminence during extension of the wrist joint.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of scaphoid bone (most commonly fractured carpal bone)

- Avascular necrosis of scaphoid bone (secondary to fracture)

- Scaphoid aplasia

- Preiser’s disease

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of scaphoid bone consists of the proximal, distal, and medial aspects of the bone that articulate with adjacent bones. It includes the radial, capitate, trapezoid, and trapezium articular facets.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Palmar and dorsal surfaces; trapezium, scaphoid, and capitate articular facets.

Articulates With: Trapezium, scaphoid, capitate, and second metacarpal bones.

Arterial Supply: Dorsal carpal branch of radial and ulnar arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the trapezoid bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the fourth to fifth years (Standring, 2016). Complete ossification occurs during early to middle adolescence.

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the trapezoid bone can be palpated proximal to the base of second metacarpal bone.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Fracture of trapezoid bone (extremely rare)

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of the trapezoid bone consists of the proximal, distal, medial and lateral aspects of the bone that articulate with adjacent bones. It includes the trapezium, scaphoid, and capitate articular facets, and the second metacarpal articular facet.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Palmar and dorsal surfaces; lunate, hamate, and pisiform articular facets.

Articulates With: Lunate, hamate, and pisiform bones.

Arterial Supply: Ulnar artery; dorsal carpal branch of radial and ulnar arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the triquetrum bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the third year (Standring, 2016). Complete ossification occurs during early adolescence.

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the triquetrum bone can be palpated on the medial aspect of the wrist during abduction of the wrist joint.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Fracture of triquetrum bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of the triquetrum bone consists of the proximal, lateral, and distal aspects of the bone that articulate with adjacent bones. It includes the lunate and hamate articular facets.

23255.name: Pisiform Articular Facet of Triquetrum Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The pisiform articular facet is the small, oval area found on the palmar aspect of the triquetrum bone. It articulates with the triquetrum articular facet of the pisiform bone, forming the pisotriquetral joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of lunate bone consists of the proximal and distal surfaces of the bone that articulate with adjacent bones. It includes the radial, triquetrum, hamate, capitate, and scaphoid articular facets.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Palmar and dorsal surfaces, and radial, scaphoid, capitate, and triquetrum articular facets.

Articulates With: Radius, triquetrum, hamate, capitate, and scaphoid bones.

Arterial Supply: Dorsal carpal branch of radial and ulnar arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the lunate bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the fourth to fifth years (Standring, 2016). Complete ossification occurs during adolescence.

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the dorsal surface of lunate bone can be palpated on the dorsal aspect of the wrist, proximal to the capitate bone, during flexion of the wrist joint.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Dislocation of lunate bone (most commonly dislocated carpal bone)

- Perilunate dislocation

- Kienböck’s disease

- Fracture of lunate bone

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Head, base, palmar and dorsal surfaces, and scaphoid and hamate articular facets.

Articulates With: Trapezoid, scaphoid, lunate, and hamate bones; second, third, and fourth metacarpal bones.

Arterial Supply: Deep palmar arch, dorsal carpal branch of radial artery, dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the capitate bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the second month after birth (Standring, 2016). Complete ossification occurs during early adolescence.

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the capitate bone can be palpated on the dorsal aspect of the wrist, proximal to the third metacarpal bone.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of the capitate bone consists of the proximal, distal, medial, and lateral aspects of the bone that articulate with adjacent bones. It includes the scaphoid, lunate, and hamate articular facets, and the second, third, and fourth metacarpal articular facets of capitate bone.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Sesamoid bone.

Key Features: Palmar and dorsal surfaces, triquetrum articular facet.

Articulates With: Triquetrum bone.

Arterial Supply: Ulnar artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the pisiform bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the ninth to twelfth years (Standring, 2016). Complete ossification occurs during middle to late adolescence.

sections.title: Variations
sections.text: In some individuals, the pisiform bone may be present in a bipartite condition, i.e., divided into two parts (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the pisiform bone can be palpated proximal to the hypothenar eminence.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Fracture of pisiform bone

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

20013.name: Triquetrum Articular Facet of Pisiform Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The triquetrum articular facet is the small, flat, oval area found on the dorsal aspect of the pisiform bone. It articulates with the pisiform articular facet of the triquetrum bone, forming the pisotriquetral joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Hook, palmar and dorsal surfaces; triquetrum, capitate, and lunate articular facets.

Articulates With: Capitate, lunate, triquetrum, and fourth and fifth metacarpal bones.

Arterial Supply: Deep palmar arch, dorsal carpal branch of radial and ulnar arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the hamate bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the third month after birth (Standring, 2016). Complete ossification occurs during middle to late adolescence.

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the hook of hamate bone can be palpated between the hypothenar eminence and the pisiform bone.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Fracture of hamate bone (common in golfers, baseball and tennis players)

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of the hamate bone consists of the proximal, distal, medial, and lateral aspects of the bone that articulate with adjacent bones. It includes the triquetrum, capitate, and lunate articular facets, and the fourth and fifth metacarpal articular facets.

19290.name: Distal Articular Facet of Fourth Metacarpal Bone
19290.latin: Facies articularis distalis ossis quarti metacarpi

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The distal articular facet of the fourth metacarpal bone is the convex, inferior area of its head. It articulates with the proximal articular facet found on the proximal phalanx of the ring finger, forming the fourth metacarpophalangeal joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Long Bone.

Key Features: Head, body, base, medial and lateral surfaces, and proximal and distal articular facets.

Articulates With: Proximal phalanx of ring finger, capitate, hamate, third and fifth metacarpal bones.

Arterial Supply: Palmar metacarpal arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the fourth metacarpal bone occurs at two ossification centers, these are found in the:

- body, which appears in utero at the ninth week;

- head, which appears within the second to third years.

These ossification centers fuse with each other during the fifteenth to nineteenth years (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
sections.text: The base of the fourth metacarpal bone can vary between individuals in terms of the number and size of its articular surfaces.

sections.title: Surface Anatomy

sections.text: The proximal articular area of the fourth metacarpal bone consists of the superior, medial, and lateral aspects of the base of the bone that articulate with adjacent bones. It includes the proximal and capitate articular facets, and the third and fifth metacarpal articular facets.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The proximal articular area of the second metacarpal bone consists of the superior, medial, and lateral aspects of the base of the bone that articulate with adjacent bones. It includes the trapezium, capitate, and proximal articular facets, and the third metacarpal articular facet.

24839.name: Distal Articular Facet of Second Metacarpal Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The distal articular facet of the second metacarpal bone is the convex, inferior area of its head. It articulates with the proximal articular facet found on the proximal phalanx of the index finger, forming the second metacarpophalangeal joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Key Features: Head, body, base, medial and lateral surfaces, and proximal and distal articular facets.

Articulates With: Proximal phalanx of index finger, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and third metacarpal.

Arterial Supply: Palmar metacarpal arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the second metacarpal bone occurs at two ossification centers, these are found in the:

- body, which appears in utero at the ninth week;

- head, which appears within the second to third years.

These ossification centers fuse with each other during the fifteenth to nineteenth years (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
sections.text: In some individuals, the second metacarpal bone can present a pseudoepiphysis at its proximal end. It does not contribute greatly to the longitudinal growth of the bone and joins the body earlier than the epiphysis of the head (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

17433.name: Proximal Articular Facet of First Metacarpal Bone
17433.latin: Facies articularis proximalis ossis primi metacarpi

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The proximal articular facet of the first metacarpal bone is the saddle-shaped, superior area of its base. It articulates with the first metacarpal articular facet of the trapezium bone, contributing to the formation of the carpometacarpal joints.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Key Features: Head, body, base, medial and lateral surfaces, and proximal and distal articular facets.

Articulates With: Proximal phalanx of thumb and trapezium bone.

Arterial Supply: Princeps pollicis artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations

sections.title: Quick Facts

Key Features: Head, body, base, medial and lateral surfaces, styloid process, and proximal and distal articular facets.

Articulates With: Proximal phalanx of middle finger, capitate, second and fourth metacarpal bones.

sections.text: In some individuals, the styloid process of the third metacarpal bone does not fuse with the rest of the bone. Instead it exists as an accessory bone, known the os styloideum, which is present between the second and third metacarpal bones (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The distal phalanx of the index finger is one of the fourteen phalangeal bones of the hand. It’s classified as a long bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: head, body, and base;

- landmarks: tuberosity and articular facet.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The distal phalanx is located distal to the middle phalanx and articulates with it at the distal interphalangeal joint.

sections.title: Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the distal phalanx of index finger occurs at two ossification centers, these are found in the:

- body, which appears in utero during the third month;

- base, which appears during the second to fourth years.

These ossification centers fuse with each other during the fifteenth to eighteenth years (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Surface Anatomy
sections.text: With regard to surface anatomy, the head, body, and base of the distal phalanx of index finger can be easily palpated.

The distal phalanx of the middle finger is one of the fourteen phalangeal bones of the hand. It’s classified as a long bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: head, body, and base;

- landmarks: tuberosity and articular facet.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The distal phalanx is located distal to the middle phalanx and articulates with it at the distal interphalangeal joint.

sections.title: Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the distal phalanx of middle finger occurs at two ossification centers, these are found in the:

- body, which appears in utero during the third month;

- base, which appears during the second to fourth years.

These ossification centers fuse with each other during the fifteenth to eighteenth years (Standring, 2016).

sections.text:
The sesamoid bones of hand are the pair of small, oval, nodule-like bones found along the palmar aspect of the thumb. The tendon of the adductor pollicis muscle contains the medial of the two sesamoid bones, while the tendon of the flexor pollicis brevis muscle contains the lateral sesamoid bone.

In some individuals, other sesamoid bones within the hand may be present and occur at the metacarpophalangeal joints of the index and little fingers.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The sesamoid bones of hand are located anterior to the first metacarpophalangeal joint, within the tendons of the adductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis muscles. The tendon of the flexor pollicis longus muscle travels between the sesamoid bones of hand.

sections.title: Function

17235.name: Articular Area of Proximal Part of Ulna

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of proximal part of ulna is the concave, superior end of the bone. It includes both the trochlear and radial notches of the ulna.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Forearm.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Key Features: Head, body, olecranon, trochlear and radial notches, and ulnar styloid process.

Articulates With: Humerus and radius.

Arterial Supply: Anterior and posterior interosseous, radial, and ulnar arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
Variations
sections.text: In some individuals, interrupted growth of the epiphyses of the ulna can result in hypoplasia, and partial or complete aplasia of the bone (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Surface Anatomy
List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of ulna (e.g., Monteggia fracture)

- Radioulnar synostosis

18552.name: Articular Area of Distal Part of Ulna

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of distal part of ulna is the convex, inferior end of the bone. It includes both the articular facet and articular circumference of the head of the ulna.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Forearm.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Key Features: Head, neck, body, radial tuberosity, radial styloid process, and ulnar notch.

Articulates With: Humerus, ulna, scaphoid bone, and lunate bone.

Arterial Supply: Anterior and posterior interosseous, radial, and ulnar arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
Variations
sections.text: In some individuals, an accessory tubercle, known as a lunar tubercle, may be present at the distal part of radius (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Surface Anatomy
List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Dislocation of elbow joint

- Radioulnar synostosis

- Radial dysplasia

- Fracture of radius (e.g., Colles’, Smith’s, Barton’s, and Galeazzi fractures)

- Madelung’s deformity

19192.name: Articular Area of Proximal Part of Radius

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of proximal part of radius is the round, superior end of the bone. It includes both the articular facet and articular circumference of the head of the radius.

16425.name: Articular Area of Distal Part of Radius

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of distal part of radius is the concave, inferior end of the bone. It includes the ulnar notch and the carpal articular surface of the radius.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Arm.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Key Features: Head, anatomical neck, greater and lesser tubercles, body, and condyle of humerus.

Articulates With: Scapula, radius, and ulna.

Arterial Supply: Brachial, anterior circumflex humeral, and deep brachial arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
Variations
Surface Anatomy
List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of humerus

- Dislocation of glenohumeral joint

- Dislocation of elbow joint

19669.name: Articular Area of Condyle of Humerus

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular area of condyle of the humerus is the convex, distal end of the bone. It includes the trochlea and capitulum.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The head of humerus (humeral head) is the smooth, spherical-like, proximal end of the bone. It is orientated in the superomedial direction and slightly posteriorly also. It is continuous inferolaterally with the anatomical neck of the humerus.

The head of humerus is covered with articular cartilage and articulates with the glenoid fossa of the scapula, thus forming the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The sternal articular surface of the clavicle is the convex, quadrangular, articular area found on the medial aspect of the sternal end of the bone. It articulates with the clavicular notch of the manubrium of sternum, forming the sternoclavicular joint, and provides an attachment site for the interclavicular ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The acromial facet of the clavicle is the smooth, oval, articular area found on the lateral aspect of the acromial end of the bone. It articulates with the acromion of the scapula, forming the acromioclavicular joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Pectoral girdle.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Key Features: Acromial end, body, sternal end, superior and inferior surfaces, conoid tubercle, and trapezoid line.

Articulates With: Manubrium of sternum and scapula.

Arterial Supply: Suprascapular artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the clavicle occurs at three ossification centers, these are found in the:

- body of the clavicle, two centers are located here and appear in utero during weeks five to six, making the clavicle the first bone to ossify;

- sternal end of the clavicle, which appears during late adolescence.

These ossification centers fuse with each other by the twenty-third year, making the clavicle the last bone to complete ossification (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
sections.text:
In males, the clavicle is generally longer, thicker, and more curved than in females. Furthermore, the acromial end of the clavicle is positioned superior to the sternal end in males, while the opposite is usually observed in females.

The left clavicle is often longer and weaker than the right clavicle and, in some individuals, the clavicle is pierced by a branch of the supraclavicular nerve.

sections.title: Surface Anatomy
List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of clavicle (most commonly fractured bone)

- Cleidocranial dysotosis/cleidocranial dysplasia

- Dislocation of sternoclavicular joint

- Dislocation of acromioclavicular joint

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Pectoral girdle.

Bone Type: Flat bone.

Key Features: Head, neck, body, coracoid process, acromion, and glenoid fossa.

Articulates With: Clavicle and humerus.

Arterial Supply: Suprascapular artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations

Variations

- Dislocation of glenohumeral joint

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The clavicular facet is the small, oval, superomedially facing, articular area found on the medial aspect of the acromion, close to its tip. It articulates with the acromial facet of the clavicle, forming the acromioclavicular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The glenoid fossa (glenoid cavity) is the pear-shaped, slightly concave, anterolaterally facing, articular area found on the lateral aspect of the head of the scapula. It articulates with the head of the humerus, forming the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint. Its margin is covered with a fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum, which deepens the concavity of the glenoid fossa, thereby improving the stability of the glenohumeral joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Neurocranium.

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Body, greater and lesser wings, medial and lateral plates of pterygoid process, sella turcica, and anterior and posterior clinoid processes.

Articulates With: Frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, zygomatic, ethmoid, and palatine bones, and vomer.

Arterial Supply: Middle meningeal and internal carotid arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the sphenoid bone occurs at many ossification centers, these are found in the:

- body, which appears in utero during the third to fifth months;

- greater and lesser wings, which appear in utero during the third month.

The ossification centers for the body of sphenoid bone fuse with each other in utero. The lesser wings fuse with the body in utero, while the greater wings fuse with the body during the first year after birth (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations

- Osteomyelitis of sphenoid bone

- Craniosynostosis

sections.text:

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Squamous, petrous, tympanic, and mastoid parts, styloid process, mandibular fossa, and zygomatic and mastoid processes.

Articulates With: Parietal, occipital, sphenoid, and zygomatic bones.

Arterial Supply: Middle meningeal, posterior auricular, and stylomastoid arteries.

sections.text:
Location: Neurocranium.

Bone Type: Flat bone.

Key Features: Frontal, occipital, sphenoidal, and mastoid angles, internal and external surfaces, parietal eminence, and superior and inferior temporal lines.

Articulates With: Opposite parietal bone, frontal, occipital, temporal, and sphenoid bones.

Arterial Supply: Middle meningeal artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of a parietal bone occurs at two ossification centers. These are found near the parietal eminence and appear in utero during the second month. They fuse with each other in utero (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: Regarding surface anatomy, the parietal eminence and temporal lines of each parietal bone can be palpated.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular facets are the smooth, convex, inferolaterally facing articular areas on the occipital condyles. They articulate with the superior articular facets of the atlas (first cervical vertebra), forming the atlantooccipital joints.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Neurocranium.

Bone Type: Flat bone.

Key Features: Squamous, basilar, and lateral parts, cerebral and cerebellar fossae, superior and inferior nuchal lines, and internal and external occipital protuberances.

Articulates With: Parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones, and atlas.

Arterial Supply: Middle meningeal artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: Regarding surface anatomy, the external occipital protuberance and superior nuchal lines of the occipital bone can be palpated.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of occipital bone

- Occipital horn syndrome

- Craniosynostosis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Neurocranium.

Bone Type: Flat bone.

Key Features: Squamous, orbital and nasal parts, supraorbital margin, superciliary arch, fossae for lacrimal glands, and zygomatic processes.

Articulates With: Parietal, ethmoid, lacrimal, nasal, zygomatic, and sphenoid bones, and maxilla.

Arterial Supply: Middle meningeal artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the frontal bone occurs at four ossification centers, these are found in the:

- right and left frontal eminences, with one center found in each, which appear in utero during the second month;

- nasal spine, with two centers found here, which appear during the tenth year.

At birth, the right and left halves of the frontal bone remains unfused, with a metopic suture (frontal suture) located between them. The right and left halves of the frontal bone fuse within the first year after birth(Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: Regarding surface anatomy, the frontal eminences, superciliary arches, supraorbital margins, and temporal lines of the frontal bone can all be palpated.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Fracture of frontal bone

- Hyperostosis frontalis interna

- Craniosynostosis

sections.text:
Location: Viscerocranium.

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Medial and lateral surfaces, superior and inferior borders, and lacrimal, maxillary, and ethmoidal processes.

Articulates With: Lacrimal, ethmoid, and palatine bones, and maxilla.

Arterial Supply: Posterior lateral nasal, facial, and maxillary arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of each inferior nasal concha occurs at one ossification center, which appears in utero during the fifth month (Standring, 2016).

- Hypoplasia of inferior nasal concha

sections.text:
Location: Viscerocranium.

Bone Type: Flat bone.

Key Features: Crest, ethmoid groove, internal and external surfaces, and superior, inferior, medial, and lateral borders.

Articulates With: Opposite nasal bone, frontal and ethmoid bones, and maxilla.

Arterial Supply: Ophthalmic and angular arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of each nasal bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears in utero during the third month (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations

sections.text: Regarding surface anatomy, the external surface of the nasal bone is subcutaneous and can be easily palpated.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Viscerocranium.

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Cribriform, perpendicular, and orbital plates, ethmoidal labyrinth, crista galli, and superior and middle nasal conchae.

Articulates With: Frontal, sphenoid, palatine, lacrimal, and nasal bones, and maxillae, inferior nasal conchae, and vomer.

Arterial Supply: Anterior and posterior ethmoidal and sphenopalatine arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the ethmoid bone occurs at three ossification centers, these are found in the:

- right and left ethmoidal labyrinths, with one center found in each, which appear in utero during the fourth to fifth months;

- perpendicular plate, which appears during the first year after birth.

The ossification centers for the ethmoidal labyrinths and perpendicular plate fuse with each during the second year (Standring, 2016).

Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of each maxilla occurs at one ossification center in its body, which appears in utero during the second month and also forms the zygomatic, frontal, alveolar, and palatine processes (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations

sections.text:

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Perpendicular and horizontal plates, pyramidal, orbital and sphenoidal processes, greater palatine groove, and conchal, ethmoidal, and nasal crests.

Articulates With: Opposite palatine bone, ethmoid and sphenoid bones, maxilla, vomer, and inferior nasal concha.

Arterial Supply: Greater palatine artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of each palatine bone occurs at one ossification center in its perpendicular plate, which appears in utero during the third month and also forms the horizontal plate and the pyramidal, orbital, and sphenoidal processes (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Variations

sections.text: Regarding surface anatomy, the horizontal plate of palatine bone can be palpated along the posterior one quarter of the hard palate.

Articulates With: Frontal, sphenoid, and temporal bones, and maxilla.

Arterial Supply: Zygomaticoorbital artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the vomer occurs at two ossification centers, with one found in the right half and the other found in the left half, which appear in utero during the second month. They begin to fuse with each other in utero during the third month, with fusion usually being completed by puberty (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Distal to mandibular canine tooth; mesial to mandibular second premolar tooth.

Eruption: 6 to 7 years (permanent).

Key Features: Crown, root, marginal ridges, central groove, and buccal and lingual cusps.

Nerve Supply: Inferior dental plexus.

Arterial Supply: Inferior alveolar artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Development
sections.text:
The permanent mandibular first premolar tooth does not have a deciduous precursor.

The permanent mandibular first premolar tooth undergoes calcification around the time of birth, with the development of the crown being completed during the second to third years. Eruption of this tooth occurs during the sixth to seventh years and the development of the root is completed during the ninth to tenth years (Nelson, 2014).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: As with all premolar teeth, the function of the mandibular first premolar tooth is to assist the mandibular canine tooth in the gripping (prehension) and tearing of food during mastication.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Nelson, S. J. (2014) Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion. 10th edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Development
sections.text: The permanent mandibular third molar tooth does not have a deciduous precursor. It undergoes calcification during the eighth to tenth years, with the development of the crown being completed during the twelfth to sixteenth years. Eruption of this tooth occurs during the seventeenth to twenty-first years and the development of the root is completed during the eighteenth to twenty-fifth years (Nelson, 2014).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: As with all molars, the mandibular third molar tooth has cusped surfaces and is specialized for the crushing or grinding (comminution) of food during mastication.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Development
sections.text:
The permanent mandibular second premolar tooth does not have a deciduous precursor.

The permanent mandibular second premolar tooth undergoes calcification during the third year, with the development of the crown being completed during the sixth to seventh years. Eruption of this tooth occurs during the eleventh to twelfth years and the development of the root is completed during the thirteenth to fourteenth years (Nelson, 2014).

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
As with all premolar teeth, the function of the mandibular second premolar tooth is to assist the mandibular canine tooth in the gripping (prehension) and tearing of food during mastication.

The mandibular second premolar tooth also assists the mandibular molar teeth with the crushing or grinding (comminution) of food during mastication.

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Head, neck, base, and anterior and posterior limbs.

Articulates With: Incus.

Arterial Supply: Anterior tympanic and stylomastoid arteries.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The stapes is the smallest of the three auditory ossicles, the other two being the malleus and incus. It is a small, stirrup-like bone that is found in the tympanic cavity of the middle ear in the temporal bone. It is classified as an irregular bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: head, neck, base, and anterior and posterior limbs;

- landmarks: articular facet of head of stapes.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The stapes is located posteromedial to the incus, articulates with the incus at the incudostapedial joint and attaches to the vestibular window of the labyrinthine wall.

sections.title: Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the stapes occurs at one ossification center, which is found in its base and appears in utero during the fourth month. The stapes is fully developed by the time of birth (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Dislocation

- Incus ankylosis

- Cholesteatoma

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The malleus is the largest of the three auditory ossicles, the other two being the incus and stapes. It is a small, hammer-like bone that is found in the tympanic cavity of the middle ear in the temporal bone. It is classified as an irregular bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: head, neck, and handle;

- landmarks: articular facet for incus and anterior and lateral processes.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The malleus is located anterolateral to the incus, articulates with the incus at the incudomallear joint and attaches to the tympanic membrane.

sections.title: Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the malleus occurs at two ossification centers, these are found in the:

- near the neck of the malleus, which appears in utero during the fourth month;

- anterior process of the malleus, which appears in utero during the sixth month.

The malleus is fully developed by the time of birth (Standring, 2016).

20305.name: Articular Facets on Head of Eighth Rib

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The head of the eighth rib contains two articular facets.

- The superior articular facet articulates with the inferior costal facet of the seventh thoracic vertebra, forming the upper part of the joint of the head of the eighth rib.

- The inferior articular facet articulates with the superior costal facet of the eighth thoracic vertebra, forming the lower part of the joint of the head of the eighth rib.

21319.name: Articular Facet of Tubercle of Eighth Rib

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The articular facet is the smooth, oval area found along the tubercle of the eighth rib. It articulates with the transverse costal facet of the eighth thoracic vertebra, forming the eighth costotransverse joint.

Overall, these articular facets on tubercles are only present on the first to tenth ribs, while the eleventh and twelfth ribs lack this bony feature.

sections.title: Description

22182.name: Articular Facet of Head of Tenth Rib

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The articular facet is the round, smooth area located on the medial aspect of the head of the tenth rib. It articulates with the costal facet of the tenth thoracic vertebra, forming the joint of the head of the tenth rib.

Overall, the first, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth ribs have a single articular facet on their heads, while the remaining ribs have two articular facets, known as the superior and inferior articular facets on heads of ribs.

sections.text:

The ossification center for the head fuses with the body of the eleventh rib within the fourteenth to twentieth years (Cunningham, Scheuer and Black, 2016).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Thoracic cage.

Bone Type: Flat bone.

Key Features: Head, body, costal end, internal and external surfaces, and superior and inferior borders.

Articulates With: Twelfth thoracic vertebra, twelfth costal cartilage.

Arterial Supply: Subcostal artery.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text:
Ossification of the twelfth rib occurs at ossification centers found in the:

- body, which appears in utero during the second month;

- head, which appears during puberty.

The ossification center for the head fuses with the body of the twelfth rib within the fourteenth to twentieth years (Cunningham, Scheuer and Black, 2016).

sections.title: Variations
Surface Anatomy
sections.text: The costal end of the twelfth rib is easily palpated and is located by palpating two ribs down from the tenth rib.

16431.name: Articular Facet of Head of Twelfth Rib

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The articular facet is the round, smooth area located on the medial aspect of the head of the twelfth rib. It articulates with the costal facet of the twelfth thoracic vertebra, forming the joint of the head of the twelfth rib.

Overall, the first, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth ribs have a single articular facet on their heads, while the remaining ribs have two articular facets, known as the superior and inferior articular facets on heads of ribs.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Ossification
sections.text: Ossification of the coccyx occurs at four ossification centers, with one ossification center found in each of its four coccygeal vertebrae that unite to form the coccyx. The ossification center for the first coccygeal vertebra appears during the first year after birth, with the other centers appearing sequentially up until the twentieth year or later. The ossification centers for the coccygeal vertebrae fuse with each other during adulthood to form one unified coccyx (Standring, 2016).

sections.text: The dorsal surface and apex of the coccyx can both be palpated at the inferior end of the vertebral column.
