sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The pterygospinous ligament is a band of fibers that connects one part of the sphenoid bone to another. In some instances, it may be replaced with muscle fibers or may be ossified.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The pterygospinous ligament extends between the spine of the sphenoid bone and the pterygospinous process on the posterior margin of the lateral pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: If ossified, this ligament may form a foramen, the pterygospinous foramen, that transmits the muscular branches of the mandibular nerve to the temporalis, masseter, and the lateral pterygoid muscles.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Mandibular neuralgia

21457.name: Sphenomandibular Ligament
alternate: Internal Lateral Ligament of Temporomandibular Joint

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The sphenomandibular ligament is an aponeurotic band derived from Meckel’s cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch of embryonic development.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The sphenomandibular ligament is usually separate from the temporomandibular joint capsule. It runs from the spine of the sphenoid bone to the lingula of the mandible. The inferior alveolar nerve is a close relation to the sphenomandibular ligament and descends between the ligament and the ramus of the mandible before entering the mandibular foramen.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The sphenomandibular ligament limits distension of the mandible inferiorly.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The stylohyoid ligament is a fibrous cord derived from the second pharyngeal arch during embryonic development. The stylohyoid ligament may be partially calcified.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The stylohyoid ligament extends from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone, thus, suspending the hyoid bone. It also forms the origin for the highest fibers of the middle pharyngeal constrictor and styloglossus muscles.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The stylohyoid ligament, as mentioned above, suspends the hyoid bone and allows for the attachment of some fibers of the middle pharyngeal constrictor and styloglossus muscles.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Eagle syndrome

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The stylomandibular ligament is formed from the thickened portion of the investing cervical fascia.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The stylomandibular ligament extends from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the angle and posterior border of the angle of the mandible, between the attachments of the masseter and medial pterygoid muscles.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The stylomandibular ligament provides attachment to some fibers of the styloglossus muscle.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The articular disc of the temporomandibular joint is located between the head of the mandibular condyle and the glenoid fossa of the temporal bone. It divides the joint into a superior and an inferior space, both filled with synovial fluid. It is oval and composed of avascular fibrous connective tissue. 

Around the periphery of the disc is a thick margin, the annulus, with a depression in the center. This depression is on the inferior surface of the disc and accommodates the articular surface of the mandibular condyle, thus stabilizes the articular disc on the condyle. The disc is divided into three distinct sections. Anteriorly and posteriorly the disc is thickened, with a thinner avascular intermediate zone. 

Around the condyle of the mandible, there is a capsular ligament that surrounds the lower joint capsule and fuses with the articular disc, holding it in place. Collateral ligaments are local thickenings of the capsular ligament, attaching to the medial and lateral poles of the condyle (Helland, 1980).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Anteriorly, the disc is attached to the upper head of the lateral pterygoid muscle. Posteriorly, the disc continues as a thick layer of loose connective tissue (the retrodiscal pad) that fuses to the posterior wall of the joint capsule.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The articular disc of the temporomandibular joint acts as an articular surface, separating the cavity into superior and inferior spaces. It may also provide lubrication for the joint and it reduces friction between the articulating surfaces.

The disc also aids in the movement of the temporomandibular joint. Gliding movements of protrusion and retrusion occur between the temporal bone and the articular disc, whereas hinge movements of depression, elevation and rotation occur between the condyle of the mandible and the articular disc. To fully depress the mandible, the articular disc and head of the mandible move anteriorly onto the articular tubercle. These movements are controlled by the upper head of lateral pterygoid anteriorly and elastic tissue in the posterior section (Helland, 1980).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Articular disc displacement

sections.title: References
sections.text: Helland, M. M. (1980) Anatomy and function of the temporomandibular joint. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther, 1(3), 145-52.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular facet of the mandible is the smooth, convex area found along the superior aspect of its head. It contributes to the formation of the temporomandibular joint, along with the mandibular fossa of temporal bone and an intervening articular disc of the temporomandibular joint.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: An articular capsule surrounds the entire temporomandibular joint. The fibers of the inferior portion of the capsule are tight and connect the condyle of the mandible to the articular disc. The upper portion of the capsule is looser, these fibers attach the articular disc to the temporal bone. Laterally the joint capsule is strengthened by the lateral ligament of the temporomandibular joint.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The articular capsule of the temporomandibular joint ensures that the joint is sealed, thus, keeping the lubricating synovial fluid within the joint. It provides passive stability to the joint by limiting the joint movement. Additionally, it provides active stability by containing numerous proprioceptive nerve endings which relay mechanical information back to the central nervous system (Ralphs & Benjamin, 1994).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Ralphs, J. R. & Benjamin, M. (1994) The joint capsule: structure, composition, ageing and disease. Journal of Anatomy, 184(Pt 3), 503-509.

19133.name: Inferior Retrodiscal Lamina of Temporomandibular Joint

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The inferior retrodiscal lamina is composed of collagenous tissue.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The inferior retrodiscal lamina attaches to the posteroinferior part of the articular disc. It extends to the posterior aspect of the mandibular condyle (Miloro & Peterson, 2012).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The inferior retrodiscal lamina is not elastic like the superior lamina, therefore, acts to maintain a strong relationship to the mandibular condyle.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Temporomandibular disorder

sections.title: References
sections.text: Miloro, M. & Peterson, L. J. (2012) Peterson's Principles of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery. People's Medical Publishing House-USA.

22489.name: Superior Retrodiscal Lamina of Temporomandibular Joint

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The superior retrodiscal lamina consists of connective tissue with many elastic fibers.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The superior retrodiscal lamina attaches to the posterosuperior part of the articular disc. It extends to the posterior wall of the mandibular fossa (the petrotympanic fissure) (Miloro & Peterson, 2012).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The superior retrodiscal lamina allows anterior translation of the articular disc over the articular eminence.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Anterior disc displacement

—Temporomandibular disorder

sections.title: References
sections.text: Miloro, M. & Peterson, L. J. (2012) Peterson's Principles of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery. People's Medical Publishing House-USA.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular surface of the mandibular fossa is the smooth, deep depression found along the anterior portion of the mandibular fossa of temporal bone. It contributes to the formation of the temporomandibular joint, along with the head of the mandible and an intervening articular disc of the temporomandibular joint.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The collateral ligaments of the temporomandibular joint connect the articular disc to the condyle of the mandible.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The collateral ligaments of the temporomandibular joint reinforce the inferior portion of the joint capsule. Direct and firm attachment of the articular disc to the mandibular condyle assures that they move simultaneously (Helland, 1980).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Helland, M. M. (1980) Anatomy and function of the temporomandibular joint. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther, 1(3), 145-52.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The synovial membrane of the temporomandibular joint is the inner layer of the articular capsule of the temporomandibular joint. It is composed of loose connective tissue with a smooth inner surface which lines the joint cavity. It may be broken up into superior and inferior parts, which lines the joint cavity above and below the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint, respectively.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The blood supply to the synovial membrane of the temporomandibular joint is via the superficial temporal artery.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The synovial membrane produces synovial fluid that fills both the upper and lower compartments of the temporomandibular joint. This fluid acts to lubricate the joint. The intermediate portion at the center of the articular disc is avascular and, therefore, gains its nutrients from the synovial fluid.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Synovitis

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The lateral ligament of the temporomandibular joint is strong triangular ligament formed by the thickened lateral portion of the joint capsule. This ligament consists of an outer oblique portion and an inner horizontal portion.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lateral ligament of the temporomandibular joint runs from the articular tubercle of the temporal bone superiorly, down past the lateral side of the temporomandibular joint, in contact with the joint capsule. It attaches to the lateral and posterior surfaces of the neck of the condylar process of the mandible.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The lateral ligament of the temporomandibular joint prevents posterior displacement of the mandibular condyle and initiates the forward movement of the articular disc when the mandible is fully depressed.

21297.name: Fibrous Layer of Articular Capsule of Atlantooccipital Joint
21297.latin: Stratum fibrosa capsulae articularis articulationis atlantooccipitalis
alternate: Fibrous Layer of Articular Capsule of Atlanto-occipital Joint
Fibrous Membrane of Articular Capsule of Atlanto-occipital Joint
Fibrous Membrane of Articular Capsule of Atlantooccipital Joint

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The atlantooccipital joint is surrounded by a joint capsule and is composed of a fibrous layer and synovial membrane. The capsule is composed of tough interwoven fibers and tends to be looser and slacker to facilitate the variety of movements associated with this joint.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The fibrous layer of the capsule attaches along the margins of the articular surfaces of the atlas and occipital bone, thus, enveloping them. These are the superior articular surfaces of the atlas and the occipital condyles. The condyles are positioned on both sides of foramen magnum. 

The fibrous layer blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament on their anteromedial aspects and with the posterior atlantooccipital membrane posteriorly.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The fibrous layer adds and maintains the stability of the atlantooccipital joint. It restricts excessive movements of the articulating surfaces by tightening as they move.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Atlantooccipital joint subluxation

—Osteoarthritis

23451.name: Synovial Membrane of Articular Capsule of Atlantooccipital Joint
23451.latin: Membrana synovialis capsulae articularis articulationis atlantooccipitalis
alternate: Synovial Layer of Articular Capsule of Atlantooccipital Joint
Synovial Membrane of Articular Capsule of Atlanto-occipital Joint

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The synovial membrane forms the inner portion of the articular capsule and is overlaid by the outer fibrous layer of the capsule. It is in contact with the margins of articular cartilages that are in close proximity to the fibrous layer insertion. They may associate with the posterior aspect of the median atlantoaxial joint.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The synovial membrane allows for the production and secretion of synovial fluid which helps to lubricate joints and prevent friction during movement. It also provides nutrition to the joint. The membrane also locks in this fluid and prevents leakage out of the capsule.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The anterior atlantooccipital membrane is a broad, densely woven, fibrous sheet. It is more durable than its posterior counterpart but doesn’t match its width.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anterior atlantooccipital membrane is a superior continuation of the anterior longitudinal ligament. It is attached from the anterior arch of the atlas to the anterior margin of foramen magnum. Laterally, it blends with the atlantooccipital joint capsules, thickening the joint capsule anteromedially. The rectus capitis anterior muscles are located anteriorly, while the alar ligaments can be found posterior to the anterior atlantooccipital membrane.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Along with the other ligaments around the atlantooccipital joint, the anterior atlantooccipital membrane maintains support and stability of the atlantooccipital joint, as well as reducing excessive movement.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Atlantooccipital subluxation

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: Fibers of the lateral atlantooccipital ligament run medial to lateral, between the lateral pert of the occipital bone to the transverse process of the first cervical vertebra (Tubbs et al, 2007).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lateral atlantooccipital ligament lies immediately deep to rectus capitis lateralis muscle. It runs from the inferior surface of the lateral part of the occipital bone, posterior to the jugular process, to the superior surface of the transverse process of the atlas.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The lateral atlantooccipital ligament limits the movement of the atlantooccipital joint, preventing anterior or posterior displacement of the cranium in relation to the spinal column.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tubbs, R. S., Stetler, W., Shoja, M. M., Loukas, M., Hansasuta, A., Liechty, P., Acakpo-Satchivi, L., Wellons, J. C., Blount, J. P., Salter, E. G. and Oakes, W. J. (2007) 'The lateral atlantooccipital ligament', Surg Radiol Anat, 29(3), pp. 219-23.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The posterior atlantooccipital membrane is a sheet of connective tissue that extends from the posterior arch of the atlas to the posterior margin of foramen magnum. Its bony attachments enable it to cover the open space between the atlas and the cranium. The posterior atlantooccipital membrane is wider but thinner than its anterior counterpart.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The posterior atlantooccipital membrane corresponds superiorly with the ligamentum flavum Laterally, it blends with the atlantooccipital joint capsules, thickening the joint capsule. Anteriorly, the ligament is adherent to the spinal dura (Zumpano, Hartwell and Jagos, 2006). Posteriorly, it is related to the rectus capitis posterior major muscle. The posterior atlantooccipital membrane, along with the posterior arch of the atlas, forms the floor the suboccipital triangle, which is bounded by small cranially inserted muscles.

The posterior atlantooccipital membrane forms an arc on its insertion to the posterior arch of the atlas, allowing for smooth passage the vertebral artery, first cervical nerve, and venous vessels from the vertebral foramina to the foramen magnum. The margin of this ligamentous arc over these neurovascular structures may be harder and stiffer than the rest of the ligament, which may contribute to reduced obstruction or adhesion to the neurovascular bundle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Given its median posterior position, the posterior atlantooccipital membrane is in a beneficial position to prevent hyperflexion of the atlas, which it achieves in conjunction with the other locally supporting ligaments.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Cervicogenic headache

sections.title: References
sections.text: Zumpano, M. P., Hartwell, S. & Jagos, C. S. (2006) Soft tissue connection between rectus capitus posterior minor and the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane: a cadaveric study. Clin Anat, 19(6), 522-7.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The superficial temporal fat pad is situated inside the temporal fossa and contributes to the soft tissue bulge seen in the anteroinferior temporal fossa. It fills in the space between the temporalis muscle and the zygomatic arch (along with the deep temporal fat pad). However, the depth of the fat pad decreases superiorly, with the temporalis muscle lying much closer to the skin. Some studies have reported the superficial temporal fat pad extending posteriorly, past the external auditory meatus (Stephan & Devine, 2009).

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
Various structures must be dissected to expose the superficial temporal fat pad (which also form its lateral relations): the skin, subcutaneous fat, temporoparietal fascia, and the superficial fascial lamina of the superficial temporal fat pad.

The vascular supply of the superficial temporal fat pad includes branching perforators from the deep and middle temporal arteries that traverse through the substance of the fat pad (Kim & Matic, 2005).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The superficial temporal fat pad contributes to face morphology.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Kim, S. & Matic, D. B. (2005) The anatomy of temporal hollowing: the superficial temporal fat pad. J Craniofac Surg, 16(4), 651-4.

Stephan, C. N. & Devine, M. (2009) The superficial temporal fat pad and its ramifications for temporalis muscle construction in facial approximation. Forensic Sci Int, 191(1-3), 70-9.

17788.name: Bursa of Tensor Veli Palatini
alternate: Bursa of Tensor Veli Palatini Muscle

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The bursa of the tensor veli palatini muscle sits between the tendon of the tensor veli palatini and the pterygoid hamulus of the sphenoid bone. Bursae exist between structures that are in close contact when moving, preventing excessive friction between the two objects.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The bursa of the tensor veli palatini muscle reduces friction and ensures smooth movement of the tensor veli palatini muscle over the pterygoid hamulus of the sphenoid bone.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The major alar cartilages are one of three paired plates of cartilage forming the lateral, cartilaginous skeleton of the external nose. It is a plate of cartilage that forms the inferior and anterior framework of the lateral wall of the external nose. It sharply recurs at its anterior-most extent to contribute to the septum. This portion is called the medial crus or septal process. In this way, it forms the anterior lateral and anterior medial borders of the nares, notably the tip of the external nose. The cartilage plate is thin and flexible, giving mobility to the external nose.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The superior margin is attached by fibrous tissue to the inferior margin of the lateral nasal cartilage, and posteriorly to three or four minor alar cartilages to complete the framework of the lateral wall of the external nose. Inferior to the major alar cartilage is flexible fibrofatty tissue that forms the posteroinferior wall of the external nose, including the lateral and posterior nares.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The major alar cartilages maintain patency of the nostrils.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Rhinoplasty

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The accessory nasal cartilages link the lateral crus of the major alar cartilages with the lateral nasal cartilages.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The lateral nasal cartilages are one of three paired plates of cartilage forming the lateral, cartilaginous skeleton of the external nose. It is triangular and forms the superolateral part of the lateral wall of the external nose. The cartilage plate is thickest anteriorly and gets thinner posteriorly.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The posterior side of this triangular cartilage continues along the nasal bone and onto the frontal process of the maxilla. The anterior side attaches to the septal cartilage on the midline. Thus, the major attachment of the external nose to the facial skeleton and to the internal nose is by the lateral nasal cartilage. The base of the triangle of cartilage articulates with the major alar nasal cartilage.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The lateral nasal cartilage fuses with the septal cartilage along the midline, ideally at an angle between 10 to 15 degrees. In this area is the internal nasal valve, essential to maintain the normal nasal airway (Park et al, 2015).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Symptomatic nasal obstruction

—Rhinoplasty

sections.title: References
sections.text: Park, J., Suhk, J. & Nguyen, A. H. (2015) Nasal Analysis and Anatomy: Anthropometric Proportional Assessment in Asians-Aesthetic Balance from Forehead to Chin, Part II. Semin Plast Surg, 29(4), 226-31.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The minor alar cartilages are paired multiple plates of cartilage forming the posterior and lateral cartilaginous skeleton of the external nose.

There are typically three or four ‘islands’ of minor alar cartilages embedded in alar fibrofatty tissue. They complete the posteroinferior lateral wall of the external nose where they attach to the frontal process of the maxilla bone, thereby attaching the external nose to the facial skeleton.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The minor alar cartilages are found in the fibrous membrane between the lateral border of the major alar cartilage and the frontal process of the maxilla.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The minor alar cartilages are the fibrofatty alar tissue contributes to the posterolateral rim of the nares, giving them flexibility.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The cartilaginous framework of the nose is anchored to the piriform aperture by fibrous tissue. The lateral crura of the major alar cartilages do not extend to the piriform aperture, thus, leaving a space that is filled by fibrofatty tissue and the minor alar cartilages.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The fibrofatty tissue contributes to the posterolateral rim of the nares, giving them flexibility.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The nasal septal cartilage is a four-sided plate of cartilage found on the median plane that separates the anterior nasal cavity and external nose into right and left halves. As such, the cartilage forms the anterior portion of the medial wall of the nose, and a transition from the external nose to the nasal cavity.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nasal septal cartilage forms the anterior medial wall of the nose. It articulates with both nasal cartilages (lateral and major alar) and nasal skeleton. Posterosuperiorly, the nasal septal cartilage attaches to the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone and, posteroinferiorly, with the vomer. These together form the cartilaginous and bony nasal septum, the entire medial wall of the nose. Inferiorly, the nasal septal cartilage articulates with the most anterior portion of the palatine processes of the maxilla. Anteroinferiorly, it contacts the recurrent, medial crus, of the major alar cartilage where it becomes part of the medial nares. The anterosuperior portion articulates with the lateral nasal cartilage.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The nasal septal cartilage completes the separation between the nasal cavities and is a very important contributor to the structural stability of the nose.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Deviated nasal septum

—Rhinoplasty

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The external ear is composed of both the auricle and the external acoustic meatus. The auricle is composed of a single plate of elastic fibrocartilage, covered by thin skin. The auricle is formed by the auricular cartilage with two exceptions. At the lobule (or earlobe) and the area between the tragus and the crus of the helix, there is no cartilage beneath the skin.

The auricular cartilage is primarily composed of the helix, the elevated outer margin, and the concha, the hollow next to the ear canal. Other cartilaginous features are the tragus, found anterior to the opening of the external acoustic meatus, the antitragus, located opposite the tragus, and the antihelix, a smaller rim parallel to the helix.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The external ear projects from the side of the head by variable amounts. The cartilaginous auricle is connected to the surrounding structures by ligaments and muscles and is continuous with the external acoustic meatus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The auricle conducts sound waves from the external environment through the external acoustic meatus towards the tympanic membrane.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Auricular hematoma

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The auditory tube has both bony and cartilaginous parts. The bony part makes up one third of the tube closest to the tympanic cavity. It beings in the wall of the tympanic cavity and descends anteromedially through the temporal bone. The end of the bony part serves as the attachment for the cartilaginous portion. 

The cartilaginous part of the auditory tube opens directly under the mucous membrane of the nasopharynx where it forms an elevation, the torus tubarius. In children the angle of the tube is more horizontal but is at an angle of 45° in adults.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The auditory tube connects the tympanic cavity and the nasopharynx.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Due to the auditory tube connecting the nasopharynx and the middle ear, it can equalize pressure in the middle ear. This is important why flying or scuba diving as the surrounding air pressure changes. Active opening of the auditory tube is needed to equalize this pressure change. This is essential to maintain normal tympanic membrane motility and, hence, important for hearing. The auditory tube is normally collapsed and opens when swallowing or with positive pressure. The auditory tube also aids in mucociliary clearance of the middle ear and protection from loud sounds.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Otitis media 

—Barotitis

—Patulois pharyngotympanic tube

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The tympanic membrane is a thin, semi-transparent membrane with an oval shape. Most of the circumference of the membrane is a thickened rim of fibrocartilage known as the anulus. The anulus contains some smooth muscle cells.

The tympanic membrane can be divided into two parts, the pars flaccida, superiorly, and the pars tensa, inferiorly. These parts are separated by the anterior and posterior mallear folds, which pass from the tympanic membrane to the malleus.

The inner surface of the tympanic membrane is convex and projects into the tympanic cavity. The handle of the malleus is firmly attached to the inner surface of the membrane. The primary innervation of the tympanic membrane is the auriculotemporal nerve, which conveys pain sensation.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The tympanic membrane forms the division between the external acoustic meatus and the tympanic cavity. The handle of the malleus is attached to its internal surface.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The tympanic membrane vibrates with the force of sound waves entering the cavity through the external acoustic meatus. This vibration is transferred from the tympanic membrane to the auditory ossicles. The anulus around the circumference of the tympanic membrane potentially plays a role in maintaining tension of the membrane and controlling blood flow.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Otitis media

—Perforation

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The malleus has three suspensory ligaments that attach to it, including the anterior, lateral, and superior ligaments. The superior ligament extends from the head of the malleus to the roof of the epitympanic recess (epitympanum).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The superior ligament of the malleus is a suspensory ligament, connecting the malleus to the tympanic wall.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The annular ligament of stapes is composed of elastic fibers and is narrower anteriorly than posteriorly.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The annular ligament of stapes connects the stapes to the oval window. The footplate of the stapes and the oval window are both covered by hyaline cartilage. Between the hyaline cartilage is a ring of elastic fibers forming the annular ligament of stapes (Mansour et al, 2013).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Since the annular ligament of stapes is narrower anteriorly, it acts like a hinge so that the stapedial base can move when the stapedius muscle contracts during acoustic oscillations. This is important for the transmission of high-frequency sounds (Mansour et al., 2013).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Calcification of annular ligament of stapes

sections.title: References
sections.text: Mansour, S., Magnan, J., Haidar, H., Nicolas, K. & Louryan, S. (2013) Comprehensive and Clinical Anatomy of the Middle Ear. Springer Berlin Heidelberg.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The posterior ligament of the incus connects the short limb (process or crus) of the incus to the fossa of the incus (fossa incudis; a small depression on the posterior wall of the tympanic cavity).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The posterior ligament of incus plays an important role in vibrations of the middle ear bones.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The malleus has three suspensory ligaments that attach to it, including the anterior, lateral, and superior ligaments. The lateral ligament of the malleus is triangular, stretching from the posterior aspect of the tympanic notch to the head of the malleus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The lateral ligament of the malleus is a suspensory ligament, connecting the malleus to the tympanic wall.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The malleus has three suspensory ligaments that attach to it, including the anterior, lateral, and superior ligaments. The anterior ligament of the malleus may contain muscle fibers called the laxator tympani muscle or musculus externus mallei (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anterior ligament of the malleus extends from the neck of the malleus to the anterior wall of the tympanic cavity. From here, collagen fibers within the ligament can either enter the petrotympanic fissure to attach to the spine of the sphenoid or continue into the sphenomandibular ligament.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The anterior ligament of the malleus is a suspensory ligament, connecting the malleus to the tympanic wall.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 41st ed. Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The stapedial membrane fills the arch formed by the anterior and posterior limbs and the base (footplate) of the stapes. This arch is also known as the obturator foramen of the stapes and is approximately 3 mm in size. The stapedial artery traverses this foramen of the stapes in the fetus.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The superior ligament of the incus is merely a mucosal fold.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The superior ligament of the incus extends from the body of the incus to the roof of the epitympanic recess (epitympanum).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The superior ligament of incus is a suspensory ligament, connecting the incus to the tympanic wall.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The medial palpebral (canthic) ligament passes from the medial ends of both tarsal plates and insets into the anterior lacrimal crest and the frontal process of the maxilla (bone forming part of the orbital cavity). As it inserts into the tarsal plates, the ligament splits to surround the lacrimal canaliculi.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The medial palpebral ligament acts as a tendon for which the orbicularis oculi muscle inserts (Robinson & Stranc, 1970).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Robinson, T. J. and Stranc, M. F. (1970) 'The anatomy of the medial canthal ligament', Br J Plast Surg, 23(1), pp. 1-7.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The orbital septum is a weak membranous sheet that attaches to the orbital margin. It is continuous with the periosteum and is thickest laterally, where it lies anterior to the lateral palpebral ligament.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The orbital septum extends into the eyelid where it blends with the tarsal plates and the superficial lamella of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle. 

Laterally, the orbital septum lies anterior to the lateral palpebral ligament, whereas medially, the orbital septum passes posteriorly to the medial palpebral ligament and the nasolacrimal sac. 

The septum is pierced by the extraocular muscle, levator palpebrae superioris, and fibrous extensions of the sheaths of inferior oblique and inferior rectus muscles. It is also pierced by nerves and vessels that pass from the orbit to the face and scalp.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: When the eyes are closed, the orbital septum and tarsal plates provide complete coverage of the eyeball. The septum also acts to keep the eyelids stable as the eye moves.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Orbital cellulitis

—Periorbital cellulitis

—Age-related eyelid defects

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The superior tarsal plate is a thin plate of dense fibrous tissue in the upper eyelid. It is crescent shaped and approximately 2.5 cm long. The superior tarsal plate is around 10 mm high at its center and is larger than the inferior tarsus.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The superior tarsal plate is located in the upper eyelid, its free border is straight and closely related to the eyelash follicles. The border closest to the orbit is convex and attached to the orbital septum. Both tarsal plates are attached to the margin of the orbit via the orbital septum and the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments. Fibers from levator palpebrae superioris attach to the superior tarsus. The superior tarsal muscle is also closely associated.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The superior tarsal plate provides support to the upper eyelid and determines the shape of the eyelid.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The suspensory ligament of the eyeball is considered a part of the fascial sheath of the eyeball.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The suspensory ligament forms a hammock-like sling underneath the eyeball, between the check ligaments of the medial and lateral rectus muscles. This ligament encloses the inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The suspensory ligament of the eyeball functions to support the eyeball and prevent downward displacement.

sections.title: Structure
Function
sections.text: The function of the superior transverse ligament is uncertain, but it is thought to act as a lever for levator palpebrae superioris muscle by transferring its line of action from an anterior-posterior direction to a superior-inferior direction. It also acts as a suspensory ligament for the upper eyelid (Codere et al, 1995).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Codere, F., Tucker, N. A. & Renaldi, B. (1995) The anatomy of Whitnall ligament. Ophthalmology, 102(12), 2016-9.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The capsulopalpebral fascia is a fibrous expansion originating from the fascial sheaths surrounding the inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles (Dutton, 2011).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The capsulopalpebral fascia attaches to the suspensory ligament of the eyeball. Fibers ascend to the inferior tarsal plate and the dermis of the lower eyelid, thus creating a crease in the skin of the lower eyelid.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The capsulopalpebral fascia is described as the analog to the levator palpebrae muscle. It inserts into the inferior tarsal plate and dermis of the lower eyelid, thus assisting with the depression of the lower eyelid when the inferior oblique and inferior rectus muscles contract.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Palpebral bags

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dutton, J. J. (2011) Atlas of Clinical and Surgical Orbital Anatomy: Expert Consult: Online and Print. Elsevier Health Sciences.

20753.name: Check Ligament of Lateral Rectus Muscle

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The check ligament of the lateral rectus muscle is an expansion of the muscular fascia overlying the lateral rectus muscle, which is a reflection of the fascial sheath of the eyeball. This expansion is triangular and strong.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The check ligament of the lateral rectus muscle runs from the muscular sheath around the lateral rectus muscle to the orbital tubercle of the zygomatic bone laterally.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The check ligament of the lateral rectus muscle limits the action of the lateral rectus muscle.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The fascial sheath of the eyeball surrounds the eye, extending from the optic nerve to the corneoscleral junction. The fascial sheath is thickened anteriorly at the attachment of the recti muscles, thus, forming a fascial ring.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
At the posterior aspect, the fascial sheath is traversed by ciliary vessels and nerves. It is also perforated by the extraocular muscle tendons, where it is reflected on to each muscle as a sheath. The reflection onto the superior oblique muscle extends to the trochlea, whereas the sheaths of the four rectus muscles are thick anteriorly but posteriorly form a thin perimysium. 

These fascial sheaths around the extraocular muscles give off important expansions to the walls of the orbit, that limits the action of the medial and lateral rectus muscles. These expansions are named the medial and lateral check ligaments. 

The sheath around the inferior rectus muscle is also thickened. It acts as a suspensory ligament of the eye due to it being continuous with the sheaths of the medial and lateral rectus muscles which are attached to the medial and lateral check ligaments.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The fascial sheath of the eyeball separates the eyeball from the surrounding orbital fat.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Sub-Tenon’s anesthesia

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The superior and inferior eyelids contain a thin, elongated plate composed of tough collagenous tissue called the tarsal plate. Each plate is convex, conforming to the shape of the anterior surface of the eyeball. It has a free straight ciliary border adjacent to the hair follicles of the eyelashes, and a convex orbital border that is attached to the orbital septum (palpebral fascia). The inferior tarsus is the smallest of the two tarsal plates. It is approximately 2.5 cm long and 4 mm high (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The free ciliary margins of the tarsal plates end approximately 2 mm from the margin of the eyelid and runs parallel to it. 

The orbital margins of the tarsal plates are bound to margins of the orbital septum and to the lateral and medial palpebral ligaments on each side. The medial palpebral (canthic) ligament passes from the medial ends of both tarsal plates and insets into the anterior lacrimal crest and the frontal process of the maxilla (bone forming part of the orbital cavity). As it inserts into the tarsal plates, the ligament splits to surround the lacrimal canaliculi. The lateral palpebral ligament, on the other hand, is poorly developed. It passes from the lateral edges of the tarsal plates to the zygomatic bone that forms part of the orbital margin.

Each tarsal plate has associated smooth muscle forming the superior and inferior tarsal muscles, which aids in elevating and depressing the upper and lower eyelids, respectively.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The superior and inferior tarsal plates provide support to the eyelids and determine the shape of each lid.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 41st ed. Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The lateral palpebral (canthic) ligament is poorly developed. It passes from the lateral edges of the superior and inferior tarsal plates to marginal (or Whitnall’s) tubercle on the zygomatic bone (forming part of the orbital margin).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The lateral palpebral ligament is responsible for the structure of the lateral canthus (Parent et al, 1993).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Parent, A. D., Das, S. K., Mallette, R. A. and Haines, D. E. (1993) 'Significance of the lateral canthal tendon in craniofacial surgery', Pediatr Neurosurg, 19(2), pp. 73-7.

20514.name: Check Ligament of Medial Rectus Muscle

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The check ligament of the medial rectus muscle is an expansion of the muscular fascia overlying the medial rectus muscle, which is a reflection of the fascial sheath of the eyeball. This expansion is triangular and strong.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The check ligament of the medial rectus muscle runs from the muscular sheath around the medial rectus muscle to the lacrimal bone medially, just posterior to the posterior lacrimal crest.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The check ligament of the medial rectus muscle limits the action of the medial rectus muscle.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The dorsal cuneonavicular ligaments are a set of three ligaments that attach the dorsal aspects of the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiform bones to the navicular bone.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The dorsal cuneonavicular ligaments help stabilize the cuneonavicular joint.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The plantar cuneonavicular ligaments are a set of three ligaments that attach the plantar aspects of the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiform bones to the navicular bone.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The plantar cuneonavicular ligaments help stabilize the cuneonavicular joint.

23280.name: Articular Capsules of Proximal Interphalangeal Joints of Foot
23280.latin: Capsulae articulares articulationum interphalangearum proximalium pedis
alternate: Joint Capsules of Proximal Interphalangeal Joints of Foot
Synovial Capsules of Proximal Interphalangeal Joints of Foot

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The articular capsules of the interphalangeal joints are loosely attached to the articular margins of the bones. It is composed of two layers. The external layer, the fibrous membrane, is composed of dense fibrous tissue. The internal layer, the synovial membrane, lines the joint cavity and is composed of loose connective tissue.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The articular capsules of the interphalangeal joints are reinforced laterally and medially by the collateral ligaments, on its plantar aspect by the plantar ligaments, and dorsally by the extensor expansion.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The articular capsule of the interphalangeal joints ensure that the joint is sealed, thus, keeping the lubricating synovial fluid within the joint. It provides passive stability to the joint by limiting the joint movement. Additionally, it provides active stability but containing numerous proprioceptive nerve endings which relay mechanical information back to the central nervous system (Ralphs and Benjamin, 1994).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Ralphs, J. R. and Benjamin, M. (1994) 'The joint capsule: structure, composition, ageing and disease', Journal of Anatomy, 184(Pt 3), pp. 503-509.

17030.name: Plantar Interphalangeal Ligaments (Proximal; Left)
alternate: Plantar Plates of Interphalangeal Joints of Foot (Proximal; Left)

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The proximal plantar interphalangeal ligaments are thick, dense, fibrocartilaginous bands, or plates, found on the plantar surface of the interphalangeal joints. They attach to the heads of the proximal phalanges and the bases of the middle phalanges.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The plantar interphalangeal ligaments blend with the collateral ligaments.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The plantar interphalangeal ligaments help increase the articulation area for the base of the phalanx and limit the degree of extension at the interphalangeal joint. They also reinforce the articular capsule surrounding the interphalangeal joints.

22914.name: Articular Capsule of Interphalangeal Joint of Great Toe
alternate: Joint Capsule of Interphalangeal Joint of Great Toe
Synovial Capsule of Interphalangeal Joint of Great Toe

sections.title: Structure

The external layer, the fibrous membrane, is composed of dense fibrous tissue. The internal layer, the synovial membrane, lines the joint cavity and is composed of loose connective tissue.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations

Additionally, it provides active stability but containing numerous proprioceptive nerve endings which relay mechanical information back to the central nervous system (Ralphs and Benjamin, 1994).

16774.name: Collateral Interphalangeal Ligaments of Foot (Proximal; Left)

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The collateral interphalangeal ligaments of the proximal interphalangeal joints are strong fibers that extend from the lateral and medial sides of the heads of the proximal phalanges to the bases of the middle phalanges. Additional fibers, also called the accessory collateral ligaments, insert into the plantar ligaments.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The collateral interphalangeal ligaments help reinforce the articular capsules surrounding the joints and stabilize the joints during plantar and dorsiflexion.

21589.name: Collateral Interphalangeal Ligaments of Foot (Great Toe; Left)

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The collateral interphalangeal ligaments of the great toe are strong fibers that extend from the lateral and medial sides of the head of the proximal phalanx to the base of the distal phalanx. Additional fibers, also called the accessory collateral ligaments, insert into the plantar ligament.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The collateral interphalangeal ligaments help reinforce the articular capsules surrounding the joints and stabilize the joints during plantar and dorsiflexion.

19435.latin: Capsulae articulares articulationum interphalangearum distalium pedis

alternate: Plantar Plates of Interphalangeal Joints of Foot (Distal; Left)

alternate: Plantar Plates of Interphalangeal Joints of Foot (Great Toe; Left)

sections.text: The plantar interphalangeal ligament of the great toe is a thick, dense, fibrocartilaginous band, or plate, found on the plantar surface of the interphalangeal joint. It attaches to the head of the proximal phalanx and the base of the middle phalanx.
