23516.latin: Ramus glandularis posterior arteriae thyreoideae superioris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior thyroid artery.

Course: Descends along the posterior border of the thyroid gland.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Posterior surface of thyroid gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior glandular branch of the superior thyroid artery arises from the superior thyroid artery, the first branch of the external carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior glandular branch of the superior thyroid artery descends along the posterior border of the thyroid gland.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches of the posterior glandular branch of the superior thyroid artery; however, it anastomoses with the inferior thyroid artery on the posterior border of the thyroid gland.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior glandular branch of the superior thyroid artery supplies the lateral and medial surfaces of the thyroid gland.

19987.name: Anterior Glandular Branch of Superior Thyroid Artery
19987.latin: Ramus glandularis anterior arteriae thyreoideae superioris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior thyroid artery.

Course: Descends along the medial border of the upper poles of the thyroid gland.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Anterior surface of thyroid gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior glandular branch of the superior thyroid artery arises from the superior thyroid artery, the first branch of the external carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior glandular branch of the superior thyroid artery descends along the medial border of the upper pole of the right and left lobes of the thyroid gland.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches of the anterior glandular branch of the superior thyroid artery, however, at the isthmus of the thyroid gland, the right and left anterior glandular branches anastomose.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior glandular branch of the superior thyroid artery supplies the anterior surface of the thyroid gland.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Terminal branch of the common carotid artery near the C4 vertebral level

Course: Travels through the carotid canal into the cranial cavity and terminates as the anterior and middle cerebral arteries

Parts: Cervical (C1), petrous (C2), lacerum (C3), cavernous (C4), clinoid (C5), ophthalmic (C6), and communicating (C7)

Branches: Meningohypophyseal trunk, ophthalmic artery, posterior communicating artery, and anterior choroidal artery

Supplied Structures: Brain, pituitary gland and stalk, orbit, optic tract, internal capsule, basal nuclei, and cerebral cortex

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The internal carotid artery is one of the two terminal branches of the common carotid artery, the other being the external carotid artery. It arises at approximately the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, typically near the C4 vertebral level.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The internal carotid artery travels superiorly to the base of the skull, where it passes through the carotid canal to enter the cranial cavity. It ends at the base of the brain by dividing into its two terminal branches, the anterior and middle cerebral arteries. The Bouthillier classification divides the internal carotid artery into seven parts:

– C1, cervical: from the bifurcation of the common carotid artery to the carotid canal.

– C2, petrous: from the carotid canal to the border of the foramen lacerum, traveling through the petrous part of the temporal bone.

– C3, lacerum: from the border of the foramen lacerum to the superior margin of the petrolingual ligament.

– C4, cavernous: from the petrolingual ligament to the anterior clinoid process (proximal dural ring).

– C5, clinoid: from the anterior clinoid process (proximal dural ring) to the cavernous sinus roof (distal dural ring).

– C6, ophthalmic: from the cavernous sinus roof (distal dural ring) to a point just proximal to the origin of the posterior communicating artery.

– C7, communicating: from the origin of the posterior communicating artery to the internal carotid artery bifurcation.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
With the exception of the communicating (C7) segment, the odd-numbered segments (C1, C3, C5) usually have no branches. The even-numbered segments (C2, C4, C6) usually have branches; however many are variable and small in morphology. Numerous small unnamed branches also arise along its course.

– C2 (petrous): caroticotympanic branches, artery of the pterygoid canal.
– C4 (cavernous): meningohypophyseal trunk (giving the tentorial marginal branch, dorsal meningeal artery, and inferior hypophyseal artery); branches to the trigeminal nerve; cavernous branches; clival branches; branches to adjacent nerves; tentorial basal branch.
– C6 (ophthalmic): ophthalmic artery, superior hypophyseal artery, meningeal branch.
– C7 (communicating): posterior communicating artery, anterior choroidal artery; terminates as the anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
Through its cavernous (C4) and ophthalmic (C6) segment branches, the internal carotid artery supplies the tentorium cerebelli and clival dura, cranial nerves traversing the cavernous sinus (CN III, IV, V, VI), pituitary gland and stalk, optic chiasm, as well as the orbit and its contents.

Through the anterior choroidal artery and its terminal branches (the anterior and middle cerebral arteries), it supplies the optic tract, posterior limb of the internal capsule, basal nuclei, and the majority of the cerebral cortex (i.e., medial and lateral surfaces of the frontal and parietal lobes, the lateral temporal lobe, and the insular cortex).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: External carotid artery.

Course: Ascends between the parotid gland and styloid process, then between the auricular cartilage and mastoid process.

Branches: Stylomastoid artery and auricular, occipital, and parotid branches.

Supplied Structures: Middle and external ear, mastoid air cells, muscles of the neck, and facial nerve.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior auricular artery arises from the posterior aspect of the external carotid artery, just above the posterior belly of digastric and the stylohyoid muscle. In 12% of cases, the posterior auricular artery may arise from the occipital artery (Tubbs et al, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior auricular artery ascends in the neck between the parotid gland and the styloid process. It then travels in a groove between the auricular cartilage and the mastoid process of the temporal bone.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
In the neck, the posterior auricular artery gives off the stylomastoid artery and several small muscular branches.

As the posterior auricular artery travels between the auricular cartilage and mastoid processes, it provides auricular and occipital branches. Additionally, the posterior auricular artery anastomosis with the auricular branch of the occipital artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
In the neck, the posterior auricular artery provided arterial supply the digastric, stylohyoid, and sternocleidomastoid muscles, as well as the parotid gland.

In the head, the posterior auricular artery provides arterial supply to the extrinsic auricular muscles (auricularis anterior, superior, and posterior), the external acoustic meatus, auricle, middle ear, facial nerve (via the stylomastoid artery), and mastoid air cells.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. & Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Common carotid artery.

Course: Ascends on either side of the neck to enter the parotid gland.

Branches: Superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, superficial temporal, and maxillary arteries.

Supplied Structures: Face, scalp, tongue, teeth, palatine tonsils, frontal, ethmoidal, sphenoidal, and maxillary sinuses, auditory tube, external and middle ear, pharynx, larynx, muscles in the neck, and thyroid gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The external carotid artery arises when the common carotid artery bifurcates into the interior and external carotid arteries, usually at the level of C4 (or the upper border of the thyroid cartilage). The external carotid artery is easily distinguishable from the internal carotid artery, since the latter has no branches in the neck.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The external carotid artery originates in the carotid triangle of the neck and lies anteromedially to the internal carotid artery. Initially, it is slightly curved, as it bends anteriorly then posteriorly and slightly laterally. As it ascends, it passes more laterally to the internal carotid artery and gives off numerous branches to become diminished in size. It enters the parotid gland behind the neck of the mandible where it gives off its terminal branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The external carotid artery gives to eight branches distributed to the head and neck. Six of these branches arise from either the anterior, posterior, or medial surface of the external carotid artery.

- The superior thyroid, lingual, and facial arteries arise from the anterior surface of the external carotid artery.

- The occipital and posterior auricular arteries arise from posterior surface of the external carotid artery.

- The ascending pharyngeal artery arises from the medial surface of the external carotid artery.

The remaining two branches of the external carotid artery arise as terminal branches within the substance of the parotid gland, the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The external carotid artery is widely distributed to structures of the head and neck. These include the face, scalp, tongue, teeth, palatine tonsil, frontal, ethmoidal, sphenoidal, and maxillary sinuses, auditory tube, external and middle ear, pharynx, larynx, muscles in the neck, and thyroid gland.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the ophthalmic (C6) part of the internal carotid artery

Course: Passes medially beneath the optic chiasm toward the median eminence and infundibulum

Branch: Descending branch along the pituitary stalk

Supplied Structures: Anterior lobe of the pituitary gland, optic chiasm, ventral hypothalamus, lower infundibulum, and pars nervosa

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior hypophyseal artery typically arises from the ophthalmic (C6) part of the internal carotid artery, or less commonly from the clinoid (C5) or communicating (C7) parts.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The superior hypophyseal artery passes medially beneath the optic chiasm to reach the median eminence of the hypothalamus and infundibulum of the pituitary gland. In this region, it forms the primary capillary network of the hypophyseal portal system which receives hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones. 

The superior hypophyseal artery anastomoses with its contralateral fellow, branches of the inferior hypophyseal artery and other small perforators; this anastomotic network provides collateral circulation to the pituitary gland.

sections.title: Branches and Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The descending branch of superior hypophyseal artery, also known as the trabecular artery or loral artery, courses inferiorly along the pituitary stalk before passing through the adenohypophyseal trabecula.

Other small unnamed branches may be present and supply the optic nerve/chiasm.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The superior hypophyseal artery supplies the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland (via the hypophyseal portal system), optic chiasm, and ventral portions of the hypothalamus.

Its descending branch supplies the lower part of the infundibulum and pars nervosa, where it anastomoses with branches of the inferior hypophyseal artery. It may also provide a minor arterial supply to the pars tuberalis.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Communicating (C7) part of the internal carotid artery

Course: Passes over the optic tract, along the cerebral peduncle, and into the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle

Branch: Uncal artery

Supplied Structures: Optic pathway, lateral geniculate body, internal capsule, globus pallidus, hippocampus, amygdaloid body, and choroid plexus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior choroidal artery (AChA) arises from the communicating (C7) part of the internal carotid artery, just distal to the origin of the posterior communicating artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior choroidal artery has two segments, cisternal and intraventricular. The cisternal segment arises from the internal carotid artery lateral to the posterior communicating artery, then crosses from lateral to medial over the optic tract and continues posteriorly along the lateral aspect of the cerebral peduncle to reach the lateral geniculate body. The artery then enters the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle through the choroidal fissure, where it terminates in the choroid plexus.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior choroidal artery is a common origin of the uncal artery and also gives off numerous small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The branches of the anterior choroidal artery supply portions of the lateral ventricle, the anterior perforated substance, the optic nerve, chiasm, tract, and radiation, the lateral geniculate body, the internal capsule and its genu, the globus pallidus, the tail of the caudate nucleus, the hippocampus, dentate gyrus, fornix, amygdaloid body, hypothalamic and thalamic nuclei, substantia nigra, and crus cerebri.

sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Communicating (C7) segment of the internal carotid artery

Course: Passes laterally through the sphenoidal (M1), insular (M2), opercular (M3), and cortical (M4) segments

Branches: Anterolateral central arteries and superior and inferior cortical divisions

Supplied Structures: Lateral frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes, insula, basal nuclei, and internal capsule

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle cerebral artery is the larger of the two terminal branches of the internal carotid artery, arising from the communicating segment (C7) lateral to the optic chiasm and at the level of the anterior perforated substance. It is the principal arterial supply to the lateral cerebral hemisphere.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The middle cerebral artery is divided into four segments (M1–M4).

– M1 (sphenoidal): represents the main trunk, from the bifurcation onward. It passes laterally and slightly anteriorly from the internal carotid artery, inferior to the anterior perforated substance and parallel to the sphenoid ridge, toward the limen insulae. The artery typically bifurcates into superior and inferior divisions at or near the genu, occasionally trifurcating. Note: the M1/M2 boundary is not universally agreed upon — landmark-based nomenclature defines M1 as ending at the genu, while endovascular convention defines it as ending at the main bifurcation; in most patients these do not coincide.

M2–M4 designate the successive territories through which the branches pass on their course from the bifurcation to their final cortical destination.

– M2 (insular): the divisions course along the insular cortex within the lateral sulcus, continuing toward the circular sulcus (of Reil) of the insula, where they make an almost perpendicular turn.

– M3 (opercular): begins at the near-perpendicular bend at the circular sulcus and the divisions travel along the frontoparietal and temporal opercula toward the superior border of the lateral sulcus.

– M4 (cortical): begins at the superior border of the lateral sulcus, where the branches emerge onto the lateral cortex. Cortical branches are broadly grouped into superior and inferior cortical parts based on their territory.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The branches of the middle cerebral artery are divided into perforating and cortical branches:

– The perforating branches are the anterolateral central arteries (lenticulostriate arteries), which arise predominantly from M1. 

– Most cortical branches arise from the superior and inferior divisions; however, the polar temporal and anterior temporal arteries typically arise directly from M1, prior to the bifurcation. Superior cortical branches include the lateral orbitofrontal, prefrontal, artery of the precentral sulcus, artery of the central sulcus, artery of the postcentral sulcus, anterior parietal, posterior parietal; inferior cortical branches include the middle temporal, posterior temporal, temporooccipital arteries, as well as the artery to the angular gyrus.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
– Deep and subcortical: the anterolateral central (lenticulostriate) arteries supply the caudate nucleus, putamen, lateral segment of the globus pallidus, and the anterior limb, genu, and posterior limb of the internal capsule.

– Cortical: the cortical branches supply the lateral surface of the frontal lobe (precentral, postcentral, superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri), the parietal lobe (supramarginal and angular gyri, superior parietal lobule), the lateral and superior temporal lobe (superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyri), the insular cortex, and the temporooccipital region.

24922.name: Clival Branches of Internal Carotid Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal carotid artery.

Course: Passes posteriorly towards the clivus.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Clivus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The clival branches of the cerebral part of the internal carotid artery are small ramifications that arise from the cerebral part of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The clival branches of the cerebral part of the internal carotid artery pass posteriorly to reach the clivus. The clivus is the sloping part of bone formed by the dorsum sellae, posterior part of body of the sphenoid bone, and the basilar part of the occipital bone.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The clival branches of the cerebral part of the internal carotid artery supply the clivus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Distal basilar artery, immediately before the posterior cerebral arteries

Course: Passes posterolaterally through the anterior pontomesencephalic (S1), lateral pontomesencephalic (S2), cerebellomesencephalic (S3), and cortical (S4) segments

Branches: Medial superior vermian branch and lateral branch

Supplied Structures: Rostral pons, cerebral peduncles, anterior cerebellar lobe, and superior cerebellar peduncle

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The superior cerebellar artery typically branches from the basilar artery just before its termination as the paired posterior cerebral arteries. 

Documented variations show it originating from the posterior cerebral artery, sharing a common trunk with the posterior cerebral artery, or, rarely, originating from the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
Following its typical origin from the distal basilar artery, the superior cerebellar artery passes posterolaterally and commonly divides into rostral and caudal trunks. The superior cerebellar artery is divided into four segments:

– Anterior pontomesencephalic (S1): passes directly inferior to the oculomotor nerve.

– Lateral pontomesencephalic (S2): begins at the lateral margin of the brainstem and often passes inferiorly along the lateral aspect of the rostral pons.

– Cerebellomesencephalic (S3): begins at the cerebellomesoencephalic fissure.

– Cortical (S4): the terminal segment, which perforates and supplies the vermis and cerebellar hemispheres.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The superior cerebellar artery divides into a medial branch, the superior vermian artery, which supplies the anterior vermis, and a lateral branch, which supplies the anterior cerebellar hemispheres.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superior cerebellar artery and its branches supply the rostral pons, the cerebral peduncles, the anterior lobe of the cerebellum, and the superior cerebellar peduncle.

sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the cranial (V4) segment of the vertebral artery

Course: Passes around the medulla oblongata, between the cerebellar tonsil and medulla, and through the cerebellomedullary fissure

Branches: Posterior spinal artery, cerebellar tonsillar branches, inferior vermian branch, and choroidal branch to the fourth ventricle

Supplied Structures: Dorsolateral medulla oblongata, inferior cerebellar peduncle, cerebellar tonsils, inferior vermis, inferior cerebellar hemisphere, and fourth ventricular choroid plexus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) typically arises from the V4 (intracranial) segment of the vertebral artery at the level of the medulla oblongata, within the cisterna magna. Its origin is variable; it may occasionally be absent, with its territory supplied by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The posterior inferior cerebellar artery can be divided into five segments: the anterior medullary, lateral medullary, tonsillomedullary, telovelotonsillar, and cortical segments. 

From its origin, the posterior inferior cerebellar artery passes anteriorly then laterally around the medulla oblongata through its anterior and lateral medullary segments. It forms an inferior loop near the median aperture of the fourth ventricle before passing between the tonsil and medulla (tonsillomedullary segment). It then traverses the cerebellomedullary fissure between the roof of the fourth ventricle and the cerebellar tonsil (telovelotonsillar segment), emerging onto the inferior surface of the cerebellar hemisphere as its cortical segment.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Along its path, the posterior inferior cerebellar artery gives rise to the posterior spinal artery, cerebellar tonsillar branches, the inferior vermian branch, and a choroidal branch to the fourth ventricle.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the dorsolateral medulla oblongata (lateral to the hypoglossal nucleus and dorsal to the olivary nucleus), the inferior cerebellar peduncle, the cerebellar tonsils, the inferior vermis, the inferior surface of the cerebellar hemisphere including the posterior lobe, the nodule, and the choroid plexus and tela choroidea of the fourth ventricle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the most caudal branch of the basilar artery

Course: Passes along the ventral pons through the cerebellopontine angle and divides near the flocculus

Branches: Rostrolateral and caudomedial branches, labyrinthine artery, and subarcuate artery

Supplied Structures: Inferolateral pons, middle cerebellar peduncle, flocculus, lateral posterior cerebellum, and fourth ventricular choroid plexus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior inferior cerebellar artery is typically the first (most caudal) branch of the basilar artery. Occasionally, it may originate with the posterior inferior cerebellar artery through a common trunk on the basilar artery or it may originate from the vertebral arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
After branching from the basilar artery, the anterior inferior cerebellar artery courses posterolaterally within the prepontine cistern along the ventral surface of the pons, passing inferior to the abducens nerve before traveling through the cerebellopontine angle alongside the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves. 

Near this location, the artery typically divides into rostrolateral and caudomedial branches. The rostrolateral branch continues laterally above the flocculus and horizontal fissure, anterior to the middle cerebellar peduncle, to terminate on the anterolateral surface of the cerebellar hemispheres. The caudomedial branch passes inferior to the flocculus, penetrates the inferior cerebellomedullary fissure, and courses along the lateral aperture.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior inferior cerebellar artery commonly gives off the labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery and the subarcuate artery near the internal acoustic meatus. It also gives off numerous small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the lateral portions of the posterior lobe of the cerebellum, the flocculus, the middle cerebellar peduncle, the inferolateral pons, and the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle via the lateral aperture.

When the labyrinthine artery arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, it also supplies the internal ear.

sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the infracallosal (A2) segment of the anterior cerebral artery

Course: Travels anteriorly along the medial frontal lobe toward the frontal pole

Branches: Small perforating branches

Supplied Structures: Medial and lateral surfaces of the frontal pole

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The frontopolar artery most commonly arises from the infracallosal (A2) segment of the anterior cerebral artery, although it has also been reported to arise from the callosomarginal artery, and rarely from the precommunicating (A1) segment or pericallosal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The frontopolar artery travels anteriorly along the medial surface of the frontal lobe toward the frontal pole, where it crosses the subfrontal sulcus.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The frontopolar artery gives off small perforating branches to the frontal pole.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The frontopolar artery supplies portions of the lateral and medial surfaces of the frontal pole.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior cerebral artery near the genu of the corpus callosum, usually from the precallosal (A3) segment

Course: Travels posteriorly along or within the cingulate sulcus

Branches: Anteromedial, intermediomedial, and posteromedial frontal branches, cingular branch, and paracentral branches

Supplied Structures: Superior frontal gyrus, cingulate gyrus, and paracentral lobule

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The callosomarginal artery arises from the anterior cerebral artery at the level of the genu of the corpus callosum, typically from the A3 (precallosal) segment.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the callosomarginal artery travels caudally (posteriorly), curving along or within the cingulate sulcus.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The branches of the callosomarginal artery are variable, but typically include the anteromedial, intermediomedial, and posteromedial frontal branches (also known as the anterior, middle, and posterior internal frontal arteries), a cingular branch, and paracentral branches. In some individuals, the frontopolar and orbitofrontal arteries may arise from the callosomarginal artery rather than from the infracallosal (A2) segment.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The branches of the callosomarginal artery primarily supply the superior frontal gyrus (via the anteromedial, intermediomedial, and posteromedial frontal branches), portions of the cingulate gyrus, and the paracentral lobule.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
The precuneate branches arise from distal end of the pericallosal artery. They are also known as the precuneal arteries. From their origin, they travel posterosuperiorly along the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere to the precuneus.

They provide an arterial supply to the inferior part of the precuneus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Callosomarginal artery or supracallosal (A4) segment of the anterior cerebral artery

Course: Runs within the cingulate or paracentral sulcus before passing superiorly along the paracentral lobule

Branches: Cortical branches to the paracentral lobule, cingulate gyrus, and lateral premotor, motor, and somatosensory cortices

Supplied Structures: Paracentral lobule, cingulate gyrus, and premotor, motor, and somatosensory cortices

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The paracentral branch (also called the paracentral artery) variably arises from the callosomarginal artery or directly from the supracallosal (A4) segment of the anterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The paracentral branch runs briefly within the cingulate or paracentral sulcus before turning superiorly to course along the paracentral lobule, often extending to the lateral surface of the premotor, motor, and somatosensory cortices.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The paracentral branch gives off cortical branches to the dorsal (superior) aspects of the paracentral lobule and the cingulate gyrus, as well as branches on the lateral surface of the cortex to the premotor, motor, and somatosensory cortices.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The paracentral branch gives off cortical branches to the superior aspect of the paracentral lobule and cingulate gyrus, as well as branches to the premotor, motor, and somatosensory cortices on the lateral surface.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
The parieto-occipital branches arise from distal end of the pericallosal artery. From their origin, they travel posteriorly along the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere to the parietal and occipital lobes.

They provide an arterial supply to parts of the parietal and occipital lobes.

21563.name: Posteromedial Frontal Branch of Callosomarginal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Callosomarginal artery or anterior cerebral artery, usually the precallosal (A3) segment

Course: Passes posteriorly and superiorly along the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus

Branches: Small unnamed terminal branches

Supplied Structures: Medial superior frontal gyrus and anterior paracentral lobule

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posteromedial frontal branch of the callosomarginal artery (also known as the posterior internal frontal artery) typically arises from the callosomarginal artery or directly from the anterior cerebral artery, most often from the precallosal (A3) segment and, less commonly, the supracallosal (A4) segment.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the posteromedial frontal branch typically passes posteriorly (caudally) and superiorly (dorsally) along the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus, terminating near the anterior surface of the paracentral lobule.

sections.title: Branches and Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posteromedial frontal branch ends as small unnamed terminal branches supplying the medial aspect of the superior frontal gyrus and the anterior aspect of the paracentral lobule.

sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Distal anterior cerebral artery from the level of the genu of the corpus callosum through the precallosal (A3), supracallosal (A4), and postcallosal (A5) segments

Course: Follows the superior surface of the corpus callosum within the pericallosal sulcus

Branches: Superior and inferior parietal branches, with variable frontal, paracentral, and central branches

Supplied Structures: Corpus callosum, medial parietal lobe, precuneus, and variably the paracentral lobule, cingulate gyrus, and medial frontal lobe

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The pericallosal artery is the portion of the anterior cerebral artery from the level of the genu of the corpus callosum distally (A3–A5 segments), from which the callosomarginal artery arises as a variable branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The pericallosal artery courses within the pericallosal sulcus, following the superior surface of the corpus callosum posteriorly from the genu along the body.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The branching of the pericallosal artery is subject to a large degree of interindividual variation. 

Its principal named cortical branches are the superior parietal and inferior parietal branches. Additional cortical branches such as the frontopolar, [anteromedial, intermediomedial, and posteromedial] frontal, and paracentral arteries typically arise from the callosomarginal artery, but may arise directly from the pericallosal artery when the callosomarginal artery is small or absent. 

Small central branches may also arise, contributing to the supply of the lamina terminalis, anterior hypothalamus, and optic chiasm, though these structures are primarily supplied by the anteromedial central arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The pericallosal artery consistently supplies the body of the corpus callosum and the medial parietal lobe, including the superior and inferior parietal lobules and the precuneus. When the callosomarginal artery is small or absent, it also variably supplies the paracentral lobule, cingulate gyrus, and medial frontal lobe. Small central branches may additionally contribute to the lamina terminalis, anterior hypothalamus, and optic chiasm.

22363.name: Medial Orbitofrontal Artery
alternate: Medial Orbitofrontal Branch of Anterior Cerebral Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the infracallosal (A2) segment of the anterior cerebral artery

Course: Travels ventrally and rostrally around the straight gyrus toward the orbitofrontal cortex

Branches: Branches to the olfactory bulb and tract, orbitofrontal cortex, and lateral orbitofrontal artery

Supplied Structures: Olfactory bulb and tract, orbital gyri, and inferomedial frontal lobe

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial orbitofrontal artery typically arises as the first branch of the infracallosal (A2) segment of the anterior cerebral artery, although in rare instances it can arise from the precommunicating (A1) segment.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The medial orbitofrontal artery travels ventrally and rostrally from its origin toward the anterior cranial fossa. It then travels around the straight gyrus, oblique to the olfactory tract and bulb, where it can penetrate the olfactory cistern before ultimately terminating in the orbitofrontal cortex.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The medial orbitofrontal artery provides five branches to the olfactory bulb and tract, four to the bulb and one to the tract. Approximately eight further small branches distribute to the orbitofrontal cortex, and two small anastomotic branches connect with the lateral orbitofrontal artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The medial orbitofrontal artery provides a primary supply to the olfactory bulb and tract. Its branches also supply aspects of the orbital gyri, the medial portion of the orbital surface, and the inferomedial portion of the frontal lobe.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

21254.name: Intermediomedial Frontal Branch of Callosomarginal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Callosomarginal artery or precallosal (A3) segment of the anterior cerebral artery

Course: Passes superiorly along the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus

Branches: Small unnamed terminal branches

Supplied Structures: Medial aspect of the superior frontal gyrus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The intermediomedial frontal branch of callosomarginal artery (also known as the middle internal frontal artery) typically arises from the callosomarginal artery or directly from the precallosal (A3) segment of the anterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the intermediomedial frontal branch typically passes superiorly (dorsally) along the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus.

sections.title: Branches and Supplied Structures
sections.text: The intermediomedial frontal branch ends as small unnamed terminal branches supplying the medial aspect of the superior frontal gyrus.

23922.name: Anteromedial Frontal Branch of Callosomarginal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Callosomarginal artery or anterior cerebral artery, usually the precallosal (A3) segment

Course: Passes anteriorly and superiorly along the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus

Branches: Small unnamed terminal branches

Supplied Structures: Medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anteromedial frontal branch of callosomarginal artery (also known as the anterior internal frontal artery) typically arises from the callosomarginal artery or directly from the anterior cerebral artery, most often from the precallosal (A3) segment and, less commonly, the infracallosal (A2) segment.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the anteromedial frontal branch typically passes anteriorly (rostrally) and superiorly (dorsally) along the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus.

sections.title: Branches and Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anteromedial frontal branch ends as small, unnamed terminal branches that distribute along the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the infracallosal (A2) segment of the anterior cerebral artery

Course: Passes anteriorly and laterally before recurring posteriorly through the anterior perforated substance

Branches: Perforating branches

Supplied Structures: Head of the caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, anterior limb and genu of the internal capsule, and rostral corona radiata

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The long striate artery (medial striate artery, recurrent artery of Heubner) typically arises from the infracallosal (A2) segment of the anterior cerebral artery, close to the junction of the anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries, or occasionally from the precommunicating (A1) segment.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The long striate artery initially courses anteriorly and laterally, parallel to the anterior cerebral artery, before recurring posteriorly toward the anterior perforated substance, through which it enters the brain.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The long striate artery enters the brain through the anterior perforated substance, giving off perforating branches to the caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, and internal capsule.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The long striate artery supplies anterior parts of the head of the caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, as well as the anterior limb and genu of the internal capsule. It may also contribute to the superior portions of the internal capsule and the rostral corona radiata.

16477.name: Lateral Orbitofrontal Artery
alternate: Lateral Orbitofrontal Branch of Middle Cerebral Artery
Lateral Frontobasal Branch of Middle Cerebral Artery
Ramus orbitofrontalis lateralis arteriae cerebri mediae
Ramus frontobasalis lateralis arteriae cerebri mediae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the superior division of the middle cerebral artery during the insular (M2) segment

Course: Travels within the anterior ramus of the lateral sulcus toward the posterolateral orbitofrontal cortex

Supplied Structures: Lateral orbitofrontal cortex, orbital parts of the middle and inferior frontal gyri, pars orbitalis, and anterior insula

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral orbitofrontal artery (lateral frontobasal artery) typically arises from the superior division of the middle cerebral artery during its insular course (M2 segment), though it may arise directly from the main MCA trunk (M1 segment), proximal to the bifurcation, or from the inferior division.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lateral orbitofrontal artery travels within the anterior ramus of the lateral (Sylvian) sulcus, between the anterosuperior aspect of the temporal lobe and the posteroinferior aspect of the frontal lobe, toward the posterolateral portion of the orbitofrontal cortex.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The lateral orbitofrontal artery gives rise to small cortical branches distributed to the lateral orbital surface of the frontal lobe.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The lateral orbitofrontal artery predominantly supplies the lateral, anterior, and posterior orbitofrontal gyri, and part of the pars orbitalis of the inferior frontal gyrus. Some perforating branches may supply part of the anterosuperior insula.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

16540.name: Anterolateral Central Arteries
alternate: Anterolateral Central Branches of Middle Cerebral Artery
Rami centrales anterolaterales arteriae mediae cerebri

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Sphenoidal (M1) segment of the middle cerebral artery

Course: Pass through the lateral cerebral cistern and anterior perforated substance, then traverse the basal nuclei and internal capsule

Supplied Structures: Caudate nucleus, putamen, lateral globus pallidus, external capsule, and internal capsule

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterolateral central arteries (lenticulostriate arteries) are small perforating arteries arising primarily from the sphenoid part (M1) of the middle cerebral artery. They are sometimes subdivided into medial and lateral lenticulostriate groups based on their position of origin along M1 (the medial group arising more proximally and the lateral group more distally). Some authors also use the term "medial lenticulostriate arteries" to refer to perforating branches of the A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery; these correspond to the anteromedial central arteries in TNA terminology.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterolateral central arteries travel through the lateral cerebral (Sylvian) cistern and pierce the anterior perforated substance to enter the brain, ascending within the external capsule along the lower lateral aspect of the lentiform complex before turning medially to traverse the basal nuclei and internal capsule.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterolateral central arteries are themselves small perforating branches; they have no named branches and distribute to much of the basal nuclei and the internal capsule.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: As their alternative name (lenticulostriate arteries) suggests, these vessels supply the lentiform nucleus and striatum (specifically the putamen, head of the caudate nucleus, and lateral segment of the globus pallidus) as well as the external capsule and the anterior limb, genu, and much of the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

18431.name: Posterior Temporal Artery
alternate: Posterior Temporal Branch of Middle Cerebral Artery
Ramus temporalis posterior arteriae cerebri mediae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the posterior insular or opercular course of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery

Course: Passes over the posterior insula and temporal operculum before continuing along the superior temporal gyrus

Supplied Structures: Posterior superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyri

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior temporal artery typically arises from the posterior portion of the inferior division's insular or opercular course, making it the most posteriorly arising of the temporal branches. It may occasionally arise from the superior division.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior temporal artery passes over the posterior insula (insular segment, M2) and along the temporal operculum (opercular segment, M3), before exiting the lateral sulcus and coursing along the superior temporal gyrus (cortical segment, M4), sending perforating branches superiorly and inferiorly within the superior and inferior temporal sulci.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The posterior temporal artery gives off numerous small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior temporal artery supplies the posterior portions of the superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyri.

sections.title: References

24908.name: Inferior Division of Middle Cerebral Artery
alternate: Inferior Trunk of Middle Cerebral Artery
Inferior Cortical Branch of Middle Cerebral Artery
Inferior Terminal Branch of Middle Cerebral Artery
Inferior Terminal Trunk of Middle Cerebral Artery
Inferior Cortical Part of Middle Cerebral Artery
Ramus corticalis inferior arteriae cerebri mediae
Ramus terminalis inferior arteriae cerebri mediae
Truncus terminalis inferior arteriae cerebri mediae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Bifurcation of the middle cerebral artery near the end of the sphenoidal (M1) segment

Course: Passes through the insular (M2), opercular (M3), and cortical (M4) segments to the lateral temporal, parietal, and occipital cortex

Branches: Anterior, middle, and posterior temporal arteries, temporooccipital artery, and artery to the angular gyrus

Supplied Structures: Lateral temporal lobe, angular gyrus, and temporooccipital region

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle cerebral artery typically bifurcates into superior and inferior divisions at or near the genu, at the end of the sphenoidal segment (M1). Occasionally, a third intermediate division is present. The terminal branches of the inferior division constitute the inferior cortical part of the middle cerebral artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior division arises at the bifurcation near the genu and travels posteriorly and inferiorly along the inferior insula, deep within the lateral sulcus (insular segment, M2), before turning along the inferior operculum (opercular segment, M3), exiting along the inferior edge of the lateral sulcus, and terminating along the lateral cortex (cortical segment, M4).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The inferior division usually gives rise to the anterior, middle, and posterior temporal arteries, the temporooccipital artery, and the artery to the angular gyrus. 

The anterior temporal and polar temporal arteries typically arise from the M1 segment, but may arise from the inferior division. 

There is also variability in the more posterior branches; the angular artery may occasionally arise from the superior division, and superior division branches, particularly the parietal arteries, may arise from the inferior division.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The inferior division and its branches supply the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, including the superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyri, the angular gyrus, and the temporooccipital region.

19722.name: Anterior Temporal Artery
alternate: Anterior Temporal Branch of Middle Cerebral Artery
Ramus temporalis anterior arteriae cerebri mediae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the sphenoidal (M1) segment of the middle cerebral artery; variably the inferior division

Course: Passes toward the temporal pole or through the insular, opercular, and cortical segments to the anterolateral temporal lobe

Supplied Structures: Anterior superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyri

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior temporal artery has a variable origin. It typically arises from the sphenoid (horizontal, M1) segment of the middle cerebral artery, near the midpoint of its horizontal course. It may also arise from the inferior division or as part of an M1 trifurcation.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The course of the anterior temporal artery varies with its origin:

– When arising from M1, it typically passes anteriorly and inferiorly over the temporal pole without deeply entering the lateral sulcus. 

– When arising from the inferior division, it passes over the anterior insula (insular segment, M2), along the temporal operculum (opercular segment, M3), before exiting the lateral sulcus and coursing along the anterolateral surface of the temporal lobe (cortical segment, M4).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior temporal artery gives off numerous small, unnamed cortical branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior temporal artery supplies the anterior portions of the superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyri. Its territory lies posterior to that of the polar temporal artery (which is specific to the temporal pole) and anterior to that of the middle temporal artery.

23175.name: Artery to Angular Gyrus
alternate: Ramus gyri angularis arteriae cerebri mediae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the terminal and largest branch of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery

Course: Passes over the posterior insula and temporal operculum before continuing across the superior temporal, supramarginal, and angular gyri

Supplied Structures: Angular and supramarginal gyri, posterior superior temporal gyrus, and superior lateral occipital lobe

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The artery to the angular gyrus is the terminal and largest branch of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery, emerging from the most posterior part of the lateral sulcus. It may occasionally arise from the superior division.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The artery to the angular gyrus passes over the posterior insula (insular segment, M2) and along the temporal operculum, including over the transverse temporal gyri (opercular segment, M3), before exiting the posterior end of the lateral sulcus and coursing horizontally over the superior temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, and angular gyrus toward the lateral occipital lobe (cortical segment, M4).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The artery to the angular gyrus gives rise to small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The artery to the angular gyrus supplies the angular gyrus, parts of the supramarginal gyrus, the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus, and the superior part of the lateral occipital lobe.

17459.name: Superior Division of Middle Cerebral Artery
alternate: Superior Trunk of Middle Cerebral Artery
Superior Cortical Branch of Middle Cerebral Artery
Superior Terminal Branch of Middle Cerebral Artery
Superior Terminal Trunk of Middle Cerebral Artery
Superior Cortical Part of Middle Cerebral Artery
Ramus corticalis superior arteriae cerebri mediae
Ramus terminalis superior arteriae cerebri mediae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Bifurcation of the middle cerebral artery near the end of the sphenoidal (M1) segment

Course: Passes through the insular (M2), opercular (M3), and cortical (M4) segments to the superior lateral cerebral cortex

Branches: Lateral orbitofrontal, prefrontal, precentral, central, postcentral, anterior parietal, and posterior parietal arteries

Supplied Structures: Anterior insula, orbitofrontal cortex, frontal gyri, precentral and postcentral gyri, and superior parietal lobule

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle cerebral artery typically bifurcates into superior and inferior divisions at or near the genu, at the end of the sphenoidal segment (M1). Occasionally, a third intermediate division or smaller branches may be present.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The superior division of the middle cerebral artery arises at the bifurcation, near the genu, and travels posteriorly and superiorly along the insular cortex, deep within the lateral (Sylvian) sulcus (insular segment, M2), toward the distal portion of the insular circular sulcus. Here it makes a sharp turn to pass along the superior aspect of the operculum (opercular segment, M3), before exiting along the superior edge of the lateral sulcus onto the lateral surface of the cerebral cortex (cortical segment, M4). 

The terminal branches of the superior division constitute the majority of the superior cortical part of the MCA.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The superior division usually gives rise to the lateral orbitofrontal artery, prefrontal artery, artery of the precentral sulcus, artery of the central sulcus, artery of the postcentral sulcus, anterior parietal artery, and posterior parietal artery. The origin of individual branches is variable; the parietal arteries in particular may occasionally arise from the inferior division.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Depending on its branches, the superior division of the middle cerebral artery may supply the anterior insular cortex, the orbitofrontal cortex, the inferior and middle frontal gyri, the precentral and postcentral gyri, and part of the superior parietal lobule.

22255.name: Middle Temporal Artery
alternate: Middle Temporal Branch of Middle Cerebral Artery
Ramus temporalis medius arteriae cerebri mediae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery

Course: Passes through the insular, opercular, and cortical segments to the lateral temporal lobe

Supplied Structures: Middle portions of the superior and middle temporal gyri and variably the inferior temporal gyrus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle temporal artery typically arises from the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery, from the mid-portion of its insular or opercular course. It may occasionally arise from the superior division.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The middle temporal artery travels along the insula (insular segment, M2) and temporal operculum (opercular segment, M3), before emerging from the mid-portion of the lateral sulcus and coursing along the lateral surface of the temporal lobe (cortical segment, M4).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The middle temporal artery gives rise to small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The middle temporal artery supplies the middle portions of the superior and middle temporal gyri, and variably the inferior temporal gyrus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
The artery of postcentral sulcus (aka anterior parietal artery) arises from the superior terminal branch of the middle cerebral artery. It travels posterosuperiorly, along the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere, towards the postcentral sulcus, which it also travels along.

It provides an arterial supply to the postcentral sulcus and the areas of the cerebral cortex that lie adjacent to it.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the superior division of the middle cerebral artery; variably the inferior or intermediate division

Course: Passes along the posterior insula and parietal operculum before continuing over the inferior parietal lobule

Supplied Structures: Supramarginal gyrus and posterior superior and inferior parietal lobules

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior parietal artery typically arises from the superior division of the middle cerebral artery, though it may arise from the inferior division or, when present, from an intermediate division.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior parietal artery travels along the posterior aspect of the long gyrus of the insula (insular segment, M2), then along the parietal operculum (opercular segment, M3), before emerging from the lateral sulcus near its posterior end and passing posterosuperiorly along the inferior parietal lobule, marking the anterior border of the supramarginal gyrus (cortical segment, M4).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The posterior parietal artery gives off numerous small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior parietal artery supplies the supramarginal gyrus and the posterior parts of the superior and inferior parietal lobules.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
The artery of central sulcus arises from the superior terminal branch of the middle cerebral artery. It travels superiorly, along the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere, towards the central sulcus, which it also travels along.

It provides an arterial supply to the central sulcus and the areas of the cerebral cortex that lie adjacent to it.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior division of the middle cerebral artery, usually from the insular (M2) segment

Course: Passes along the insula and frontoparietal operculum before continuing within the precentral sulcus

Supplied Structures: Posterior superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri, precentral gyrus, and anterior subcentral gyrus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The artery of the precentral sulcus arises from the superior division of the middle cerebral artery, typically from the M2 (insular) segment.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The artery of the precentral sulcus travels along the insula before turning at the circular sulcus (of Reil) to pass along the frontoparietal operculum (opercular segment, M3), exiting the lateral sulcus and coursing along the lateral surface of the frontal lobe within the precentral sulcus (cortical segment, M4).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The artery of the precentral sulcus gives off numerous small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The artery of the precentral sulcus supplies the posterior parts of the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri as well as the precentral gyrus. It may also supply the anterior part of the subcentral gyrus (within the lateral sulcus).

24830.name: Prefrontal Artery
alternate: Prefrontal Branch of Middle Cerebral Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior division of the middle cerebral artery during the insular (M2) segment

Course: Passes through the insular, opercular, and cortical segments to the prefrontal cortex

Supplied Structures: Inferior, middle, and superior frontal gyri and anterior insula

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The prefrontal artery typically arises from the superior division of the middle cerebral artery during its insular course (M2 segment) and may share a common origin with the lateral orbitofrontal artery. It may occasionally arise from the inferior division.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The prefrontal artery arises from the superior division of the middle cerebral artery, coursing along the insular cortex (M2) before turning at the circular sulcus of the insula to pass along the frontal operculum (M3). It exits the lateral sulcus anteriorly onto the lateral surface of the frontal lobe, coursing over the prefrontal cortex (M4).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The prefrontal artery gives off numerous small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The prefrontal artery supplies parts of the inferior frontal gyrus, most of the middle frontal gyrus, and part of the superior frontal gyrus. Some perforating branches may supply part of the anterior insula.

24960.name: Parietal Branch of Medial Occipital Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The parietal branch arises from medial occipital artery. It travels superiorly to the parietal lobe, which it provides an arterial supply to.

24370.name: Posterior Temporal Branch of Lateral Occipital Artery
24370.latin: Ramus temporalis posterior arteriae occipitalis lateralis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the lateral occipital artery; variably the posterior cerebral, parietooccipital, or calcarine branch

Course: Passes posterolaterally along the basal temporal and occipital lobes

Branch: Variably gives rise to the lateral posterior choroidal artery

Supplied Structures: Caudal parahippocampal, lingual, fusiform, and inferior temporal gyri and inferior occipital cortex

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior temporal branch typically arises from the lateral occipital artery, though it may arise directly from the posterior cerebral artery or occasionally from the parietooccipital or calcarine branches of the medial occipital artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the posterior temporal branch passes posterolaterally along the basal surface of the temporal and occipital lobes.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The posterior temporal branch gives off numerous small, unnamed perforating branches. The lateral posterior choroidal artery may occasionally arise from it.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior temporal branch supplies the caudal parahippocampal, lingual, fusiform, and inferior temporal gyri, and the inferior occipital cortex.

23607.name: Calcarine Branch of Medial Occipital Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Medial occipital artery

Course: Passes posteriorly within the calcarine sulcus toward the occipital pole

Supplied Structures: Primary visual cortex, walls of the calcarine sulcus, posterior cuneus, and lingual gyrus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The calcarine branch arises from the medial occipital artery. It is occasionally duplicated (reported in approximately 10% of hemispheres).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the calcarine branch passes posteriorly within the calcarine sulcus, coursing toward the occipital pole.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The calcarine branch gives rise to multiple small cortical branches distributed to the walls of the calcarine sulcus and adjacent cortex.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The calcarine branch is the principal arterial supply to the primary visual cortex (area V1), supplying the walls of the calcarine sulcus, the posterior cuneus, and the lingual gyrus (medial occipitotemporal gyrus).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Terminal branch of the posterior cerebral artery near the junction of the postcommunicating (P2) and quadrigeminal (P3) parts

Course: Passes posteriorly along the posteromedial cerebral hemisphere toward the occipital pole

Branches: Dorsal branch to the corpus callosum, parietooccipital branch, calcarine branch, and occipitotemporal branch

Supplied Structures: Medial and basal occipital lobe, cuneus, posterior precuneus, lingual gyrus, splenium, and primary visual cortex

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial occipital artery is one of two terminal branches of the posterior cerebral artery, the other being the lateral occipital artery. It arises in the region of the P2–P3 junction as the posterior cerebral artery passes posteriorly around the midbrain.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the medial occipital artery courses posteriorly along the posteromedial aspect of the cerebral hemisphere, passing successively through the territories of the parietal and occipital lobes toward the occipital pole.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The medial occipital artery gives rise to four primary named branches: the dorsal branch to the corpus callosum, the parietooccipital branch, the calcarine branch, and the occipitotemporal branch.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Through its branches, the medial occipital artery supplies the medial and basal occipital lobe. Its territory includes the cuneus, posterior precuneus, lingual gyrus, as well as the splenium of the corpus callosum. The calcarine branch supplies the primary visual cortex (area V1) along the walls of the calcarine sulcus.

20705.name: Parietooccipital Branch of Medial Occipital Artery
alternate: Parieto-occipital Branch of Medial Occipital Artery
Parietal Branch of Medial Occipital Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Proximal or middle portion of the medial occipital artery

Course: Passes superiorly within the parietooccipital sulcus between the cuneus and precuneus

Branches: Cuneal and precuneal cortical branches

Supplied Structures: Parietooccipital sulcus, cuneus, precuneus, and variably the posterior superior parietal lobule

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The parietooccipital branch arises from the medial occipital artery, typically from its proximal or mid portion, distal to the origin of the dorsal branch to the corpus callosum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the parietooccipital branch courses superiorly and enters the parietooccipital sulcus, running along the sulcus between the cuneus inferiorly and the precuneus superiorly.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The parietooccipital branch gives rise to cortical branches distributed to the walls of the parietooccipital sulcus and the adjacent medial occipital and parietal cortex, including cuneal and precuneal branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The parietooccipital branch supplies the walls of the parietooccipital sulcus, the cuneus, and the precuneus. Branches may extend to the posterior part of the superior parietal lobule on the medial surface.

20347.name: Anterior Temporal Branch of Lateral Occipital Artery
20347.latin: Ramus temporalis anterior arteriae occipitalis lateralis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lateral occipital artery

Course: Passes anteriorly and laterally along the basal temporal lobe toward the temporal pole

Supplied Structures: Anterior inferior temporal gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and uncus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior temporal branch of the lateral occipital artery (anterior inferior temporal artery) arises from the lateral occipital artery as one of its cortical branches.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the anterior temporal branch passes anteriorly and laterally along the basal surface of the temporal lobe toward the temporal pole, running along the inferior temporal and parahippocampal gyri.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior temporal branch gives off numerous small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior temporal branch supplies the anterior basal temporal lobe, including portions of the inferior temporal gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and uncus.

18813.name: Dorsal Branch of Medial Occipital Artery
alternate: Splenial Branch of Medial Occipital Artery
Ramus corporis callosi dorsalis arteriae occipitalis medialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the medial occipital artery; variably its parietooccipital or calcarine branches

Course: Passes superiorly around the splenium and anastomoses with the pericallosal artery

Supplied Structures: Splenium and collateral supply to the body of the corpus callosum

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal branch to the corpus callosum (splenial artery; posterior pericallosal artery) usually arises as a direct branch of the medial occipital artery. Its exact point of origin is variable; it may also arise from the parietooccipital or calcarine branches of the medial occipital artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the dorsal branch to the corpus callosum courses superiorly around the splenium of the corpus callosum, where it anastomoses with branches of the pericallosal artery.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The dorsal branch to the corpus callosum gives off a few small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The dorsal branch to the corpus callosum supplies the splenium of the corpus callosum and provides a collateral supply to the body of corpus callosum via its anastomosis with the pericallosal artery.

16827.name: Middle Temporal Branch of Lateral Occipital Artery
16827.latin: Ramus temporalis medius arteriae occipitalis lateralis
alternate: Intermediate Temporal Branch of Lateral Occipital Artery
Ramus temporalis intermedius arteriae occipitalis lateralis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the lateral occipital artery; variably the posterior cerebral artery

Course: Passes laterally along the basal temporal lobe toward the middle inferior temporal gyrus

Supplied Structures: Parahippocampal, fusiform, and inferior temporal gyri

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle temporal branch (middle inferior temporal artery) arises from the lateral occipital artery, though it may arise directly from the posterior cerebral artery. It is the most variable of the temporal branches and may be absent.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the middle temporal branch passes laterally along the basal surface of the temporal lobe, terminating along the middle part of the inferior temporal gyrus.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The middle temporal branch gives off a few small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The middle temporal branch supplies portions of the parahippocampal, fusiform, and inferior temporal gyri.

20648.name: Occipitotemporal Branch of Medial Occipital Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Distal medial occipital artery

Course: Passes anteroinferiorly along the basal occipital lobe toward the occipitotemporal junction

Supplied Structures: Lingual gyrus and adjacent basal occipital cortex

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The occipitotemporal branch arises from the distal portion of the medial occipital artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the occipitotemporal branch courses anteroinferiorly along the basal surface of the occipital lobe toward the occipitotemporal junction.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The occipitotemporal branch gives rise to small cortical branches distributed to the basal occipital and posterior temporal cortex.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The occipitotemporal branch supplies the lingual gyrus (medial occipitotemporal gyrus) on the basal surface of the occipital lobe. Its territory is adjacent to, and may partially overlap with, that of the posterior temporal branches of the lateral occipital artery laterally, and the calcarine branch superiorly.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Terminal cortical branch of the posterior cerebral artery

Course: Passes across the parahippocampal gyrus and along the ventral temporal and occipital lobes

Branches: Anterior, middle, and posterior temporal branches

Supplied Structures: Uncus, parahippocampal gyrus, fusiform gyrus, and inferior temporal gyrus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral occipital artery typically arises as one of the terminal cortical branches of the posterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lateral occipital artery courses across the parahippocampal gyrus before sending terminal branches along the ventral surface of the temporal and occipital lobes.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The lateral occipital artery gives rise to anterior, middle, and posterior temporal branches, as well as numerous small unnamed perforating branches. The posterior lateral choroidal artery may occasionally arise from it.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The lateral occipital artery supplies portions of the uncus and the parahippocampal, fusiform, and inferior temporal gyri.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Communicating (C7) part of the internal carotid artery

Course: Passes anteromedially into the longitudinal fissure, curves around the genu of the corpus callosum, and continues posteriorly

Parts: Precommunicating (A1), infracallosal (A2), precallosal (A3), supracallosal (A4), and postcallosal (A5)

Branches: Anterior communicating, long striate, orbitofrontal, frontopolar, callosomarginal, and pericallosal arteries

Supplied Structures: Medial frontal and parietal lobes, corpus callosum, cingulate gyrus, internal capsule, caudate nucleus, putamen, and anterior hypothalamus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior cerebral artery arises from the communicating segment (C7) of the internal carotid artery, distal to the origin of the ophthalmic artery, ventral to the ipsilateral optic nerve and anterior to the optic chiasm.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
After emerging from the communicating segment (C7) of the internal carotid artery, the anterior cerebral artery travels anteromedially above the optic nerve toward the longitudinal fissure, where the paired arteries are connected by the anterior communicating artery. Within the longitudinal fissure, the artery gives rise to two major branches, the pericallosal and callosomarginal arteries, before curving around the genu of the corpus callosum. It then continues posteriorly along the upper surface of the corpus callosum toward the parietooccipital sulcus.

The anterior cerebral artery is classified into five segments:

– A1 (precommunicating): from the internal carotid artery to the anterior communicating artery.

– A2 (infracallosal): from the anterior communicating artery to the genu of the corpus callosum.

– A3 (precallosal): curving around the genu of the corpus callosum.

– A4 (supracallosal): running over the body of the corpus callosum.

– A5 (postcallosal): continuing beyond the splenium toward the parietooccipital sulcus.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The anterior cerebral artery gives off branches in a segmental pattern. 

– The A1 segment gives rise to the anteromedial central arteries, including short striate, supraoptic, anterior perforating, and preoptic branches. At the A1/A2 junction, the anterior communicating artery connects the paired arteries and gives off suprachiasmatic, median commissural, and median callosal branches. 

– The A2 segment gives rise to the long striate artery, medial and posterior orbitofrontal arteries, frontopolar artery, and pericallosal artery, along with perforanting branches to the hypothalamus, septum pellucidum, anterior commissure, and fornix. 

– The A3 segment gives rise to the callosomarginal artery, which supplies the medial frontal lobe via anteromedial, intermediomedial, and posteromedial frontal branches, a cingular branch, and paracentral branches. 

– The A4 segment gives off paracentral and precuneate branches, and the A5 segment gives off superior and inferior parietal, parietooccipital, and inferior callosal branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surfaces of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the medial frontal gyrus, paracentral lobule, and precuneus, as well as the cortical representation of the contralateral lower limb. 

It also supplies the corpus callosum (rostrum, genu, and body), cingulate gyrus, olfactory cortex, straight gyrus, and medial orbital gyrus. 

Via its central and perforating branches, it supplies the head of the caudate nucleus, anterior putamen, adjacent internal capsule, septum pellucidum, anterior commissure, anterior columns of the fornix, anterior hypothalamus, and lamina terminalis.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of the vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction

Course: Ascends within the basilar sulcus along the ventral pons and terminates as the posterior cerebral arteries

Branches: Anterior inferior cerebellar, pontine, superior cerebellar, posterior cerebral, and variably labyrinthine arteries

Supplied Structures: Pons, rostral medulla oblongata, cerebellum, inner ear, midbrain, thalamus, and medial and inferior occipital and temporal lobes

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The basilar artery is formed by the merging of the two vertebral arteries, typically at the pontomedullary junction.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin at the pontomedullary junction, the basilar artery ascends along the ventral surface of the pons, within the basilar sulcus, before terminating at the level of the midbrain as the paired posterior cerebral arteries.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: From its origin near the pontomedullary junction to its terminal bifurcation at the midbrain, the basilar artery gives rise to the anterior inferior cerebellar arteries, pontine arteries, and superior cerebellar arteries, before terminating as the paired posterior cerebral arteries. It may occasionally give rise to the labyrinthine artery directly.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The basilar artery and its branches supply the pons, the rostral medulla oblongata, the anteroinferior and superior cerebellum, the inner ear (via the labyrinthine artery); through the posterior cerebral arteries, it supplies the midbrain, thalamus, and the medial and inferior surfaces of the occipital and temporal lobes

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Communicating (C7) part of the internal carotid artery

Course: Passes posteriorly, medial to the oculomotor nerve, to join the posterior cerebral artery

Branches: Posteromedial central arteries and tuberothalamic artery

Supplied Structures: Anterior thalamus, hypothalamus, mammillary bodies, subthalamus, optic chiasm and tract, and oculomotor nerve

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior communicating artery is a short branch arising from the communicating (C7) part of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior communicating artery extends posteriorly, passes medial to the oculomotor nerve (CN III), and joins the posterior cerebral artery. This connection forms part of the cerebral arterial circle (of Willis).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The posterior communicating artery gives rise to a number of named branches, e.g. the posteromedial central arteries (arising along its entire length), which pierce the posterior perforated substance, as well as the tuberothalamic artery (arising from its middle third). 

It also gives off numerous unnamed perforating branches to the thalamus and hypothalamus, and nearby cranial nerves.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
Through its branches, the posterior communicating artery supplies the anterior thalamus, hypothalamus, mammillothalamic tract, mammillary bodies, subthalamus, and the lateral wall of the third ventricle. 

It also contributes to the supply of the optic chiasm/tract, and oculomotor nerve.
