sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
The right posterior cerebral artery is one of the two terminal branches of the basilar artery, the other being the left posterior cerebral artery.

From its origin, it travels posterolaterally around the superior part of the pons, in a manner that is parallel to, but superior to, the superior cerebellar artery. It then travels along the inferomedial surface of the posterior part of the cerebral hemisphere. It ends by dividing into two terminal branches; these are the medial and lateral occipital arteries.

For descriptive purposes, the posterior cerebral artery is described as having a precommunicating part and a postcommunicating part. The precommunicating part is the portion of the artery that lies proximal to the posterior communicating artery, while the postcommunicating part is the portion of the artery that lies distal to it.

Along it path, the precommunicating part of the posterior cerebral artery gives off arteries that travel to the pons, midbrain, thalamus, and pineal body; while the postcommunicating part gives off arteries that travel to the midbrain, thalamus, and choroid plexuses of the 3rd and 4th ventricles.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Terminal branches of the basilar artery

Course: Passes around the cerebral peduncle through the precommunicating (P1), postcommunicating (P2), quadrigeminal (P3), and cortical (P4) parts

Branches: Thalamoperforating, collicular, thalamogeniculate, posterior choroidal, hippocampal, lateral occipital, and medial occipital arteries

Supplied Structures: Thalamus, midbrain, hippocampal formation, posterior corpus callosum, and medial occipital, parietal, and temporal cortex

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The posterior cerebral arteries are the terminal branches of the basilar artery, typically arising at the level of the superior border of the pons, anterior to the midbrain. 

In a fetal configuration (present in approximately 15–25% of individuals), the posterior cerebral artery receives its dominant supply from the internal carotid artery via an enlarged posterior communicating artery rather than from the basilar artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
From its origin at the pontomesencephalic junction within the interpeduncular cistern, the posterior cerebral artery passes posterolaterally around the cerebral peduncle, superior to the tentorium cerebelli, before reaching the medial occipital surface.

The artery is divided into four parts, corresponding to the P1–P4 segment classification:

– Precommunicating part (P1): from the basilar tip to the junction with the posterior communicating artery, within the interpeduncular cistern.

– Postcommunicating part (P2): from the posterior communicating artery junction, coursing through the ambient cistern around the midbrain (often subdivided into P2A [anterior] and P2P [posterior]).

– Quadrigeminal part (P3): from the posterior edge of the midbrain through the quadrigeminal cistern to the parietooccipital sulcus.

– Cortical part (P4): the terminal portion, running within the parietooccipital sulcus onward.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The branches of the posterior cerebral artery can be organized by segment:

– Precommunicating part (P1): posteromedial central arteries, thalamoperforating artery, collicular artery.

– Postcommunicating part (P2): posteromedial central arteries, posterolateral central arteries, thalamogeniculate artery (distal P2), posterior medial choroidal artery, posterior lateral choroidal artery, anterior hippocampal artery, middle hippocampal artery, posterior hippocampal artery.

– Quadrigeminal part (P3): lateral occipital artery (with anterior, middle, and posterior temporal branches).

– Cortical part (P4): medial occipital artery (dorsal branch to the corpus callosum, parietooccipital branch, calcarine branch, and occipitotemporal branch).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The posterior cerebral artery supplies structures across three broad territories:

– Deep and subcortical: thalamus, midbrain (cerebral peduncles, colliculi, tegmentum), pineal gland, medial and lateral geniculate bodies, choroid plexuses of the third ventricle and lateral ventricle, splenium of the corpus callosum.

– Limbic and temporal: hippocampal formation, parahippocampal gyrus, cingulate gyrus (posterior), ventral surface of the temporal lobe.

– Medial occipital and parietal: cuneus, posterior precuneus, lingual gyrus, primary visual cortex (calcarine sulcus).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Junction of the precommunicating (A1) and infracallosal (A2) segments of the anterior cerebral arteries

Course: Short transverse connection between the two anterior cerebral arteries, dorsal to the optic chiasm

Branches: Anteromedial central arteries, suprachiasmatic branch, median commissural branch, and median callosal branch

Supplied Structures: Subcallosal and paraterminal gyri, anterior commissure, lamina terminalis, preoptic hypothalamus, fornix, corpus callosum, and optic chiasm

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior communicating artery is a short midline vessel connecting the two anterior cerebral arteries at the junction of their precommunicating (A1) and infracallosal (A2) segments, just before they enter the longitudinal fissure.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior communicating artery travels transversely to connect the two anterior cerebral arteries at the base of the frontal lobes, dorsal to the optic chiasm.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior communicating artery gives rise to anteromedial central arteries, including the suprachiasmatic branch, median commissural branch, and median callosal branch, along with smaller unnamed perforating branches to the lamina terminalis and preoptic hypothalamus.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior communicating artery supplies the subcallosal and paraterminal gyri, anterior commissure, lamina terminalis, preoptic hypothalamus, septal area, paraolfactory areas, and anterior columns of the fornix. Via the median callosal branch, it also contributes to the supply of the corpus callosum, and via the suprachiasmatic branch, to the optic chiasm.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the anterior choroidal artery; variably the middle or posterior cerebral artery

Course: Travels along the ventral surface of the uncus before penetrating it

Supplied Structures: Uncus, piriform cortex, parahippocampal gyrus, and head of the hippocampus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The uncal artery has a variable origin, arising most commonly from the anterior choroidal artery and less often directly from the middle cerebral artery or the posterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The uncal artery travels a short distance along the ventral surface of the uncus before penetrating it.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The uncal artery gives off numerous small, unnamed cortical/perforating branches, and it often forms an anastomosis with the anterior hippocampal artery from the posterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The uncal artery supplies the uncus, as well as portions of the piriform cortex, the parahippocampal gyrus, and the head of the hippocampus.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Isolan, Gustavo Rassier, Antônio Carlos Huf Marrone, Luiz Carlos Porcellos Marrone, et al., 2021. Vascularization of the Uncus – Anatomical Study and Clinical Implications. Surgical Neurology International 12 : 393. doi:10.25259/SNI_616_2021

Standring, S., Tubbs, S.R., 2025. Gray’s Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 43rd ed. Elsevier.

Vanderah, T.W., Gould, D.J., 2025. Nolte’s The Human Brain: An Introduction to its Functional Anatomy, 9th ed. Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Basilar artery along the anterior surface of the pons

Course: Pass posterolaterally to penetrate the anterior and lateral pons

Branches: Paramedian, short circumflex, and long circumflex branches

Supplied Structures: Pons and regions of the trigeminal, abducens, facial, and vestibulocochlear nerves

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The pontine arteries are small perforating arteries that arise directly from the basilar artery along the anterior surface of the pons. On average, seven pontine arteries branch from each side of the basilar artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The pontine arteries can vary slightly in their course, but generally these arteries branch from the basilar artery and travel slightly posterolaterally to perforate the anterior and lateral surfaces of the pons. Those that penetrate near their origin from the basilar artery are referred to as paramedian branches, those that continue slightly laterally before penetrating are referred to as short circumflex branches, and those that travel further laterally along the pons before penetrating are referred to as long circumflex branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The pontine arteries give off numerous small, unnamed perforating branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: In addition to supplying a large portion of the pons, the pontine arteries supply the regions of the trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII), and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves as they emerge from the pons and pontomedullary junction.

sections.text:

Kwiatkowska, Magdalena, Radosław Rzepliński, and Bogdan Ciszek, 2023. Anatomy of the Pontine Arteries and Perforators of the Basilar Artery in Humans. Journal of Anatomy 243 (6), 997–1006. doi:10.1111/joa.13927

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Meningohypophyseal trunk

Course: Passes medially across the cavernous sinus toward the neurohypophysis

Branches: Superior and inferior branches

Supplied Structures: Pars nervosa and lower infundibulum

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior hypophyseal artery is a small branch of the meningohypophyseal trunk, a short artery arising from the cavernous part (C4) of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior hypophyseal artery passes medially across the cavernous sinus toward the lateral surface of the neurohypophysis (the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland), where it forms an anastomosis with the corresponding artery of the opposite side.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The inferior hypophyseal artery usually arises as a single artery and divides into superior and inferior branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: These branches of the inferior hypophyseal artery primarily supply the pars nervosa (neurohypophysis) and contribute to the vascular supply of the lower infundibulum. They may also form anastomoses with branches of the superior hypophyseal arteries.

sections.text:

17440.name: Sternocleidomastoid Branch of Superior Thyroid Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior thyroid artery.

Course: Descends laterally and crosses the carotid sheath to reach the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Middle portion of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The sternocleidomastoid branch of the superior thyroid artery arises from the superior thyroid artery, the first branch of the external carotid artery. However, the sternocleidomastoid branch may arise directly from the external carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The sternocleidomastoid branch of the superior thyroid artery extends laterally, crossing the carotid sheath to reach the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The sternocleidomastoid branch of the superior thyroid artery supplies the middle portion of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior thyroid artery.

Course: Travels superiorly, anterior to the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae and medial to the phrenic nerve.

Branches: Spinal branches.

Supplied Structures: Scalenus anterior, longus cervicis, cervical vertebral bodies, and the spinal cord and its meningeal layers.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ascending cervical artery can originate from the inferior thyroid artery as it turns medially to run posterior to the carotid sheath and its contents. Alternatively, the ascending cervical artery can originate directly from the thyrocervical trunk.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the ascending cervical artery ascends between the scalenus anterior and longus cervicis muscles, just medial to the phrenic nerve, and ascends along the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae. Along its course, the artery anastomoses with the vertebral, ascending pharyngeal, and deep cervical arteries.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: One or two small spinal branches travel through the intervertebral foramina to supply the vertebral bodies and the contents of the vertebral canal.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ascending cervical artery and its branches provide an arterial supply to the scalenus anterior and longus cervicis muscles of the neck, vertebrae bodies, and the contents of the vertebral canal.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: External carotid artery.

Course: Descends from the anterior surface of the external carotid artery.

Branches: Superior laryngeal artery, sternocleidomastoid, cricothyroid, infrahyoid, and anterior, posterior, and lateral glandular branches.

Supplied Structures: Sternocleidomastoid, cricothyroid, and infrahyoid strap muscles, thyroid gland, and tissue of the upper part of the larynx.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior thyroid artery usually arises as the first branch of the external carotid artery, just inferior to the greater cornu of the hyoid bone. However, the superior thyroid artery may arise from the division of the common carotid artery, from the subclavian artery, or share a common trunk with the lingual and facial arteries (Tubbs et al, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior thyroid artery descends from the anterior surface of the external carotid artery along the lateral border of the thyrohyoid muscle. It extends towards the apex of the lobe of the thyroid gland.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The superior thyroid artery gives rise to several branches, including the superior laryngeal artery, which pierces through the thyrohyoid membrane to enter the larynx.

It also gives rise to muscular branches including the sternocleidomastoid, cricothyroid, and infrahyoid branches. Finally, it gives rise to several glandular branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superior thyroid artery supplies the upper part of the larynx via the superior laryngeal artery. It also supplies the sternocleidomastoid, cricothyroid, and infrahyoid strap muscles via its muscular branches. The glandular branches of the superior thyroid artery provide an extensive blood supply to the thyroid gland.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. & Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

22379.name: Infrahyoid Branch of Superior Thyroid Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior thyroid artery.

Course: Extends along the inferior border of the hyoid bone.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Infrahyoid strap muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The infrahyoid branch of the superior thyroid artery arises from the superior thyroid artery, the first branch of the external carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The infrahyoid branch of the superior thyroid artery extends along the inferior border of the hyoid bone, deep the thyrohyoid muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches of the infrahyoid branch of the superior thyroid artery; however, it does form an anastomosis with its fellow branch from the opposite side.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The infrahyoid branch of the superior thyroid artery supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles, including sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and omohyoid.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Thyrocervical trunk.

Course: Ascends anterior to scalenus anterior, turns medially at the transverse process of the sixth cervical vertebra and descends on the longus cervicis muscle to the inferior margin of the thyroid gland.

Branches: Ascending cervical and inferior laryngeal arteries; muscular, pharyngeal, esophageal, tracheal, and glandular branches.

Supplied Structures: Scalenus anterior, longus cervicis, infrahyoid, and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles, spinal cord, cervical vertebral bodies, laryngopharynx, esophagus, trachea, thyroid and parathyroid glands.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior thyroid artery originates as a terminal branch of the thyrocervical trunk, anterior to the scalenus anterior muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the inferior thyroid artery travels superomedially along the medial border of the scalenus anterior muscle, posterior to the carotid sheath and anterior to the vertebral artery. On the left, the artery is crossed anteriorly by the thoracic duct. Just inferior to the transverse process of the sixth cervical vertebra, the artery descends on the longus cervicis muscle and usually travels anterior to the recurrent laryngeal nerve to reach the inferior margin of the thyroid gland.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The inferior thyroid artery gives off named arteries and many branches, which anastomose with other vessels to supply the structures of the neck. These include the ascending cervical and inferior laryngeal arteries, and the muscular, pharyngeal, esophageal, tracheal, and glandular branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: As the inferior thyroid artery has many branches, it supplies numerous structures in the neck. This includes the scalenus anterior, longus cervicis, infrahyoid, and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles. Small branches supply the cervical vertebral bodies, spinal cords, and the meningeal layers surrounding it. The laryngopharynx, esophagus, and inferior part of the larynx are supplied by branches of the inferior thyroid artery. The posterior and inferior parts of the thyroid gland and parathyroid glands are partly supplied by glandular branches.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Subclavian artery.

Course: Ascends medial to the scalenus anterior muscle.

Branches: Suprascapular, transverse cervical, and inferior thyroid arteries.

Supplied Structures: Structures of the neck and scapular region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The thyrocervical trunk arises from the anterior surface of the first part of the subclavian artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The thyrocervical trunk is a short thick vessel that ascends just medial to the scalenus anterior muscle and divides almost immediately from its origin.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The suprascapular artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk and passes inferolaterally across the scalenus anterior muscle to reach the superior scapular border.

The transverse cervical artery arises just superior to the suprascapular artery and takes a lateral course across the occipital triangle of the neck.

The inferior thyroid artery is the largest terminal branch of the thyrocervical trunk. It ascends anterior to the scalenus anterior muscle. Sometimes, the ascending cervical artery may arise directly from the thyrocervical trunk, but it usually arises from the inferior thyroid artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
Branches from the thyrocervical trunk supply various structures of the neck and scapular region.

- The suprascapular artery supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles and part of the sternocleidomastoid and the subclavius muscles.

- The transverse cervical artery supplies trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles.

- The inferior thyroid artery supplies the inferior poles of the thyroid gland, parathyroid gland, larynx, pharynx, infrahyoid muscles, longus colli, scalenus anterior, and the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles.

16726.name: Cricothyroid Branch of Superior Thyroid Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior thyroid artery.

Course: Crosses medially above the anterior cricothyroid muscle towards the median cricothyroid ligament.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Cricothyroid muscle and median cricothyroid ligament.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The cricothyroid branch of the superior thyroid artery arises from the superior thyroid artery, the first branch of the external carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The cricothyroid branch of the superior thyroid artery extends medially along the upper border of the cricothyroid muscle, towards the median cricothyroid ligament.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches of the cricothyroid branch of the superior thyroid artery; however, it does form an anastomosis with its fellow branch from the opposite side.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The cricothyroid branch of the superior thyroid artery supplies the cricothyroid muscle and median cricothyroid ligament.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lingual artery.

Course: Along the superior border of the hyoid bone.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Suprahyoid muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The suprahyoid branch of the lingular artery arises from the lingual artery, a branch of the external carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The suprahyoid traverses medially along the superior border of the hyoid bone.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the suprahyoid branch anastomosis with its fellow branch from the opposite side.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The suprahyoid branch of the lingual artery supplies the suprahyoid muscles, including hyoglossus, geniohyoid, mylohyoid, and stylohyoid.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Facial artery.

Course: Passes anteriorly under the chin.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Digastric, genioglossus, hyoglossus, mylohyoid, and platysma muscles, skin of the chin and lower lip.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The submental artery is the largest cervical branch arising from the facial artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: As the facial artery leaves the submandibular gland, it gives off the submental artery. The submental artery passes anteriorly, passing over the mylohyoid muscle and deep to the anterior belly of the digastric muscle. It ascends over the mandible at the chin.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The submental artery supplies the anterior belly of the digastric muscle and the overlying platysma muscle and skin. It forms an anastomosis with the sublingual branch of the lingual artery and the mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar artery, which provide arterial supply to the genioglossus, hyoglossus, and mylohyoid muscles. Additionally, the terminal branches of the submental artery anastomosis with the inferior labial artery and mental branch of the inferior alveolar artery, thus, supplying the chin and lower lip (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

19861.name: Mylohyoid Branch of Inferior Alveolar Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior alveolar artery.

Course: Descends in the mylohyoid groove on the inner surface of the ramus of the mandible.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Mylohyoid muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar artery arises from the inferior alveolar artery before it enters the mandibular canal.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar artery pierces the sphenomandibular ligament and descends to the mylohyoid muscle on the inner surface of the ramus of the mandible, accompanied by the mylohyoid nerve in the mylohyoid groove.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar artery anastomosis with the submental branch of the facial artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar artery supplies the mylohyoid muscle.

19349.name: Lower Sternocleidomastoid Branch of Occipital Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Occipital artery.

Course: Descend posteriorly to enter the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lower sternocleidomastoid branch of the occipital artery arises from the occipital artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
There are two sternocleidomastoid branches that arise from the occipital artery, the upper and lower sternocleidomastoid branches.

The lower sternocleidomastoid branch arises near the origin of the occipital artery from the posterior aspect of the external carotid artery. The lower sternocleidomastoid branch descends posteriorly, traversing the hypoglossal nerve and internal jugular vein and enters the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches. The lower sternocleidomastoid branch of the occipital artery forms an anastomosis with the sternocleidomastoid branch of superior thyroid artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The sternocleidomastoid branches of the occipital artery help supply the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

19388.name: Upper Sternocleidomastoid Branch of Occipital Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Occipital artery.

Course: Descend posteriorly to enter the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The upper sternocleidomastoid branch of the occipital artery arises from the occipital artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
There are two sternocleidomastoid branches that arise from the occipital artery, the upper and lower sternocleidomastoid branches.

The upper sternocleidomastoid branch of the occipital artery arises where the occipital artery is crossed by the accessory nerve. The upper sternocleidomastoid branch descends posteriorly, passing the internal jugular vein superficially, to enter the sternocleidomastoid muscle along with the accessory nerve.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The sternocleidomastoid branches of the occipital artery help supply the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Occipital Artery.

Course: Descends over the obliquus capitis superior muscle.

Branches: Superficial and deep branches.

Supplied Structures: Trapezius and deep muscles of neck.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The descending branch of the occipital artery arises from the occipital artery as it passes over the obliquus capitis superior muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The descending branch of the occipital artery descends over the obliquus capitis superior muscle of the suboccipital triangle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The descending branch of the occipital artery divides into superficial and deep branches and forms an anastomosis with the superficial cervical artery (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The descending branch of the occipital artery helps supply the suboccipital muscles, including the obliquus capitis inferior and superior muscles and rectus capitis posterior major and minor muscles. Additionally, it provides arterial supply to the trapezius, splenius capitis, and cervicis muscles, and the occipital belly of the occipitofrontalis muscle (Dorland, 2011; Netter, 2011).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Saunders/Elsevier.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

19283.name: Deep Descending Branch of Occipital Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Descending branch of the occipital Artery.

Course: Descends deep to the semispinalis capitis and cervicis muscles.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Deep muscles of the neck.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep descending branch of the occipital artery arises from the descending branch of the occipital artery as it passes over the obliquus capitis superior muscle (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep descending branch of the occipital artery enters the suboccipital triangle and runs deep to the semispinalis capitis muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the deep descending branch of the occipital artery anastomosis with the vertebral artery and the deep cervical artery. This anastomosis forms a collateral circulation after ligation of the common carotid or subclavian arteries (Gray & Lewis, 1918).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The deep descending branch of the occipital artery helps supply the semispinalis capitis and cervicis muscles and the muscles of the suboccipital triangle.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Gray, H. & Lewis, W. H. (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body. Lea & Febiger.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Facial artery.

Course: Enter the submandibular gland.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Submandibular gland, lymph nodes, and overlying skin.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The glandular branches of the facial artery arise from the facial artery as it passes over the lateral surface of the submandibular gland. There may be three or four large glandular branches.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The glandular branches of the facial artery are short arteries that enter the submandibular gland adjacent to their origin. Some branches are prolonged and can reach surrounding lymph nodes and skin.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The glandular branches of the facial artery supply the submandibular gland. Additionally, it may also supply surrounding lymph nodes and overlying skin.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Costocervical trunk.

Course: Travels posteriorly, superior to the first rib, then ascends to the level of second cervical vertebra.

Branches: Spinal branches.

Supplied Structures: Semispinalis capitis and semispinalis cervicis muscles, the spinal cord, and vertebral canal.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep cervical artery originates as one of two terminal branches from the costocervical trunk, the other being the supreme intercostal artery. The artery can also arise directly from the second part of the subclavian artery in 8 to 10% of people (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the deep cervical artery travels posteriorly through the space between the neck of the first rib and the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra, superior to the eighth cervical nerve. It then travels superiorly to the level of the second cervical vertebra, between the semispinalis capitis and semispinalis cervicis muscles.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The deep cervical artery gives off a spinal branch that supplies the vertebral canal and spinal cord at the level of the seventh cervical vertebra. Along its course, the deep cervical artery anastomoses with the deep branch of the descending branch of the occipital artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The deep cervical artery supplies the semispinalis capitis and cervicis muscles. As it ascends, it also supplies the spinal cord and vertebral canal in the neck.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: First (left) or second (right) part of subclavian arteries.

Course: Arches backwards to the neck of first rib.

Branches: Supreme intercostal and deep cervical arteries.

Supplied Structures: Upper two intercostal spaces, vertebral column, deep cervical muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The costocervical trunk arises from the posterior surface of the first part of the subclavian artery on the left, or the second part of the subclavian artery on the right.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The costocervical trunk arches posteriorly over the cervical pleura towards the neck of the first rib.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The costocervical trunk terminates by dividing into the supreme intercostal and deep cervical arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The branches of the costocervical trunk supply arterial blood to structures of the first and second intercostal spaces, vertebral column, and cervical muscles of the back proper (deep muscles of the back).

17113.name: Superficial Descending Branch of Occipital Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Descending branch of the occipital Artery.

Course: Courses deep to the splenius capitis muscle.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Trapezius muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial descending branch of the occipital artery arises from the descending branch of the occipital artery as it passes over the obliquus capitis superior muscle (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial descending branch of the occipital artery runs deep to the splenius capitis muscle. It then pierces it to reach the trapezius muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superficial descending branch of the occipital artery helps supply the splenius capitis and trapezius muscles.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Maxillary artery.

Course: Ascends in infratemporal fossa and enters the middle cranial fossa via the foramen spinosum.

Branches: Superior tympanic artery; Accessory meningeal, petrosal, frontal, and parietal branches; Lacrimal anastomotic branch.

Supplied Structures: Dura mater and cranium.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle meningeal artery arises from the first part of the maxillary artery as it passes through the infratemporal fossa. Sometimes, it may arise from a common trunk with the inferior alveolar artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The middle meningeal artery ascends within the infratemporal fossa between the sphenomandibular ligament and the lateral pterygoid muscle. It passes between the roots of the auriculotemporal nerve emerging from the mandibular nerve. The middle meningeal artery passes lateral to the tensor veli palatini muscle and enters the foramen spinosum to reach the middle cranial fossa. It traverses anteriorly within a groove (the groove for the middle meningeal artery), then terminates by dividing into frontal and parietal branches. The branches of the middle meningeal artery upwards, passing over the pterion and towards the vertex of the skull.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The middle meningeal artery gives rise to several branches including the accessory meningeal, petrosal, frontal, and parietal branches. Additionally, it gives rise to the superior tympanic artery and forms an anastomosis with a branch of the lacrimal artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The middle meningeal artery supplies the dura mater of the brain and the cranial bones.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Extradural hemorrhage

17738.name: Meningeal Branches of Internal Carotid Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal carotid artery.

Course: Passes over the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Meninges and bone of anterior cranial fossa.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The meningeal branch of the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery is a small branch arising from the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The meningeal branch of the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery traverses over the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone of the anterior cranial fossa.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the meningeal branch of the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery may anastomose with rami of the posterior ethmoidal artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The meningeal branch of the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery supplies the meninges and bone of the anterior cranial fossa.

24536.name: Accessory Branch of Middle Meningeal Artery
alternate: Ramus meningeus accessorius arteriae meningeae mediae
Ramus meningicus accessorius arteriae meningeae mediae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Middle meningeal artery.

Course: Ascends in the infratemporal fossa and passes through the foramen ovale to become intracranial.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Extracranial: lateral and medial pterygoid muscles and tensor veli palatini muscle; greater wing and lateral pterygoid process of sphenoid bone, mandibular nerve and otic ganglion; Intracranial: trigeminal ganglion, cavernous sinus and surrounding dura mater.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The accessory branch of the middle meningeal artery arises from the middle meningeal artery in the infratemporal fossa. However, sometimes it may arise directly from the maxillary artery, in which case it is named the accessory meningeal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The accessory branch of the middle meningeal artery ascends in the infratemporal fossa in close related to the levator veli palatini muscle and deep to the mandibular nerve. The artery then passes into the middle cranial fossa of the cranium via the foramen ovale.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The accessory branch of the middle meningeal artery principally supplies extracranial structures, including the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles and the tensor veli palatini muscle. Additionally, it provides arterial supply to the greater wing and lateral pterygoid processes of the sphenoid bone, the mandibular nerve and otic ganglion. After the accessory branch of the middle meningeal nerve passes into the middle cranial fossa, it supplies the trigeminal ganglion, the walls of the cavernous sinus, and surrounding dura mater.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Meningohypophyseal trunk.

Course: Descends on the clivus.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Adjacent meninges.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal meningeal artery is a small branch arising from the meningohypophyseal trunk, as short trunk arising from the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal meningeal artery descends on the surface of the clivus (Hendrix et al, 2014).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The dorsal meningeal artery supplies the meninges adjacent to the clivus.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Hendrix, P., Griessenauer, C., Foreman, P., Loukas, M., S Fisher, W., Rizk, E., Shoja, M. & Tubbs, R. S. (2014) Arterial Supply of the Upper Cranial Nerves: A Comprehensive Review, 27.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Occipital artery.

Course: Ascends with internal jugular vein to reach the posterior cranial fossa.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Dura matter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The meningeal branch of the occipital artery consists of one or more variable branches that arise from the occipital artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The meningeal branch of the occipital artery accompanies the internal jugular vein through the jugular foramen of the skull to reach the posterior cranial fossa (Gray & Lewis, 1918).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The meningeal branch of the occipital artery supplies the dura matter of the posterior cranial fossa.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Gray, H. & Lewis, W. H. (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body. Lea & Febiger.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Vertebral Artery.

Course: Travel posteriorly in posterior cranial fossa.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Occipital bone, diploe, and falx cerebelli.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The meningeal branches of the vertebral artery arise from the suboccipital part of the vertebral artery, close to the foramen magnum. They arise as anterior and posterior branches.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From their origin, the meningeal branches of the vertebral artery travel posteriorly within the posterior cranial fossa, between the occipital bone and the dura mater.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The meningeal branches of the vertebral artery supply the occipital bone and its diploe, and the falx cerebelli in the posterior cranial fossa.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Neuromeningeal trunk.

Course: Traverses the hypoglossal foramen of skull.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Bones and dura mater of the posterior cranial fossa.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The neuromeningeal trunk gives rise to several meningeal branches, which enter the skull via numerous foramina, including the foramen lacerum, hypoglossal canal, and jugular foramen.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: One meningeal branch traverses the hypoglossal canal to enter the posterior cranial fossa.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The meningeal branch traversing the hypoglossal canal helps supply the bones and dura matter of the posterior cranial fossa (Hacein-Bey et al, 2002).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Hacein-Bey, L., Daniels, D. L., Ulmer, J. L., Mark, L. P., Smith, M. M., Strottmann, J. M., Brown, D., Meyer, G. A. & Wackym, P. A. (2002) The Ascending Pharyngeal Artery: Branches, Anastomoses, and Clinical Significance. American Journal of Neuroradiology, 23(7), 1246.

19635.name: Branches of Internal Carotid Artery to Nerves

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal carotid artery.

Course: Passes posteriorly through the cavernous and inferior petrosal sinuses.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Nerves of the wall of the cavernous and inferior petrosal sinuses.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The branches of the internal carotid artery to nerves are a small group of arteries arising from the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The branches of the internal carotid artery to nerves pass posteriorly through the cavernous and inferior petrosal sinuses.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The branches of the internal carotid artery to nerves supply the nerves of the walls of the cavernous and inferior petrosal sinuses (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

24113.name: Tentorial Basal Branch of Internal Carotid Artery
24113.latin: Ramus basalis tentoria arteriae carotidis internae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal Carotid Artery.

Course: Runs along the attachment of the tentorium cerebelli to the petrous part of temporal bone.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Tentorium cerebelli.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The tentorial basal branch of the internal carotid artery is a small branch that arises from the posterior aspect of the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The tentorial basal branch of the internal carotid artery extends along the tentorial cerebelli where it attaches to the petrous part of the temporal bone.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The tentorial basal branch of the internal carotid artery supplies the base of the tentorium cerebelli.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Neuromeningeal trunk.

Course: Traverses the jugular foramen of skull.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Bones and dura mater of posterior cranial fossa.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior meningeal artery arises from the neuromeningeal trunk, and is considered the terminal branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior meningeal artery traverses the jugular foramen to enter the posterior cranial fossa and can reach the cerebellar fossa.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior meningeal artery supplies the dura mater and bone of the posterior cranial fossa (Hacein-Bey et al, 2002).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Hacein-Bey, L., Daniels, D. L., Ulmer, J. L., Mark, L. P., Smith, M. M., Strottmann, J. M., Brown, D., Meyer, G. A. & Wackym, P. A. (2002) The Ascending Pharyngeal Artery: Branches, Anastomoses, and Clinical Significance. American Journal of Neuroradiology, 23(7), 1246. Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

16661.name: Anterior Meningeal Branch of Anterior Ethmoidal Artery
16661.latin: Ramus meningeus anterior arteriae ethmoideae anterioris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior ethmoidal artery.

Course: Ascends into the anterior cranial fossa.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Dura mater.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior meningeal branch of the anterior ethmoidal artery arises from the anterior ethmoidal artery as it passes through the anterior ethmoidal canal.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior meningeal branch of the anterior ethmoidal artery exits the anterior ethmoidal canal via the anterior ethmoidal foramen to enter the anterior cranial fossa, just at the anterior end of the lateral edge of the cribriform plate.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior meningeal branch of the anterior ethmoidal artery helps supply the dura mater of the anterior cranial fossa (Pamir et al, 2010).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Pamir, M. N., Black, P. M. L. & Fahlbusch, R. (2010) Meningiomas: A Comprehensive Text. Saunders/Elsevier.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Neuromeningeal trunk.

Course: Traverses the foramen lacerum of skull.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Bones and dura mater adjacent to the foramen lacerum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The neuromeningeal trunk gives rise to several meningeal branches, which enter the skull via numerous foramina, including the foramen lacerum, hypoglossal canal, and jugular foramen.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The carotid branch traverses the foramen lacerum with the internal carotid artery to enter the middle cranial fossa.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The carotid branch of the neuromeningeal trunk helps supply the bones and dura matter adjacent to the foramen lacerum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Supraorbital artery.

Course: Passes through the frontal bone.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Diploe of the frontal bone and frontal sinus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The diploic branch of the supraorbital artery is a small branch arising from the supraorbital artery as it passes through the supraorbital foramen/notch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The diploic branch of the supraorbital artery passes into the diploe (or spongy bone) of the frontal bone at the supraorbital margin.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The diploic branch of the supraorbital artery supplies the spongy bone of the frontal bone at the supraorbital margin, as well as the mucosal lining of the frontal sinus (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

21948.name: Tentorial Marginal Branch of Internal Carotid Artery
21948.latin: Ramus maringalis tentoria arteriae carotidis internae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Meningohypophyseal trunk.

Course: Along the free edge of the tentorium cerebelli.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Margin of tentorium cerebelli.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The tentorial marginal branch of the internal carotid artery is a small branch arising from the meningohypophyseal trunk, as short trunk arising from the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The tentorial marginal branch of the internal carotid artery travels along the free edge of the tentorium cerebelli to reach the tentorial notch.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: As its name suggests, the tentorial marginal branch of the internal carotid artery supplies the margin of the tentorium cerebelli.

16721.name: Petrosal Branch of Middle Meningeal Artery
alternate: Ramus petrosus superficialis arteriae meningeae mediae
Ramus pyramidis superficialis arteriae meningeae mediae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Middle meningeal artery.

Course: Enters hiatus for greater petrosal nerve.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Facial nerve, geniculate ganglion, and tympanic cavity.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery arises from the middle meningeal artery in the region of the petrous part of the temporal bone.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From the petrous part of the temporal bone, the petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery enters the hiatus for the greater petrosal nerve (facial hiatus or Torin’s hole).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery forms an anastomosis with the stylomastoid artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery supplies the facial nerve, geniculate ganglion, and tympanic cavity.

22764.name: Branch of Middle Meningeal Artery to Trigeminal Ganglion
22764.latin: Ramus ganglionaris trigeminalis arteriae meningeae mediae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Middle meningeal artery.

Course: Passes medially in the middle cranial fossa towards the trigeminal ganglion.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Trigeminal Ganglion and its roots.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The branch of the middle meningeal artery to the trigeminal ganglion arises from the middle meningeal artery just after it passes through the foramen spinosum to enter the middle cranial fossa.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The branch of the middle meningeal artery passes medially in the middle cranial fossa towards the trigeminal ganglion.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The branch of the middle meningeal artery supplies the trigeminal ganglion and its roots.

20244.name: Frontal Branch of Middle Meningeal Artery
alternate: Anterior Branch of Middle Meningeal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Middle meningeal artery.

Course: Within the grooves of the sphenoid and parietal bones.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Dura mater of the anterior portion of the brain.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The frontal branch of the middle meningeal artery is one of two arteries that arise from the middle meningeal artery after it passes through the foramen spinosum to enter the cranial cavity. The frontal branch is much larger than the parietal branch of the middle meningeal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The frontal branch of the middle meningeal artery crosses over the greater wing of the sphenoid bone and enters the sphenoparietal canal, a groove in the sphenoid angle of the parietal bone. The frontal branch divides into numerous rami that extend between the dura mater and the cranium, with some rami extending as far as the vertex.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, it does anastomose with its fellow branch of the opposite side.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The frontal branch of the middle meningeal artery supplies the anterior portion of dura mater and cranium.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Extradural hemorrhage

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Occipital artery.

Course: Enters cranial cavity through the mastoid foramen.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Dura matter and mastoid cells.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The mastoid branch of the occipital artery arises from the occipital artery as it passes within the occipital groove of the temporal bone, medial to the mastoid process and its muscular attachments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The mastoid branch of the occipital artery enters the posterior cranial fossa of the cranial cavity through the mastoid foramen.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The mastoid branch of the occipital artery supplies the dura matter and mastoid cells.

23408.name: Meningeal Branch of Posterior Ethmoidal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior ethmoidal artery.

Course: Ascends into the anterior cranial fossa.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Dura mater.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The meningeal branch of the posterior ethmoidal artery arises from the posterior ethmoidal artery as it passes through the posterior ethmoidal canal.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The meningeal branch of the posterior ethmoidal artery exits the posterior ethmoidal canal via the posterior ethmoidal foramen to enter the anterior cranial fossa, just at the posterior end of the lateral edge of the cribriform plate.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the meningeal branch of the posterior ethmoidal artery may anastomose with meningeal branches of the internal carotid artery and with the middle meningeal artery (Pamir et al, 2010).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The meningeal branch of the posterior ethmoidal artery helps supply the dura mater of the medial third of the floor of the anterior cranial fossa (Pamir et al, 2010).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Pamir, M. N., Black, P. M. L. & Fahlbusch, R. (2010) Meningiomas: A Comprehensive Text. Saunders/Elsevier.

21535.name: Branches of Internal Carotid Artery to Trigeminal Ganglion
21535.latin: Rami ganglionares trigeminales arteriae carotidis internae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal Carotid Artery.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Trigeminal ganglion.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The branches of the internal carotid artery to the trigeminal ganglion are short branches that arise from the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: As the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery passes medial to the trigeminal ganglion in the cavernous sinus, it gives of short branches directly to the trigeminal ganglion.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The branches of the internal carotid artery to the trigeminal ganglion supply the trigeminal ganglion.

20863.name: Cavernous Branch of Internal Carotid Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal carotid artery.

Course: Passes posteriorly through the cavernous sinus.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Wall of the cavernous sinus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The cavernous branch of the internal carotid artery is a small artery arising from the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The cavernous branch of the internal carotid artery passes posteriorly through the cavernous sinus.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The cavernous branch of the internal carotid artery supplies the wall of the cavernous sinus.

21760.name: Parietal Branch of Middle Meningeal Artery
alternate: Posterior Branch of Middle Meningeal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Middle meningeal artery.

Course: On the squamous part of the temporal bone.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Dura mater of the posterior portion of the brain.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The parietal branch of the middle meningeal artery is one of two arteries that arise from the middle meningeal artery after it passes through the foramen spinosum to enter the cranial cavity. The parietal branch is much smaller than the frontal branch of the middle meningeal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The parietal branch of the middle meningeal artery turns backwards on the squamous part of the temporal bone to reach the lower border of the parietal bone. The parietal branch divides into numerous rami that extend between the dura mater and the cranium.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, it does anastomose with its fellow branch of the opposite side.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The parietal branch of the middle meningeal artery supplies the posterior portion of dura mater and cranium.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Cavernous (C4) part of the internal carotid artery

Course: Passes posteromedially within the cavernous sinus before dividing

Branches: Inferior hypophyseal artery, tentorial marginal branch, and dorsal meningeal artery

Supplied Structures: Tentorium cerebelli, dura of the clivus and posterior cranial fossa, neurohypophysis, and cranial nerves III, IV, and VI

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The meningohypophyseal trunk, also known as the posterior trunk, is a short branch arising from the posterior aspect of the cavernous (C4) part of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The meningohypophyseal trunk is short, passing posteromedially from the internal carotid artery within the cavernous sinus before dividing into its terminal branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The meningohypophyseal trunk typically gives rise to three branches, namely the:

– inferior hypophyseal artery

– tentorial marginal branch

– dorsal meningeal artery

Anatomical variation is common; any of these branches may arise directly from the cavernous segment (C4) of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The meningohypophyseal trunk supplies the tentorium cerebelli and the dura of the clivus and posterior cranial fossa, as well as the neurohypophysis, and oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nerves (cranial nerves III, IV, and VI). It also forms an anastomosis with branches of the external carotid artery.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Agosti, Edoardo, A. Yohan Alexander, Danielle D. Dang, et al., 2025. Origin and Course Cavernous Internal Carotid Artery Branches from the Endoscopic Endonasal Perspective: Cadaveric Study and Analysis Clinical Implications. Operative Neurosurgery 28 (5), 687–96. doi:10.1227/ons.0000000000001392

Allen, Jason W., Anthony J. G. Alastra, and Peter K. Nelson, 2005. Proximal Intracranial Internal Carotid Artery Branches: Prevalence and Importance for Balloon Occlusion Test. Journal of Neurosurgery 102 (1), 45–52. doi:10.3171/jns.2005.102.1.0045

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The carotid sinus is a dilated area at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery and the proximal end of the internal carotid artery.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: Visceral afferent fibers convey information from the carotid sinus via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CNIX).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The carotid sinus is a baroreceptor (pressorecptor), which monitors changes in arterial blood pressure.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Carotid sinus syndrome

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: First part of the subclavian artery

Course: Ascends through the cervical transverse foramina and foramen magnum, then passes along the medulla oblongata to form the basilar artery

Parts: Cervical (V1), vertebral (V2), suboccipital (V3), and cranial (V4)

Branches: Anterior and posterior meningeal branches, anterior and posterior spinal arteries, posterior inferior cerebellar artery, and medullary and muscular branches

Supplied Structures: Spinal cord, medulla oblongata, cerebellum, and posteroinferior cranial dura mater

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vertebral artery arises from the posterosuperior aspect of the first part of the subclavian artery, close to the lateral aspect of the vertebral bodies. Rarely, the left vertebral artery may arise directly from the aortic arch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The vertebral artery is divided into four parts:

– Cervical (V1): from its origin on the first part of the subclavian artery, the vertebral artery travels superiorly between the longus colli and scalenus anterior muscles.

– Vertebral (V2): it enters the transverse foramen of the C6 vertebra and ascends through the transverse foramina of the remaining cervical vertebrae.

– Suboccipital (V3): after passing through the transverse foramen of the atlas (C1), the artery travels along the groove on the superior aspect of the posterior arch of C1, then passes through the atlantooccipital membrane and dura mater before entering the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum.

– Cranial (V4): the artery continues superiorly and gradually moves medially along the anterior surface of the medulla oblongata before merging with the contralateral vertebral artery to form the basilar artery at the pontomedullary junction.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The vertebral artery has numerous branches and is the principal vessel of the vertebrobasilar system. Its named branches include the anterior and posterior meningeal branches, the anterior and posterior spinal arteries, the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, and medullary arteries, as well as muscular branches to the deep cervical musculature. 

At the pontomedullary junction, the two vertebral arteries unite to form the basilar artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The vertebral artery and its branches supply the spinal cord, the medulla oblongata, the cerebellum, and the posteroinferior dura mater of the cranial cavity. Together with the contralateral vertebral artery, it forms the basilar artery, which continues the posterior circulation supply to the pons, midbrain, and posterior cerebral hemispheres.

sections.text:
Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R., 2013. Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 7th ed.  Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: External carotid artery.

Course: Passes between the neck of the mandible and sphenomandibular ligament, through the infratemporal fossa. Passes the inferior head of the lateral pterygoid muscle and enters the pterygopalatine fossa.

Branches: middle meningeal, inferior alveolar, deep auricular, anterior tympanic, deep temporal, masseteric, buccal, pterygoid, posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, pharyngeal, descending palatine, and sphenopalatine arteries and the artery of the pterygoid canal.

Supplied Structures: Upper and lower jaws and teeth, muscles of mastication, ears, nose, meninges, and palate.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The maxillary artery is one of the two terminal branches of the external carotid artery. The transverse facial artery forms the other terminal branch and is much smaller than the maxillary artery. Both arteries are initially embedded in the parotid gland behind the neck of the mandible.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From the parotid gland, the maxillary artery passes anteriorly between the neck of the mandible and the sphenomandibular ligament to traverse the infratemporal fossa. It may pass either medial or lateral to the lower head of the lateral pterygoid muscle to enter the pterygopalatine fossa via the pterygomaxillary fissure. If the maxillary artery passes medial to the lateral pterygoid muscle, it must loop laterally between the upper and lower heads of the lateral pterygoid muscle to access the pterygomaxillary artery (Standring, 2016)

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The maxillary artery may be divided into three parts according to its location. The first part, or bony portion, of the maxillary artery is located between the neck of the mandible and sphenomandibular ligament. This portion gives rise to two major branches, the middle meningeal and inferior alveolar arteries, as well as the smaller deep auricular, anterior tympanic, and accessory meningeal (when it arises from the maxillary artery) arteries. All of these branches enter bone.

The second part, or the muscular portion, of the maxillary artery is the part associated with the lateral pterygoid muscle. This portion gives rise to the deep temporal, masseteric, buccal, and pterygoid arteries. These branches supply muscles.

The third part, or pterygopalatine portion, of the maxillary artery lies within the pterygopalatine fossa. This portion gives rise to terminal branches of the maxillary artery and is named similarly to the branches of the maxillary nerve. They include the posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, pharyngeal, descending palatine, and sphenopalatine arteries and the artery of the pterygoid canal.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The maxillary artery is widely distributed, thus supplies many structures, including the upper and lower jaw and teeth, muscles of mastication, ears, nose, meninges, and palate.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ophthalmic artery.

Course: Pierce the sclera near the optic nerve.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Choroid.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The short posterior ciliary arteries arise from the ophthalmic artery. There are usually about seven arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The short posterior ciliary arteries extend anteriorly towards the eyeball and divide into 15–20 branches (Standring, 2016). They then pierce the sclera of the eyeball near the optic nerve.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the short posterior ciliary arteries form an anastomosis with branches from the central retinal artery at the optic disc.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The short posterior ciliary arteries supply the choroid of the eyeball.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal carotid artery.

Course: Enters the orbit and travels along the medial wall between the superior oblique and medial rectus muscles.

Branches: Lacrimal, supraorbital, ciliary, muscular, posterior ethmoidal, anterior ethmoidal, palpebral, supratrochlear, and external nasal arteries, central artery of retina, recurrent meningeal branch.

Supplied Structures: Eyeball, orbit, facial structures.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ophthalmic artery arises from the cerebral part of the internal carotid artery, just as it exits the cavernous sinus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ophthalmic artery enters the orbit, inferolateral to the optic nerve, via the optic canal and lies within the common tendinous ring. It continuous anteriorly briefly, before passing medially and crosses over the optic nerve. The ophthalmic artery continues along the medial wall of the orbit, passing between the superior oblique and medial rectus muscles.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The branches of the ophthalmic artery include the central retinal artery, lacrimal artery, muscular branches, long and short ciliary arteries, supraorbital arteries, posterior and anterior ethmoidal arteries, medial palpebral arteries, and the terminal supratrochlear and external (dorsal) nasal arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ophthalmic artery supplies many structures including the eyeball, structures of the orbit, and adjacent facial structures.

18191.name: Recurrent Meningeal Branch of Lacrimal Artery
alternate: Anastomotic Branch of Lacrimal Artery with Middle Meningeal Artery
Anastomotic Branch of Middle Meningeal Artery with Lacrimal Artery
Ramus anastomoticus arteriae lacrimalis cum arteria meningea media

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lacrimal artery.

Course: Exits the orbit via the superior orbital fissure

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Lacrimal gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The recurrent meningeal branch arises from the lacrimal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The recurrent meningeal branch exits the orbit via the lateral aspect of the superior orbital fissure.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the recurrent meningeal branch of the lacrimal artery forms an anastomosis with the middle meningeal artery. Therefore, enlargement of this anastomosis accounts for the occasional origin of the lacrimal artery from the middle meningeal artery (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The recurrent meningeal branch of the lacrimal artery helps supply the lacrimal gland.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ophthalmic artery.

Course: Runs inside the optic nerve to reach the eyeball.

Branches: Superior and inferior nasal and temporal branches.

Supplied Structures: Retina.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The central retinal artery is the small, first branch of the ophthalmic artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The central retinal artery arises just below the optic nerve. For a short time, it lies inferiorly in the dural sheath surrounding the optic nerve, and then enters the optic nerve to course towards the retina (extraocular part). It enters the eyeball through the cribriform plate (lamina cribrosa), where it gives of several branches (intraocular part).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The intraocular part of the central retinal artery divides into superior and inferior temporal, and superior and inferior nasal branches, each of which supply a quadrant of the retina.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The central retinal artery supplies the retina of the eyeball.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ophthalmic artery.

Course: Pierce the sclera near the optic nerve.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Iris, ciliary body, and choroid.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The long posterior ciliary arteries arise from the ophthalmic artery. There are usually two arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The long posterior ciliary arteries extend anteriorly and pierce the sclera of the eyeball near the optic nerve. They travel anteriorly in the suprachoroid layer of the choroid, in the medial and lateral horizontal planes of the eyeball.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the long posterior ciliary arteries divide in the ciliary body and form an anastomosis with the anterior ciliary arteries. This forms the major arterial circle of the iris (Forrester et al., 2008).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The long posterior ciliary arteries supply the choroid, ciliary body and iris of the eyeball.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Forrester, J. V., Dick, A. D., McMenamin, P. G. & Roberts, F. (2008) The Eye: Basic Sciences in Practice. Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ophthalmic artery.

Course: Traverses anteriorly in the orbital cavity above the lateral rectus muscle.

Branches: Lateral palpebral arteries, anastomotic branch with middle meningeal artery.

Supplied Structures: Lacrimal gland, superior and inferior eyelids, and conjunctiva.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lacrimal artery is one of the largest branches arising from the ophthalmic artery. It usually arises within the orbital cavity, close to the optic foramen. However, occasionally, it may arise before the ophthalmic artery enters the orbital cavity.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lacrimal artery accompanies the lacrimal nerve along the superior surface of the lateral rectus muscle to reach the lacrimal gland. Here, it supplies the gland. It ends in the conjunctiva and the lateral sides of both the upper and lower eyelids and the lateral palpebral arteries.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
After the lacrimal artery reaches the lacrimal gland, it continues anteriorly as the lateral palpebral arteries, which supply the eyelids and conjunctiva.

The lacrimal artery gives off an anastomotic branch with the middle meningeal artery. This recurrent meningeal branch passes backwards through the lateral aspect of the superior orbital fissure to anastomose with a branch of the middle meningeal artery (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The lacrimal artery provides a blood supply primarily to the lacrimal gland. Indirectly, it supplies the eyelids and conjunctiva via the lateral palpebral arteries.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

19685.name: Dorsal Nasal Artery
alternate: Dorsal Nasal Branch of Ophthalmic Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ophthalmic artery.

Course: Emerges on the face between the trochlea and medial palpebral ligament.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Lacrimal sac and dorsum of nose.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal nasal artery arises as one of the two terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery, the other being the supratrochlear artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal nasal artery emerges on the face between the trochlea and the medial palpebral ligament.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The dorsal nasal artery provides rami to the nasolacrimal sac, then divides into two terminal branches. One branch anastomosis with the angular artery, a terminal branch of the facial artery. Another branch extends down the dorsum of the nose and anastomoses with its fellow from the opposite side.

19581.name: Occipital Branch of Posterior Auricular Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior auricular artery.

Course: Passes posteriorly to the scalp behind the ear.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Epicranius and sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The occipital branch of the posterior auricular artery arises from the posterior auricular artery as it ascends in the groove between the mastoid process of the temporal bone and the cartilage of the ear.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The occipital branch of the posterior auricular artery passes posteriorly over the sternocleidomastoid muscle to the scalp above and behind the ear.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the occipital branch of the posterior auricular artery anastomosis with the occipital branches of the occipital artery (Gray & Lewis, 1918).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The occipital branch of the posterior auricular artery provides arterial supply to the occipitofrontalis and temporoparietalis muscles and the epicranial aponeurosis (collectively known as the epicranius muscle). Additionally, it may supply the upper portion of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Gray, H. & Lewis, W. H. (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body. Lea & Febiger.

Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Saunders/Elsevier.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Maxillary artery.

Course: Between the ramus of the mandible and the lateral pterygoid muscle.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Medial and lateral pterygoid muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery are a variable number of arteries that arise from the maxillary artery as it passes between the ramus of the mandible and the lateral pterygoid muscle.

sections.title: Course
