sections.text: The pterygoid branches of the maxillary arteries ascend or descend from their origins to reach either the lateral or medial pterygoid muscles.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery provide arterial supply to the lateral and medial pterygoid muscles.

19865.name: Lateral Nasal Branch of Facial Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Facial artery.

Course: Medially over the lateral surface of the nose.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Ala and dorsum of the nose.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral nasal branch of the facial artery arises from the facial artery as it ascends on the lateral side of the nose. Sometimes, the lateral nasal branch may arise from the superior labial artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lateral nasal branch of the facial artery extends medially over the side of the nose.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The lateral nasal branch of the facial artery supplies the ala and dorsum of the nose. Additionally, it forms an anastomosis with its fellow branch from the opposite side.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ophthalmic artery.

Course: Ascends on the forehead.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Skin and muscle of forehead.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The supratrochlear artery arises as one of the two terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery, the other being the external nasal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Accompanied by the supratrochlear nerve, the supratrochlear artery leaves the orbit superomedially. It ascends on the forehead.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the supratrochlear artery anastomosis with the supraorbital artery and its fellow from the opposite side.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The supratrochlear artery supplies the skin and muscle of the forehead.

16694.name: Parotid Branch of Superficial Temporal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial temporal artery.

Course: Within the substance of the parotid gland.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Parotid gland and temporomandibular joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The parotid branch of the superficial temporal artery arises from the temporal artery as it ascends through the substance of the parotid gland, posterior to the neck of the mandible.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ramifications of the parotid branch of the superficial temporal artery travel through the substance of the parotid gland, where some rami reach the temporomandibular joint.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The parotid branch of the superficial temporal artery provides arterial blood supply to the parotid gland and temporomandibular joint.

18729.name: Frontal Branch of Superficial Temporal Artery
alternate: Anterior Branch of Superficial Temporal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial temporal artery.

Course: Ascends over the frontal bone.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis muscle, adjacent skin and pericranium.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The frontal branch of the superficial temporal artery arises from the superficial temporal artery as one of its terminal branches, approximately 2.5 cm above the zygomatic arch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The frontal branch of the superficial temporal artery passes superiorly towards the frontal eminence of the frontal bone.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the frontal branch of the superficial temporal artery anastomosis with its fellow artery on the opposite side.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The frontal branch of the superficial temporal artery supplies the frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis muscle and the adjacent skin and pericranium.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial temporal artery.

Course: Upper border of zygomatic arch towards the lateral orbital angle.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Orbicularis oculi muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The zygomaticoorbital artery arises from the superficial temporal artery. In some instance, it may arise from the middle temporal artery or the parietal branch of the superficial temporal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The short zygomaticoorbital artery courses medially towards the lateral angle of the orbit on the upper border of the zygomatic arch. It is located between the two layers of the temporal fascia.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the zygomaticoorbital artery may anastomose with the lacrimal and palpebral branches of the ophthalmic artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The zygomaticoorbital artery provides arterial supply to the orbicularis oculi muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Maxillary artery.

Course: Exits the orbit via the infraorbital canal and then emerges onto the face through the infraorbital foramen.

Branches: Anterior and middle superior alveolar arteries.

Supplied Structures: Maxilla and its sinus, maxillary dental arcade, inferior eyelid, cheek, and nose.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The infraorbital artery arises from the third part of the maxillary artery as it passes through the pterygopalatine fossa. Sometimes, it may share a common trunk with the posterior superior alveolar artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The infraorbital artery ascends to the orbit of the eye, entering it through the inferior orbital fissure. The infraorbital artery exits the orbit via the infraorbital canal of the maxillary bone. It emerges onto the face through the infraorbital foramen.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Within the infraorbital canal, the infraorbital artery gives rise to the anterior and middle superior alveolar arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The infraorbital artery supplies numerous structures. The anterior and middle superior alveolar arteries supply the teeth of the upper jaw and the maxillary sinus, while the terminal ramifications of the infraorbital artery supply the skin of the inferior eyelid, cheek, and nose.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lacrimal artery.

Course: Passes along the lateral wall of the orbit and enters the face via zygomaticofacial foramen.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Skin of the cheek.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lacrimal artery accompanies the lacrimal nerve along the superior surface of the lateral rectus muscle. Here, it gives off two zygomatic branches, the zygomaticofacial and the zygomaticotemporal arteries (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The zygomaticofacial artery accompanies the zygomaticofacial nerve in the lateral wall of the orbit. It enters the cheek via the zygomaticofacial foramen (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the zygomaticofacial artery anastomosis with the zygomaticoorbital arteries in the face.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The zygomaticofacial artery supplies the overlying skin of the cheek.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Saunders/Elsevier.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Facial artery.

Course: Ascends to the medial angle of the orbit.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Lacrimal sac, orbicularis oculi muscle, and lower eyelid.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The angular artery is the terminal portion of the facial artery. However, if the facial artery is deficient, the angular artery is replaced by either the nasal branch of the ophthalmic artery, the transverse facial artery, or the maxillary artery (Tubbs et al, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The angular artery continues to ascend on the face to the medial angle of the orbit, within the fibers of the levator nasolabialis muscle. The angular artery is usually small, and its course is variable.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The angular artery provides arterial supply to the lacrimal sac, orbicularis oculi muscle, and lower eyelid. Additionally, it anastomosis with the external nasal artery (or dorsal nasal branch of the ophthalmic artery).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. & Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Maxillary artery.

Course: Passes forwards over the lateral pterygoid muscle.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Buccinator muscle and skin and mucosa overlying it.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The buccal artery arises from the maxillary artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The buccal artery passes forwards between the lateral pterygoid plate and the tendon of the temporalis muscle to reach the buccinator muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the buccal artery may anastomose with branches of the facial and infraorbital arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The buccal artery supplies the buccinator muscle and overlying skin, and the adjacent mucosa in the mouth.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Maxillary artery.

Course: Passes through the mandibular notch to the deep surface of the masseter muscle.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Masseter muscle and temporomandibular joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The masseteric artery arises from the maxillary artery posterior to the tendon of the temporalis muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The masseteric artery passes through the mandibular notch with the masseteric nerve. It enters the deep surface of the masseter muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the masseteric artery anastomoses with masseteric branches of the facial artery and with the transverse facial branch of the superficial temporal artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The masseteric artery supplies the masseter muscle, while some of its ramifications may provide arterial supply to the temporomandibular joint.

23157.name: Parietal Branch of Superficial Temporal Artery
alternate: Posterior Branch of Superficial Temporal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial temporal artery.

Course: Curves upwards and backwards.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Auricularis anterior, posterior, and superior muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The parietal branch of the superficial temporal artery arises from the superficial temporal artery as one of its terminal branches, approximately 2.5 cm above the zygomatic arch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The parietal branch of the superficial temporal artery passes posterosuperiorly, superficial to the temporal fascia.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the parietal branch of the superficial temporal artery anastomosis with its fellow artery on the opposite side, as well as the posterior auricular and occipital arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The parietal branch of the superficial temporal artery supplies the auricularis anterior, posterior, and superior muscles.

20835.name: Inferior Labial Artery
alternate: Inferior Labial Branch of Facial Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Facial artery.

Course: Along the margin of the lower lip.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Inferior labial glands, mucous membranes, and lower part of orbicularis oris muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior labial artery arises from the facial artery as it nears the angle of the mouth. It is much smaller and less tortuous than the superior labial artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior labial artery passes anterosuperiorly, deep to the depressor anguli oris. It pierces the orbicularis oris to course along the margin of the lower lip, between the orbicularis oris and the mucous membrane of the lip.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The inferior labial artery supplies the inferior labial glands, the overlying mucous membrane, and the lower part of orbicularis oris muscle. Additionally, the inferior labial artery anastomosis with the submental arteries and the mental branch of the inferior alveolar artery, thus, supplying the chin and lower lip (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ophthalmic artery.

Course: Posterior to the nasolacrimal sac.

Branches: Posterior conjunctival arteries, superior and inferior palpebral arches.

Supplied Structures: Eyelids.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial palpebral artery arises from the ophthalmic artery, below the trochlea of the superior oblique muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The medial palpebral artery descends posterior to the nasolacrimal sac. As it reaches the medial aspect of the eyelids, it divides into the superior and inferior medial palpebral arteries and enters the superior and inferior eyelids, respectively. They extend laterally to anastomose with the lateral palpebral arteries.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The medial palpebral arteries, together with the lateral palpebral arteries, provide important anastomotic arches within the upper and lower eyelids.

The medial palpebral arteries also give rise to the posterior conjunctival arteries that supply the conjunctiva and lacrimal caruncle.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The medial palpebral arteries supply the upper and lower eyelids.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial temporal artery.

Course: Medially across the face.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Structures of the parotid region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The transverse facial artery arises from the superficial temporal artery before it emerges from the parotid gland. Sometimes, it may arise directly from the external carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The transverse facial artery passes medially within the parotid gland. It passes of the masseter muscle, between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct, and accompanied by branches of the facial nerve.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches of the transverse facial artery; however, it does ramify to supply numerous structures and forms anastomoses with the facial, masseteric, buccal, lacrimal, and infraorbital arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The transverse facial artery supplies the parotid gland and duct, the orbicularis oris and masseter muscles, and adjacent skin. Additionally, when the facial artery is deficient, the transverse facial artery may replace the arterial supply to the face.

19839.name: Mental Branch of Inferior Alveolar Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior alveolar artery.

Course: Travels within the mandibular canal and exits through the mental foramen.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Chin.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The mental branch of the inferior alveolar artery arises from the inferior alveolar artery as it passes within the mandibular canal.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The mental branch of the inferior alveolar artery leaves the mandibular canal through the mental foramen.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no branches, however, the mental branch of the inferior alveolar artery anastomosis with the submental and inferior labial arteries, and with its fellow from the opposite side.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The mental branch of the inferior alveolar artery supplies the mylohyoid muscle and chin.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: External carotid artery.

Course: Passes on the posterior aspect of the submandibular gland, curves around the inferior aspect of the mandible to enter the face, and ascends to the angle of the mouth and along the lateral aspect of the nose.

Branches: Ascending palatine, submental, inferior and superior labial, and angular arteries; tonsillar, glandular, and lateral nasal septal branches.

Supplied Structures: Face, palate, tonsils, and submandibular gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The facial artery arises from the external carotid artery in the carotid triangle of the neck. It emerges just above the lingual artery and the greater cornu of the hyoid bone. Sometimes, the facial artery arises from the external carotid artery through a common trunk with the lingual artery (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
When the facial artery arises from the external carotid artery, it is covered only by the platysma, fascia, and skin. It passes anterosuperiorly, deep to the digastric and stylohyoid muscles. It arches upwards within a groove on the posterior aspect of the submandibular gland, then turns downwards towards the inferior border of the mandible, while sitting in a lateral groove of the submandibular gland.

The facial artery curves around the inferior border of the mandible to enter the face, anterior to the masseter muscle and deep to skin and fat. It ascends to the angle of the mouth, passing deep to the zygomaticus major and risorius muscles and superficial to buccinator and levator anguli oris muscles. It continues to ascend along the lateral side of the nose and ending at the medial angle of the orbit.

Throughout its course, the facial artery is tortuous, most likely to adapt to movements of the pharynx, mandible, lips, and cheeks.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The facial artery gives rise to several branches supplying structures in the face and neck.

In the neck, the facial artery gives rise to the ascending palatine and submental arteries, and the tonsillar and glandular branches. In the face, the facial artery gives rise to the inferior and superior labial arteries, and the lateral nasal septal branches. Distal to these tributaries, the facial artery continues as the angular artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The facial artery supplies the glandular tissue including the submandibular gland and palatine tonsils. It supplies muscles of facial expression, muscles found below the chin, and the soft palate. Additionally, it supplies overlying fascia and skin.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. & Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Supraorbital artery.

Course: Ascends superficially on the forehead.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Skin and muscles of forehead and scalp.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep branch of the supraorbital artery arises from the ophthalmic artery as it emerges from the supraorbital foramen/notch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep branch of the supraorbital artery ascends on the forehead.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, it forms and anastomoses with the superficial temporal and supratrochlear arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The deep branch of the supraorbital artery supplies the skin and muscles of the forehead and scalp.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: External carotid artery.

Course: Ascends to the scalp.

Branches: Transverse facial, zygomaticoorbital, and middle temporal arteries, parotid, anterior auricular, occipital, frontal, and parietal branches.

Supplied Structures: Structures of the parotid and temporal regions.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial temporal artery arises as a small terminal branch of the external carotid artery, within the substance of the parotid gland and posterior to the neck of the mandible.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial temporal artery ascends superficially, passing over the zygomatic process of the temporal bone. It continues to ascend, with the auriculotemporal nerve, to the scalp for about 4 cm. It terminates by dividing into its terminal frontal and parietal branches. Because of its superficial location, the pulse of the superficial temporal artery can be palpable immediately anterior to the tragus of auricle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The superficial temporal artery provides several named branches, including the transverse facial, zygomaticoorbital, and middle temporal arteries. Additionally, it provides parotid, anterior auricular, occipital, frontal, and parietal branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superficial temporal artery provides arterial supply to the skin and muscles of the side of the face and scalp. It also supplies the parotid gland and temporomandibular joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior lateral and medial palpebral arteries.

Course: Along the margin of the upper eyelid.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Upper eyelid.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior palpebral arch arises from the anastomoses between the lateral and medial palpebral arterial branches of the upper eyelid.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior palpebral arch extends the length of the upper eyelid, sitting just above (2 mm) the margin of the eyelid (Yanoff and Duker, 2013).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superior palpebral arch supplies the superior eyelid.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Yanoff, M. & Duker, J. S. (2013) Ophthalmology E-Book: Expert Consult: Online and Print. Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior lateral and medial palpebral arteries.

Course: Along the margin of the lower eyelid.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Lower eyelid.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior palpebral arch arises from the anastomoses between the lateral and medial palpebral arterial branches of the lower eyelid.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior palpebral arch extends the length of the lower eyelid, sitting just below the margin of the eyelid.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The inferior palpebral arch supplies the inferior eyelid.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Maxillary artery.

Course: Ascends between the temporalis muscle and the epicranium.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Temporalis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior deep temporal artery arises from the maxillary artery as it passes between the ramus of the mandible and the lateral pterygoid muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior deep temporal artery ascends above the level of the zygomatic arch, under the cover of the tendon of the temporalis muscle. The artery then travels between the temporalis muscle and the pericranium, thus producing grooves within the bone.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the posterior deep temporal artery anastomoses with the middle temporal branch of the superficial temporal artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior deep temporal artery supplies the posterior portion of the temporalis muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Maxillary artery.

Course: Ascends between the temporalis muscle and the epicranium.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Temporalis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior deep temporal artery arises from the maxillary artery as it passes between the ramus of the mandible and the lateral pterygoid muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior deep temporal artery ascends above the level of the zygomatic arch, under the cover of the tendon of the temporalis muscle. The artery then travels between the temporalis muscle and the pericranium, thus producing grooves within the bone.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the anterior deep temporal artery anastomoses with the middle temporal branch of the superficial temporal artery. Additionally, the anterior deep temporal artery anastomosis with the lacrimal artery by ramifications that perforate the zygomatic bone and greater wing of the sphenoid bone.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior deep temporal artery supplies the anterior portion of the temporalis muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lacrimal artery.

Course: Extends from lacrimal gland to the lateral aspect of the eyelids.

Branches: Marginal and peripheral arterial arcades.

Supplied Structures: Lateral sides of superior and inferior eyelids and the conjunctiva.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral palpebral arteries are the terminal continuation of the lacrimal artery after it supplies the lacrimal gland.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lateral palpebral arteries continue from the lacrimal gland to reach the lateral aspect of the upper and lower eyelids. Within the eyelids, the arteries course medially to anastomose with the medial palpebral arteries (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The lateral palpebral arteries, together with the medial palpebral arteries, provide important anastomotic arches within the upper and lower eyelids. These include the superior and inferior marginal arterial arcades and the superior peripheral arterial arcade.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The lateral palpebral arteries supply the upper and lower eyelids and the conjunctiva.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

17822.name: Parotid Branch of Posterior Auricular Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior auricular artery.

Course: Short branch extending into the parotid gland.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Parotid gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The parotid branch of the posterior auricular artery is a small vessel arising from the posterior auricular artery as it ascends between the styloid process and the parotid gland.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The course of the parotid branch is short, since the posterior auricular artery passes behind the parotid gland. The parotid branch penetrates the substance of the parotid gland to supply it.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: No named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The parotid branch of the posterior auricular artery supplies the parotid gland.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial temporal artery.

Course: Pierces temporal fascia to reach the temporalis muscle.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Temporalis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle temporal artery arises from the superficial temporal artery just superior to the zygomatic arch. It is not to be confused with the temporal branch of the medial cerebral artery, which is also known as the middle temporal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The middle temporal artery pierces the temporal fascia and ascends on the squamous part of the temporal bone in the groove for the middle temporal artery, just anterior to the external acoustic meatus.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, occasionally it can give off the zygomaticoorbital artery. Additionally, the middle temporal artery anastomoses with the deep temporal arteries arising from the maxillary artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The middle temporal artery provides arterial supply to the temporalis muscle.

19639.name: Superior Labial Artery
alternate: Superior Labial Branch of Facial Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Facial artery.

Course: Along the margin of the lower lip.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Superior labial glands, mucous membranes, and upper part of orbicularis oris muscle and associated muscle, nose.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior labial artery arises from the facial artery as it passes the angle of the mouth. It is much larger and more tortuous than the inferior labial artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior labial artery passes anterosuperiorly, coursing along the margin of the upper lip, between the orbicularis oris and the mucous membrane of the lip.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The superior labial artery provides a nasal septal branch to the nose. Additionally, when the facial artery is deficient, the superior labial artery may provide arterial supply to the nose via alar branches (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superior labial artery supplies the superior labial glands, overlying mucosa, upper part of orbicularis oris, zygomaticus major and minor, depressor septi nasi, levator anguli oris, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, levator labii superioris, nasalis, and risorius, and nasal septum (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Saunders/Elsevier.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ophthalmic artery.

Course: Travels anterior in the orbital cavity and exits via the supraorbital foramen/notch.

Branches: Superficial, deep, and diploic branches.

Supplied Structures: Forehead, muscles of upper orbit, upper eyelid, and frontal sinus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The supraorbital artery arises from the ophthalmic artery as it passes medially and crosses the optic nerve in the orbital cavity.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The supraorbital artery ascends in the orbital cavity, medial to the superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris muscles. It then accompanies the supraorbital nerve between the orbital roof and the levator palpebrae superioris muscle. It exits the orbit via the supraorbital foramen/notch.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The supraorbital artery divides into superficial and deep branches after it emerges from the supraorbital foramen/notch. Additionally, it has a diploic branch at the supraorbital margin.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The supraorbital artery supplies the superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris muscles as it passes over them in the orbit. It also supplies the skin and muscles of the forehead via its superficial and deep branches. The diploic branch of the supraorbital artery supplies the spongy bone of the frontal bone at the supraorbital margin, as well as the frontal sinus (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lacrimal artery.

Course: Passes along the lateral wall of the orbit and enters the temporal fossa via zygomaticotemporal foramen.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Skin of the temporal fossa.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lacrimal artery accompanies the lacrimal nerve along the superior surface of the lateral rectus muscle. Here, it gives off two zygomatic branches, the zygomaticofacial and the zygomaticotemporal arteries (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The zygomaticotemporal artery accompanies the zygomaticotemporal nerve in the lateral wall of the orbit. It enters the temporal fossa via the zygomaticotemporal foramen (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the zygomaticotemporal artery anastomosis with the deep temporal arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The zygomaticotemporal artery supplies the overlying skin of the temporal fossa.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Saunders/Elsevier.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Supraorbital artery.

Course: Ascends superficially on the forehead.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Skin and muscles of forehead.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial branch of the supraorbital artery arises from the ophthalmic artery as it emerges from the supraorbital foramen/notch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial branch of the supraorbital artery ascends on the forehead.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, it forms and anastomoses with the superficial temporal and supratrochlear arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superficial branch of the supraorbital artery supplies the skin and muscles of the forehead.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ascending pharyngeal artery.

Course: Ascends in the head.

Branches: Inferior tympanic artery and meningeal branches.

Supplied Structures: Tympanic cavity and meninges.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The neuromeningeal trunk arises from the ascending pharyngeal artery. In some instances, it may arise from the occipital or posterior auricular artery (Hacein-Bey et al, 2002).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The neuromeningeal trunk continues to ascend towards the skull.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The neuromeningeal trunk gives rise to several meningeal branches and the inferior tympanic artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The neuromeningeal artery indirectly supplies the tympanic cavity and the meninges.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Hacein-Bey, L., Daniels, D. L., Ulmer, J. L., Mark, L. P., Smith, M. M., Strottmann, J. M., Brown, D., Meyer, G. A. & Wackym, P. A. (2002) The Ascending Pharyngeal Artery: Branches, Anastomoses, and Clinical Significance. American Journal of Neuroradiology, 23(7), 1246.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The carotid body is an ovoid mass of tissue that lies either posterior to the bifurcation of the common carotid artery or between its branches.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The carotid body is enclosed within a fibrous capsule and receives a rich blood supply from the adjacent external carotid artery. It is composed of Glomus type I cells that store a number of neurotransmitters (such as dopamine, serotonin, adrenaline) and Glomus type II cells, which act as support cells.

Visceral afferent fibers convey information from the carotid body via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), as well as contributions from the cervical sympathetic trunk and vagus nerve (CN X).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor, which monitors the oxygen levels in arterial blood. When stimulated by hypoxia (deficient oxygen), hypercapnia (elevated CO2), or low pH in the blood, the carotid body is involved in a reflex that results in increased rate and volume of ventilation via respiratory centers in the brainstem (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Carotid body paraganglioma

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior thyroid artery.

Course: Travels superiorly with the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Mucous membrane and muscles of the larynx.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior laryngeal artery originates from the inferior thyroid artery as it ascends in the neck.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior laryngeal artery travels superiorly on the lateral margin of the trachea with the inferior laryngeal nerve, which is the terminal portion of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The inferior laryngeal artery enters the larynx at the lower border of the inferior constrictor muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches of the inferior laryngeal artery;, however, it anastomoses with the contralateral artery and the ipsilateral superior laryngeal artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: As the inferior laryngeal artery enters the larynx, it supplies the mucous membrane and the intrinsic muscles of the larynx.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: As the inferior laryngeal artery enters the larynx, it supplies the mucous membrane and the intrinsic muscles of the larynx.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior thyroid artery.

Course: Pierces the thyrohyoid membrane.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Upper part of larynx.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior laryngeal artery arises from the superior thyroid artery, the first branch of the external carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior laryngeal artery extends medially and deep to the thyrohyoid muscle. It pierces through the thyrohyoid membrane to enter the larynx. It is accompanied by the internal laryngeal nerve.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches of the superior laryngeal artery; however, it forms an anastomosis with the inferior laryngeal branch of the inferior thyroid artery. Additionally, the superior laryngeal artery forms an anastomosis with its fellow branch from the opposite side.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superior laryngeal artery supplies the tissues of the upper part of the larynx.

17028.name: Anterior Auricular Branches of Superficial Temporal Artery
17028.latin: Rami auriculares anteriores arteriae temporalis superficialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial temporal artery.

Course: Around the auricular cartilage.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Lateral aspect of auricle and external acoustic meatus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior auricular branches of the superficial temporal artery arise from the superficial temporal artery as it travels anterior to the auricle of the ear.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior auricular branches of the superficial temporal artery pass around the auricle of the ear.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the anterior auricular branches of the superficial temporal artery anastomose with the auricular branches of the posterior auricular artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior auricular branches of the superficial temporal artery supply the lateral aspect of the auricle and the external acoustic meatus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior auricular artery.

Course: Enters the stylomastoid foramen.

Branches: Posterior tympanic artery, mastoid and stapedial branches.

Supplied Structures: Walls of tympanic cavity, mastoid air cells, and stapedius muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The stylomastoid artery is a branch arising from the posterior auricular artery, a posterior branch of the external carotid artery. Sometimes, the stylomastoid artery may arise from the occipital artery (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The stylomastoid artery ascends to enter the stylomastoid foramen, a small foramen located between the mastoid and styloid processes of the temporal bone, which transmits the facial nerve.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The stylomastoid artery gives off the posterior tympanic artery, and small mastoid and stapedial branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The stylomastoid artery provides arterial supply to the facial nerve as it travels with it in the stylomastoid foramen. Additionally, the stylomastoid artery supplies blood to the tympanic cavity, mastoid antrum air cells, and semicircular canals.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. & Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

18772.name: Superior Tympanic Artery
alternate: Ramus tympanicus superior arteriae meningeae mediae
Superior Tympanic Branch of Middle Meningeal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Middle meningeal artery.

Course: Semicanal for tensor tympani.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Tensor tympani muscle and mucosa of the semicanal for tensor tympani.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior tympanic artery is a small branch arising from the middle meningeal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior tympanic artery traverses the semicanal for the tensor tympani muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superior tympanic artery supplies the tensor tympani muscle and mucosa of the semicanal for tensor tympani.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal carotid artery.

Course: Passes from the carotid canal to the tympanic cavity.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Tympanic cavity.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The caroticotympanic arteries arise from the petrous part of the internal carotid artery as it travels through the carotid canal.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The caroticotympanic arteries pass from the carotid canal to the tympanic cavity via the caroticotympanic canaliculi.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the caroticotympanic arteries form anastomoses with the anterior and posterior tympanic arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The caroticotympanic arteries supply the tympanic cavity and the osseous part of the auditory (Eustachian or pharyngotympanic) tube.

23424.name: Auricular Branch of Posterior Auricular Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior auricular artery.

Course: Ascend behind the ear.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Auricle and adjacent skin.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The auricular branch of the posterior auricular artery arises from the posterior auricular artery as it ascends in the groove between the mastoid process of the temporal bone and the cartilage of the ear.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The auricular branch of the posterior auricular artery ascends behind the ear, underneath the auricularis posterior muscle (Gray & Lewis, 1918).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the auricular branch ramifies and some branches curve around the margin of the cartilage, while others perforate it to reach the anterior surface. The ramifications of the auricular branch anastomosis with the anterior auricular branches and parietal branch of the superficial temporal artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The auricular branch of the posterior auricular artery supplies the auricle and adjacent skin. Additionally, it contributes to the blood supply to the auricularis anterior, posterior, and superior muscles (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Gray, H. & Lewis, W. H. (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body. Lea & Febiger.

Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Saunders/Elsevier.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Maxillary artery.

Course: Ascends towards the external acoustic meatus.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Skin of auditory canal, tympanic membrane, and temporomandibular joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep auricular artery is a small branch arising from the maxillary artery near its origin.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep auricular artery ascends within the infratemporal fossa towards the external acoustic meatus. It pierces the osseous and cartilaginous wall to reach internal structures.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The deep auricular artery provides arterial supply to the skin lining the external acoustic meatus and part of the tympanic membrane. It also provides rami to the temporomandibular joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Occipital artery.

Course: Traverses the scalp laterally towards the ear.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Medial aspect of pinna of the ear.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The auricular branch of the occipital artery is an inconstant branch arising from the occipital artery (Dorland, 2011). As the occipital artery ascends tortuously in dense superficial fascia of the scalp, between the skin and occipital belly of occipitofrontalis muscle, it gives off the auricular branch of the occipital artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The auricular branch of the occipital artery courses laterally within the superficial fascia of the scalp towards the posterior aspect of the ear.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the auricular branch of the occipital artery anastomosis with the posterior auricular artery behind the ear.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The auricular branch of the occipital artery provides arterial supply to the auricle (pinna) of the ear (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

19360.name: Posterior Tympanic Artery
alternate: Posterior Tympanic Branch of Stylomastoid Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Stylomastoid artery.

Course: Travels with chorda tympani to enter the tympanic cavity.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Tympanic cavity.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior tympanic artery arises from the stylomastoid artery, a branch of the posterior auricular artery, as it passes through the facial canal.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior tympanic artery leaves the facial canal with the chorda tympani via the posterior canaliculus to enter the tympanic cavity (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the posterior tympanic artery and the anterior tympanic artery (branch of the maxillary artery) forms a vascular circle on the internal surface of the tympanic membrane. Additionally, it anastomosis with the artery of the pterygoid canal and the caroticotympanic arteries in the tympanic cavity mucosa (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior tympanic artery supplies the posterior aspect of the tympanic cavity.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

22161.name: Labyrinthine Artery
alternate: Ramus meatus acustici interni arteriae cerebelli inferioris anterioris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Usually the anterior inferior cerebellar artery; variably the basilar, superior cerebellar, or posterior inferior cerebellar artery

Course: Passes through the internal acoustic meatus with the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves

Branches: Anterior vestibular, vestibulocochlear, and cochlear arteries

Supplied Structures: Internal ear

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The labyrinthine artery most often arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery; however, it may also arise from the basilar, superior cerebellar, or posterior inferior cerebellar arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The labyrinthine artery runs posterolaterally and passes through the internal acoustic meatus. It accompanies the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves and the labyrinthine vein.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The labyrinthine artery gives rise to the anterior vestibular, vestibulocochlear, and cochlear arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The labyrinthine artery supplies the structures of the internal ear.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Haidara, Aderehime, Johann Peltier, Yvan Zunon-Kipre, Hermann Adonis N’da, Landry Drogba, and Daniel Le Gars, 2015. Microsurgical Anatomy of the Labyrinthine Artery and Clinical Relevance. Turkish Neurosurgery 25 (4), 539–43. doi:10.5137/1019–5149.JTN.9136–13.0

Standring, S., Tubbs, S.R., 2025. Gray’s Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 43rd ed. Elsevier.

Tempski, Jonasz, Grzegorz Fibiger, Katarzyna Majka, et al., 2025. Surgical Anatomy of the Labyrinthine Artery - a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Neurosurgical Review 48 (1), 464. doi:10.1007/s10143–025–03592–0

Vanderah, T.W., Gould, D.J., 2025. Nolte’s The Human Brain: An Introduction to its Functional Anatomy, 9th ed. Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Neuromeningeal trunk.

Course: Passes through the inferior tympanic canaliculus of temporal bone.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Tympanic cavity.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior tympanic artery arises as a small branch from the proximal aspect of the neuromeningeal trunk. However, sometimes, it may arise between the pharyngeal branches and neuromeningeal trunk as they bifurcate from the ascending pharyngeal artery (Hacein-Bey et al., 2002).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior tympanic artery traverses the inferior tympanic canaliculus (tympanic canaliculus or Jacobson’s canaliculus) of the petrous part of the temporal bone. It accompanies the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The inferior tympanic artery supplies the medial wall of the tympanic cavity.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Hacein-Bey, L., Daniels, D. L., Ulmer, J. L., Mark, L. P., Smith, M. M., Strottmann, J. M., Brown, D., Meyer, G. A. & Wackym, P. A. (2002) The Ascending Pharyngeal Artery: Branches, Anastomoses, and Clinical Significance. American Journal of Neuroradiology, 23(7), 1246.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Maxillary artery.

Course: Passes through the petrotympanic fissure to reach the middle ear.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Mucosa of middle ear.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior tympanic artery is a small branch arising from the maxillary artery near its origin.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior tympanic artery ascends in the infratemporal fossa and passes through the petrotympanic fissure, a small opening posterior to the articular surface of the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone. The anterior tympanic artery accompanies the chorda tympani nerve to the middle ear.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the anterior tympanic artery forms an anastomosis with the caroticotympanic artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior tympanic artery supplies the mucosa of the middle ear.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Pharyngeal trunk.

Course: Medially towards the cartilaginous part of the auditory tube.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Auditory tube.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The Eustachian branch of the pharyngeal trunk is a small irregular branch arising from the pharyngeal trunk as it ascends in the neck.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The Eustachian branch traverses medially towards the auditory tube.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The Eustachian branch supplies the cartilaginous part of the auditory tube.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior division of internal iliac artery.

Course: Descends posteriorly between the piriformis and coccygeus (ischiococcygeus) muscles to enter the gluteal region through the greater sciatic foramen.

Branches: Artery to sciatic nerve.

Supplied Structures: Pelvic diaphragm, piriformis, quadratus femoris, biceps femoris, gluteus maximus, skin of buttock, and posterior thigh.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior gluteal artery originates as the larger terminal branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The inferior gluteal artery descends posteriorly from its origin. It passes anterior to the sacral plexus and piriformis muscle and passes between the first and second (or second and third) anterior rami of the sacral nerves. The inferior gluteal artery then descends between the piriformis and coccygeus muscles to enter the gluteal region through the lower part of the greater sciatic foramen.

The inferior gluteal artery continues to descend between the greater trochanter of femur and the ischial tuberosity, along with the sciatic and posterior femoral cutaneous nerves, to enter the thigh.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The inferior gluteal artery often gives off an artery to sciatic nerve, which accompanies the sciatic nerve along its course. However, the origin of this artery may vary (Georgakis and Soames, 2008).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The inferior gluteal artery supplies the coccygeus, iliococcygeus (levator ani), piriformis, gluteus maximus, superior gemellus, and biceps femoris muscles. It also supplies the skin of the buttock and posterior thigh.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Georgakis, E. and Soames, R. (2008) 'Arterial supply to the sciatic nerve in the gluteal region', Clin Anat, 21(1), pp. 62-5.

16426.name: Deep Branch of Superior Gluteal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior gluteal artery.

Course: Laterally and deep to gluteus medius.

Branches: and inferior branches of the deep branch of the superior gluteal artery.

Supplied Structures: Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fascia latae muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: As the superior gluteal artery exits the greater sciatic foramen, superior to the piriformis, it divides into the superficial and deep branch of the superior gluteal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep branch runs laterally between the gluteus medius and the ilium. It then runs on the gluteus minimus and divides into superior and inferior branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The deep branch of the superior gluteal divides into the superior and the inferior branches of the deep branch of the superior gluteal artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The deep branch supplies the gluteus medius, the gluteus minimus, and the tensor fascia latae muscles.

23107.name: Inferior Branch of Superior Gluteal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep branch of superior gluteal artery.

Course: Inferolaterally between gluteus medius and gluteus minimus.

Branches: No named branches.

Supplied Structures: Gluteus medius and minimus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep branch of the superior gluteal artery runs laterally between the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, where it divides into superior and inferior branches.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior branch runs laterally along the gluteus minimus.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: It gives small branches to the gluteus medius and the gluteus minimus. It also forms anastomoses with the ascending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: It aids in the arterial supply of the gluteus medius and the gluteus minimus muscles and lateral aspect of the hip via its anastomoses.

18329.name: Superficial Branch of Superior Gluteal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior gluteal artery.

Course: It gives several small branches that pierce the gluteus maximus and travel towards superficially.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Gluteus maximus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: As the superior gluteal artery exits the greater sciatic foramen, superior to the piriformis, it divides into superficial and deep branches.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial branch pierces the deep surface of the gluteus maximus, while other branches perforate the tendinous attachment of the gluteus maximus.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Several branches of the superficial branch travel within the gluteus maximus muscle.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superficial branch supplies the gluteus maximus and gives cutaneous supply to the skin surrounding the sacrum. It also anastomoses with branches of the lateral sacral artery.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior gluteal artery.

Course: Descends with sciatic nerve.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Sciatic nerve.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The artery that accompanies the sciatic nerve is a derivative of the inferior gluteal artery. In fetal development, the inferior gluteal artery is larger, and is continuous with the popliteal artery. Postnatally, it diminishes in size and becomes the artery to the sciatic nerve.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The artery to the sciatic nerve descends with the sciatic nerve through the gluteal region and the posterior thigh.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: As the name suggests, the artery to the sciatic nerve artery supplies the sciatic nerve.

17159.name: Superior Branch of Superior Gluteal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep branch of superior gluteal artery.

Course: Laterally between gluteus medius and minimus muscles.

Branches: Anastomoses with the deep circumflex iliac artery and a branch of the lateral circumflex artery.

Supplied Structures: Gluteus medius and minimus muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep branch of the superior gluteal artery runs laterally between the gluteus medius and minimus muscles and divides into a superior and an inferior branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior branch runs along the superior border of the gluteus minimus muscle as far as the anterior superior iliac spine.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: It anastomoses with the deep circumflex iliac artery and also with the ascending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: It aids in the arterial supply of the gluteus medius and the gluteus minimus muscles. It also aids in the supply of the ileum and lateral aspect of the hip via its anastomoses.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior division of internal iliac artery.

Course: Descends posteriorly leaving the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen.

Branches: Superficial and deep branches.

Supplied Structures: Ilium, skin of gluteal region, and the piriformis, obturator internus, gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, and gluteus minimus muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior gluteal artery is the continuation of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery and forms its largest branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior gluteal artery extends posteriorly between the lumbosacral trunk and first anterior ramus of the sacral nerve, or between the first and second anterior rami of the sacral nerves. It passes above the piriformis muscle and leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: As the superior gluteal artery enters the gluteal region, it divides into superficial and deep branches. The deep branch of superior gluteal artery courses between gluteus medius muscle and the ilium to further subdivide into superior and inferior branches. The superficial branch pierces the gluteus maximus muscle.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
As the superior gluteal artery courses through the pelvis, it supplies the piriformis and obturator internus muscles and sends a nutrient branch to the ilium.

The superficial branch of superior gluteal artery enters the gluteus maximus muscle giving off numerous branches to this large muscle. It also supplies the skin over the sacrum.

The superior division of the deep branch of the superior gluteal artery extends along the superior border of gluteus minimus to the anterior superior iliac spine. The inferior division of the deep branch of the superior gluteal artery passes through gluteus minimus to supply it and gluteus medius muscle.

21860.name: Superficial Branch of Medial Plantar Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Medial plantar artery at the medial cuneiform bone.

Course: Travels distally along the medial aspect of the first metatarsal, deep to the flexor hallucis brevis muscle.

Branches: Forms anastomoses with the first plantar metatarsal artery.

Supplied Structures: Plantar aspect of the foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial branch arises from the medial plantar artery at the level of the tarsometatarsal joint, between the medial cuneiform and the first metatarsal.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial branch of the medial plantar artery courses distally, deep to the flexor hallucis brevis muscle, along the medial aspect of the first metatarsal (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The superficial branch of the medial plantar artery forms an anastomosis with first plantar metatarsal artery, approximately at the level of the metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe. The vessel then continues as the plantar digital artery of the great toe (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superficial branch of the medial plantar artery supplies the medial aspect of the plantar surface of the foot.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Netter Basic Science Series: Saunders/Elsevier.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by the anastomosis between the lateral plantar and deep plantar arteries.

Course: Arches over the metatarsal bones, deep to the lumbrical muscles.

Branches: Plantar metatarsal arteries and perforating branches.

Supplied Structures: Plantar aspect of the sole of the foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The plantar arch originates from the lateral plantar artery at the base of the fifth metatarsal artery. In some rare instances, the lateral plantar artery forms an anastomosis with the medial plantar artery, deep to the plantar aponeurosis and superficial to the flexor digitorum brevis muscle. This is referred to as the superficial plantar arch. In this instance, the plantar arch is called the deep plantar arch (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the plantar arch courses from the base of the fifth metatarsal to the space between the first and second metatarsals, the first intermetatarsal space. Here it joins the deep plantar artery. The plantar arch lies deep to the lumbricals, the tendons of the flexor digitorum longus muscles, and the oblique head of the adductor hallucis muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The plantar arch gives off three to four perforating branches, which anastomose with the dorsal metatarsal arteries. Secondly, four plantar metatarsal arteries arise from the plantar arch. These run distally along the lateral four metatarsals and form the plantar digital arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The plantar arch gives muscular and cutaneous supply to the sole of the foot and toes.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal metatarsal arteries at the metatarsophalangeal joint.

Course: Distally to the tip of the distal phalanx.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Dorsal aspect of the toes.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal digital arteries arise from the dorsal metatarsal arteries at the level of the metatarsophalangeal joint. Each dorsal metatarsal artery divides into two dorsal digital arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal digital arteries run along the medial and lateral aspects of adjacent digits. The first and fifth dorsal metatarsal arteries run distally along the medial aspect of the great toe and the lateral aspect of the little toe, respectively.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The dorsal digital arteries give cutaneous, muscular, and articular supply to the dorsal aspect of the digits of the foot. In particular, they contribute to the supply of the dorsal interossei, the lumbricals, and the extensor digitorum brevis muscles.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsalis pedis artery.

Course: Passes laterally in an arch across the base of the metatarsal bones.

Branches: Dorsal metatarsal arteries.

Supplied Structures: Dorsum of the foot and the lateral four digits.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The arcuate artery arises from the dorsalis pedis artery. There are many variations of the arcuate artery, which are related to the variations of the dorsalis pedis artery.

- In approximately one third of individuals, the arcuate artery arises at the first metatarsal joint where it tends to give off the second to fourth dorsal metatarsal arteries.

- In approximately one fifth of individuals, the arcuate artery arises at the cuneonavicular joint.

- In one third of individuals the arcuate artery is absent (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The arcuate artery forms an arch as it travels laterally along the proximal portion of the metatarsals. The artery sits deep to the extensor digitorum longus and brevis muscles.

It may terminate in the lateral aspect of the foot, where it may form an anastomosis with the lateral tarsal artery and plantar arteries.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The arcuate artery gives off the second to fourth dorsal metatarsal arteries, which travel distally over the dorsal interossei muscles. They then bifurcate into two dorsal digital branches, which run distally on both the medial and lateral aspects of adjacent toes.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The arcuate artery contributes to the supply of the dorsum of the foot.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsalis pedis artery.

Course: Laterally, deep to the extensor digitorum brevis muscle, towards the lateral aspect of the foot.

Branches: Contributes to the lateral malleolar network.

Supplied Structures: Lateral aspect of the tarsal bones and its respective intertarsal joints.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral tarsal artery arises from the dorsalis pedis artery. It may originate at the junction of the head and neck of the talus bone (in approximately 60% of individuals), at the ankle joint (in approximately 20% of individuals), or distal to the talonavicular joint (in approximately 20% of individuals) (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the lateral tarsal artery extends laterally, deep to the extensor digitorum brevis muscle, and contributes to the lateral malleolar network.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the lateral tarsal artery aids in the formation of the lateral malleolar network via its anastomosis with the lateral malleolar branches of the fibular artery, anterior lateral malleolar artery, and the perforating branch of the fibular artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The lateral tarsal artery supplies the extensor digitorum brevis muscle and the articulations between the tarsal bones.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior tibial artery.

Course: Travels distally to the base of the first metatarsal.

Branches: Medial and lateral tarsal, arcuate, first dorsal metatarsal, and deep plantar arteries.

Supplied Structures: Dorsum of the foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The dorsalis pedis artery arises from the anterior tibial artery. In up to 5% of individuals, it may arise from the perforating branch of the fibular artery (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

The dorsalis pedis artery may be enlarged if the main plantar arterial supply is diminished. Conversely, it is absent in approximately 12% of individuals and may be replaced by an enlarged perforating branch from the fibular artery (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The dorsalis pedis artery runs distally along the talocrural joint and tarsal bones, deep to the extensor hallucis brevis muscle. The deep fibular nerve sits lateral to the dorsalis pedis artery.

The dorsalis pedis artery continues along the dorsal aspect of the foot, between the long tendons of the extensor hallucis longus muscle medially and the extensor digitorum longus muscle laterally. These tendons provide important anatomical landmarks in order to avoid the vasculature during surgery (Standring, 2016). They are also important in finding the dorsalis pedis pulse. In the region of the navicular bone, the vessel is superficial and can be palpated when the ankle is in slight dorsiflexion (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013). This pulse point is important clinically, whereby a weak pulse is indicative of vascular occlusion and arterial disease.

The dorsalis pedis artery reaches the first intermetatarsal space and passes between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle, into the plantar aspect of the foot. Here, where it gives rise to the deep plantar artery, which joins the deep plantar arch.

The dorsalis pedis often strays either medially or laterally from the route described above; however, lateral deviation is more common (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: As the dorsalis pedis runs along the tarsal bones, it gives off the medial and lateral tarsal arteries. As it reaches the proximal head of the first metatarsal bone, it gives off the arcuate artery. It continues to the proximal end of the first intermetatarsal space where it gives off the first dorsal metatarsal artery, before traveling into the plantar aspect of the foot as the deep plantar artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The dorsalis pedis artery contributes to the supply of the extensor hallucis brevis and the extensor digitorum brevis muscles. It may also send some twigs to the long tendons of the dorsal aspect of the foot.

It supplies some of the surrounding bones, namely the navicular bone, and gives cutaneous supply to the dorsal aspect of the foot.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Dorsalis pedis pulse

- Vascular occlusive disorder of the lower limb

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn. Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior medial malleolar artery, medial malleolar branches of the posterior tibial artery, medial tarsal arteries, and medial plantar artery.

Course: Forms an anastomotic network around the medial malleolus.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Subcutaneous tissue of medial malleolar region.

sections.title: Origin
Course
sections.text: The medial malleolar network is an anastomotic network of vessels that course along the medial malleolus of the tibia.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The medial malleolar network contributes to the arterial supply of the adductor hallucis muscle, as well as the overlying fascial and cutaneous tissue of the medial malleolar region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Plantar arch.

Course: Distally in the intermetatarsal spaces.

Branches: Plantar digital arteries.

Supplied Structures: Plantar aspect of the foot and toes.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: There are four plantar metatarsal arteries that arise from the plantar arch and are numbered sequentially from the first to fourth plantar metatarsal arteries. A fifth plantar metatarsal artery arises from the lateral plantar artery and is named the plantar metatarsal branch of the lateral plantar artery (Netter, 2011). It runs along the lateral aspect of the fifth metatarsal.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The plantar metatarsal arteries course distally, on the plantar side of the plantar interossei in the intermetatarsal space.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The plantar metatarsal arteries give rise to the common plantar digital arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The plantar metatarsal arteries provide an arterial supply to the plantar aspect of the foot and digits.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Netter Basic Science Series: Saunders/Elsevier.

19461.name: Perforating Branches of Plantar Metatarsal Arteries
alternate: Anterior Perforating Branches to Dorsal Metatarsal Arteries

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Plantar metatarsal arteries.

Course: Travel from the plantar to dorsal aspect of the foot.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Collateral supply between dorsal and plantar aspects of the metatarsals and phalanges.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Four perforating branches arise from the distal ends of each of the four plantar metatarsal arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From their origins at the distal ends of the intermetatarsal spaces, the perforating branches of the plantar metatarsal arteries travel through the first to fourth intermetatarsal spaces and anastomose with the dorsal metatarsal arteries.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries provide an arterial supply to the structures of the first to fourth intermetatarsal spaces and adjacent structures. They also aid in the formation of a collateral vascular supply to the metatarsal and phalangeal regions of the foot.

21339.name: Deep Plantar Artery
alternate: Ramus plantaris profunda arteriae dorsalis pedis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsalis pedis artery.

Course: Passes between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Sole of the foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep plantar artery originates from the dorsal pedis artery at the base of the first metatarsal bone.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the deep plantar artery enters the first intermetatarsal space between the heads of the first interosseous muscle. As it reaches the plantar region of the foot, it joins with the lateral plantar artery to form the plantar arch.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The deep plantar artery gives muscular and cutaneous supply to the sole of the foot.

19537.name: Anterior Lateral Malleolar Artery
alternate: Lateral Malleolar Branches of Peroneal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior tibial artery.

Course: Descends inferiorly to lateral aspect of the ankle.

Branches: Contributes to the lateral malleolar network.

Supplied Structures: Inferior tibiofibular joint and lateral aspect of the ankle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior lateral malleolar artery arises from the anterior tibial artery on the anterior surface of the distal tibia.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior lateral malleolar artery travels inferolaterally, deep to the tendons of the extensor digitorum longus and the fibularis tertius muscles to wrap around the lateral malleolus of the fibula.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches, however, the anterior lateral malleolar artery anastomoses with the perforating and lateral malleolar branches of the fibular artery and the lateral tarsal artery to form the lateral malleolar network.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior lateral malleolar artery supplies the lateral aspect of the ankle and the inferior tibiofibular joint.

19753.name: Plantar Metatarsal Branch of Lateral Plantar Artery
19753.latin: Ramus metatarsalis plantaris arteriae plantaris lateralis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Terminal continuation of the lateral plantar artery.

Course: Travels laterally, then distally along the lateral side of the fifth metatarsal.

Branches: Plantar digital artery.

Supplied Structures: Lateral side of the sole of foot and little toe.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The plantar metatarsal branch is the terminal continuation of the lateral plantar artery after it gives rise to the plantar arch (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: Course
