sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The circumflex scapular artery provides origin for an unnamed branch which travels to the subscapular fossa and anastomoses with the vessels on the anterior surface of the scapula (Standring, 2016). Another unnamed branch descends on the lateral border and runs between the two teres muscles, then posterior to the inferior angle where it anastomosis with the dorsal scapular artery. There are additional small muscular branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The circumflex scapular artery gives muscular branches to the teres major, infraspinatus, posterior deltoid, and the long head of the triceps brachii muscles, as well as contributing to the anastomotic network of the scapula. Additionally, there are cutaneous branches that supply the skin overlying the scapula.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior division of the internal iliac artery.

Course: Loops around the ischial spine, then travels anteriorly within the perineum.

Branches: Inferior anorectal, perineal, and urethral arteries, artery of bulb of the vestibule/penis, deep artery of the clitoris/penis, and dorsal artery of clitoris/penis.

Supplied Structures: Rectum, anal canal, urethra, and external genitalia.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The internal pudendal artery originates from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The internal pudendal artery crosses anterior to the piriformis muscle, the inferior gluteal artery, and the sacral plexus.

It courses in an inferolateral direction towards the inferior aspect of the greater sciatic foramen and exits the pelvic cavity between the piriformis and the ischiococcygeus muscles.

Within the gluteal region, it curves posteriorly around the ischial spine, where it traverses the lesser sciatic foramen and enters the perineum. It travels anteriorly, within the pudendal canal, along the walls of the ischioanal canal and gives off the inferior anorectal artery.

The artery continues anteriorly within the pudendal canal (Alcock’s canal) with the pudendal vein and nerve. The canal is formed from the surrounding connective tissue and the fascia of the obturator internus muscle. As the artery courses anteriorly, in the region of the ischial ramus, it continues along the perineal membrane.

In females, it divides into its two terminal branches, the deep artery of the clitoris and dorsal artery of clitoris. The male equivalents are the deep artery of the penis and the dorsal artery of the penis.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
As the internal pudendal artery travels anteriorly, it gives off a series of branches. These include the inferior anorectal, perineal, and urethral arteries. 

In females, it also gives rise to the artery of the bulb of the vestibule, deep artery of the clitoris, and dorsal artery of the clitoris. In males, it gives rise to the deep and the dorsal arteries of the penis and the artery of the bulb of the penis.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The internal pudendal artery supplies the inferior rectum and anal canal, the external genitalia, and perineum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal pudendal artery.

Course: Pierces the perineal membrane.

Branches: Transverse perineal artery, posterior scrotal artery and artery of bulb of penis (males) or posterior labial artery and artery of vestibule (females).

Supplied Structures: Perineum and skin of external genitalia.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The perineal artery originates in the distal anterior portion of the pudendal canal as a branch of the internal pudendal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: After branching from the internal pudendal artery, the perineal artery travels anteriorly in the deep perineal pouch. It pierces the perineal membrane to enter the superficial perineal pouch. Here it runs between the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus muscles.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The perineal artery sometimes gives off a small transverse perineal artery. In males, the artery terminates into the posterior scrotal arteries and the artery of the bulb of the penis. In females, the artery terminates as the posterior labial arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The perineal artery supplies the perineum and skin of the external genitalia.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Perineal artery.

Course: Medially towards the perineal body.

Branches: Anastomoses with inferior anorectal arteries, and the posterior scrotal arteries and artery of bulb of penis (males) or posterior labial arteries and arteries of the vestibule (females).

Supplied Structures: Superficial transverse perineal, levator ani, and external anal sphincter muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The transverse perineal artery is a small branch that originates from the perineal artery in the superficial perineal pouch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The transverse perineal artery passes medially, inferior to the superficial transverse perineal muscle to reach the perineal body.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The transverse perineal artery does not give off any branches. It forms anastomoses with the inferior anorectal arteries and its contralateral branch. In males, it also anastomoses with the posterior scrotal arteries and the artery of the bulb of the penis. In females, the artery anastomoses with the posterior labial artery and the artery of the vestibule.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The small transverse perineal arteries supply the superficial transverse perineal, the levator ani, and the external anal sphincter muscles.

25473.name: Prostatic Branches of Inferior Vesical Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior vesical artery.

Course: Pass towards the prostate.

Branches: Anterior and posterolateral branches.

Supplied Structures: Prostate.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The prostatic branches typically arise from the inferior vesical artery (a branch of the internal iliac artery) near the junction of the bladder and prostate.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: After branching, the prostatic branches quickly divide and pierce the capsule of the prostate.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The prostatic branches divide into anterior and posterolateral branches, which give rise to urethral and capsular branches (MacLennan, 2012).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterolateral branch supply the bulk of the prostate, while the anterior branch supplies only the anterolateral portion of the gland (MacLennan, 2012).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Prostatectomy
—Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
—Prostate Cancer

sections.title: References
sections.text: MacLennan, G. T. (2012) Hinman's Atlas of Urosurgical Anatomy. Elsevier/Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior vesical artery.

Course: Follows the ductus deferens through the inguinal canal into the scrotum.

Branches: Ureteric branches of artery of ductus deferens.

Supplied Structures: Ductus deferens and seminal vesicle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The artery of the ductus deferens arises from the superior vesical artery, a branch of the patent part of the umbilical artery. Occasionally, it may arise from the inferior vesical artery (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The artery of the ductus deferens passes inferior from the superior vesical artery to reach the ductus deferens. The artery follows the ductus deferens within the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal and into the scrotum. In the scrotum, this artery will anastomose with the testicular artery.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The artery of the ductus deferens gives rise to ureteric branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The artery of the ductus deferens supplies the ductus deferens, as well as the superior seminal vesicle.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Prostatectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal artery of penis.

Course: Pierces the tunica albuginea. 

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Corpora cavernosa.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior epigastric artery.

Course: Enters the spermatic cord through the deep inguinal ring, travels the length of the cord, terminating at the tail of the epididymis.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Spermatic cord and tail of the epididymis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The cremasteric artery arises from the inferior epigastric artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The cremasteric artery passes through the deep inguinal ring to run the length of the spermatic cord, between the external and internal spermatic fascia. It terminates at the tail of the epididymis.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the cremasteric artery supplies small anastomotic branches that communicate with branches of the testicular and epididymal arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The cremasteric artery supplies the cremaster and the other layers of the spermatic cord, as well as the tail of the epididymis (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Vasectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

25469.name: Prostatic Branches of Middle Anorectal Artery
alternate: Prostatic Branches of Middle Rectal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Middle anorectal artery.

Course: Pass anteriorly and superiorly towards the prostate.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Prostate.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The prostate is mainly supplied by the prostatic branches that typically arise from the inferior vesical artery. Occasionally small branches from the middle anorectal artery will supply the inferior aspects of the bladder.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The prostatic branches from the middle anorectal artery (if present) will course anteriorly and superiorly to supply the posterior and inferior portions of the prostate.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The prostatic branches from the middle anorectal artery supply the posterior and inferior portions of the prostate.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Prostatectomy
—Benign prostatic hyperplasia
—Prostate cancer

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Abdominal aorta.

Course: Travels from abdominal aorta to the testis

Branches: Ureteric and epididymal branches.

Supplied Structures: Ureter, testes, and epididymis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The testicular arteries arise from the abdominal aorta, below the renal arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The testicular arteries descend obliquely, inferiorly and laterally, and retroperitoneally. The right testicular artery passes anterior to the inferior vena cava, and posterior to the middle colic and ileocolic arteries and the distal ileum. The left testicular artery passes posterior to the inferior mesenteric vein, left colic artery, and descending colon (Standring, 2020). 

Once they enter the pelvis, they pass anterior to the genitofemoral nerves, the ureters, and external iliac arteries. They traverse the deep inguinal ring to enter the inguinal canal, and, within the spermatic cord, they pass to the scrotum.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The testicular arteries give rise to ureteric and epididymal branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The testicular arteries provide arterial supply to the ureters, testes, and epididymis.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Testicular biopsy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Femoral artery.

Course: Travels medially from femoral artery.

Branches: Anastomosis with internal pudendal artery.

Supplied Structures: Skin of abdomen and external genitalia.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial external pudendal artery arises from the medial surface of the proximal third of the femoral artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the artery travels medially, pierces the cribriform fascia (part of the superficial fascia of the thigh covering the saphenous opening) and travels anterior to the spermatic cord in males or the round ligament of uterus in females to reach the external genitalia.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches; however, the superficial external pudendal artery anastomosis with the internal pudendal artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superficial external pudendal artery supplies the skin of the inguinal region and external genitalia.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal pudendal artery.

Course: Penetrates the perineal membrane to enter the crus and supply the crus and corpus cavernosum of the body. 

Branches: Helicine branches. 

Supplied Structures: Corpora cavernosa of the penis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep artery of the penis is one of two terminal branches of the internal pudendal artery, the other being the dorsal artery of the penis.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep artery of the penis penetrates the perineal membrane to enter the corpora cavernosa in the crus of the penis. It continues towards the glans penis.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Within each corpus cavernosum, the deep artery of the penis gives off several helicine branches. They open directly into the vascular spaces supported and enclosed by the trabeculae (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The deep artery of the penis supplies the corpora cavernosa in the crus, body, and glans of the penis.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Penile erection

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal pudendal artery.

Course: Passes superior through the perineal membrane to enter the bulb of the penis.

Branches: Urethral branches.

Supplied Structures: Bulbourethral gland, bulb of penis, spongy (penile) urethra, corpus spongiosum, and glans penis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The artery of the bulb of the penis is a branch of the internal pudendal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The artery of the bulb of the penis passes superior (deep) through the perineal membrane to enter the bulb of the penis (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The artery of the bulb of the penis gives rise to urethral branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The artery of the bulb of the penis supplies the bulbourethral gland, bulb of the penis, spongy urethra, corpus spongiosum, and glans penis (MacLennan, 2012).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Catheter placement

sections.title: References
sections.text:
MacLennan, G. T. (2012) Hinman's Atlas of Urosurgical Anatomy. Elsevier/Saunders.
Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal artery of penis.

Course: Pierces the tunica albuginea. 

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Corpus spongiosum and spongy urethra.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: As the dorsal artery of the penis passes towards the glans penis, it gives off several circumflex arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The circumflex arteries extend around the body of the penis towards its ventral surface.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The circumflex arteries of the penis supply the corpus spongiosum and spongy urethra (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

25037.name: Anterior Scrotal Arteries
alternate: Scrotal Branches of Deep External Pudendal Artery
Rami scrotales arteriae pudendalis externae profundae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep external pudendal artery.

Course: Descend inferiorly to the anterior scrotum.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Anterior wall of the scrotum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The anterior scrotal arteries arise from the deep external pudendal artery as it passes posterior to the spermatic cord.

The anterior labial arteries are the female equivalent of the anterior scrotal arteries. They provide an arterial supply to the anterior part of the labia majora.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior scrotal arteries pass inferior to the anterior wall of scrotum. They sit parallel to the rugae of the scrotum and are limited by the raphe (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior scrotal arteries supply the anterior wall of the scrotum.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal pudendal artery.

Course: Penetrates the perineal membrane to reach the body of the penis. 

Branches: Circumferential and perforating arteries.

Supplied Structures: Superficial tissues of the penis, glans penis, and corpora cavernosa.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal artery of the penis arises as one of two terminal branches from the internal pudendal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal artery of the penis pierces the perineal membrane at its anterior margin to reach the dorsal surface of the body of the penis. This artery passes along its dorsal surface towards the glans penis, medial to the dorsal nerve.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The dorsal artery of the penis gives rise to circumferential and perforating arteries (Diallo et al., 2013). It also forms anastomoses with branches of the deep artery of the penis and the urethral artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The dorsal artery of the penis supplies the superficial tissues of the penis, the glans penis, corpus spongiosum, spongy urethra, and corpora cavernosa.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Diallo, D., Zaitouna, M., Alsaid, B., Quillard, J., Droupy, S., Benoit, G. and Bessede, T. (2013) 'What is the origin of the arterial vascularization of the corpora cavernosa? A computer-assisted anatomic dissection study', J Anat, 223(5), pp. 489-94.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Femoral artery.

Course: Crosses the thigh to reach the perineum and scrotum (male) or labia majora (female).

Branches: Anterior scrotal (male) or labial branches (female).

Supplied Structures: Skin of perineum and external genitalia.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep external pudendal artery arises from the medial surface of the proximal third of the femoral artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep external pudendal artery takes a horizontal course and travels medially over the pectineus and adductor longus muscles to enter the anterior aspect of the urogenital triangle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: In males, the deep external pudendal artery gives off anterior scrotal branches. In females, the deep external pudendal artery gives off anterior labial branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The deep external pudendal artery provides an arterial supply to the skin of the external genitalia and perineum.

25051.name: Posterior Scrotal Arteries
alternate: Posterior Scrotal Branches of Perineal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Perineal artery.

Course: Pass anterior and inferior through the superficial perineal space.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Skin of scrotum and dartos muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior scrotal arteries are typically the terminal branches of the perineal artery, a main branch of the internal pudendal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior scrotal arteries pierce the perineal membrane between the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus muscles to enter the superior perineal space (pouch). The posterior scrotal arteries (equivalent to the posterior labial arteries in females) travel inferiorly along the posterior portion of the scrotum.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior scrotal arteries supply the scrotal skin and dartos muscle.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Vasectomy
—Testicular cancer

25464.name: Helicine Branches of Deep Artery of Penis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep artery of penis.

Course: Pass into the cavernous spaces of the corpus cavernosum.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Corpus cavernosum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The helicine branches are terminal branches of the deep artery of the penis.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: These short terminal branches pass in multiple directions from their origin to eventually open directly into the vascular spaces in the corpus cavernosum, supported and enclosed by trabeculae (Standring, 2020). The shape of these vessels will change based on the erectile state of the penis. When flaccid, the vessels will be contracted and tortuous; when erect, the vessels will be straight and dilated.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The helicine branches of the deep artery of the penis supply the corpora cavernosa.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

20807.name: Ureteric Branches of Common Iliac Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Common iliac artery.

Course: Laterally towards the ureter.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Ureter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Ureteric branches arise from the common iliac artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the common iliac artery approach the ureter on its medial aspect.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the common iliac artery supply the inferior portion of the abdominal portion of the ureter.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Renal Artery.

Course: Branches from the renal artery near to the renal hilum.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Superior third of the ureter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Small ureteric branches arise from the renal artery, just as it enters the kidney at the renal hilum. The ureter emerges from the kidney at the same location.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ureteric branches pass immediately to the ureter and form an arterial plexus around it.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Ramifications of the ureteric branches form arterioles and capillaries that supply the tissues of the ureter. These form anastomoses with ureteric branches from the abdominal aorta.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Anatomical variation in the arterial supply of the ureter is common. This long structure is supplied segmentally by overlapping arteries from several sources. The superior third of the ureter is supplied by the ureteric branches of the renal artery.

25476.name: Ureteric Branches of Artery of Ductus Deferens

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Artery of ductus deferens.

Course: Pass towards the urethra.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Distal ureter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Near the bladder and the ductus deferens, several ureteric branches arise from the artery of the ductus deferens.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ureteric branches will pass superiorly along the distal ureter, anastomosing with more proximal branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the artery of the ductus deferens supply the distal ureter.

22654.name: Ureteric Branches of Inferior Vesical Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior vesical artery.

Course: Medially towards the ureter.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Ureter and trigone of bladder.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Ureteric branches arise from the inferior vesical artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the inferior vesical artery approach the ureter on its lateral aspect.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the inferior vesical artery supply the inferior part of the pelvic portion of the ureter, as well as the trigone of the bladder (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Testicular artery.

Course: Towards the ureters.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Portion of the abdominal ureters.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Ureteric branches originate from the testicular artery as it descends adjacent to the ureters within the abdominal cavity.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the testicular artery travel a short distance to the ureter.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the testicular artery supply the ureters in the region where the testicular artery and the ureter lie in close proximity to each other within the abdominal cavity.

20964.name: Ureteric Branches of Internal Iliac Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal iliac artery.

Course: Medially towards the ureter.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Ureter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Ureteric branches arise from the internal iliac artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the internal iliac artery approach the ureter on its lateral aspect.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the internal iliac artery supply the superior part of the pelvic portion of the ureter.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Abdominal aorta.

Course: Laterally towards the ureter.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Ureter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Ureteric branches arise from the inferior portion of the abdominal aorta.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the abdominal aorta approach the medial aspect of the ureter.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ureteric branches of the abdominal aorta supply the inferior part of the abdominal portion of the ureter.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal pudendal artery.

Course: Passes through the perineal membrane, through corpus spongiosum to reach the glans penis (male).

Branches: No branches.

Supplied Structures: Urethra (males and females), corpus spongiosum, and glans penis (males).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The urethral artery originates in the superficial perineal pouch, just inferior to the perineal membrane.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
In males, the urethral artery passes medially to travel through the corpus spongiosum to reach the glans penis. It travels through the perineal membrane, through corpus spongiosum and into the glans penis.

As the urethra is much shorter in females, the urethral artery is much small in caliber and is not always present. In these cases, the urethra is supplied by the vaginal and inferior vesical arteries.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The urethral artery does not give off any branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: In males, the urethral artery supplies the urethra, corpus spongiosum, and glans penis. In females, the urethral artery may be present and supplies the urethra.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Segmental arteries of kidney.

Course: Extend outward from near the renal papillae within the renal columns.

Branches: The interlobar arteries bifurcate into arcuate arteries just as they reach the renal cortex, and these branches travel in opposite directions across the cortex.

Supplied Structures: Renal columns.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The renal segmental arteries give rise to renal interlobar arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Renal interlobar arteries pass from the renal pelvis side (deep) to the cortex side (superficial) along the renal columns on either side of a renal pyramid.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The interlobar arteries bifurcate just as they reach the renal cortex (juxtamedullary zone of the cortex) sending arcuate arteries in opposite directions that parallel the external surface of the kidney.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The interlobar arteries supply the renal columns, and will ultimately, through one or more generations of branches, provide the afferent glomerular input of the nephron.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior branch of renal artery.

Course: Passes posterior to the renal pelvis, superiorly and laterally.

Branches: Interlobar branches.

Supplied Structures: Posterior lobe of the kidney.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior segmental artery is the direct continuation of the posterior branch of the renal artery. Its name changes as it passes through the hilum of the kidney (renal sinus).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior segmental artery passes posterior to the renal pelvis and travels laterally, more or less horizontally.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The posterior segmental artery gives rise to interlobar branches, usually one for each renal pyramid within the posterior lobe of the kidney.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior segmental artery supplies the posterior lobe of the kidney, which includes all of the central-posterior surface of the kidney. This excludes the superior and inferior poles and a small posterolateral portion (Rani et al., 2014).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - The segmental arteries of the kidney are virtual end arteries. They supply non-overlapping “segments” of kidney tissue. In other words, the segments are defined by the vascular territories of the segmental arterial branches. This has important implications in kidney segmental resection.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Rani, N., Singh, S., Dhar, P. and Kumar, R. (2014) 'Surgical importance of arterial segments of human kidneys: an angiography and corrosion cast study', Journal of clinical and diagnostic research : JCDR, 8(3), pp. 1-3.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior branch of renal artery.

Course: Passes anterior to the renal pelvis, superiorly and laterally.

Branches: Interlobar branches.

Supplied Structures: Superior (or apical) lobe of the kidney.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior segmental artery of the kidney is one of four branches of the anterior branch of the renal artery that usually occurs in the hilum of the kidney (renal sinus).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior segmental artery of the kidney passes anterior to the renal pelvis, steeply superior and laterally towards the superior pole of the kidney.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The superior segmental artery of the kidney gives rise to interlobar branches, usually one for each renal pyramid within the apical and superior lobes of the kidney.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superior segmental artery of the kidney supplies the superior (or apical) lobe of the kidney. This includes the entire superior pole, including the anterior and posterior surfaces of the kidney (Rani et al., 2014).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - The segmental arteries of the kidney are virtual end arteries. They supply non-overlapping “segments” of kidney tissue. In other words, the segments are defined by the vascular territories of the segmental arterial branches. This has important implications in kidney segmental resection.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Rani, N., Singh, S., Dhar, P. and Kumar, R. (2014) 'Surgical importance of arterial segments of human kidneys: an angiography and corrosion cast study', Journal of clinical and diagnostic research : JCDR, 8(3), pp. 1-3.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior branch of renal artery.

Course: Passes anterior to the renal pelvis, inferiorly and laterally

Branches: Interlobar branches.

Supplied Structures: Inferior lobe of the kidney.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior segmental artery is one of four branches of the anterior branch of the renal artery that usually occurs in the hilum of the kidney (renal sinus).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior segmental artery passes anterior to the renal pelvis, inferiorly and laterally towards the inferior pole of the kidney.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The inferior segmental artery gives rise to interlobar branches, usually one for each renal pyramid within the inferior lobe of the kidney.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The inferior segmental artery supplies the inferior lobe of the kidney, which encompasses the whole of the inferior pole of the kidney, including the anterior and posterior surfaces (Rani et al., 2014).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - The segmental arteries of the kidney are virtual end arteries. They supply non-overlapping “segments” of kidney tissue. In other words, the segments are defined by the vascular territories of the segmental arterial branches. This has important implications in kidney segmental resection.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Rani, N., Singh, S., Dhar, P. and Kumar, R. (2014) 'Surgical importance of arterial segments of human kidneys: an angiography and corrosion cast study', Journal of clinical and diagnostic research : JCDR, 8(3), pp. 1-3.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Renal artery primarily.

Course: Passes around the external surface of the kidney then penetrating the renal capsule.

Branches: Perirenal, perforating, and anastomotic branches.

Supplied Structures: Primarily perirenal fat but may serve as a source of collateral circulation for the kidney parenchyma via penetrating branches.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: There are three sets of capsular arteries: superior, middle, and inferior (Boijsen, 1959). For the most part, capsular arteries typically arise from the renal artery before dividing into anterior and posterior divisions. However, they may arise from other neighboring arteries such as the abdominal aorta, inferior suprarenal artery, or gonadal artery. Additionally, there may be multiple arteries from multiple sources.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Since the capsular artery is an extrarenal artery, it does not penetrate the parenchyma of the kidney via the hilar aspect. Instead, it passes around the external surface of the kidney before penetrating the renal capsule.

sections.title: Branches
Supplied Structures
sections.text: The capsular branches supply the perirenal fat capsule and provides a source of collateral circulation with the arterial supply of the renal parenchyma primarily served by the intrarenal arterial system.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - The capsular artery complex can serve as an important source of collateral circulation in an ischemic kidney (Meyers et al., 1967).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Boijsen, E. (1959) 'Angiographic studies of the anatomy of single and multiple renal arteries', Acta Radiol Suppl, 183, pp. 1-135.

Meyers, M. A., Friedenberg, R. M., King, M. C. and Meng, C.-H. (1967) 'The Significance of the Renal Capsular Arteries', The British Journal of Radiology, 40(480), pp. 949-956.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Left lateral side of abdominal aorta.

Course: Passes approximately at a right angle from the aorta and travels laterally into the renal hilum.

Branches: Inferior suprarenal, ureteric, anterior and posterior renal arteries.

Supplied Structures: Left kidney, part of the suprarenal gland, and left superior ureter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The left renal artery originates at the left lateral margin of the aorta, slightly superior to the origin of the right renal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The left renal artery passes anteriorly to the left renal vein, across the left crus of the diaphragm, entering the kidney at the renal hilum.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The left renal artery branches into the inferior suprarenal and ureteric arteries, and the terminal branches of the anterior and posterior renal branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The renal artery supplies the perirenal fat, renal capsule, and cortex and medulla of the kidney. The renal artery is one of the three arteries that supply the suprarenal gland, where it supplies the inferior portion of this endocrine gland.

It is one of several sets of segmental arteries that supply the ureter. The renal artery supplies the superior most portion of the ureter.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Accessory renal arteries

- Renal artery stenosis

- Hypertension

19008.name: Anterior Inferior Segmental Artery of Kidney

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior branch of renal artery.

Course: Passes anterior to the renal pelvis, laterally and slightly inferiorly.

Branches: Interlobar branches.

Supplied Structures: Anteroinferior lobe of the kidney.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior inferior segmental artery is one of four branches of the anterior branch of the renal artery that usually occurs in the hilum of the kidney (renal sinus).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior inferior segmental artery passes anterior to the renal pelvis, laterally and angled slightly inferiorly.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior inferior segmental artery gives rise to interlobar branches, usually one for each renal pyramid within the anteroinferior lobe of the kidney.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior inferior segmental artery supplies the anteroinferior lobe of the kidney, which includes the central anteroinferior region, extending to the lateral aspect and slightly onto the posterior surface of the kidney (Rani et al., 2014).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - The segmental arteries of the kidney are virtual end arteries. They supply non-overlapping “segments” of kidney tissue. In other words, the segments are defined by the vascular territories of the segmental arterial branches. This has important implications in kidney segmental resection.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Rani, N., Singh, S., Dhar, P. and Kumar, R. (2014) 'Surgical importance of arterial segments of human kidneys: an angiography and corrosion cast study', Journal of clinical and diagnostic research : JCDR, 8(3), pp. 1-3.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Renal artery.

Course: Segmental renal branches enter the kidney at renal hilum.

Branches: Segmental arterial branches.

Supplied Structures: Kidney.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior branch of the renal artery is formed by the bifurcation of the renal artery into two main branches next to, or at, the renal hilum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior branch of the renal artery travels almost horizontally. Along its lateral course, the artery travels posteriorly to the renal vein, and anteriorly to the ureter.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The number of anterior renal branches varies between individuals. There may be up to five segmental arterial branches. The branches continue to divide, passing to the renal columns within the cortex of the kidney, before terminating as the glomeruli of the nephron.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior branch of the renal artery supplies the medulla and cortex of the kidney.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Renal Artery.

Course: Enters kidney at the renal hilum.

Branches: Segmental arterial branches.

Supplied Structures: Kidney.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior branch of the renal artery is formed by the bifurcation of the renal artery into two main branches next to, or at, the renal hilum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior branch of the renal artery travels almost horizontally. The artery takes a lateral course and travels posteriorly to the ureter.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The number of posterior branches of the renal artery varies between individuals. They continue to divide, passing to the renal columns within the cortex of the kidney, before terminating as the glomeruli of the nephron.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior branch of the renal artery supplies the medulla and cortex of the kidney.

19263.name: Anterior Superior Segmental Artery of Kidney

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior branch of renal artery.

Course: Passes anterior to the renal pelvis, superiorly and laterally.

Branches: Interlobar branches.

Supplied Structures: Anterosuperior lobe of the kidney.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior superior segmental artery is one of four branches of the anterior branch of the renal artery that usually occurs in the hilum of the kidney (renal sinus).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior superior segmental artery passes anterior to the renal pelvis, superiorly and laterally towards the superior pole of the kidney. It does not ascend as steeply as the superior segmental artery. It does not extend into the superior pole.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior superior segmental artery gives rise to interlobar branches, usually one for each renal pyramid within the anterosuperior lobe of the kidney.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior superior segmental artery supplies the anterosuperior lobe of the kidney, which includes the central anterosuperior region, extending to the lateral aspect and slightly onto the posterior surface of the kidney. It can be considered to include the inferior-most portion of the superior pole (Rani et al., 2014).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - The segmental arteries of the kidney are virtual end arteries. They supply non-overlapping “segments” of kidney tissue. In other words, the segments are defined by the vascular territories of the segmental arterial branches. This has important implications in kidney segmental resection.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Rani, N., Singh, S., Dhar, P. and Kumar, R. (2014) 'Surgical importance of arterial segments of human kidneys: an angiography and corrosion cast study', Journal of clinical and diagnostic research : JCDR, 8(3), pp. 1-3.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Right lateral side of abdominal aorta.

Course: Passes approximately at a right angle from the aorta and travels laterally into the renal hilum.

Branches: Inferior suprarenal, ureteric, and anterior and posterior renal arteries.

Supplied Structures: Right kidney, part of the suprarenal gland, and right superior ureter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The right renal artery originates at the right lateral margin of the aorta, slightly inferior to the origin of the left renal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The right renal artery passes anteriorly to the left renal vein, across the right crus of the diaphragm, entering the kidney at the renal hilum.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The right renal artery branches into the inferior suprarenal arteries, the ureteric artery, and the terminal branches of the anterior and posterior renal branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The renal artery supplies the perirenal fat, renal capsule, and cortex and medulla of the kidney. The renal artery is one of the three arteries that supply the suprarenal gland, where it supplies the inferior portion of this endocrine gland.

It is one of several sets of segmental arteries that supply the ureter. The renal artery supplies the superior most portion of the ureter.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Accessory renal arteries

- Renal artery stenosis

- Hypertension

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior division of internal iliac artery (males) or branch of the vaginal artery (females).

Course: Travels anteriorly to lower portion of bladder and ramifies along its surface.

Branches: Prostatic artery and the artery of the ductus deferens (males).

Supplied Structures: Bladder, prostate, seminal glands, distal ureter, and ductus deferens.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
In males, the inferior vesical artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. Sometimes, the vessel may arise directly from the middle anorectal artery.

In females, the inferior vesical artery is a branch of the vaginal artery. The vaginal artery is a homologue of the inferior vesical arteries in males as it arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior vesical artery travels anteriorly from its origin to enter the lateral ligament of the bladder.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
In males, the inferior vesical artery branches into the prostatic artery and occasionally the artery of the ductus deferens. However, the artery to the ductus deferens is normally a branch of the superior vesical artery.

In females, the artery does not branch, but it does form anastomosis with the superior vesical artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
In males, the artery supplies the bladder, prostate, seminal glands, distal ureter, and ductus deferens.

In females, the artery ramifies on the surface of the bladder in order to supply it.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal iliac artery.

Course: Travels anteriorly to abdominal wall, then superiorly to the umbilicus.

Branches: Superior vesical arteries and the artery to ductus deferens.

Supplied Structures: Superior bladder, inferior ureter, ductus deferens, and seminal vesicle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Paired umbilical arteries arise from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. It is usually an early proximal branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The umbilical artery passes anteromedially across the pelvis to the anterior abdominal wall. It then passes superiorly, along the inner surface of the anterior wall. Right and left arteries pass medially as they ascend to converge on the umbilicus. In the fetus, this vessel is entirely patent and passes through the abdominal wall at the umbilicus, into the umbilical cord to the placenta. After birth the vessel becomes fibrotic, except for the most proximal, pelvic portion that gives off the superior vesical arteries. The occluded part of the umbilical artery forms the medial umbilical folds, which are located along the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
Up to four superior vesical arteries arise from the proximal part of the umbilical artery.

In males, the artery may give off a branch to the ductus deferens. However, there is considerable anatomical variation in the origin of this vessel. The artery to the ductus deferens may branch exclusively from the superior vesical arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The umbilical artery supplies the superior portion of the bladder. In males, the artery gives off variable branches that supply the ductus deferens, testis and seminal vesicle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Peritoneal folds produced by the non-pelvic remnant of the embryonic umbilical artery originating from approximately the apex of the bladder.

Course: Passes superiorly along the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall.

Branches: No branches.

Supplied Structures: Patent vessel that returns blood from fetal systemic circulation to the placenta but becomes occluded by fibrotic tissue in the adult.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The medial umbilical ligament is one of three (one single, and two paired) folds of peritoneum on the anterior abdominal wall, that are produced by underlying structures.

The paired medial umbilical ligaments are formed from the remaining fibrous tissue of the occluded umbilical artery. They originate distal to the superior vesical arteries, approximately at the apex of the bladder, where they become occluded. Proximal to this point, the umbilical artery remains patent, and branches into the superior vesical artery, that supply the bladder.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The medial umbilical ligaments pass superiorly along the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall, between the layers of the peritoneum and transversalis fascia. They converge with their contralateral partner, by passing medially towards the umbilicus.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: No branches are given off by the umbilical artery distal to the superior vesical arteries.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: In the fetus, the umbilical artery returns deoxygenated, nutrient depleted blood f to the placenta. In the adult, the structure becomes fibrotic and occluded.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Proximal patent part of umbilical artery.

Course: Multiple branches pass medially to the superior aspect of the bladder.

Branches: Ureteric artery and artery to ductus deferens (male).

Supplied Structures: Superior portion of the bladder and the inferior portion of the ureter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior vesical arteries arise from the patent portion of the umbilical artery as it passes anteriorly towards the abdominal wall.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The small superior vesical arteries pass medially to the superior aspect of the bladder.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The superior vesical arteries give off a ureteric branch that supplies the inferior portion or the ureter. In males, the superior vesical artery gives off the artery to ductus deferens.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superior vesical artery supplies the superior portion of the bladder and superior part of the intrapelvic portion of the ureter. In males, the artery to the ductus deferens accompanies the ductus to the testis.

17003.name: Right Marginal Branch of Right Coronary Artery
17003.latin: Ramus marginalis dexter arteriae coronariae dextrae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Right coronary artery.

Course: Inferiorly along right cardiac border of right ventricle.

Branches: Several small unnamed branches.

Supplied Structures: Contributes to the supply of the right ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The right marginal branch of the right coronary artery arises from the right coronary artery along the right cardiac border.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The right marginal branch courses inferiorly towards the apex of the heart.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The right marginal branch ramifies as it descends towards the apex.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The right marginal branch contributes to the supply of the right ventricle.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Coronary artery disease

- Coronary atherosclerosis

- Coronary bypass graft

- Coronary angioplasty

- Coronary occlusion

- Coronary revascularization

- Coronary artery fistula

20489.name: Sinuatrial Nodal Branch of Right Coronary Artery
20489.latin: Ramus nodi sinuatrialis arteriae coronariae dextrae
alternate: Sino-atrial Nodal Branch of Right Coronary Artery
Sinoatrial Nodal Branch of Right Coronary Artery
Sinu-atrial Nodal Branch of Right Coronary Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Right coronary artery.

Course: Initially, between aorta and right atrial appendage. It then winds around superior vena cava.

Branches: Several small unnamed branches and a larger branch to the crista terminalis.

Supplied Structures: Sinuatrial node and adjacent portions of the atria.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The sinuatrial branch is one of the small atrial branches. It arises on the anterior aspect of the right atrium. However, it may originate along the lateral or sometimes the poster aspect of the right atrium (Standring, 2016). The sinuatrial nodal artery may also arise from the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery in 40% of individuals (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013; Pejković et al., 2008).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The sinuatrial nodal branch typically courses between the right atrial appendage and the aorta. Despite its variable origin, it winds around the superior vena cava and gives off small branches as it courses towards the sinuatrial node.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are several small branches which extend along the right and left atria. It also gives a larger branch to the crista terminalis, which courses through the sinuatrial node.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The sinuatrial nodal branch contributes to the vascular supply of the right atrium and supplies the sinuatrial node.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Coronary artery disease

- Coronary atherosclerosis

- Coronary bypass graft

- Coronary angioplasty

- Coronary occlusion

- Coronary revascularization

- Coronary artery fistula

23484.name: Conal Branch of Right Coronary Artery
23484.latin: Ramus coni arteriosi arteriae coronariae dextrae
alternate: Conus Branch of Right Coronary Artery
Right Conal Branch of Right Coronary Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Right coronary artery.

Course: Inferiorly along the conus arteriosus.

Branches: Small unnamed branches.

Supplied Structures: Conus arteriosus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The conal branch is the first branch of the right coronary artery. It may arise from the anterior aortic sinus in up to one third of individuals where it may occasionally be called the third coronary artery (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The conal branch of the right coronary artery is a small artery that courses in an anteroinferior direction over the upper portion of the right ventricle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The conal branch of the right coronary artery has many small unnamed branches that may anastomose with the branches of the left interventricular artery. In this case, they form an anastomotic ring (annulus of Vieussens) which encircles the outflow tract of the right ventricle (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The conal branch of the right coronary artery supplies the region of the conus arteriosus.

18678.name: Inferior Left Ventricular Branch of Circumflex Artery of Heart
18678.latin: Ramus inferior ventriculi sinistri arteriae circumflexae cordis
alternate: Inferior Left Ventricular Branch of Left Coronary Artery
Posterior Left Ventricular Branch of Circumflex Artery of Heart
Posterior Left Ventricular Branch of Circumflex Branch of Left Coronary Artery
Posterior Left Ventricular Branch of Left Coronary Artery
Ramus inferior ventriculi sinistri arteriae coronariae sinistrae
Ramus posterior ventriculi sinistri arteriae circumflexae cordis
Ramus posterior ventriculi sinistri arteriae coronariae sinistrae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Circumflex artery of heart.

Course: Descends on the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface of heart.

Branches: Several small branches.

Supplied Structures: Inferior (diaphragmatic) surface of heart.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior left ventricular branch arises from the circumflex artery on the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior left ventricular branch descends along the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface of the left ventricle towards the apex. It is accompanied by the posterior vein of the left ventricle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The inferior left ventricular branch gives rise to several small unnamed branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The inferior left ventricular branch of the circumflex artery contributes to the supply of the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Coronary artery disease

- Coronary atherosclerosis

- Coronary bypass graft

- Coronary angioplasty

- Coronary occlusion

- Coronary revascularization

- Coronary artery fistula

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Proximal portion of ascending aorta.

Course: Within coronary sulcus.

Branches: Circumflex and anterior interventricular arteries.

Supplied Structures: Left atrium, majority of left ventricles, portion of right ventricle, anterior two thirds of interventricular septum, atrioventricular bundle, and sinuatrial node.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The coronary arteries are the first branches of the thoracic aorta and the only branches of the ascending aorta, arising from its proximal portion below the sinutubular junction.

The left coronary artery arises from the left coronary aortic sinus. It is larger in diameter than the right coronary artery, since it provides vascular supply to a greater portion of the myocardium and epicardium. Occasionally, there is a double origin, and this corresponds to the two main branches of the left coronary artery, namely the circumflex and the anterior interventricular arteries.

The arteries are subepicardial but may be more deeply embedded in regions such as the interventricular grooves. In addition, they are covered by adipose tissue and may be somewhat hidden on initial inspection of the heart during cadaveric dissection.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The left coronary artery sits between the pulmonary trunk and the left atrial appendage. It courses towards the atrioventricular groove en route to the left cardiac border. This portion does not typically have any branches; however, a small atrial branch may arise and on a rare occasion it may give off the sinuatrial nodal artery (Standring, 2016).

Within the atrioventricular groove, the left coronary artery bifurcates into the circumflex and anterior interventricular arteries. The distance between its origin and its first branch is variable.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
There are two main branches of the left coronary artery, the circumflex and anterior interventricular branches. The circumflex branch travels within the coronary sulcus from the anterior aspect to the posterior aspect of the heart. The anterior interventricular branch is often considered a continuation of the left coronary artery. It descends within the anterior interventricular sulcus (Standring, 2016).

Variations in the branching pattern of the coronary arteries exist, where the posterior interventricular branch may arise from the left coronary artery (33% of individuals) (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The left coronary artery supplies the majority of the left ventricle, a narrow portion of the right ventricle, the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, and the majority of the left atrium.

The arterial supply to the diaphragmatic surface of the heart is the most variable in terms of right or left coronary arterial supply. Its supply is related to which vessel is dominant. The term dominant does not refer to the amount of cardiac tissue supplied by the arteries, but from which coronary artery that gives rise to the inferior interventricular artery (aka the posterior descending artery [PDA] or posterior interventricular artery). This artery supplies the diaphragmatic inferolateral wall of the left ventricle. The right coronary artery is dominant in 67% of individuals (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

17349.name: Anterior Interventricular Artery
alternate: Anterior Interventricular Branch of Left Coronary Artery
Left Anterior Descending Branch of Left Coronary Artery
Ramus descendens anterior arteriae coronariae sinistrae
Ramus interventricularis anterior arteriae coronariae sinistrae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Left coronary artery.

Course: Descends within the coronary sulcus.

Branches: Diagonal, anterior septal, right and left atrial and ventricular branches.

Supplied Structures: Adjacent portions of right and left ventricle, anterior two thirds of interventricular septum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: There are two main branches of the left coronary artery, the circumflex and anterior interventricular branches. The anterior interventricular branch is often considered a continuation of the left coronary artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery descends within the anterior interventricular groove and is accompanied by the great cardiac vein. This artery usually reaches the apex, but it may extend beyond the apex to the posterior (inferior) aspect of the heart. Here, it meets the terminal portion of the posterior interventricular artery.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The right and left anterior ventricular arteries are branches of the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery. The right branches are small and few, but the left branches are large and course obliquely across the left-hand side of the heart. One particular branch on the left is the diagonal artery which is described separately. In addition, several septal branches course along the interventricular septum to supply the anterior two-thirds of the septum as well as the atrioventricular bundle. Occasionally there is a left conal branch which anastomoses with the conal branch of the right coronary artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior interventricular branch of left coronary artery supplies the adjacent portions of right and left ventricle. It also supplies the anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum as well as the atrioventricular bundle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The atrial branches course superiorly on the left atrium.

sections.title: Branches

sections.title: Supplied Structures

18983.name: Diagonal Branch of Anterior Interventricular Artery
alternate: Lateral Branch of Anterior Interventricular Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior interventricular artery.

Course: Descends along anterior surface of left ventricle.

Branches: No named branches.

Supplied Structures: Anterior surface of the left ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The diagonal branch is a common variant which is present in 33–50% of individuals (Standring, 2016). It is the largest branch that arises from the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The diagonal branch descends along the anterior (or sternocostal) surface of the left ventricle, parallel to the anterior interventricular artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The diagonal branch contributes to the supply of the anterior surface of the left ventricle.

17065.name: Ventricular Branches of Right Coronary Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Right coronary artery.

Course: Inferiorly along the right ventricle.

Branches: Several small unnamed branches.

Supplied Structures: Right ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
There are a series of ventricular branches that arise from the right coronary artery and can be divided into anterior and posterior ventricular branches.

Between the origin of the right coronary artery and the origin of the right marginal artery, there are a series of small branches that supply the anterior aspect of the right atrium and ventricle. Of these branches there are usually two or three anterior ventricular branches. There are also two or three posterior ventricular branches that originate between the right marginal artery and the posterior interventricular sulcus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ventricular branches course inferiorly along the anterior and posterior (inferior) aspects of the right ventricle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The ventricular branches ramify as they descend towards the apex along the right ventricle.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ventricular branches contribute to the supply of the right ventricle.

18330.name: Atrioventricular Nodal Branch of Right Coronary Artery

Course: It extends from the region of posterior interventricular sulcus towards atrioventricular node.

Branches: No named branches.

Supplied Structures: Atrioventricular node.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The atrioventricular nodal branch arises from the right coronary artery near the posterior interventricular sulcus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The atrioventricular nodal branch has a short course from the external surface of the heart near the origin of the posterior interventricular artery. It then courses inferiorly through the interatrial septum towards the atrioventricular node.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches of the atrioventricular nodal branch.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The atrioventricular nodal branch supplies the atrioventricular node.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:

Course: Inferiorly on diaphragmatic surface of left ventricle

Branches: Several small unnamed branches

Supplied Structures: Contributes to the supply of the left ventricle

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The right inferolateral branch arises from the right coronary artery after it has reached the left ventricle on the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle. This branch is a common variation of the branching pattern of the right coronary artery on the diaphragmatic surface. Other variations do not have this branch and the final branch of the right coronary artery is the posterior interventricular artery (Tubbs et al., 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The right inferolateral branch runs inferiorly towards the apex of the heart along the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The right inferolateral branch gives off several small unnamed branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The right inferolateral branch contributes to the supply of the left ventricle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Circumflex branch of the left coronary artery.

Course: It descends along the left cardiac border of the left ventricle.

Branches: Several small unnamed branches.

Supplied Structures: Left ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The left marginal branch arises from the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery and it is often calledreferred to as the obtuse marginal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The left marginal branch runs approximately perpendicular to the circumflex artery. It courses inferiorly on the left ventricle along the left cardiac border (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The left marginal branch gives rise to several small unnamed branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The left marginal branch contributes to the supply of the left ventricle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Proximal portion of the ascending aorta.

Course: It runs in the coronary sulcus from the anterior aspect heart to the posterior interventricular sulcus.

Branches: Conus, atrial, and ventricular branches; right marginal arteries; atrioventricular nodal, sinuatrial nodal, posterior interventricular, and right posterolateral branches.

Supplied Structures: Right atrium, most of right ventricle, a portion of the left ventricle (inferior surface), posterior one third of the interventricular septum, sinuatrial node (in approx. 60% of individuals) and the atrioventricular node (in approx. 80% of individuals).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The coronary arteries are the first branches of the thoracic aorta and the only branches of the ascending aorta, arising from its proximal portion below the sinutubular junction.

The right coronary artery arises from the right coronary aortic sinus. It is smaller in diameter than the left coronary artery. The arteries are subepicardial but may be more deeply embedded in regions such as the interventricular grooves. In addition, they are covered by adipose tissue and may be somewhat hidden on initial inspection of the heart during cadaveric dissection.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The right coronary artery first courses in an anterior direction, then towards the right where it sits between the right atrial appendage and the pulmonary trunk to reach the coronary sulcus (atrioventricular groove). In this groove, it descends towards the right in a near vertical manner, along the right cardiac border. It then curves posteriorly where it reaches the junction between the interatrial and the interventricular grooves (the cardiac crux).

The position of the termination of the artery is variable. It often terminates to the left of the crux where it frequently joins the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The conus branch is the first branch of the right coronary artery. There are a series of small branches that supply the anterior aspect of the right atrium and ventricle. Of these branches there are usually two or three anterior ventricular branches.

The next branch is the right marginal artery. It is the largest of the ventricular branches and runs inferiorly where it almost reaches the apex. There are also a series of posterior ventricular branches. It then gives the posterior interventricular artery and often the right posterolateral branch of the right coronary artery.

The right coronary artery usually gives off both the sinuatrial nodal branch and the atrioventricular nodal branch (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The right coronary artery supplies almost the entire right ventricle, as well as the right atrium and a portion of the left atrium. It supplies the posterior one third of the interventricular septum. It also contributes to the supply of the conduction system, including the sinuatrial node and the atrioventricular node.

The arterial supply to the diaphragmatic surface of the heart is the most variable in terms of right or left coronary arterial supply. Its supply is related to which vessel is dominant. The term dominant does not refer to the amount of cardiac tissue supplied by the arteries, but from which coronary artery that gives rise to the inferior interventricular artery (aka the posterior descending artery [PDA] or posterior interventricular artery). This artery supplies the diaphragmatic inferolateral wall of the left ventricle. The right coronary artery is dominant in 67% of individuals (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

Course: Inferiorly within posterior interventricular sulcus towards the apex.

Branches: Several small unnamed branches.

Supplied Structures: Posterior one third of the interventricular septum and adjacent portions of the right and left ventricles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior interventricular artery arises from the right coronary artery in 60% of individuals (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior interventricular artery descends within the posterior interventricular sulcus towards the apex of the heart.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are several small unnamed branches that arise from the inferior interventricular artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures

20694.name: Circumflex Artery of Heart
alternate: Circumflex Branch of Left Coronary Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Left coronary artery.

Course: Within coronary sulcus from anterior to posterior aspect of the heart.

Branches: Atrial, left marginal, and posterior left ventricular branches.

Supplied Structures: Left atrium and ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: There are two main branches of the left coronary artery. These are the circumflex and the anterior interventricular branches.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The circumflex artery travels along the anterior aspect of the heart, within the atrioventricular groove. Here, the left atrial appendage sits over the vessel anteriorly. As the name suggests, the circumflex branch curves to the left and becomes posterior, still within the atrioventricular groove. It continues as far as “the crux” and gives off the posterior interventricular artery in hearts with left coronary dominance (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The branches of the circumflex artery include the left marginal and anterior ventricular branches, which run parallel to the diagonal artery. The artery to the sinuatrial node may arise from the anterior portion of the circumflex artery. The artery to the atrioventricular node arises near the crux in 20% of individuals as a branch of the posterior interventricular artery when left dominance occurs (Standring, 2016). The posterior left ventricular branches in this case are diminished.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The circumflex branch contributes to the supply of the left atrium and ventricle.

sections.text:
