sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Along right atrium.

Course: Within the posterior portion of the coronary sulcus.

Tributaries: Small unnamed veins.

Drainage: Right atrium and ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The small cardiac vein originates along the right atrium.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The small cardiac vein follows the course of the right marginal artery and crosses deep to the right coronary artery as it travels to the coronary sinus. It drains into the coronary sinus near its termination.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The small cardiac vein is formed by the union of small unnamed veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The small cardiac vein contributes to the drainage of the posterior portion of the right atrium and ventricles.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Within the anterior interventricular sulcus near the apex of the heart.

Course: Superiorly.

Tributaries: Small unnamed veins.

Drainage: Left ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior interventricular vein arises near the apex of the heart within the anterior interventricular groove.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior interventricular vein courses superiorly where it becomes the great cardiac vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior interventricular vein is formed by the union of small unnamed veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior interventricular vein contributes to the drainage of the inferior portion of the left ventricle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: The cardiac apex.

Course: Superiorly within the posterior interventricular sulcus.

Tributaries: Small unnamed veins.

Drainage: Inferior (diaphragmatic) surface of the heart.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle cardiac vein originates at the cardiac apex.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The middle cardiac vein courses superiorly within the posterior interventricular groove and drains into the coronary sinus. Within in the posterior interventricular groove, it is accompanied by the posterior interventricular artery.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The middle cardiac vein is formed by the union of small unnamed veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The middle cardiac vein drains the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface of the heart.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle.

Course: Superiorly to the coronary sinus.

Tributaries: Small unnamed veins.

Drainage: Left ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior vein of the left ventricle originates along the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior vein of the left ventricle courses superiorly along the left ventricle to drain into the coronary sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior vein of the left ventricle is formed by the union of small unnamed veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior vein of the left ventricle contributes to the venous drainage of the left ventricle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior interventricular sulcus.

Course: Superiorly within the anterior interventricular sulcus then within the coronary sulcus to the coronary sinus.

Tributaries: Left marginal, ventricular, atrial, and oblique veins.

Drainage: Left ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The great cardiac vein originates at the apex of the heart as the anterior interventricular vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The great cardiac vein ascends within the anterior interventricular groove then courses to the left to the posterior aspect of the heart where it enters the coronary sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The great cardiac vein receives its tributaries from the left side of the heart via the left marginal vein, as well as the ventricular and atrial veins. It receives the oblique vein at the inferior (posterior) surface of the heart as it courses towards the coronary sinus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The great cardiac vein drains most of the left side of the heart.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior interventricular region.

Course: Along the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface of the heart in the region of the coronary sulcus and runs through the myocardium to drain into the right atrium.

Tributaries: The great, middle, and small cardiac veins, the posterior vein of the left ventricle, the oblique vein of the left atrium, and the left marginal vein.

Drainage: External aspect of the myocardium of the heart.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The coronary sinus is approximately 2–3 cm long and sits at the junction of the atrioventricular sulcus and the posterior interventricular sulcus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The coronary sinus sits between the inferior vena cava and the atrioventricular opening between the right atrium and ventricle. The inner opening of the coronary sinus may be covered by the Thebesian valve (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The great, middle, and small cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus. Additionally, it receives the posterior vein of the left ventricle, the oblique vein of the left atrium, and the left marginal vein (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016; Standring, 2016). Occasionally, if the coronary sulcus is absent, venous drainage of the heart is completed by drainage into the pulmonary trunk (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The coronary sinus delivers deoxygenated blood from the myocardium to the right atrium.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: The inferior margin of the heart.

Course: Superiorly along the right ventricle.

Tributaries: Several unnamed veins.

Drainage: Right atrium and ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The right marginal vein arises along the right ventricle at the inferior border of the heart, the junction between the anterior (sternocostal) and inferior (diaphragmatic) surfaces of the heart.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The right marginal vein courses superiorly towards the right atrium where it drains into the right atrium. However, it may also unite with the anterior cardiac veins (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The right marginal vein is formed by the union of several small unnamed veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The right marginal vein contributes to the drainage of the right atrium and ventricle.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Structures Drained

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Along the right ventricle.

Course: Around the right coronary artery, draining into the right atrium.

Tributaries: Small unnamed veins.

Drainage: Anterior aspect of the right ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: There are typically between two and five anterior cardiac veins that sit on the right ventricle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior cardiac veins travel superiorly and follow the ventricular branches of the right coronary artery. They then course over the right coronary artery within the coronary sulcus and drain into the right atrium.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior cardiac veins are formed by the union of small unnamed veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior cardiac veins contribute to the drainage of the anterior aspect of the right ventricle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lateral aspect of left ventricle.

Course: Superiorly along left cardiac border.

Tributaries: Small unnamed veins.

Drainage: Left ventricle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The left marginal vein originates on the left ventricle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: It courses with the left marginal artery as it travels superiorly along the left cardiac border. It drains into the great cardiac vein or the coronary sinus (Standring, 2016, Tubbs et al., 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The left marginal vein is formed by the union of small unnamed veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The left marginal vein contributes to the venous drainage of the left ventricle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inguinal region of the superficial fascia of the anterior abdominal wall.

Course: Runs inferiorly to drains into the long saphenous vein or femoral vein.

Tributaries: Thoracoepigastric vein and tributaries of the paraumbilical veins.

Drainage: Skin of medial thigh, external genitalia, and pubic symphysis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial epigastric vein originates in the inguinal region of the superficial fascia of the anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the vein travels inferiorly, within the superficial fascia of the abdominal wall, to drain into the long saphenous vein or femoral vein, close to the saphenous opening.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superficial epigastric vein receives tributaries from the paraumbilical and thoracoepigastric vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superficial epigastric vein drains the skin of the medial thigh, the external genitalia, and the pubic symphysis.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Between the internal abdominal oblique and transversus abdominis muscle in the anterior abdominal wall.

Course: Travels posterolaterally then medially towards the ascending lumbar vein.

Tributaries: Lumbar vertebral plexus.

Drainage: Posterior, lateral, and anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lumbar veins originate in the anterior abdominal wall, between the internal abdominal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. At their origin, the lumbar veins form anastomoses with the lower intercostal, subcostal, and lumbar veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lumbar veins accompany the corresponding lumbar arteries and are equivalent to the posterior intercostal veins. From its origin, the first lumbar vein travels posterolaterally then medially, between the transversus abdominis and the internal abdominal oblique muscles, towards the ascending lumbar vein. The ascending lumbar veins then join with the subcostal vein to form the azygos vein on the right, and the hemiazygos vein on the left.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The lumbar veins receive the lumbar vertebral plexus. Additionally, they form anastomoses with the lower intercostal, subcostal epigastric, circumflex iliac, and lateral thoracic veins anteriorly.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The lumbar veins drain the posterior, lateral, and anterior abdominal wall.

Course: Travels posterolaterally then medially towards the ascending lumbar vein.

Tributaries: Lumbar vertebral plexus.

Drainage: Posterior, lateral, and anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Origin

The ascending lumbar vein then joins with the subcostal vein to form the azygos vein on the right, and the hemiazygos vein on the left.

sections.title: Tributaries

sections.title: Structures Drained

sections.title: Origin

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the lumbar veins accompany the corresponding lumbar arteries and are equivalent to the posterior intercostal veins. From its origin, the fourth lumbar vein travels posterolaterally then medially, between the transversus abdominis and the internal abdominal oblique muscles, towards the ascending lumbar vein. The ascending lumbar vein then joins with the subcostal vein to form the azygos vein on the right, and the hemiazygos vein on the left.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The lumbar veins receive the lumbar vertebral plexus. Additionally, they form anastomoses with the lower intercostal, subcostal epigastric, circumflex iliac, and lateral thoracic veins anteriorly.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The lumbar veins drain the posterior, lateral, and anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Between the internal abdominal oblique and transversus abdominis muscle in the anterior abdominal wall.

Course: Travels posterolaterally then medially towards the ascending lumbar vein.

Tributaries: Lumbar vertebral plexus.

Drainage: Posterior, lateral, and anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lumbar veins originate in the anterior abdominal wall, between the internal abdominal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. At their origin, the lumbar veins form anastomoses with the lower intercostal, subcostal, and lumbar veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lumbar veins accompany the corresponding lumbar arteries and are equivalent to the posterior intercostal veins. From its origin, the second lumbar vein travels posterolaterally then medially, between the transversus abdominis and the internal abdominal oblique muscles, towards the ascending lumbar vein. The ascending lumbar vein then joins with the subcostal vein to form the azygos vein on the right, and the hemiazygos vein on the left.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The lumbar veins receive the lumbar vertebral plexus. Additionally, they form anastomoses with the lower intercostal, subcostal epigastric, circumflex iliac, and lateral thoracic veins anteriorly.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The lumbar veins drain the posterior, lateral, and anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Common iliac vein.

Course: Vertical course, anterior to the transverse process of lumbar vertebra.

Tributaries: Lumbar veins.

Drainage: Posterolateral abdominal wall.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ascending lumbar veins ascend from the common iliac veins in the pelvis, at approximately the level of the fifth lumbar vertebrae.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From their origin, the paired ascending lumbar veins runs vertically, anterior to the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae. They connect ipsilateral lumbar veins, iliolumbar, and common iliac veins. The azygos vein arises from the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and the subcostal vein. The hemiazygos vein arises from the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and the subcostal vein. The ascending lumbar veins and the azygos veins connect the inferior vena cava and the superior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The lumbar azygos vein usually enters the ascending lumbar vein. Additionally, it connects the lumbar veins from the ipsilateral side, but it can also connect the common iliac vein and iliolumbar vein. Blood flow in the lumbar veins can run in any direction.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Through the lumbar veins, the ascending lumbar veins drain the posterior and lateral abdominal wall into the azygos vein on the right, and the hemiazygos vein on the left.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises from within the rectus sheath.

Course: Ascends within the rectus sheath to drain into the internal thoracic vein.

Tributaries: Muscular and cutaneous tributaries.

Drainage: Anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior epigastric vein originates in the superior aspect of the rectus sheath, posterior to the rectus abdominis muscle, and forms an anastomosis with the inferior epigastric vein below.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the vein ascends within the rectus sheath, posterior to the rectus abdominis muscles, to drain into the internal thoracic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Along its course, the superior epigastric vein receives tributaries from small muscular and cutaneous branches. At its inferior portion, it forms an anastomosis with the inferior epigastric vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The vein drains the anterior abdominal wall and the diaphragm.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises from within the rectus sheath.

Course: Travels inferiorly, within the rectus sheath to drain into the external iliac vein.

Tributaries: Pubic, and obturator branch of the interior epigastric vein.

Drainage: Anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior epigastric vein arises from within the rectus sheath in the superior aspect of the anterior abdominal wall. At its origin, the vein will form anastomoses with the superior epigastric vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the inferior epigastric vein, descends in a relatively straight course, within the rectus sheath, posterior to the rectus abdominis muscle, to drain into the external iliac vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Small tributaries of the inferior epigastric vein drain the skin around the umbilicus and anastomose with terminal branches of the umbilical vein. Additionally, the vein receives the pubic and the obturator branch the inferior epigastric vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The muscular and cutaneous branches drain the muscles, peritoneum, aponeurosis, and skin of the anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Common iliac vein.

Course: Vertical course, anterior to the transverse process of lumbar vertebra.

Tributaries: Lumbar veins.

Drainage: Posterolateral abdominal wall.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ascending lumbar veins ascend from the common iliac veins in the pelvis, at approximately the level of the fifth lumbar vertebrae.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From their origin, the paired ascending lumbar veins runs vertically, anterior to the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae. They connect ipsilateral lumbar veins, iliolumbar, and common iliac veins. The azygos vein arises from the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and the subcostal vein. The hemiazygos vein arises from the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and the subcostal vein. The ascending lumbar veins and the azygos veins connect the inferior vena cava and the superior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The lumbar azygos vein usually enters the ascending lumbar vein. Additionally, it connects the lumbar veins from the ipsilateral side, but it can also connect the common iliac vein and iliolumbar vein. Blood flow in the lumbar veins can run in any direction.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Through the lumbar veins, the ascending lumbar veins drain the posterior and lateral abdominal wall into the azygos vein on the right, and the hemiazygos vein on the left.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior surface of respiratory diaphragm.

Course: Ascend through the middle mediastinum.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Pericardium, respiratory diaphragm, and mediastinal part of parietal pleura.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The pericardiacophrenic veins arise from the superior surface of the respiratory diaphragm.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, each pericardiacophrenic vein ascends through the middle mediastinum. It travels between the pleura and the lateral surface of the pericardium, then anterior to the lung root. Through its course, it is accompanied by the pericardiacophrenic artery and phrenic nerve. The pericardiacophrenic veins drain into the right and left brachiocephalic veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the pericardiacophrenic veins form an anastomosis with the superior phrenic and musculophrenic veins to ensure constant drainage of the diaphragm.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The pericardiacophrenic veins drain the pericardium, respiratory diaphragm, and mediastinal part of parietal pleura.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of small tributaries.

Course: Along superior surface of respiratory diaphragm.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Superior surface of diaphragm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior phrenic veins are formed by the union of small venules on the superior surface of the respiratory diaphragm.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior phrenic veins course along the superior surface of the respiratory diaphragm and are accompanied by the superior phrenic arteries. They descend posteriorly to unite with the hemiazygos and azygos veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, they do form an anastomosis with the musculophrenic and pericardiacophrenic veins to ensure constant drainage of the diaphragm.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior phrenic veins drain the vertebral portion of the respiratory diaphragm.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of small tributaries.

Course: Along superior surface of respiratory diaphragm.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Superior surface of diaphragm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior phrenic veins are formed by the union of small venules on the superior surface of the respiratory diaphragm.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior phrenic veins course along the superior surface of the respiratory diaphragm and are accompanied by the superior phrenic arteries. They descend posteriorly to unite with the hemiazygos and azygos veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, they do form an anastomosis with the musculophrenic and pericardiacophrenic veins to ensure constant drainage of the diaphragm.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior phrenic veins drain the vertebral portion of the respiratory diaphragm.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of small tributaries.

Course: Travel along the inferior surface of the diaphragm.

Tributaries: Multiple small tributaries.

Drainage: Diaphragm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Small vessels located along the inferior surface of the diaphragm join the inferior phrenic veins along its course.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
There are often two left and one right inferior phrenic veins. The left veins drain into either the left renal or suprarenal veins, or directly into the inferior vena cava. The right inferior phrenic vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

Along their course, the inferior phrenic veins cross the crura and the central tendon of the diaphragm. The left inferior phrenic vein travels posterior to the esophagus, and the right inferior phrenic vein passes posterior to the inferior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Small tributaries join the inferior phrenic veins along its course.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The left inferior phrenic vein receives esophageal branches, while the right inferior phrenic vein drains the caval opening of the diaphragm. Both inferior phrenic veins drain the inferior surface of the diaphragm.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anorectal venous plexus.

Course: Travels through the ischioanal fossa to drain into the internal pudendal vein.

Tributaries: Rectal venous plexus.

Drainage: Lower third of the rectum and anal canal.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior anorectal vein is formed in the rectal venous plexus surrounding the anal canal and rectum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The vein travel through the ischioanal fossa to drain into the systemic venous circulation, via the internal pudendal veins, at the posterior end of the pudendal canal.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior anorectal vein receives tributaries from the anorectal venous plexus. It also forms anastomoses with the middle and superior anorectal veins via the anorectal venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior anorectal vein drains the mucosa and muscular layers of the lower third of the rectum and anal canal.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Lower gastrointestinal bleeding

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Within the left portion of the liver.

Course: Joins the intermediate (middle) hepatic vein and terminates in the inferior vena cava.

Tributaries: Umbilical fissure vein.

Drainage: Left portion of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The left hepatic vein originates within the left portion of the liver between the medial and lateral sectors.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The left hepatic vein typically joins the middle hepatic vein as it travels posterosuperior through the left portion of the liver, before it ultimately drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The left hepatic vein receives an umbilical fissure vein, which typically runs between segments III and IV of the liver.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The left hepatic vein drains the left portion of the liver, associated with segments II, III, and occasionally IV.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Liver transplantation

- Hepatic resections

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein at the transpyloric plane.

Course: Travels obliquely within the free edge of the hepatoduodenal ligament (lesser omentum) to the porta hepatis of the liver.

Tributaries: Superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, splenic, left and right gastric, posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal, and cystic veins.

Drainage: Gastrointestinal tract, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The hepatic portal vein is formed from the union of the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein at the level of the transpyloric plane (L1/L2). Anatomical variations in the origin of the hepatic portal vein are common. In approximately one third of individuals, the inferior mesenteric vein also contributes to the formation of the hepatic portal vein, by merging at the confluence of the superior mesenteric and the splenic vein (Kimura, 2000).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The hepatic portal vein is formed posterior to the neck of the pancreas. It ascends obliquely for approximately 8 cm alongside the common bile duct and hepatic artery proper, within the free edge of the hepatoduodenal ligament (lesser omentum). The hepatic portal vein enters the liver at the right end of the porta hepatis and bifurcates into left and right portal veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
The hepatic portal vein and its tributaries (splenic, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric veins) form the Hepatic Portal System.

The left and right gastric veins drain into the hepatic portal vein at the level of the first part (or superior part) of the duodenum. The posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein drains directly into the hepatic portal vein near the head of the pancreas. The middle colic vein may also drain directly into the hepatic portal vein. The cystic veins may drain directly into the hepatic portal vein or into the left and right portal veins.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The hepatic portal vein drains nutrient-rich venous blood from the gastrointestinal tract, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder into the liver. Blood from the gastrointestinal tract is processed, and toxins, including pharmaceutical agents, are filtered in the sinusoids of the liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Pringle Maneuver 

- Cirrhosis of the liver

- Porto-systemic shunts

sections.title: References
sections.text: Kimura, W. (2000) 'Surgical anatomy of the pancreas for limited resection', J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Surg, 7(5), pp. 473-9.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal inferior portion of the duodenum, head and uncinate process of the pancreas.

Course: Travels from right to left to drain into the superior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: Venous arcades.

Drainage: Dorsal duodenum, head and uncinate process of the pancreas.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein arises from the inferior dorsal surface of the duodenum and the head and uncinate process of the pancreas.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein travels from right to left along the curvature of the duodenum and pancreatic head and uncinate process to drain directly into the superior mesenteric vein. Occasionally, the anterior and posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal veins may merge to form a singular inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein before draining into the superior mesenteric vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein receives small venous arcades.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein drains the dorsal surface of the second and third portion of the duodenum and the dorsal surface of the head and uncinate process of the pancreas.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Whipple procedure

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Along the surface of the cecum.

Course: Travels from inferolateral to superomedial to join the appendicular veins as the ileocolic vein and ultimately the superior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Cecum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The cecal veins (anterior and posterior) originate along the surface of the cecum near the ileocecal junction.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The cecal veins travel superomedially from the cecum (lower right quadrant) to merge with the appendicular veins as the ileocolic vein, which will then drain into the superior mesenteric vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The cecal veins drain the cecum.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Appendectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises from the surface of the appendix.

Course: Travels superiorly towards the ileocecal junction and drains into ileocolic vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Appendix.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The appendicular vein arises along the surface of the appendix within the mesoappendix.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the appendicular vein travels superiorly to merge with the cecal veins or the ileocolic vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The appendicular vein drains the appendix.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
-Appendectomy

- Acute appendicitis

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises along the greater curvature of the stomach.

Course: Travels inferomedially along the greater curvature of the stomach to drain into the superior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: Occasionally the right colic vein and/or the superior pancreaticoduodenal vein.

Drainage: Greater omentum and distal body and antrum of the stomach.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The right gastroomental vein arises along the greater curvature of the stomach.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The right gastroomental vein travels medially along the greater curvature in the superior portion of the gastrocolic ligament. Prior to the pylorus, the vein passes posterior to drain into the superior mesenteric vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Occasionally the right colic vein and/or the superior pancreaticoduodenal vein will join the right gastroomental vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The right gastroomental vein drains the greater omentum and the distal body and antrum of the stomach.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Gastrectomy

- Gastric lymphadenectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed within the root of the mesentery by the union of tributaries from the terminal ileum, cecum, and vermiform appendix.

Course: Ascends within the mesentery and passes anterior to the third part of the duodenum and uncinate process of the pancreas. It then travels posterior to the neck of the pancreas and unites with the splenic vein to form the hepatic portal vein.

Tributaries: Posterior, anterior, inferior pancreaticoduodenal veins, pancreatic, right gastroomental, jejunal, ilial, ileocolic, middle colic, right colic, and splenic veins.

Drainage: Small intestines, part of large intestine, and pancreas.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior mesenteric vein is formed within the root of the mesentery by the union of tributaries from the terminal ileum, cecum, and vermiform appendix.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The superior mesenteric vein ascends along the root of the mesentery. Along its course, it travels between the two layers of the mesentery and is joined by tributaries draining the small intestines, parts of the large intestine, stomach, and pancreas.

The vein travels anterior to the third part of the duodenum and anterior to the uncinate process of the pancreas. It then travels posterior to the neck of the pancreas and unites with the splenic vein to form the hepatic portal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Along its course, the superior mesenteric vein receives tributaries from the posterior, anterior, inferior pancreaticoduodenal, pancreatic, right gastro-omental, jejunal, ilial, ileocolic, middle colic, and right colic veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior mesenteric vein drains blood from the small and large intestines, and accessory organs of digestion into the portal venous system. These structures include the jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon, parts of the stomach, greater omentum, duodenum, and pancreas.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Cirrhosis

- Portal Hypertension

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arise along the anterior abdominal wall and the diaphragm.

Course: Travels posterosuperior along the falciform ligament to drain into the left hepatic portal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Portion of the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The paraumbilical veins arise along the anterior abdominal wall and the inferior surface of the diaphragm.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The small paraumbilical veins travel posterosuperior from their origin along the falciform ligament to typically drain venous blood into the left hepatic portal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, they do anastomosis with other veins along the anterior abdominal wall including the superior epigastric veins (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The paraumbilical veins drain a portion of the anterior abdominal wall and the diaphragm.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Cirrhosis

- Portal Hypertension

- Caput Medusae

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises along the transverse colon.

Course: Travels inferiorly and posteriorly from the transverse colon to drain into the superior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: Small, unnamed tributaries.

Drainage: Proximal two thirds of the transverse colon.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle colic vein originates along the surface of the transverse colon within the transverse mesocolon.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The middle colic vein travels inferiorly from the surface of the transverse colon through the transverse mesocolon. Typically, the middle colic vein drains directly into the superior mesenteric vein (~63%) or the gastrocolic trunk of Henle, the common trunk formed by the confluence of the right gastroomental and right colic veins (~29%) (Standring, 2016; Maki et al., 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The middle colic vein is often continuous with branches of the right and left colic veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The middle colic vein supplies the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Transverse colectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Maki, Y., Mizutani, M., Morimoto, M., Kawai, T., Nakagawa, M., Ozawa, Y., Takeuchi, M., Maki, H., Kurosaka, K. and Shibamoto, Y. (2016) 'The variations of the middle colic vein tributaries: depiction by three-dimensional CT angiography', Br J Radiol, 89(1063), pp. 20150841.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of several splenic branches at the hilum of the spleen.

Course: Horizontal course, posterior to the body of the pancreas. Unites with superior mesenteric vein to form the hepatic portal vein.

Tributaries: Several segmental branches of the splenic vein, short gastric, left gastroomental, posterior gastric, and pancreatic veins.

Drainage: Spleen, pancreas, and stomach.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The splenic vein is formed at the hilum of the spleen by the union of several segmental branches, within the lienorenal ligament.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The splenic vein travels retroperitoneally and parallel to the body and tail of the pancreas. Posterior to the neck of the pancreas, the splenic vein unites with the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
Multiple segmental branches of the splenic vein unite to form the splenic vein.

Short gastric, the left gastroomental, and pancreatic veins drain into the splenic vein directly or into the segmental branches. Along its course, the splenic vein also receives the posterior gastric vein.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Several splenic tributaries unite to form the splenic vein at the hilum of the spleen. The left gastroepiploic vein empties into the splenic vein within the gastrosplenic ligament. Three to five short gastric veins drain the fundus and the upper part of the greater curvature of the stomach. In approximately one third of individuals, the left gastric vein terminates at the splenic vein (Ohkubo, 2000).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
-Opitz (thrombophlebitic splenomegaly)

- Portal hypertension

sections.title: References
sections.text: Ohkubo, M. (2000) 'Aberrant left gastric vein directly draining into the liver', Clin Anat, 13(2), pp. 134-7.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises along the junction of the pylorus and the duodenum.

Course: Travels superiorly from the surface of the gastroduodenal junction to drain into the right gastric vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Gastroduodenal junction.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The prepyloric veins originate on the surface of the pylorus, near the duodenum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The prepyloric veins pass superior and posterior to drain into the right gastric vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The prepyloric veins drain the region of the gastroduodenal junction.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed as a continuation of the anorectal venous plexus.

Course: Travels through the mesorectum and mesocolon to continue as the inferior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: Anorectal venous plexus.

Drainage: Upper two thirds of the rectum and upper anal canal.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior anorectal vein is formed in the rectal submucosa as a continuation of tributaries from the anorectal venous plexus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior anorectal vein travels through the upper mesorectum to the root of the sigmoid mesocolon. The vessel ascends and continues as the inferior mesenteric vein. Along its course, the superior anorectal veins travel to the left of the superior anorectal artery, within the sigmoid mesocolon.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superior anorectal vein is a continuation of the tributaries of the anorectal venous rectal plexus. The veins in the plexus form anastomoses with the middle and inferior anorectal veins. The vessels establish a connection between the portal venous system and the systemic venous system.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior anorectal vein drains the upper two-thirds of the rectum, the internal part of the anorectal venous plexus, and the upper anal canal.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hemorrhoids (thromboses in the external venous plexus)

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises along the fundus of the stomach.

Course: Travels inferiorly and posteriorly to drain into the splenic vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Fundus and upper greater curvature of the stomach.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The short gastric veins arise along the surface of the fundus and upper greater curvature of the stomach.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The short gastric veins (typically 3-5) pass inferiorly and posteriorly from the surface of the fundus and upper greater curvature of the stomach to drain into the splenic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The short gastric veins drain the fundus and upper greater curvature of the stomach.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Splenectomy

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises along the surface of the body and tail of the pancreas.

Course: Travels posteriorly to drain principally into the splenic vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Body and tail of the pancreas.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The small pancreatic veins arise along the surface of the body and tail of the pancreas.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The pancreatic veins typically travel posteriorly from the surface of the body and tail of the pancreas to drain into the splenic vein, which is embedded in the posterior surface of the pancreas.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The pancreatic veins drain the body and tail of the pancreas.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Whipple procedure

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Along the surface of the jejunum.

Course: Travels superiorly towards the superior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: Straight veins of jejunum.

Drainage: Jejunum and the mesentery.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The jejunal veins originate on the surface of the jejunum as short, straight veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The jejunal veins begin as straight veins, which then form small loops within the mesentery.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The jejunal veins receive the straight veins of the jejunum.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The jejunal veins drain the jejunum and the mesentery.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: A collection of veins located in the sigmoid mesocolon.

Course: Ascend in the sigmoid mesocolon to drain into the inferior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Sigmoid colon and mesocolon.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Multiple sigmoid veins form vasa recta within the sigmoid mesocolon.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Sigmoid veins ascend intraperitoneally within the sigmoid mesocolon to drain into the inferior mesenteric vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The sigmoid veins are terminal veins. They form anastomoses with the sigmoid arteries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Sigmoid veins drain the distal part of the descending colon, the sigmoid colon, and sigmoid mesocolon.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises along the ascending colon.

Course: Travels from right to left to join the superior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Ascending colon.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The right colic vein originates along the surface of ascending colon.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Typically, the right colic vein travels from right to left to join the superior mesenteric vein. Occasionally, the right colic vein will join the right gastroepiploic or inferior pancreaticoduodenal veins to form a gastrocolic trunk, which drains into the superior mesenteric vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The right colic vein drains the ascending colon.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Right hemicolectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal superior surface duodenum and head of the pancreas.

Course: Circular course along the dorsal surface of the pancreas, where it typically drains into the hepatic portal vein directly.

Tributaries: Venous arcades.

Drainage: Dorsal superior aspect of the head of pancreas and duodenum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein arises along the dorsal surface of the pancreatic head and duodenum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein has a circular course along the dorsal surface of the superior pancreatic head and duodenum. Typically, it will travel from right to left to ultimately drain into the hepatic portal vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein receives small venous arcades.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein drains the dorsal surface of the distal first and second portion of the duodenum and the dorsal surface of the pancreatic head.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Whipple procedure

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: A continuation of the superior anorectal vein.

Course: Long retroperitoneal course running anterior to the left psoas major muscle.

Tributaries: Superior rectal, sigmoid, left colic, and transverse (inferior) pancreatic veins.

Drainage: Large intestines.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior mesenteric vein is formed as a continuation of the superior anorectal vein in the lesser pelvis.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior mesenteric vein has a long retroperitoneal course. From its origin it ascends in the pelvis, anterior to the left psoas major muscle. Initially, it runs medial to the left ureter and gonadal vessels. It then passes over these structures and continues to ascend within the abdomen. At the level of the duodenojejunal flexure, the course becomes intraperitoneal, and it drains directly into the splenic vein (or the confluence of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins) (Kimura, 2000).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The main tributaries of the inferior mesenteric vein are the superior anorectal and sigmoid veins, and the union of the ascending and descending branch of the left colic vein. A transverse (inferior) pancreatic vein may also be present and join the inferior mesenteric vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text:
The inferior mesenteric vein is one of the major vessels of the hepatic venous portal system. It drains nutrient rich venous blood from the lower gastrointestinal tract into the liver, where it is processed and filtered, before entering the systemic circulation.

The inferior mesenteric vein drains mainly the large intestines via the sigmoid and left colic veins. This includes the distal third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Kimura, W. (2000) 'Surgical anatomy of the pancreas for limited resection', J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Surg, 7(5), pp. 473-9.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises along the distal transverse colon and descending colon.

Course: Travels from left to right to join the inferior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: Ascending and descending tributaries.

Drainage: Distal one third of transverse colon and descending colon.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The left colic vein originates along the surface of the distal one third of the transverse colon and the descending colon.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ascending and descending branches of the left colic vein converge to form the left colic vein just medial to the descending colon. The left colic vein then travels from left to right to join the inferior mesenteric vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The left colic vein receives ascending and descending tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The left colic vein drains the distal third of the transverse colon and descending colon.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Left hemicolectomy

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ventral inferior portion of the duodenum, pancreatic head, and uncinate process.

Course: Travels from right to left eventually drain into the superior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: Venous arcades.

Drainage: Ventral duodenum, pancreatic head, and pancreatic uncinate process.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein arises from the ventral surface of the duodenum, pancreatic head, and uncinate process.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein travels from right to left along the curvature of the duodenum and pancreatic head and uncinate process to drain directly into the superior mesenteric vein. Occasionally, the anterior and posterior branches may merge to form a singular interior pancreaticoduodenal vein prior to draining into the superior mesenteric vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein receives small venous arcades.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein drains the ventral surface of the second and third portion of the duodenum and the ventral surface of the pancreatic head and uncinate process.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Whipple procedure

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ventral superior surface of duodenum and pancreatic head.

Course: Circular course along the ventral surface of the pancreas with variable drainage locations.

Tributaries: Venous arcades.

Drainage: Ventral superior pancreatic head and duodenum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein arises along the ventral surface of the pancreatic head and often forms a venous arcade with the anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein counterpart.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein takes a circular course along the ventral surface of the superior pancreatic head. The terminal drainage point can be variable for this vein. There are two common courses for this vein to drain. The first is for the anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein to join with its posterior counterpart as the superior pancreaticoduodenal vein, which drains into the hepatic portal vein directly. The second is for the anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein to join the right gastroomental vein, which drains into the superior mesenteric vein directly (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein receives small venous arcades.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein drains the ventral surface of the distal first and second portion of the duodenum and the ventral surface of the pancreatic head.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Whipple procedure

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises along the lesser curvature of the stomach.

Course: Travels posterior and medial from lesser curvature of the stomach to the portal vein.

Tributaries: Lower esophageal veins.

Drainage: Lesser curvature of the stomach and distal esophagus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The left gastric vein originates along the lesser curvature of the stomach.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The left gastric vein ascends along the lesser curvature of the stomach towards the gastroesophageal junction. Then it turns posterior and medial towards to the liver. The left gastric vein typically drains into the hepatic portal vein but can also drain into the splenic vein or rarely, directly into the left branch of the hepatic portal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The left gastric vein receives the lower esophageal veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The left gastric vein drains the distal esophagus and the upper body and fundus of the stomach.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Gastrectomy

- Gastric lymphadenectomy

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior aspect of stomach.

Course: Passes inferiorly along the posterior aspect of the stomach to drain into the splenic vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Middle posterior aspect of stomach.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: One or more posterior gastric veins may arise on the posterior aspect of the stomach.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior gastric veins descend along the middle portion of the posterior surface of the stomach and drain into the splenic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior gastric veins drain the middle part of the posterior aspect of the stomach.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Portal hypertension

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Along the surface of the ileum.

Course: Travels superiorly towards the superior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: Straight veins of the ileum.

Drainage: Ileum and the mesentery.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ileal veins originate on the surface of the ileum as short, straight veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ileal veins begin as straight veins, which then form small loops with adjacent straight veins, which ultimately drain directly into the superior mesenteric vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The ileal veins receive the straight veins of the ileum.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The ileal veins drain the ileum and the mesentery.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Junction of the ileum and cecum.

Course: Travels obliquely from the ileocecal junction to drain into the superior mesenteric vein.

Tributaries: Appendicular and cecal veins.

Drainage: Distal ileum, cecum, appendix, and proximal ascending colon.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ileocolic vein originates adjacent to the ileocolic artery near the surface of the ileum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The appendicular and cecal veins merge to form the ileocolic vein. The ileocolic vein travels obliquely from the lower right quadrant of the abdomen, superiorly and medially towards to the midline of the body. The ileocolic vein drains directly into the superior mesenteric vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The ileocolic vein receives the appendicular and cecal veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The ileocolic vein drains the distal ileum, appendix, cecum, and proximal ascending colon.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Appendectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Surface of the body of the gallbladder.

Course: Travels inferiorly along the body and neck of the gallbladder to drain into the hepatic portal veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Gallbladder and cystic ducts.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: There are typically numerous cystic veins. Those that drain the superior surface lie between the liver and the body of the gallbladder. The remaining veins lie on the inferomedial surface of the body and neck of the gallbladder.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The cystic veins draining the superior surface of the gallbladder traditionally drain directly into segmental portal veins within the liver. Cystic veins draining the other aspects of the gallbladder typically drain into the hepatic portal vein directly (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The cystic veins drain the gallbladder and cystic ducts.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Cholecystectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises along the medial portion of the lesser curvature of the stomach.

Course: Travels medially along the lesser curvature of the stomach to drain into the hepatic portal vein.

Tributaries: Prepyloric vein.

Drainage: Lesser curvature of the stomach.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The right gastric vein arises along the medial portion of the lesser curvature of the stomach.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The right gastric vein travels medially along the lesser curvature of the stomach, passes under the peritoneum on the posterior wall of the lesser sac. It then drains directly into the portal vein near the first part of the duodenum (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The right gastric vein receives the prepyloric vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The right gastric vein drains the lesser curvature of the stomach.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Gastrectomy

- Gastric lymphadenectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises along the greater curvature of the stomach.

Course: Travels superolateral along the greater curvature of the stomach to drain into the splenic vein.

Tributaries: Small, unnamed tributaries.

Drainage: Anterior and posterior body of the stomach and greater omentum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The left gastroomental vein arises along the greater curvature of the stomach.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The left gastroomental vein travels superolateral along the greater curvature of the stomach, between layers of the gastrocolic ligament, and drains into the splenic vein within the gastrosplenic ligament (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The left gastroomental vein receives small, unnamed tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The left gastroomental vein drains the anterior and posterior body of the stomach and greater omentum.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Gastrectomy

- Gastric lymphadenectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

24681.name: Right Branch of Hepatic Portal Vein

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: One of two major branches from the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Divides into numerous branches within the right half of the liver.

Branches: Anterior and posterior branches.

Supplied Structures: Right half of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The hepatic portal vein gives rise to a right branch near the porta hepatis of the liver.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The right branch of the hepatic portal vein is shorter than the left branch, measuring about 2–3 cm long (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The right branch of the hepatic portal vein typically divides into anterior and posterior branches that will supply segments V and VIII and segments VI and VII, respectively. The anterior branch occasionally gives a branch to supply part of segment I. Generally, the branching pattern of the right branch of the hepatic portal vein is more variable than the left branch (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The right branch of the hepatic portal vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to the right half of the liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Liver transplantation

- Hepatic resection

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

22248.name: Posterior Right Branch of Hepatic Portal Vein
22248.latin: Ramus dexter posterior venae portae hepatis
alternate: Lateral Right Branch of Hepatic Portal Vein
Ramus dexter lateralis venae portae hepatis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Right branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Travels from left to right at the point of branching from the right branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Branches: Segment VI and VII veins.

Supplied Structures: Segments VI and VII of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein arises immediately after the hepatic portal vein bifurcates into the left and right branches.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein travels from left to right in the parenchyma of the right liver.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The posterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein typically terminates by dividing into segment VI and VII veins.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to segments within the right half of the liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Liver transplantation

- Hepatic resection

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Travels superiorly to enter segment VII of the liver.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Segment VII of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The segment VII vein originates from the terminal end of the posterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein where it bifurcates into the segment VI and the segment VII veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The segment VII vein travels inferiorly to enter segment VII of the liver.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The segment VII vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to segment VII of the liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hepatic resection

16680.name: Anterior Right Branch of Hepatic Portal Vein
16680.latin: Ramus dexter anterior venae portae hepatis
alternate: Medial Right Branch of Hepatic Portal Vein
Ramus dexter medialis venae portae hepatis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Right branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Travels from left to right at the point of branching from the right branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Branches: Segment V and VIII branches.

Supplied Structures: Segment V and VIII of the right half of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein arises immediately after the hepatic portal vein bifurcates into the left and right branches.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein travels from left to right in the parenchyma of the right liver.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Typically, the anterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein terminates as branches for segments V and VIII, and occasionally a branch to segment I (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to segments within the right half of the liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Liver transplantation

- Hepatic resection

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

18623.name: Caudate Branches of Hepatic Portal Vein
18623.latin: Rami lobi caudati venae portae hepatis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Typically originates from the right branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Travels into the caudate lobe of the liver.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Segment I of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The caudate branches of the hepatic portal vein typically originate from the right branch of the hepatic portal vein, though it may have branches from both the left and right branch of the hepatic portal vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: There are numerous caudate branches of the hepatic portal vein that originate predominately from the right branch of the hepatic portal vein. There may be, on average, more than four caudate branches (Kumon, 2017). Upon entering the caudate lobe, these branches continue to branch into smaller venous branches, which ultimately terminate as portal venules. These portal venules drain into the hepatic sinusoids.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The caudate branches supply nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to segment I of the liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hepatic resection

sections.title: References
sections.text: Kumon, M. (2017) 'Anatomical Study of the Caudate Lobe with Special Reference to Portal Venous and Biliary Branches Using Corrosion Liver Casts and Clinical Application', Liver Cancer, 6(2), pp. 161-170.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Travels superiorly to enter segment VIII of the liver.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Segment VIII of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The segment VIII vein originates from the terminal end of the anterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein where it bifurcates into the segment V and the segment VIII veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The segment VIII vein travels superiorly to enter segment VIII of the liver.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The segment VIII supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to segment VIII of the liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hepatic resection

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Travels inferiorly to enter segment VI of the liver.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Segment VI of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The segment VI vein originates from the terminal end of the posterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein where it bifurcates into the segment VI and the segment VII veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The segment VI vein travels inferior to enter segment VI of the liver.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The segment VI vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to segment VI of the liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hepatic resection

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Travels inferiorly to enter the segment V of the liver.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Segment V of liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The segment V vein originates from the terminal end of the anterior right branch of the hepatic portal vein where it bifurcates into the segment V and the segment VIII veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The segment V vein travels inferior to enter segment V of the liver.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The segment V vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to segment V of the liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hepatic resection

17637.name: Umbilical Part of Left Branch of Hepatic Portal Vein
17637.latin: Pars umbilicalis rami sinistri venae portae hepatis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Portion of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein distal to the connection of the ligamentum venosum

Course: Provides main branches for liver segments II, III, and IV.

Branches: Segment II, III, IV, and I veins.

Supplied Structures: Left half of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The umbilical part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein is the segment of the left hepatic portal vein distal to the area that the ligamentum venosum (left umbilical vein) merges.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The umbilical part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein continues throughout the left portion of the liver.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The umbilical part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein provides segmental branches to II, III, and IV of the liver. It may also give a branch to segment I of the liver. These branches continue to branch into smaller venous branches, which ultimately terminate as portal venules. These portal venules drain into the hepatic sinusoids.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The umbilical part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hepatic resection

21226.name: Transverse Part of Left Branch of Hepatic Portal Vein
21226.latin: Pars transversa rami sinistri venae portae hepatis
alternate: Horizontal Part of Left Branch of Hepatic Portal Vein

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: First segment of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Extends from the bifurcation of the hepatic portal vein to the ligamentum venosum.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Left half of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The transverse part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein originates as the first segment of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The transverse part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein begins at the bifurcation of the hepatic portal vein. This vein spans from the bifurcation to the point of connection to the obliterated left umbilical vein (also known as the ligamentum venosum).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The transverse part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein continues as the umbilical part, which ultimately supplies the left part of the liver.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The transverse part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to the left liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Liver transplantation

- Hepatic resection

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Umbilical part of left branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Travels anterior and slightly inferior to enter segment III of the liver.

Branches: None.

Structures Supplied: Segment III of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The segmental III vein originates from the umbilical part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: After branching from the umbilical part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein, the segmental III vein travels anteriorly and slightly inferior to enter segment III of the liver (Standring, 2016).. This vein continues to branch into smaller venous branches, which ultimately terminate as portal venules. These portal venules drain into the hepatic sinusoids.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The segmental III vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to segment III of the left liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hepatic resection

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Umbilical part of left branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Travels laterally from the left branch of the hepatic portal vein to enter segment II of the liver.

Branches: None.

Structures Supplied: Segment II of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The segmental II vein originates from the umbilical part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: After branching from the umbilical part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein, the segmental II vein travels laterally to enter segment II of the liver (Standring, 2016). This vein continues to branch into smaller venous branches, which ultimately terminate as portal venules. These portal venules drain into the hepatic sinusoids.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The segmental II vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to segment II of the left liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hepatic resection

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Umbilical part of left branch of the hepatic portal vein.

Course: Travels anterior and slightly inferior from the left branch of the hepatic portal vein to enter segment IV of the liver.

Branches: None.

Structures Supplied: Segment IV of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The segmental IV vein originates from the umbilical part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: After branching from the umbilical part of the left branch of the hepatic portal vein, the segmental IV vein travels anteriorly and slightly inferior to enter segment IV of the liver. This vein continues to branch into smaller venous branches, which ultimately terminate as portal venules. These portal venules drain into the hepatic sinusoids.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The segmental IV vein supplies nutrient-rich venous blood from the digestive tract to segment IV of the left liver.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hepatic resection

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Medial portion of anorectal venous plexus.

Course: Travels through the mesorectum to drain into the internal iliac vein.

Tributaries: Anorectal venous plexus.

Drainage: Medial third of rectum and mesorectum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle anorectal veins are formed in the anorectal venous plexus surrounding the anal canal and rectum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The number and caliber of middle anorectal vessels are highly variable. They originate within the anorectal venous plexus and travel along the surface of levator ani to drain into the systemic circulation via the internal iliac veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
