sections.text: The middle anorectal veins communicate with the external anorectal plexus. They may also receive tributaries from the bladder, seminal gland (or vesicle), and prostate in males, or the posterior portion of the vagina in females. They also form anastomoses with the superior and inferior anorectal veins through the anorectal venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: They drain the middle one third of the rectum and mesorectum via the anorectal venous plexus and the muscularis externa of the ampulla of the anal canal.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Along the thoracic esophagus.

Course: Posteriorly to the azygos, hemiazygos, and accessory hemiazygos veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Thoracic esophagus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The esophageal veins are small veins that drain blood from the thoracic esophagus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The esophageal veins extend posteriorly to reach the azygos, hemiazygos, and accessory hemiazygos veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the bronchial veins may receive blood from the esophageal veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The esophageal veins are responsible for draining blood from the thoracic esophagus. The cervical esophagus is drained by the inferior thyroid vein, while the abdominal esophagus is drained by branches of the left gastric vein.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Esophageal varices

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Continuation of the central vein of the suprarenal gland.

Course: The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein or inferior phrenic vein. The right suprarenal vein drains into the inferior vena cava.

Tributaries: Various veins within the substance of the suprarenal gland.

Drainage: Suprarenal gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The suprarenal vein is a continuation of the central vein of the suprarenal gland.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The suprarenal vein exits the gland at the hilum. They continue inferiorly and medially. The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein or the inferior phrenic vein. The right renal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The central vein of the suprarenal gland receives veins from within the substance of the suprarenal gland. These unite to empty into the suprarenal vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The suprarenal vein drains the substance of the suprarenal gland.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Within the main portal fissure.

Course: Joins the left hepatic vein and terminates in the inferior vena cava.

Tributaries: Small branches draining segments IV, V and VIII of the liver.

Drainage: Central section of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The intermediate (middle) hepatic vein originates in the main portal fissure between the right and left halves of the liver.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The intermediate hepatic vein typically joins the left hepatic vein as it travels posterosuperior through the liver, before it ultimately drains directly into the inferior vena cava (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The intermediate hepatic vein receives small branches draining venous blood directly from segments, IV, V, and VIII of the liver.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The intermediate hepatic vein drains the central aspect of the liver, associated with segments IV, V, and VIII.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Liver transplantation and hepatic resections

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Network of vessels surrounding anal canal and inferior rectum.

Course: Vessels lie within the mucosa of the rectum and upper anal canal, draining them via the inferior, middle, and superior anorectal veins.

Tributaries: Connects with vesical plexus (males) or uterovaginal plexus (females).

Drainage: Rectum and upper anal canal.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anorectal venous plexus predominantly surrounds the anal canal and the lower part of the rectum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The plexus consists of a network of internal (submucosal) and external (subepithelial) veins that connects anteriorly with the vesical plexus in males or the uterovaginal plexus in females. Veins within the anorectal venous plexus normally appear varicose (dilated and tortuous).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anorectal venous plexus may receive tributaries from the vesical plexus in males or the uterovaginal plexus in females.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The plexus drains into the systemic circulation via the inferior and middle anorectal veins (through the internal pudendal and internal iliac veins, respectively), and the portal venous circulation via the superior anorectal vein (through the inferior mesenteric vein).

Due to its drainage into both the systemic and portal venous system, the anorectal venous plexus acts as an area of portacaval anastomosis.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hemorrhoids (thromboses in the external venous plexus)

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Continuation of the central vein of the suprarenal gland.

Course: The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein or inferior phrenic vein. The right suprarenal vein drains into the inferior vena cava.

Tributaries: Various veins within the substance of the suprarenal gland.

Drainage: Suprarenal gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The suprarenal vein is a continuation of the central vein of the suprarenal gland.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The suprarenal vein exits the gland at the hilum. They continue inferiorly and medially. The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein or the inferior phrenic vein. The right renal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The central vein of the suprarenal gland receives veins from within the substance of the suprarenal gland. These unite to empty into the suprarenal vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The suprarenal vein drains the substance of the suprarenal gland.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Within the right portion of the liver.

Course: Runs posterosuperior through the right half of the liver to drain directly into the inferior vena cava.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Right portion of the liver.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The right hepatic vein originates within the right portion of the liver, between the medial and lateral sectors.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The right hepatic vein travels posterosuperior through the right portal fissure of the liver to drain directly into the inferior vena cava near the caudate lobe of the liver (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The right hepatic vein drains the entirety of segments VI and VII and a portion of segments V and VIII, depending on the drainage that passes into the middle hepatic vein (Tani et al., 2016).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Liver transplantation

- Hepatic resections

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tani, K., Shindoh, J., Akamatsu, N., Arita, J., Kaneko, J., Sakamoto, Y., Hasegawa, K. and Kokudo, N. (2016) 'Venous drainage map of the liver for complex hepatobiliary surgery and liver transplantation', HPB (Oxford), 18(12), pp. 1031-1038.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by the union of the facial vein with the anterior division of the retromandibular vein.

Course: Descends in the neck to empty into the internal jugular vein.

Tributaries: Lingual vein.

Drainage: Face.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The facial vein pierces the investing layer of deep cervical fascia below the border of the mandible. Here it unites with the anterior branch of the retromandibular vein to form the common facial vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The common facial vein descends in the neck and crosses over the external carotid artery to eventually enter the internal jugular vein below the hyoid bone. An atypical drainage of the vein into subclavian or external jugular has been reported as well (A and Rabi, 2011).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The lingual vein joins the common facial vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The common facial vein typically drains into the internal jugular vein at approximately the level of the hyoid bone.

sections.title: References
sections.text: A, B. and Rabi, S. (2011) 'Anatomical variations in termination of common facial Vein', JCDR, 5(1), pp. 24-27.

17398.name: Parietal Tributaries of Superficial Temporal Vein
alternate: Posterior Tributaries of Superficial Temporal Vein

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of small vessels overlying the parietal bone.

Course: Unites with frontal tributaries to form superficial temporal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Drains the muscles and skin of the temporal region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The parietal tributaries of the superficial temporal vein arise as a plexus of small veins overlying the parietal bone.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The parietal tributaries descend over the temporal region and unites with the frontal tributaries to form the superficial temporal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the parietal ramifications may anastomose posteriorly with the posterior auricular and occipital veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The parietal tributaries of the superficial temporal vein drain the muscles and skin of the temporal region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises on the face, close to the lower eyelid, by the union of several small tributaries.

Course: Passes posteriorly in the orbital floor to empty into the pterygoid venous plexus. 

Tributaries: Anterior and middle superior alveolar veins.

Drainage: Inferior orbit and its adjacent facial structures.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The infraorbital vein arises on the face, close to the lower eyelid, by the union of several small venous tributaries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Accompanied by the infraorbital artery and the infraorbital nerve, the infraorbital vein passes posteriorly through the infraorbital foramen, infraorbital canal, and infraorbital groove. It drains through the inferior orbital fissure into the pterygoid venous plexus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The infraorbital vein receives the anterior and middle superior alveolar veins. It also communicates with the inferior ophthalmic and facial veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The infraorbital vein drains the inferior orbit and its adjacent facial structures, including lower eyelid, part of the cheek, the side of the external nose, and the upper lip.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of tributaries at the lateral angle of the orbit.

Course: Pierces the temporal fascia and passes backwards between the two layers of the deep temporal fascia to drain into the superficial temporal vein.

Tributaries: Zygomaticotemporal vein.

Drainage: Temporalis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle temporal vein originates from two to four tributaries at the lateral orbital angle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The middle temporal vein passes backwards, downwards, and outwards in the temple region. It pierces the temporal fascia, then passes back between the superficial and deep layers of the deep temporal fascia, while being embedded within the superficial temporal fat pad (horizontal segment). As the vein courses posteriorly within the temporal fat pad, it makes a large curve downward in front of the ear and drains into superficial temporal vein, before it enters the parotid gland.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The middle temporal vein receives the zygomaticotemporal vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The middle temporal vein drains blood from the temporalis muscle and the tissue of the temporal region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior temporal region above the zygomatic arch.

Course: Runs posteriorly across the temple to join with the middle temporal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Temporal region above the zygomatic arch.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The zygomaticotemporal vein originates in the anterior temporal region above the zygomatic arch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The zygomaticotemporal vein passes posteriorly to join with the middle temporal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The zygomaticotemporal vein receives drainage mainly from the temporal area above the zygomatic arch.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by the union of supratrochlear and supraorbital veins.

Course: Descends downwards and backwards, behind the facial artery and becomes the facial vein, distal to its junction with the superior labial vein.

Tributaries: External nasal, superior and inferior ophthalmic, and superior and inferior palpebral veins. Communicates with the cavernous sinus.

Drainage: Venous drainage from the lateral aspect of the nose, forehead, orbit, and eyelids.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The angular vein is formed by the union of supratrochlear and supraorbital veins, near the medial canthus of the eye.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The angular vein descends downwards and backwards on the face behind the facial artery, but with a straighter course. It passes underneath the zygomaticus major muscle and joins with the superior labial vein. The angular vein changes its name to facial vein, distal to its junction with the superior labial vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The angular vein connects with the cavernous sinus via the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins. Additional tributaries include the external nasal veins and the superior and inferior palpebral veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Accompanying the angular artery, the angular vein descends along the lateral aspect of the nose, draining the superficial structures of the face.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Cavernous sinus thrombosis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Originates from a venous network on the forehead.

Course: Descends medially towards the bridge of the nose, then diverges to reach the medial canthus of the eye to join with the supraorbital vein.

Tributaries: Nasal arch.

Drainage: Muscles and skin of the forehead.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The supratrochlear vein begins on the forehead. It originates from a venous network that is connected to the frontal tributaries of the superﬁcial temporal vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The supratrochlear vein arises as a single trunk from this venous network and runs downwards to reach the bridge of the nose, close to the midline. Here it runs in parallel with its counterpart from the other side. They then diverge and descend laterally towards the medial canthus of the eye, where they join the supraorbital vein to form the angular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The supratrochlear veins are joined by a nasal arch across the nose.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The supratrochlear veins drain the muscles and skin of the forehead.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Occipital region of the scalp.

Course: Passes superficially over the posterior triangle to drain into the external jugular vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Scalp overlying the occipital region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior jugular vein forms from the confluence of several superficial veins in the occipital region of the scalp.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior jugular vein descends obliquely along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, then passes superficially over the posterior triangle of the neck. It usually drains into the external jugular vein, by may drain into the internal jugular vein, jugular venous arch, or brachiocephalic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior jugular vein drains venous blood from skin, subcutaneous tissue, and superficial muscles in the posterosuperior neck and posterior scalp region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Side of the face over the masseter muscle.

Course: Runs transversely across the face between the zygomatic arch and parotid duct to enter the parotid gland.

Tributaries: Parotid vein.

Drainage: Masseter muscle and parotid duct.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The transverse facial vein originates from a network of branches on the side of the face over the masseter muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The transverse facial vein runs transversely and posteriorly across the side of the face, between the parotid duct and the lower border of the zygomatic arch and accompanied by branches of facial nerve. Inside the parotid gland, it drains into superficial temporal or retromandibular veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The transverse facial vein receives tributaries from the parotid gland and anastomoses anteriorly with the facial vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The transverse facial vein drains venous blood from the masseter muscle and other muscles of the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Upper eyelid.

Course: Course along the upper eyelid to the angular vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Upper eyelid.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior palpebral vein is formed by small veins in the upper eyelid.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior palpebral vein travels along the surface of the upper eyelid and courses medially to reach the angular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior palpebral vein drains blood from the upper eyelid.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Temporal region.

Course: Descend and drain into the pterygoid plexus.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Temporalis muscle and subcutaneous tissue in the temporal region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep temporal veins emerge from the temple region, deep to the temporalis muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep temporal veins course inferiorly to reach the pterygoid plexus of veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the deep temporal veins may form a venous web over the temple region by connecting with other tributaries of the middle temporal vein, including superciliary, zygomaticotemporal, and posterior deep temporal veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep temporal veins drain the temporalis muscle and subcutaneous tissue.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of small veins around the mental region.

Course: Passes through the mental foramen and combines with an incisive branch to ascend as the inferior alveolar vein inside the mandibular canal.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Facial muscles in the mental region and overlying subcutaneous tissues.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The mental vein forms from a small network of superficial veins over the mental protuberance.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The mental vein passes through the mental foramen to enter the mandible. Here, it combines with an incisive branch to form the inferior alveolar nerve, which ascends inside the mandibular canal.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The mental vein drains the facial muscles in the mental region and the overlying subcutaneous tissues.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by the union of frontal and parietal ramifications.

Course: Descends over the temporal region and into the parotid gland to join with the maxillary vein.

Tributaries: Middle temporal, transverse facial, and anterior auricular veins and branches draining the parotid gland and temporomandibular joint; Communicates anteriorly, posteriorly, and on the vertex with various venous channels.

Drainage: Drains the muscles and skin of the temporal region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial temporal vein arises from a frontoparietal venous plexus on the side of the head extending all the way up to the vertex. The plexus communicates with various veins anteriorly and posteriorly, and at the vertex with corresponding veins from the other side.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial temporal vein passes laterally from the temporal region over the zygomatic arch and enters the parotid gland. It descends further inside the gland and joins with the maxillary vein to form the retromandibular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superficial temporal vein receives the middle temporal, anterior auricular, and transverse facial veins. Additional tributaries from the parotid gland and temporomandibular joint may also join.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superficial temporal vein drains the muscles and skin of the temporal region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From a venous plexus on the posterior scalp.

Course: Pierces the cranial attachment of trapezius and turns deep into the suboccipital triangle to drain into the internal jugular vein. It may also drain into the external jugular vein via the posterior auricular vein.

Tributaries:

Deep cervical and mastoid and occipital emissary veins.

Drainage: Posterior scalp.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The occipital vein originates from a small network or plexus of veins on the posterior scalp in a region spanning from the superior nuchal line to the vertex of the skull.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The occipital vein emerges as a single vessel from the plexus on the posterior scalp. It pierces the cranial attachment of trapezius muscle and turns deep. It follows the course of the occipital artery and ends by draining into the internal jugular vein. It may also drain into the external jugular vein indirectly via the posterior auricular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The occipital vein receives the deep cervical vein. Additionally, emissary veins connect the occipital vein to the intracranial venous sinuses via the mastoid (with the transverse sinus) and occipital (with the confluence of sinuses) emissary veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The occipital vein drains the muscles and skin of the occipital region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Masseter muscle.

Course: Accompanies the masseteric artery to reach the pterygoid plexus of veins in the infratemporal fossa.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Masseter muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The masseteric vein arises from the deep surface of the masseter muscle, between the muscle and the ramus of the mandible.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The masseteric vein accompanies the corresponding masseteric artery (from the maxillary artery) and nerve (from the mandibular nerve). The vein ascends between the masseteric muscle and the ramus of the mandible. It passes over the mandibular notch and enters the infratemporal fossa to reach the pterygoid plexus of veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The masseteric vein drains the masseter muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Parotid gland.

Course: Drain directly into the pterygoid plexus and the retromandibular, facial, and transverse facial veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Parotid gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The parotid veins originate as small local tributaries in the substance of the parotid gland.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The parotid veins are short and have a vast drainage system via the pterygoid plexus of veins or into the retromandibular, facial, and transverse facial veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The parotid veins drain the parenchyma and the connective tissue of the parotid gland.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Forehead.

Course: Passes medially above the orbit to join with the supratrochlear vein, forming the angular vein.

Tributaries: Frontal diploic vein; communicates with the superior ophthalmic (via the nasofrontal vein), superficial temporal, and transverse facial veins.

Drainage: Drains the forehead, eyebrow, and upper eyelid.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The supraorbital vein originates on the forehead near the zygomatic process of the frontal bone, from its anastomosis with the branches of the superficial and middle temporal veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The supraorbital vein passes medially above the orbital opening, superficial to the frontalis muscle, and joins with the supratrochlear vein near the medial canthus of the eye to form the angular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The supraorbital vein gives off a branch which passes through the supraorbital notch, the nasofrontal vein, which subsequently joins with the superior ophthalmic vein. The supraorbital vein also receives the frontal diploic vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The supraorbital vein drains the forehead, eyebrow, and upper eyelid.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Angular vein.

Course: Crosses the anteroinferior angle of the masseter muscle and runs superficial to the submandibular gland to join with the anterior division of retromandibular vein, forming the common facial vein.

Tributaries: Angular, deep facial, superior and inferior labial, external nasal, external palatine, inferior palpebral, submental, parotid, and transverse facial veins. Communicates with the pterygoid plexus of veins and the cavernous sinus.

Drainage: Face, soft palate, tonsils, parotid gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The facial vein is a direct continuation of the angular vein that occurs at the approximate level of the inner canthus of the eye. It is usually called the facial vein once below the adjoining level of the superior labial vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The angular vein continues as the facial vein, running downwards and backwards behind the facial artery, but with a straighter course. It crosses the anteroinferior angle of the masseter muscle, piercing the deep fascia. It crosses over the submandibular gland and joins the anterior division of retromandibular vein below the angle of the mandible to form the common facial vein. The latter drains into the internal jugular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
The facial vein connects with the pterygoid plexus of veins (via the deep facial vein) and with the cavernous sinus (through the pterygoid plexus).

Additional tributaries include the deep facial, superior and inferior labial, external nasal, external palatine, inferior palpebral, submental, parotid, and transverse facial veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Due to its vast number of tributaries, the facial vein drains several structures including the lips, nose, forehead, anterior scalp, tonsils, soft palate, eyelids, parotid and submandibular glands, and the region under the mandible.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Cavernous sinus thrombosis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From the buccinator muscle.

Course: Joins the pterygoid plexus.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Buccinator muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The buccal vein arises from the outer surface of the buccinator muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The buccal vein drains into pterygoid plexus behind the masseter muscle.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The buccal vein provides venous drainage for the buccinator muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Near the midpoint of the orbicularis oris muscle.

Course: Courses laterally along the upper lip to drain into facial vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Upper lip.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior labial vein originates close to the midpoint of the orbicularis oris muscle in the upper lip region.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior labial vein courses along the upper lip to drain into the facial vein near the lateral angle of the mouth.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superior labial vein anastomosis with the superior labial vein of the opposite side. It may also receive ramifications from the nasal septum and the ala of the nose.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior labial vein drains the region of the upper lip and lower nasal septum and lower lateral wall of the nose.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Surface of the nose.

Course: Descend on the dorsum of the nose to drain into angular vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Ala and dorsum of the nose.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The external nasal veins originate on the dorsum of the nose close to the medial angle of the eye.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The external nasal veins descend on either side of the dorsum of the nose to drain into the angular veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The external nasal veins drain the superficial tissues and skin of the dorsum and ala of the nose.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From the eyebrow or the upper eyelid.

Course: Runs posteriorly across the temple to drain into branches of the middle temporal vein.

Tributaries: None. 

Drainage: Muscles and superficial tissues in the temple region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superciliary vein originates from the eyebrow or the upper eyelid.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superciliary vein runs posteriorly across the temple to unite with the zygomaticotemporal vein, thus, forming the middle temporal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the superciliary vein forms a venous web over the temple region by connecting with other tributaries of the middle temporal vein, including zygomaticotemporal deep temporal veins (Tansatit, Apinuntrum and Phetudom, 2015).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superciliary vein drains the muscles and superficial tissues in the temple region into middle temporal vein. From the middle temporal vein, the blood is eventually poured into the superficial temporal vein.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tansatit, T., Apinuntrum, P. and Phetudom, T. (2015) 'An Anatomical Study of the Middle Temporal Vein and the Drainage Vascular Networks to Assess the Potential Complications and the Preventive Maneuver During Temporal Augmentation Using Both Anterograde and Retrograde Injections', Aesthetic Plast Surg, 39(5), pp. 791-9.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Pterygoid plexus.

Course: Passes forwards over the buccinator muscle to connect with the facial vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Pterygoid plexus to the facial vein.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep facial vein is a branch of the pterygoid plexus and serves as a deep connection with the facial vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The deep facial vein courses forwards from the infratemporal fossa deep to the masseter muscle and the body of the mandible. It passes over the buccinator muscle to reach the facial vein.

The pterygoid plexus of veins is linked with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins. Infections from the face can spread in a retrograde direction from the facial vein, through the pterygoid plexus to the cavernous sinus and cause thrombosis of the cavernous sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep facial vein drains the rostral aspect of the pterygoid plexus to the facial vein.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Cavernous sinus thrombosis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Near the midpoint of the orbicularis oris muscle.

Course: Courses laterally along the lower lip to drain into facial vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Lower lip.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior labial veins originate close to the midpoint of the orbicularis oris muscle in the lower lip region.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior labial vein courses along the lower lip to drain into the facial vein near the lateral angle of the mouth.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior labial vein anastomosis with the inferior labial vein of the opposite side. Additionally, it may anastomose with the mental branch of the inferior alveolar vein before running laterally and emptying into the facial vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior labial vein drains the region of the lower lip.

17982.name: Frontal Tributaries of Superficial Temporal Vein
alternate: Anterior Tributaries of Superficial Temporal Vein

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of small vessels overlying the frontal bone.

Course: Unites with parietal tributaries to form superficial temporal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Drains the muscles and skin of the temporal region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The frontal tributaries of the superficial temporal vein arise as a plexus of small veins overlying the frontal bone.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The frontal tributaries descend over the temporal region and unites with the parietal tributaries to form the superficial temporal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the frontal ramifications may anastomose anteriorly with the supraorbital and supratrochlear veins. Some rami may cross over the vertex to communicate with the corresponding veins of the opposite side.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The frontal tributaries of the superficial temporal vein drain the muscles and skin of the temporal region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lower eyelid.

Course: Course along the lower eyelid.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Lower eyelid.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior palpebral vein is formed by small tributaries in the lower eyelid.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior palpebral vein travels along the surface of the lower eyelid and courses medially to reach the angular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior palpebral vein drains venous blood from the lower eyelid into the angular vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Connects the right and left supratrochlear veins.

Course: Arches over the bridge of the nose.

Tributaries: None.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The nasal arch arises from the supratrochlear vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From the supratrochlear vein on one side, the nasal arch crosses over the bridge of the nose to reach on to its counterpart on the other side.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The nasal arch allows for a communication between the two supratrochlear veins.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inside the maxilla.

Course: Ascends in the maxilla to reach the infraorbital vein running in the floor of the orbit.

Tributaries: Venous tributaries come from the maxillary incisor and canine teeth.

Drainage: Anterior teeth and the anterior part of the maxillary sinus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior superior alveolar vein arises as a network of veins around the alveolar sockets of the anterior teeth (upper incisors and canines) and from the anterior part of the maxillary sinus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The venous channels of the anterior superior alveolar vein ascend in the maxilla to reach the floor of the orbit and drain into the infraorbital vein coursing along the orbital floor.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior superior alveolar vein receives tributaries from the upper front teeth.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior superior alveolar vein drains the anterior teeth (upper incisors and canine) and the anterior part of the maxillary sinus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Hard palate.

Course: Passes through the greater palatine foramina in the hard palate and ascend through the palatine canal in the maxilla to reach the pterygoid plexus of veins in the infratemporal fossa.

Tributaries: Lesser palatine veins.

Drainage: Hard palate and gingiva.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The greater palatine veins arise from the lateral margins of the hard palate.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The greater palatine veins pass through the greater palatine foramina in the posterolateral angle of the hard palate. These accompany their corresponding arterial palatine branches from the maxillary artery and ascend through the palatine canal in the maxilla. Here, they join with the lesser palatine veins which course through the lesser palatine foramina to enter the palatine canal. The palatine veins drain into the pterygoid plexus of veins inside the infratemporal fossa.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The greater palatine vein receives a lesser palatine vein in the palatine canal.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The greater palatine vein drains the hard palate and the gingiva.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Begins near the anterior border of hyoglossus muscle.

Course: Accompanies the hypoglossal nerve.

Tributaries: Deep lingual and sublingual veins.

Drainage: Inferior and deep structures of the tongue.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep lingual vein joins the sublingual vein (from the sublingual gland) near the anterior border of the hyoglossus muscle to form vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The vena comitans travel backwards along with the hypoglossal nerve in a loop-like fashion. It joins with the dorsal lingual vein to form the lingual vein, which eventually drains into the internal jugular vein via the common facial vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The vena comitans receives the deep lingual and sublingual veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The vena comitans drains the Inferior and deep structures of the tongue.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: On the dorsum and sides of the tongue.

Course:

Passes posteriorly on dorsum of the tongue and joins the vena comitans of hypoglossal nerve.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Dorsum and sides of the tongue.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal lingual vein begins on the dorsum and sides of the tongue.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal lingual vein passes posteriorly and joins the vena comitans of hypoglossal nerve to form the lingual vein. It eventually drains into the internal jugular vein near the greater cornu of the hyoid bone.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The dorsal lingual vein drains the dorsum and sides of the tongue.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Soft palate.

Course: Passes through the lesser palatine foramina in the hard palate and ascend through the palatine canal in the maxilla. It joins the greater palatine vein here.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Tissues and muscles of the soft palate.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lesser palatine veins arise from the soft palate.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lesser palatine veins pass through the lesser palatine foramina in the posterolateral angle of the hard palate. These accompany their corresponding arterial palatine branches from the maxillary artery and ascend through the palatine canal in the maxilla. Here, they join with the greater palatine veins which course through the greater palatine foramina to enter the palatine canal. The palatine veins drain into the pterygoid plexus of veins inside the infratemporal fossa.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The lesser palatine veins drain the soft palate.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inside the maxilla.

Course: Emerges from maxillary tuberosity and passes through the pterygomaxillary fissure to join the maxillary artery inside the pterygopalatine fossa.

Tributaries: Venous tributaries come from the maxillary molar and premolar teeth and the maxillary air sinus.

Drainage: Maxillary molar and premolar teeth and the maxillary air sinus and the buccal mucosa.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior superior alveolar vein arises as venous branches from the bony mandible, in areas around the maxillary molar and premolar teeth and the maxillary air sinus, and other venous branches from the buccal mucosa.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior superior alveolar vein emerges from the maxillary tuberosity and runs through the pterygomaxillary fissure to enter the pterygopalatine fossa, where it unites with the maxillary vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Venous tributaries of the posterior superior alveolar vein come from around the maxillary molar and premolar teeth and the maxillary air sinus and from the buccal mucosa.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior superior alveolar vein drains the molar and premolar areas of the maxilla, the maxillary air sinus, and buccal mucosa.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by the union of small veins in the roots and pulp of the incisive teeth.

Course: Travels through the mandibular canal to drain into the inferior alveolar vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Incisive teeth of lower jaw.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The incisive vein is formed by the union of small veins arising in the roots and pulp of the incisor teeth of the mandible.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The incisive vein descends within the mandibular canal, accompanied by the terminal end of the inferior alveolar nerve and the incisive branch of the inferior alveolar artery. It joins with the mental vein, thus forming the inferior alveolar vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The incisive vein drains the incisive teeth of the lower jaw.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Tip of the tongue.

Course: Runs backwards on the inferior surface of the tongue and joins the sublingual vein to form the vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Tip and inferior surfaces of the tongue.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep lingual vein begins near the tip of the tongue.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Following its commencement at the tip of the tongue, the deep lingual vein runs backwards on its inferior surface, in close approximation with the mucous membrane. The deep lingual vein joins the sublingual vein near the anterior border of the hyoglossus muscle. This results in formation of the vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve, which runs back and accompanies the hypoglossal nerve in a plane between mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep lingual vein drains the tip and inferior surfaces of the tongue.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: On the dorsal lateral surface of the tongue

Course: Follows the course of the lingual artery and drains into the internal jugular vein.

Tributaries: Dorsal lingual vein vena comitans of hypoglossal nerve.

Drainage: Tongue.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lingual vein originates on the dorsal, inferior, and lateral surface of the tongue. It is formed by the union of the dorsal lingual vein and the vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lingual vein follows the course of the lingual artery and joins with the common facial vein, which drains into the internal jugular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The lingual vein receives the deep lingual and sublingual veins via the vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve and the dorsal lingual vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The lingual vein drains venous blood from the tongue.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by the union of incisive and mental veins.

Course: Travels through the mandibular canal to exit the mandibular foramen and enters the infratemporal fossa.

Tributaries: Incisive and mental veins.

Drainage: Lower jaw and teeth.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior alveolar vein is formed by the union of incisive and mental veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior alveolar vein ascends within the mandibular canal, along with its arterial and nervous counterparts. It exits the mandibular foramen and enters the infratemporal fossa. Here, it passes between the sphenomandibular ligament and the ramus of the mandible to ascend behind the lateral pterygoid muscle.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior alveolar vein receives the incisive and mental veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior alveolar vein drains the lower jaw and teeth into the maxillary vein inside the infratemporal fossa.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inside the maxilla.

Course: Ascends in the maxilla to reach the infraorbital vein running in the floor of the orbit.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Drains the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus (extending towards the canine and lateral incisor teeth).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle superior alveolar vein arises as a network of veins in the upper jaw (maxilla) situated along the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus. These might extend to drain the lateral incisors and canines.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The venous channels ascend in the maxilla to reach the floor of the orbit and drain into the infraorbital vein coursing along the orbital floor.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The middle superior alveolar vein drains the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus (extending towards the canine and lateral incisor teeth).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ventral surface of the tongue.

Course: Joins posteriorly with the deep lingual vein to form the vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Ventral tongue and sublingual glands.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The two sublingual veins are found on the ventral surface of the tongue, one on either side of the midline.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The sublingual vein joins the deep lingual vein along its posterior course, near the anterior border of the hyoglossus muscle, to form vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The sublingual vein provides venous drainage for the ventral tongue and the sublingual glands.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Network of veins.

Course: Situated inside the infratemporal fossa, deep to the lateral pterygoid muscle.

Tributaries: Deep temporal, masseteric, buccinator, external palatine, alveolar, parotid, infraorbital, inferior ophthalmic, and sphenopalatine veins, and vein of pterygoid canal.

Drainage: Upper and lower jaws and teeth, muscles of mastication, ear, nose, eye, meninges, and palate.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The pterygoid plexus is a venous plexus formed by a network of veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The pterygoid plexus is situated inside the infratemporal fossa, partly deep to the lateral pterygoid muscle.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
The pterygoid plexus has several tributaries including sphenopalatine, deep temporal, masseteric, buccinator, external palatine, alveolar, parotid, infraorbital, and inferior ophthalmic veins, and vein of the pterygoid canal.

Anteriorly, the plexus connects with the facial vein via the deep facial vein. Posteriorly, it connects with the retromandibular vein via the maxillary vein. It connects rostrally with the cavernous sinus through emissary veins that pass through the sphenoidal emissary foramen, foramen ovale, and foramen lacerum in the base of the skull to enter the cranial cavity.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The tributaries of the pterygoid plexus provide venous drainage to the structures which are supplied by the branches of the maxillary artery. Hence, tributaries of the pterygoid plexus provide venous drainage of the nasal cavity, the paranasal sinuses, the nasopharynx, the lateral wall and the roof of the oral cavity, the maxillary and mandibular teeth, and the musculature of the infratemporal fossa. The inferior ophthalmic vein, which drains structures of the bony orbit, has variable anatomy, and may be found as a tributary of the pterygoid plexus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by the union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins.

Course: Descends within the parotid gland and emerges behind its apex.

Tributaries: Parotid veins.

Drainage: Face and temporal region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins, within the parotid gland. It lies deep to the facial nerve and superficial to the external carotid artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The retromandibular vein descends within the parotid gland, along with the external carotid artery. It emerges behind the apex of the gland where it divides into anterior and posterior divisions. The anterior division combines with the facial vein to form the common facial vein. The posterior division joins with the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The retromandibular vein receives tributaries from the parotid veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The retromandibular vein drains structures of the face and temporal region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Nasal cavity.

Course: Serve as the vena comitans of the ethmoidal arteries and accompany them along their course.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Roof and upper medial and lateral walls of the nasal cavity, ethmoidal air sinuses, dorsum of the nose, and dura mater (in the anterior cranial fossa).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ethmoidal veins originate in the mucosa of the nasal cavity.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ethmoidal veins serve as the vena comitans of the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries. They accompany the corresponding arteries to enter ethmoidal canals in the medial wall of the orbit to reach the superior ophthalmic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The ethmoidal veins drain venous blood from the roof and upper medial and lateral walls of the nasal cavity, ethmoidal air sinuses, dorsum of the nose, and the dura mater (in the anterior cranial fossa).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From the submucosal plexus in the nasal cavity.

Course: Passes through sphenopalatine foramen to enter pterygoid plexus.

Tributaries: Nasal veins.

Drainage: Nasal cavity.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Inside the nasal cavity, the mucosa is densely vascularized in the posterior part of the septum and in the region of the middle and the inferior conchae. These veins give rise to sphenopalatine vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The sphenopalatine vein runs backwards through the sphenopalatine foramen, which is situated at the junction of the palatine bone and the sphenoid bone in the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa. From here, the sphenopalatine vein enters the infratemporal fossa to drain into the pterygoid plexus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The sphenopalatine vein receives the nasal veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The sphenopalatine vein drains the posterior nasal cavity.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Mucosa of the nasal cavity.

Course: Ascend over the septum and lateral walls of the nasal cavity and merge to form the sphenopalatine vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Nasal cavity.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Inside the nasal cavity, the mucosa is densely vascularized in the posterior part of the septum and in the region of the middle and the inferior conchae.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The nasal veins join together to give rise to the sphenopalatine vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: None.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The nasal veins drain the mucosa of the nasal cavity.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein.

Course: Descends obliquely, superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and drains into the subclavian vein.

Tributaries: Anterior and posterior jugular, transverse cervical, and suprascapular veins.

Drainage: Face, scalp, and neck.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The external jugular vein originates at a point close to the angle of the mandible, just beneath or in the parotid gland. It is formed by the merging of the posterior branch of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From the angle of the mandible, the external jugular vein makes a descent towards the middle aspect of the clavicle. It courses obliquely, superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, but deep to the platysma muscle, superficial fascia, and the skin. At this point, it traverses the deep fascia and terminates as it inserts into the subclavian vein, either anterior or lateral to the scalenus anterior muscle. At its insertion point into the subclavian vein, the external jugular vein has valves. However, these valves are not known to prevent regurgitation. There is a portion of the external jugular vein (between the insertion point into the subclavian vein and an area that is 4 cm superior the clavicle) that is dilated and thus is often referred to as a sinus (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The external jugular vein receives several veins including the posterior and anterior jugular, transverse cervical, and the suprascapular veins. Within the parotid gland, a branch of the internal jugular vein joins the external jugular vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The external jugular vein drains blood from the face, scalp, and neck.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Forms a paratonsillar venous plexus which covers over the fibrous capsule of the tonsil and is situated inside the paratonsillar space.

Course: Pierces the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle to reach the pterygoid venous plexus. 

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Tonsils.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The external palatine vein arises from the paratonsillar venous plexus that lies exterior to the fibrous capsule of the tonsil, inside the paratonsillar space. The paratonsillar plexus is formed by the tonsillar veins which travel along the fibrous septa within the lobules of the tonsil to reach the fibrous capsule.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The paratonsillar space is separated from the surrounding parapharyngeal space by the pharyngobasilar fascia, the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle, and the buccopharyngeal fascia. The external palatine vein arises from the paratonsillar (pericapsular) venous plexus and pierces through the three aforementioned structures to join the pterygoid venous plexus inside the parapharyngeal space. It may also drain into the facial or internal jugular veins or the pharyngeal plexus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The external palatine vein drains the venous blood from the tonsils.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Tonsillectomy

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Parenchyma of the tonsil.

Course: Course externally to reach the paratonsillar space and join the facial vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Tonsils.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Numerous tonsillar veins originate from the parenchyma of the tonsils.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The tonsillar veins travel along the numerous septa which arise from the tonsillar capsule to penetrate the tonsillar parenchyma and dividing the tonsillar tissue into various lobes. The tonsillar veins drain externally into the facial vein or pharyngeal plexus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The tonsillar veins drain the tonsils.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Tonsillectomy

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The vein of the pterygoid canal accompanies the corresponding nerve and artery as it travels through the pterygoid canal. It descends, draining structures of the pharynx and empties into the pterygoid plexus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of pharyngeal veins posterolateral to the pharynx.

Course: Passes laterally to the internal jugular vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Pharynx.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The pharyngeal plexus is formed by the union of several pharyngeal veins along the posterolateral aspect on the external surface of the pharynx.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The pharyngeal plexus extends laterally to drain into the internal jugular vein. Sometimes, it may drain into the facial, lingual, or superior thyroid veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the pharyngeal plexus may communicate with the pterygoid plexus. Additionally, emissary veins may connect the pharyngeal plexus with the cavernous sinus, thus connecting intracranial venous sinuses with the extracranial veins (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The pharyngeal plexus drains the pharynx.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of the inferior petrosal and sigmoid sinuses.

Course: Descends in the carotid sheath

Tributaries: Superior and middle thyroid, lingual, common facial, sternocleidomastoid, pharyngeal, ascending pharyngeal, and occipital veins.

Drainage: Skull, brain, superficial face, and most of the neck.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The internal jugular vein is formed by the union of the sigmoid and inferior petrosal venous sinuses. Here, the internal jugular vein is dilated as the superior bulb lying in the posterior part of the tympanic floor.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The internal jugular vein passes through the jugular foramen and accompanies the internal carotid artery and vagus nerve within the carotid sheath. It lies deep to and is separated from the external carotid artery by the styloglossus and stylopharyngeus muscles and glossopharyngeal nerve.

The internal jugular vein continues to descend until it reaches the subclavian vein just behind the sternal end of the clavicle. Here, they join to form the brachiocephalic vein. Just like at its origin, near its termination, the internal jugular vein has a dilation called the inferior bulb.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The internal jugular vein receives the superior and middle thyroid, lingual, common facial, sternocleidomastoid, pharyngeal, ascending pharyngeal, and occipital veins. At its junction with the subclavian vein, it usually receives the thoracic duct on the left, or the right lymphatic duct on the right-hand side.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The internal jugular vein is the major venous vessel for the skull, brain, superficial face, and the neck.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Jugular venous pulse

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anteroinferior part of the orbit from the union of small tributaries.

Course: Runs posteriorly along the floor of the orbit.

Tributaries: Inferior vorticose veins.

Drainage: Eyeball, orbit, and facial structures.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior ophthalmic vein arises at the anteroinferior part of the orbit (near the infraorbital margin) by confluence of small ciliary and muscular tributaries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior ophthalmic vein runs posteriorly along the floor of the orbit and drains into the superior ophthalmic vein to subsequently drain into the cavernous sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior ophthalmic vein receives the inferior vorticose veins that drain the inferior portions of the choroid of the eyeball.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior ophthalmic vein drains parts of the orbit (including lower eyelid, lacrimal sac, eyeball, and lateral rectus muscles) into the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Supraorbital vein.

Course: Passes inferiorly to join the superior ophthalmic vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Serves as a connection between the supraorbital and superior ophthalmic veins.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The nasofrontal vein arises from the supraorbital vein at the supraorbital notch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The nasofrontal vein courses inferiorly to connect with the superior ophthalmic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The nasofrontal vein acts as a communication between the supraorbital and superior ophthalmic veins.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From the venules inside the retina.

Course: Accompanies central retinal artery in the optic nerve.

Tributaries: Superior and inferior nasal and temporal branches.

Drainage: Retina.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The central retinal vein arises from the union of the superior and inferior nasal and temporal venules in the retina.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
Within the eyeball, the intraocular part of the central retina vein does not share a similar distribution with the arteries. Arteries, which lie more superficially, can often cross over the veins. In individuals with severe hypertension, the arteries press on the veins causing dilations of the veins.

The extraocular part of the central retinal vein accompanies the central retinal artery within the optic nerve. It is short and drains into the cavernous sinus directly, or into the superior ophthalmic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The central retinal vein receives the superior and inferior nasal and temporal venules, which each drain a quadrant of the retina.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The central retinal vein is responsible for draining the retina of the eyeball.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superomedial orbital rim.

Course: It accompanies the ophthalmic artery along its course, passing through the superior orbital fissure to reach the cavernous sinus.

Tributaries: Superior vorticose, nasofrontal, central retinal, ethmoidal, lacrimal, and inferior ophthalmic veins.

Drainage: Eyeball, structures of the orbit, and adjacent facial structures.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior ophthalmic vein originates at the superomedial orbital rim, where it is formed by the union of two tributaries/roots. The superior root is the orbital continuation of the supraorbital vein, while the inferior root is the terminal pat of the angular vein. On entry into the orbit, the two roots join to form the superior ophthalmic vein just posterior to the trochlea and medial to the tendinous insertion of the superior rectus muscle (Cheung and McNab, 2003).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior ophthalmic vein lies inside the retrobulbar fat where it is embedded in and supported by connective tissue septal layers. The vein accompanies the ophthalmic artery along its course, lying between the optic nerve and superior rectus muscle. It passes through the superior orbital ﬁssure, above the common tendinous ring of the recti muscles to reach the cavernous sinus (Cheung and McNab, 2003).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superior ophthalmic vein receives two superior vorticose veins, the central retinal vein, ethmoidal veins, nasofrontal vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior ophthalmic vein drains the eyeball, structures of the orbit, and adjacent facial structures.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Cavernous sinus thrombosis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Between the sclera and the fascial sheath of the eyeball.

Course: Run posteriorly to drain into inferior ophthalmic vein.

Tributaries: Episcleral veins.

Drainage: Choroid of eyeball.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vorticose veins emerge from the episcleral space between the sclera and the fascial sheath of the eyeball (Tenon’s capsule).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior vorticose veins run posteriorly on the sclera and drain into inferior ophthalmic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The vorticose veins receive the episcleral veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The vorticose veins drain the choroid of the eyeball.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises from the lacrimal gland as one, and sometimes two, branches that join to form the lacrimal vein.

Course: Runs along the upper border of the lateral rectus muscle to reach the posterior orbit where it drains into the superior ophthalmic vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Lacrimal gland, upper eyelid, and conjunctiva.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lacrimal vein arises in the lacrimal gland in the anterolateral part of the orbit. It arises from the gland as one, or sometimes two, branches that join to form the lacrimal vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lacrimal vein runs along the upper border of the lateral rectus muscle in close approximation with the lacrimal nerve and artery. As it extends to the posterior part of the orbit, the vein approaches the lateral border of the superior rectus muscle where it drains into the superior ophthalmic vein (Cheung and McNab, 2003).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The lacrimal vein drains the lacrimal gland, upper eyelid, and conjunctiva.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Cheung, N. and McNab, A. A. (2003) 'Venous anatomy of the orbit', Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci, 44(3), pp. 988-95.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Between the sclera and the fascial sheath of the eyeball.

Course: Run posteriorly to drain into superior ophthalmic vein.

Tributaries: Episcleral veins.

Drainage: Choroid of eyeball.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vorticose veins emerge from the episcleral space between the sclera and the fascial sheath of the eyeball (Tenon’s capsule).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior medial vortex vein has a shorter course and drains into the ﬁrst part of the superior ophthalmic vein; whereas, the superior lateral vortex vein runs a longer route. After its emergence from the episcleral space superolateral to the origin of the optic nerve, it runs posteriorly for some distance to drain into either the lacrimal vein or the second part of the superior ophthalmic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The vorticose veins receive the episcleral veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The vorticose veins drain the choroid of the eyeball.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The anterolateral pontine veins are found along the anterolateral aspect of the pons. They are tributaries of the superior petrosal sinus and drain blood from the pons.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The inferior cerebral veins drain the area below the cerebral hemispheres into the cavernous and transverse sinuses. Those on the surface of the frontal lobe join the superior cerebral veins, and through these open into the superior sagittal sinus. Those of the temporal lobe branch with the middle cerebral and basal veins, and join the cavernous, sphenoparietal and superior petrosal sinuses.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins from the anterolateral medullary surface

Course: Longitudinally along the anterolateral medulla, communicating with the vein of medullopontine sulcus superiorly and spinal venous channels inferiorly

Tributaries: Small veins from the olive, pyramid, and lateral medullary surface

Drainage: Primarily drains the anterolateral medulla

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterolateral medullary vein usually begins from small veins on the anterolateral surface of the medulla.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterolateral medullary vein courses longitudinally along the anterolateral medulla, near the pyramid and olive. It commonly communicates with the vein of medullopontine sulcus superiorly and spinal or lateral medullary venous channels inferiorly.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterolateral medullary vein receives small tributaries from the olive, pyramid, and adjacent lateral medullary surface. Transverse medullary veins may connect it with anteromedian or posteromedian medullary venous channels.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The anterolateral medullary vein primarily drains the anterolateral medulla. Its drainage territory includes the surface near the olive, pyramid, and adjacent lateral medullary region.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins on the posterior midline surface of the medulla oblongata

Course: Courses along the posterior median sulcus toward cerebellomedullary and spinal venous pathways

Tributaries: Small veins from the posterior medulla oblongata and inferior fourth ventricular region

Drainage: Primarily drains the posterior medulla oblongata

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posteromedian medullary vein usually begins from small veins on the posterior midline surface of the medulla.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posteromedian medullary vein courses along the posterior median sulcus of the medulla. It commonly communicates superiorly with veins near the cerebellomedullary fissure (e.g., vein of lateral recess of fourth ventricle) and inferiorly with posterior spinal venous channels.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The posteromedian medullary vein receives small tributaries from the posterior medullary surface and adjacent inferior fourth ventricular region. Transverse medullary veins may connect it with lateral and anterior medullary venous channels.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The posteromedian medullary vein primarily drains the posterior surface of the medulla. Its territory includes the posterior midline medullary region and nearby inferior fourth ventricular surface.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2000. The posterior fossa veins. Neurosurgery 47 (3 Suppl), S69–S92. doi:10.1097/00006123-200009001-00012

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Confluence of superficial cortical veins along the posterior lateral sulcus

Course: Anteriorly along the lateral sulcus toward the cavernous or sphenoparietal sinus region

Tributaries: Frontosylvian, parietosylvian, and temporosylvian veins, plus the anastomotic veins of Trolard and Labbé

Drainage: Lateral frontal, parietal, and temporal cortex bordering the lateral sulcus

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial middle cerebral vein usually begins where superficial cortical veins converge along the posterior part of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial middle cerebral vein courses anteriorly along the lateral sulcus toward the skull base. It most commonly drains into the cavernous sinus or sphenoparietal sinus region, with variable anastomotic connections to superior or inferior superficial cerebral veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The main tributaries of the superficial middle cerebral vein are frontal, parietal, and temporal veins from cortical regions bordering the lateral sulcus (a.k.a., fronto-/parieto-/temporosylvian veins), together with the superior anastomotic vein (of Trolard) and the inferior anastomotic vein (of Labbé).

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The superficial middle cerebral vein primarily drains lateral frontal, parietal, and temporal cortex adjacent to the lateral sulcus, including opercular regions and sometimes superficial insular territory.

sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of the superior thalamostriate, anterior septal, and superior choroidal veins near the foramen of Monro

Course: Posteriorly in the tela choroidea along the roof of the third ventricle to form the great cerebral vein

Tributaries: Anterior septal, superior thalamostriate, superior choroidal, lateral direct, medial atrial, posterior septal, caudate, striate, fornical, and choroid plexus veins

Drainage: Deep periventricular and subependymal cerebral territories

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The internal cerebral vein typically forms near the posterior margin of the interventricular foramen (of Monro) from the union of the superior thalamostriate vein with the anterior septal vein or the superior choroidal vein; all three vessels may contribute at or near this point.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: After forming, the internal cerebral vein turns posteriorly and courses near the midline within the tela choroidea in the roof of the third ventricle. In the pineal region, the paired internal cerebral veins unite inferior and posterior to the splenium to form the great cerebral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The most consistent tributaries of the internal cerebral vein are the anterior septal, superior thalamostriate, and superior choroidal veins. Variable tributaries include lateral direct, medial atrial, posterior septal, caudate, striate, fornical, callosal, and small choroid plexus veins.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The internal cerebral vein primarily drains deep periventricular and subependymal territories, including the septal region, caudate nucleus, internal capsule, deep frontal and parietal white matter, choroid plexus, fornix, corpus callosum, atrial and occipital horn regions, and nearby dorsal thalamic or diencephalic territory.
