sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small superficial veins from the lateral and dorsolateral midbrain

Course: Along the lateral mesencephalic groove toward pontomesencephalic and petrosal venous pathways

Tributaries: Lateral cerebral peduncle, lateral mesencephalic groove, dorsolateral midbrain, posterior mesencephalic, peduncular, pontomesencephalic, pontotrigeminal, and petrosal venous channels

Drainage: Lateral and dorsolateral midbrain, including lateral cerebral peduncle and lateral tegmental surface

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral mesencephalic vein usually originates from small superficial veins on the lateral and dorsolateral surface of the midbrain, including veins near the lateral cerebral peduncle and lateral mesencephalic groove.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lateral mesencephalic vein courses along or near the lateral mesencephalic groove on the lateral midbrain, between the cerebral peduncle region anteriorly and lateral tegmental surface posteriorly. It continues inferiorly toward the pontomesencephalic region and may communicate superiorly with the basal or posterior mesencephalic venous pathways and inferiorly with pontomesencephalic, pontotrigeminal, or petrosal venous channels.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The lateral mesencephalic vein receives small tributaries from the lateral cerebral peduncle region, lateral mesencephalic groove, and adjacent dorsolateral midbrain. Variable communicating channels may connect it with the posterior mesencephalic, peduncular, transverse pontine, pontomesencephalic, pontotrigeminal, and petrosal venous pathways.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The lateral mesencephalic vein primarily drains the lateral and dorsolateral midbrain, including the lateral cerebral peduncle region, lateral mesencephalic groove region, and adjacent lateral tegmental surface. Through variable connections, it may also participate in drainage of nearby posterior mesencephalic, pontomesencephalic, and upper lateral pontine territories.

sections.text:

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2000. The posterior fossa veins. Neurosurgery 47 (3 Suppl), S69–S92. doi:10.1097/00006123-200009001-00012

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins from the anterior and lateral surfaces of the pons

Course: Course transversely across the pons toward the petrosal venous system

Tributaries: Small pontine surface veins and communicating pontomesencephalic or pontomedullary channels

Drainage: Primarily drain the anterior and lateral pons

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The transverse pontine veins usually begin from small veins on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the pons.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The transverse pontine veins course horizontally or obliquely across the pontine surface. They commonly connect the anteromedian pontine venous network with lateral pontine, pontotrigeminal, and petrosal venous outflow pathways.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The transverse pontine veins receive small surface tributaries from the anterior and lateral pons. They may also communicate with the anteromedian pontomesencephalic vein, anterolateral pontomesencephalic vein, vein of medullopontine sulcus, and petrosal vein.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The transverse pontine veins primarily drain the anterior and lateral surfaces of the pons. Their drainage may include adjacent pontomesencephalic and pontomedullary surface territories through variable communicating channels.

sections.text:

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2000. The posterior fossa veins. Neurosurgery 47 (3 Suppl), S69–S92. doi:10.1097/00006123-200009001-00012

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The posterolateral medullary vein runs posteriorly and laterally around the medulla oblongata. Draining the medulla oblongata the posterolateral medullary vein empties into either the adjacent dural venous sinuses, inferior petrosal sinus or the superior bulb of the jugular vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of tributaries from the anterior cerebellum, middle cerebellar peduncle, lateral pons, and cerebellopontine fissure

Course: Courses through the cerebellopontine angle to the superior petrosal sinus

Tributaries: Veins from the cerebellopontine fissure, transverse pontine region, lateral recess of the fourth ventricle, anterior cerebellar hemisphere, middle cerebellar peduncle, and petrosal cerebellar surface

Drainage: Drains the cerebellopontine angle, anterior cerebellar hemisphere, middle cerebellar peduncle, lateral pons, and cerebellopontine fissure

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The petrosal vein usually forms from the convergence of tributaries from the anterior cerebellum, middle cerebellar peduncle, lateral pons, and cerebellopontine fissure region.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The petrosal vein courses through the cerebellopontine angle toward the petrosal surface of the posterior fossa. It usually terminates in the superior petrosal sinus, often through a short common trunk.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The tributaries of the petrosal vein commonly include veins from the cerebellopontine fissure, transverse pontine region, lateral recess of the fourth ventricle, anterior cerebellar hemisphere, middle cerebellar peduncle, and petrosal cerebellar surface.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The petrosal vein primarily drains the cerebellopontine angle region. Its drainage territory includes portions of the anterior cerebellar hemisphere, middle cerebellar peduncle, lateral pons, and adjacent cerebellopontine fissure.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Matsushima, T., Rhoton, A.L. Jr., de Oliveira, E., Peace, D., 1983. Microsurgical anatomy of the veins of the posterior fossa. J. Neurosurg. 59 (1), 63–105. doi:10.3171/jns.1983.59.1.0063

Matsushima, T., Rhoton, A.L. Jr., Lenkey, C., 1983. Microsurgery of the fourth ventricle: Part 1. Microsurgical anatomy. Neurosurgery 11 (5), 631–667. doi:10.1227/00006123-198211000-00001

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2000. The posterior fossa veins. Neurosurgery 47 (3 Suppl), S69–S92. doi:10.1097/00006123-200009001-00012

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial middle cerebral venous network near the posterior lateral sulcus

Course: Posteriorly and inferiorly across the lateral temporal lobe to the transverse sinus region

Tributaries: Variable cortical veins from lateral temporal and adjacent parietal cortex

Drainage: Lateral temporal lobe, especially inferior and posterior temporal cortex, with adjacent parietal cortex

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior anastomotic vein (of Labbé) usually forms from the superficial middle cerebral venous network near the posterior part of the lateral sulcus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior anastomotic vein courses posteriorly and inferiorly across the lateral surface of the temporal lobe. It most commonly drains into the transverse sinus or nearby transverse-sigmoid region.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior anastomotic vein receives a variable set of superficial cortical veins from the lateral temporal cortex and adjacent parietal cortex.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The inferior anastomotic vein primarily drains the lateral temporal lobe, especially the inferior and posterior temporal cortex, and may also drain adjacent parietal cortex.

sections.text:

Miabi, Z., Midia, R., Rohrer, S.E., Hoeffner, E.G., Vandorpe, R., Berk, C.M., Midia, M., 2004. Delineation of lateral tentorial sinus with contrast-enhanced MR imaging and its surgical implications. AJNR Am. J. Neuroradiol. 25 (7), 1181–1188.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins from the medial and basal frontal lobe near the optic chiasm

Course: Posteriorly along the optic chiasm and optic tract, joining the deep middle cerebral and inferior thalamostriate veins to form the anterior segment of the basal vein

Tributaries: Subcallosal, paraterminal, parolfactory, olfactory sulcus, posterior orbitofrontal, and basal forebrain veins

Drainage: Medial and basal frontal region near the subcallosal, paraterminal, parolfactory, olfactory, and posterior orbitofrontal areas

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior cerebral vein usually forms at the anterior base of the brain from small veins of the medial and basal frontal lobe near the optic chiasm, prechiasmatic cistern, and lamina terminalis region.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior cerebral vein courses posteriorly along the superior or superolateral margin of the optic chiasm and then near the optic tract within the basal cisterns. Near the anterior perforated substance, it commonly joins the deep middle cerebral vein and inferior thalamostriate veins to form the anterior segment of the basal vein. The right and left anterior cerebral veins may communicate through an anterior communicating vein near the optic chiasm.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The tributaries of the anterior cerebral vein are small and variable. They commonly include veins from the subcallosal region, paraterminal gyrus, parolfactory area, olfactory sulcus, posterior orbitofrontal surface, basal forebrain, and anterior perforated substance.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The anterior cerebral vein primarily drains the anterior medial and basal frontal lobe, especially cortex and adjacent white matter near the subcallosal and paraterminal regions, straight gyrus, posterior orbitofrontal surface, and olfactory groove. It may also receive nearby basal forebrain drainage close to the optic chiasm, lamina terminalis, and anterior perforated substance.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The caudal peduncular vein is located in the caudal cerebellar peduncle and is a tributary of the superior petrosal vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins from the midbrain near the interpeduncular fossa, cerebral peduncle, and lateral midbrain surface

Course: Around the posterior and lateral midbrain through the ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns to the great cerebral vein, posterior internal cerebral vein, or basal vein

Tributaries: Cerebral peduncle, interpeduncular, lateral midbrain, posterior midbrain, and variable tectal veins

Drainage: Midbrain surface, especially cerebral peduncle, lateral midbrain, posterior midbrain, and variable collicular territory

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior mesencephalic vein usually arises from small venous channels on the midbrain near the interpeduncular fossa, cerebral peduncle, and lateral midbrain surface.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior mesencephalic vein courses around the posterior and lateral midbrain through the ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns. It ascends toward the pineal region and usually drains into the great cerebral vein, posterior internal cerebral vein, or adjacent basal venous pathway.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The tributaries of the posterior mesencephalic vein usually include small veins from the cerebral peduncle, interpeduncular fossa, lateral midbrain surface, and posterior midbrain near the tectal plate. Small tectal veins from the superior and inferior colliculi may communicate with this pathway near the quadrigeminal cistern.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The posterior mesencephalic vein primarily drains the midbrain surface, especially the cerebral peduncle, lateral midbrain surface, posterior midbrain near the tectal plate, and small surface veins near the interpeduncular fossa. It may also receive variable drainage from the superior and inferior colliculi.

sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The lateral inferior cerebellar veins drain both the posterior lobes of the cerebellum and the cerebellar tonsils as they run from their origin backwards and superiorly emptying into the transverse sinus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Near the anterior perforated substance from anterior cerebral, deep middle cerebral, and inferior thalamostriate veins

Course: Posteriorly through basal cisterns around the cerebral peduncle and midbrain to the great cerebral vein

Tributaries: Anterior cerebral, deep middle cerebral, inferior thalamostriate, inferior ventricular, medial temporal, thalamic, peduncular, and lateral mesencephalic veins

Drainage: Basal forebrain, deep lateral sulcus and insular region, medial temporal lobe, thalamus, cerebral peduncle, and lateral midbrain

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The basal vein (of Rosenthal) usually forms near the anterior perforated substance from the convergence of the anterior cerebral vein, deep middle cerebral vein, and inferior thalamostriate veins. It may also receive posterior frontoorbital and olfactory venous channels near its origin.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: After forming, the basal vein courses posteriorly through the basal cisterns, passing along the cerebral peduncle and curving around the side of the midbrain. It continues through the ambient and quadrigeminal cistern regions and usually drains into the great cerebral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior segment of the basal vein commonly receives the anterior cerebral, deep middle cerebral, inferior thalamostriate, posterior frontoorbital, and olfactory veins. Its middle and posterior segments may receive inferior ventricular, medial temporal, peduncular, thalamic, and lateral mesencephalic veins.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The basal vein carries venous blood from the basal forebrain, hypothalamus and mammillary bodies, anterior perforated substance and nearby inferior parts of the basal nuclei, deep lateral sulcus and insular region, limbic/medial temporal lobe), temporal horn region, thalamus, cerebral peduncle, and lateral midbrain.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

Suzuki, Y., Matsumoto, K., 2001. Variations of the basal vein: identification using three-dimensional CT angiography. AJNR Am. J. Neuroradiol. 22 (4), 670–676.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The medial superior cerebellar veins drain the superior vermis as they run from their origin backwards and upwards draining into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins from the anterior midbrain and upper medial pons

Course: Courses along the anteromedian pontomesencephalic surface near the basilar sulcus

Tributaries: Small veins from the cerebral peduncle, pontomesencephalic sulcus, and medial pons

Drainage: Primarily drains the ventral midbrain and upper medial pons

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anteromedian pontomesencephalic vein usually begins from small veins on the ventral midbrain and upper medial pons near the pontomesencephalic junction.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anteromedian pontomesencephalic vein is a single midline vessel, coursing along the anteromedian surface of the pontomesencephalic region close to the basilar sulcus. Its superior arms drain into the interpeduncular veins, while inferiorly it is continuous with the vein of medullopontine sulcus and communicates with the anteromedian medullary vein. It also communicates with the vein of pontomesencephalic sulcus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anteromedial pontomesencephalic vein receives small tributaries from the cerebral peduncle, pontomesencephalic sulcus, and medial surface of the upper pons. Variable connections may occur with interpeduncular, transverse pontine, and anterior pontine venous channels.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The anteromedial pontomesencephalic vein primarily drains the anterior midbrain and upper medial pons. Its territory includes the ventral surface near the cerebral peduncle, pontomesencephalic junction, and adjacent basilar surface of the pons.

sections.text:

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2000. The posterior fossa veins. Neurosurgery 47 (3 Suppl), S69–S92. doi:10.1097/00006123-200009001-00012

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The posterior mesencephalic veins drain the posterior aspects of the midbrain. Originating close to the cerebellar peduncles the posterior mesencephalic veins run superiorly, emptying into the great cerebral vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small pial veins from superior, superolateral, and medial cerebral surfaces

Course: Ascend toward the superior sagittal sinus as bridging veins

Tributaries: Cortical veins from frontal, parietal, and occipital regions

Drainage: Superior, superolateral, and superomedial cerebral cortex with adjacent superficial white matter

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior cerebral veins usually begin as small pial veins from the superior, superolateral, and medial surfaces of the cerebrum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The superior cerebral veins course in cortical sulci toward the midline, pass through the subarachnoid space, and pierce the dura as bridging veins. 

They usually terminate in the superior sagittal sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
The superior cerebral veins receive cortical veins from frontal and parietal regions, with variable contributions from adjacent medial and superior convexity surfaces.

Named cortical tributaries include the orbitofrontal, frontopolar, and frontal veins anteriorly; the precentral, central (rolandic), and postcentral veins; and the parietal and occipital veins posteriorly.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The superior cerebral veins drain the superior, superolateral, and superomedial cerebral cortex and adjacent superficial white matter, including the frontal, central, parietal, and occipital regions.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Kiliç, T., Akakin, A., 2008. Anatomy of cerebral veins and sinuses. Front. Neurol. Neurosci. 23, 4–15. doi:10.1159/000111256

Uddin, M., Haq, T., Rafique, M.Z., 2006. Cerebral venous system anatomy. J. Pak. Med. Assoc. 56 (11), 516–519.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins from the interpeduncular fossa and adjacent cerebral peduncle

Course: Courses in the interpeduncular cistern toward the basal venous system

Tributaries: Small veins from the cerebral peduncle, posterior perforated substance, and nearby midbrain surface

Drainage: Primarily drains the ventral midbrain near the interpeduncular fossa

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The interpeduncular vein usually begins from small venous channels in the interpeduncular fossa and adjacent ventral midbrain near the cerebral peduncle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The interpeduncular vein courses within the interpeduncular cistern along the ventral surface of the midbrain. It commonly communicates with posterior communicating, peduncular, and basilar venous channels before draining toward the basal vein or nearby mesencephalic venous network.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The interpeduncular vein receives small tributaries from the posterior perforated substance, cerebral peduncle, and adjacent ventral surface of the midbrain. Variable communicating channels may connect it with posterior mesencephalic and pontomesencephalic veins.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The interpeduncular vein primarily drains the ventral midbrain near the interpeduncular fossa. Its drainage territory includes small surface veins from the cerebral peduncle region, posterior perforated substance region, and nearby mesencephalic venous network.

sections.text:

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2000. The posterior fossa veins. Neurosurgery 47 (3 Suppl), S69–S92. doi:10.1097/00006123-200009001-00012

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The internal occipital veins drain the posterior inferior aspects of the cerebral hemispheres running anteriorly they empty into the great cerebral vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins on the anterior midline surface of the medulla

Course: Along the anterior median fissure, communicating with the vein of medullopontine sulcus superiorly and anterior spinal venous channels inferiorly

Tributaries: Small veins from the pyramids and anterior medullary surface

Drainage: Primarily drains the anterior medulla

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anteromedian medullary vein usually begins from small veins on the anterior midline surface of the medulla.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anteromedian medullary vein courses along the anterior median fissure between the medullary pyramids. It commonly communicates superiorly with the vein of medullopontine sulcus and inferiorly with anterior spinal venous channels.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anteromedian medullary vein receives small tributaries from the medullary pyramids and adjacent anterior surface of the medulla. Transverse medullary veins may communicate with it along its course.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The anteromedian medullary vein primarily drains the anterior surface of the medulla. Its territory includes the region of the medullary pyramids and nearby anterior midline venous network.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2000. The posterior fossa veins. Neurosurgery 47 (3 Suppl), S69–S92. doi:10.1097/00006123-200009001-00012

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small pial veins from the inferolateral and basal temporal and occipital surfaces, with contribution from the uncal vein

Course: Posteriorly or medially, chiefly via the inferior anastomotic vein (of Labbé) into the transverse sinus

Tributaries: Uncal, temporal, basal temporal, occipital, and basal occipital veins

Drainage: Inferolateral and basal temporal and occipital lobes

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior cerebral veins arise as small pial veins from the inferolateral and basal surfaces of the temporal and occipital lobes, with the uncal vein contributing drainage from the uncus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior cerebral veins course posteriorly or medially, draining predominantly via the inferior anastomotic vein (of Labbé) into the transverse sinus, with additional communications toward the superficial middle cerebral vein, basal vein, cavernous sinus, sphenoparietal sinus, or superior petrosal sinus. More posterior basal temporal and basal occipital veins may drain directly to the transverse sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The tributaries of the inferior cerebral veins include the uncal vein, temporal veins, basal temporal veins, occipital veins, and basal occipital veins.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The inferior cerebral veins primarily drain the inferolateral and basal temporal and occipital lobes.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Kubo, M., Kuwayama, N., Massoud, T.F., Hacein-Bey, L., 2022. Anatomy of intracranial veins. Neuroimaging Clin. N. Am. 32 (4), 637–661. doi:10.1016/j.nic.2022.05.002

Ota, T., 2024. Functional cerebral venous anatomy from the viewpoint of venous collaterals Part I, supratentorial superficial and deep venous system. Stroke Vasc. Interv. Neurol. 4 (2), e001050. doi:10.1161/SVIN.123.001050

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins on the anterior, lateral, or posterior medullary surface

Course: Course transversely around the medulla oblongata between longitudinal medullary veins

Tributaries: Small surface veins from the medulla oblongata

Drainage: Drain segmental surface territories of the medulla oblongata

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The transverse medullary veins usually begin from small surface veins on the medulla.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The transverse medullary veins course transversely or obliquely around the medullary surface. They connect longitudinal venous channels, including anteromedian, anterolateral, and posteromedian medullary veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The transverse medullary veins receive small tributaries from nearby anterior, lateral, or posterior medullary surfaces. Their tributaries are usually short regional veins rather than consistently named branches.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The transverse medullary veins primarily drain segmental areas of the medullary surface. They also help connect anterior, lateral, and posterior medullary venous drainage pathways.

sections.text:

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2000. The posterior fossa veins. Neurosurgery 47 (3 Suppl), S69–S92. doi:10.1097/00006123-200009001-00012

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The lateral superior cerebellar veins drain the anterior lobes of the cerebellum as they run from their origin backwards and inferiorly emptying into the transverse sinus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of the right and left internal cerebral veins, with the basal veins commonly joining near this confluence

Course: Through the quadrigeminal cistern around the splenium to form the straight sinus with the inferior sagittal sinus

Tributaries: Internal cerebral, basal, pineal, tectal, posterior callosal, and superior vermian veins

Drainage: Deep cerebral structures, medial temporal region, posterior corpus callosum, pineal-tectal region, and variable superior cerebellar territory

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is an unpaired midline vein formed by the union of the right and left internal cerebral veins beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum. The basal veins commonly join at or near this confluence.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The great cerebral vein passes posteriorly and superiorly through the quadrigeminal cistern around the splenium of the corpus callosum. It joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The principal tributaries of the great cerebral vein are the internal cerebral veins and basal veins. Variable tributaries include pineal, tectal, posterior callosal, and superior vermian veins.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The great cerebral vein carries venous blood from deep cerebral structures drained by the internal cerebral and basal veins, including the thalami, basal nuclei, deep white matter, choroid plexus, medial temporal structures, posterior corpus callosum, pineal and tectal regions, and variable superior cerebellar territory.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Pterygoid plexus.

Course: Accompanies the first part of the maxillary artery and enters the parotid gland to unite with the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein.

Tributaries: Pterygoid plexus.

Drainage: Upper and lower jaws and teeth, muscles of mastication, ear, nose, eye, meninges, and palate.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The maxillary veins are formed by the confluence of veins from the pterygoid plexus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The maxillary veins accompany the ﬁrst part of the maxillary artery. They pass backwards between the sphenomandibular ligament and the neck of the mandible. They enter the parotid gland to join the superficial temporal vein, forming the retromandibular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The maxillary veins receive the venous blood from the pterygoid plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The maxillary veins drain the upper and lower jaw and teeth, muscles of mastication, ear, nose, meninges, and palate.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by the splitting of the retromandibular vein into its anterior and posterior divisions.

Course: Joins with the facial vein to form the common facial vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Face and temporal region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior division of the retromandibular vein is formed within the lower parotid gland by the splitting of the retromandibular vein into its anterior and posterior divisions.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior division of the retromandibular vein combines with the facial vein to form the common facial vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior division of the retromandibular vein drains structures of the face and temporal region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Parenchyma of thyroid gland.

Course: Passes obliquely to join the internal jugular vein.

Tributaries: Superior laryngeal and cricothyroid veins.

Drainage: Thyroid gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior thyroid veins originate from a glandular venous plexus. The venous plexus is also linked to the middle and inferior thyroid veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior thyroid vein passes laterally from its glandular point of origin and is accompanied by the superior thyroid artery. The superior thyroid vein crosses anterior to the common carotid artery and drains into the internal jugular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Superior thyroid vein receives the superior laryngeal and cricothyroid veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior thyroid vein drains the thyroid gland.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Parenchyma of thyroid gland.

Course: Passes inferiorly and obliquely to join the internal jugular vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Thyroid gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle thyroid vein originates from a glandular venous plexus. The venous plexus is also linked to the superior and inferior thyroid veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The middle thyroid vein descends from its glandular point of origin, crosses anterior to the common carotid artery, and drains into the internal jugular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The middle thyroid vein drains the thyroid gland.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Parenchyma of thyroid gland.

Course: Passes inferiorly and obliquely to join the brachiocephalic vein.

Tributaries: Inferior laryngeal, tracheal, and esophageal veins.

Drainage: Thyroid gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior thyroid veins originate from a glandular venous plexus. The venous plexus is also linked to the superior and middle thyroid veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The inferior thyroid veins descend from their glandular point of origin, travel superficial to the trachea, and insert into the brachiocephalic veins, posterior to the manubrium of the sternum. As the right inferior thyroid vein makes its descent, it crosses the brachiocephalic trunk near its termination point in the right brachiocephalic vein (Standring, 2016).

The inferior thyroid veins lie superficial to the trachea, inferior to the lower borders of the thyroid gland, deep to the sternocleidomastoid, sternothyroid and sternohyoid muscles, and relatively anteromedial to the left and right common carotid arteries.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior thyroid vein receives the tracheal, the esophageal, and the inferior laryngeal veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior thyroid vein drains the thyroid gland.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dura mater.

Course: Descends with middle meningeal artery, passes through foramen spinosum and enters the maxillary vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Dura mater.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle meningeal vein originates within the dura matter.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The middle meningeal vein descends with the middle meningeal artery, passing through the foramen spinosum and emptying into the maxillary vein or the pterygoid plexus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The middle meningeal vein drains the dura mater.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Connections: Connects the sigmoid sinus or jugular bulb with the vertebral venous plexus

Course: Passes through the condylar canal

Tributaries: Small suboccipital, condylar, and vertebral venous channels

Drainage: Communicates between posterior fossa sinuses and craniocervical veins

sections.title: Connections
sections.text: The condylar emissary vein connects the sigmoid sinus or jugular bulb region with the suboccipital and vertebral venous plexuses.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The condylar emissary vein passes through the condylar canal near the occipital condyle. It forms an important venous communication at the craniocervical junction.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The condylar emissary vein receives small tributaries from the suboccipital venous plexus, vertebral venous plexus, condylar region, and posterior fossa dural venous channels.

sections.title: Drainage pathway
sections.text: The condylar emissary vein provides communication between the sigmoid sinus or jugular bulb and extracranial craniocervical venous pathways.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Connections: Connects scalp veins with the superior sagittal sinus

Course: Passes through the parietal foramen

Tributaries: Small scalp, diploic, and meningeal veins

Drainage: Communicates between extracranial parietal veins and the superior sagittal sinus

sections.title: Connections
sections.text: The parietal emissary vein connects veins of the parietal scalp and skull with the superior sagittal sinus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The parietal emissary vein passes through the parietal foramen near the posterior part of the parietal bone. It may communicate with diploic veins as it crosses the skull.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The parietal emissary vein receives small tributaries from parietal scalp veins, diploic veins, and nearby meningeal veins. The size and presence of this vein are variable.

sections.title: Drainage pathway
sections.text: The parietal emissary vein provides a communication between extracranial parietal venous channels and the superior sagittal sinus.

sections.title: References

Tubbs, R.S., Shoja, M.M., Loukas, M., 2016. Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley Blackwell, Hoboken.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Connections: Connects posterior auricular or occipital veins with the sigmoid sinus

Course: Passes through the mastoid foramen

Tributaries: Small scalp, diploic, and mastoid venous channels

Drainage: Communicates between extracranial posterior scalp veins and the sigmoid sinus

sections.title: Connections
sections.text: The mastoid emissary vein connects posterior auricular or occipital scalp veins with the sigmoid sinus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The mastoid emissary vein passes through the mastoid foramen in the temporal bone. It may communicate with diploic and mastoid venous channels along its course.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The mastoid emissary vein receives small tributaries from posterior auricular, occipital, diploic, and mastoid venous channels. Its size is variable and it may be prominent on one side.

sections.title: Drainage pathway
sections.text: The mastoid emissary vein provides a communication between extracranial posterior scalp veins and the sigmoid sinus.

sections.title: References

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Connections: Connects occipital scalp veins with the confluence, occipital sinus, or marginal sinus region

Course: Passes through an occipital emissary foramen when present

Tributaries: Small occipital scalp, diploic, and posterior fossa dural veins

Drainage: Communicates between occipital scalp veins and posterior dural venous sinuses

sections.title: Connections
sections.text: The occipital emissary vein connects occipital scalp veins with posterior dural venous sinuses, commonly near the confluence, occipital sinus, or marginal sinus region.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The occipital emissary vein passes through an occipital emissary foramen when present. Its course and size vary considerably between individuals.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The occipital emissary vein receives small tributaries from occipital scalp veins, diploic veins of the occipital bone, and nearby posterior fossa dural veins.

sections.title: Drainage pathway
sections.text: The occipital emissary vein provides communication between extracranial occipital veins and posterior dural venous sinuses.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

Tubbs, R.S., Shoja, M.M., Loukas, M., 2016. Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley Blackwell, Hoboken.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Connections: Connects the cavernous sinus region with the pterygoid venous plexus

Course: Passes through or around the foramen ovale with mandibular nerve-related structures

Tributaries: Small sphenoid, meningeal, cavernous, and pterygoid venous channels

Drainage: Communicates between cavernous and extracranial infratemporal venous pathways

sections.title: Connections
sections.text: The venous plexus of foramen ovale connects skull-base venous channels near the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid venous plexus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The venous plexus of foramen ovale passes through or around the foramen ovale in the sphenoid bone, near the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. It forms part of the emissary venous network of the middle cranial fossa.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The venous plexus of foramen ovale receives small tributaries from the cavernous sinus region, sphenoid dura, middle meningeal venous channels, and pterygoid venous plexus.

sections.title: Drainage pathway
sections.text: The venous plexus of foramen ovale provides communication between intracranial cavernous or meningeal venous pathways and the extracranial pterygoid venous plexus.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

Tubbs, R.S., Shoja, M.M., Loukas, M., 2016. Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley Blackwell, Hoboken.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Connections: Network of small veins surrounding the internal carotid artery, within the carotid canal and cavernous region

Course: Surrounds the petrous and cavernous segments of the internal carotid artery

Tributaries: Small cavernous, petrosal, and carotid canal venous channels

Drainage: Communicates with cavernous, petrosal, and skull-base venous pathways

sections.title: Connections
sections.text: The internal carotid venous plexus is a network of small veins surrounding the internal carotid artery, especially within the carotid canal and cavernous region.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The internal carotid venous plexus follows the petrous and cavernous segments of the internal carotid artery. It communicates with the cavernous sinus and adjacent skull-base venous channels.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The internal carotid venous plexus receives small tributaries from the cavernous sinus region, carotid canal, petrous temporal bone, and nearby petrosal venous pathways.

sections.title: Drainage pathway
sections.text: The internal carotid venous plexus provides communication between the cavernous sinus, petrosal venous channels, and small veins of the carotid canal region.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Situated mainly in the occipital bone.

Course: Run through the diploic channels between the outer and inner tables of the cortical bone in the posterior occipital region.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Occipital bone.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The occipital diploic vein is situated mainly in the occipital bone.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Diploic channels are situated in the diploe or the spongy layer, between the outer and inner tables of the cortical bones. The occipital diploic veins represent a network of valveless intraosseous veins which course primarily through the occipital bone.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
There are no named tributaries; however, the occipital diploic vein communicates with the posterior temporal diploic vein.

Emissary veins such as the emissary mastoid vein and some occipital (and parietal) emissary veins link the occipital (and posterior temporal) diploic veins with the veins of the posterior scalp and neck (in the suboccipital venous plexus).

The occipital diploic vein opens either externally into the occipital vein (suboccipital plexus of veins), or internally into the transverse sinus or into the confluence of the sinuses (Garcia-Gonzalez et al., 2009).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The occipital diploic vein drains the occipital bone.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Garcia-Gonzalez, U., Cavalcanti, D. D., Agrawal, A., Gonzalez, L. F., Wallace, R. C., Spetzler, R. F. and Preul, M. C. (2009) 'The diploic venous system: surgical anatomy and neurosurgical implications', Neurosurg Focus, 27(5), pp. E2.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior skull.

Course: Run through the diploic channels between the outer and inner tables of the frontal cortical bone.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Frontal bone.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The frontal diploic veins are situated in the frontal bone of the skull, in an area topographically delimited by the bregma, glabella, and pterion.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Diploic channels are situated in the diploe or the spongy layer, between the outer and inner tables of the cortical bones. The frontal diploic veins represent a network of valveless intraosseous veins which run through the diploic channels in the frontal bone of the skull. They drain into the supraorbital vein and/or the superior sagittal sinus (Garcia-Gonzalez et al., 2009).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Frontal diploic veins on either side receive small unnamed tributaries near their origin that run along the superolateral aspect of the frontal sinus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The frontal diploic veins drain the frontal bone of the skull.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Garcia-Gonzalez, U., Cavalcanti, D. D., Agrawal, A., Gonzalez, L. F., Wallace, R. C., Spetzler, R. F. and Preul, M. C. (2009) 'The diploic venous system: surgical anatomy and neurosurgical implications', Neurosurg Focus, 27(5), pp. E2.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Situated chiefly in the parietal bone.

Course: Run through the diploic channels between the outer and inner tables of the cortical bone of the parietal bone near the asterion.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Parietal bone.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior temporal diploic vein is located mainly in the parietal bone, in a region which is topographically delimited by the bregma, pterion, asterion, and lambda.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Diploic channels are situated in the diploe or the spongy layer, between the outer and inner tables of the cortical bones. The posterior temporal diploic veins represent a network of valveless intraosseous veins which course primarily through the parietal bone, running anteriorly and dorsomedially relative to the midline. These have a draining point posteriorly close to the asterion or posterosuperior mastoid area (Garcia-Gonzalez et al., 2009).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
There are no named tributaries; however, the posterior temporal diploic veins connect with the petrosquamosal sinus, mastoid emissary vein, and sigmoid, transverse, and superior petrosal sinuses to form a complex system that drains the superior sagittal sinus and forms a communication between the extracranial and intracranial venous systems. Sometimes, rich anastomoses exist between the posterior and anterior temporal diploic veins and the occipital diploic veins. Emissary veins, such as the emissary mastoid vein and some parietal and occipital emissary veins, link the posterior temporal and occipital diploic veins with the veins of the posterior scalp and neck (suboccipital venous system). 

The posterior temporal diploic veins terminate in the transverse sinus (and sigmoid sinus), through an aperture at the mastoid angle of the parietal bone or through the mastoid foramen (Garcia-Gonzalez et al., 2009).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior temporal diploic veins drain chiefly the parietal bones of the skull.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Garcia-Gonzalez, U., Cavalcanti, D. D., Agrawal, A., Gonzalez, L. F., Wallace, R. C., Spetzler, R. F. and Preul, M. C. (2009) 'The diploic venous system: surgical anatomy and neurosurgical implications', Neurosurg Focus, 27(5), pp. E2.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Confined chiefly to the frontal bone and anterior parietal bone.

Course: Run through the diploic channels between the outer and inner tables of the cortical bone of the parietal and frontal bones near the pterion.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Parietal and frontal bone.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior temporal diploic veins are confined chiefly to the frontal and anterior parietal bones of the skull and are topographically located in an area delimited by the bregma, frontozygomatic suture, pterion, and asterion. There are certain areas in the anterior skull region, where the frontal and anterior temporal diploic veins overlap.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Diploic channels are situated in the diploe or the spongy layer, between the outer and inner tables of the cortical bones. The anterior temporal diploic veins represent a network of valveless intraosseous veins which run dorsocaudally through the diploic channels near the pterion. The pterion is surrounded by multiple small venous channels and the anterior temporal diploic veins have draining points in all pterional areas. The main trunk can be followed upward almost parallel to the border of the squamous temporal bone and coronal sutures. The main trunk of the anterior temporal diploic vein can be seen running towards the midline where it drains into the superior sagittal sinus. It may also pierce the greater wing of sphenoid bone to drain into the sphenoparietal sinus (Garcia-Gonzalez et al., 2009).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, it does form an anastomosis with the frontal and posterior temporal diploic veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior temporal diploic veins drain the parietal and frontal bones.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Garcia-Gonzalez, U., Cavalcanti, D. D., Agrawal, A., Gonzalez, L. F., Wallace, R. C., Spetzler, R. F. and Preul, M. C. (2009) 'The diploic venous system: surgical anatomy and neurosurgical implications', Neurosurg Focus, 27(5), pp. E2.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Upper part of the larynx.

Course: Passes laterally to enter the superior thyroid vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Larynx.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior laryngeal vein begins in the upper aspect of the larynx.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior laryngeal vein accompanies the superior laryngeal artery. It passes laterally in the neck, deep to the thyrohyoid muscle, to reach and drain into the superior thyroid vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior laryngeal vein, along with the inferior laryngeal vein, provides venous drainage of the larynx.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lower part of the larynx.

Course: Descends to enter the inferior thyroid vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Larynx.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior laryngeal vein begins in the lower aspect of the larynx.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior laryngeal vein accompanies the inferior laryngeal artery. It descends in the neck to reach and drain into the inferior thyroid vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior laryngeal vein, along with the superior laryngeal vein, provides venous drainage of the larynx.

19091.name: Inferior Bulb of Internal Jugular Vein

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The inferior bulb of the internal jugular vein is a dilation of the internal jugular vein near its termination with the subclavian vein. It is located within the supraclavicular fossa, a depression between the two heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The inferior bulb also contains two valves above it.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Central vein cannulation

24502.name: Superior Bulb of Internal Jugular Vein

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The superior bulb of the internal jugular vein is a dilation of the internal jugular vein at its origin, where the sigmoid and inferior petrosal sinuses join. It lies below the posterior part of the tympanic floor.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: In the suboccipital region from the union of communicating branch of the occipital veins and tributaries from the suboccipital muscles. 

Course: Descends between semispinalis cervicis and capitis, then passes over the neck of the first rib to drain into the vertebral vein.

Tributaries: Vertebral venous plexuses.

Drainage: Suboccipital region, cervical part of vertebral column, deep muscles of the neck.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep cervical vein originates in the suboccipital region, from the union of a communicating branch of the occipital veins with tributaries from the suboccipital muscles.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep cervical vein descends between the semispinalis cervicis and capitis muscles, accompanied by the deep cervical artery. The vein then passes between the neck of the first rib and the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra to drain into the vertebral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The deep cervical vein receives tributaries from the vertebral venous plexuses.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep cervical vein drains venous blood from the suboccipital region, the adjacent vertebral column, and from the deep muscles of the neck.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Course: Courses parallel to the sternocleidomastoid artery to traverse over the hypoglossal nerve and drain into internal jugular vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The sternocleidomastoid vein originates from the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The sternocleidomastoid vein runs parallel to the sternocleidomastoid artery, which arises from the occipital artery proximal to the crossing point of the hypoglossal nerve over the occipital artery.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The sternocleidomastoid vein drains venous blood from the sternocleidomastoid muscle tissue and eventually drains into the internal jugular vein.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: An accessory vertebral vein may arise from the vertebral vein as it forms a venous plexus around the vertebral artery. The accessory vertebral vein continues to descend in the foramina transversaria as far as the seventh cervical vertebra, where it then passes between the apex of the lung and the subclavian artery to join the brachiocephalic vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Under the chin.

Course: Descends superficially to drain into the external jugular vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Anterior neck.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior jugular vein is the smallest of the jugular veins and its size is inversely proportional to that of the external jugular vein. It originates from the convergence of superficial veins under the mandible.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior jugular vein travels inferiorly from its point of origin, within the subcutaneous tissue or deep to the superficial layer of the deep cervical fascia, between the anterior edge of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and the anterior median line. When the anterior jugular vein arrives at the root of the neck, it courses laterally, deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, but superficial to the infrahyoid muscles. It terminates by either opening into the terminal aspect of the external jugular vein or directly into the subclavian vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
There are no named tributaries; however, the anterior jugular vein may receive the laryngeal veins and infrequently, a small thyroid vein (Standring, 2016). 

The left and right anterior jugular veins are devoid of valves and form the large transverse jugular venous arch in the suprasternal space by merging at the midlines, just superior to the manubrium of the sternum. The jugular venous arch receives the inferior thyroid vein tributaries (Standring, 2016; Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior jugular vein drains blood from the anterior part of the neck.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Suprahyoid muscles.

Course: Runs along the superior border of the hyoid bone to reach the lingual vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Suprahyoid muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The suprahyoid vein originates in the parenchyma of the suprahyoid muscles.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The suprahyoid vein accompanies its corresponding suprahyoid artery along the superior border of the hyoid bone. It drains into the lingual vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The suprahyoid vein drains venous blood from the suprahyoid muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The left and right anterior jugular veins merge in the midline, thus forming a large transverse jugular venous arch in the suprasternal space, just superior to the manubrium of the sternum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Suboccipital triangle.

Course: Descends in the foramina transversaria of the upper six cervical vertebrae.

Tributaries: Intervertebral, anterior vertebral, and deep cervical veins.

Drainage: Vertebral column and suboccipital region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vertebral vein originates from a venous plexus in the suboccipital triangle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The vertebral vein descends in the foramina transversaria of the upper six cervical vertebrae and forms a plexus around the vertebral artery. After emerging from the foramen transversarium of the sixth cervical vertebra, the vertebral vein descends anterolateral to the vertebral artery. It passes behind the internal jugular vein and anterior to the first part of the subclavian artery, before draining superoposteriorly into the brachiocephalic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The vertebral vein receives the intervertebral, anterior vertebral, and deep cervical veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The vertebral vein drains the muscles of the suboccipital triangle and the cervical part of the vertebral column.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Submental triangle.

Course: Passes laterally over the submandibular gland near the angle of the mandible to drain into facial vein.

Tributaries: Submandibular vein.

Drainage: Submental region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The submental vein originates from a network of vessels situated inside the submental triangle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Following its origin inside the submental triangle, the submental vein turns laterally, passes over the submandibular gland near the angle of the mandible and drains into the facial vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the submental vein may communicate with the anterior jugular veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The submental vein drains the muscles and superficial tissues inside the submental triangle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Around the transverse processes of the upper cervical vertebrae.

Course: Descends in the neck to drain into the vertebral vein.

Tributaries: Anterior external vertebral venous plexus.

Drainage: Vertebral column.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior vertebral vein begins in the upper neck, as a venous plexus around the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior vertebral vein descends in the neck, anterior to the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, close to the attachments of the scalenus anterior and longus capitis muscles. It is accompanied by the ascending cervical artery. The anterior vertebral vein drains into the vertebral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior vertebral vein receives tributaries from the anterior external vertebral venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior vertebral vein drains the vertebral column.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Cricothyroid membrane.

Course: Passes laterally to reach the superior thyroid vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Cricothyroid membrane and muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The cricothyroid vein originates as a confluence of small tributaries draining the cricothyroid membrane and muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The cricothyroid vein is accompanied by the corresponding cricothyroid artery. It passes laterally to drain into the superior thyroid vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the cricothyroid vein may anastomose with its fellow vein of the opposite side. This could sometimes lead to the formation of a common cricothyroid vein in the midline, which then descends on the surface of the thyroid gland.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The cricothyroid vein drains venous blood from the cricothyroid membrane and muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by the splitting of the retromandibular vein into its anterior and posterior divisions.

Course: Joins with the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Face and temporal region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior division of the retromandibular vein is formed within the lower parotid gland by the splitting of the retromandibular vein into its anterior and posterior divisions.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior division of the retromandibular vein combines with the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein, which then descends across the sternocleidomastoid muscle and into the supraclavicular fossa.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior division of the retromandibular vein drains structures of the face and temporal region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Tympanic cavity.

Course: Accompanies the facial nerve from the tympanic cavity into the facial canal to the stylomastoid foramen.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Tympanic cavity, tympanic antrum, mastoid air cells, and the semicircular canals.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The stylomastoid vein originates from a network of veins inside the tympanic cavity.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The stylomastoid vein accompanies the facial nerve from the tympanic cavity and travels inside the facial canal to reach the stylomastoid foramen. It drains into posterior auricular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The stylomastoid vein drains the tympanic cavity, tympanic antrum, mastoid air cells, and the semicircular canals.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Behind the ear, superficial to the temporal fascia.

Course: Descends behind the ear towards the lower pole of the parotid gland.

Tributaries: Stylomastoid vein.

Drainage: Assists with the draining of the muscles and skin of the scalp behind the ear.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior auricular vein arises as a single channel, from a small parietooccipital plexus of veins on the side of the head and superficial to the temporal fascia.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior auricular vein descends behind the ear and joins with the posterior division of the retromandibular vein to form the external jugular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the posterior auricular vein forms an anastomosis with tributaries of the occipital and the superficial temporal veins. Along its descent, the posterior auricular vein may also receive tributaries from the stylomastoid vein and from the auricle.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior auricular vein assists with the draining of the muscles and skin of the scalp behind the ear.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From the mucosa of the mastoid antrum.

Course: Run medially and emerge onto the posterior surface of the petrous temporal bone at the subarcuate fossa.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Mucosa of the tympanic cavity.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The tympanic vein arises as a small group of veins from the mucosa of the mastoid antrum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The tympanic vein runs medially through the arch formed by the superior semicircular canal and emerges onto the posterior surface of the petrous part of the temporal bone at the subarcuate fossa. They may drain into the superior petrosal sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The tympanic veins drain the tympanic cavity.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of various venous tributaries from the vestibule of the inner ear.

Course: Runs parallel to the vestibular aqueduct before draining into the inferior petrosal, sigmoid sinus, or superior bulb of internal jugular vein.

Tributaries: Small tributaries.

Drainage: Vestibule and semicircular canals.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vein of the vestibular aqueduct is formed by the union of venous tributaries draining the vestibule and semicircular canals of the internal ear (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The vein of the vestibular aqueduct runs parallel to the vestibular aqueduct and the endolymphatic duct, prior to its opening into the inferior petrosal, sigmoid sinus, or the superior bulb of internal jugular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The vein of the vestibular aqueduct receives the small veins draining the vestibule and the semicircular canals.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The vein of the vestibular aqueduct drains blood from the vestibule and the semicircular canals.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: Courses from the inner ear through the internal acoustic meatus or nearby petrous bone

Tributaries: Small veins from the cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals, and vestibulocochlear nerve region

Structures drained: Inner ear and internal acoustic meatus region

Termination: Drains into the inferior or superior petrosal sinus, petrosal vein, or jugular bulb

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: As the labyrinthine vein drains the membranous and bony labyrinth of the inner ear, it courses with the vestibulocochlear nerve region through the internal acoustic meatus or adjacent petrous temporal bone pathways.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The labyrinthine vein receives small veins from the cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals, and internal acoustic meatus region. Small channels near the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves may communicate with it.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The labyrinthine vein drains the inner ear, including cochlear and vestibular venous territories. It may also drain small venous channels from the internal acoustic meatus region.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: Common termination sites for the labyrinthine vein include the inferior petrosal sinus, superior petrosal sinus, petrosal vein, or jugular bulb.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of various venous tributaries from the cochlear part of the inner ear.

Course: Runs parallel to the cochlear aqueduct before draining into the inferior petrosal sinus.

Tributaries: Common modiolar and vestibulocochlear veins.

Drainage: Cochlea and semicircular canals.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vein of the cochlear aqueduct is formed by the union of various venous tributaries from the cochlear part of the inner ear.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The vein of the cochlear aqueduct runs parallel to the cochlear aqueduct by the side of the middle ear, prior to its opening into the inferior petrosal sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
The vein of the cochlear aqueduct receives blood from the various venous tributaries, including the common modiolar vestibulocochlear veins. The confluence of these venous tributaries is located at the bottom of the scala tympani near the round window, prior to their opening into the vein of cochlear aqueduct.

The vein of the cochlear aqueduct also receives two communicating veins from the mucoperiosteum of the middle ear. One arises from the mucoperiosteum of the cochlear surface, which runs parallel to the vein of cochlear aqueduct, before draining into it, while the other is from a network of mucoperiosteal vessels near the round window that communicate directly with the vein of cochlear aqueduct (Watanabe, Nakashima and Yanagita, 1988).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The vein of the cochlear aqueduct receives blood from the scala vestibuli and tympani via the common modiolar veins, and from the cochlea, saccule, and semicircular canals via the vestibulocochlear vein.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Watanabe, Y., Nakashima, T. and Yanagita, N. (1988) 'Venous communications of the cochlea after acute occlusion of the vein of the cochlear aqueduct', Arch Otorhinolaryngol, 245(6), pp. 340-3.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior aspect of external ear.

Course: Drain directly into the superficial temporal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, and superficial muscles anterior to the external ear and external acoustic meatus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior auricular veins arise from the anterior aspect of the external ear.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior auricular veins have a short course and drain into the superficial temporal (or retromandibular) vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior auricular veins drain the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and superficial muscles in the anterior auricular region, the ear lobule, and the external acoustic meatus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: Courses along the superior border of the petrous temporal bone

Tributaries: Cavernous sinus, petrosal vein, cerebellar veins, and brainstem veins

Structures drained: Cavernous sinus, cerebellopontine angle, anterior cerebellum, and lateral brainstem

Termination: Drains into the transverse-sigmoid junction or sigmoid sinus

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: The superior petrosal sinus courses along the superior border of the petrous part of the temporal bone, within the attached margin of the tentorium cerebelli. It connects the cavernous sinus with the transverse-sigmoid region.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superior petrosal sinus receives the cavernous sinus anteriorly and commonly receives the petrosal vein, cerebellar veins, and small brainstem venous tributaries. It may also receive tentorial and meningeal veins.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The superior petrosal sinus drains the cavernous sinus, cerebellopontine angle region, anterior cerebellar surface, and lateral brainstem venous pathways.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: The superior petrosal sinus usually terminates at the transverse-sigmoid junction or directly into the sigmoid sinus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: S-shaped continuation of the transverse sinus in the posterior cranial fossa

Tributaries: Transverse sinus, superior petrosal sinus, mastoid and condylar emissary veins, and cerebellar veins

Structures drained: Major cerebral, cerebellar, dural, and skull venous outflow

Termination: Becomes the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: The sigmoid sinus is the S-shaped continuation of the transverse sinus along the posterolateral skull base. It courses in the sigmoid sulcus of the temporal and occipital bones toward the jugular foramen.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The sigmoid sinus receives the transverse sinus, superior petrosal sinus, mastoid emissary veins, condylar emissary veins, and small cerebellar or meningeal veins. It may also communicate with diploic and extracranial venous channels.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The sigmoid sinus carries major venous outflow from the cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, posterior fossa dura, and skull. It is the final intracranial dural venous sinus pathway before jugular venous drainage.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: The sigmoid sinus exits the cranial cavity through the jugular foramen and continues as the internal jugular vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: Venous channel around the margin of the foramen magnum

Tributaries: Occipital sinus, vertebral venous plexus, condylar veins, and inferior posterior fossa veins

Structures drained: Foramen magnum dura, lower cerebellar, medullary, and craniocervical venous regions

Termination: Communicates with the sigmoid sinus, jugular bulb, and vertebral venous plexus

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: The marginal sinus courses around the margin of the foramen magnum within the dura of the posterior cranial fossa. It forms an important venous ring at the craniocervical junction.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The marginal sinus receives the occipital sinus, small dural veins near the foramen magnum, condylar emissary veins, and venous channels from the medullary and inferior cerebellar region. It also communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The marginal sinus drains the dura around the foramen magnum and adjacent posterior fossa venous territory. It may also receive drainage from lower medullary, inferior cerebellar, and craniocervical venous pathways.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: The marginal sinus communicates with the sigmoid sinus, jugular bulb, condylar venous channels, and vertebral venous plexus.

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2002. The cerebral veins. Neurosurgery 51 (4 Suppl), S159–S205. doi:10.1097/00006123-200210001-00005

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Continuation of the cranial part of anterior internal vertebral venous plexus or from a primary head vein.

Course: Consists of interconnecting venous channels between layers of dura mater on the clivus.

Tributaries: Numerous connections exist with surrounding venous channels, such as inferior petrosal sinuses, internal vertebral venous plexus, cavernous and superior petrosal sinuses, marginal sinus, venous network of the hypoglossal canal, condylar emissary veins, and the inferior surface of clivus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: There is contradictory evidence in the literature regarding the origin of the basilar venous plexus. Some believe that it arises as a continuation of the cranial part of the anterior internal vertebral venous plexus. Others found no anatomical link between the two and postulated that the basilar plexus of veins is likely derived from a primary head vein (de Caro et al., 1990).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The basilar sinus and plexus consist of interconnecting venous channels between layers of dura mater on the clivus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
The basilar venous plexus has numerous connections with the venous channels around it. For instance, it interconnects the inferior petrosal sinuses and joins posteroinferiorly with the internal vertebral venous plexus. Anteriorly, it has additional connections with the cavernous and superior petrosal sinuses. If the marginal sinus enlarges, it may also join anteriorly with the basilar plexus of veins. The basilar plexus indirectly communicates with the pterygoid plexus and facial veins through the cavernous sinus and superior ophthalmic vein, respectively.

There are additional intraosseous connections between the basilar plexus and the inferior side of the clivus via the basilar canal and connections with the venous network of the hypoglossal canal and condylar emissary veins (Tubbs et al., 2007).

sections.title: References
sections.text:

Tubbs, R. S., Hansasuta, A., Loukas, M., Louis Jr., R. G., Shoja, M. M., Salter, E. G. and Oakes, W. J. (2007) 'The basilar venous plexus', Clinical Anatomy, 20(7), pp. 755-759.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
There are usually three irregularly shaped venous spaces, or lacunae, present inside the dura mater, on either side of the superior sagittal sinus. They can be considered as the lateral extensions of the sinus. These include a small frontal, a large parietal, and intermediate occipital lacunae. The venous lacunae could potentially become confluent in elderly people and form large single spaces on either side of the superior sagittal sinus.

Most of the cerebral veins from the outer surface of the cerebral hemispheres open into the venous lacunae and numerous arachnoid granulations project into them from below. The venous lacunae also drain diploid, emissary, and meningeal veins.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: Courses along the free inferior margin of the falx cerebri

Tributaries: Small veins from the falx, medial cerebral hemisphere, and corpus callosum region

Structures drained: Falx cerebri and adjacent medial cerebral territory

Termination: Joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: The inferior sagittal sinus courses along the free inferior margin of the falx cerebri. It lies superior to the corpus callosum and below the superior sagittal sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior sagittal sinus receives small veins from the falx cerebri and adjacent medial surfaces of the cerebral hemispheres. Small callosal or cingulate venous channels may also communicate with it.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The inferior sagittal sinus drains the falx cerebri and adjacent medial cerebral territory, including small veins near the corpus callosum and cingulate region.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: The inferior sagittal sinus usually joins the great cerebral vein near the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli to form the straight sinus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: Midline sinus in the attached falx cerebelli

Tributaries: Inferior cerebellar, dural, and marginal sinus tributaries

Structures drained: Posterior fossa dura, inferior cerebellar region, and craniocervical venous pathways

Termination: Drains superiorly to the confluence or inferiorly to the marginal sinus

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: The occipital sinus is a midline dural venous sinus within the attached margin of the falx cerebelli. It courses between the confluence of sinuses and the foramen magnum region.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The occipital sinus may receive small dural veins, inferior cerebellar veins, and communicating channels from the marginal sinus and vertebral venous plexus. Its size and presence are variable.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The occipital sinus drains posterior fossa dura and may receive venous blood from inferior cerebellar and craniocervical venous territories.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: The occipital sinus may drain superiorly into the confluence of sinuses, inferiorly into the marginal sinus, or both.
