sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: Courses laterally from the confluence of sinuses along the attached margin of the tentorium

Tributaries: Superior sagittal, straight, occipital, tentorial, and cerebellar venous inputs

Structures drained: Posterior cerebral, cerebellar, meningeal, and diploic territories

Termination: Continues as the sigmoid sinus

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: The transverse sinus courses laterally from the confluence of sinuses within the attached margin of the tentorium cerebelli, following the transverse sulcus of the occipital bone and curving toward the mastoid region. The right and left sinuses are commonly asymmetric e.g., the right transverse sinus may arise from the confluence of sinuses receiving the superior sagittal sinus, while the left connects more directly with the straight sinus. The right sinus is dominant in the majority of individuals.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The tributaries of the transverse sinus include the superior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, occipital sinus, tentorial sinuses, and superior or inferior cerebellar veins. The pattern of right and left transverse sinus dominance is variable.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The transverse sinus receives venous drainage from posterior cerebral, cerebellar, meningeal, and diploic territories. It also serves as a major outflow route for superficial and deep cerebral venous drainage that reaches the confluence of sinuses.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: The transverse sinus usually continues as the sigmoid sinus at the transverse-sigmoid junction near the posterolateral skull base.

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2002. The cerebral veins. Neurosurgery 51 (4 Suppl), S159–S205. doi:10.1097/00006123-200210001-00005

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: Courses along the lesser wing of the sphenoid toward the cavernous sinus

Tributaries: Dural, diploic, superficial middle cerebral, and anterior temporal venous channels

Structures drained: Sphenoid wing, anterior temporal dura, and variable superficial cerebral drainage

Termination: Drains into the cavernous sinus or nearby skull-base venous pathways

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: The sphenoparietal sinus courses along the lesser wing of the sphenoid toward the cavernous sinus. It lies near the anterior part of the middle cranial fossa.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The sphenoparietal sinus may receive dural veins, diploic veins, superficial middle cerebral venous drainage, and small anterior temporal or sphenoid wing venous channels. Its tributary pattern is variable.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The sphenoparietal sinus drains the sphenoid wing region, adjacent dura, and variable superficial cerebral venous channels near the lateral sulcus and anterior temporal region.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: The sphenoparietal sinus commonly drains into the cavernous sinus, although some drainage may pass through nearby skull-base or meningeal venous pathways.

sections.text:

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2002. The cerebral veins. Neurosurgery 51 (4 Suppl), S159–S205. doi:10.1097/00006123-200210001-00005

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: Courses along the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli

Tributaries: Great cerebral vein, inferior sagittal sinus, and tentorial or cerebellar veins

Structures drained: Deep cerebral, medial cerebral, tentorial, and cerebellar territories

Termination: Drains into the confluence of sinuses or a transverse sinus

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: The straight sinus courses posteriorly along the junction between the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli. It forms where the inferior sagittal sinus joins the great cerebral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The major tributaries of the straight sinus are the great cerebral vein and inferior sagittal sinus. It may also receive tentorial veins, posterior callosal veins, and superior cerebellar or vermian venous channels.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The straight sinus drains deep cerebral venous blood carried by the great cerebral vein, medial cerebral drainage from the inferior sagittal sinus, and variable tentorial or cerebellar venous contributions.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: The straight sinus usually terminates at the confluence of sinuses or preferentially into one transverse sinus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Origin: paired dural venous sinuses that are found on either side of the sella turcica.

– Course: extends anteriorly up to the medial end of the superior orbital fissure and posteriorly to the apex of the petrous temporal bone.

– Tributaries: superior ophthalmic and superficial cerebral veins and sphenoparietal sinus. Communicates with the transverse sinus, internal jugular vein, pterygoid plexus of veins, facial vein, and the opposite cavernous sinus via intercavernous sinuses and basilar plexus.

– Drainage: orbit and the anterior part of the brain.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The cavernous sinuses are paired dural venous sinuses that are found on either side of the sella turcica (body of sphenoid), occupying a space between the periosteal and meningeal layers of the dura matter. The internal aspect of the cavernous sinus is divided into several spaces or caverns by trabeculae.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The cavernous sinus extends anteriorly up to the medial end of the superior orbital fissure, while posteriorly, it reaches up to the apex of the petrous part of the temporal bone. The floor of the sinus is formed by the periosteal dura mater. The lateral wall, roof, and medial walls are formed by the meningeal layer of dura mater.

Several important structure course through the cavernous sinus and in its lateral wall. For instance, cranial nerves, including the oculomotor, trochlear, and ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of trigeminal nerve run inside the lateral wall of the sinus. The internal carotid artery and the abducent nerve pass through the center of the sinus.

sections.title: Tributaries
Structures Drained
sections.text: The cavernous sinus drains the orbit and the anterior part of the brain.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Cavernous sinus thrombosis

– Caroticocavernous sinus fistula

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: Courses along the attached superior margin of the falx cerebri

Tributaries: Superior cerebral veins, diploic veins, meningeal veins, and lateral lacunae

Structures drained: Superior and medial cerebral hemispheres, dura, and skull

Termination: Usually drains into the confluence of sinuses

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: The superior sagittal sinus courses in the attached superior margin of the falx cerebri from the frontal region toward the occipital region. It lies in the midline along the superior border of the cranial vault.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superior sagittal sinus receives superior cerebral veins, diploic veins, meningeal veins, and venous blood from lateral lacunae. Arachnoid granulations commonly project into the sinus and adjacent lacunae.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The superior sagittal sinus drains the superior and medial surfaces of the cerebral hemispheres, adjacent dura, and skull. It is a major superficial cerebral venous outflow pathway.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: The superior sagittal sinus usually terminates at the confluence of sinuses, often continuing preferentially into one transverse sinus depending on venous dominance.

Rhoton, A.L. Jr., 2002. The cerebral veins. Neurosurgery 51 (4 Suppl), S159–S205. doi:10.1097/00006123-200210001-00005

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Connects the two cavernous sinuses on either side of sella turcica.

Course: Lies within the anterior attached border of the diaphragma sellae.

Tributaries: Small irregular sinuses inferior to the pituitary gland drain into the intercavernous sinuses.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The intercavernous sinus is unpaired sinus which lies within the attached border of the diaphragma sellae.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The intercavernous sinus forms a complete circular venous sinus around the sella turcica.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Small irregular sinuses inferior to the pituitary gland drain into the intercavernous sinuses.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The intercavernous sinus connects the two cavernous sinuses situated on either side of the sella turcica. Like other venous sinuses, the connection is valveless and the blood can flow between the two cavernous sinuses in a bidirectional fashion.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location/Course: Courses in the petroclival fissure from the cavernous sinus to the jugular foramen

Tributaries: Cavernous sinus, basilar plexus, labyrinthine and brainstem-related veins

Structures drained: Cavernous sinus, clival, inner ear, and skull-base venous pathways

Termination: Drains into the jugular bulb or internal jugular vein

sections.title: Location/Course
sections.text: The inferior petrosal sinus courses along the petroclival fissure between the petrous temporal bone and clivus. It extends from the cavernous sinus to the jugular foramen.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior petrosal sinus receives venous blood from the cavernous sinus, basilar plexus, and small clival or meningeal veins. It may also receive labyrinthine, pontine, or medullary venous communications.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The inferior petrosal sinus drains the cavernous sinus and skull-base venous pathways near the clivus and petrous temporal bone. It also participates in communication with the basilar plexus and posterior fossa venous system.

sections.title: Termination
sections.text: The inferior petrosal sinus usually terminates in the jugular bulb or upper internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Along the bronchi.

Course: Travel posteriorly to join the azygos vein on the right and accessory hemiazygos vein on the left.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Bronchi and hilar structures.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The bronchial veins originate on the dorsal aspect of the left and right bronchi.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
From their origin, the right and left bronchial veins travel posteriorly to their terminations at the azygos vein on the right and the accessory hemiazygos vein, or sometimes the superior intercostal vein, on the left.

It is important to note that bronchial vessels are a part of the systemic circulation, not the pulmonary circulation. They are not involved in the gas exchange that takes place at the alveoli between the blood and inspired air, although some distal bronchial vessels do anastomose with pulmonary vessels.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The bronchial veins receive blood from the bronchi, hilar structures, such as lymph nodes, and visceral pleura adjacent to the hilum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Gluteal region.

Course: Passes though the greater sciatic foramen to drain into the internal iliac vein.

Tributaries: Lateral sacral veins.

Drainage: Muscles of the buttocks, upper thigh, and hip bones.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Deep and superficial ramifications of the superior gluteal vein unite in the gluteal region to form the superior gluteal vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the superior gluteal vein enters the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen, superior to piriformis muscles. They drain into the internal iliac vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superior gluteal veins may receive tributes from the lateral sacral veins. It also forms anastomoses with the lateral circumflex femoral vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior gluteal vein drains gluteus minimums, gluteus maximus, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae muscles, the hip joint, and ilium.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Gluteal region.

Course: Travels deep to gluteus maximus and enters the pelvic cavity through the greater sciatic foramen to drain into the internal iliac vein.

Tributaries: Medial circumflex femoral vein and venules from the gluteus maximus muscle.

Drainage: Posterior thigh and gluteal region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior gluteal veins in the gluteus maximus muscle in the gluteal region.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin the inferior gluteal vein courses deep to the gluteus maximus and inferior to the piriformis muscle. It travels through the greater sciatic foramen, with the corresponding artery, to drain into the anterior division of internal iliac vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior gluteal vein receives blood from the medial circumflex femoral vein and venules of the gluteus maximus muscle. The gluteal veins communicate with tributaries from the femoral region via the medial and lateral circumflex veins. Therefore, they provide an alternative route for venous return in conditions in which the femoral vein may be occluded (Moore et al, 2013).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior gluteal vein drains muscle of the posterior thigh and gluteal region. This includes the coccygeus, levator ani, piriformis, quadratus femoris, hamstrings, gluteus maximus muscles, and the sciatic nerve.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Piriformis syndrome

sections.title: References
sections.text: Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep hypogastric region.

Course: Travels along the iliac crest to drain into the external iliac vein.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: External iliac vein.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep circumflex vein is formed by the venules draining the deep hypogastric region of the trunk wall.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the deep circumflex vein courses anteromedially along the iliac crest to join with the external iliac vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep circumflex vein drains blood directly from the deep hypogastric region of the abdominal wall.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Inguinal hernia

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of iliac, spinal, and lumbar branches.

Course: Travel medially from the medial border of psoas major to drain into common iliac veins.

Tributaries: Fourth and fifth lumbar and iliac vein and spinal branches.

Drainage: Iliacus, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, ilium, posterior lumbar and sacral regions.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: From its origin, the iliolumbar vein receives anastomotic tributaries from the fourth and fifth lumbar veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The iliolumbar vein courses inferiorly along the sacrospinous joint to drain into the internal iliac vein, or more commonly into the common iliac vein. It often bifurcates and drains into both the internal iliac and the common iliac veins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
The iliolumbar vein drains the fourth and fifth lumbar veins.

The spinal branches of the iliolumbar vein drain into the iliolumbar vein and pass through the intervertebral foramen between the fifth lumbar vertebrae and sacrum.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The iliolumbar vein drains the structures of the iliac fossae and the lumbar and sacral region. This includes the Iliacus, psoas major, and quadratus lumborum muscles.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of unnamed anterior and posterior tributaries, encircling the obturator foramen.

Course: Drains into the internal iliac vein or inferior epigastric vein.

Tributaries: Anterior, posterior, and pubic tributaries.

Drainage: Pelvic muscles and hip joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The obturator vein originates from the union of unnamed anterior and posterior tributaries that encircle the obturator foramen, between the obturator externus muscle and the obturator membrane.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the obturator vein runs in the medial compartment of the thigh and passes through the obturator canal to reach the pelvis. It travels inferior to and with the obturator artery and nerve. The obturator vein runs posteriorly and superiorly on the lateral pelvic wall and drains into the internal iliac vein or inferior epigastric vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The obturator vein receives anterior and posterior ramifications, which run in relation to the adductor brevis muscle. In the pelvis, the obturator vein will also receive a pubic branch. The pubic branch of the obturator vein will form a connection with its fellow from the opposite side.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The obturator vein drains the pelvic muscles and the hip joint. The anterior tributary of the obturator vein drains the obturator and adductor muscles. The posterior tributary supplies the proximal portion of the hamstring muscles.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Head of the femur.

Course: Pass over the neck of the femur to reach the medial and lateral circumflex femoral veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Head and neck of the femur.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The retinacular veins originate in the region of the head of the femur.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The retinacular veins descend over the neck of the femur to drain into the lateral and medial circumflex femoral veins, which in turn drain into the deep femoral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The retinacular veins drain the head and neck of the femur.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial fascia of the inguinal region.

Course: Travels inferiorly and medially to drain into the great saphenous vein or femoral vein.

Tributaries: No tributaries.

Drainage: Inguinal region and anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial circumflex iliac vein originates superficially within the superficial fascia of the inguinal region.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the vein takes an oblique course medially, along the course of the inguinal ligament, then descends into the great saphenous vein or femoral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries of the superficial circumflex iliac vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superficial circumflex iliac vein drains the inguinal region and the abdominal wall.

20433.name: Posterior Arch Vein
alternate: Posterior Accessory Saphenous Vein of Leg

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: At the medial malleolus.

Course: Ascends in the calf to join the great saphenous vein distal to the knee joint.

Tributaries: Perforating veins.

Drainage: Foot and ankle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior arch vein arises at the medial malleolus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior arch vein ascends in the calf, parallel to the great saphenous vein. It drains into the great saphenous vein distal to the knee joint.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Perforating veins from the posterior tibial veins join the posterior arch vein, rather than the great saphenous vein directly (Meissner, 2005).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior arch vein receives blood from the foot and ankle.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Meissner, M. H. (2005) Lower extremity venous anatomy. Seminars in interventional radiology, 22(3), 147-156.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Behind the lateral malleolus.

Course: Ascends in the posterior leg to the knee joint and drains into the popliteal vein.

Tributaries: Perforating veins.

Drainage: Foot, ankle, and posterior leg.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The small saphenous vein is a continuation of the lateral marginal vein and originates behind the lateral malleolus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The small saphenous vein ascends superficially in the posterior leg. It passes lateral to the calcaneal tendon and ascends in the subcutaneous tissue of the calf. It passes between the two heads of the gastrocnemius muscle to enter the popliteal fossa. It drains into the popliteal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The small saphenous vein receives perforating veins that connects it to the fibular and anterior tibial veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The small saphenous vein drains blood from the lateral foot and calf.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lateral side of the dorsum of the foot.

Course: Passes behind the lateral malleolus and continues as the small saphenous vein.

Tributaries: Dorsal venous arch.

Drainage: Dorsum and sole of the lateral aspect of the foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral marginal vein forms at the lateral side of the dorsal aspect of the foot by veins arising from the superficial parts of the sole of the foot.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lateral marginal vein passes behind the lateral malleolus and continues as the small saphenous vein which ascends in the leg.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The lateral marginal vein communicates with the dorsal venous arch.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The lateral marginal vein drains the dorsum of the foot and the superficial parts of the sole of the foot.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal surface of the toes.

Course: Pass towards the clefts of the toes and unite to form the dorsal metatarsal veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Toes.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal digital veins of the foot arise from a venous plexus in the dorsal aspect of the toes.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal digital veins of the foot extend towards the clefts of the toes, where they receive perforating veins from the plantar digit veins. They continue as the dorsal metatarsal veins in the intermetatarsal spaces of the foot.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The dorsal digital veins of the foot receive ramifications from the plantar digital veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The dorsal digital veins of the foot drain blood from the dorsal surfaces of the toes.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Continuation of the plantar digital veins.

Course: Pass within the intermetatarsal spaces and unite in a plantar venous arch.

Tributaries: Intercapitular veins.

Drainage: Plantar surface of the foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The plantar metatarsal veins are the continuations of the plantar digital veins at the clefts of the toes.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The plantar metatarsal veins pass proximally in the intermetatarsal spaces and unite to form the plantar venous arch at the proximal end of the metatarsal bones.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The plantar metatarsal veins receive the intercapitular veins, short vessels that pass between the heads of the metatarsal bones and connecting to the plantar metatarsal veins. These veins tend not to have any valves and the blood flow is bidirectional. In some instances valves may be present and face towards the superficial system, thus, allowing blood to pass from the plantar to dorsal systems (Kelikian, 2012).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The plantar metatarsal veins drain blood from the plantar aspect of the foot.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Kelikian, A. S. (2012) Sarrafian's Anatomy of the Foot and Ankle: Descriptive, Topographic, Functional. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Continuation of the dorsal digital veins of the foot.

Course: Pass within the intermetatarsal spaces and unite in a dorsal venous arch.

Tributaries: Intercapitular veins.

Drainage: Dorsal surface of the foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal metatarsal veins are the continuation of the dorsal digital veins at the clefts of the toes.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal metatarsal veins pass proximally in the intermetatarsal spaces and unite to form the dorsal venous arch at the proximal end of the metatarsal bones.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The dorsal metatarsal veins receive the intercapitular veins, short vessels that pass between the heads of the metatarsal bones and connecting to the plantar metatarsal veins. These veins tend not to have any valves and the blood flow is bidirectional. In some instances valves may be present and face towards the superficial system, thus, allowing blood to pass from the plantar to dorsal systems (Kelikian, 2012).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The dorsal metatarsal veins drain blood from the dorsal aspect of the foot.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Kelikian, A. S. (2012) Sarrafian's Anatomy of the Foot and Ankle: Descriptive, Topographic, Functional. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Medial side of the dorsum of the foot.

Course: Passes behind the medial malleolus and continues as the great saphenous vein.

Tributaries: Dorsal venous arch.

Drainage: Dorsum and sole of the medial aspect of the foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial marginal vein forms at the medial side of the dorsal aspect of the foot by veins arising from the superficial parts of the sole of the foot.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The medial marginal vein passes behind the medial malleolus and continues as the great saphenous vein which ascends in the leg.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The medial marginal vein communicates with the dorsal venous arch.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The medial marginal vein drains the dorsum of the foot and the superficial parts of the sole of the foot.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of the dorsal metatarsal veins.

Course: Arches over the proximal ends of the metatarsal bones, draining into the medial and lateral marginal veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Dorsal aspect of the foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal venous arch is formed by the union of the dorsal metatarsal veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal venous arch passes over the proximal ends of the metatarsal bones. On either side of the foot, the dorsal venous arch connects with the lateral and medial marginal veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The dorsal venous arch drains blood from the dorsal aspect of the foot.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Plantar surface of the toes.

Course: Pass towards the clefts of the toes and unite to form the plantar metatarsal veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Toes.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The plantar digital veins arise from a venous plexus in the plantar aspect of the toes.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The plantar digital veins extend towards the clefts of the toes, where they receive perforating veins from the dorsal digit veins. They continue as the plantar metatarsal veins in the intermetatarsal spaces of the foot.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The plantar digital veins send ramifications to the dorsal digital veins of the foot.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The plantar digital veins drain blood from the plantar surfaces of the toes.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of tributaries from the medial and posterior aspect of the thigh.

Course: Runs in the posteromedial thigh and opens into great saphenous vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Medial and posterior superficial parts of thigh.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The accessory saphenous vein is formed posteriorly from the union of tributaries from the medial and posterior aspect of the thigh.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The accessory saphenous vein may not always be present. At its origin, the accessory saphenous vein is superficial as it runs just below the superficial fascia. As it ascends in the posteromedial thigh, the vein becomes deeper in order to drain into the proximal great saphenous vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The accessory saphenous vein drains the medial and posterior parts of the superficial thigh, including the skin and subcutaneous tissue.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: -Varicose veins

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of the dorsal venous arch of the foot and the dorsal veins of the great toe.

Course: Takes a long course from the foot to the proximal thigh to drain into the femoral vein.

Tributaries: Perforating, accessory saphenous, external pudendal, and posterior arch veins.

Drainage: Foot and leg.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The great saphenous vein originates in the foot from the union of the dorsal venous arch of the foot and the dorsal veins of the great toe.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The great saphenous vein is the longest vein in the body, as it travels superficially through the entire length of the lower limb. It ascends from the foot, anterior to the medial malleolus, and travels in an anteroposterior direction along the medial surface of the tibia to the knee joint. It runs posterior to the medial condyle of the femur and the medial border of the patella. From there it runs along the medial aspect of the superficial thigh to drain into the femoral vein, at the saphenous opening in the fascia latae.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Tributaries of the great saphenous vein include perforating veins from the deep veins of the lower limb, accessory saphenous, external pudendal, and the posterior arch veins. Additionally, the medial marginal, superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac may drain into the great saphenous vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The many tributaries of the great saphenous vein drain the foot, leg, thigh, inguinal region, and lower abdominal wall.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
-Varicose Veins

-Thrombophlebitis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Around the proximal femur.

Course: Horizontal course to drain into the femoral or deep femoral vein.

Tributaries: Retinacular veins.

Drainage: Hip joint and thigh muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral circumflex femoral vein is formed by the union of unnamed ascending, transverse, and descending tributaries, that follow a similar pattern to the branches of the lateral circumflex femoral artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the lateral circumflex femoral vein takes a horizontal course and runs medially around the proximal shaft of the femur bone to drain into the femoral or deep femoral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
The lateral circumflex femoral vein receives the retinacular veins which drain the head and neck of the femur. Additionally, the lateral circumflex femoral vein receives ascending and transverse tributaries. However due to variation they are not officially named. Additionally, it forms an anastomosis with the superficial tributary of medial circumflex femoral vein.

The ascending tributary of the lateral circumflex femoral vein courses inferiorly along the intertrochanteric line at the anterior aspect of the neck of the femur, until it drains into the lateral circumflex vein.

The transverse tributary is the smallest tributary of the lateral circumflex femoral vein. It pierces vastus lateralis muscle and runs anterior to vastus intermedius muscle. It forms anastomoses with the transverse tributary of medial circumflex vein (deep to gluteus maximus muscles), the inferior gluteal vein, and first perforating vein in the thigh.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The lateral circumflex femoral vein drains the proximal deep thigh, including the head, neck, and proximal shaft of the femur.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Around the proximal femur.

Course: Horizontal course to drain into the femoral or deep femoral vein.

Tributaries: Retinacular veins.

Drainage: Hip joint and thigh muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial circumflex femoral vein is formed by the union of unnamed deep, superficial, ascending, transverse, and acetabular tributaries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the medial circumflex femoral vein takes a horizontal course and runs anterolaterally in the gluteal region. It runs between pectineus and iliopsoas muscles and receives many tributaries. It enters the distal part of the femoral triangle and drains into the femoral or deep femoral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The medical circumflex femoral vein receives the retinacular veins which drain the head and neck of the femur. Additionally, the medial circumflex femoral vein receives deep, superficial, ascending, transverse, and acetabular tributaries. These unnamed tributaries closely follow the course of the branches of the medial circumflex femoral vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The medial circumflex femoral vein drains the proximal deep thigh, including the head, neck, and proximal shaft of the femur. The ascending and deep tributaries communicate with the gluteal veins, and the descending tributary communicates with the popliteal vein. The superficial and transverse tributaries communicate with the inferior gluteal, lateral circumflex femoral, and the first perforating veins. Acetabular tributaries drain the head of the femur and the acetabulum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Popliteal region.

Course: Travels between adductor muscles to join the femoral vein in the anterior compartment of the thigh.

Tributaries: Inferior gluteal, medial and lateral circumflex femoral veins, and muscular branches. 

Drainage: Adductor, extensor, and flexor muscles of the thigh.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep femoral vein is one of the main veins of the thigh. It originates distally in the popliteal region.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep femoral vein runs posterior to the deep femoral artery as it traverses the entire length of the thigh. It joins the femoral vein approximately 3 cm distal to the inguinal ligament (Standring, 2016). Along its course, the vein passes between the adductor muscles and anastomoses with the popliteal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
Proximally, the medial and lateral circumflex femoral veins drain into the deep femoral vein, just inferior to the inguinal ligament. Distally, muscular branches join the vein along its course in the thigh.

The deep femoral vein anastomoses proximally with the inferior gluteal veins and distally with the popliteal vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep femoral vein drains the adductor magnus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, pectineus, quadratus femoris, and iliopsoas muscles.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Continuation of the popliteal vein.

Course: Ascends posterolateral to the femoral artery and continues as the external iliac vein.

Tributaries: Deep femoral, long saphenous, lateral and medial circumflex femoral, superficial epigastric, and perforating veins.

Drainage: Lower limb.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The femoral vein originates as a continuation of the popliteal vein, after it passes through the adductor hiatus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The femoral vein ascends in the thigh. It runs with the femoral artery and nerve in the femoral sheath. The femoral vein continues proximally, passing deep to the inguinal ligament, where it becomes the external iliac vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The deep femoral vein joins the femoral vein 3 cm distal to the inguinal ligament (Standring, 2016). The great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein at the saphenous opening. The lateral and medial circumflex femoral veins join the femoral vein or the deep femoral vein. Additionally, the femoral vein receives perforating veins from the great saphenous vein, thus connecting the superficial venous system of the lower limb with the deep venous system.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The femoral vein drains the lower limb.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of the anterior and posterior tibial veins.

Course: Ascends in the popliteal fossa and becomes the femoral vein at the opening of the adductor magnus muscle.

Tributaries: Small saphenous, genicular, and sural veins.

Drainage: Knee, leg, ankle, and foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The popliteal vein arises by the union of the anterior and posterior tibial veins at the distal border of the popliteus muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The popliteal vein ascends in the popliteal fossa, accompanied by the popliteal artery. It is usually more superficial to the artery, but in some cases, it may pass deep to the artery. The popliteal vein becomes the femoral vein as it passes through the adductor hiatus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The popliteal vein receives the small saphenous, genicular, and sural veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The popliteal vein receives blood from the deep veins coming from the knee, leg, ankle, and foot.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Deep vein thrombosis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferomedial aspect of the knee.

Course: Passes posteriorly to drain into the popliteal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Knee joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior medial genicular vein arises at the inferomedial aspect of the knee.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior medial genicular vein passes posteriorly and horizontally across the medial condyle of the tibia to drain into the popliteal vein. It accompanies the inferior medial genicular artery.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior medial genicular vein drains blood from the knee joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior aspect of the knee.

Course: Accompanies the middle genicular artery and drains into the popliteal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Knee joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The middle genicular vein arises at the posterior aspect of the knee.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The middle genicular vein drains into the popliteal vein. It accompanies the middle genicular artery.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The middle genicular vein drains blood from the knee joint, including the cruciate ligaments and the synovial capsule.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superomedial aspect of the knee.

Course: Passes posteriorly to drain into the popliteal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Knee joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior medial genicular vein arises at the superomedial aspect of the knee.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior medial genicular vein passes posteriorly and horizontally across the medial condyle of the femur to drain into the popliteal vein. It accompanies the superior medial genicular artery.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior medial genicular vein drains blood from the knee joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferolateral aspect of the knee.

Course: Passes posteriorly to drain into the popliteal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Knee joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior lateral genicular vein arises at the inferolateral aspect of the knee.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior lateral genicular vein passes posteriorly and horizontally across the lateral condyle of the tibia to drain into the popliteal vein. It accompanies the inferior lateral genicular artery.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The inferior lateral genicular vein drains blood from the knee joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterolateral knee.

Course: Passes posteriorly around the neck of the fibula to drain into the popliteal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Soleus muscle and the knee joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The circumflex fibular vein arises at the anterolateral aspect of the knee.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The circumflex fibular vein accompanies the circumflex fibular branch of the posterior tibial artery. It passes over the lateral aspect of the neck of the fibula and through the soleus muscle to drain into the popliteal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The circumflex fibular vein drains the knee joint and the soleus muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superomedial aspect of the knee.

Course: Ascends medially to drain into the femoral vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Knee joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The descending genicular vein arises at the superomedial aspect of the knee.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The descending genicular vein ascends medially, accompanied by the branches of the descending genicular artery. It drains into the femoral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The descending genicular vein drains blood from the medial aspect of the knee joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superolateral aspect of the knee.

Course: Passes posteriorly to drain into the popliteal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Knee joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior lateral genicular vein arises at the superolateral aspect of the knee.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior lateral genicular vein passes posteriorly and horizontally across the lateral condyle of the femur to drain into the popliteal vein. It accompanies the superior lateral genicular artery.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior lateral genicular vein drains blood from the knee joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lateral aspect of the foot.

Course: Ascends in the lateral compartment of the leg and empties into the posterior tibial vein.

Tributaries: Perforating veins.

Drainage: Lateral aspect of the foot and ankle, and the lateral leg.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The fibular veins form the venae comitantes of the fibular artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The fibular veins ascend in the lateral compartment of the leg, between the tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus muscles. Proximally, it is found deep to the soleus muscle. It terminates by draining into the posterior tibial vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The fibular veins receive the perforating veins. They anastomosis with the superficial veins of the leg and with the anterior tibial veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The fibular veins drain the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg, fibularis longus and brevis. It also receives blood from the soleus muscle, the lateral and posterior aspects of the calcaneus bone, and the deep structures of the foot.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Medial aspect of the ankle.

Course: Ascends in the posterior compartment of the leg and unites with the anterior tibial veins to form the popliteal vein.

Tributaries: Fibular and perforating veins.

Drainage: Foot, ankle, and posterior leg.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior tibial veins are formed by the union of the medial and lateral plantar veins. It forms the venae comitantes of the posterior tibial arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior tibial veins ascend deep to the flexor retinaculum and posterior to the medial malleolus. It then passes deep to the transverse muscular septum and the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles in the posterior compartment of the leg. They unite with the anterior tibial veins at the distal end of the popliteus muscle. This union forms the popliteal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The posterior tibial veins receive the fibular and the perforating veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior tibial veins drain the plantar aspect of the foot, the medial ankle, and the muscles of the posterior compartment of the leg.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsum of the foot.

Course: Ascends in the anterior compartment of the leg and unites with the posterior tibial veins to form the popliteal vein.

Tributaries: Perforating veins and dorsalis pedis vein.

Drainage: Dorsal aspect of the foot and ankle, the tibiofibular and knee joints, and the anterior leg.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior tibial veins form the venae comitantes of the dorsal pedis and anterior tibial arteries.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior tibial veins ascend in the anterior compartment of the leg, between the tibia and fibula. They pass posteriorly through the interosseous membrane and unite with the posterior tibial veins at the distal end of the popliteus muscle. This union forms the popliteal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior tibial veins receive the dorsalis pedis vein and the perforating veins in the ankle and leg.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior tibial veins drain the dorsal aspect of the foot and ankle, the tibiofibular and knee joints, and the anterior leg, including the tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and brevis, and the fibularis longus muscles.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary, 32nd edition. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Each head of the gastrocnemius muscle.

Course: Drains into the popliteal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Gastrocnemius muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The sural veins follow the same path as the sural arteries, originating in the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The sural veins pass within the popliteal fossa and drain into the popliteal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, in some cases, the sural vein may receive the small saphenous veins (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The sural veins drain the muscles of the calf, including gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Plantar surface of the foot.

Course: Unites with the lateral plantar vein to form the posterior tibial vein.

Tributaries: Plantar venous arch.

Drainage: Foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial plantar vein arises on the medial aspect of the foot.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The medial plantar vein passes between the abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis muscles, accompanied by the medial plantar artery. They unite with the lateral plantar vein to form the posterior tibial vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The medial plantar vein receives the plantar venous arch.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The medial plantar vein drains the medial aspect of the foot, including the abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, and quadratus plantae muscles (Ricci et al, 2014).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Plantar vein thrombosis

sections.title: References
sections.text: Ricci, S., Moro, L. & Antonelli Incalzi, R. (2014) The foot venous system: anatomy, physiology and relevance to clinical practice. Dermatol Surg, 40(3), 225-33.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of the metatarsal veins.

Course: Proximal end of the first interosseous space to the base of the fifth metatarsal bone.

Tributaries: Plantar metatarsal veins.

Drainage: Foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The plantar venous arch arises from the union of the metatarsal veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The plantar venous arch, accompanied by the plantar arterial arch, extends from the first interosseous space to the base of the fifth metatarsal bone (Ricci et al, 2014). It is drained by the medial and lateral plantar veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The plantar venous arch receives the plantar metatarsal veins, which are connected to the dorsal metatarsal veins via intercapitular veins, thus, connecting the plantar venous arch with the dorsal venous arch.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The plantar venous arch drains blood from the digits of the foot and surrounding plantar muscles.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Ricci, S., Moro, L. & Antonelli Incalzi, R. (2014) The foot venous system: anatomy, physiology and relevance to clinical practice. Dermatol Surg, 40(3), 225-33.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Plantar surface of the foot.

Course: Unites with the lateral plantar vein to form the posterior tibial vein.

Tributaries: Plantar venous arch.

Drainage: Foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial plantar vein arises on the medial aspect of the foot.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The medial plantar vein passes between the abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis muscles, accompanied by the medial plantar artery. They unite with the lateral plantar vein to form the posterior tibial vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The medial plantar vein receives the plantar venous arch.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The medial plantar vein drains the medial aspect of the foot, including the abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, and quadratus plantae muscles (Ricci et al, 2014).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Plantar vein thrombosis

sections.title: References
sections.text: Ricci, S., Moro, L. & Antonelli Incalzi, R. (2014) The foot venous system: anatomy, physiology and relevance to clinical practice. Dermatol Surg, 40(3), 225-33.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep venous network of the foot.

Course: Accompanies the dorsalis pedis artery along the proximal foot and drains into the anterior tibial vein.

Tributaries: Medial and lateral ankle perforating veins.

Drainage: Deep structures of the foot.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsalis pedis veins are the venae comitantes of the dorsalis pedis artery. There are usually two veins surrounding the artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsalis pedis veins travel deep in the dorsum of the foot, deep to the dorsal fascia and lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus muscle.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The dorsalis pedis veins are connected to the superficial venous system. The anteromedial malleolar vein, a medial perforating vein of the ankle, connects the dorsalis pedis veins to the great saphenous vein. The anterolateral malleolar vein, a lateral perforating vein of the ankle, connects the dorsalis pedis veins to the small saphenous vein. The dorsalis pedis veins continue proximally as the anterior tibial veins (Kelikian, 2012).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The dorsalis pedis veins drain the deep structures of the foot.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Kelikian, A. S. (2012) Sarrafian's Anatomy of the Foot and Ankle: Descriptive, Topographic, Functional. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Greater saphenous vein.

Course: Passes laterally crossing the ankle joint to reach the anterior tibial veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Ankle joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anteromedial malleolar vein is usually present and comes from the great saphenous vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anteromedial malleolar vein passes laterally across the ankle joint, beneath the tendons for extensor hallucis longus and tibialis anterior muscles. It drains into the anterior tibial or dorsalis pedis veins (Kelikian, 2012).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anteromedial malleolar vein drains the ankle joint.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Kelikian, A. S. (2012) Sarrafian's Anatomy of the Foot and Ankle: Descriptive, Topographic, Functional. Wolters Kluwer Health.

21310.name: Upper Posterior Tibial Perforating Veins
alternate: Paratibial Perforating Vein of Mid Third of Leg

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior arch vein.

Course: Proximal aspect of the leg.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Unites with posterior tibial veins.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The upper posterior tibial perforating veins originate from the superficially placed posterior arch vein in the proximal portion of the leg.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The upper posterior tibial perforating veins pass from the posterior arch vein to the posterior tibial veins, thus shunting blood from the superficial veins into the deep veins (Caggiati et al., 2014).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The upper posterior tibial perforating veins connect the superficial venous system of the lower limb with the deep venous system. The perforating veins shunt blood in one direction, from superficial veins to the high-pressured deep veins. The perforating veins contain valves to prevent the flow of blood from deep to superficial.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Varicose veins

sections.title: References
sections.text: Caggiati, A., Mendoza, E., Murena-Schmidt, R. & Lattimer, C. R. (2014) Anatomy of the Superficial Veins, in Mendoza, E., Lattimer, C. R. & Morrison, N. (eds), Duplex Ultrasound of Superficial Leg Veins. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg, 19-47.

24392.name: Perforating Veins of Small Saphenous Vein

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small saphenous vein.

Course: Several veins found along the course of the small saphenous vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Unite with the fibular vein.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The small saphenous vein has four constant perforating veins found over the length of the vein. They connect the small saphenous vein to the fibular vein. The most proximal two perforating veins, May’s perforating veins, connect the small saphenous veins with the muscular veins draining the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles and terminate in the fibular (or peroneal) veins. The para-Achillean perforating vein, or Bassi’s perforating vein, is located next to the calcaneal tendon. Finally, a direct perforating vein found below the lateral malleolus connects the small saphenous vein to the fibular vein (Caggiati et al, 2014).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The perforating veins of the small saphenous vein connect the superficial venous system of the lower limb with the deep venous system. The perforating veins shunt blood in one direction, from superficial veins to the high-pressured deep veins. The perforating veins contain valves to prevent the flow of blood from deep to superficial.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Varicose veins

sections.title: References
sections.text: Caggiati, A., Mendoza, E., Murena-Schmidt, R. & Lattimer, C. R. (2014) Anatomy of the Superficial Veins, in Mendoza, E., Lattimer, C. R. & Morrison, N. (eds), Duplex Ultrasound of Superficial Leg Veins. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg, 19-47.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior arch vein.

Course: Distal aspect of the leg.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Unites with posterior tibial veins.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior tibial perforating veins originate from the superficially placed posterior arch vein in the distal portion of the leg. There are usually three veins (Caggiati et al, 2014).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior tibial perforating veins pass from the posterior arch vein to the posterior tibial veins, thus shunting blood from the superficial veins into the deep veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior tibial perforating veins connect the superficial venous system of the lower limb with the deep venous system. The perforating veins shunt blood in one direction, from superficial veins to the high-pressured deep veins. The perforating veins contain valves to prevent the flow of blood from deep to superficial.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Ulcerations

sections.title: References
sections.text: Caggiati, A., Mendoza, E., Murena-Schmidt, R. & Lattimer, C. R. (2014) Anatomy of the Superficial Veins, in Mendoza, E., Lattimer, C. R. & Morrison, N. (eds), Duplex Ultrasound of Superficial Leg Veins. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg, 19-47.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Connection between the dorsal and plantar venous system.

Course: Between the heads of the metatarsal bones.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Connect the dorsal and plantar venous systems.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The intercapitular veins are short vessels that connect the superficial dorsal and the deep plantar venous systems.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The intercapitular veins are short vessels that pass between the heads of the metatarsal bones. These veins tend not to have any valves and the blood flow is bidirectional. In some instances valves may be present and face towards the superficial system, thus, allowing blood to pass from the plantar to dorsal systems (Kelikian, 2012).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Kelikian, A. S. (2012) Sarrafian's Anatomy of the Foot and Ankle: Descriptive, Topographic, Functional. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Great saphenous vein.

Course: Pierce deep fascia to enter the adductor canal.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Femoral vein.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: There are three direct perforating veins of the adductor canal, two found in the upper and middle third of the thigh (Dodd’s perforating veins), and one in the distal thigh (Hunter’s perforating vein). These perforating veins join the great saphenous vein with the femoral vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The perforating veins of the thigh connect the superficial venous system of the lower limb with the deep venous system. The perforating veins shunt blood in one direction, from superficial veins to the high-pressured deep veins. The perforating veins contain valves to prevent the flow of blood from deep to superficial.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Varicose veins

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small saphenous vein.

Course: Passes medially crossing the ankle joint to reach the anterior tibial veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Ankle joint and tibiofibular syndesmosis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterolateral malleolar vein is usually present and comes from the small saphenous vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterolateral malleolar vein passes medially across the ankle joint, forming a lateral malleolar venous circle. It drains into the anterior tibial veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterolateral malleolar vein drains the ankle joint and the tibiofibular syndesmosis (Kelikian, 2012).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Kelikian, A. S. (2012) Sarrafian's Anatomy of the Foot and Ankle: Descriptive, Topographic, Functional. Wolters Kluwer Health.

17323.name: Paratibial Perforating Vein
alternate: Paratibial Perforating Vein of Upper Third of Leg

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Great saphenous vein.

Course: Found below the knee joint.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Unites with the posterior tibial veins.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The paratibial perforating vein, or Boyd’s perforating vein, is a constant vein found below the knee joint.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The paratibial vein passes from the great saphenous vein to the posterior tibial veins. Other paratibial veins may be found more distally in the leg (Caggiati et al, 2014).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The paratibial perforating vein connects the superficial venous system of the lower limb with the deep venous system. The perforating veins shunt blood in one direction, from superficial veins to the high-pressured deep veins. The perforating veins contain valves to prevent the flow of blood from deep to superficial.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Caggiati, A., Mendoza, E., Murena-Schmidt, R. & Lattimer, C. R. (2014) Anatomy of the Superficial Veins, in Mendoza, E., Lattimer, C. R. & Morrison, N. (eds), Duplex Ultrasound of Superficial Leg Veins. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg, 19-47.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior mediastinum.

Course: Superiorly to the brachiocephalic veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Contents of the anterior mediastinum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The mediastinal veins originate in the anterior mediastinum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: They ascend through the anterior and superior mediastinum, where they unite with the left and right brachiocephalic veins. However, they may also drain into the azygos vein or superior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The mediastinal veins drain structures of the anterior and superior mediastinum including, mediastinal lymph nodes, areolar tissue (fat), pericardium, and thymus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Thymus gland.

Course: Superiorly to the left brachiocephalic vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Thymus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The thymic veins originate on the posterior surface of the thymus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From the gland, the thymic veins ascend in the superior mediastinum, draining into the left brachiocephalic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The thymic veins are responsible for draining the thymus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Second intercostal space.

Course: Anteriorly within the intercostal space.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Intercostal space, sternum, and skin.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior intercostal veins are small venae comitantes of the anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior intercostal veins course through their corresponding intercostal spaces. They drain the blood anteriorly, where the most superior veins drain into the internal thoracic vein and inferior veins drain into the musculophrenic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, they do form an anastomosis with the posterior intercostal veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior intercostal veins drain the muscles of the intercostal space, the sternum, and overlying skin.

sections.text:
Origin: Ninth intercostal space.

Course: Anteriorly within the intercostal space.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Intercostal space, sternum, and skin.

sections.title: Quick Facts

Course: Posteriorly within the intercostal space.

Tributaries: Dorsal branch and intervertebral veins.

Drainage: Intercostal space, back, and skin.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The left superior intercostal vein is formed by the union of the second and third, and sometimes the fourth, posterior intercostal veins on the left-hand side.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the left superior intercostal vein travels anteriorly, crossing the arch of aorta. It is lateral to the left vagus nerve and medial to the left phrenic nerve. It joins the posterior aspect of the left brachiocephalic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The left superior intercostal vein may receive the bronchial and left pericardiacophrenic veins. In some instances, it may connect with the accessory hemiazygos vein inferiorly.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Since the left superior intercostal vein receives the second and third posterior intercostal veins, it indirectly drains the muscles of the intercostal space, muscle of the back, vertebral column, and overlying skin.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The subcostal vein originates under the twelfth rib.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The subcostal vein runs with the subcostal artery inferior to the twelfth rib and anterior to the twelfth thoracic vertebral body. Inferior to the diaphragm, the subcostal vein unites with the ascending lumbar vein to form the azygos vein on the right and the hemiazygos vein on the left. The vein pierces the aponeurosis of transversus abdominis muscle and travels between it and the internal abdominal oblique muscle.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The subcostal veins receive dorsal branches, similar to the intercostal veins. It forms anastomoses with the superior epigastric, lower posterior intercostal, and lumbar veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The subcostal vein drains the upper posterior abdominal wall, inferior to the twelfth ribs.

sections.text:
Origin: Union of the second and third right posterior intercostal veins.

Course: Descends towards the azygos vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Intercostal space, back, and skin.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The right superior intercostal vein is formed by the union of the second and third, and sometimes the fourth, posterior intercostal veins on the right-hand side.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the right superior intercostal vein travels inferiorly to reach the azygos vein. It is one of the last tributaries of the azygos vein before it returns blood to the superior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Since the right superior intercostal vein receives the second and third posterior intercostal veins, it indirectly drains the muscles of the intercostal space, muscle of the back, vertebral column, and overlying skin.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of tributaries from the inferior intercostal spaces.

Course: Ascends obliquely along the margin of the ribs.

Tributaries: Lower anterior intercostal veins.

Drainage: Lower intercostal spaces and respiratory diaphragm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The musculophrenic veins originate from the union of anterior intercostal veins of the lower intercostal spaces.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The musculophrenic vein ascends obliquely along the margin of the ribs and drains into the internal thoracic veins at the level of the sixth costal cartilage.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The musculophrenic vein receives the anterior intercostal veins and tributaries from the superior surface of the respiratory diaphragm.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The musculophrenic veins drain the muscles of the intercostal space, abdominal wall, diaphragm, and lower part of the pericardium.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Continuation of musculophrenic and superior epigastric veins.

Course: Superiorly to the corresponding brachiocephalic vein.

Tributaries: Anterior intercostal and perforating cutaneous veins.

Drainage: Intercostal space, sternum, and skin.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The internal thoracic veins are vena commitantes of the inferior half of the internal thoracic artery and are the continuation of the musculophrenic and superior epigastric veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The internal thoracic veins ascend posterior to the upper six costal cartilages, lateral to the sternum. At the level of the third costal cartilage, the venae comitantes unite forming a single right and left internal thoracic vein, which continue to ascend medial to the internal thoracic artery. The internal thoracic vein drains into the brachiocephalic vein on its corresponding side.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior intercostal veins and perforating tributaries drain into the internal thoracic veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The thoracic veins drain the corresponding intercostal spaces via the anterior intercostal veins. Perforating tributaries accompany the perforating arterial branches and anterior cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves (anterior rami of thoracic nerves) to drain the overlying skin.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The perforating veins of the hand refer to the communicating branches that connect the superficial venous palmar arch with the dorsal venous network of the hand (or dorsal venous arch).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: The branches of this vein unite within the axilla.

Course: Short course to the axillary artery.

Tributaries: Deltoid, pectoral, acromial, and clavicular branches.

Drainage: Deltoid, pectoral, acromial, and clavicular regions.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Smaller veins unite to form the thoracoacromial vein. These include its deltoid, pectoral, acromial, and clavicular branches.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The thoracoacromial vein forms at the superior end of the pectoralis minor muscle. It has a short course where it almost immediately unites with the axillary vein, at the level of the coracoid process of the scapula (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The thoracoacromial vein is formed by the union of the deltoid, pectoral, acromial, and clavicular branches.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The thoracoacromial vein contributes to the venous drainage of the deltoid, pectoral, acromial, and clavicular regions.

sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limit ed.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal digital veins.

Course: Proximally, along dorsal aspect of the metacarpals.

Tributaries: Perforating branches from the palmar metacarpal veins.

Drainage: Hand.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal metacarpal veins arise from the unification of adjacent dorsal digital veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal metacarpal veins run between the interosseous spaces in a proximal direction. They drain into the dorsal venous network of the hand (Moore et al., 2013).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The dorsal metacarpal veins, which accompany the dorsal metacarpal arteries, receive perforating branches from the palmar metacarpal veins (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The dorsal metacarpal veins contribute to the venous drainage of the hand.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Cephalic vein.

Course: Superomedially to basilic vein.

Tributaries: Branches from deep veins of the forearm.

Drainage: Collateral drainage of the forearm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The median cubital vein originates from the cephalic vein within the forearm, 2.5 cm below the lateral epicondyle of the humerus (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The median cubital vein courses in a superomedial direction, across the bicipital aponeurosis and joins the basilic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The median cubital vein may receive the median antebrachial vein and tributaries from the deep median vein. If the median cubital vein is enlarged, the majority of the blood is transferred from the cephalic vein to basilic vein and the upper portion of the cephalic vein is reduced (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The median cubital vein gives a collateral route for venous return in the forearm (Tubbs et al., 2016).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial palmar arch.

Course: Posteriorly, to dorsal digital veins.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: Palmar aspect of hand.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The intercapitular veins connect the superficial venous palmar arch with the dorsal digital veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The intercapitular veins course posteriorly from the palmar to the dorsal aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superficial venous system is the primary drainage of the hand. The palmar venous drainage is insufficient and blood of the palm of the hand is drained primarily by the dorsal venous network via the intercapitular veins (Doyle and Botte, 2003, Tubbs et al., 2016).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Palmar digital veins.

Course: Laterally within web space of the digits of the hand.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: Digits of the hand.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The transverse natatory veins originate from the palmar digital veins (Chung and Steinbach, 2009).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The transverse natatory veins course within the webbed spaces between the proximal aspect of the digits, deep to the superficial transverse metacarpal ligament (i.e., the natatory ligament) (Doyle and Botte, 2003; Chung and Steinbach, 2009).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The transverse natatory veins contribute to the venous drainage of the digits of the hand.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small unnamed veins.

Course: Proximally, along medial and lateral aspects of each digit.

Tributaries: Intercapitular vein.

Drainage: Digits of the hand.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: There are several small veins in the digits of the hand, which unite to form the dorsal digital veins (Doyle and Botte, 2003).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: There are two dorsal digital veins that course along both sides of the digits. Once they arrive at the digital commissure, they form a venous arcade which forms the dorsal metacarpal veins (Tubbs et al., 2016, Doyle and Botte, 2003).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Palmar digital veins connect to the dorsal digital veins via intercapitular veins, which drains blood into the dorsal aspect of the hand (Doyle and Botte, 2003).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The dorsal digital veins drain the digits of the hand.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal metacarpal and dorsal digital veins.

Course: Proximally, extends across the dorsal aspect of metacarpals.

Tributaries: Dorsal digital, intercapitular, and dorsal metacarpal veins.

Drainage: Dorsal aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal venous network of the hand arises from the unification of the dorsal metacarpal and dorsal digital veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal anastomosis forms an asymmetrical dorsal network and, in 70% of individuals, forms a dorsal arch (Tubbs et al., 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The dorsal venous network receives the dorsal digital, dorsal metacarpal, and intercapitular veins. The veins of the dorsal venous network coalesce on the radial aspect with digital veins of the thumb and form the cephalic vein. Conversely, on the ulnar aspect, the network coalesces with the digital veins of the little finger and forms the basilic vein (Doyle and Botte, 2003).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superficial venous system is the primary drainage of the hand. The palmar venous drainage is insufficient and blood of the palm of the hand is drained primarily by the dorsal venous network via the intercapitular veins (Doyle and Botte, 2003, Tubbs et al., 2016).
