sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal venous network.

Course: Superiorly along forearm.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: Hand and forearm.

sections.title: Origin
Course
sections.text: The accessory cephalic vein courses in a superolateral direction along the posterior aspect of the forearm. It ends by uniting with the cephalic vein below the elbow (Standring, 2016, Doyle and Botte, 2003).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The accessory cephalic vein contributes to the drainage of the hand and forearm.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Doyle, J. R. and Botte, M. J. (2003) Surgical Anatomy of the Hand and Upper Extremity. LWW medical book collection: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Smaller unnamed veins.

Course: Proximally, along the digits towards the metacarpals.

Tributaries: Oblique veins.

Drainage: Digits.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Smaller vessels within the digits coalesce to form the palmar digital veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The palmar digital veins course proximally along the palmar aspect on either side of the digits. The palmar digital veins are typically accompanied by the proper palmar digital arteries (Doyle and Botte, 2003).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The oblique veins arise from the palmar digital veins and unite with the dorsal digital veins (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The palmar digital veins contribute to the venous drainage of the digits.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Doyle, J. R. and Botte, M. J. (2003) Surgical Anatomy of the Hand and Upper Extremity. LWW medical book collection: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lateral aspect of dorsal venous network of the hand.

Course: Superiorly along anterolateral forearm and arm.

Tributaries: Accessory cephalic, median cubital, and branches from deep veins.

Drainage: Hand, forearm, and arm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial veins on the lateral aspect of the dorsum of the hand unite to form the cephalic vein. This occurs at the anatomical snuffbox (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The cephalic vein courses superiorly on the anterolateral aspect of the forearm. Distally it lies adjacent to the superficial branch of the radial nerve; however, proximally it runs alongside the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (Standring, 2016, Tubbs et al., 2016).

In the arm, the cephalic vein runs proximally along the lateral aspect to reach the deltopectoral groove. Finally, the cephalic vein pierces the clavipectoral fascia with the thoracoacromial vein. It typically drains into the axillary vein; however, it may also drain into the basilic vein or the internal jugular vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
Within the forearm, the cephalic vein communicates with median antebrachial and basilic veins via the median cubital vein (Doyle and Botte, 2003). If the median cubital vein is enlarged, then the majority of the blood is transferred from the cephalic vein to the basilic vein and the upper portion of the cephalic vein is reduced (Standring, 2016).

The cephalic vein receives tributaries from the deep veins at the elbow, including the radial and ulnar veins. It also receives the accessory cephalic vein in 45% of individuals (Tubbs et al., 2016)

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The cephalic vein contributes to the venous drainage of the hand, forearm, and arm.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Cannulation

- Venipuncture

- Central venous lines

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Doyle, J. R. and Botte, M. J. (2003) Surgical Anatomy of the Hand and Upper Extremity. LWW medical book collection: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Medial aspect dorsal venous network.

Course: Superiorly along medial aspect of forearm and arm.

Tributaries: Median cubital and median antebrachial veins, branches from deep veins of the forearm.

Drainage: Hand, forearm, and arm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The basilic vein forms from the dorsal venous network at the ulnar aspect of the dorsal hand. The basilic vein is larger than the cephalic vein (Tubbs et al., 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The basilic vein runs proximally from the dorsal aspect of the hand, along the medial border of the forearm. As it approaches the elbow, it becomes anteriorly placed on the forearm.

In the arm, it ascends posterior to the biceps brachii muscle, alongside the anterior and posterior components of the medial cutaneous nerve (Standring, 2016). It pierces the brachial fascia in the middle one third of the arm and drains into the brachial veins to form the axillary vein (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The basilic vein receives the median cubital and, commonly, the median antebrachial veins (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The basilic vein aids in the venous drainage of the hand, forearm, and arm.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial palmar arch.

Course: Superiorly along the forearm.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: Palmar aspect of the hand and anterior forearm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The median antebrachial vein arises from the superficial veins of the palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The median antebrachial vein courses superiorly and drains into the median cubital vein or directly into the basilic vein. However, in up to a quarter of individuals, it may divide distal to the elbow where one branch joins the cephalic vein and the other joins the basilic vein (Tubbs et al., 2016, Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The median antebrachial vein contributes to the venous drainage of the palmar aspect of the hand and anterior forearm.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Intravenous injections

- Blood sampling

- Venipuncture

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Common palmar veins.

Course: Palmar aspect of the metacarpals.

Tributaries: Common palmar digital and intercapitular veins.

Drainage: Palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial palmar arch is formed by a venous network of palmar veins including the common palmar digital veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial and deep palmar venous arches accompany the arterial palmar arches. The common palmar digital veins join the superficial veins, while the palmar metacarpal veins join the deep venous palmar arch (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superficial palmar arch receives the common palmar digital veins via a network of superficial palmar vessels. It shunts blood to the dorsal aspect of the hand via the intercapitular veins (Doyle and Botte, 2003).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superficial venous system is the primary drainage of the hand. The palmar venous drainage is insufficient and blood of the palm of the hand is drained primarily by the dorsal venous network via the intercapitular veins (Doyle and Botte, 2003, Tubbs et al., 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Doyle, J. R. and Botte, M. J. (2003) Surgical Anatomy of the Hand and Upper Extremity. LWW medical book collection: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Several smaller veins unite within the infraspinous fossa to become the circumflex scapular vein.

Course: Laterally to the subscapular vein.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: Infraspinous fossa of the scapula.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Several smaller veins unite to form the circumflex scapular veins within the infraspinous fossa.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The circumflex scapular vein is the vena comitantes of the circumflex scapular artery. It courses laterally towards and unites with the thoracodorsal vein to form the subscapular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The circumflex scapular vein drains the region of the infraspinous fossa.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of small vessels in the trapezius muscle.

Course: Passes within the posterior triangle of the neck to enter the external jugular vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Trapezius muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The transverse cervical vein begins in the trapezius muscle as small tributaries that unite.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, it traverses the posterior triangle of the neck and crosses the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle. The transverse cervical vein drains into the external jugular vein (80%), the subclavian vein (12%), or both (8%) (Haas and Weiglein, 2009).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The transverse cervical vein helps drain the trapezius muscle.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Haas, F. and Weiglein, A. (2009) 'CHAPTER 21 - Trapezius flap', in Wei, F.-C. & Mardini, S. (eds.) Flaps and Reconstructive Surgery. Edinburgh: W.B. Saunders, pp. 249-269.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Brachial veins.

Course: Superiorly, from inferior border of teres major to external border of the first rib.

Tributaries: Brachial, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral, long thoracic, subscapular, thoracodorsal, thoracoepigastric, lateral thoracic, superior thoracic, basilic, and cephalic veins, branches of the thoracoacromial vein.

Drainage: Upper limb, scapular, and pectoral regions.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The axillary vein originates from the unification of the brachial veins with the basilic vein. This occurs at the inferior border of the teres major muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: As the axillary vein course superiorly, it sits medial to the axillary artery. The axillary vein is divided into three parts in the same manner as the axillary artery (Moore et al., 2013). The first part sits proximal to the pectoralis minor muscle, the second part sits posterior to the pectoralis minor muscle, and the third part lies distal to the pectoralis minor muscle. The axillary vein continues superiorly to the external border of the first rib, where it is renamed the subclavian vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The axillary vein receives the brachial veins and basilic vein at its origin. It is then joined by the cephalic vein just inferior to the clavicle. The remaining tributaries roughly parallel the branches of the axillary artery, including the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral, subscapular, branches of the thoracoacromial, lateral thoracic, and superior thoracic veins. The axillary vein also receives the thoracoepigastric veins, which are formed from the vessels originating from the inguinal region uniting with the axillary region (Moore et al., 2013).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The axillary vein contributes to the venous drainage of the scapular, axillary, pectoral, and brachial regions.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial epigastric vein.

Course: Superiorly along anterolateral thoracic wall.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: Superficial region of anterolateral thoracic wall.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The thoracoepigastric vein arises from the superficial epigastric vein in the inguinal region (Moore et al., 2013).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The thoracoepigastric vein courses superiorly within the subcutaneous tissue of the anterolateral thoracic wall. It ends by draining into the axillary vein directly or via the lateral thoracic vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The thoracoepigastric vein drains the superficial portion of the anterolateral thoracic wall. It also provides a link between the femoral vein and the axillary vein, and thus, connects the regions drained by the inferior vena cava and superior vena cava. In cases where the inferior vena cava is blocked, the thoracoepigastric vein may be increased in size.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Axillary vein.

Course: Superomedially, to the internal jugular vein where it forms the brachiocephalic vein.

Tributaries: External jugular vein and thoracic duct (left) or right lymphatic duct (right).

Drainage: Entire upper limb.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The subclavian vein is the continuation of the axillary vein. It originates from the external border of the first rib.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The subclavian vein courses medially and runs between the distal margin of the scalenus anterior and sternocleidomastoid muscles. At the medial border of the scalenus anterior muscle, it terminates by joining the internal jugular vein, thus forming the brachiocephalic vein. There are two valves approximately 2 cm prior to its unification with the internal jugular vein, which ensure unidirectional blood flow into the brachiocephalic vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The subclavian vein receives the external jugular vein. The thoracic duct drains into the left subclavian vein and the right lymphatic duct drains into the right subclavian vein. The subclavian vein then unites with the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The subclavian vein receives all the deoxygenated blood from the upper limb.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Subclavian vein puncture

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of veins in the supraspinous fossa of scapula.

Course: Accompanies the suprascapular artery.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Supraspinatus muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The suprascapular vein forms by the union of small tributaries on the supraspinous fossa of the scapula.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The suprascapular vein accompanies its corresponding artery. It passes superior to the superior transverse ligament, continuing medially, deep to the inferior belly of omohyoid muscle. It traverses the anterior aspect of the scalenus anterior muscle and deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle to drain into the external jugular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries of the suprascapular vein; however, it does for an anastomosis with the transverse cervical and circumflex scapular veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The suprascapular vein drains the supraspinatus muscle and surrounding tissue.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Unification of the circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal vein.

Course: Short course to axillary vein.

Tributaries: Thoracodorsal and circumflex scapular veins.

Drainage: Muscles of the scapular region and latissimus dorsi muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The subscapular vein is the vena comitantes to the subscapular artery. It originates when the circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal veins unite.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The subscapular vein has a short course and runs superiorly.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The subscapular vein is formed by the unification of two large tributaries. These are the thoracodorsal and circumflex scapular veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Via its tributaries, the subscapular vein drains the scapular region, as well as the latissimus dorsi muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Medial border of the scapula.

Course: Ascends along the medial scapular border.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Rhomboid, latissimus dorsi, ascending (or inferior) part of the trapezius, and scalenus anterior muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal scapular vein begins along the medial border of the scapula.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal scapular vein ascends along the scapula and accompanies the dorsal scapular artery and nerve. It drains into the subclavian vein, or in some cases, into the external jugular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The dorsal scapular vein helps drain the muscles of the back, including the rhomboids, latissimus dorsi, the ascending (or inferior) part of the trapezius, and the scalenus anterior muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins at the proximal humerus.

Course: Medially towards the axillary vein.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: Proximal humerus and glenohumeral joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior circumflex humeral vein arises from smaller vessels anterior to the neck of the humerus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior circumflex humeral vein courses medially towards the axillary vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior circumflex humeral vein contributes to the drainage of the proximal humerus and the glenohumeral joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Within the latissimus dorsi muscle.

Course: Superiorly to the subscapular vein.

Tributaries: No named branches.

Drainage: Latissimus dorsi muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Several smaller veins unite to form the thoracodorsal vein within the fibers of the latissimus dorsi muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The thoracodorsal vein courses superiorly within the latissimus dorsi muscle, along with the thoracodorsal artery and nerve. It then unites with the circumflex scapular vein to form the subscapular vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The thoracodorsal vein drains the latissimus dorsi muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of smaller veins on the lateral thoracic wall.

Course: Superiorly along the lateral thoracic wall, draining into the axillary vein.

Tributaries: Lateral mammary branches of lateral thoracic vein.

Drainage: Pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, and serratus anterior muscles, the breasts.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral thoracic vein is formed by the union of smaller veins that drain the lateral part of the anterior thoracic wall.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the lateral thoracic vein travels superiorly along the lateral thoracic wall. It ends by draining into the axillary vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Along its course, its lateral mammary branches drain into lateral thoracic vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Overall, the lateral thoracic veins and its tributaries provide venous drainage to the pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, and serratus anterior muscles, as well as the mammary glands.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small veins at the proximal humerus.

Course: Medially towards the quadrangular space.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: Proximal humerus and glenohumeral joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior circumflex humeral vein arises from the union of smaller vessels posterior to the neck of the humerus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior circumflex humeral vein courses medially away from the humerus. It traverses the quadrangular space, a space formed by the borders teres major, teres minor, long head of the triceps, and the humerus. The posterior circumflex humeral vein is accompanied by its arterial counterpart and the axillary nerve. It ends by draining into the axillary vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior circumflex humeral vein contributes to the drainage of the proximal humerus and the glenohumeral joint.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of small veins.

Course: Accompanying the superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries.

Tributaries: No named branches.

Drainage: Area around the elbow.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The collateral veins form around the elbow joint.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The collateral veins of the elbow joint accompany the superior and inferior collateral arteries and drain into the brachial veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Overall, the collateral veins of the elbow joint contribute to the venous drainage of the elbow region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial and ulnar veins.

Course: Superiorly in the arm, accompanying the brachial artery as far as the inferior margin of the subscapularis muscle.

Tributaries: Deep brachial, superior ulnar collateral, and inferior ulnar collateral veins.

Drainage: Arm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The brachial veins arise from the unification of the radial and ulnar arteries at the level of the distal arm.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: There are usually two brachial veins on the medial and lateral aspects of the brachial artery. They course superiorly along the medial aspect of the arm. At the level of the inferior edge of the subscapularis muscle, the brachial veins join the basilic vein to form the axillary vein. Pulsations from the artery help venous return (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013; Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The tributaries of the brachial veins are similar to those of the brachial arteries. These include the deep brachial, superior collateral, and inferior collateral veins. There are also numerous anastomoses with the superficial veins (Doyle and Botte, 2003).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The brachial veins provide deep venous drainage to the arm.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Doyle, J. R. and Botte, M. J. (2003) Surgical Anatomy of the Hand and Upper Extremity. LWW medical book collection: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep palmar arch.

Course: Superiorly, along the medial aspect of the forearm.

Tributaries: Superficial veins of the forearm, anterior and posterior interosseous veins.

Drainage: Hand, medial and posterior aspect of forearm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ulnar veins form as the continuation of the medial aspect of the deep palmar arch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ulnar veins are the venae comitantes of the ulnar artery and follow the course of the artery along the medial aspect of the forearm. The radial and ulnar veins unite near the elbow and continue as the brachial veins in the arm (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
There are two sets of venae comitantes in the forearm, the radial and ulnar veins, which receive the superficial and deep palmar venous arches. The deep palmar arch mainly drains into the radial veins. The bulk of the palmar superficial venous blood is shunted to the dorsal aspect of the hand; however, the remainder of blood in the superficial palmar arch primarily drains into the ulnar vein (Doyle and Botte, 2003).

At the wrist, superficial veins connect with the radial and ulnar veins. Along the forearm, the radial and ulnar veins receive tributaries from the anterior and posterior interosseous veins, as well as muscular branches (Standring, 2016, Moore et al., 2013).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Overall, the ulnar vein and its tributaries contribute to the venous drainage of the forearm via the interosseous veins and through the ulnar vein itself. It also contributes to the drainage of the palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Doyle, J. R. and Botte, M. J. (2003) Surgical Anatomy of the Hand and Upper Extremity. LWW medical book collection: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep venous palmar arch.

Course: Superiorly along anterior aspect of the interosseous membrane between the radius and ulna.

Tributaries: No named branches.

Drainage: Anterior and posterior forearm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior interosseous vein is formed by the union of dorsal and palmar carpal veins. The anterior interosseous veins accompany its corresponding artery and unite with posterior interosseous veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the anterior interosseous vein travels superiorly along the anterior aspect of the interosseous membrane. It ends by draining into the ulnar vein, near the elbow joint.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Along its course, small unnamed branches drain into anterior interosseous vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Overall, the anterior interosseous vein and its tributaries provide venous drainage to the muscles of the anterior forearm.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial recurrent vein.

Course: Superiorly in the arm.

Tributaries: Medial collateral and radial recurrent veins.

Drainage: Posterior aspect of the arm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep brachial vein is a continuation of the radial recurrent vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep brachial vein courses superiorly along the arm.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: In the distal arm, the middle collateral and radial recurrent veins join the deep brachial vein. In the proximal arm, it unites with the deltoid branch of the deep brachial vein, the brachial vein, and with the superficial venous drainage via the basilic vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep brachial vein contributes to the drainage of the posterior aspect of the arm.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Palmar digital veins.

Course: Proximally, along the metacarpals.

Tributaries: No named branches.

Drainage: Palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The palmar metacarpal veins are formed as the palmar digital veins coalesce at the level of the distal metacarpals.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The palmar metacarpal veins course proximally from the palmar digital veins along the palmar aspect of the metacarpals and drains into the deep palmar venous arch.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The palmar metacarpal veins are connected to the superficial and dorsal venous systems by a series of small interconnecting vessels (Doyle and Botte, 2003).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The palmar metacarpal veins aid in the drainage of the palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Doyle, J. R. and Botte, M. J (2003) ‘ Surgical Anatomy of the Hand and Upper Extremity’ Lippincott, Williams and Wilkins PA:USA.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The perforating veins of the forearm refer to the communicating branches that connect the anterior and posterior interosseous veins. Additionally, other perforating veins of the forearm connect the superficial venous system with the deep system.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ulnar vein.

Course: Superiorly along proximal ulna and unites with the superior ulnar collateral vein.

Tributaries: No named branches.

Drainage: Area around the elbow.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior ulnar recurrent vein originates the ulnar vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the posterior ulnar recurrent vein travels superiorly along the proximal portion of the ulna and the posterior aspect of the medial epicondyle of the humerus. It ends by draining into superior ulnar collateral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Overall, the posterior ulnar recurrent vein contributes to the venous drainage of the elbow region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Palmar metacarpal veins.

Course: Along the distal bases of the second to fifth metacarpals.

Tributaries: Palmar digital and palmar metacarpal veins.

Drainage: Palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep palmar arch arises from the palmar metacarpal veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep palmar arch drains primarily into the radial veins on lateral aspects of the forearm, but also drains into the ulnar veins on the medial aspect of the distal forearm.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The deep palmar arch receives the palmar digital veins of the thumb, palmar metacarpal veins, and the connecting veins from the superficial arch.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep palmar arch aids in the venous drainage of the palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ulnar vein.

Course: Superiorly along proximal ulna and unites with the inferior ulnar collateral vein.

Tributaries: No named branches.

Drainage: Area around the elbow.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the anterior ulnar recurrent vein travels superiorly along the proximal portion of the ulna and the anterior aspect of the medial epicondyle of the humerus. It ends by draining into the inferior ulnar collateral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Overall, the anterior ulnar recurrent vein contributes to the venous drainage of the elbow region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal metacarpal veins.

Course: Proximally, along the metacarpals.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Dorsal aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep dorsal veins of the hand arise from the dorsal metacarpal veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep dorsal veins of the hand course proximally, deep to the fascia and accompanied by the dorsal metacarpal arteries. It drains into the dorsal venous network of the hand.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep dorsal veins of the hand aid in the drainage of the dorsal aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep palmar arch.

Course: Superiorly, in the lateral aspect of the forearm and unites with the ulnar vein to form the brachial veins.

Tributaries: Radial recurrent vein.

Drainage: Forearm and hand.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The radial veins form a continuation of the lateral aspect of the deep palmar arch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The radial veins are venae comitantes of the radial artery and follow the arterial course along the lateral aspect of the forearm. The radial and ulnar veins unite near the elbow and continue as the brachial veins. The radial veins are smaller than the ulnar veins (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
There are two sets of venae comitantes in the forearm, the radial and ulnar veins, which receive the superficial and deep palmar venous arches. The deep palmar arch mainly drains into the radial veins. The bulk of the palmar superficial venous blood is shunted to the dorsal aspect of the hand; however, the remainder of blood in the superficial palmar arch primarily drains into the ulnar vein (Doyle and Botte, 2003).

At the wrist, superficial veins connect with the radial and ulnar veins. Along the forearm, the radial and ulnar veins receive tributaries from the anterior and posterior interosseous veins as well as muscular branches (Standring, 2016, Moore et al., 2013)

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The radial vein and its tributaries drain the lateral aspect of the anterior forearm and the palmar and dorsal aspects of the hand.

sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial vein.

Course: Superiorly along proximal radius and unites with the deep brachial vein.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: Area around the elbow.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The radial recurrent vein originates from the radial vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the radial recurrent vein travels superiorly along the proximal portion of the radius and then on the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. It ends by draining into the deep brachial vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Overall, the radial recurrent vein contributes to the venous drainage of the elbow region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of veins from dorsal venous carpal network.

Course: Superiorly along posterior aspect of the interosseous membrane between the radius and ulna.

Tributaries: No named tributaries.

Drainage: Posterior forearm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior interosseous vein is formed by the union of the dorsal carpal venous network.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the posterior interosseous vein travels superiorly along the posterior aspect of the interosseous membrane between the radius and the ulna. It ends by draining into a collateral vein at the elbow joint.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Overall, the posterior interosseous vein and its tributaries provide venous drainage to the muscles of the posterior forearm.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Venous network originates in testes (males) or broad ligament (females).

Course: Veins in the plexus unite to form a single testicular vein (males) or ovarian vein (females).

Tributaries: Small spermatic veins (males) or small tubal ovarian veins (females).

Drainage: Testes and epididymis (males) or ovaries and uterine tubes (females).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
In males, the pampiniform plexus is formed from the union of multiple spermatic veins that surround the testis and epididymis.

In females, the pampiniform plexus is formed from tubal branches from the ovarian veins, within the mesovarium of the broad ligament and suspensory ligament of the ovary.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
In both males and females, the pampiniform plexus drains into the gonadal veins (testicular/ovarian veins). The plexus is much larger in males than it is in females.

In males, the plexus runs anterior to the ductus deferens, through the superficial inguinal ring and traverses the inguinal canal. The veins of the plexus unite to form the testicular veins. The right testicular vein drains into the inferior vena cava, while the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein. 

In females, the tubal branches of the pampiniform plexus are located within the mesovarium and the suspensory ligament of the ovary. The plexus drains into the ovarian veins. The right ovarian vein drains into the inferior vena cava, while the left ovarian vein drains into the left renal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: In males, the pampiniform plexus receives small spermatic veins. In females, the pampiniform plexus receives tubal branches from the ovarian veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text:
The pampiniform venous plexus is much larger and is more functionally important in males than in females. In males, the pampiniform plexus surrounds and drains the spermatic cord, testis and epididymis. For normal spermatogenesis to occur, the temperature of the testis has to remain at approximately 3 °C lower than the abdominal body temperature. This is achieved, in-part, by a counter-flow heat exchange system, between the pampiniform plexus veins and the testicular artery (Standring, 2016).

In females, the pampiniform plexus is a vine-like structure that drains the ovaries and part of the uterine tubes into the left and right ovarian veins.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: External genitalia and skin of lower abdomen.

Course: Passes superomedially to join the greater saphenous vein.

Tributaries: Anterior scrotal and superficial dorsal vein of penis (male); anterior labial and superficial dorsal vein of clitoris (female)

Drainage: External genitalia and skin of lower abdomen.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The external pudendal vein forms from veins in the skin of the external genitalia of males (anterior scrotum and prepuce and shaft of the penis) and females (anterior labia majora). It receives some contribution from the skin of the inferior anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The external pudendal vein has a short course that passes superomedially from the anterior scrotum/labia and penis/clitoris. In most cases, it joins the greater saphenous vein just before it passes through the saphenous opening to join the femoral vein. Occasionally, it can pass through the opening before directly draining into the femoral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The external pudendal vein receives the anterior scrotal and superficial dorsal vein of penis (male), or the anterior labial and superficial dorsal vein of clitoris (female).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The external pudendal vein drains the skin of anterior scrotum/labia and penis/clitoris, including the prepuce.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From the deep dorsal veins of penis or clitoris.

Course: Ascends through the lesser and greater pelvis to drain into the internal iliac vein. It passes through the pudendal canal, lesser sciatic foramen, and greater sciatic foramen.
 
Tributaries: Inferior anorectal vein, vein of the bulb of penis or vestibule, posterior scrotal or labial veins, perineal veins, deep dorsal vein of the penis or clitoris, crural and urethral veins.

Drainage: External genitalia and perineum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The venae comitantes of the internal pudendal artery unite to form a single internal pudendal vein at the superior aspect of the perineal membrane.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The internal pudendal vein follows the course of the internal pudendal artery and pudendal nerve, eventually draining into the internal iliac vein. 

Along its course, the internal pudendal vein travels through the pudendal canal on the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa. It ascends through the perineum and passes through the lesser sciatic foramen. It then travels within the gluteal region, inferior to the piriformis muscle, and passes through the greater sciatic foramen to enter the true pelvis.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
The internal pudendal vein receives many tributaries of the urogenital region including:
- inferior anorectal vein
- perineal veins
- deep dorsal vein of penis or clitoris
- crural veins
- vein of the bulb of penis or vestibule
- urethral veins
- posterior scrotal or labial veins. 

In females, the distal portion of the vagina is also drained by the internal pudendal vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The internal pudendal veins drain the organs, skin, and muscles of  the external genitalia, perineum, and surrounding structures.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Prostate.

Course: Passes into the vesical venous plexus or the internal iliac veins.

Tributaries: Deep dorsal veins of penis.

Drainage: Prostate.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The prostatic venous plexus is located along the anterolateral surface of the prostate.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Blood within the plexus will drain either into the vesical venous plexus (superiorly) or the internal iliac veins (posterolateral). This plexus also communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus posteriorly, which provides a potential avenue for malignancy to enter the vertebral column (Standring, 2020; MacLennan, 2012).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The deep dorsal vein of the penis drains into the prostatic venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The prostatic venous plexus drains the deeper tissue of the prostate.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Prostatectomy
—Prostate cancer
—Benign Prostatic Hypertrophy

sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Skin and connective tissue of anterior scrotum.

Course: Subcutaneous veins converge superolaterally and drain into the external pudendal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Skin of anterior scrotum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior scrotal veins are a collection of veins the originate in the skin and connective tissue of anterior scrotum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
These superficial veins course subcutaneously across the anterior surface of the scrotum drain into the external pudendal vein. There are abundant anastomoses between the anterior and posterior scrotal veins superolaterally. This dense superficial network of scrotal veins facilitates temperature regulation of the testes, which is important given the high rate of germ cell production occurring there.

The external pudendal vein drains into the greater saphenous vein and eventually into the femoral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior scrotal veins drain the skin of the anterior scrotum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Corpus spongiosum of penis.

Course: Passes around the penis in the fascia of the penis to the dorsal midline and terminates in the deep dorsal vein.

Tributaries: Emissary veins.

Drainage: Glans penis, corpus spongiosum and corpora cavernosa of body of penis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The circumflex veins originate in the corpus spongiosum of the penis. They are only present in the distal two thirds of the penis.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The circumflex veins pass around the circumference of the penile body, within and deep to the fascia of the penis (Buck’s fascia). They drain into the deep dorsal vein. There are usually between 3 and 10 circumflex veins (Standring, 2020). 

Engorgement of the erectile tissue bodies of the penis compresses venous outflow, including circumflex and emissary veins and venous plexuses. This blocks blood return (veno-occlusive mechanism) leading to accumulation of blood and penile erection.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The circumflex veins receive emissary veins (draining the subalbugineal venous plexus). In some instances, the circumflex veins may receive tributaries from communicating veins in the subcutaneous tissue of the penis (Quartey, 2006).

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The circumflex veins drain the glans penis and the erectile tissues in the distal two thirds of the body of the penis.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Quartey, J. K. M. (2006) 'Anatomy and Blood Supply of the Urethra and Penis', in Schreiter, F. and Jordan, G.H. (eds.) Urethral Reconstructive Surgery. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg, pp. 11-17.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Bulb of the penis.

Course: Pass to the internal pudendal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Bulb of penis and bulbourethral gland.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vein of the bulb of the penis originates in the bulb of the penis, the rounded portion at the base of the penis that contains the bulbourethral (Cowper’s) glands and their efferent ducts.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The veins of the bulb of the penis pass laterally to empty into the internal pudendal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The veins of the bulb of the penis drain blood from the bulb of the penis and bulbourethral glands.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Arises in midline of the penis between the crura.

Course: Travels to the hilum of the penis to drain into the internal pudendal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Crura of penis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The crural veins are short veins that originate in the midline of the penis between the crura.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The crural veins travel to the hilum of the penis to drain into the internal pudendal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The crural veins drain the crura of the penis.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Fascia and contents of spermatic cord.

Course: Ascends in the cremasteric fascia entering the abdominal cavity by passing along the inguinal canal. It joins the inferior epigastric vein at the level of the deep inguinal ring.

Tributaries:

Drainage: Spermatic cord.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The cremasteric vein is formed by small venules that pass from the cremaster layer of the spermatic fascia that contains the cremaster muscle fibers. It also receives contributions from the pampiniform plexus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The cremasteric vein ascends within the spermatic cord between the internal and external spermatic fascia. It passes through the superficial inguinal ring across the inguinal canal and into the abdominal cavity through the deep inguinal ring. It has a short intraabdominal course before joining the inferior epigastric vein.

The cremasteric vein serves as an alternate pathway for venous return of blood from the testis, which is normally via the testicular vein into the inferior vena cava. Blood may shunt across the pampiniform plexus into the cremasteric vein into the inferior epigastric vein, thus, a potential source of varicocele (Hamada, Esteves and Agarwal, 2015).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The cremasteric vein drains the three layers of the spermatic fascia (external, cremasteric and internal), and their contents. These structures make up the spermatic cord.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Varicocele

sections.title: References
sections.text: Hamada, A., Esteves, S. C. and Agarwal, A. (2015) Varicocele and Male Infertility: Current Concepts, Controversies and Consensus. Springer International Publishing.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Bulb of penis (males) or vestibule of vagina (females).

Course: Travels inferiorly through the pudendal canal to drain into internal pudendal vein.

Tributaries: Posterior scrotal vein and vein of the bulb of penis (males) or posterior labial vein and deep vein of the clitoris (females).

Drainage: Superficial perineal muscles and scrotum (males) or bulb of vestibule (females).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The perineal vein originates in the bulb of penis (males) or bulb of vestibules (females).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the perineal vein travels from the superficial space and runs backwards between bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus muscles. It pierces the perineal membrane and runs through the pudendal canal to drain into the internal pudendal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
In males, the perineal vein receives tributaries from the posterior scrotal vein and the vein of the bulb of penis.

In females, the perineal vein receives tributaries from the posterior labial vein and the deep vein of the clitoris (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The perineal vein drains the skin of the perineum and external genitalia. During sexual arousal, the perineal vein is compressed by the bulbospongiosus muscles, pushing blood into the body of the penis (males) or clitoris (females) to aid in erection (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Netter Basic Science Series: Saunders/Elsevier.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of venules along the transverse perineal muscle.

Course: Travels horizontally on surface of the transverse perineal muscle to drain into perineal vein.

Tributaries: No tributaries.

Drainage: Transverse perineal muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The transverse perineal vein may not always be present. It originates as a branch of the perineal vein, close to the superficial transverse perineal muscle.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the transverse perineal vein runs horizontally on the surface of the transverse perineal muscle to drain into the perineal vein (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The transverse perineal vein does not receive any tributaries. It forms an anastomosis with the corresponding transverse perineal vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The transverse perineal vein drains the superficial transverse perineal muscle in the superficial perineal space.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Netter Basic Science Series: Saunders/Elsevier.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Skin of posterior scrotum.

Course: Passes posteriorly to empty into the internal pudendal vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Posterior scrotum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior scrotal vein arises in the skin and fascia of the posterior scrotum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The posterior scrotal vein passes from the posterior scrotum superiorly and posteriorly to empty into the internal pudendal vein.

A potential shunt exists between the external iliac vein (via anterior scrotal veins) and the internal iliac vein (via posterior scrotal veins) that, when exploited, can lead to varicocele (varicose veins of scrotal veins) (Patel, 2017).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior scrotal vein drains the skin and fascial layers of the posterior scrotum.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Varicocele

sections.title: References
sections.text: Patel, A. P. (2017) 'Anatomy and physiology of chronic scrotal pain', Transl Androl Urol, 6(Suppl 1), pp. S51-s56.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Pampiniform plexus.

Course: Ascends in the abdominal cavity to drain into the inferior vena cava (on right side) and left renal vein (on left side).

Tributaries: Pampiniform plexus and ureteral veins.

Drainage: Drains testes, epididymis, ureter, and cremaster muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The testicular veins arise from the terminal ends of the pampiniform plexuses, at around the level of the superficial inguinal ring.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The testicular veins enter the abdomen and ascend. The right testicular vein empties directly into the inferior vena cava, while the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The testicular veins receive the pampiniform plexus and tributaries from the ureter.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The testicular veins drain the testes, epididymis, ureter, and cremasteric muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Pampiniform plexus.

Course: Ascends in the abdominal cavity to drain into the inferior vena cava (on right side) and left renal vein (on left side).

Tributaries: Pampiniform plexus and ureteral veins.

Drainage: Drains testes, epididymis, ureter, and cremaster muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The testicular veins arise from the terminal ends of the pampiniform plexuses, at around the level of the superficial inguinal ring.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The testicular veins enter the abdomen and ascend. The right testicular vein empties directly into the inferior vena cava, while the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The testicular veins receive the pampiniform plexus and tributaries from the ureter.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The testicular veins drain the testes, epididymis, ureter, and cremasteric muscle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Glans penis and distal two thirds of penile shaft.

Course: Travels unpaired along the dorsal midline deep to the superficial penile fascia. Passes inferior to the public symphysis and terminates in the prostatic plexus.

Tributaries: Receives input from circumflex and emissary veins via a capillary plexus.

Drainage: Glans penis, corpus spongiosa, and corpora cavernosa.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep dorsal vein of the penis is formed by a collection of circumflex veins, which pass around the circumference of the penile shaft, with 3-10 joining the deep dorsal vein along its distal two thirds.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The deep dorsal vein of the penis travels on the dorsal aspect of the shaft of the penis deep to the superficial (Colle’s) and deep (Buck’s) penile fascia. It lies in the dorsal midline groove between the paired corpora cavernosa. Eventually the vein passes inferior to the pubic symphysis at the level of the suspensory ligament of the penis. It terminates by draining into the prostatic plexus.

Engorgement of the erectile tissue bodies of the penis compresses venous outflow, including circumflex and emissary veins and venous plexuses. This blocks blood return (veno-occlusive mechanism) leading to accumulation of blood and penile erection.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The deep dorsal vein of the penis receives circumflex veins directly and emissary Veins via a subtunical capillary plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep dorsal vein of the penis drains the glans penis and the distal two thirds of the corpus spongiosum and corpora cavernosa erectile tissue bodies.

Course: Veins in the plexus unite to form a single testicular vein (males) or ovarian vein (females).

Tributaries: Small spermatic veins (males) or small tubal ovarian veins (females).

Drainage: Testes and epididymis (males) or ovaries and uterine tubes (females).

In females, the pampiniform plexus is a vine-like structure that drains the ovaries and part of the uterine tubes into the left and right ovarian veins.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Prepuce and shaft skin of penis.

Course: Travels subcutaneously along the dorsum of the penis towards its base and empties into the superficial external pudendal veins.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Skin and superficial fascia of penis, prepuce of penis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial dorsal veins of the penis arise in the skin and superficial fascia of prepuce of penis and shaft of penis.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial dorsal veins of the penis travel deep to the skin and between the superficial (Colle’s) and deep (Buck’s) fascia of the penis. It empties into the superficial external pudendal veins, and eventually into the greater saphenous vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superficial dorsal veins of the penis drain the skin and superficial fascia of prepuce of penis and shaft of penis.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Penile urethra.

Course: Passes along the length of the urethra.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Urethra and corpus spongiosum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The urethral veins originate along the length of the penile urethra.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The urethral veins enter the bulb of the penis and unite with veins there to form the bulbourethral veins. They eventually terminate in the internal pudendal vein (Quartey, 2006).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The urethral veins drain the urethra and corpus spongiosum.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Quartey, J. K. M. (2006) 'Anatomy and Blood Supply of the Urethra and Penis', in Schreiter, F. and Jordan, G.H. (eds.) Urethral Reconstructive Surgery. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg, pp. 11-17.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Convergence of the renal arcuate veins.

Course: Pass from superficial to deep within the renal columns and drain into the renal veins.

Tributaries: Renal arcuate veins.

Drainage: Renal cortex and medulla.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The renal arcuate veins converge along the corticomedullary junction at the superficial end of each renal column to form the interlobar veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From the corticomedullary junction at the superficial end of the renal columns, the interlobar veins travel parallel to the axis of the column from superficial to deep. There is one interlobar vein per column (lobe). Each vein accompanies an interlobar renal artery.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The interlobar veins receive the arcuate veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The interlobar veins drain the renal cortex and medulla.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of anterior and posterior branches of renal veins at the renal hilum.

Course: Horizontal course to reach the inferior vena cava.

Tributaries: The left renal vein receives the left testicular (males) or ovarian (females) vein, left suprarenal vein, a communication with the lumbar veins, hemi-azygos and inferior phrenic veins. There are no tributaries of the right renal vein.

Drainage: The kidneys.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The renal veins originate from the union of the anterior and posterior branches, which are formed at the base of the renal pyramids.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
Both renal veins take a retroperitoneal, horizontal course to drain into the inferior vena cava. As they run towards the inferior vena cava, they travel anterior to the renal arteries.

The left renal vein is much longer than the right renal vein as it has to travel over the aorta in order to reach the inferior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Due to the location of the inferior vena cava on the right-hand side of the body, the left renal vein is longer and receives more tributaries than the right renal vein. The left renal vein receives the left gonadal vein at approximately a 90-degree angle, the left suprarenal vein, a communicating branch from the lumbar veins and often, hemiazygos, and inferior phrenic vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The renal veins are large caliber veins that drain the medulla and cortex of the kidneys.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: A network of vessels that surround the fundus of the bladder and prostate (males) or the upper part of the urethra and neck of the bladder (females). 

Course: The network of vessels surrounds the urethra and bladder and drains into the vesical veins.

Tributaries: Dorsal vein of the clitoris (females). 

Drainage: Bladder and prostate (males), or clitoris and urethra (females).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vesical venous plexus is a network of vessels that surround the upper part of the urethra and neck of the bladder in females. In males, the plexus of vessels surrounds the fundus of the bladder and prostate.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The plexus communicates with the vaginal and uterovaginal plexuses (female) or prostatic plexus (male). The plexus drains mainly into the inferior vesical vein and into the internal iliac vein. Often, it may drain into the vertebral venous plexus via the sacral veins. For descriptive purposes, the veins in the vesical plexus may be named the superior vesical veins and the inferior vesical veins.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: In females, the dorsal vein of the clitoris drains into the vesical venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The vesical venous plexus is directly associated with the bladder. In females, the plexus drains the urethra and clitoris. In males, it receives tributaries from the prostate (Moore et al., 2013).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The bladder is drained by the vesical venous plexus. The superior aspect of the plexus is drained into the superior vesical vein, and the inferior aspect of the plexus is drained into the inferior vesical vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Originates on the anterior surface of sacrum.

Course: Ascends on the anterior surface of sacrum to drain into the common iliac vein.

Tributaries: No tributaries.

Drainage: Anterior surface of sacrum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The median sacral vein is a singular vein that originates on the anterior surface of the sacrum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the vein ascends on the anterior surface of the sacrum to drain into the common iliac vein, at approximately the level of the fourth lumbar vertebrae.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The median sacral vein drains the ventral surface of the sacrum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Pars spongiosa of the vertebral bodies.

Course: Passes horizontally through the vertebral bodies.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Vertebrae.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The basivertebral veins originate from venous sinuses within the pars spongiosa of the vertebral bodies.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The basivertebral veins run horizontally through the vertebral bodies, emerging through the foramina of the vertebral bodies.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the basivertebral veins communicate anteriorly with the anterior external vertebral venous plexus and posteriorly with the anterior internal vertebral venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The basivertebral veins drain the vertebral bodies.

21975.name: Anterior Internal Vertebral Venous Plexus (Cervical; Right)
alternate: Anterior Internal Epidural Venous Sinus (Cervical; Right)

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior epidural space.

Course: Posterior to the vertebral bodies in the vertebral canal.

Tributaries: Basivertebral veins.

Drainage: Vertebrae, epidural space, spinal cord, and local tissue.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior internal vertebral plexus arises from a network of vessels located within the vertebral canal, posterior to the vertebral bodies of all 33 vertebrae. Their main channels are located on either side of the posterior longitudinal ligament with several smaller vessels traversing the ligament.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior internal vertebral venous plexus is composed of valveless veins, which are free to anastomose with other components of the vertebral venous plexus. Additionally, around the foramen magnum, the venous plexus communicates with the dural venous sinuses, and with the deep veins of the neck and pelvis. It communicates laterally with the intervertebral veins which drain the vertebral venous plexus into the vertebral vein in the neck, the posterior intercostal veins in the thorax, and the lumbar and lateral sacral veins caudally.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior internal vertebral venous plexus receives the basivertebral veins and tributaries from the spinal veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior internal vertebral venous plexus drains the vertebrae, epidural space, spinal cord, and local tissue.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Spinal epidural hematoma

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior to the vertebral bodies.

Course: Extends the entire length of the vertebral column.

Tributaries: The basivertebral vein.

Drainage: Vertebrae and local tissue.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior external vertebral venous plexus is formed by a network of interconnected vessels located anterior to the vertebral bodies.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior external vertebral venous plexus is found along the entire length of the vertebral column, from the foramen magnum to the sacral hiatus. It is most developed in the cervical region.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior external vertebral venous plexus is a valveless network, which is free to anastomose with other components of the vertebral venous plexus. It communicates with the basivertebral and intervertebral veins and venules from local tissues.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior external vertebral venous plexus drains blood from the vertebrae, as well as muscle and connective tissues located close by.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Arteriovenous malformation

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior external vertebral venous plexus is formed by a network of interconnecting vessels running posterior to the vertebral laminae, around and between the spinous process.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior external vertebral venous plexus is a valveless network located along the entire length of the spinal column.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The posterior external vertebral venous plexus communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus and joins with the vertebral, posterior intercostal, and lumbar veins.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior to the vertebral arches.

Course: Extends the entire length of the vertebral column.

Tributaries: Posterior internal vertebral venous plexus.

Drainage: Vertebrae and local tissue.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior external vertebral venous plexus is formed by a network of interconnecting vessels running posterior to the vertebral laminae, around and between the spinous process.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior external vertebral venous plexus is a valveless network located along the entire length of the spinal column.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The posterior external vertebral venous plexus communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus and joins with the vertebral, posterior intercostal, and lumbar veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior external vertebral venous plexus drains the bony tissues and some soft tissues surrounding the spinous processes and laminae.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Arteriovenous malformation

17611.name: Posterior Internal Vertebral Venous Plexus (Sacral; Left)
alternate: Posterior Internal Epidural Venous Sinus (Sacral; Left)

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior epidural space.

Course: Anterior to the vertebral arches in the vertebral canal.

Tributaries: Posterior external vertebral venous plexus.

Drainage: Vertebrae, epidural space, spinal cord, and local tissue.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior internal venous plexus is formed by a network of vessels located within the vertebral canal, anterior to the vertebral arches and lining the posterior aspect of the epidural space. They are in ruminant formation in the cervical region but more developed caudally.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The posterior internal venous plexus is composed of valveless veins, which are free to anastomose with the posterior external vertebral venous plexus.

Additionally, around the foramen magnum, the venous plexus communicates with the occipital and sigmoid sinuses, the basilar plexus, and the condylar emissary veins. It communicates laterally with the intervertebral veins which drain the vertebral venous plexus into the vertebral vein in the neck, the posterior intercostal veins in the thorax, and the lumbar and lateral sacral veins caudally.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The posterior internal venous plexus receives blood from the posterior external vertebral venous plexus, carrying blood from outside the vertebral canal inside.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The posterior internal vertebral venous plexus drains the vertebrae, epidural space, spinal cord, and local tissue.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Spinal epidural hematoma

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Network of vessels on the pelvic surface of the sacrum.

Course: Drains into the middle and lateral sacral veins.

Tributaries: Sacral intervertebral veins.

Drainage: Sacrum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The sacral venous plexus is a network of vessels that originates caudal to the lumbosacral junction.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The sacral venous plexus normally forms a symmetrical hexagonal network of vessels on the pelvic surface of the sacrum, that drains into the lateral branch of the hypogastric vein. A sacral ladder is formed from anastomoses created by transversely orientated pre-sacral veins that unite the medial and lateral sacral veins (Zeit and Cope, 1983).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The sacral venous plexus receives blood from the sacral intervertebral veins and forms anastomoses with the lumbar and pelvic veins.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The sacral venous plexus drains the surrounding sacrum.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Zeit, R. M. and Cope, C. (1983) 'Anatomy of the sacral venous plexus', AJR Am J Roentgenol, 140(1), pp. 143-4.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior surface of sacrum.

Course: Ascends on the anterior surface of the sacrum and drains into the internal iliac or superior gluteal vein.

Tributaries: Spinal branches.

Drainage: Anterior surface of the sacrum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral sacral veins are paired veins that originate on the inferior portion of the sacrum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the lateral sacral veins ascend on the anterior surface of the sacrum, lateral to the median sacral vein and artery, to drain into the internal iliac or superior gluteal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text:
The lateral sacral veins form an anastomosis with the vertebral venous plexuses. This provides an alternative collateral pathway for blood to reach the inferior or superior vena cava.

Spinal tributaries travel through the pelvic sacral foramen and drain into the lateral sacral vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The lateral sacral veins drain the anterior surface of the sacrum.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Venous metastases

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Pars spongiosa of the vertebral bodies.

Course: Passes horizontally through the vertebral bodies.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Vertebrae.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The basivertebral veins originate from venous sinuses within the pars spongiosa of the vertebral bodies.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The basivertebral veins run horizontally through the vertebral bodies, emerging through the anterior and posterior foramina of the vertebral bodies.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries; however, the basivertebral veins communicate anteriorly with the anterior external vertebral venous plexus and posteriorly with the anterior internal vertebral venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The basivertebral veins drain the vertebral bodies.
