sections.title: Structure
sections.text: Endolymphatic duct is a canal-like structure, which is the non-sensory component of the membranous labyrinth. It is given off from the confluence of utricular and saccular ducts (utriculosaccular duct) within the bony vestibule. It exits the vestibule through the osseus vestibular aqueduct and subsequently terminates in the epidural space of the posterior cranial fossa.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
Proximally, the endolymphatic duct is slightly dilated to form an endolymphatic sinus. Distally, the endolymphatic duct ends in a blind pouch called the endolymphatic sac, located on the posterior surface of the petrous portion of the temporal bone, where it is in contact with the dura mater. The distal end of the sac overlaps the sigmoid sinus in as many as 40% of the cases (Lo et al, 1997).

In humans, tubularity develops within the endolymphatic sac and reaches adult complexity by 3–4 years of age.

The epithelial lining of the endolymphatic duct comprises of flattened, cuboidal or cylindrical cells. The stroma surrounding the endolymphatic duct and the sac is loose and voluminous due to an extensive capillary network, unlike the remaining portions of the membranous labyrinth, which comprise of thin, smooth-walled channels. The supportive stroma gradually condenses as the endolymphatic sac merges with the dura mater distally.

The endolymphatic duct and the sac both contain endolymph, while there is no perilymph space surrounding them.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Meniere’s disease

sections.title: References
sections.text: Lo, W. W., Daniels, D. L., Chakeres, D. W., Linthicum, F. H., Ulmer, J. L., Mark, L. P. & Swartz, J. D. (1997) The endolymphatic duct and sac. American Journal of Neuroradiology, 18(5), 881.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The lower end of the posterior semicircular duct is dilated medially to form a sac-like structure called the posterior ampulla. It opens into the lower posterior part of the utricle, within the bony vestibule. This dilated ampulla contains sensory hair cells. Numerous stereocilia and a single large kinocilium can be seen emerging from the apices of the hair cells. These are embedded in a gelatinous substance called the cupula, which extends to the roof of the ampulla. The longest stereocilium is the one nearest to the kinocilium gradually decreasing in length with accordance to their distance to the kinocilium.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The posterior ampulla opens anteriorly into the lower back part of the utricle within the bony vestibule. It lies just underneath the opening of the posterior non-ampullated end of the lateral semicircular duct.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The ampulla of the posterior semicircular duct helps detect the angular acceleration/deceleration of the head during its rotatory movements in a left-right frontal axis (coronal plane), e.g. when one moves the side of the head to touch his shoulders.

When the head changes position, the endolymph in the lateral semicircular duct lags behind due to inertia and bends the cupula and the stereocilia of the hair cells. The mechanical stimulation of the hair cells (due to deflection of the stereocilia) sends electrical signals to the brain. Movement towards the kinocilium depolarizes the hair cells causing stimulation, whereas movement away from the kinocilium hyperpolarizes the hair cell decreasing firing of the afferent neuron.

Within approximately 10 seconds of achieving constant motion, the endolymph catches up with the movement of the lateral semicircular duct and the cupula is no longer affected, stopping the sensation of acceleration generated in the posterior ampulla (Khan & Chang, 2013; Tascioglu, 2005).

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The utriculosaccular duct is part of the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear. It is formed by the union of the utricular and saccular ducts and, thus, interconnects the utricle and saccule.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The utriculosaccular duct serves as a conduit for the longitudinal flow of endolymph from the cochlea, through the saccule and subsequently towards the utricle.

The endolymphatic duct is given off from the confluence of utricular and saccular ducts (utriculosaccular duct) within the bony vestibule. It ends up in the endolymphatic sac.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The common membranous limb refers to the common conduit formed by the union of the posterior non-ampullated end of the anterior (superior) semicircular duct with the upper non-ampullated end of the posterior semicircular duct. This serves as the combined port of entry of both semicircular ducts into the utricle (Tascioglu, 2005).

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The common membranous limb opens into the posterior utricle (inside the bony vestibule). It lies above the opening of the non-ampullated end of the lateral (horizontal) semicircular duct.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Tascioglu, A. B. (2005) Brief review of vestibular system anatomy and its higher order projections, 4.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The ductus reuniens is the part of the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear, which connects the lower part of the saccule to the cochlear duct near its vestibular extremity. It has sometimes been referred in the literature as a continuation of the Reissner’s membrane, approximately 0.7mm in length and 0.225mm in diameter at the narrowest portion.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The endolymph within the membranous labyrinth flows longitudinally from the cochlear duct towards the endolymphatic duct and sac via the ductus reuniens and saccule.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Meniere’s disease

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: midbrain, between the tegmentum posteriorly and cerebral peduncle anteriorly

– The compact part contains dopaminergic neuromelanin-containing neurons; the reticular part contains mainly GABAergic neurons

– Function: regulates voluntary movement through basal nuclei circuitry

– Arterial supply: perforating branches of the posterior cerebral and basilar arteries

– Degeneration of compact part neurons underlies major motor features of Parkinson disease

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The substantia nigra is a bilateral nuclear mass of the midbrain composed of neuronal cell bodies and glia, divided into two relatively distinct regions:

– The compact part (pars compacta) consists of dopaminergic neurons containing the pigment neuromelanin, which gives the structure its characteristic dark appearance and its name. 

– The reticular part (pars reticulata) consists predominantly of GABAergic neurons.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The substantia nigra lies in the midbrain, between the tegmentum posteriorly and the cerebral peduncle anteriorly, extending throughout the rostrocaudal length of the midbrain. 

The compact part occupies the more posterior position, adjacent to the tegmentum; the reticular part lies anteriorly, immediately posterior to the cerebral peduncle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The substantia nigra is functionally related to the circuitry of the basal nuclei and involved in the regulation of voluntary movement.

The compact part projects dopaminergic fibers via the nigrostriatal pathway to the striatum (i.e., caudate nucleus and putamen), modulating the balance between the direct and indirect pathways of basal ganglia output. 

The reticular part, together with the medial/internal segment of the globus pallidus, forms the principal output of the basal ganglia, projecting GABAergic fibers to the thalamus and brainstem.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The substantia nigra is supplied by perforating branches of the posterior cerebral and basilar arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous blood drains via the basal vein (of Rosenthal) to the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and subsequently the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Parkinson disease: degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the compact part disrupts nigrostriatal input to the striatum, producing the cardinal features of bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and postural instability.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Medial subdivision of the globus pallidus; major output nucleus of basal nuclei

– Location: medial to lateral segment, separated by medial medullary lamina

– Sends inhibitory projections to thalamus and subthalamic nucleus

– Component of the direct pathway for movement facilitation

– Arterial supply: anterior choroidal artery; middle cerebral artery (anterolateral central arteries)

– Venous drainage: inferior thalamostriate veins → internal cerebral vein → great cerebral vein (of Galen)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The globus pallidus is a wedge-shaped deep cortical nucleus that is divided into medial (internal) and lateral (external) segments by a thin layer of white matter called the internal medullary lamina. The medial segment is the smaller of the two.

Both segments are predominantly made up of large multipolar GABAergic neurons.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The medial (internal) segment of the globus pallidus internus is the innermost portion of the lentiform nucleus, laying directly lateral to the internal capsule, and medial to the lateral segment. 

The medial segment is connected to the lateral segment by pallidopallidal fibers. It also projects pallidothalamic fibers to the thalamus, which are organized into two main bundles: the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus. 

– The ansa lenticularis emerges from the medial segment and courses ventrally and medially, looping around the posterior limb of the internal capsule toward the thalamus.

– The lenticular fasciculus passes more dorsally through the internal capsule and subthalamic region before also reaching the thalamus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The globus pallidus is mainly associated with regulation of voluntary movement. The medial segment acts largely an output nucleus, sending fibers mainly to the thalamus.

In the “direct pathway,” the dorsal striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen) sends inhibitory signals to the medial segment, which in turn sends inhibitory signals to the thalamus.

In the “indirect pathway,” the dorsal striatum sends inhibitory signals to the lateral segment of the globus pallidus, which then sends inhibitory signals to the subthalamic nucleus. The subthalamic nucleus sends excitatory (glutamatergic) signals back to the medial segment, which then sends inhibitory signals to the thalamus.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The anterolateral central (lenticulostriate) arteries, which arise from the M1 segment of middle cerebral artery, are the main blood supply of the globus pallidus. Additional supply is provided by the anterior choroidal artery and perforating branches of the anterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The inferior thalamostriate veins drain the lentiform nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus) which drains into the internal cerebral vein, the great cerebral vein and the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
–Parkinson disease: Increased inhibitory output from the medial segment of the globus pallidus (GPi) suppresses thalamocortical activity, contributing to bradykinesia and rigidity. The GPi is a principal target for deep brain stimulation (DBS) and pallidotomy, both of which aim to reduce this excessive inhibitory output and improve motor symptoms.

– Dystonia: The GPi is also a recognised deep brain stimulation target for refractory dystonia, where GPi stimulation reduces abnormal sustained muscle contractions.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: subthalamus, inferior to the thalamus, medial to the internal capsule, and below the zona incerta

– Biconvex lens-shaped gray matter nucleus with glutamatergic projection neurons

– Function: excites basal nuclei output regions and regulates voluntary movement

– Arterial supply: posterior cerebral, posterior communicating, and anterior choroidal artery branches

– Lesions may cause contralateral hemiballismus; deep brain stimulation is used in Parkinson disease

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The subthalamic nucleus is the principal gray matter structure of the subthalamus, a transitional zone of the diencephalon lying inferior to the thalamus, lateral to the hypothalamus, and medial to the internal capsule.

It is a biconvex, lens-shaped nucleus composed of neuronal cell bodies and glia, containing small interneurons intermixed with large multipolar cells.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The subthalamic nucleus lies medial to the internal capsule, just rostral to where it becomes continuous with the crus cerebri. 

The zona incerta lies dorsal to it, separating it from the thalamus. The rostral poles of the red nucleus and substantia nigra extend into the subthalamic region.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The subthalamic nucleus is unique within the basal nuclei circuitry in that its neurons are glutamatergic, projecting excitatory fibers predominantly to the medial/internal segment of the globus pallidus and to the reticular part of the substantia nigra, driving inhibitory basal nuclei output. 

It also projects to the lateral/external segment of the globus pallidus. It receives GABAergic input from the lateral segment of the globus pallidus and afferents from the cerebral cortex via the subthalamic fasciculus.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The subthalamic nucleus is supplied by perforating branches of the posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries, with contributions from the anterior choroidal artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The subthalamic nucleus is drained via the basal vein (of Rosenthal) to the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Hemiballismus: lesion of the subthalamic nucleus (most commonly from infarction) results in sudden, wild, flinging involuntary movements of the contralateral limbs (dyskinesia).

– Parkinson disease: the subthalamic nucleus is overactive in Parkinson disease due to loss of dopaminergic input to the striatum; deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus is an established surgical treatment.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Lateral subdivision of the globus pallidus; intrinsic nucleus of basal nuclei

– Location: lateral to medial segment, medial to putamen

– Projects to subthalamic nucleus as part of indirect pathway

– Functions: movement suppression via indirect pathway

– Arterial supply: middle cerebral artery (anterolateral central arteries)

– Venous drainage: inferior thalamostriate veins → internal cerebral vein → great cerebral vein (of Galen)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The globus pallidus is a wedge-shaped deep cortical nucleus that is divided into medial (internal) and lateral (external) segments by a thin layer of white matter called the internal medullary lamina. The lateral segment is the larger of the two.

Both segments are predominantly made up of large multipolar GABAergic neurons.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The lateral (external) segment of the globus pallidus is the intermediate portion of the lentiform nucleus, lying directly between the medial segment (medially) and the putamen (laterally).

The two segments of the globus pallidus are interconnected through pallidopallidal fibers. The lateral segment also has direct connections to the subthalamic nucleus via pallidosubthalamic fibers.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The globus pallidus is mainly associated with regulation of voluntary movement. 

In the “indirect pathway,” the dorsal striatum sends inhibitory signals to the lateral segment of the globus pallidus, which then sends inhibitory signals to the subthalamic nucleus. The subthalamic nucleus sends excitatory (glutamatergic) signals back to the medial segment, which then sends inhibitory signals to the thalamus.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The anterolateral central (lenticulostriate) arteries, which arise from the M1 segment of middle cerebral artery, are the main blood supply of the globus pallidus. Additional supply is provided by the anterior choroidal artery and perforating branches of the anterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The inferior thalamostriate veins drain the lentiform nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus) which drains into the internal cerebral vein, the great cerebral vein and the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Huntington disease: Preferential degeneration of striatal neurons projecting to the lateral segment of the globus pallidus (GPe) reduces inhibitory input to the GPe, disinhibiting the subthalamic nucleus and disrupting basal nuclei circuitry, contributing to the characteristic characteristic involuntary movements (chorea) of the condition.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Large C-shaped structure along the lateral wall of the lateral ventricles

– Composed of head, body, and tail; forms dorsal striatum with putamen

– Predominantly GABAergic medium-sized spiny neurons

– Functions: movement planning, learning, memory, reward, motivation, emotion

– Arterial supply: anterior cerebral artery (long striate artery); middle cerebral artery (anterolateral central arteries); anterior choroidal artery (tail)

– Venous drainage: caudate veins → superior thalamostriate vein → internal cerebral vein

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The caudate nucleus is a large C-shaped structure located deep to the cerebral cortex near the thalamus.  It consists of a head, body, and tail, with the terminal portion adjacent to the hippocampus and amygdaloid body. 

The majority of neurons within the caudate are medium-sized spiny neurons that principally release the neurotransmitter GABA.  

The caudate nucleus and putamen may be collectviely referred to as the dorsal striatum, sometimes referred to simply as the striatum, or neostriatum.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The head of the caudate nucleus lies along the lateral wall of the lateral ventricle; the body is further lateral to the lateral ventricle; and the tail is located just above the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle. 

The terminal portion of the tail is adjacent to the hippocampus and amygdaloid body. The inferior portion of the head of the caudate nucleus is continuous with the inferior portion of the putamen above the anterior perforated substance. The body is mainly separated from the lenticular nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus) by the internal capsule. The caudate nuclei lie close to the centrally located thalamus. The corpus callosum lies superior (dorsal) to the head and body of the caudate nucleus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The caudate nucleus is involved in planning and initiation of movement, as well as learning, memory, reward, motivation, and emotion.

The anterior portion (head) of the caudate nucleus has connections to the medial and lateral prefrontal cortices and is involved with executive functioning and working memory. In addition, it receives information from the prefrontal and motor cortices related to the planning of movements. 

The tail of the caudate nucleus has connections to the inferior temporal pole and is involved in the control of movement and processing visual information.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The major arteries supplying the caudate nucleus are: 

– Head: Long striate artery (a.k.a. medial striate/long central artery, recurrent artery of Heubner) and anterolateral central arteries (lenticulostriate arteries)

– Body: Anterolateral central arteries (lenticulostriate arteries, M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery)

– Tail: Anterior choroidal artery

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage of the caudate nucleus is provided by several caudate veins, which drain into the superior thalamostriate vein (terminal vein) or directly into the internal cerebral vein.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
–Huntington disease: Characterised by preferential degeneration of caudate nucleus neurons, producing progressive choreiform movements, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbance. Caudate atrophy is a recognised imaging finding and contributes to the characteristic "box-car" appearance of the lateral ventricles on MRI.

– Obsessive-compulsive disorder: The caudate nucleus forms part of the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit implicated in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD); hyperactivity within this circuit is associated with the compulsive behaviours characteristic of the condition.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Largest component of the basal nuclei; lateral part of lentiform nucleus

– Location: deep to insular cortex, lateral to globus pallidus

– Composed predominantly of GABAergic medium-sized spiny neurons

– Functions: motor preplanning, motor learning, emotion, reward

– Arterial supply: middle cerebral artery (anterolateral central arteries); anterior choroidal artery

– Venous drainage: inferior thalamostriate veins → internal cerebral vein → great cerebral vein (of Galen)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The putamen is the lateral component of the lentiform nucleus, located adjacent to the lateral (external) segment of the globus pallidus. It is structurally and histologically similar to the caudate nucleus; for this reason, the putamen can also be grouped with the caudate nucleus to form the dorsal striatum, which is also sometimes referred to simply as the striatum, or neostriatum. 

The putamen is composed predominantly of GABAergic medium-sized spiny neurons.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The putamen is located deep to the insular cortex, separated from it by the claustrum. The putamen is located lateral to the globus pallidus (lateral segment), separated by the Lateral (external) medullary lamina.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The putamen has multiple functions: the anterior putamen has connections with association cortical areas (particularlyee prefrontal regions), and the posterior portion connects with the primary motor and supplementary motor cortical areas. 

Together with the caudate nucleus, the putamen is the main site of cortical input to the basal nuclei. It functions in motor preplanning and movement modulationok give. Additional roles relate to learning, memory, emotions, and other types of cognitive processing. The putamen also contributes to the modulation of sensory and motor aspects of pain.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The anterolateral central (lenticulostriate) arteries, which arise from the M1 segment of middle cerebral artery, are the main blood supply to the putamen.Additional supply is provided by the anterior choroidal artery and perforating branches of the anterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The inferior thalamostriate veins drain the lentiform nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus) which drains into the internal cerebral vein, the great cerebral vein and the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Parkinson disease: Associated with degeneration of the nigrostriatal pathway, reducing dopaminergic input to the putamen and disrupting motor circuit function, producing bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor.

sections.title: References
sections.text: FIPAT, 2017. Terminologia Neuroanatomica. Federative International Programme for Anatomical Terminology. https://fipat.library.dal.ca.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Oval elevation on the dorsal surface of the caudal medulla oblongata, just lateral to the gracile tubercle

– Surface manifestation of the underlying cuneate nucleus

– Function: overlies the cuneate nucleus, which relays fine discriminative touch, pressure, vibration, and proprioception from the ipsilateral upper limb, shoulder, and neck (T5 and above); contributes to the posterior columns and medial lemniscus

– Arterial supply: posterior inferior cerebellar (PICA) and posterior spinal arteries (+ minor vertebral artery contribution)

– Venous drainage: dorsal medullary veins → posterior spinal veins and internal vertebral venous plexus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The cuneate tubercle is an oval elevation on the dorsal surface of the caudal medulla oblongata, oriented parallel to the long axis of the brainstem. It is paired, lying 4–5 mm lateral to the midline, just lateral and slightly rostral to the gracile tubercle. It is a surface manifestation of the underlying cuneate nucleus.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The cuneate tubercles lie on either side of the midline, just lateral to the gracile tubercles. Superficially lies the subarachnoid space and meninges; deep to it is the cuneate nucleus. Its rostral limit corresponds to the level at which the medulla oblongata transitions from closed to open. Inferiorly, the cuneate fasciculus continues as an elongated band into the spinal cord.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The cuneate tubercle overlies the cuneate nucleus, which receives large-diameter myelinated primary somatosensory afferents from the ipsilateral body at T5 and above, conveying fine discriminative touch, pressure, vibration, and proprioception from the upper limb, shoulder, and neck. Together with the gracile tubercle and their respective fasciculi, they form the posterior columns, giving rise to the medial lemniscus.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The major arterial supply to the region of the cuneate tubercle and nucleus is derived from the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and the posterior spinal artery. Minor contributions come from long circumferential branches of the vertebral arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage of the area of the cuneate tubercle converges on small dorsal medullary veins that drain primarily to posterior spinal veins.  Additional flow may include the anterior spinal vein and the internal vertebral venous plexus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Dorsal column syndrome: Damage to the cuneate tubercle or cuneate nucleus causes ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception in the upper limb.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Vanderah, T.W., 2026. Nolte's The Human Brain: An Introduction to Its Functional Anatomy, 9th ed. Elsevier, Amsterdam.

Standring, S., Tubbs, S.R., 2025. Gray’s Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 43rd ed. Elsevier, Amsterdam.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Oval elevation on the dorsal surface of the caudal medulla oblongata, on either side of the posterior median sulcus

– Surface manifestation of the underlying nucleus gracilis; its rostral limit is the obex

– Function: overlies the nucleus gracilis, which relays fine discriminative touch, pressure, vibration, and proprioception from the ipsilateral lower limb, pelvis, and abdomen (T6 and below); contributes to the dorsal columns and medial lemniscus

– Arterial supply: posterior inferior cerebellar (PICA) and posterior spinal arteries (+ minor vertebral artery contribution)

– Venous drainage: dorsal medullary veins → posterior spinal veins and internal vertebral venous plexus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The gracile tubercle is an oval elevation on the dorsal surface of the caudal medulla oblongata, oriented parallel to the long axis of the brainstem. It is a surface manifestation of the underlying nucleus gracilis.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The gracile tubercles are paired, lying on either side of the posterior median sulcus. Superficially lies the subarachnoid space with its meninges; deep to it is the gracile nucleus. 

Its rostral limit is the obex, where the medulla oblongata transitions from closed to open. Inferiorly, the gracile fasciculus continues as an elongated band into the spinal cord. Laterally lies the cuneate fasciculus, terminating rostrally in the cuneate tubercle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The gracile tubercle overlies the nucleus gracilis, which receives large-diameter myelinated primary somatosensory afferents from the ipsilateral body at T6 and below, conveying fine discriminative touch, pressure, vibration, and proprioception from the lower limb, pelvis, and abdomen. Together with the cuneate tubercle and their respective fasciculi, they form the dorsal columns, giving rise to the medial lemniscus.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The major arterial supply to the region of the gracile tubercle and nucleus is derived from the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and the posterior spinal artery. Minor contributions come from long circumferential branches of the vertebral arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage of the area of the gracile tubercle converges on small dorsal medullary veins that drain primarily into posterior spinal veins with additional flow to the anterior spinal vein and internal vertebral venous plexus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Dorsal column syndrome: Results from damage to the gracile fasciculus or gracile nucleus, causing ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception from the lower limb and lower trunk.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Vanderah, T.W., 2026. Nolte's The Human Brain: An Introduction to Its Functional Anatomy, 9th ed. Elsevier, Amsterdam.

Standring, S., Tubbs, S.R., 2025. Gray’s Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 43rd ed. Elsevier, Amsterdam.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Most caudal division of the brainstem

– Continuous with the spinal cord at the cervicomedullary junction

– Contains nuclei of cranial nerves IX–XII and cardiovascular and respiratory control centers

– Arterial supply: anterior spinal artery, vertebral arteries, posterior inferior cerebellar artery, and posterior spinal arteries

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The medulla oblongata (myencephalon) is the most caudal division of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord at the cervicomedullary junction. It comprises an open portion rostrally, where the fourth ventricle lies on its dorsal surface, and a closed portion caudally, where the central canal is enclosed within the tissue. 

The dorsal surface presents the gracile and cuneate tubercles, overlying the gracile and cuneate nuclei. The ventral surface presents two prominent features: the pyramids, which carry the corticospinal fibers, and the inferior olives, which overlie the inferior olivary nuclei.

The medulla oblongata contains the nuclei of cranial nerves IX, X, and XII, and the cranial root of cranial nerve XI, within its tegmentum.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The medulla oblongata lies between the pons superiorly and the spinal cord inferiorly, within the posterior cranial fossa. It exits the posterior cranial fossa through the foramen magnum, where it becomes continuous with the spinal cord at the cervicomedullary junction. 

The cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) lies posterior to the medulla oblongata, between it and the inferior surface of the cerebellum. Anteriorly, the medulla oblongata is related to the lower clivus, and the premedullary cistern contains the vertebral arteries along its ventral surface.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The medulla oblongata contains the nuclei of cranial nerves IX–XII, mediating swallowing, phonation, tongue movement, and parasympathetic innervation of the thoracic and abdominal viscera. 

It houses the cardiovascular and respiratory control centers, including the vasomotor center and the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups, and the nucleus of the solitary tract, which integrates visceral afferent information. 

The medulla oblongata also serves as the conduit for ascending somatosensory pathways and descending motor pathways between the pons and spinal cord. The corticospinal tract decussates at the caudal medulla oblongata, at the level of the foramen magnum.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The medulla oblongata is supplied by four vessels:

– The anterior spinal artery supplies the pyramids and medial medulla oblongata, including the hypoglossal nucleus and medial lemniscus. 

– The vertebral arteries supply the ventrolateral medulla oblongata, including the inferior olivary nuclei and spinothalamic tracts. 

– The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) supplies the dorsolateral medulla oblongata, including the nucleus ambiguus, nuclei of the solitary tract, and posterior nucleus of vagus nerve. 

– The posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal medulla oblongata including the gracile and cuneate nuclei. 

The blood supply to nuclei and axonal tracts is variable as the vascular territories overlap and shift as one moves rostrally and caudally through the medulla oblongata.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
Venous drainage of the medulla oblongata can be organized into three routes:

– Anterior drainage is collected by the anteromedian and anterolateral medullary veins, which drain inferiorly into the anterior spinal vein. 

– Posterior drainage passes via the posteromedian medullary vein and the vein of the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle into the posterior spinal veins. 

– Lateral drainage is carried by radicular veins accompanying cranial nerves IX–XII, draining into the inferior petrosal sinus, the occipital sinus, or the superior bulb of the jugular vein.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome): dorsolateral medullary infarction, typically from PICA occlusion, producing ipsilateral facial numbness, Horner syndrome, and ataxia with contralateral body pain and temperature loss.

– Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine syndrome): medial medullary infarction from anterior spinal or vertebral artery occlusion, producing contralateral hemiplegia, proprioceptive loss, and ipsilateral hypoglossal palsy.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Paired longitudinal elevations on the ventral surface of the medulla oblongata, flanking the anterior median fissure

– Formed by the descending axons of the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract

– Function: transmit upper motor neuron fibers from the motor cortex to the spinal cord, mediating voluntary motor control of the limbs and trunk

– Arterial supply: anterior spinal artery

– Venous drainage: anteromedian, anterolateral, and transverse medullary veins → petrosal sinuses

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The pyramids are longitudinal elevations on the ventral surface of the medulla oblongata, formed by the descending axons of the corticospinal tract (pyramidal fibers).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The pyramids are paired structures flanking the ventral midline, separated from each other by the anterior median fissure. Lateral to each pyramid lies the olive, with the hypoglossal nerve emerging from the groove between them (the preolivary sulcus).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The pyramids transmit corticospinal fibers carrying upper motor neuron axons from the motor cortex to the spinal cord, mediating voluntary motor control of the limbs and trunk.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The pyramids are supplied by the anterior spinal artery, which runs in the anterior median fissure along their medial border.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
Blood is drained through a venous plexus via the anteromedian, anterolateral, and transverse medullary veins, ultimately draining to the petrosal sinuses.

Drainage through the anterior spinal vein is also possible.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine syndrome): medial medullary infarction from anterior spinal or vertebral artery occlusion, producing contralateral hemiplegia, proprioceptive loss, and ipsilateral hypoglossal palsy.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Middle division of the brainstem

– Comprises the basilar pons and tegmentum

– Contains nuclei for cranial nerves V–VIII

– Arterial supply: basilar artery, anterior inferior cerebellar artery, and superior cerebellar artery

– Venous drainage: pontine veins, basal vein, cerebellar veins, petrosal sinuses, and transverse sinuses

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The pons is the middle division of the brainstem, recognizable by its prominent ventral enlargement. It comprises two parts, namely the:

– basilar pons, which contains the descending corticospinal and corticopontine fibers and the transverse pontocerebellar fibers; 
– tegmentum, which contains the cranial nerve nuclei for cranial nerves V–VIII and the ascending and descending tracts of the pontine core. 

The middle cerebellar peduncles emerge from the lateral aspect of the basilar pons and connecting it to the cerebellum.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The pons is located between the midbrain superiorly and the medulla oblongata inferiorly; it lies within the posterior cranial fossa, anterior to the cerebellum and posterior to the clivus.

The prepontine cistern lies anterior to the basilar pons and contains the basilar artery, which runs in the basilar sulcus along the ventral midline. The cerebellopontine angle cisterns flank the pons laterally, at the junction with the cerebellum and the petrous portion of the temporal bone.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The pons relays sensory information from the body to the brain and transmits descending corticospinal fibers from the cerebral cortex to the spinal cord. 

The nuclei of cranial nerves V–VIII are located within the pons, mediating facial sensation and movement, horizontal eye movements, auditory sensation, and vestibular function.

Pontocerebellar fibers cross in the basilar pons and pass via the middle cerebellar peduncles to the cerebellum, contributing to the planning and coordination of movement. 

The pontine reticular formation contains the paramedian pontine reticular formation, which serves as the horizontal gaze center, and the pontine respiratory group (comprising the pneumotaxic center in the upper pons and the apneustic center in the lower pons) which modulates the respiratory rhythm generated in the medulla oblongata.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The pons is supplied primarily by the basilar artery which runs along its ventral length. Pontine or paramedian branches serve the ventral pons while long circumferential branches of the basilar artery serve more lateral and dorsal portions of the pons. There is also a lesser contribution of the superior cerebellar and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries to the dorsolateral pons.

The pons is supplied primarily by the basilar artery, which runs along its ventral surface. Paramedian pontine branches of the basilar artery supply the medial basilar pons and tegmentum, short circumferential branches supply the anterolateral pons, and long circumferential branches supply the lateral and dorsal pons. 

The anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) supplies the dorsolateral pons and the region of the cerebellopontine angle, and the superior cerebellar artery (SCA) contributes to the supply of the rostral pons.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
Venous drainage of the pons is collected by the anteromedian and anteromedial pontine veins and their tributaries, draining into the basilar venous plexus anteriorly. 

Pontine veins drain variably into the basal vein (of Rosenthal), the adjacent cerebellar veins, the petrosal and transverse sinuses, or the venous plexus of the foramen ovale. 

The vein of the pontomesencephalic sulcus and the vein of the pontomedullary sulcus connect the pontine venous system superiorly and inferiorly respectively.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Locked-in syndrome: loss of voluntary movement of all limbs and the lower cranial nerves with preservation of consciousness and vertical eye movements, resulting from bilateral infarction of the ventral pons disrupting the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts while sparing the reticular formation.

– Basilar artery occlusion: occlusion of the basilar artery causing ischemia of the pons, cerebellum, and midbrain. It presents with altered consciousness, quadriplegia, and cranial nerve deficits, and carries high mortality without prompt revascularization.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Ovoid elevation on the ventral surface of the medulla oblongata, lateral to the pyramid

– Formed by the underlying inferior olivary nucleus

– Function: projects via the olivocerebellar tract through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral cerebellum, where climbing fibers synapse on Purkinje cells; contributes to motor learning

– Arterial supply: vertebral artery and posterior inferior cerebellar artery

– Venous drainage: anteromedian, anterolateral, and transverse medullary veins → petrosal sinuses

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The olive is an ovoid elevation on the ventral surface of the medulla oblongata, formed by the underlying inferior olivary nucleus.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The olive lies lateral to the pyramid, separated from it by the preolivary sulcus, from which the rootlets of the hypoglossal nerve emerge. 

The superior olivary nucleus, despite the shared name, is a separate structure located in the pons and does not contribute to the olive.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The inferior olivary nucleus projects via the olivocerebellar tract through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral cerebellum, where its climbing fibers synapse on Purkinje cells. It plays a role in motor learning through repetition.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The olive is supplied primarily by branches of the vertebral artery and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). 

The anterior spinal artery may supply the deeper portions of the inferior olivary nucleus.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Blood is drained through a venous plexus via the anteromedian, anterolateral, and transverse medullary veins, ultimately draining to the petrosal sinuses.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: –Hypertrophic olivary degeneration: Damage to any component of the dentatorubroolivary circuit (Guillain-Mollaret triangle, connecting the dentate nucleus, red nucleus, and inferior olivary nucleus via the superior cerebellar peduncle and central tegmental tract) causes transsynaptic degeneration of the olive, which undergoes characteristic hypertrophy rather than atrophy.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
The middle cerebellar peduncle (aka brachium points) is the largest of the cerebellar peduncles. The fibers originate in the pontine nucleus, cross the midline in the basilar pons and emerge on the opposite side as large bundles along the lateral side of the pontine tegmentum into the cerebellum.

Some uncrossed pontocerebellar fibers in this peduncle are distributed chiefly to the cortex of the cerebellar hemisphere with some collateral fibers passing to the cerebellar nuclei.

Fibers of the pontine nuclei primarily relay motor signals from the primary motor cortex to the cerebellum to modulate motor outputs of the brain.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Largest of the three cerebellar lobes; lies between the primary fissure and the posterolateral fissure

– Superior surface posterior to the primary fissure; inferior surface to the posterolateral fissure, separating it from the flocculonodular lobe

– Related superiorly to the tentorium cerebelli; inferior surface overlies the caudal pons and rostral medulla and contributes to the roof of the fourth ventricle

– Function: shift from spinocerebellar to pontocerebellar function; oculomotor control, working memory, language, executive function, and emotional processing

– Arterial supply: anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The posterior lobe is the largest of the three cerebellar lobes.

On the superior surface, the posterior lobe lies posterior to the primary fissure (preclival fissure) and extends to the horizontal fissure (intercrural fissure); on the inferior surface, it continues from the horizontal fissure to the posterolateral fissure, which separates it from the flocculonodular lobe.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The posterior lobe lies in the posterior cranial fossa. Its superior surface is related to the tentorium cerebelli. 

At the horizontal fissure the lobe bends sharply to form the inferior surface, which lies over the caudal pons and rostral medulla and contributes to the roof of the fourth ventricle. 

Laterally, the inferior surface is related to the inner surface of the squamous part of the occipital bone, immediately lateral to the foramen magnum.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The posterior lobe reflects a broad shift from spinocerebellar (sensorimotor) to pontocerebellar (cognitive) function. 

Spinocerebellar functions are retained in the anteromedial aspects of the posterior quadrangular lobule (HVI) and the pyramis (lobule VIII), contributing to sensorimotor integration and postural control. 

The pontocerebellar territory comprises vermal portions immediately posterior to the primary fissure as well as most of the posterior cerebellar hemispheres; it contributes to oculomotor control, anticipatory postural adjustments, higher cognitive functions including working memory, language and executive function, and affective and emotional processing via its limbic connections. 

The uvula (lobule IX) and tonsils (HIX) contain a third representation of motor and cognitive networks.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The posterior lobe is supplied by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), both branches of the vertebrobasilar system. 

The PICA gives rise to an inferior vermian branch, which supplies the inferior aspect of the vermis, and tonsillar branches, which supply the cerebellar tonsils. 

The relative territories of AICA and PICA vary considerably between individuals; one artery is often dominant and supplies a larger territory than the other.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The posterior lobe is drained by superficial cerebellar veins. Veins of the superior and inferior surfaces drain into the transverse sinus; the anterior veins drain into the inferior petrosal sinus or sigmoid sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Ataxia: lesions of the lateral posterior lobe (cerebellar hemispheres) typically produce appendicular ataxia, characterised by dysmetria, intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia affecting the limbs ipsilateral to the lesion.

– Cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome (Schmahmann syndrome): disruption of posterior lobe connections with prefrontal, parietal, temporal, and limbic cortices produces deficits in executive function, visuospatial cognition, language, and affect regulation, without prominent motor signs.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Midline strip of cerebellar cortex separating the two cerebellar hemispheres

– Cortical gray matter over a white matter core, folded into dense parallel folia; C-shaped in midsagittal section

– Subdivided into 10 lobules (I–X); primary fissure divides anterior (I–V) and posterior (VI–IX) portions; posterolateral fissure separates the nodule (X)

– Function: largely spinocerebellar (posture, axial musculature); portion posterior to the primary fissure pontocerebellar; nodule and uvula vestibular

– Arterial supply: superior vermian artery (from SCA) and inferior vermian artery (from PICA)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The vermis (lit. "worm") is an approximately 1.25–2.0 cm midline strip of cerebellar cortex separating the two cerebellar hemispheres. Like the hemispheres, it comprises an overlying layer of cortical gray matter and an underlying core of white matter, folded into dense parallel folia. Along its length, it contains the same cell types and intrinsic circuitry as the hemispheres but varies significantly in its afferent and efferent connections.

In midsagittal section, the vermis appears C-shaped, with the open ends abutting the roof of the fourth ventricle; it therefore stretches from the most anterosuperior end to the posterior extent of the cerebellum at the horizontal fissure, then turns and extends to its most anteroinferior border.

sections.title: Parts
sections.text:
The vermis is subdivided by fissures into 10 lobules, designated by Roman numerals I–X in the widely used Larsell nomenclature, which largely overlaps with the classical lobule names. 

The primary fissure divides the vermis into an anterior portion (lobules I–V) and a posterior portion (lobules VI–IX). The posterolateral fissure separates lobules I–X from the nodule (lobule X), the vermal component of the flocculonodular lobe and vestibulocerebellum. 

Much of the vermis is generally designated as spinocerebellum, however the portion posterior to the primary fissure is often considered as pontocerebellum, while the nodule is vestibulocerebellum.

sections.title: Anatomical Location and Relations
sections.text:
The vermis occupies the midline of the cerebellum, running along both its superior and inferior surfaces. 

Superiorly, it lies just inferior to the straight sinus within the tentorium cerebelli. Posteriorly, it lies within the posterior cerebellar notch, where the falx cerebelli—a small midline infolding of dura mater containing the occipital sinus—partially separates the two cerebellar hemispheres. 

At its anterosuperior extent, the lingula of the vermis extends onto the superior medullary velum, the thin membrane forming the anterior roof of the fourth ventricle. On the inferior surface, the nodule of the vermis rests on the inferior medullary velum, a thin layer of ependyma; together they contribute to the roof of the fourth ventricle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The functional character of the vermis varies along its anterior-posterior extent.

Although the vermis is generally considered spinocerebellar in character—receiving proprioceptive input from the trunk and limbs via the spinocerebellar tracts and contributing to the maintenance of posture and coordination of axial musculature—the portion posterior to the primary fissure is considered pontocerebellar.

This posterior region contributes to oculomotor control, affective and emotional processing via its limbic connections, and anticipatory postural adjustments via cortical motor input.

The posterior vermis is additionally described as the limbic cerebellum, while the uvula and nodule contribute to vestibular function, integrating vestibular input to maintain balance and spatial orientation.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The vermis is supplied by two arterial territories. 

The superior surface is supplied by the superior vermian artery, a branch of the superior cerebellar artery (SCA). 

The inferior surface vermis is supplied by the inferior vermian artery, a branch of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA).

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage of the vermis follows the arterial territories, with superior vermian veins draining into the great cerebral vein and/or the straight sinus, and inferior vermian veins draining into the straight sinus or confluence of sinuses.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Truncal ataxia: Damage to the vermis results in truncal ataxia, characterised by instability of the trunk and axial musculature, leading to a wide-based, unsteady gait and difficulty maintaining posture. Unlike hemispheric lesions, limb coordination is typically preserved.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– White matter core of the cerebellum; tree-like branching pattern in sagittal and transverse section

– Formed by axons passing through the three pairs of cerebellar peduncles, which form the trunk of the tree

– Contains four pairs of cerebellar nuclei

– Lies deep to the cerebellar cortex, with folia forming the appearance of leaves at the distal branches

– Function: conveys afferent and efferent signals, including Purkinje cell and climbing fiber axons of cerebellar circuitry

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The arbor vitae (lit. "tree of life") is the white matter core of the cerebellum, visible in sagittal and transverse section as a tree-like branching pattern.

It is formed by the convergence of axons passing through the three pairs of cerebellar peduncles, which convey axons into and out of the cerebellum, forming the "trunk" of the tree. Within its substance are embedded four pairs of cerebellar nuclei. 

Axons from the cerebellar peduncles arborize into progressively finer branches, with the dense, regularly arranged folia of the cerebellar cortex forming the appearance of "leaves" at the distal ends of the finest branches.

sections.title: Anatomical Location and Relations
sections.text:
The arbor vitae lies deep to the cerebellar cortex and extends throughout the cerebellum. Embedded within it are the four pairs of cerebellar nuclei. 

Its base is continuous with the three pairs of cerebellar peduncles (superior, middle and inferior) that connect the cerebellum to the rest of the central nervous system.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The arbor vitae is the cerebellar white matter, containing myelinated axons that convey afferent and efferent signals to and from the cerebellar cortex, analogous to the corona radiata of the cerebral hemispheres. 

It carries the axons of Purkinje cells projecting from the cerebellar cortex to the cerebellar nuclei, as well as climbing fibers from the inferior olivary nucleus projecting back to the Purkinje cells, forming a fundamental component of cerebellar circuitry.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Lobule HX; hemispheric counterpart of the nodule (X); paired lateral components of the flocculonodular lobe

– Connected to the nodule by relatively long pedicles ending in tufts of cortical tissue

– Anterior to the tonsils (HIX) and biventral lobules (HVIII), separated from them by the posterolateral fissure

– Distal pedicles lie posterior to the middle cerebellar peduncle, closely related to the lateral apertures of the fourth ventricle (foramina of Luschka)

– Function: vestibulocerebellum; with the nodule, balance, gait, gaze stabilization, vestibuloocular reflex, and optokinetic nystagmus

sections.title: Anatomical Location and Relations
sections.text:
The flocculus (HX) is the hemispheric counterpart of the nodule, forming the lateral components of the flocculonodular lobe. There are two, extending laterally to the right and left, connected to the nodule by relatively long pedicles ending in tufts of cortical tissue.

The flocculi are anterior to the tonsils and biventral lobules of the posterior lobe, separated from them by the posterolateral fissure.

The distal pedicles and cortex of the flocculus lie posterior to the middle cerebellar peduncle and are closely related to the lateral apertures of the fourth ventricle (foramina of Luschka), which communicate with the cerebellopontine cisterns of the subarachnoid space.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
Lobules as a whole do not correspond to precise functional divisions; however, the flocculus forms part of the vestibulocerebellum—the phylogenetically oldest part of the cerebellum— by virtue of its extensive connections with the vestibular nuclear complex, projecting directly to the vestibular nuclei. 

Together with the nodule it plays an important role in balance, coordinating gait, and stabilising gaze during eye, head, and neck movements. It is specifically implicated in the vestibuloocular reflex and optokinetic nystagmus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
The middle cerebellar peduncle (aka brachium points) is the largest of the cerebellar peduncles. The fibers originate in the pontine nucleus, cross the midline in the basilar pons and emerge on the opposite side as large bundles along the lateral side of the pontine tegmentum into the cerebellum.

Some uncrossed pontocerebellar fibers in this peduncle are distributed chiefly to the cortex of the cerebellar hemisphere with some collateral fibers passing to the cerebellar nuclei.

Fibers of the pontine nuclei primarily relay motor signals from the primary motor cortex to the cerebellum to modulate motor outputs of the brain.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
The superior cerebellar peduncle (aka rostral cerebellar peduncle, or brachium conjunctivum) consists of a large bundle of nerve fibers emerges from the cerebellum along the lateral wall of the fourth ventricle into the tegmentum where most of its fibers decussate.

The fibers originate from the dentate and interpositus nuclei. They terminate in the contralateral red nucleus and parts of the ventrolateral, ventral intermediate and central lateral nuclei of the thalamus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
The inferior cerebellar peduncle (aka caudal cerebellar peduncle) is a thick, large bundle of nerve fibres that emerge from the posterolateral surface of the upper medulla. It extends under the lateral recesses of the rhomboid fossa and curves superiorly into the cerebellum, caudomedial to the middle cerebellar peduncle.

The fibres originate from spinal neurons and medullary relay nuclei. Each peduncle connects the spinal cord and medulla oblongata with the cerebellum and comprises the small, medial juxtarestiform body and large, lateral restiform body.

The peduncles carry many types of input and output fibers which integrate proprioceptive sensory input with motor vestibular functions such as balance and postural maintenance.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Lobule HIX; hemispheric extension of the uvula (IX) of the vermis; most anterior component of the posterior lobe in the hemisphere

– Posterior border: secondary fissure, separating them from the biventral lobule (HVIII)

– Anterior border: posterolateral fissure, separating them from the flocculonodular lobe (X/HX)

– Rests against the squamous part of the occipital bone on either side of the foramen magnum

– Function: pontocerebellum; third representation of motor and cognitive networks — language, verbal fluency, autobiographical recall, and motor planning

sections.title: Anatomical Location and Relations
sections.text:
The cerebellar tonsils (HIX) are paired ovoid lobules on the inferior surface of the cerebellum, forming the hemispheric extension of the uvula (lobule IX) of the vermis. 

They are separated posteriorly from the biventral lobule (HVIII) by the secondary fissure (postpyramidal fissure), and anteriorly from the flocculonodular lobe by the posterolateral fissure. They represent the most anterior component of the posterior lobe in the cerebellar hemisphere. 

The tonsils expand laterally from the uvula between the secondary and posterolateral fissures, partially covering the medial part of the biventral lobule superomedially, and the nodule inferomedially.

The tonsils rest against the internal surface of the squamous part of the occipital bone on either side of the foramen magnum, where they are vulnerable to herniation in the context of raised intracranial pressure.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
Lobules as a whole do not correspond to precise functional divisions; however, the cerebellar tonsils belong to the pontocerebellum and have been identified as containing a third representation of motor and cognitive networks, distinct from the primary sensorimotor representation in the anterior lobe and the secondary representation in the pyramis (lobule VIII). 

Functional imaging studies suggest contributions to cognitive functions including language processing, verbal fluency and autobiographical recall, as well as motor planning and action observation.

sections.text:
The inferior cerebellar peduncle (aka caudal cerebellar peduncle) is a thick, large bundle of nerve fibres that emerge from the posterolateral surface of the upper medulla. It extends under the lateral recesses of the rhomboid fossa and curves superiorly into the cerebellum, caudomedial to the middle cerebellar peduncle.

The fibres originate from spinal neurons and medullary relay nuclei. Each peduncle connects the spinal cord and medulla oblongata with the cerebellum and comprises the small, medial juxtarestiform body and large, lateral restiform body.

The peduncles carry many types of input and output fibers which integrate proprioceptive sensory input with motor vestibular functions such as balance and postural maintenance.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: most anterosuperior part of the cerebellum, anterior to the primary fissure, under the tentorium cerebelli

– Vermis: lingula (I), central lobule (II/III), culmen (IV/V); hemispheres: vincingulum (HI), wing of central lobule (HII/HIII), anterior quadrangular lobule (HIV/HV)

– Function: forms much of the spinocerebellum; refines motor output and maintains truncal balance, posture, and gait

– Arterial supply: superior cerebellar artery (SCA)

– Venous drainage: anterior and superior superficial cerebellar veins into the superior petrosal and transverse sinuses

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The anterior (cranial) lobe is the most anterosuperior portion of the cerebellum, lying anterior to the primary fissure. It is triangular in shape when viewed from above, with its base along the anterior margin of the cerebellum and its apex pointing posteriorly toward the midline.

The anterior lobe occupies approximately one quarter of the superior cerebellar surface in the hemispheres, but comprises most of the vermis visible on the superior surface.

In the vermis, the anterior lobe contains the lingula (lobule I), central lobule (II/III), and culmen (IV/V). In the cerebellar hemispheres, it contains the vincingulum (lobule HI), wing of the central lobule (HII/HIII), and anterior quadrangular lobule (HIV/HV).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The tentorium cerebelli lies directly superior to the anterior lobe, and the fourth ventricle lies anterior to it. The anterior lobe is separated from the posterior lobe by the primary fissure. Anteriorly, it is related to the inferior colliculi and the superior medullary velum.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The anterior lobe comprises much of the spinocerebellum, receiving proprioceptive and sensory input from the trunk, limbs, head and neck via the spinocerebellar and trigeminocerebellar tracts. 

By comparing the intended motor program with ongoing movement, it enables real-time adjustments that smooth and refine motor output. It is particularly important for the maintenance of truncal balance, posture and gait, and for the coordination of axial and proximal limb musculature. 

Output is directed via the fastigial nucleus to the brainstem and via the interposed nuclei to the cerebral cortex, modulating descending motor pathways.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The anterior lobe is primarily supplied by the superior cerebellar artery (SCA), a branch of the basilar artery. 

The SCA divides into a medial (superior vermian) branch, which supplies the anterior part of the vermis, and a lateral (hemispheric) branch, which supplies the anterior part of the cerebellar hemispheres.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The anterior lobe is drained by anterior and superior superficial cerebellar veins, which empty into the superior petrosal and transverse sinuses.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Anterior lobe syndrome: gait ataxia (with lower limb ataxia and wide-based, unsteady gait) resulting from degeneration of the anterior cerebellar lobe, classically associated with chronic alcohol use and underlying nutritional (thiamine) deficiency.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Thin membranous sheet on the midline separating the anterior horns and bodies of the lateral ventricles

– Forms as two laminae separated by the cavum septi pellucidi, which fuse after birth

– Contains neuronal cell bodies and myelinated axons

– Attaches to corpus callosum superiorly/anteriorly and fornix inferiorly/posteriorly

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The septum pellucidum is a thin membranous sheet that is located on the midline. Embryologically, it forms as two laminae. During fetal development these laminae are separated by a transient cavity called the cavum septi pellucidi. Shortly after birth these laminae fuse together. The septum pellucidum contains both neuronal cell bodies and myelinated axons.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The septum pellucidum is a thin vertically oriented membrane that sits deep within the midline of the brain. It separates the anterior horns and bodies of the lateral ventricles. Superiorly and anteriorly, the septum pellucidum attaches to the corpus callosum while inferiorly and posteriorly it attaches to the fornix.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Cavum septi pellucidi: Persistence of the embryological cavity between the two laminae, is a common incidental finding on MRI; when large, it may be associated with psychiatric conditions including schizophrenia.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Deep, nearly vertical groove separating the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe

– Runs from near the lateral sulcus to the superomedial border and onto the paracentral lobule

– Separates the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus) from the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus)

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The central sulcus is a relatively deep, nearly vertical groove on the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere that separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe. It runs almost the entire length of the hemisphere from near the lateral sulcus to the superomedial border, where it typically wraps onto the medial surface and extends into the paracentral lobule for up to 1 cm. Generally, it does not reach the lateral sulcus, being separated from it by the subcentral gyrus. 

The central sulcus separates the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus from the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S., 2021. Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: posterior to frontal lobe, superior to temporal lobe, anterior to occipital lobe

– Contains postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex), superior and inferior parietal lobules, precuneus

– Functions: somatosensory processing, spatial awareness, visuospatial processing, attention, language comprehension

– Arterial supply: anterior cerebral artery (medial parts); middle cerebral artery (lateral parts)

– Venous drainage: superior cerebral veins → superior sagittal sinus; parietal tributaries → superficial middle cerebral vein

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The parietal lobe is a large portion of the cerebral cortex located posterior to the frontal lobe, superior to the temporal lobe, and anterior to the occipital lobe. It contains the postcentral gyrus, superior parietal lobule, inferior parietal lobule, supramarginal gyrus, angular gyrus, and precuneus.

Like most of the cerebral cortex, the parietal lobe predominantly consists of six-layered isocortical gray matter overlying subcortical white matter.

Functional areas: Primary somatosensory cortex, somatosensory association cortex, parietotemporooccipital association cortex.

Brodmann areas: 3, 1, 2, 5, 7, 23, 26, 29, 30, 31, 39, 40 and 43.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The parietal lobe extends from the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere laterally and inferiorly toward the lateral sulcus. 

Anteriorly, it is bounded by the central sulcus; the most anterior gyrus of the parietal lobe, the postcentral gyrus, contains the primary somatosensory cortex. 

Posteriorly, the boundary with the occipital lobe is indistinct on the lateral surface but is commonly approximated by a line extending from the parietooccipital sulcus to the preoccipital notch. 

On the medial surface, the precuneus extends posteriorly to the parietooccipital sulcus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The parietal lobe is primarily involved in somatosensory integration. Somatosensory information relayed from the body through the thalamus is processed within the primary somatosensory cortex of the postcentral gyrus. Further processing occurs within somatosensory association cortical regions located posterior to the primary somatosensory cortex.

The parietotemporooccipital (PTO) association area functions as a heteromodal association cortex integrating visual, auditory, and somatosensory information. It contributes to higher-order functions including spatial awareness, visuospatial processing, attention, reading, writing, object recognition, and language comprehension. 

Portions of the inferior parietal lobule in the dominant hemisphere contribute to the sensory language area (Wernicke's area), which is involved in the comprehension of spoken and written language.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The medial portions of the parietal lobe are supplied by branches of the anterior cerebral artery, particularly paracentral and parietal branches arising variably from the callosomarginal and pericallosal arteries.

The lateral portions of the parietal lobe are supplied by superior cortical branches of the middle cerebral artery, including the artery of the central sulcus, anterior parietal artery, artery of the postcentral sulcus, and posterior parietal artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
The parietal lobe is drained by superficial and deep cerebral veins. 

Ascending lateral and medial parietal veins, part of the superior cerebral veins, drain predominantly into the superior sagittal sinus. Inferolateral parietal regions may also drain through parietal tributaries of the superficial middle cerebral vein.

Descending medial parietal veins, contribute to the deep venous system by draining into the inferior sagittal sinus and great cerebral vein (of Galen), which ultimately drain into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Thought processHemispatial neglect: Lesions of the non-dominant (typically right) inferior parietal lobe produce contralateral hemispatial neglect, in which the patient fails to attend to stimuli on the opposite side of space despite intact primary sensation and vision.

– Gerstmann syndrome: Lesions of the dominant (typically left) angular gyrus produce Gerstmann syndrome, characterised by the tetrad of agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation.

– Balint syndrome: Bilateral posterior parietal lesions produce Balint syndrome, comprising simultanagnosia (inability to perceive more than one object at a time), optic ataxia (impaired visually guided reaching), and ocular apraxia (difficulty directing gaze voluntarily).

– Contralateral sensory loss: Damage to the parietal lobe, particularly the postcentral gyrus and superior parietal lobule, impairs contralateral discriminative touch, proprioception, and stereognosis, reflecting disruption of somatosensory processing and integration.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: anterior parietal lobe, extends from longitudinal cerebral fissure to lateral sulcus

– Separated from precentral gyrus by central sulcus; corresponds to Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2

– Contains primary somatosensory cortex; somatotopically organized

– Arterial supply: anterior cerebral artery (paracentral branches); middle cerebral artery (artery of postcentral sulcus, artery of central sulcus)

– Venous drainage: superior cerebral veins (central vein) → superior sagittal sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The postcentral gyrus is a vertically oriented cerebral cortical gyrus located in the anterior portion of the parietal lobe, corresponding primarily to Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2, and constituting part of the primary somatosensory cortex. 

It is predominantly composed of six-layered, granular isocortical gray matter; area 3b is koniocortical, characterised by a particularly prominent inner granular layer (layer IV).

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The postcentral gyrus is the most anterior gyrus of the parietal lobe of the cerebrum. It extends from the medial surface in the longitudinal cerebral fissure up and then laterally and inferiorly down to the lateral sulcus in a vertical manner.

Anteriorly, the postcentral gyrus is separated from the precentral gyrus by the central sulcus. Posteriorly, it is separated from the superior and inferior parietal lobules by the postcentral sulcus. Medially, it continues as the posterior paracentral gyrus, which is connected with the anterior paracentral gyrus to form the paracentral lobule. 

The inferior portions of the postcentral and precentral gyri may become continuous around the inferior end of the central sulcus, forming the subcentral gyrus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The postcentral gyrus contains the primary somatosensory cortex and is the principal cortical site for processing somatosensory information relayed from the thalamus, including touch, proprioception, pain, and temperature sensation.

The primary somatosensory cortex is somatotopically organized, with the trunk and upper extremity represented on the superolateral surface, while the face and tongue are represented more inferolaterally. 

Medially, the somatosensory representation continues into the posterior paracentral gyrus, where the lower limb and pelvic floor regions are represented.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The medial portion of the postcentral gyrus, including its continuation into the posterior paracentral gyrus, is supplied by paracentral branches of the callosomarginal artery (branch of the anterior cerebral artery).  Branches of the pericallosal artery may also contribute to the blood supply of the postcentral gyrus or replace the callosomarginal supply depending on anatomical variation.

The lateral convexity of the postcentral gyrus is supplied by branches of the middle cerebral artery, including the artery of postcentral sulcus and artery of central sulcus.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
The postcentral gyrus is drained primarily by superior cerebral veins (namely the central vein (of Rolando)), which empty into the superior sagittal sinus. 

Additional lateral drainage is facilitated via parietal tributaries of the superficial middle cerebral vein.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Middle and anterior cerebral artery stroke: Infarction involving the postcentral gyrus may result in contralateral somatosensory deficits including impaired touch, proprioception, pain, and temperature sensation.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Band of myelinated axons connecting left and right temporal lobes and limbic structures

– Location: anterior wall of third ventricle; appears round in midsagittal section

– Facilitates interhemispheric transfer of visual, auditory, and olfactory information

– Contributes to memory, emotion, speech, hearing, and instinctive behaviors

sections.title: Structure/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The anterior commissure is a band of myelinated axons that cross the midline and connect the left and right hemispheres, specifically the temporal lobes and several structures of the limbic system. In a midsagittal section, it is found along the anterior wall of the third ventricle and appears round. 

In a coronal section, it appears as a bow-shaped band of fibers running across the midline just below the fornix and above the portion of the third ventricle visible at this level.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The function of the anterior commissure is not fully established. It is an important component of the limbic system and is thought to facilitate interhemispheric transfer of visual, auditory, and olfactory information, particularly between the temporal lobes. It has also been implicated in pain perception, olfaction, and chemoreception. Consequently, it is considered to contribute to functions such as memory, emotion, speech and hearing, instinctive behaviors, and sexual behavior.(Shah et al., 2019)

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Deep groove (Sylvian fissure) bounding the frontal and parietal lobes above and the temporal lobe below

– Divided into a superficial part (posterior, anterior ascending, and anterior horizontal rami) and a deep part

– Insula lies within the deep part; the middle cerebral artery runs within the sulcus

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure) is a deep groove on the lateral surface of the cerebrum, forming the boundary between the frontal and parietal lobes above and the temporal lobe below. It is often referred to as a fissure, indicating that it is deeper than most cerebral sulci. 

The lateral sulcus is divided into superficial and deep parts: 

– the superficial part, visible on the lateral surface, gives off a posterior ramus, an anterior ascending ramus, and an anterior horizontal ramus;

– the deep part lies below the external surface and is divided into sphenoidal and operculoinsular compartments.

The insula lies buried within the deep part of the lateral sulcus, and the middle cerebral artery runs within the sulcus, giving off branches to the lateral cortex.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Transsylvian surgical approach: The lateral sulcus is opened (Sylvian fissure split) to provide access to deep structures including the insula, basal nuclei, thalamus, and anterior circulation aneurysms, while preserving the overlying frontal and temporal lobes.
