sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: lateral and inferolateral cerebral surfaces, inferior to lateral sulcus

– Contains superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyri; transverse temporal gyri on superior surface

– Functions: hearing (audition), language comprehension, memory, emotional processing; sensory language area (of Wernicke) in dominant hemisphere

– Arterial supply: middle cerebral artery (temporal branches); posterior cerebral artery (temporal branches of lateral occipital artery)

– Venous drainage: inferior temporal veins → inferior anastomotic vein (of Labbé) → transverse sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The temporal lobe is an elongated cortical subdivision located on the lateral and inferolateral surfaces of the cerebrum. It contains the superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyri, as well as the transverse temporal gyri on its superior surface.

Like most of the cerebral cortex, the temporal lobe predominantly consists of six-layered isocortical gray matter overlying subcortical white matter.

Functional areas: Primary and secondary auditory cortices, auditory association cortex, parietotemporooccipital association cortex, and sensory language area (of Wernicke; part of the posterior language area).

Brodmann areas: 20, 21, 22, 37, 38, 41, and 42.

Note: Structures located along the medial aspect of the temporal lobe (e.g., hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, uncus, and entorhinal cortex) are considered part of the limbic lobe under the classification given by the Terminologia Neuroanatomica.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The temporal lobe lies inferior to the lateral sulcus and extends posteriorly toward the occipital lobe.

Superiorly, it is separated from the frontal and parietal lobes by the lateral sulcus. Posteriorly, the boundary with the parietal and occipital lobes is indistinct on the lateral surface and is conventionally approximated by a line drawn from the preoccipital (temporooccipital) notch to the parietooccipital sulcus, with the temporoparietal boundary marked by a perpendicular line from the posterior end of the lateral sulcus.

On the basal surface, the temporooccipital boundary is considered to run approximately along a line extending between the preoccipital notch laterally to the parahippocampal-lingual junction medially.

Medially, the temporal lobe borders the limbic lobe and contains the inferior (temporal) horn of the lateral ventricle. Inferiorly, it rests on the middle cranial fossa.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The temporal lobe supports a wide range of functions, including hearing (audition), language comprehension, memory, and emotional processing. 

The auditory cortices occupy the transverse temporal gyri on the superior surface of the superior temporal gyrus, within the lateral sulcus. The medial temporal region—classified under the limbic lobe in the Terminologia Neuroanatomica but functionally integrated with the temporal lobe—contributes to memory through the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, and parahippocampal cortex, and to emotional processing through the amygdaloid body. 

In the dominant hemisphere (most commonly the left), the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus contributes to the sensory language area (of Wernicke), which is centrally involved in language comprehension.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The lateral and superior surfaces of the temporal lobe are supplied by temporal branches of the middle cerebral artery. The inferior (basal) surface is supplied by temporal branches of the lateral occipital artery, a branch of the posterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
The lateral and inferior (basal) surfaces of the temporal lobe are drained by inferior temporal veins, which empty primarily into the inferior anastomotic vein (of Labbé), but also into the transverse sinus or superior petrosal sinus. 

Tributaries of the superficial middle cerebral vein, which terminates in the cavernous or sphenoparietal sinus, also drain the superolateral aspect. 

Like all cerebral veins, these vessels are highly variable in size and territory.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Sensory/receptive aphasia (Wernicke aphasia): Damage to the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus, most commonly due to middle cerebral artery infarction, produces sensory aphasia, i.e., fluent but meaningless speech with severely impaired language comprehension.

– Auditory deficits: Bilateral lesions of the superior temporal gyrus, where the primary and secondary auditory cortices are located, cause cortical deafness; unilateral lesions produce subtler deficits due to bilateral auditory representation.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: small gyrus on medial cerebral surface, posterior to subcallosal gyrus

– Lies posterior to posterior paraolfactory sulcus, anterior to lamina terminalis

– Functions: emotional processing, memory through septal and hippocampal connections

– Arterial supply: anterior communicating artery (subcallosal artery); anterior cerebral artery (cortical branches)

– Venous drainage: tributaries → basal vein (of Rosenthal) → great cerebral vein (of Galen)/straight sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The paraterminal gyrus is a small gyrus on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, forming part of the limbic lobe. 

It corresponds to Brodmann area 25 and is composed of proisocortex, transitional between isocortex and three-layered allocortex.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The paraterminal gyrus is posterior to the subcallosal gyrus, which is located on the medial cerebral cortex and is best seen on a mid-sagittal section. 

It lays posterior to the posterior paraolfactory sulcus, anterior to the lamina terminalis and third ventricle, and inferior to the rostrum of the corpus callosum. 

Confusingly, it is often used interchangeably with the subcallosal gyrus, but it is in fact posterior to and distinct from the subcallosal gyrus.

It is connected to the dentate gyrus via the stria longitudinalis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The paraterminal gyrus is often functionally treated as part of the broader subcallosal area in most of the literature, where individual contributions of the subcallosal gyrus and paraterminal gyrus are difficult to distinguish. 

As part of this region, it is likely involved in emotional processing, particularly sadness, and contributes to memory through septal and hippocampal connections.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The paraterminal gyrus is supplied by anteromedial central arteries arising from the anterior communicating artery (specifically the subcallosal artery in most individuals), with additional supply from cortical branches of the anterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The paraterminal gyrus is drained by tributaries of the basal vein (of Rosenthal), which empties into either the cavernous sinus anteriorly or the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and straight sinus posteriorly.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Alzheimer disease: The paraterminal gyrus, as part of the basal forebrain, shows early imaging changes (including white matter alterations on diffusion tensor imaging) in Alzheimer disease, and has been proposed as a potential biomarker region for early diagnosis.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: large gyrus on medial cerebral surface, arching over corpus callosum

– Subdivided into anterior, mid-, posterior cingulate cortex, and retrosplenial cortex; corresponds to Brodmann areas 23, 24, 26, 29, 30, 31, 32

– Functions: emotional processing, autonomic regulation, motor planning, pain processing, memory; key node of default mode network

– Arterial supply: anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal and callosomarginal arteries); posterior cerebral artery (posterior portions)

– Venous drainage: medial cerebral veins → inferior sagittal sinus; anterior cerebral vein → basal vein (of Rosenthal)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The cingulate gyrus is a large, prominent gyrus on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, forming the major component of the limbic lobe. 

The cingulate gyrus can be subdivided into the anterior cingulate cortex (BA 32), midcingulate cortex (BA 24), posterior cingulate cortex (BA 23, 31), and retrosplenial cortex (BA 26, 29, 30), and continues posteriorly as the isthmus of the cingulate gyrus.

Its cytoarchitecture varies considerably along its length. The posterior cingulate cortex is composed of six-layered isocortical gray matter. The anterior cingulate and midcingulate cortices are agranular or dysgranular, lacking a distinct inner granular layer (layer IV). The retrosplenial cortex is periallocortex, transitional between allocortex and isocortex, with fewer than six layers.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The cingulate gyrus arches over the corpus callosum on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, separated from it inferiorly by the callosal sulcus and bounded superiorly by the cingulate sulcus. 

It extends from the subcallosal area anteriorly, where it is continuous with the paraterminal gyrus beneath the rostrum of the corpus callosum, and continues posteriorly as the isthmus of the cingulate gyrus, which curves around the splenium of the corpus callosum and continues onto the medial temporal surface as the parahippocampal gyrus.

The cingulate gyrus lies medial to the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes, separated from them by the cingulate sulcus and its branches. It has numerous neural connections with other cerebral regions including the orbitofrontal cortex, basal ganglia, prefrontal cortex, and the insula.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The cingulate gyrus contributes to a wide range of functions reflecting its extensive connections with cortical and subcortical structures:

– The anterior cingulate cortex serves as a relay between the prefrontal cortex and the limbic system, contributing to emotional processing, autonomic regulation, motor planning, and the affective component of pain. 

– The midcingulate cortex contains the cingulate motor areas and integrates pain, negative affect, and cognitive control with motor output. 

– The posterior cingulate cortex is interconnected with visual, auditory, and somatosensory association areas, contributing to multimodal memory, and is a key node of the default mode network.
 

– The retrosplenial cortex contributes to spatial navigation, scene processing, and memory.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The cingulate gyrus is supplied predominantly by the pericallosal and callosomarginal arteries, terminal branches of the anterior cerebral artery. The posterior cingulate gyrus and isthmus also receive supply from the posterior cerebral artery, namely the dorsal branch to the corpus callosum (of the medial occipital artery).

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
The cingulate gyrus is drained predominantly via the deep venous system:

– Small medial cerebral veins empty into the inferior sagittal sinus, which runs along the free margin of the falx cerebri just above the corpus callosum. 
- The anterior cingulate cortex may additionally drain via the anterior cerebral vein into the basal vein (of Rosenthal). 

Both pathways ultimately reach the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and straight sinus. 

Additional drainage may reach the superior sagittal sinus via small ascending superior cerebral veins.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Schizophrenia: Structural and functional abnormalities of the anterior cingulate cortex, including reduced gray matter volume and altered connectivity, are associated with deficits in attention, cognitive control, and emotional regulation.

– Subfalcine herniation: Mass effect from a unilateral supratentorial lesion can displace the cingulate gyrus beneath the free margin of the falx cerebri, potentially compressing the anterior cerebral artery and causing secondary infarction.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Largest lobe of the brain; located anterior to central sulcus

– Bounded posteriorly by central sulcus, inferiorly by lateral sulcus

– Contains precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) and prefrontal cortex

– Functions: motor control, executive function, language (motor language area of Broca)

– Arterial supply: anterior cerebral artery (medial surfaces); middle cerebral artery (lateral surfaces)

– Venous drainage: superior cerebral veins → superior sagittal sinus; superficial middle cerebral vein → cavernous sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The frontal lobe is the most anterior lobe of the cerebral hemisphere, located anterior to the central sulcus and superior to the lateral sulcus. It includes the precentral gyrus, superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri, as well as the orbitofrontal cortex on the inferior surface.

The frontal lobe consists of an outer isocortex (gray matter) overlying subcortical white matter. The majority is six-layered isocortex; parts of the posterior frontal lobe (i.e., Brodmann areas 4, 6, and 44) is heterotypical, comprising agranular and dysgranular cortex.

Functional areas: Primary motor cortex, premotor cortex, supplementary motor area, frontal eye fields, prefrontal cortex, and motor language area (of Broca).

Brodmann areas: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 24, 25, 32, 33, 44, 45, 46, and 47.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The frontal lobe forms the anterior portion of the cerebral hemisphere. 

Posteriorly, it is bounded by the central sulcus, which separates it from the parietal lobe. Inferiorly, the lateral sulcus separates it from the temporal lobe. Medially, the frontal lobe is continuous with the limbic lobe along the cingulate gyrus on the medial surface of the hemisphere. Inferiorly, the orbital surface rests within the anterior cranial fossa.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The anterior portions of the frontal lobe, particularly the prefrontal cortex, are involved in higher-order cognitive functions including planning, executive function, working memory, attention, motivation, emotional regulation, personality, and social behavior.

The posterior portions of the frontal lobe are involved in motor control, with the primary motor cortex located in the precentral gyrus and the premotor cortex situated anterior to it.

The frontal lobe also contains the frontal eye fields, which are important for visual attention and eye movements, particularly voluntary saccades and smooth pursuit eye movements.

The motor language area (of Broca) in the inferior frontal gyrus is essential for language production.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The frontal lobe receives blood from two arteries: the anterior cerebral artery and the middle cerebral artery. The middle cerebral artery supplies most of the lateral cortical regions visible from the side while the anterior cerebral artery supplies most of the midline of the frontal cortex.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Motor/expressive aphasia (Broca aphasia): Infarction involving the motor language area (of Broca) in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus causes expressive aphasia, characterised by non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension.

– Contralateral hemiparesis: Infarction of the primary motor cortex (typically from middle cerebral artery occlusion affecting the lateral surface, or anterior cerebral artery occlusion affecting the medial surface) produces contralateral weakness, with lower limb predominance in ACA territory and upper limb/face predominance in MCA territory.

– Executive dysfunction: Prefrontal lesions from trauma, tumour, or neurodegeneration impair planning, impulse control, working memory, and personality, as seen in frontal lobe syndrome.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Gyrus immediately anterior to the central sulcus

– Location: between central sulcus (posterior) and precentral sulcus (anterior)

– Contains primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4)

– Functions: voluntary motor control; somatotopic organization (motor homunculus)

– Arterial supply: anterior cerebral artery (medial surface); middle cerebral artery (lateral surface)

– Venous drainage: superior cerebral veins → superior sagittal sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The precentral gyrus is a vertically oriented cerebral cortical gyrus located in the posterior portion of the frontal lobe.

Unlike most isocortex (neocortex), the precentral gyrus is composed of agranular isocortical gray matter, lacking a distinct inner granular layer (layer IV).

The precentral gyrus corresponds primarily to Brodmann area 4 and contains the primary motor cortex.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The precentral gyrus is the most posterior gyrus of the frontal lobe. It extends superiorly toward the longitudinal cerebral fissure and inferiorly toward the lateral sulcus. 

Anteriorly, it is separated from the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri by the precentral sulcus. Posteriorly, it is separated from the postcentral gyrus by the central sulcus. Medially, the precentral gyrus continues as the anterior paracentral gyrus within the paracentral lobule. 

Inferiorly, the inferior portions of the precentral and postcentral gyri may become continuous around the inferior end of the central sulcus, forming the subcentral gyrus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The precentral gyrus contains the primary motor cortex. It contains upper motor neurons whose axons descend through the internal capsule to form the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts.

The primary motor cortex is somatotopically organized, with the lower extremity represented most medially, followed by the trunk and upper extremity, while the face and tongue are represented more laterally.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The medial portion of the precentral gyrus, including its continuation into the anterior paracentral gyrus, is supplied by paracentral branches of the callosomarginal artery (branch of the anterior cerebral artery).  The pericallosal artery may also contribute to or replace the callosomarginal supply depending on anatomical variation.

The lateral convexity of the precentral gyrus is supplied by branches of the middle cerebral artery, including the artery of precentral sulcus and artery of central sulcus.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
The precentral gyrus is drained primarily by superior cerebral veins, namely the precentral vein and central vein (of Rolando), which empty into the superior sagittal sinus. 

Additional lateral drainage is facilitated via frontal tributaries of the superficial middle cerebral vein.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
–Middle cerebral artery infarction: Infarction in the middle cerebral artery territory involving the lateral precentral gyrus produces contralateral upper motor neuron weakness predominantly affecting the contralateral face and upper limb, reflecting the somatotopic organization of the primary motor cortex.

– Anterior cerebral artery infarction: Infarction in the anterior cerebral artery territory involving the medial precentral gyrus and anterior paracentral gyrus produces contralateral lower limb weakness, reflecting damage to the medial primary motor cortex.

sections.text:

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: posterior cortical subdivision, behind parietal and temporal lobes

– Contains cuneus and lingual gyrus (medial), superior/middle/inferior occipital gyri (lateral)

– Functions: visual processing; primary visual cortex (V1) around calcarine sulcus; visual association cortices (V2–V5)

– Arterial supply: posterior cerebral artery (medial occipital and lateral occipital branches); middle cerebral artery (temporooccipital branches)

– Venous drainage: superficial cerebral veins → superior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, transverse sinuses

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The occipital lobe is the posterior cortical subdivision of the cerebrum, located behind the parietal and temporal lobes. On its medial surface it contains the cuneus and lingual gyrus. The lingual gyrus continues onto the basal surface, where it lies medial to the occipital part of the fusiform gyrus. The lateral surface contains the superior, middle, and inferior lateral occipital gyri.

Like most of the cerebral cortex, the occipital lobe primarily consists of six-layered isocortical gray matter overlying subcortical white matter. The primary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus however is koniocortical; this region is distinguished by the occipital stripe (of Gennari), a macroscopically visible stripe of densely myelinated axons in cortical layer IV.

Functional areas: Primary visual cortex (V1), and visual association cortices (V2-V5).

Brodmann areas: 17, 18, and 19.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The occipital lobe is the most posterior part of the cerebral cortex.

Its anterior boundary is indistinct on the lateral surface and is conventionally approximated by a line drawn from the parietooccipital sulcus to the preoccipital (temporooccipital) notch. 

On the medial surface, the parietooccipital sulcus clearly separates the occipital lobe from the parietal lobe. 

On the basal surface, the temporooccipital boundary is considered to run approximately along a line extending between the preoccipital notch laterally and the parahippocampal-lingual junction medially. 

Inferiorly, the occipital lobe rests on the tentorium cerebelli.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The occipital lobe is the primary site of visual processing in the cerebral cortex. Visual information is relayed from the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus to the primary visual cortex (V1) surrounding the calcarine sulcus, establishing retinotopic representation of the contralateral visual field, with the upper visual field represented below the sulcus (in the lingual gyrus) and the lower visual field represented above it (in the cuneus).

Higher-order visual processing occurs in the surrounding visual association cortices, contributing to object and face recognition, color perception, motion detection, depth and distance perception, and visuospatial processing.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The medial, basal, and inferolateral surfaces of the occipital lobe are supplied by the posterior cerebral artery:

– the mediobasal surface by the occipitotemporal and calcarine branches of the medial occipital artery, 

– the laterobasal surface by the posterior temporal branches of the lateral occipital artery. 

The superolateral surface is supplied by the temporooccipital branch(es) of the middle cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Superficial cerebral veins drain blood from the occipital lobe and send it to a number of dural sinuses, including the superior sagittal sinus, the straight sinus, the transverse sinuses, and the confluence of sinuses.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Homonymous hemianopia: Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes, most commonly from posterior cerebral artery infarction affecting the primary visual cortex.

– Cortical blindness: Complete loss of vision from bilateral occipital lobe injury despite intact eyes and optic pathways.

– Visual agnosia: Impaired recognition of objects, faces, or colors from lesions of the visual association cortices.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The parieto-occipital sulcus (aka parieto-occipital fissure) is a deep, slightly vertical groove that is located on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, at the division between the parietal and occipital lobes. Its lower portion projects forward to fuse with the anterior end of the calcarine sulcus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: medial cerebral surface, encircling corpus callosum and diencephalon in ring-like configuration

– Comprises subcallosal area, paraterminal gyrus, cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and uncus

– Functions: emotional processing, memory, motivation, autonomic regulation; contains primary olfactory cortex

– Arterial supply: anterior cerebral artery (cingulate gyrus); anterior communicating artery (subcallosal/paraterminal); posterior cerebral artery (parahippocampal gyrus, uncus)

– Venous drainage: deep venous system → basal vein (of Rosenthal) → great cerebral vein (of Galen) → straight sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The limbic lobe is a cortical subdivision of the cerebrum on the medial surface, encircling the corpus callosum and the diencephalon in a curved, ring-like configuration. Under the Terminologia Neuroanatomica, the limbic lobe comprises the subcallosal area, paraterminal gyrus, cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and uncus.

Like most of the cerebral cortex, the limbic lobe consists of six-layered isocortical gray matter (isocortex) in its cingulate component, transitioning to less differentiated three- to five-layered cortex (mesocortex and allocortex) in its mesial temporal components, including the entorhinal cortex and adjacent hippocampal formation.

Functional areas: limbic association cortex and primary olfactory (piriform) cortex.

Brodmann areas: 23-36.

Note: the term "limbic lobe" is used variably in the literature. Some older and broader usages extend it to include adjacent subcortical structures (amygdala, hippocampus proper, mammillary bodies, fornix, septal nuclei); these are more accurately considered part of the limbic system rather than the limbic lobe proper.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The limbic lobe occupies the central area of the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, forming a semi-continuous ring-shaped region from the subcallosal area anteriorly, passing posteriorly over the corpus callosum as the cingulate gyrus, before continuing anteriorly onto the parahippocampal gyrus and uncus.

It is separated from the adjacent frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes by a series of sulci collectively termed the limbic sulcus, including the cingulate sulcus superiorly, the subparietal sulcus posterosuperiorly, and the collateral sulcus laterally on the basal temporal surface.

The limbic lobe surrounds the corpus callosum and the diencephalon, and lies medial to the lateral ventricle along most of its course.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The limbic lobe contributes to emotional processing, memory, motivation, and autonomic regulation, functioning as the cortical component of the broader limbic system.

It plays a central role in the medial limbic circuit (Papez circuit) and serves as the major cortical interface between the hippocampal formation and the isocortex (neocortex), supporting episodic memory and emotional learning. It is also a key node of the default mode and salience networks, and contains the primary olfactory cortex within the uncus.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The limbic lobe has a complex arterial supply reflecting its C-shape around the corpus callosum and diencephalon. 

The cingulate gyrus is supplied predominantly by the anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal and callosomarginal branches). The subcallosal and paraterminal gyri are supplied by anteromedial central arteries of the anterior communicating artery. 

The parahippocampal gyrus and uncus are supplied predominantly by the posterior cerebral artery, with additional contributions from the anterior choroidal and middle cerebral arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
The limbic lobe is drained predominantly via the deep venous system. The cingulate gyrus drains into the inferior sagittal sinus, with additional contribution to the superior sagittal sinus via small ascending bridging veins. 

The subcallosal area, paraterminal gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and uncus drain via tributaries into the basal vein (of Rosenthal) and/or the internal cerebral veins, which join to form the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and reach the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Alzheimer disease: Pathology begins in the transentorhinal region (parahippocampal gyrus), spreads through limbic structures (Braak stages III-IV "limbic stages"), and eventually reaches isocortex; the limbic lobe is genuinely central to AD's progression.

– Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy: Involves the uncus, parahippocampal gyrus, and hippocampus together.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The subcallosal area (aka subcallosal gyrus, or parolfactory area of Broca) is a small triangular region of the cerebral cortex on the medial surface of the hemisphere in front of the paraterminal gyrus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Largest white matter commissure; approximately 200 million myelinated axons connecting cerebral hemispheres

– Location: floor of longitudinal cerebral fissure, above lateral ventricles

– Five parts: rostrum, genu, trunk (body), isthmus, splenium

– Function: interhemispheric communication supporting bilateral coordination of sensory, motor, and cognitive functions

– Arterial supply: anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal artery); posterior cerebral artery (dorsal branch to splenium)

– Venous drainage: callosal and callosocingulate veins → internal cerebral veins → great cerebral vein (of Galen) → straight sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The corpus callosum is the largest white matter commissure in the brain, a massive bundle of approximately 200 million myelinated axons that connects the two cerebral hemispheres. It accounts for about 80% of interhemispheric connections, with the remainder carried by the anterior and hippocampal commissures. 

The corpus callosum is approximately 10 cm in length and consists of five parts from anterior to posterior: the rostrum, genu, trunk (body), isthmus, and splenium.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The corpus callosum is a single, large midline white-matter commissure of the telencephalon, positioned in the floor of the the longitudinal cerebral fissure and above the lateral ventricles. 

On midsagittal view, it is bordered superiorly by the cingulate gyrus (from which it is separated by the callosal sulcus) and inferiorly by the septum pellucidum. 

Fibers from the genu form the forceps minor, connecting the frontal lobes; fibers from the splenium form the forceps major, connecting the occipital lobes; and fibers from the body radiate laterally as the corona radiata to reach the rest of the cerebral cortex.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The corpus callosum serves as the primary axonal bridge between the two cerebral hemispheres, and therefore constitutes the primary route for interhemispheric communication. This enables the integration and transfer of sensory, motor, and cognitive information between the left and right cerebral hemispheres, and supports bilateral coordination by connecting both homologous regions (corresponding areas of the two hemispheres) and heterologous regions (non-corresponding areas).

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The pericallosal artery, a branch of the anterior cerebral artery, is the primary source of blood for the corpus callosum. A portion of the splenium is supplied by the dorsal branch to the corpus callosum (of the medial occipital artery), a branch of the posterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The corpus callosum is drained by small intrinsic tributaries (callosal and callosocingulate veins) of the internal cerebral veins, then via the great cerebral vein (of Galen) into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Multiple sclerosis: The corpus callosum is commonly affected in MS, with demyelination of its axons producing characteristic periventricular lesions visible on MRI ("Dawson's fingers").

– Agenesis/dysgenesis of the corpus callosum: Congenital absence, partial development, or malformed development of the corpus callosum, producing difficulties with tasks requiring interhemispheric integration of information.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Thin membrane of gray matter forming the anterior wall of the third ventricle

– Spans from the rostrum of the corpus callosum to the optic chiasm

– Contains the vascular organ (circumventricular organ with fenestrated capillaries lacking a blood-brain barrier)

– Function: structural boundary; vascular organ → senses blood osmolality and contributes to regulation of thirst, body temperature, and fever responses

– Arterial supply: perforating branches of anterior cerebral and communicating arteries

– Venous drainage: tributaries of anterior cerebral vein into the basal vein (of Rosenthal)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The lamina terminalis is a thin membrane of gray matter forming the anterior wall of the third ventricle. 

It represents the rostral end of the neural tube and spans from the rostrum of the corpus callosum superiorly to the optic chiasm inferiorly. Embedded within it is the vascular organ (organum vasculosum) of the lamina terminalis, a circumventricular organ characterized by fenestrated capillaries that lack a blood-brain barrier.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The lamina terminalis lies anterior to the third ventricle, with the anterior commissure embedded within its substance. Laterally, it is continuous with the columns of the fornix. 

Anteriorly, it is related to the anterior cerebral arteries and the anterior communicating artery.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The lamina terminalis itself serves primarily as a structural boundary of the third ventricle. 

Its functional significance derives largely from the vascular organ, which, lacking a blood-brain barrier, directly senses blood osmolality and circulating cytokines. The vascular organ plays a role in regulating thirst and water intake, body temperature, and fever responses via its connections with the hypothalamus.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The lamina terminalis is supplied by perforating branches of the anterior cerebral arteries and the anterior communicating artery, arising from the cerebral arterial circle (of Willis).

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage of the lamina terminalis occurs via small tributaries of the anterior cerebral vein, which drains into the basal vein (of Rosenthal).

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Vascular organ lesions: Damage to the vascular organ of the lamina terminalis disrupts osmosensing and thirst regulation, contributing to disorders of water homeostasis including diabetes insipidus and hyperosmolar states.

– Lamina terminalis corridor: The lamina terminalis is an important neurosurgical access route to the third ventricle and hypothalamus, used in the surgical management of third ventricular tumors and obstructive hydrocephalus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The indium grime (aka supracallosal gyrus) is a band of grey matter that runs along the dorsal surface of the corpus callosum. It is continuous with the stria terminalis and septal nucleus rostrally, and the dentate gyrus caudally.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– X-shaped crossing of optic nerve fibers at the base of the diencephalon

– Nasal retinal fibers decussate; temporal retinal fibers remain ipsilateral

– Lies anterior to the tuber cinereum and pituitary stalk, superior to the pituitary gland, and inferior to the floor of the third ventricle

– Function: directs visual information from each visual hemifield to the contralateral cerebral hemisphere

– Arterial supply: superior hypophyseal arteries; venous drainage: cavernous sinus

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Bilateral white matter tract conveying retinal ganglion cell axons from the optic chiasm to central targets

– Carries information representing the contralateral visual hemifield

– Course: optic chiasm → around cerebral peduncle → lateral border of hypothalamus → lateral geniculate nucleus

– Function: visual relay to primary visual cortex via optic radiation; projections to superior colliculus, pretectal nuclei, and suprachiasmatic nucleus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The optic chiasm is an X-shaped crossing of the optic nerve fibers situated at the base of the diencephalon, in the floor of the third ventricle. 

Nasal retinal fibers from each eye decussate at the chiasm, while temporal retinal fibers remain ipsilateral, ensuring that visual information from each visual hemifield is directed to the contralateral cerebral hemisphere.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The optic chiasm lies anterior to the tuber cinereum and pituitary stalk, superior to the pituitary gland within the suprasellar cistern, and inferior to the floor of the third ventricle. 

The optic nerves enter anterolaterally and the optic tracts exit posterolaterally. Laterally lie the internal carotid arteries; the anterior communicating artery passes anterosuperiorly.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The optic chiasm transmits visual information from the retina toward the thalamus. 

By allowing nasal retinal fibers to cross while temporal retinal fibers remain ipsilateral, it ensures that visual information from the right visual field is conveyed to the left cerebral hemisphere and from the left visual field to the right hemisphere. 

These fibers continue in the optic tracts to synapse primarily in the lateral geniculate nucleus before being relayed to the visual cortex.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The optic chiasm is supplied by the superior hypophyseal arteries from the internal carotid artery (ICA), with contributions from branches of the anterior cerebral, anterior communicating, and posterior communicating arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage of the optic chiasm is facilitated via small veins passing into the cavernous sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Bitemporal hemianopia: Compression of the optic chiasm from below (most commonly by a pituitary adenoma or craniopharyngioma) damages the crossing nasal retinal fibers, causing loss of the temporal visual fields bilaterally. This pattern of visual field loss is pathognomonic of chiasmal compression.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Located between the inferior surface of the cerebral cortex and the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

Branches: Olfactory tract.

Supply: Conveys the sense of smell.

sections.title: Location
sections.text: The olfactory bulb sits just intracranially to the cribriform plate. It receives input from olfactory nerves located in the nasal epithelium.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: At its posterior margin, the olfactory bulb becomes the olfactory tract.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The olfactory bulb is sensory, organizing and conveying the sense of smell. Fibers from the olfactory bulb travel posteriorly in the olfactory tract to reach the olfactory cortex in the temporal lobe of the brain.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Anosmia

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Bilateral white matter tract conveying retinal ganglion cell axons from the optic chiasm to central targets

– Carries information representing the contralateral visual hemifield

– Course: optic chiasm → around cerebral peduncle → lateral border of hypothalamus → lateral geniculate nucleus

– Function: visual relay to primary visual cortex via optic radiation; projections to superior colliculus, pretectal nuclei, and suprachiasmatic nucleus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The optic tract is a bilateral white matter tract conveying retinal ganglion cell axons from the posterior margin of the optic chiasm to their central targets. 

Each tract contains fibers from the temporal hemiretina of the ipsilateral eye and the nasal hemiretina of the contralateral eye, such that each tract carries information representing the contralateral visual hemifield.

Fibers within the tract are organized by functional subtype rather than strict retinotopy, with magnocellular axons superficially and parvocellular axons more deeply situated.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
From the optic chiasm, each optic tract curves posterolaterally around the cerebral peduncle, passing along the lateral border of the hypothalamus before reaching the lateral geniculate nucleus. 

The anterior choroidal artery crosses the optic tract twice along this course on its way to supply the crus cerebri and lateral geniculate body.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The majority of optic tract fibers (approximately 90%) terminate in the lateral geniculate nucleus, which relays visual information to the primary visual cortex via the optic radiation. 

The remaining fibers leave the tract at the superior brachium and project to the superior colliculus, pretectal nuclei, and suprachiasmatic nucleus. Superior colliculus projections contribute to reflexive eye movements; pretectal projections mediate the pupillary light reflex via the accessory nuclei of oculomotor nerve (Edinger–Westphal nuclei); and projections to the suprachiasmatic nucleus from intrinsically photosensitive ganglion cells entrain circadian rhythms.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Contralateral homonymous hemianopia: A lesion of the optic tract interrupts all fibers carrying information from the contralateral visual hemifield, producing loss of vision in that hemifield in both eyes; unlike more posterior lesions, optic tract lesions typically produce incongruent field defects owing to the incomplete spatial segregation of axons within the tract.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Sheet of gray matter on the ventral surface of the brain

– Location: lateral to optic chiasm, medial to uncus, posterior to olfactory striae

– Conduit for perforating arteries supplying basal nuclei and internal capsule

– Arterial supply: middle cerebral artery (anterolateral central arteries); anterior cerebral artery; anterior choroidal artery

– Venous drainage: basal vein → great cerebral vein (of Galen) → straight sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The anterior perforated substance is a sheet of gray matter containing neuronal cell bodies. It is perforated by several small arteries and veins, giving rise to the name.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anterior perforated substance is located on the ventral surface of the brain. It sits lateral to the optic chiasm, medial to the uncus of the temporal lobe, and posterior to the medial and lateral olfactory stria. The intermediate olfactory stria penetrates the anterior perforated substance.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The anterior perforated substance serves as a conduit for numerous small perforating arteries (primarily branches of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries) that supply deep structures of the brain, including the basal nuclei and internal capsule. It also forms part of the basal forebrain and is associated with nearby olfactory and limbic regions. A specific neuronal processing role has not been defined.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The anterior perforated substance receives blood from three different arteries. Lateral lenticulostriate arteries from the middle cerebral artery are the most well known. However, the anterior cerebral and anterior choroidal arteries also contribute branches to the anterior perforated substance.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The basal vein drains the anterior perforated substance into the great cerebral vein (of Galen, which drains into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The diagonal band of Broca is a tract of nerve fibres located on the posterior border of the anterior perforated substance. It passes between the parolfactory area and the amygdala.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The arcuate nucleus of thalamus is the small area of the ventral posteromedial nucleus that projects to the lower part of the postcentral gyrus of the cerebral cortex. It is in this structure that the fibers of the secondary trigeminal tract and the gustatory lemniscus terminate.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Largest nuclear complex in the human thalamus, occupying the posterior pole

– Comprise anterior, medial, lateral, and inferior pulvinar nuclei

– Continuous anteriorly with the lateral posterior nucleus, forming the pulvinar-LP complex

– Connected with association cortices, posterior cingulate gyrus, insular cortex, and somatosensory areas

– Function: visuospatial processing, attention, and higher-order cognitive functions

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The pulvinar nuclei form the largest nuclear complex in the human thalamus, occupying the posterior pole of the thalamus. They comprise four subdivisions: the anterior, medial, lateral, and inferior pulvinar nuclei, each with distinct cortical targets.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The pulvinar nuclei lie at the posterior end of the thalamus, continuous anteriorly with the lateral posterior nucleus, together forming the pulvinar-LP complex with shared connectivity. 

They receive subcortical input from the superior colliculus and visual system, and are interconnected with the parietal, occipital, temporal, and prefrontal association cortices, the posterior cingulate gyrus, the insular cortex, and somatosensory areas. 

The inferior pulvinar nucleus additionally receives direct retinal input and contains a complete retinotopic representation.

sections.title: Function
Arterial Supply
sections.text: The posterior cerebral artery supplies blood to the pulvinar nuclei, primarily via the thalamoperforating or thalamogeniculate branches.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The internal cerebral vein drains the pulvinar nuclei into the great cerebral vein (of Galen), and then on into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Lies at the anterior pole of the ventral nuclear group of the thalamus

– Comprises a principal part and a magnocellular part

– Receives input from the globus pallidus and reticular part of the substantia nigra

– Function: motor relay nucleus involved in planning and initiation of voluntary movements

– Arterial supply: thalamoperforating branches and tuberothalamic artery; venous drainage: internal cerebral veins

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The ventral anterior nucleus (VA) lies at the anterior pole of the ventral nuclear group of the thalamus. It comprises two subdivisions: a principal part (VApc) and a magnocellular part (VAmc).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The ventral anterior nucleus lies in the anterior thalamus, lateral to the internal medullary lamina and anterior to the ventral lateral nucleus. 

The principal part (VApc) receives input from the medial/internal segment of the globus pallidus, and the magnocellular part (VAmc) from the reticular part of the substantia nigra. 

Corticothalamic afferents arrive from the premotor cortex and frontal eye fields, with efferents projecting to widespread frontal lobe regions.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The ventral anterior nucleus acts together with the ventral lateral nucleus as a motor relay nucleus, transmitting and modulating output from the basal nuclei to the premotor cortex. 

It is involved in the planning and initiation of voluntary movements.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The ventral anterior nucleus is supplied primarily by the thalamoperforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery, with the anterior portion also receiving supply from the tuberothalamic artery arising from the posterior communicating artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The ventral anterior nucleus is drained by the internal cerebral veins to the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Basal nuclei disorders: As a relay for basal nuclei output, the ventral anterior nucleus is implicated in the motor deficits of Parkinson disease and other basal nuclei disorders. Thalamotomy targeting VA has historically been used to treat tremor and rigidity.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Vanderah, T.W., Gould, D.J., 2025. Nolte’s The Human Brain: An Introduction to its Functional Anatomy, 9th ed. Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Nucleus of the posterior nuclear group of the thalamus

– Anterior pole extends into the bifurcation of the internal medullary lamina

– Receives input from the pretectum, superior colliculus, and hippocampus

– Projects to cingulate, retrosplenial, parahippocampal, presubicular, and parietal cortical areas

– Function: suggested role in memory, limbic function, and visuospatial processing

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The laterodorsal nucleus (LD) is a nucleus of the posterior nuclear group of the thalamus. Its anterior pole extends into the bifurcation of the internal medullary lamina, rendering it continuous with the anterior nuclear group; this is the basis for its classification with the anterior nuclei in the Terminologia Neuroanatomica (TNA).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The laterodorsal nucleus lies in the posterior/dorsal thalamus, with its anterior pole within the bifurcation of the internal medullary lamina. It receives subcortical input from the pretectum, superior colliculus, and hippocampus, and projects to the cingulate, retrosplenial, and parahippocampal cortices, the presubiculum, and the parietal cortex.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The laterodorsal nucleus shares connectivity with the anterior nuclei, projecting to the cingulate gyrus and receiving hippocampal input, suggesting a role in memory and limbic function. Its connections with the pretectum and superior colliculus also suggest involvement in visuospatial processing, though its precise functional significance remains unclear.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The posterior cerebral artery supplies blood to the laterodorsal nucleus, primarily via the thalamoperforating or thalamogeniculate branches.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The laterodorsal nucleus is drained by the internal cerebral veins to the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and the straight sinus.

sections.title: References
sections.text:

Vanderah, T.W., Gould, D.J., 2025. Nolte’s The Human Brain: An Introduction to its Functional Anatomy, 9th ed. Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
The ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus is involved in the integration and modulation of sensory information on its way from the body to the somatosensory cortex and ascending reticular activating system.

It receives its input from the spinothalamic, trigeminothalamic, and medial and spinal lemniscus tracts that convey sensory information from the body to the brain.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Nucleus of the posterior nuclear group of the thalamus

– Lies between the laterodorsal nucleus anteriorly and the pulvinar nuclei posteriorly

– Continuous with the pulvinar nuclei; together referred to as the pulvinar-LP complex

– Interconnected with parietal, occipital, and temporal association cortices

– Function: involved in visuospatial processing, attention, and higher-order cognitive functions

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The lateral posterior nucleus (LP) is a nucleus of the posterior (dorsal) nuclear group of the thalamus, lying between the laterodorsal nucleus anteriorly and the pulvinar nuclei posteriorly, with which it is continuous. Together they are sometimes referred to as the pulvinar-LP complex, sharing similar connectivity.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lateral posterior nucleus lies on the dorsolateral surface of the thalamus. It receives subcortical input from the superior colliculus and is interconnected with the parietal, occipital, and temporal association cortices, the cingulate gyrus, and the medial parahippocampal cortex.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The lateral posterior nucleus functions as an association nucleus, sharing similar roles with the pulvinar nuclei. Through its connections with the parietal, occipital, and temporal association cortices and via input from the superior colliculus, it is involved in visuospatial processing, attention, and higher-order cognitive functions.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The posterior cerebral artery supplies blood to the lateral posterior nucleus, primarily via the thalamoperforating or thalamogeniculate branches.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The internal cerebral vein drains the lateral posterior nucleus into the great cerebral vein, and then into the straight sinus.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S., Tubbs, R.S., 2026. Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 43rd ed. Elsevier.

Crossman, A.R., 2025. Neuroanatomy: An Illustrated Colour Text, 7th ed. Elsevier.

Vanderah, T.W., Gould, D.J., 2025. Nolte’s The Human Brain: An Introduction to its Functional Anatomy, 9th ed. Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Enclosed within the anterior bifurcation of the internal medullary lamina

– Comprise the anterodorsal, anteromedial, and anteroventral nuclei

– Receive input from the hippocampus via the fornix and mammillary bodies

– Function: principal thalamic relay for the limbic system; involved in declarative memory, alertness, and attention

– Arterial supply: thalamoperforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery; venous drainage: internal cerebral vein

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The anterior nuclei of the thalamus are enclosed within the anterior bifurcation of the internal medullary lamina and comprise three nuclei: the anterodorsal (AD), anteromedial (AM), and anteroventral (AV) nuclei.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The anterior nuclei of the thalamus receive input from the limbic system, specifically the hippocampus via the fornix, and the mammillary bodies. Efferents from the anterior nuclei go to the cingulate gyrus as well as frontal association cortical regions. The anterior nuclei sit lateral to the lateral walls of the third ventricle, anterior to the interthalamic adhesion. 

Although separated from the anterior nuclei by the internal medullary lamina, the lateral dorsal nucleus is often functionally associated with the anterior nuclei.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The anterior nuclei form part of the medial limbic circuit (of Papez) and serve as the principal thalamic relay for the limbic system. They receive input from the mammillary bodies via the mammillothalamic tract (itself receiving hippocampal input via the fornix) and project to the cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and entorhinal cortex. 

The hippocampus also projects directly to the anterior nuclei via the postcommissural fornix. This circuitry underlies the acquisition and consolidation of declarative memory, and the anterior nuclei are also implicated in the regulation of alertness and attention.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The anterior thalamic nuclei are primarily supplied by the thalamoperforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The internal cerebral vein drains blood from the anterior thalamus to the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and then to the straight sinus.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S., Tubbs, R.S., 2026. Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 43rd ed. Elsevier.

Crossman, A.R., 2025. Neuroanatomy: An Illustrated Colour Text, 7th ed. Elsevier.

Vanderah, T.W., Gould, D.J., 2025. Nolte’s The Human Brain: An Introduction to its Functional Anatomy, 9th ed. Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Large nucleus on the medial surface of the thalamus, medial to the internal medullary lamina

– Comprises magnocellular, parvocellular, and paralaminar divisions

– Reciprocal connections with the prefrontal and premotor cortex

– Function: principal thalamic relay to the prefrontal cortex; involved in working memory, attention, decision-making, mood, and emotion

– Arterial supply: posterior cerebral artery branches; venous drainage: internal cerebral vein

sections.title: Structure
Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The mediodorsal nucleus lies medial to the internal medullary lamina, at the level of the interthalamic adhesion. 

Medially it borders the third ventricle; laterally the internal medullary lamina separates it from the lateral nuclear group. 

It has extensive reciprocal connections with the prefrontal and premotor cortex, and receives input from the olfactory system, limbic system, amygdala, and insular cortex.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The mediodorsal nucleus is the principal thalamic relay to the prefrontal cortex. The magnocellular division relays olfactory and limbic input to the orbitofrontal and medial prefrontal cortex; the parvocellular division is reciprocally connected with the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, and supplementary motor area. It plays a key role in higher cognitive functions including working memory, attention, decision-making, and modulation of mood and emotion.

Bilateral damage produces deficits comparable to those seen after prefrontal lesions, including transient amnesia and changes in affect.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The posterior cerebral artery supplies blood to the mediodorsal nucleus, primarily via the thalamoperforating or thalamogeniculate branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA).

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The internal cerebral vein drains the mediodorsal nucleus into the great cerebral vein (of Galen), and then on into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Thalamic amnesia: Bilateral damage to the mediodorsal nucleus (as occurs in Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency) causing anterograde amnesia and cognitive dysfunction, reflecting disruption of prefrontal-thalamic circuitry.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Standring, S., Tubbs, R.S., 2026. Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 43rd ed. Elsevier.

Crossman, A.R., 2025. Neuroanatomy: An Illustrated Colour Text, 7th ed. Elsevier.

Vanderah, T.W., Gould, D.J., 2025. Nolte’s The Human Brain: An Introduction to its Functional Anatomy, 9th ed. Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Thin, Y-shaped sheet of myelinated axons within the thalamus

– Divides the thalamus into medial, lateral, and anterior regions

– Intralaminar nuclei are embedded within the lamina itself

– Function: carries afferent and efferent fibers passing to and from thalamic nuclei

– Arterial supply: posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries; venous drainage: internal cerebral veins

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The internal medullary lamina is a thin, Y-shaped sheet of myelinated axons that divides the thalamus into three main regions: the medial thalamus medial to the lamina, the lateral thalamus lateral to it, and the anterior thalamus enclosed within the anterior bifurcation. The intralaminar nuclei are embedded within the lamina itself.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
Function
sections.text:
The internal medullary lamina carries afferent and efferent fibers passing to and from the thalamic nuclei. 

The intralaminar nuclei embedded within it (e.g., centromedian and parafascicular nuclei) project diffusely to the cerebral cortex and striatum, contributing to arousal, attention, and consciousness.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The thalamus is supplied by branches of the posterior cerebral artery and the posterior communicating artery. The thalamoperforating artery supplies the anterior third of the thalamus and the thalamogeniculate artery supplies the posterior two thirds. 

Additional contributions come from the posterior and anterior choroidal arteries and minor branches of the posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The thalamus is drained by the internal cerebral veins, which pass into the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and then into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Connects the median eminence of the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland

– Comprises the pars tuberalis of the adenohypophysis surrounding the infundibulum of the neurohypophysis

– Transmits the hypophysial portal vessels, carrying hypothalamic releasing hormones to the adenohypophysis

– Transmits axons of the hypothalamoneurohypophysial tract, conveying antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) and oxytocin to the neurohypophysis

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The pituitary stalk is a funnel-shaped structure connecting the median eminence of the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland. It comprises the pars tuberalis of the adenohypophysis, which surrounds the infundibulum of the neurohypophysis—the latter being a direct downward extension of the hypothalamus.

It transmits the hypophysial portal vessels, carrying hypothalamic releasing hormones to the adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary gland), and axons of the hypothalamoneurohypophysial tract, conveying antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) and oxytocin to the neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary gland).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Olfactory tract.

Course: Run on either side of the anterior perforated substance and enter the cerebral cortex proper.

Branches: None.

Supply: Convey olfactory information to the cerebral cortex, particularly the septal nuclei and primary olfactory cortex.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The olfactory striae originate under the inferior surface of the cerebral cortex at the olfactory trigone. This area just anterior to the anterior perforated substance is the point at which the olfactory tract bifurcates into medial and lateral olfactory striae. However, the existence of the medial olfactory stria is disputed within the literature (Sakamoto et al, 1999).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The medial olfactory stria runs medially, anterior to the anterior perforated substance. It penetrates the cortex and sends axons to the septal nuclei and through the anterior commissure to the contralateral olfactory cortex.

The lateral olfactory stria runs laterally, anterior to the anterior perforated substance. It penetrates the uncus where it sends axons to the primary olfactory cortex.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The medial olfactory stria connects to the limbic system via the septal nuclei and the contralateral olfactory cortex via the anterior commissure.

The lateral olfactory stria contains the fibers classically associated with smell and its axons run to the primary olfactory cortex in the uncus.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Sakamoto, N., Pearson, J., Shinoda, K., Alheid, G. F., Olmos, J. S. d. & Heimer, L. (1999) Chapter I - The human basal forebrain. Part I. An overview, in Bloom, F. E., Björklund, A. & Hökfelt, T. (eds), Handbook of Chemical NeuroanatomyElsevier, 1-55.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Ovoid elevation on the posteroinferior surface of the thalamus; part of the metathalamus

– Lies lateral to the medial geniculate body and inferior to the pulvinar nuclei

– Site of termination of the optic tract; projects third-order visual fibers to the primary visual cortex via the optic radiation

– Function: relays visual information from retinal ganglion cells to the primary visual cortex, preserving a precise retinotopic map

– Arterial supply: thalamogeniculate branch of the posterior cerebral artery, with contributions from the anterior choroidal artery

– Venous drainage: superior and/or inferior thalamostriate veins

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The lateral geniculate body is an ovoid elevation on the posteroinferior surface of the thalamus, forming part of the metathalamus alongside the medial geniculate body. It contains the lateral geniculate nucleus, through which ascending visual fibers are relayed to the cerebral cortex.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The lateral geniculate body lies on the posterior inferior surface of the thalamus, lateral to the medial geniculate body and inferior to the pulvinar nuclei. 

The lateral geniculate nucleus, which it contains, is the site of termination of the optic tract, which consists of second-order neurons of the central visual pathway. The lateral geniculate nucleus projects third-order visual fibers to the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The lateral geniculate nucleus/body relays visual information from the retinal ganglion cells of both eyes to the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe via the optic radiation. It maintains a precise retinotopic map, preserving the spatial organization of the visual field throughout the relay.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The lateral geniculate nucleus receives blood primarily from the thalamogeniculate branch of the posterior cerebral artery. Additional contributions from branches of the anterior choroidal artery are also present.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage of the lateral geniculate body is facilitated via the superior thalamostriate vein and/or inferior thalamostriate veins, as per the thalamus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Homonymous hemianopia: Lesions of the lateral geniculate body cause a contralateral homonymous visual field defect, with the pattern varying according to the extent and location of the lesion.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The septal nuclei are a group of nuclei located anterior to the anterior commissure and corpus callosum. They are divided into a dorsal septal nucleus, lateral septal nucleus, medial septal nucleus and a triangular septal nucleus. The septal nuclei have reciprocal connections with numerous subcortical structures. They primarily project into the hippocampus and hypothalamus and receive fibres from the medial olfactory stria. They are often considered part of the limbic system due to their extensive connections with these structures, however they actually lie close to the cerebrum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Small, cone-shaped midline endocrine gland; forms part of the epithalamus

– Circumventricular organ lacking a blood-brain barrier

– Lies rostrodorsal to the superior colliculi and posterior to the stria medullaris thalami, within the quadrigeminal cistern

– Function: synthesizes melatonin (regulating sleep-wake patterns across circadian and seasonal cycles)

– Arterial supply: posterior choroidal branches of posterior cerebral artery

– Venous drainage: tributaries of great cerebral vein (of Galen) into the straight sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The pineal gland is a small, cone-shaped midline endocrine gland, approximately 8 mm in diameter, and forms part of the epithalamus.

It is classified as a circumventricular organ, lacking a blood-brain barrier, which permits direct exchange between its secretory cells and the bloodstream.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The pineal gland lies rostrodorsal to the superior colliculi and posterior to the stria medullaris thalami, situated within the quadrigeminal cistern. 

The great cerebral vein (of Galen) lies immediately superior to it. Its stalk contains the pineal recess, a posterior extension of the third ventricle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The pineal gland synthesizes melatonin, a serotonin-derived hormone that regulates sleep-wake patterns across both circadian and seasonal cycles.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The pineal gland is supplied by the posterior choroidal branches of the posterior cerebral artery. As a circumventricular organ, it lacks a blood-brain barrier and is in direct contact with the fenestrated capillaries of its vascular supply.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The pineal gland is drained by small tributaries of the great cerebral vein (of Galen), which empties into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Pineal tumors (pineocytoma, pineoblastoma, germinoma): Tumors of the pineal region may compress the dorsal midbrain causing Parinaud syndrome, or obstruct the aqueduct of midbrain causing obstructive hydrocephalus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Olfactory bulb.

Course: Runs posteriorly from the olfactory bulb to the anterior perforated substance on the inferior surface of the cerebral cortex.

Branches: Olfactory striae.

Supply: Conveys the sense of smell.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The olfactory tract originates at the posterior margin of the olfactory bulbs.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The olfactory tract runs parallel to and on either side of the midline on the inferior surface of the brain. The tract runs posteriorly to the anterior perforated substance where it bifurcates and penetrates the brain as the olfactory striae.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The olfactory tract bifurcates to give rise to the olfactory striae. Typically, there is a medial stria and a lateral stria.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The olfactory tract conveys sensory information. It supplies the sense of olfaction to the brain, specifically the primary olfactory cortex which is located in the uncus, and entorhinal cortex of the temporal lobe. Additionally, axons that form the olfactory tract will target the amygdala and other parts of the limbic system.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Anosmia

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The pituitary gland (aka hypophysis, or pituitary body) gland is connected to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum and lies in the sella turcica. The pituitary has two main parts; the anterior pituitary (aka adenohypophysis) and the posterior pituitary (aka neurohypophysis). It is under the control of the hypothalamus and forms a link between the brain and endocrine system. The adenohypophysis receives signals from parvocellular neurons and the neurohypophysis receives signals from magnocellular neurons to secrete nine hormones.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Most ventral subdivision of the diencephalon, inferior/ventral to the thalamus

– Forms the floor and lateral wall of the third ventricle; ventral surface marked by the mammillary bodies and tuber cinereum

– Composed of numerous nuclei across anterior (chiasmatic), intermediate (tuberal), and posterior (mammillary) areas

– Function: regulates homeostasis, autonomic activity, endocrine secretion via the pituitary gland, and behavioral responses

– Arterial supply: perforating arteries from the cerebral arterial circle (of Willis), with contributions from the anterior choroidal and superior hypophyseal arteries

– Venous drainage: cavernous sinus, basal vein (of Rosenthal), and hypothalamohypophyseal portal system to the anterior pituitary

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The hypothalamus is a major neuroendocrine center and the principal regulator of the autonomic nervous system, with extensive connections to the limbic system and pituitary gland. It is composed of numerous nuclei (i.e., collections of neuronal cell bodies) organized across anterior (chiasmatic), intermediate (tuberal) and posterior (mammillary) hypothalamic areas, which serve distinct functions including endocrine secretion, autonomic regulation, and behavioral responses.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The hypothalamus is the most ventral part of the diencephalon, lying beneath the thalamus. Its medial extent forms the floor and lateral wall of the third ventricle. On the base of the brain, the ventral surface of the hypothalamus is marked by the mammillary bodies and the tuber cinereum, from the apex of which extends the pituitary stalk.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Through its connections with the autonomic nervous system and limbic system, its release of hormones and control over the pituitary gland, the hypothalamus plays a key role in homeostasis, influencing hunger, thirst and body temperature as well as reproductive function, sleep and emotional responses.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The hypothalamus is supplied by several perforating arteries arising from the cerebral arterial circle (of Willis). The anterior hypothalamus receives contributions from the anteromedial central arteries, arising from the A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery. The posterior hypothalamus is supplied by the posterolateral central arteries arising from the posterior cerebral artery (PCA), including the artery of tuber cinereum, tuberothalamic (premammillary) artery, as well as the hypothalamic and mammillary branches of PCA. 

The anterior choroidal artery also contributes branches to the tuber cinereum and hypothalamic nuclei, and the superior hypophyseal artery, arising from the internal carotid artery, supplies the infundibulum and median eminence.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
The hypothalamus drains via small veins into the cavernous sinus and the basal vein (of Rosenthal). 

A functionally important component of hypothalamic venous drainage is the hypothalamohypophyseal portal system, in which venous blood from the hypothalamic median eminence flows through portal vessels in the infundibulum to the anterior pituitary, carrying hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones directly to their target cells in the adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary gland).

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Diabetes insipidus: Deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), most commonly from damage to the posterior hypothalamus or infundibulum, causing polyuria and polydipsia.

– Narcolepsy: Loss of orexin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, causing excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, and disrupted sleep-wake regulation.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Midline white matter tract carrying fibers between the hippocampal formations and the diencephalon and forebrain

– Formed by convergence of the crura; divides into the columns of the fornix at the interventricular foramen (of Monro)

– Function: central conduit of the medial limbic circuit (of Papez) underlying declarative memory

– Arterial supply: posterior choroidal arteries

– Venous drainage: internal cerebral vein to the great cerebral vein and straight sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The body of the fornix is a midline white matter tract, carrying efferent and afferent fibers between the hippocampal formations and the diencephalon and forebrain.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The body of the fornix forms where the two crura converge anterior and superior to the hippocampal commissure. 

It runs anteriorly adherent to the inferior surface of the septum pellucidum, forming the inferomedial boundary of the body of the lateral ventricle, until it reaches the interventricular foramen (of Monro), where it divides into the columns of the fornix.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The body of the fornix relays hippocampal efferent fibers (principally toward the mammillary bodies, septal nuclei, and anterior thalamic nuclei), and conveys afferent fibers projecting back to the hippocampus, forming a central conduit of the medial limbic circuit (of Papez) underlying declarative memory.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The body of the fornix is mainly supplied via the posterior choroidal arteries from the posterior cerebral arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The internal cerebral vein drains the body of the fornix to the great cerebral vein and then on to the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Amnesia: Lesions of the body of the fornix (e.g., from trauma, tumor, or surgical injury) disrupt hippocampal output and can cause significant anterograde amnesia.

– Seizure propagation: The body of the fornix may serve as a pathway for the bilateral spread of epileptic activity between the temporal lobes.
