Mark, L.P., Daniels, D.L., Naidich, T.P., 1993. The fornix. AJNR Am. J. Neuroradiol. 14 (6), 1355–1358.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Transverse sheet of commissural fibers connecting the two hippocampal formations

– Lies inferior to the splenium, where the crura converge; continuous with the body of the fornix

– Function: bilateral integration of memory encoding and spatial-cognitive processing

– Arterial supply: posterior medial choroidal artery (posterior cerebral artery)

– Venous drainage: septum pellucidum and internal cerebral veins to the great cerebral vein

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The hippocampal commissure (commissure of the fornix; psalterium) is a transverse sheet of commissural fibers and glia that crosses the midline, connecting the two hippocampal formations.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The commissure lies immediately inferior to the splenium of the corpus callosum, where the two crura of the fornix converge. Inferolaterally, it is continuous with the crura, which diverge toward the hippocampi; superiorly and anteriorly, it is continuous with the body of the fornix.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The hippocampal commissure interconnects the limbic lobes bilaterally, enabling coordination between the hippocampal and parahippocampal regions of each hemisphere. This is thought to support bilateral integration of memory encoding and spatial-cognitive processing.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The commissure is supplied principally by the posterior medial choroidal artery, a branch of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA).

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The fornix is drained mainly by the veins of the septum pellucidum and the internal cerebral veins, which typically pass caudally to drain into the great cerebral vein and then the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Amnesia: Disruption of the commissure (e.g., from surgical sectioning, trauma, or compression) can impair interhemispheric memory transfer, contributing to anterograde amnesia.

– Seizure propagation: The commissure of the fornix provides a pathway for epileptic activity to spread between the temporal lobes; it may be targeted in refractory temporal lobe epilepsy.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Paired white matter bundles carrying fibers between the hippocampus and the diencephalon and forebrain

– Pass beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum, converging at the hippocampal commissure to form the body of the fornix

– Function: component of the medial limbic circuit (of Papez) underlying memory

– Arterial supply: posterior lateral choroidal and anterior choroidal arteries

– Venous drainage: septum pellucidum and internal cerebral veins to the great cerebral vein

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The crura of the fornix (singular: crus) are paired white matter bundles carrying efferent fibers from the hippocampus toward the diencephalon and forebrain, as well as afferent fibers traveling to the hippocampus.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The crura pass superiorly and anteriorly beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum, superior and medial to the pulvinar nuclei, forming the inferomedial margin of the body of the lateral ventricle. 

The two crura converge toward the midline, where the hippocampal commissure connects them before they join to form the body of the fornix.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The crura transmit efferent fibers from the hippocampus toward the mammillary bodies, septal nuclei, and anterior thalamic nuclei, as well as afferent fibers projecting to the hippocampus, forming a component of the medial limbic circuit (of Papez) underlying memory. 

There is evidence of functional lateralization, with the left crus primarily associated with verbal memory and the right with visuospatial memory, though this remains an area of ongoing research.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The crura of the fornix are primarily supplied by the posterior lateral choroidal artery (a branch of the posterior cerebral artery), which travels through the choroidal fissure between the pulvinar nuclei and fimbria of the fornix, and by branches of the anterior choroidal artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The fornix is drained mainly by the veins of the septum pellucidum and the internal cerebral veins, which typically pass caudally to drain into the great cerebral vein and then the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Amnesia: Damage to the crura of the fornix (e.g., from trauma, surgical injury, or compression) disrupts hippocampal output and can cause anterograde amnesia, impairing the formation of new declarative memories.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Small, almond-shaped mass of gray matter in the rostral temporal lobe, deep to the uncus

– Nuclei organized into basolateral, centromedial, and olfactory (superficial cortex-like) groups

– Functions: arousal, attention, fear responses, stress adaptation, goal-directed behavior, social behavior, olfaction

– Arterial supply: anterior choroidal artery

– Venous drainage: basal vein (of Rosenthal) → great cerebral vein (of Galen) → straight sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The amygdaloid body is a small, almond-shaped mass of gray matter located deep to the uncus of the limbic lobe. 

Its nuclei are organized into three groups: the basolateral nuclear group, the centromedial nuclear group, and the olfactory amygdala (also termed the superficial cortex-like group), which comprises the anterior amygdaloid area and the cortical nuclei.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The amygdaloid body lies deep to the uncus, anterior to the hippocampus and the tip of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, and is contiguous with the tail of the caudate nucleus. The stria terminalis arises from the amygdaloid body and courses along the medial aspect of the tail of the caudate nucleus to terminate at the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis.

The basolateral group has extensive reciprocal connections with the cerebral cortex, while the centromedial group projects primarily to the hypothalamus and brainstem.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The amygdaloid body is involved in a broad range of functions, including arousal and attention, fear responses, adaptation to stress, goal-directed behavior, social behavior, olfaction, food intake, and sexual behavior. These diverse roles reflect its multimodal afferent input from cortical and subcortical regions. 

It is best characterised by its role in associating external stimuli with emotional significance. Lesions are associated with an overly placid manner, flat affect, and inability to discern emotion in others.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The anterior choroidal artery supplies blood to the amygdaloid body.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
The basal vein (of Rosenthal) drains the amygdaloid body to the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and then on to the straight sinus. 

Variable additional drainage may occur via the superficial middle cerebral vein to the cavernous sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Temporal lobe epilepsy: Amygdaloid involvement is common, with seizure foci arising from or propagating through the amygdaloid body; associated with fear auras and automatisms (involuntary, repetitive motor behaviors such as lip-smacking or hand-fumbling occurring without conscious awareness).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Paired fiber bundles formed by bifurcation of the body of the fornix

– Each column has precommissural (anterior to the anterior commissure) and postcommissural fibers

– Descend anterior to the interventricular foramen (of Monro) toward the mammillary bodies

– Function: postcommissural fibers to the mammillary bodies (medial limbic circuit, of Papez); precommissural fibers to the septal nuclei and hypothalamus

– Arterial supply: subcallosal artery; venous drainage: internal cerebral vein to the great cerebral vein

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The columns of the fornix are paired fiber bundles formed by the bifurcation of the body of the fornix, carrying efferent and afferent fibers between the hippocampal formation and subcortical targets. Each column contains precommissural fibers (passing anterior to the anterior commissure) and postcommissural fibers (passing posterior to it).

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The columns descend anteriorly to the interventricular foramen (of Monro), arching inferiorly through the lateral wall and floor of the third ventricle within the hypothalamus, before terminating principally at the mammillary bodies. 

The precommissural fibers diverge toward the septal nuclei and anterior hypothalamus.

sections.title: Function
Arterial Supply
sections.text: The columns of the fornix are primarily supplied by the subcallosal artery, a member of the anteromedian central arteries arising from the anterior communicating artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The internal cerebral vein drains the columns of the fornix to the great cerebral vein and then on to the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Amnesia: Damage to the columns of the fornix (e.g., from surgical injury, third ventricular tumors, or infarction) disrupts hippocampal output to the mammillary bodies and can cause severe anterograde amnesia.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Location: ventral surface of the diencephalon

– Arterial Supply: posterior communicating artery

– Function: episodic/spatial memory

– Venous Drainage: basal vein

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The mammillary bodies are small, rounded nuclei composed of grey matter.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The mammillary bodies are readily visible from the ventral surface of the brain, sitting at the posterior limit of the hypothalamus, anterior to the interpeduncular fossa. They receive a large number of fibers from the hippocampus via the fornix.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The mammillary bodies are a part of the limbic system and play a role in both episodic memory and spatial memory.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The primary source of arterial supply for the mammillary bodies is the posterior communicating artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The mammillary bodies are drained by the basal vein into the great cerebral vein, and then on into the straight sinus.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2021). Gray’s Anatomy: the Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd ed. Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Tightly folded, multilayered gray matter structure in the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle

– Comprises CA1–CA4 fields; part of the hippocampal formation (with dentate gyrus and subiculum)

– Functions: spatial and temporal memory, orientation, declarative memory formation

– Arterial supply: hippocampal arteries (branches of posterior cerebral artery); anterior choroidal artery

– Venous drainage: basal vein (of Rosenthal) → great cerebral vein (of Galen) → straight sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The hippocampus proper (hippocampus proprius; cornu ammonis) is a tightly folded, multilayered gray matter structure that protrudes into the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, forming part of the inner ring of the limbic lobe. It is composed of the CA1, CA2, CA3, and CA3h/CA4 fields (CA = cornu ammonis).

The hippocampus proper forms part of the hippocampal formation, which classically also includes the dentate gyrus and subiculum. Some definitions of the hippocampal formation further include closely related parahippocampal regions such as the entorhinal cortex, presubiculum, and parasubiculum.

The hippocampus was named due to its shape which was said to resemble that of a seahorse (Greek = hippokampos).

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The hippocampus proper occupies the floor of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle and curves posteriorly, where it becomes continuous with the fimbria of the hippocampus. The amygdaloid body lies immediately anterior, while the entorhinal cortex is located both anterior and inferior.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The hippocampus proper plays a role in spatial and temporal memory and orientation, and is best known for its involvement in the formation of declarative memories. Deficits in hippocampal function are associated with the inability to form new memories relating to facts and events.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The primary arterial supply to the hippocampus comes from the hippocampal arteries (anterior, middle, and posterior), branches of the posterior cerebral artery. Hippocampal branches of the anterior choroidal artery also contribute, particularly to the anterior hippocampus.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The basal vein (of Rosenthal) drains blood from the hippocampus into the great cerebral vein, and then on into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
— Anterograde amnesia: Selective hippocampal damage results in an inability to form new declarative memories, with relative preservation of remote and procedural memory.

— Alzheimer disease: Hippocampal atrophy is an early and characteristic feature, correlating with progressive deficits in episodic memory.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Dorsal surface (roof) of the midbrain, the quadrigeminal plate, posterior to the mesencephalic aqueduct

– Comprises four elevations: paired superior and inferior colliculi, separated by a cruciform sulcus

– Function: superior colliculi coordinate reflexive eye and head movements; inferior colliculi relay auditory information and contribute to the startle response

– Arterial supply: collicular artery (quadrigeminal artery) from the posterior cerebral artery (+ superior cerebellar artery)

– Venous drainage: basal vein (of Rosenthal) and great cerebral vein (of Galen)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The tectum of the midbrain (quadrigeminal plate) is the dorsal surface of the midbrain, deep to which lies the mesencephalic aqueduct. 

It comprises four rounded elevations: the paired superior colliculi and paired inferior colliculi, separated by a cruciform sulcus.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The tectum of the midbrain sits posterior to the mesencephalic aqueduct (cerebral aqueduct) where it forms the roof of the midbrain.

It lies posterior to the periaqueductal gray matter and is bordered anteriorly by the tegmentum and is continuous inferiorly with the superior medullary velum.

sections.title: Function
Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The tectum is largely supplied by the collicular artery (quadrigeminal artery), a branch of the precommunicating part of the posterior cerebral artery. 

The superior cerebellar artery also contributes to the blood supply of the colliculi.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
Veins of the tectum drain into the basal vein (of Rosenthal) and the great cerebral vein (of Galen). 

The basal vein courses in the ambient cistern lateral to the midbrain before joining the great cerebral vein, which lies immediately dorsal to the tectum in the quadrigeminal cistern and drains to the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Dorsal midbrain syndrome (Parinaud syndrome): Compression of the superior colliculi, most commonly by pineal region tumors, produces a characteristic triad of upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and pupillary light-near dissociation.

sections.text:

Standring, S., Tubbs, S.R., 2025. Gray’s Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 43rd ed. Elsevier, Amsterdam.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Large paired bundles of descending fibers forming the ventral surface of the midbrain; continuation of the posterior limb of the internal capsule

– Carry corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine fibers; separated by the interpeduncular fossa

– Function: mediate voluntary movement and relay cortical input to the cerebellum via the pontine nuclei

– Arterial supply: peduncular branches of the posterior cerebral artery (+ basilar and superior cerebellar arteries)

– Venous drainage: basal vein (of Rosenthal) → great cerebral vein

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The cerebral peduncle (also termed the crus cerebri or basis pedunculi) is a large bundle of descending white matter fibers forming the anterior part of the midbrain. It consists principally of corticospinal, corticonuclear (corticobulbar), and corticopontine fibers arising from the ipsilateral cerebral cortex. 

Note that "cerebral peduncle" in its traditional, broader sense has been used to refer to all midbrain tissue anterior to the tectum of the midbrain, i.e., the crus cerebri, substantia nigra, and tegmentum of the midbrain.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The cerebral peduncle lies on the anterior (ventral) surface of the midbrain, anterior to the substantia nigra. The two peduncles are separated by the interpeduncular fossa, from which the oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges. 

Rostrally, the cerebral peduncle is continuous with the posterior limb of the internal capsule; caudally, its fibers fan out into the basal part of the pons.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The cerebral peduncle transmits descending motor and corticocerebellar projections from the cerebral cortex. 

Corticospinal and corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibers pass through the peduncle to reach spinal cord motor neurons and brainstem cranial nerve nuclei respectively, mediating voluntary movement of the limbs, trunk, and face. 

Corticopontine fibers synapse in the ipsilateral pontine nuclei, which project via the middle cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral cerebellum, contributing to motor coordination and broader cerebellar functions including cognitive processing.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The cerebral peduncle is supplied by perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery and the posterior communicating artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The cerebral peduncles are drained via several small veins (e.g., interpeduncular, anteromedial and anterolateral pontomesencephalic, posterior and lateral mesencephalic veins) which largely empty into the basal vein (of Rosenthal), which courses around the cerebral peduncle to the great cerebral vein.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Weber syndrome: Occlusion of a perforating branch of the posterior cerebral artery may damage the cerebral peduncle together with the adjacent fascicles of the oculomotor nerve (CN III). This produces contralateral spastic hemiplegia (from corticospinal fibre damage) combined with ipsilateral ptosis, pupillary dilation, and lateral strabismus (from CN III involvement).

Standring, S., Tubbs, S.R., 2025. Gray’s Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 43rd ed. Elsevier, Amsterdam.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Caudal pair of elevations of the tectum (quadrigeminal plate)

– Multilayered, comprising central, pericentral, and external nuclei

– Function: major relay in the ascending auditory pathway, receiving input via the lateral lemniscus and projecting to the medial geniculate body; contributes to the auditory startle response

– Arterial supply: collicular artery from the posterior cerebral artery (+ superior cerebellar artery)

– Venous drainage: basal vein (of Rosenthal) and great cerebral vein (of Galen)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The inferior colliculus is a multilayered structure comprising central, pericentral, and external nuclei containing neuronal cell bodies and axons. It forms the caudal pair of elevations of the tectum (quadrigeminal plate).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The inferior colliculi form the caudal pair of elevations of the tectum and are continuous inferiorly with the superior medullary velum. Each is separated from the superior colliculus above and contralateral inferior colliculus by the transverse and vertical components of the cruciform sulcus, respectively. 

The brachium of the inferior colliculus runs anterolaterally from the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus, conveying ascending auditory fibers.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The inferior colliculus is a major relay station in the ascending auditory pathway, receiving convergent input from multiple brainstem auditory nuclei (including the cochlear nuclei, superior olivary complex, and nuclei of the lateral lemniscus) via the lateral lemniscus, and integrating these signals before projecting to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus. It also receives descending input from the auditory cortex and contributes to the auditory startle response.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The posterior cerebral artery supplies blood to the inferior colliculus via the collicular artery. 

Alternatively, blood can be supplied by branches of the superior cerebellar artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
Veins of the superior and inferior colliculi drain into the basal vein (of Rosenthal) and the great cerebral vein (of Galen). 

The basal vein courses in the ambient cistern lateral to the midbrain before joining the great cerebral vein, which lies immediately dorsal to the tectum in the quadrigeminal cistern and drains to the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Central auditory processing deficit: Unilateral inferior colliculus lesions may produce contralateral auditory deficits and impaired sound localization; bilateral lesions cause more severe auditory processing impairment.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Vanderah, T.W., 2026. Nolte's The Human Brain: An Introduction to Its Functional Anatomy, 9th ed. Elsevier, Amsterdam.

Standring, S., Tubbs, S.R., 2025. Gray’s Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 43rd ed. Elsevier, Amsterdam.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Rostral pair of elevations of the tectum, below the pineal gland

– Multilayered: seven alternating gray and white layers; superficial layers form a retinotopic map of the contralateral visual field, deep layers integrate multisensory input and give descending motor projections

– Function: coordinate reflexive eye and head movements, including saccades and orienting toward visual stimuli

– Arterial supply: collicular artery (quadrigeminal artery) from the posterior cerebral artery (+ superior cerebellar artery)

– Venous drainage: basal vein (of Rosenthal) and great cerebral vein (of Galen)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The superior colliculus is a multilayered structure comprising seven alternating layers of gray and white matter, divided functionally into superficial layers, which receive retinal and visual cortical input and form a retinotopic map of the contralateral visual field, and deep layers, which integrate multisensory input and give rise to descending motor projections.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The superior colliculi form the rostral pair of elevations of the tectum, lying below the pineal gland. Each is separated from the inferior colliculus below and contralateral superior colliculus by the transverse and vertical components of the cruciform sulcus, respectively. 

The superior colliculi lie dorsal to the mesencephalic aqueduct and periaqueductal gray matter.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The superior colliculi are involved in the coordination of eye and head movements. Visual inputs from the retina and visual cortex are integrated by the superior colliculus to control subconscious orienting responses, including saccades and reflexively orienting toward stimuli.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The superior and inferior colliculi are largely supplied by the collicular artery (quadrigeminal artery), a branch of the precommunicating part of the posterior cerebral artery. 

The superior cerebellar artery also contributes to the blood supply of the colliculi.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
Veins of the superior and inferior colliculi drain into the basal vein (of Rosenthal) and the great cerebral vein (of Galen). 

The basal vein courses in the ambient cistern lateral to the midbrain before joining the great cerebral vein, which lies immediately dorsal to the tectum in the quadrigeminal cistern and drains to the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Dorsal midbrain syndrome (Parinaud syndrome): Compression of the superior colliculi, most commonly by pineal region tumors, produces a characteristic triad of upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and pupillary light-near dissociation.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Posterior extension of the lateral ventricle into the occipital lobe

– Most variable part of the lateral ventricle; absent in some individuals

– Contains no choroid plexus; lined by ependyma and filled with cerebrospinal fluid

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The occipital horn (posterior horn) of the lateral ventricle extends posteriorly from the atrium into the occipital lobe. It is the most variable part of the lateral ventricle in size and shape, and is absent in some individuals. It contains no choroid plexus and is lined by ependymal cells and filled with cerebrospinal fluid. On coronal sections it appears rounded; on sagittal sections it presents as a blind-ending recess extending toward the occipital pole.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Junction of the body, posterior horn, and inferior horn, posterior to the thalamus

– Bounded by the tail of the caudate nucleus (laterally) and the fornix (medially)

– Contains the glomus (prominent choroid plexus tuft); lined by ependyma and filled with cerebrospinal fluid

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The atrium (trigone) of the lateral ventricle is the junction between the body, posterior horn, and inferior horn, situated just posterior to the thalamus where the ventricle curves inferiorly. 

It is bounded laterally by the tail of the caudate nucleus and medially by the fornix. A prominent tuft of choroid plexus, the glomus, is located within the atrium. It is lined by ependymal cells and filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Small band of gray matter connecting the medial surfaces of the left and right thalami

– Crosses through the lumen of the third ventricle

– Absent in approximately 20–30% of individuals

– Does not appear to serve as a functional commissure/functional significance remains unclear

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The interthalamic adhesion is a small band of gray matter connecting the medial surfaces of the left and right thalami, crossing through the lumen of the third ventricle. It is absent in approximately 20–30% of individuals.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The interthalamic adhesion is best appreciated in midsagittal section as a small rounded protrusion within the third ventricle, connecting the two thalami across the midline.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
Despite containing axons of neurons, the interthalamic adhesion does not appear to serve as a functional commissure; no significant interhemispheric communication has been demonstrated in humans. 

Its functional significance remains unclear, and its absence appears to have no detectable neurological consequences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Single midline opening on the posterior fourth ventricle (foramen of Magendie)

– Passes cerebrospinal fluid into the cisterna magna

– One of three fourth-ventricle openings, with the paired lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka)

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The median aperture (foramen of Magendie) is a single midline opening on the posterior surface of the fourth ventricle, through which cerebrospinal fluid passes into the cisterna magna and the subarachnoid space. 

It is located posterior to the pons and medulla and anterior to the cerebellum, and is one of three openings of the fourth ventricle, alongside the paired lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Curves anteroinferiorly from the atrium into the temporal lobe

– Tail of the caudate nucleus in its roof, hippocampus in its floor, amygdala at its tip

– Choroid plexus along the choroidal fissure; the optic radiation (Meyer loop) curves around it

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The temporal horn (inferior horn) of the lateral ventricle curves anteroinferiorly from the atrium into the temporal lobe. 

The tail of the caudate nucleus runs along its lateral roof, the hippocampus forms its floor, and the amygdala lies just anterior to its tip, with the uncus immediately medial.

Choroid plexus is present along the choroidal fissure on its inferomedial wall. The anterior bundle of the optic radiation (Meyer loop) curves around its lateral aspect. It is lined by ependymal cells and filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-filled cavity between cerebellum posteriorly and pons and rostral medulla anteriorly

– Continuous rostrally with cerebral aqueduct and caudally with central canal

– Tent-like roof and diamond-shaped floor (rhomboid fossa)

– Roof formed by superior and inferior medullary vela; T-shaped choroid plexus carried by inferior medullary velum

– Cerebrospinal fluid exits via median aperture (foramen of Magendie) and lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The fourth ventricle is a cerebrospinal (CSF)-filled cavity lying between the cerebellum posteriorly and the pons and rostral medulla anteriorly, continuous rostrally with the cerebral aqueduct and caudally with the central canal at the obex. 

It has a triangular profile in sagittal section with a tent-like roof, and a diamond-shaped floor (the rhomboid fossa) when viewed posteriorly. It is lined by ependyma. The roof is formed by the superior medullary velum cranially and the inferior medullary velum caudally; the latter consists largely of tela choroidea and carries the T-shaped choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle, whose horizontal limbs extend into the lateral recesses and protrude through the lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The fourth ventricle is bounded ventrally by the pons and rostral medulla and dorsally by the cerebellum, reaching its greatest width at the pontomedullary junction. Cerebrospinal fluid exits through the median aperture (foramen of Magendie) into the cisterna magna and through the lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka) into the cerebellopontine angle cisterns.

sections.title: Floor
sections.text:
The rhomboid fossa is divided by a median sulcus into two symmetrical halves, each further subdivided by the sulcus limitans into a medial eminence and a lateral vestibular area. 

In the superior part, the facial colliculus marks the nucleus of abducens nerve, overlain by the looping fibres of the facial nerve.  The locus coeruleus lies lateral to the sulcus limitans, visible as a region of bluish-gray pigmentation. Striae medullares cross the floor horizontally at the level of the lateral apertures. 

In the inferior part, the hypoglossal and vagal trigones overlie their respective nuclei; the area postrema lies at the caudal limit of the floor adjacent to the obex.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Obstructive hydrocephalus: Mass lesions within or adjacent to the fourth ventricle may obstruct cerebrospinal fluid outflow, producing dilation of the entire ventricular system; raised infratentorial pressure may precipitate posterior fossa herniation

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The choroid plexus consists of a network of capillaries and ependymal cells that line the internal walls of the ventricles of the brain. It is responsible for the production of cerebrospinal fluid that fills the ventricles of the brain, and flushes metabolites out of the brain. The choroid plexus produces around half a litre of cerebrospinal fluid per day.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Extends from the interventricular foramen (of Monro) to the atrium

– Bounded by the body of the caudate nucleus (laterally), septum pellucidum (medially), and the thalamus and fornix (inferiorly)

– Choroid plexus on its inferior surface; lined by ependyma and filled with cerebrospinal fluid

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The central part (body) of the lateral ventricle extends from the interventricular foramen (of Monro) anteriorly to the atrium posteriorly.

It is bounded laterally by the body of the caudate nucleus, medially by the septum pellucidum (which separates the two lateral ventricles), and inferiorly by the thalamus and body of the fornix. 

Choroid plexus is present on its inferior surface, between the fornix and thalamus. It is lined by ependymal cells and filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Narrow canal, approximately 1–2 mm in diameter, extending through dorsal quarter of midbrain

– Continuous rostrally with caudal third ventricle and caudally with fourth ventricle

– Lined by ependyma and lacks choroid plexus

– Surrounded by periaqueductal gray matter

– Tectum lies dorsal to aqueduct; tegmentum lies ventral to aqueduct

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The aqueduct of the midbrain, commonly referred to as the cerebral aqueduct, is a narrow canal, approximately 1–2 mm in diameter and roughly circular in transverse section, extending through the dorsal quarter of the midbrain in the midline. 

Rostrally, it is continuous with the caudal third ventricle immediately inferior to the posterior commissure; caudally, it opens into the fourth ventricle at the midbrain–pons junction. It is lined by ependyma and, unlike the remainder of the ventricular system, lacks choroid plexus.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The periaqueductal gray matter completely surrounds the aqueduct, forming a zone of small, closely packed cells that is continuous with hypothalamic gray matter rostrally and the floor of the fourth ventricle caudally.

The tectum of the midbrain lies dorsal to the aqueduct, while the tegmentum lies ventral to it; the anterior surface of the aqueduct demarcates these two regions.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Aqueductal stenosis: Narrowing or occlusion of the aqueduct is the most common cause of congenital hydrocephalus; it results in dilation of the third and both lateral ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Most anterior and superior part of the lateral ventricle, anterior to the interventricular foramen (of Monro)

– Bounded by the corpus callosum (above and anteriorly), head of the caudate nucleus (laterally), and septum pellucidum (medially)

– Contains no choroid plexus; lined by ependyma and filled with cerebrospinal fluid

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The frontal horn is the most anterior and superior portion of the lateral ventricle, extending into the frontal lobe anterior to the interventricular foramen (of Monro), at which point it becomes continuous with the body of the lateral ventricle.

It is bounded anteriorly and superiorly by the genu and body of the corpus callosum, laterally by the head of the caudate nucleus, and medially by the septum pellucidum. Unlike other parts of the lateral ventricle, it contains no choroid plexus. It is lined by ependymal cells and filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Narrow, slit-like midline cavity derived from the primitive forebrain vesicle

– Walls: thalami and hypothalami laterally; lamina terminalis, columns of fornices, and anterior commissure anteriorly

– Floor: optic chiasm, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, and mammillary bodies

– Recesses: supraoptic, infundibular, suprapineal, and pineal recesses

– Communicates with lateral ventricles via interventricular foramina (of Monro) and with fourth ventricle via aqueduct of the midbrain

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The third ventricle is a narrow, slit-like midline cavity derived from the primitive forebrain vesicle. Its walls are formed by the following structures:

– Lateral walls: medial surfaces of the thalami (superior) and hypothalami (inferior), separated by the hypothalamic sulcus

– Anterior wall: lamina terminalis, columns of the fornices, and anterior commissure

– Posterior wall: pineal gland, habenular commissure, and posterior commissure

– Floor: optic chiasm, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, and mammillary bodies (anterior to posterior)

– Roof: tela choroidea and overlying fornices

The interthalamic adhesion (massa intermedia), a band of gray matter connecting the medial surfaces of the two thalami, spans the cavity and is present in the majority of individuals.

sections.title: Recesses
Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The third ventricle communicates anterosuperiorly with the lateral ventricles via the interventricular foramina (of Monro), located between the columns of the fornix and the anterior nuclei of the thalami.

Posteroinferiorly, it is continuous with the aqueduct of the midbrain (cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius), which traverses the midbrain to communicate with the fourth ventricle.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Obstructive hydrocephalus: Dilation of the lateral and third ventricles resulting from stenosis or occlusion of the cerebral aqueduct, most commonly due to congenital stenosis, tumor, or hemorrhage

– Colloid cyst: Benign cyst arising at the interventricular foramen that may cause acute obstructive hydrocephalus by blocking CSF flow between the lateral and third ventricles.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Paired opening at the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle (foramen of Luschka)

– Passes cerebrospinal fluid into the subarachnoid space (pontocerebellar cistern)

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lateral aperture (foramen of Luschka) is a paired opening at the lateral edge of the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle, through which cerebrospinal fluid passes from the ventricular system into the subarachnoid space, specifically the pontocerebellar cistern.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Bilateral narrow orifices connecting each lateral ventricle with the third ventricle

– Choroid plexus continuous through each foramen

– Boundaries: column of fornix anterosuperiorly; anterior pole of thalamus posteriorly

– Two foramina converge at anterior end of third ventricle, giving V-shaped appearance in coronal section

– Choroidal fissure originates at the interventricular foramen

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The interventricular foramina (of Monro) are bilateral narrow orifices connecting each lateral ventricle with the third ventricle. The choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle is continuous through the foramen with the choroid plexus of the third ventricle, forming part of the posterior wall of the foramen before continuing as two narrow strands in the roof of the third ventricle. The choroidal fissure originates at the interventricular foramen and extends in a C-shaped arc around the thalamus into the temporal horn.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Each interventricular foramen is bounded anterosuperiorly by the column of the fornix and posteriorly by the anterior pole of the thalamus. The two foramina converge at the anterior end of the third ventricle, giving a V-shaped appearance in coronal section, with the body of the fornix lying above and the thalami lateral to each foramen.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Colloid cyst: Benign cyst arising at the interventricular foramen that may cause acute obstructive hydrocephalus by blocking cerebrospinal fluid flow between the lateral and third ventricles.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The supra-optic recess is located anteriorly on the lateral surface of the third ventricle, superior to the infundibular recess. It extends anteriorly towards the upper surface of the optic chiasm.

It is responsible for the production of cerebrospinal fluid that fills the ventricles of the brain, and flushes metabolites out of the brain. sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The infundibular recess is located anteriorly on the lateral surface of the third ventricle, inferior to the supraoptic recess. It extends anteriorly towards the pituitary infundibulum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The suprapineal recess is a small extension located posteriorly on the lateral surface of the third ventricle, superior to the pineal recess. It extends posteriorly above the pineal body.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The pineal recess is a small extension located posteriorly on the lateral surface of the the third ventricle, inferior to the suprapineal recess. It extends posteriorly into the pineal body.

19055.name: Periosteal Cranial Dura (Calvaria; Right)
alternate: Endosteal Layer of Cranial Dura Mater (Calvaria; Right)

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The cranial dura mater is the most superficial of the three meningeal layers and covers the entire brain down to the foramen magnum, where it is continuous with the spinal dura mater. The cranial dura mater is a tough, fibrous, two-layer structure with the outer or periosteal dura forming the periosteum of the cranial bones and the inner of meningeal dura laying against the underlying arachnoid mater. For the most part these two dural layers are adhered, but they can be visualized at some dural sinuses where the venous cavity separates the periosteal and meningeal dural layers. The dura is pierced by bridging veins, which carry blood from the brain; emissary veins, which bring blood from the overlying bone; and arachnoid granulations, which bring cerebrospinal fluid to venous sinuses.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The periosteal cranial dura mater is adherent to the inner surfaces of the cranial bones, especially along the sutures and the foramina at the cranial base. It is continuous with the pericranium, covering the outer surfaces of the cranial bones, through the cranial sutures and the foramina. Additionally, it is continuous with the periosteum of the orbit via the superior orbital fissure.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Epidural hematoma

- Subdural hematoma

- Headache

sections.text: The cranial dura mater is the most superficial of the three meningeal layers and covers the entire brain down to the foramen magnum, where it is continuous with the spinal dura mater. The cranial dura mater is a tough, fibrous, two-layer structure with the outer or periosteal dura forming the periosteum of the cranial bones and the inner of meningeal dura laying against the underlying arachnoid mater. For the most part these two dural layers are adhered, but they can be visualized at some dural sinuses where the venous cavity separates the periosteal and meningeal dural layers. sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The meningeal cranial dura mater is closely applied to the surface of the brain. Additionally, it provides sheaths for each of the cranial nerves as they exit through their cranial foramina. The sheaths fuse with the epineurium of the nerve as it exits the skull. The dural sheath of the optic nerve is continuous with the sclera of the eyeball. The meningeal cranial dura also fuses with the outer adventitia of the major vessels, e.g. the internal carotid artery, when it enters the cranial cavity.

Since the meningeal cranial dura mater is in close contact with the brain, it reflects inwards at certain points known as dural folds. The first is the falx cerebri in which the meningeal dura runs down in the longitudinal fissure separating the two cerebral hemispheres. Second is the tentorium cerebelli, a dural fold that separates the cerebellum below from the cerebrum above. A third fold, the falx cerebelli, runs perpendicular to the tentorium cerebelli and separates the two cerebellar hemispheres. Lastly, the diaphragma sellae surrounds the pituitary stalk.

sections.text:
- Epidural hematoma

- Subdural hematoma

- Headache

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The cranial dura mater is the most superficial of the three meningeal layers and covers the entire brain down to the foramen magnum, where it is continuous with the spinal dura mater. The cranial dura mater is a tough, fibrous, two-layer structure with the outer or periosteal dura forming the periosteum of the cranial bones and the inner of meningeal dura laying against the underlying arachnoid mater. For the most part these two dural layers are adhered, but they can be visualized at some dural sinuses where the venous cavity separates the periosteal and meningeal dural layers. The dura is pierced by bridging veins, which carry blood from the brain; emissary veins, which bring blood from the overlying bone; and arachnoid granulations, which bring cerebrospinal fluid to venous sinuses.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The meningeal cranial dura mater is closely applied to the surface of the brain. Additionally, it provides sheaths for each of the cranial nerves as they exit through their cranial foramina. The sheaths fuse with the epineurium of the nerve as it exits the skull. The dural sheath of the optic nerve is continuous with the sclera of the eyeball. The meningeal cranial dura also fuses with the outer adventitia of the major vessels, e.g. the internal carotid artery, when it enters the cranial cavity.

Since the meningeal cranial dura mater is in close contact with the brain, it reflects inwards at certain points known as dural folds. The first is the falx cerebri in which the meningeal dura runs down in the longitudinal fissure separating the two cerebral hemispheres. Second is the tentorium cerebelli, a dural fold that separates the cerebellum below from the cerebrum above. A third fold, the falx cerebelli, runs perpendicular to the tentorium cerebelli and separates the two cerebellar hemispheres. Lastly, the diaphragma sellae surrounds the pituitary stalk.

sections.text:
- Epidural hematoma

- Subdural hematoma

- Headache

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The tentorium cerebelli is a large fold of the meningeal cranial dura mater that serves to separate the occipital lobe from the underlying cerebellum and brainstem.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The tentorium cerebelli has both a left and right side which come together with the falx cerebri at the straight sinus. It provides separation between the cerebrum above and the cerebellum below. The tentorium cerebelli wraps centrally toward the brainstem where it blends in with the dural layers overlying the clinoid processes of the sphenoid bone. This central margin leaves only an oval hole called the tentorial incisure, though which the brain and brainstem are connected. Several prominent dural sinuses are formed at least in part by the tentorium cerebelli, namely the transverse sinuses, the straight sinus, the superior petrosal sinuses, and the confluence of sinuses.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Uncal herniation

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The falx cerebelli is a small fold of the meningeal cranial dura mater. It separates the right and left cerebellar hemispheres.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The falx cerebelli is continuous with and on the inferior side of the tentorium cerebelli. It runs vertically in the same orientation as the falx cerebri, but due to its location inferior to the tentorium cerebelli, it separates the cerebellar hemispheres. On its external surface, the falx cerebelli runs from the internal occipital protuberance down to the foramen magnum.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The diaphragma sellae is a flat piece of dura mater extending from the tuberculum sellae posteriorly towards the dorsum sellae and posterior clinoid processes. It roofs the hypophyseal fossa of the sella turcica with the exception of a small hole in the center, through which the pituitary stalk passes.

sections.text: Standring, S. (2021). Gray’s Anatomy: the Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd ed. Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The falx cerebri is a large fold of the meningeal cranial dura mater that projects down into the longitudinal fissure, separating the left and right cerebral hemispheres.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The falx cerebri is the largest fold of meningeal dura mater in the cranium. It runs from the crista galli of the ethmoid bone anteriorly, back to the straight sinus and tentorium cerebelli posteriorly. Its superior margin forms the superior sagittal sinus while its inferior margin lays just above the corpus callosum and contains the inferior sagittal sinus.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The arachnoid mater is the middle of the three meningeal layers. It is a thin opaque layer that sends wispy fibers inward to the pia mater, forming the spider web appearance that gives the arachnoid mater its name. Where it overlies a dural venous sinus, the arachnoid mater can develop arachnoid granulations, extensions of the arachnoid that pierce the dura and allow cerebrospinal fluid to flow out of the subarachnoid space and into venous sinuses. The cranial arachnoid mater is similar in function and appearance to the spinal arachnoid mater.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The arachnoid mater lies against the dura mater, being held away from the brain and pia mater by the presence of cerebrospinal fluid. This space found between the pia and the arachnoid mater is the subarachnoid space and contains cerebrospinal fluid.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Subarachnoid hemorrhage

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The spinal dura mater is a tough fibrous membrane that protects and encloses the spinal cord. It arises at the foramen magnum, to which it is attached. It also blends with the posterior aspects of the bodies of the second and third cervical vertebrae and to the posterior longitudinal ligament. Otherwise, it forms a distinctive layer that is separated from the tissues surrounds the vertebral column by an epidural space. Deep to the spinal dura is the subdural space, a potential space that separates it from the spinal arachnoid.

Distally, at around the level of the second sacral vertebra, the dura begins to taper and invests the thin, delicate filum terminale internum to form the filum terminale externum (or the coccygeal ligament). It descends to the posterior coccyx to blend with its periosteum.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The spinal dura mater forms the dural sac, running from the foramen magnum rostrally to the S2 vertebrae caudally. The spinal dura extends laterally with nerve roots to cover nerves as they emerge from the spinal canal. The dura mater blends with the epineurium of the spinal nerves.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The filum terminale externum is composed of both pia mater and dura mater and is the terminal portion of the filum terminale. The pia mater that contributes to the filum terminale internum merges with the overlaying spinal dura. It starts within a few centimeters of the coccyx and terminates when the filum terminale externum attaches to the coccyx.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The filum terminale externum is located where the pia and dura mater layers merge, and is approximately 5cm long (Standring, 2016). It is the terminal end of the filum terminale and helps anchor the spinal cord to the coccyx.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The denticulate ligaments are thin sheets of collagen that extend laterally from the spinal pia mater. They extend out and form triangular shaped attachments to the overlying dura mater.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The denticulate ligaments extend from the foramen magnum rostrally down to the level of the T12 vertebra caudally. On each side, there are typically 18-21 triangular extensions which attach to the spinal dura mater, lateral to the spinal cord. They are thought to help stabilize the spinal cord. The lateral extensions of the denticulate ligaments can be seen laying between the dorsal and ventral nerve roots.

The filum terminale internum forms the majority of the length of the filum terminale and is generally the portion seen in cadaveric specimens. The filum terminale internum is composed of pia mater. In cadaveric specimens, it often is distinguishable from spinal nerve roots due to its silvery to opaque appearance.

sections.text: Spinal pia mater is similar to cranial pia mater in both structure and position. The spinal pia mater is wrapped directly on the spinal cord and invests within the ventral median fissure and dorsal sulci of the spinal cord. Spinal pia mater is a very thin, largely transparent, fibrous membrane.

Because it is so thin and largely transparent, it is generally not visible. It appears somewhat opaque, with a white to silver color, as it forms the denticulate ligaments and filum terminale.

Because it is so thin and largely transparent, it is generally not visible. It appears somewhat opaque, with a white to silver color, as it forms the denticulate ligaments and filum terminale.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: Arachnoid mater is a thin opaque layer that sends wispy fibers inward to the pia mater. This created the spider web appearance that gives the arachnoid mater its name. The spinal arachnoid mater has a similar function and appearance to the cranial arachnoid mater. It is the middle of the three meningeal layers.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The arachnoid mater is located adjacent to the dura mater, separated from it by the potential subdural space. It is also separated from the spinal cord and pia mater by the presence of cerebrospinal fluid in the subarachnoid space. At the level of the second sacral vertebra, the arachnoid mater fuses with the dura mater.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The central canal is the portion of the ventricular system of the central nervous system that is specific to the spinal cord. It originates when the embryonic neural tube folds together forming a lumen. It carries cerebrospinal fluid in early years but is often partially or wholly obliterated in adults.

The central canal is generally oval in shape with the longer axis running dorsoventral. It is lined with a single layer of ependymal cells and either filled with cerebrospinal fluid or is no longer patent. Just before its terminus within the conus medullaris, the central canal will expand to form a larger cavity.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The central canal is continuous with the fourth ventricle, originating at the obex rostrally and ending in the conus medullaris caudally. Within the spinal cord, it is found centrally within the grey commissure that connects the left and right sides. It is surrounded by grey matter that is classified as Rexed lamina X. The terminal expansion of the central canal is called the ventriculus terminalis of Krause (Saker et al., 2016).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Syringomyelia

sections.title: References
sections.text: Saker, E., Henry, B. M., Tomaszewski, K. A., Loukas, M., Iwanaga, J., Oskouian, R. J. and Tubbs, R. S. (2016) 'The Human Central Canal of the Spinal Cord: A Comprehensive Review of its Anatomy, Embryology, Molecular Development, Variants, and Pathology', Cureus, 8(12), pp. e927.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The spinal cord is composed of two types or regions, the inner gray matter and the surrounding white matter. White matter is rich in myelinated axons and this results in a whiter visual appearance in unstained tissue, relative to the darker gray matter. When viewed in cross section, white matter is essentially all of the spinal cord other than the central butterfly shape of gray matter. White matter is composed of dense tracts of neuronal axons that are heavily myelinated by glial cells known as oligodendrocytes. These bundles or tracts of fibers, sometimes referred to as fasciculi, carry information up towards the brain or down to the appropriate spinal cord level.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The spinal cord white matter varies in thickness depending on location, with the upper cervical levels having more white matter and the sacral regions having the least. This is due to the fact that all information to the entire body must travel up and down through cervical levels, while only information pertaining to lower limb and genital regions is found in the sacral levels.

The white matter is broken down into three major regions, or funiculi. The dorsal funiculus lays dorsal to the gray matter, the lateral funiculus is located lateral to the gray matter, and the ventral funiculus is located ventral to the gray matter. Within each region multiple tracts, each of which is called a fasciculus, carry information that is either ascending or descending.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Paralysis

- Hypertonia

- Spasticity

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The spinal cord is composed of two types or regions, the inner gray matter and the surrounding white matter. Gray matter is rich in neuronal cell bodies and this results in a darker visual appearance in unstained tissue. When viewed in cross section, gray matter often appears to be shaped like a butterfly or an H.

Gray matter is often divided into different regions that are best seen when looking at cross sections. The dorsal horns run from the dorsolateral surface of the spinal cord and are the sites of sensory input to interneurons. This horn can be divided into different lamina, each of which are associated with different modalities and inputs.

The lateral horns, which are sometimes difficult to see, project almost directly laterally and are the site at which autonomic neuronal cell bodies are located.

The ventral horns, which form the thickest part of the gray matter and are located ventrally, are the site at which primary motor neurons are located. Motor and autonomic axons project out of the ventral horns in a ventrolateral direction.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The gray matter forms an H or butterfly shape when seen in cross section. At the center lies the central canal, the evolutionary equivalent of the brain’s ventricles. This canal can carry cerebrospinal fluid through teen years, after which it is generally obliterated.

On both right and left sides, the gray matter has a dorsal horn corresponding to sensation, a lateral horn corresponding to autonomics, and a ventral horn corresponding to motor control. The dorsal horn can be subdivided into six different laminae, termed Rexed laminae. More commonly, three regions of the dorsal horn are discussed: the substantia gelatinosa, the nucleus proprius, and the dorsal nucleus.

The lateral horn has two Rexed laminae, but the most relevant feature is the intermediolateral nucleus.

The ventral horn also has two Rexed laminae and indistinct clusters of primary motor neuron cell bodies.

22077.name: Spinal Ganglion of Coccygeal Nerve
alternate: Dorsal Root Ganglion of Coccygeal Nerve
Spinal Ganglion of Spinal Nerve Co

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The spinal ganglion of the coccygeal nerve is the swelling of the proximal posterior root of the coccygeal nerve. It is located within the sacral hiatus. This ganglion contains cell bodies of the somatic sensory afferents carrying information towards the spinal cord from the skin over the coccyx bone.

17706.name: Anterior Root of Coccygeal Nerve
alternate: Anterior Root of Spinal Nerve Co

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Emerges from sacral hiatus.

Course: Inferiorly towards the coccygeal plexus.

Branches: No branches.

Supply: Motor innervation to muscles of the perineum and external anal sphincter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior root of the coccygeal nerve originates as a series of rootlets that emerge from the ventrolateral surface of the spinal cord. These quickly merge to form the anterior root.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior root emerges from the sacral hiatus and runs inferiorly to form the coccygeal plexus, with the fifth sacral nerve, close to the coccyx bone.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no branches of the anterior nerve roots.

sections.title: Supplied Structures & Function
sections.text: The anterior root of the coccygeal nerves sends motor innervation to muscles of the perineum and external anal sphincter.

21787.name: Posterior Root of Coccygeal Nerve
alternate: Dorsal Root of the Coccygeal Nerve
Posterior Root of Spinal Nerve Co
Sensory Root of the Coccygeal Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: In or just medial to the first sacral foramen.

Course: Medially from the sacral hiatus and superiorly within the vertebral canal towards the posterior surface of the appropriate spinal cord level.

Branches: Unnamed rootlets just prior to entering the spinal cord.

Supply: Sensory innervation to the skin over the coccyx.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior root of the first sacral nerve originates in, or just medial, to the sacral hiatus. It is at this point that the first sacral nerve splits into anterior and posterior roots.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior root of the coccygeal nerve runs medially through the sacral hiatus into the vertebral canal. Here it runs superiorly towards its corresponding spinal cord level in a large bundle of nerve roots called the cauda equina. The posterior root splits into smaller rootlets before entering the dorsal aspect of the spinal cord.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The posterior root of the coccygeal nerve branches into several smaller rootlets shortly before entering the dorsal aspect of the spinal cord.

sections.title: Supplied Structures & Function
sections.text: The posterior root of the coccygeal nerve supplies sensory innervation to the skin over the coccyx.

24682.name: Anterior Root of First Cervical Nerve
alternate: Anterior Root of Spinal Nerve C1
Motor Root of First Cervical Nerve
Ventral Root of First Cervical Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterolateral sulcus of spinal cord.

Course: Laterally towards the posterior arch of atlas and the occipital bone.

Branches: None.

Supply: Somatic efferent fibers to the first cervical nerve, geniohyoid, infrahyoid, and prevertebral muscles and the muscles bordering the suboccipital triangle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior root of the first cervical nerve forms from a series of rootlets that emerge from the anterolateral sulcus of the first cervical spinal segment.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The anterior root of the first cervical nerve runs laterally and inferiorly away from the first cervical spinal segment towards a foramen located between the posterior arch of atlas and the occipital bone. Roughly within this foramen, the anterior root merges with the posterior root to form the first cervical nerve.

Size and direction of the spinal roots vary. For instance, the upper cervical roots are short and run horizontally to exit the vertebral canal through the foramen.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior root of the first cervical nerve merges with the posterior root to form the first cervical nerve and does so without branching.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The somatic motor efferents pass through the spinal nerve itself and into either the posterior ramus or the anterior ramus of the first cervical nerve.

Those passing through the anterior ramus contribute to the cervical plexus. It innervates the infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and superior belly of omohyoid). The thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles are also innervated by the anterior ramus of the first cervical nerve via a communicating branch to the hypoglossal nerve.

Fibers that pass through the posterior ramus (or suboccipital nerve) enter the suboccipital triangle to innervate muscles including the rectus capitis posterior major and minor, obliquus capitis superior and inferior, and semispinalis capitis.

19421.name: Anterior Root of Second Cervical Nerve
alternate: Anterior Root of Spinal Nerve C2
Motor Root of Second Cervical Nerve
Ventral Root of Second Cervical Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterolateral sulcus of spinal cord.

Course: Laterally towards the intervertebral foramen.

Branches: None.

Supply: Motor innervation to the infrahyoid and anterior prevertebral muscles, obliquus capitis inferior, longissimus capitis, semispinalis capitis and splenius capitis muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior root of the second cervical nerve forms from a series of rootlets that emerge from the anterolateral sulcus of the second cervical spinal segment.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The anterior root of the second cervical nerve runs laterally and inferiorly away from the second cervical spinal segment towards the intervertebral foramen located between the atlas (C1 vertebra) above and the axis (C2 vertebra) below. Roughly within this intervertebral foramen, the anterior root merges with the posterior root to form the second cervical nerve.

Size and direction of the spinal roots vary. For instance, the upper cervical roots are short and run horizontally to exit the vertebral canal through the foramen.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior root of the second cervical nerve merges with the posterior root to form the second cervical nerve and does so without branching.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The somatic motor efferents pass through the spinal nerve itself and into either the posterior ramus or the anterior ramus of the first cervical nerve.

Those passing through the anterior ramus contribute to the cervical plexus. It innervates the infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid and inferior belly of omohyoid) via the ansa cervicalis. Other muscles innervated include the anterior prevertebral muscles, including rectus capitis anterior and lateralis and longus colli muscles.

Fibers that pass through the posterior ramus innervate the obliquus capitis inferior muscle via communications sent from the greater occipital nerve to the suboccipital nerve. Fibers which pass through the smaller lateral branch of the posterior ramus innervate the longissimus capitis, semispinalis capitis, and splenius capitis muscles.

24126.name: Anterior Root of Sixth Cervical Nerve
alternate: Anterior Root of Spinal Nerve C6
Motor Root of Sixth Cervical Nerve
Ventral Root of Sixth Cervical Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterolateral sulcus of spinal cord.

Course: Laterally towards the intervertebral foramen.

Branches: None.

Supply: Motor innervation to muscles of upper limb, shoulder, and back.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior root of the sixth cervical nerve forms from a series of rootlets that emerge from the anterolateral sulcus of the sixth cervical spinal segment.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The anterior root of the sixth cervical nerve runs laterally and inferiorly away from the sixth cervical spinal segment towards the intervertebral foramen located between the fifth and sixth cervical vertebrae. Roughly within this intervertebral foramen, the anterior root merges with the posterior root to form the sixth cervical nerve.

Size and direction of the spinal roots vary. For instance, the upper cervical roots are short and run horizontally to exit the vertebral canal through the foramen.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior root of the sixth cervical nerve merges with the posterior root to form the sixth cervical nerve and does so without branching.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The somatic motor efferents pass through the spinal nerve itself and into either the posterior ramus or the anterior ramus of the sixth cervical nerve. 

Those passing through the anterior ramus convey motor fibers to the superior trunk of the brachial plexus. Fibers that enter the lateral cord of the brachial plexus help innervate muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm (biceps brachii, coracobrachialis, brachialis), pectoralis major, pronator teres, and flexor carpi radialis. Fibers that enter the posterior cord provide motor innervation to the subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi, deltoid, teres minor, triceps, brachioradialis, anconeus, extensor carpi radialis longus, and supinator. Some fibers also contribute to the innervation of the subclavius and supra- and infraspinatus muscles. 

Fibers that pass through the posterior ramus innervate the longissimus colli, splenius colli, iliocostalis colli, multifidus, semispinalis colli, semispinalis capitis, and trapezius.

20236.name: Anterior Root of Fifth Cervical Nerve
alternate: Anterior Root of Spinal Nerve C5
Motor Root of Fifth Cervical Nerve
Ventral Root of Fifth Cervical Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterolateral sulcus of spinal cord.

Course: Laterally towards the intervertebral foramen.

Branches: None.

Supply: Motor innervation to muscles of upper limb, shoulder, and back.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior root of the fifth cervical nerve forms from a series of rootlets that emerge from the anterolateral sulcus of the fifth cervical spinal segment.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The anterior root of the fifth cervical nerve runs laterally and inferiorly away from the fifth cervical spinal segment towards the intervertebral foramen located between the fourth and fifth cervical vertebrae. Roughly within this intervertebral foramen, the anterior root merges with the posterior root to form the fifth cervical nerve.

Size and direction of the spinal roots vary. For instance, the upper cervical roots are short and run horizontally to exit the vertebral canal through the foramen.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The anterior root of the fifth cervical nerve merges with the posterior root to form the fifth cervical nerve and does so without branching.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The somatic motor efferents pass through the spinal nerve itself and into either the posterior ramus or the anterior ramus of the fifth cervical nerve. 

Those passing through the anterior ramus convey motor fibers to the superior trunk of the brachial plexus. Fibers that enter the lateral cord of the brachial plexus help innervate muscles of the anterior compartment of arms (biceps brachii, coracobrachialis, brachialis), pectoralis major, various muscles of the anterior forearm and some intrinsic hand muscles. Fibers that enter the posterior cord provide motor innervation to the subscapularis and teres major, latissimus dorsi, deltoid, teres minor, and brachioradialis.

Fibers that pass through the posterior ramus innervate the longissimus colli, splenius colli, iliocostalis colli, multifidus, semispinalis colli, semispinalis capitis, and trapezius.

sections.text:

Other muscles innervated include the anterior prevertebral muscles, including the longus capitis and longus colli, and lateral prevertebral muscles, including the middle scalene muscle.

Fibers that pass through the posterior ramus innervate semispinalis capitis, longissimus capitis, splenius capitis, and multifidus muscles.

24767.name: Posterior Root of Second Cervical Nerve
alternate: Dorsal Root of Second Cervical Nerve
Posterior Root of Spinal Nerve C2
Sensory Root of Second Cervical Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Second cervical nerve.

Course: Medially towards the posterior side of the spinal cord.

Branches: None.

Supply: Afferent fibers from the dorsal rami transmit sensory information from the scalp and the posterior auricular region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior root of the second cervical nerve originates just lateral to or in the intervertebral foramen, between the C2 vertebra (axis) below and the C1 vertebra (atlas) above. This corresponds to the point where the cervical nerve splits into anterior and posterior roots.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior root of the second cervical nerve runs medially towards the posterior side of the spinal cord. Adjacent to the appropriate spinal cord level, the posterior root splits into smaller rootlets, which enter the posterior spinal cord in line with the dorsal horn of the gray matter.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no branches of the posterior root of the second cervical nerve. The proximal end of the posterior root has a bulge called the spinal (or dorsal root) ganglion, which is the location of the neuronal cell bodies of the neurons that form the posterior root.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Sensory cutaneous fibers ending in the greater occipital nerve receive information from the scalp. The second cervical nerve also serves as a conduit for the sensory neurons innervating the meninges and the proprioceptive nerve endings from the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

19389.name: Posterior Root of First Cervical Nerve
alternate: Dorsal Root of First Cervical Nerve
Posterior Root of Spinal Nerve C1
Sensory Root of First Cervical Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: First cervical nerve.

Course: Medially towards the posterior side of the spinal cord.

Branches: None.

Supply: Afferent fibers from somatic and visceral sensory receptors send information from the meninges and atlantooccipital joint to the spinal cord.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The posterior root of the first cervical nerve originates just lateral to or in the intervertebral foramen, between the occipital bone and the atlas (C1 vertebra). This corresponds to the point where the cervical nerve splits into anterior and posterior roots.

The posterior root of the first cervical nerve is much smaller in comparison to its corresponding anterior root. It is often absent in about 8% of the population, while others report that is it frequently or never present (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior root of the first cervical nerve runs medially towards the posterior side of the spinal cord. Adjacent to the appropriate spinal cord level, the posterior root splits into smaller rootlets, which enter the posterior spinal cord in line with the dorsal horn of the gray matter.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no branches of the posterior root of the first cervical nerve. The proximal end of the posterior root has a bulge called the spinal (or dorsal root) ganglion, which is the location of the neuronal cell bodies of the neurons that form the posterior root.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The posterior root of the first cervical nerve carries all afferents from the first cervical nerve to the first cervical spinal segment of the spinal cord.

Small filaments from the meninges and the atlantooccipital joint join the suboccipital nerve (or the posterior ramus) which conveys sensory information to the first cervical nerve and its posterior root (Ouaknine & Nathan, 1973).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Ouaknine, G. & Nathan, H. (1973) Anastomotic connections between the eleventh nerve and the posterior root of the first cervical nerve in humans. J Neurosurg, 38(2), 189-97.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. & Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

19447.name: Posterior Root of Third Cervical Nerve

sections.text:

Course: Medially towards the posterior side of the spinal cord.

Branches: None.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior root of the third cervical nerve originates just lateral to or in the intervertebral foramen, between the second and third cervical vertebrae. This corresponds to the point where the cervical nerve splits into anterior and posterior roots.

23212.name: Spinal Ganglion of Eighth Cervical Nerve
alternate: Dorsal Root Ganglion of Eighth Cervical Nerve
Posterior Root Ganglion of Eighth Cervical Nerve
Sensory Ganglion of Eighth Cervical Nerve
Spinal Ganglion of Spinal Nerve C8

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The spinal ganglion (dorsal root ganglion or posterior root ganglion) is a sensory ganglion found at the proximal end of the posterior root of each spinal nerve. 

The spinal ganglion of the eighth cervical nerve conveys sensory information from the periphery to the dorsal horn of the first cervical spinal segment of the spinal cord.

It contains cell bodies or nuclei of the afferent nerve fibers, which are derived from neural crest cells and comprise pseudounipolar neurons. These afferent neurons convey cutaneous somatic sensory signals, such as touch, temperature and pain, from the skin above the trapezius and the medial side of the upper limb. In addition, visceral sensations from glands and blood vessels from the skin in the same region are also conveyed to the central nervous system.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The spinal ganglion (dorsal root ganglion or posterior root ganglion) is a sensory ganglion found at the proximal end of the posterior root of each spinal nerve. 

The spinal ganglion of the first cervical nerve conveys sensory information from the periphery into the dorsal horn of the first cervical spinal segment of the spinal cord.

It contains cell bodies or nuclei of the afferent nerve fibers, which are derived from neural crest cells and comprise pseudounipolar neurons. The afferent neurons convey somatic sensory signals from the meninges and the atlantooccipital joint to the suboccipital nerve (or the posterior ramus) which conveys sensory information to the first cervical nerve and on to the spinal ganglion (Ouaknine and Nathan, 1973). The dorsal root ganglion of the first cervical nerve is often absent or may be rudimentary (Dorland, 2011).
