21396.name: Anterior Division of Superior Trunk of Brachial Plexus
21396.latin: Divisio anterior trunci superioris plexus brachialis
alternate: Anterior Division of Upper Trunk of Brachial Plexus
Divisio ventralis trunci superioris plexus brachialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superior trunk of the brachial plexus.

Course: Forms posterior to the mid-clavicle and runs inferolaterally to the formation of the lateral cord, posterior to the first segment of the axillary artery.

Branches: No branches. Contributes to the lateral cord which in turn gives rise to three nerves.

Supply: Sensory and motor innervation. Supplies sensory innervation for the skin of the lateral palmar digits and surfaces of the hand, and lateral skin of the forearm. Motor innervation is to the anterior compartment muscles of the arm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The origin of the anterior division of the superior trunk is from the superior trunk itself. This occurs when the trunk bifurcates into anterior and posterior divisions. It carries fibers from the C5 and C6 spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The anterior division forms roughly posterior to the mid-clavicle. It runs inferolaterally, posterior to the first segment of the axillary artery. Lateral to the first rib and posterior to the axillary artery, the anterior division of the superior trunk merges with the anterior division of the middle trunk to form the lateral cord.

The divisions of the brachial plexus run within the prevertebral fascia or its inferior extension, the axillary sheath.

sections.title: Branches
Supplied Structures
Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial nerve (C5).

Course: Arises from the radial nerve before it enters the spiral groove.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Skin of the back of the arm from the insertion of the deltoid to the olecranon process of ulna.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior brachial cutaneous nerve is a branch of the radial nerve.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: In the upper part of the arm, the radial nerve descends posterolaterally through the lower triangular space to enter the radial groove along with the profunda brachii vessels. Before entering the spiral groove in the midarm, it gives off the posterior brachial cutaneous nerve (which innervates a strip of skin overlying the triceps muscle).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior brachial cutaneous nerve provides cutaneous innervation to the skin of the back of the arm, from the insertion of the deltoid to the olecranon process of ulna.

24067.name: Superior Lateral Brachial Cutaneous Nerve
alternate: Superior Lateral Cutaneous Nerve of Arm

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Axillary nerve (C5-C6).

Course: Loops around the deltoid muscle to become superficial.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Skin of the posterior arm and inferior deltoid region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve arises from the axillary nerve. It contains sensory nerve fibers which eventually relay the sensory information to the dorsal horns of the C5 and C6 cervical segments of the spinal cord.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve exits the axilla via the quadrangular space to enter the posterior scapular region, as the distal continuation of the axillary nerve. It loops around the posterior aspect of the deltoid muscle and travels superiorly to innervate the skin of the posterior arm, including the skin over the inferior part of the deltoid.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: No named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve carries general sensations from the skin over the posterior arm and the inferior part of the deltoid muscle region.

17288.name: Inferior Lateral Brachial Cutaneous Nerve
alternate: Inferior Lateral Cutaneous Nerve of Arm

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial nerve (C5—C6).

Course: Arises from the radial nerve in the spiral groove.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Skin of the lower half of the lateral side of the arm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve arises from the radial nerve and contains sensory nerve fibers from the C5—C6 spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve arises from the radial nerve as it descends inside the spiral radial groove against the bony humerus, between the lateral and medial heads of triceps muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The sensory nerve fibers from the inferior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve eventually end up relaying sensory cutaneous information to the C5 and C6 cervical segments of the spinal cord.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The inferior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve provides cutaneous sensory innervation to the lower half of the lateral side of the arm

19690.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Medial Head of Triceps Brachii
19690.latin: Ramus capitis medialis musculi tricipitis brachii nervi radialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial nerve (C6—C8).

Course: Two muscular branches to the medial head of triceps brachii arise from the radial nerve, one before and one after the nerve enters the radial groove. 

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Medial head of triceps brachii muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A motor nerve branch to the medial head of triceps brachii muscle originates from the radial nerve and contains motor nerve fibers from the C6—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The radial nerve comes off from the posterior cord in the lower part of the axilla. Here it runs behind the third part of axillary artery while lying against the muscles of the posterior wall of the axilla, i.e., subscapularis, teres major, and latissimus dorsi muscles. 

In the upper part of the arm, it descends posterolaterally (with the profunda brachii vessels) through the lower triangular space, between the shaft of the humerus, long head of triceps brachii, and teres major muscles. The nerve then enters the radial groove along with the profunda brachii vessels. It descends downwards and laterally between the lateral and medial heads of the triceps muscle, while in contact with the humerus. 

The radial nerve innervates the medial head of triceps brachii both proximally and distally. The most proximal of the two branches to the medial head arises from the radial nerve before it enters the radial groove while the second distal one arises as the nerve descends inside the radial groove. The later descends further to innervate the anconeus muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of the radial nerve to medial head of triceps provides motor innervation to the medial head of triceps muscle. The radial nerve gives off several branches to innervate all three heads of the triceps brachii muscle.

24286.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Anconeus

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial nerve (C6—C8).

Course: Arises from the radial nerve as it descends inside the radial groove. 

Branches: No named branches. 

Supply: Anconeus muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The muscular branch to the anconeus muscle arises from the radial nerve (C6—C8 cervical spinal segments).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The radial nerve passes through the lower triangular space to descend inside the spiral radial groove against the humerus, between the lateral and medial heads of triceps muscle. Two muscular branches are given off in the groove to the lateral and medial heads of triceps muscle. The second branch of the radial nerve to the medial head of the triceps brachii also innervates the anconeus muscle. This is the more distal of the two branches that innervates the medial head of the triceps brachii, after which it passes through the medial head in the posterior compartment of the arm and continues distally to provide innervation for the anconeus muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of the radial nerve to anconeus provides motor innervation to the anconeus muscle.

18565.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Lateral Head of Triceps Brachii
18565.latin: Ramus capitis lateralis musculi tricipitis brachii nervi radialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial nerve (C6—C8).

Course: Arises from the radial nerve as it descends in the radial groove. 

Branches: No named branches. 

Supply: Lateral head of triceps brachii muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Motor nerve branch to the lateral head of triceps brachii muscle originates from the radial nerve and contains motor nerve fibers from the C6—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The radial nerve comes off from the posterior cord in the lower part of the axilla. Here it runs behind the third part of axillary artery while lying against the muscles of the posterior wall of the axilla, i.e., subscapularis, teres major, and latissimus dorsi muscles. 

In the upper part of the arm, it descends posterolaterally (with the profunda brachii vessels) through the lower triangular space, between the shaft of the humerus, long head of triceps brachii, and teres major muscles. The nerve then enters the radial groove along with the profunda brachii vessels. It descends downwards and laterally between the lateral and medial heads of the triceps muscle, while in contact with the humerus. The radial nerve innervates the lateral head of the triceps brachii as it travels deep to the muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of the radial nerve to lateral head of triceps provides motor innervation to the lateral head of triceps muscle. The radial nerve gives off several branches to innervate all three heads of the triceps brachii muscle.

20355.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Long Head of Triceps Brachii
20355.latin: Ramus capitis longi musculi tricipitis brachii nervi radialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial nerve (C6—C8).

Course: Arises from the radial nerve as it passes through the lower triangular space in the arm. 

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Long head of triceps brachii muscle

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A motor nerve branch to the long head of triceps brachii muscle originates from the radial nerve and contains motor nerve fibers from the C6—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The radial nerve comes off from the posterior cord in the lower part of the axilla. Here it runs behind the third part of axillary artery while lying against the muscles of the posterior wall of the axilla, i.e., subscapularis, teres major, and latissimus dorsi muscles. 

In the upper part of the arm, it descends posterolaterally (with the profunda brachii vessels) through the lower triangular space, between the shaft of the humerus, long head of triceps brachii, and teres major muscles. While passing through the space (before entering the spiral groove), the radial nerve provides muscular innervation to the long head of triceps brachii muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of the radial nerve to the long head of triceps provides motor innervation to the long head of triceps muscle. The radial nerve gives off several branches to innervate all three heads of the triceps brachii muscle.

21487.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Brachialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial nerve (C7).

Course: Arises from the radial nerve as it descends inside the radial groove.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Brachialis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A nerve to brachialis muscle originates from the radial nerve and contains motor nerve fibers from the seventh cervical spinal segment (C7).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
In the upper part of the arm, the radial nerve descends posterolaterally (with the profunda brachii vessels) through the lower triangular space, between the shaft of the humerus, long head of triceps brachii, and teres major muscles. The nerve then enters the radial groove along with the profunda brachii vessels. It descends downwards and laterally between the lateral and medial heads of the triceps muscle, while in contact with the humerus. 

In the lower part of the arm, it pierces the lateral intermuscular septum and passes into the anterior compartment of the arm to reach the cubital fossa where it lies between the brachialis muscle medially and brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus muscles laterally.

In the cubital fossa, a muscular branch of the radial nerve innervates a small lateral section of the brachialis muscle with fibers originating from C7. The remaining part of the muscle is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve originating from C5-C6 spinal segments.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of the radial nerve to brachialis provides motor innervation to the brachialis muscle.

16627.name: Muscular Branch of Musculocutaneous Nerve to Brachialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5—C7).

Course: Musculocutaneous nerve descends between brachialis and biceps brachii muscles, sending branches to innervates these muscles. 

Branches: None.

Supply: Brachialis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The muscular branch to brachialis muscle arises from the musculocutaneous nerve (C5—C7).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
Following its origin from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus, the musculocutaneous nerve leaves the axilla and enters the anterior compartment of the arm by piercing the coracobrachialis muscle. In the arm, it runs downwards and laterally between the biceps brachii superficially and brachialis deeper to reach the lateral side of the tendon of the biceps.

As the nerve descends between the two muscles, the muscular branches to biceps brachii are given off from the main nerve at a mean distance of 19–31 cm from the acromial process. 

Different patterns of innervation of the brachialis muscle have been recorded. In the first pattern. In the more common first pattern (Type 1), only one primary motor branch emerges from the musculocutaneous nerve and splits into two or three secondary branches that entered the muscle. In the second branching pattern (Type 2), the muscle is innervated by two primary branches with different origins on the main nerve trunk and each branch makes its own way to a different part of the brachialis muscle (Pacha Vicente et al., 2005).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Muscular branches from the musculocutaneous nerve provide motor innervation to the flexor muscles of the anterior arm, including the brachialis muscle.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Pacha Vicente, D., Forcada Calvet, P., Carrera Burgaya, A. and Llusá Pérez, M. (2005) 'Innervation of biceps brachii and brachialis: Anatomical and surgical approach', Clin Anat, 18(3), pp. 186-94.

24758.name: Muscular Branch of Musculocutaneous Nerve to Coracobrachialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5—C7).

Course: Pierces through the coracobrachialis muscle to enter the flexor compartment of the arm. 

Branches: None.

Supply: Coracobrachialis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The muscular branch to coracobrachialis arises from the musculocutaneous nerve (C5—C7).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
In most cases, when the musculocutaneous nerve arises from within the axilla, it pierces the coracobrachialis muscle and innervates it (Rea, 2016). 

Sometimes, the musculocutaneous nerve does not pierce the coracobrachialis muscle; rather it travels down adhering with the median nerve. In this case, the common median and musculocutaneous trunk innervates the coracobrachialis (and biceps) muscle, while the musculocutaneous nerve alone supplies the brachialis only (Pacha Vicente et al., 2005). In some other cases, a communicating branch connects the musculocutaneous and median nerves.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Muscular branch of the musculocutaneous nerve provides motor innervation to coracobrachialis muscle.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —biceps reflex

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Pacha Vicente, D., Forcada Calvet, P., Carrera Burgaya, A. and Llusá Pérez, M. (2005) 'Innervation of biceps brachii and brachialis: Anatomical and surgical approach', Clin Anat, 18(3), pp. 186-94.
Rea, P. (2016) Essential Clinically Applied Anatomy of the Peripheral Nervous System in the Head and Neck. Elsevier Science.

20512.name: Muscular Branch of Musculocutaneous Nerve to Short Head of Biceps Brachii
20512.latin: Ramus musculi capitis brevis musculi bicipitis brachii nervi musculocutanei

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5—C7).

Course: Musculocutaneous nerve descends between brachialis and biceps brachii muscles, sending branches to innervates these muscles. 

Branches: None.

Supply: Short head of the biceps brachii muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The muscular branch to the short head of the biceps brachii muscle arises from the musculocutaneous nerve (C5—C7).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
Following its origin from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus, the musculocutaneous nerve leaves the axilla and enters the anterior compartment of the arm by piercing the coracobrachialis muscle. In the arm, it runs downwards and laterally between the biceps brachii superficially and brachialis deeper to reach the lateral side of the tendon of the biceps.

As the nerve descends between the two muscles, the muscular branches to biceps brachii are given off from the main nerve, at a distance of 11–13 cm from the acromial process. Usually a single branch arises from the main musculocutaneous nerve, which then splits into two secondary branches. One of these branches innervates the long head while the other innervates the short head (Type 1 pattern). In some other cases, the two branches are issued directly from two distinct points of the main nerve trunk and each branch makes its own way to each muscular head of the biceps (Type 2). In fewer cases, there are two branches given off from the musculocutaneous nerve. The proximal one splits into two secondary branches and each one supplies one head of the biceps muscle. The distal primary branch innervates the common belly of the biceps brachii (Type 3) (Pacha Vicente et al., 2005).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Muscular branches from the musculocutaneous nerve provide motor innervation to the flexor muscles of the anterior arm, including the muscular branch to the short head of biceps brachii.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Biceps reflex 

—Nerve transfer surgery

sections.title: References
sections.text: Pacha Vicente, D., Forcada Calvet, P., Carrera Burgaya, A. and Llusá Pérez, M. (2005) 'Innervation of biceps brachii and brachialis: Anatomical and surgical approach', Clin Anat, 18(3), pp. 186-94.

22210.name: Muscular Branch of Musculocutaneous Nerve to Long Head of Biceps Brachii
22210.latin: Ramus musculi capitis longi musculi bicipitis brachii nervi musculocutanei

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5—C7).

Course: Musculocutaneous nerve descends between brachialis and biceps brachii muscles, sending branches to innervates these muscles. 

Branches: None.

Supply: Long head of the biceps brachii muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The muscular branch to the long head of the biceps brachii muscle arises from the musculocutaneous nerve (C5—C7).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
Following its origin from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus, the musculocutaneous nerve leaves the axilla and enters the anterior compartment of the arm by piercing the coracobrachialis muscle. In the arm, it runs downwards and laterally between the biceps brachii superficially and brachialis deeper to reach the lateral side of the tendon of the biceps.

As the nerve descends between the two muscles, the muscular branches to biceps brachii are given off from the main nerve, at a distance of 11–13 cm from the acromial process. Usually a single branch arises from the main musculocutaneous nerve, which then splits into two secondary branches. One of these branches innervates the long head while the other innervates the short head (Type 1 pattern). In some other cases, the two branches are issued directly from two distinct points of the main nerve trunk and each branch makes its own way to each muscular head of the biceps (Type 2). In fewer cases, there are two branches given off from the musculocutaneous nerve. The proximal one splits into two secondary branches and each one supplies one head of the biceps muscle. The distal primary branch innervates the common belly of the biceps brachii (Type 3) (Pacha Vicente et al., 2005).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Muscular branches from the musculocutaneous nerve provide motor innervation to the flexor muscles of the anterior arm, including the muscular branch to the long head of biceps brachii.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Biceps reflex 

—Nerve transfer surgery

sections.title: References
sections.text: Pacha Vicente, D., Forcada Calvet, P., Carrera Burgaya, A. and Llusá Pérez, M. (2005) 'Innervation of biceps brachii and brachialis: Anatomical and surgical approach', Clin Anat, 18(3), pp. 186-94.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Median nerve (C6—C8).

Course: Proximal to the flexor retinaculum, the palmar branch arises and runs above the retinaculum.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Skin over thenar eminence and lateral two thirds of the palm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The palmar branch originates from the median nerve above the flexor retinaculum and contains nerve fibers which carry sensory information to the C6-C8 segments of the cervical spinal cord.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Inside the cubital fossa, the median nerve lies medial to the brachial artery and deep to bicipital aponeurosis. The nerve exits the cubital fossa, passes between the two heads of the pronator teres and between the humeroulnar and radial heads of the flexor digitorum superficialis muscle. It descends distally down the forearm between the flexor digitorum superficialis and the flexor digitorum profundus muscle. Before the nerve enters the carpal tunnel, it gives off a palmar (or volar) branch, immediately above the flexor retinaculum. This cutaneous branch crosses over the flexor retinaculum to reach the skin over the thenar eminence and palm region.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: No named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The palmar branch of the median nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin over the thenar eminence and the lateral two thirds of the palm.

20232.name: Palmar Branch of Ulnar Nerve
alternate: Palmar Cutaneous Branch of Ulnar Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ulnar nerve.

Course: Descends along with the main nerve trunk, crosses over the flexor retinaculum and reaches the medial palmar region.

Branches: None.

Supply: Skin over hypothenar eminences.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The palmar branch of ulnar nerve arises from the main trunk of the nerve proximal to the flexor retinaculum. It contains nerve fibers which relay sensory information to the C8, T1 cervical and thoracic segments of the spinal cord.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Following its origin from the ulnar nerve in the forearm, the palmar cutaneous branch descends along with the main nerve trunk. It crosses over the flexor retinaculum to reach the skin over the hypothenar eminence (medial palmar region) (Engber and Gmeiner, 1980).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The palmar branch of the ulnar nerve provides cutaneous innervation to the medial palm (over the hypothenar eminence).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Engber, W. D. and Gmeiner, J. G. (1980) 'Palmar cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve', J Hand Surg Am, 5(1), pp. 26-9.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ulnar nerve. 

Course: The ulnar nerve crosses over the flexor retinaculum to divide into superficial and deep terminal branches. The superficial branch innervates palmaris brevis and becomes cutaneous to palmar aspect of medial one and half fingers. 

Branches: Common Palmar Digital branch of ulnar nerve, muscular branch of ulnar nerve to hypothenar muscles.

Supply: Hypothenar muscles (abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi brevis, and opponens digiti muscles), palmaris brevis muscle, and skin of palmar aspect of medial one and a half digits.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial branch arises as one of the two terminal branches of the ulnar nerve at the distal border of the flexor retinaculum.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ulnar nerve crosses the wrist between the tendons of flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis muscles. It divides into superficial and deep terminal branches at the distal border of the flexor retinaculum. The superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis and becomes cutaneous to provide digital branches to medial one and a half digits.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The superficial branch gives off nerve fibers to the hypothenar muscles and then becomes the common palmar digital nerve. It further subdivides into proper palmar digital nerves for innervating the skin of adjacent sides of the ring and little fingers.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superficial branch of the ulnar nerve provides branches that innervate the hypothenar muscles (abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi brevis, and opponens digiti muscles), palmaris brevis muscle, and skin of palmar aspect of medial one and a half digits.

24968.name: Proper Palmar Digital Branches of Ulnar Nerve
24968.latin: Rami digitales palmares proprii nervi ulnaris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Common palmar digital nerves of ulnar nerve (or directly from the superficial terminal branch of ulnar nerve; C8-T1).

Course: Travel through the digits with their corresponding digital arteries and veins. 

Branches: None.

Supply: Skin of the medial one and a half digits (little finger and medial half of the ring finger).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The proper palmar digital nerve for the medial side of the little finger arises directly from the superficial terminal branch of ulnar nerve. Those for the interdigital skin between the adjacent side of the little and ring fingers arise from the common palmar digital branches of the ulnar nerve.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The ulnar nerve enters the palm by passing superficial to the flexor retinaculum and lateral to pisiform bone, while being covered by a superficial slip of the retinaculum (volar carpal ligament). At the distal border of retinaculum, the nerve terminates by dividing into its superficial and deep branches.

Just distal to the pisiform bone, the superficial branch gives off two palmar digital branches. The medial of the two branches is a proper palmar digital nerve which innervates the skin of the medial side of the little finger. The lateral branch is a common palmar digital nerve, which further divides into two proper palmar digital nerves. These innervate the skin of adjacent sides of the ring and little fingers. It also sends a communicating branch to the palmar digital nerves of the median nerve.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Sensory nerve fibers through the proper palmar digital branches of the ulnar nerve eventually end up relaying sensory information into the C8 & T1 cervical and thoracic segments of the spinal cord.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Cutaneous sensory innervation to the skin of the medial one and a half digits (little finger and medial half of the ring finger).

20394.name: Dorsal Digital Branches of Ulnar Nerve
alternate: Ulnar Dorsal Digital Nerves of Hand

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Dorsal branch of ulnar nerve (C8-T1).

Course: Extend over the dorsal aspect of the hand to the little, ring, and middle fingers.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Medial half of the back of hand and medial two and half fingers.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal digital nerves arise from the dorsal branch of ulnar nerve (C8-T1 spinal segments) at the level of the pisiform bone.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal branch of ulnar nerve descends with the main trunk of ulnar nerve almost to the pisiform bone. Here it passes backwards to divide into three (and sometimes two) dorsal digital nerves. The first branch enters the medial side of the little finger; the second branch enters the adjacent sides of the little and ring finger; and the third branch, if present, enters the adjacent sides of the ring and middle fingers.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The dorsal digital nerves of the ulnar nerve provide sensory cutaneous innervation to the skin of the medial half of the back of hand and the skin of the dorsal aspect of the medial two and half fingers.

18411.name: Proper Palmar Digital Branches of Median Nerve
18411.latin: Rami digitales palmares proprii nervi mediani
alternate: Proper Volar Digital Branches of Median Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve (C6—C8).

Course: Median nerve enters the palm underneath the flexor retinaculum and divides into medial and lateral division. The medial division gives off common palmar digital branches for second and third interdigital clefts, which further give off proper palmar digital branches.

Branches: None.

Supply: Adjoining sides of index, middle, and ring fingers in the second and third interdigital clefts.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The proper palmar digital nerves arise from the common palmar digital branches of the median nerve, below the flexor retinaculum (C6—C8).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The median nerve enters the palm by passing deep to the flexor retinaculum, where it lies in the narrow space of the carpel tunnel in front of the ulnar bursa enclosing the long flexor tendons of the forearm. Immediately below the retinaculum, the nerve divides into lateral and medial divisions.

The medial division divides into common palmar digital nerves, which give rise to the proper palmar (or volar) digital nerves for the second and third interdigital clefts, supplying the adjoining sides of the index, middle, and ring fingers. The common palmar digital branches for the medial one and half digits come from the ulnar nerve. The lateral division gives off a muscular branch to thenar muscles and three digital branches for the lateral one and half digits (including thumb).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: Proper palmar (or volar) digital nerves from the common digital branches of the median nerve innervate the adjoining sides of index, middle, and ring fingers in the second and third interdigital clefts. The various digital branches of the median nerve supply the palmar aspect of the skin of the lateral three and a half digits, the nail beds, and skin on the dorsal aspect of the middle and distal phalanges of the same digits. On the contrary, the lateral division gives off digital branches directly to the lateral one and half digits.

17876.name: Common Palmar Digital Branches of Ulnar Nerve
17876.latin: Rami digitales palmares communes nervi ulnaris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial branch of ulnar nerve (C8-T1).

Course: Deep to the superficial palmar arch and corresponding digital arteries and veins.

Branches: Proper palmar digital nerves of ulnar nerve.

Supply: Skin of ring and little fingers.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The common palmar digital branches arise from the superficial branch of ulnar nerve, below the flexor retinaculum in the palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The ulnar nerve enters the palm by passing superficial to the flexor retinaculum and lateral to pisiform bone, while being covered by a superficial slip of the retinaculum (volar carpal ligament). At the distal border of retinaculum, the nerve terminates by dividing into its superficial and deep branches.

Just distal to the pisiform bone, the superficial branch gives off two palmar digital branches. The medial of the two branches is a proper palmar digital nerve which innervates the skin of the medial side of the little finger. The lateral branch is a common palmar digital nerve, which further divides into two proper palmar digital nerves. These innervate the skin of adjacent sides of the ring and little fingers. It also sends a communicating branch to the palmar digital nerves of the median nerve. 

The common palmar digital nerves of the ulnar nerve have a similar course as those from the median nerve. They traverse deep to the superficial palmar arch and its associated digital vessels.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Proper palmar (or volar) digital nerves arise from the common digital branches of the ulnar nerve inside the palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The common palmar digital branches of the ulnar nerve provide cutaneous sensory innervation to the skin of adjacent sides of the ring and little fingers.

20774.name: Muscular Branch of Ulnar Nerve to Palmar Interossei
20774.latin: Ramus musculorum interosseorum palmarium nervi ulnaris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep branch of ulnar nerve (C8, T1).

Course: The deep branch passes backwards through the hypothenar muscles. It turns laterally within the concavity of the deep palmar arch and innervates the medial two lumbricals, palmar and dorsal interossei, flexor pollicis brevis, and adductor pollicis muscles.

Branches: None.

Supply: Palmar interossei.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ulnar nerve crosses the wrist between the tendons of flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis muscles. It divides into superficial and deep branches at the distal border of the flexor retinaculum. The muscular branches to the palmar interosseous muscles come off from the deep branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep branch of ulnar nerve passes backwards between the abductor and flexor digiti minimi, and then between the opponens digiti minimi and the fifth metacarpal bone, lying on the hook of the hamate. Finally, it turns laterally within the concavity of the deep palmar arch and innervates the medial two lumbricals, palmar and dorsal interossei, flexor pollicis brevis, and adductor pollicis muscles.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of ulnar nerve to palmar interossei provides motor innervation to the three palmar interosseous muscles in the hand.

17258.name: Muscular Branch of Ulnar Nerve to Flexor Pollicis Brevis
17258.latin: Ramus musculi flexoris pollicis brevis nervi ulnaris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep branch of ulnar nerve.

Course: Crosses the palmar aspect of hand.

Branches: None.

Supply: Deep part of flexor pollicis brevis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ulnar nerve crosses the wrist between the tendons of flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis muscles. It divides into superficial and deep terminal branches at the distal border of the flexor retinaculum. Sometimes, the muscular branch to the deep part of flexor pollicis brevis muscle comes off from the deep branch of ulnar nerve via the nerve to the palmar interossei. Whereas, the superficial head of the muscle receives its innervation from the median nerve.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep branch of ulnar nerve passes backwards between the abductor and flexor digiti minimi, and then between the opponens digiti minimi and the fifth metacarpal bone, lying on the hook of the hamate. Finally, it turns laterally within the concavity of the deep palmar arch and innervates the medial two lumbricals and interossei, as the nerve crosses the palm. The deep branch terminates by supplying the adductor pollicis and occasionally the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis muscles.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: No named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscle branch of ulnar nerve to flexor pollicis brevis supplies motor innervation to the deep part of flexor pollicis brevis muscle in the hand.

21695.name: Muscular Branch of Ulnar Nerve to Dorsal Interossei
21695.latin: Ramus musculorum interosseorum dorsalium nervi ulnaris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep branch of ulnar nerve (C8, T1).

Course: The deep branch passes backwards through the hypothenar muscles. It turns laterally within the concavity of the deep palmar arch and innervates the medial two lumbricals, palmar and dorsal interossei, flexor pollicis brevis, and adductor pollicis muscles.

Branches: None.

Supply: Dorsal interossei.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ulnar nerve crosses the wrist between the tendons of flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis muscles. It divides into superficial and deep branches at the distal border of the flexor retinaculum. The muscular branches to the dorsal interosseous muscles come off from the deep branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep branch of ulnar nerve passes backwards between the abductor and flexor digiti minimi, and then between the opponens digiti minimi and the fifth metacarpal bone, lying on the hook of the hamate. Finally, it turns laterally within the concavity of the deep palmar arch and innervates the medial two lumbricals, palmar and dorsal interossei, flexor pollicis brevis, and adductor pollicis muscles.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of ulnar nerve to dorsal interossei provides motor innervation to the four dorsal interosseous muscles in the hand.

22538.name: Muscular Branch of Ulnar Nerve to Lumbricals 3–4
22538.latin: Ramus musculorum lumbricalium tertii et quarti nervi ulnaris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep branch of ulnar nerve (C8, T1).

Course: The deep branch passes backwards through the hypothenar muscles. It turns laterally within the concavity of the deep palmar arch and gives muscular branches to the fourth and fifth lumbricals and the eight palmar and dorsal interosseous muscles, as the nerve crosses the palm.

Branches: None.

Supply: Third and fourth lumbrical muscles.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ulnar nerve crosses the wrist between the tendons of flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis muscles. It divides into superficial and deep branches at the distal border of the flexor retinaculum. The muscular branches to the fourth and fifth lumbrical muscles originate from the deep branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep branch of ulnar nerve passes backwards between the abductor and flexor digiti minimi, and then between the opponens digiti minimi and the fifth metacarpal bone, lying on the hook of the hamate. Finally, it turns laterally within the concavity of the deep palmar arch and gives off muscular branches to the medial fourth and fifth lumbricals and eight palmar and dorsal interosseous muscles, as the nerve crosses the palm. The deep branch innervates most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of ulnar nerve to lumbricals 3–4 provides motor innervation to third and fourth lumbricals muscles.

20478.name: Muscular Branch of Ulnar Nerve to Palmaris Brevis
20478.latin: Ramus musculi palmaris brevis nervi ulnaris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial branch of ulnar nerve (C8, T1).

Course: The ulnar nerve crosses the wrist to divide into superficial and deep terminal branches.

Branches: None.

Supply: Palmaris brevis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ulnar nerve crosses the wrist between the tendons of flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis muscles. It divides into superficial and deep branches at the distal border of the flexor retinaculum. The muscular branches to the palmaris brevis muscle originates from the superficial branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis and becomes cutaneous to provide common and proper digital branches to the medial one and a half digits.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of ulnar nerve to palmaris brevis provides motor innervation to the palmaris brevis muscle in the hand.

17792.name: Muscular Branch of Ulnar Nerve to Adductor Pollicis
17792.latin: Ramus musculi adductoris pollicis nervi ulnaris

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep branch of ulnar nerve (C8, T1).

Course: The deep branch passes backwards through the hypothenar muscles. It turns laterally within the concavity of the deep palmar arch and innervates the medial two lumbricals, interossei, flexor pollicis brevis, and adductor pollicis muscles.

Branches: None.

Supply: Adductor pollicis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ulnar nerve crosses the wrist between the tendons of flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis muscles. It divides into superficial and deep branches at the distal border of the flexor retinaculum. The muscular branch to the adductor pollicis muscle comes off from the deep branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep branch of ulnar nerve passes backwards between the abductor and flexor digiti minimi, and then between the opponens digiti minimi and the fifth metacarpal bone, lying on the hook of the hamate. Finally, it turns laterally within the concavity of the deep palmar arch and innervates the medial two lumbricals, interossei, flexor pollicis brevis, and adductor pollicis muscles.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of ulnar nerve to adductor pollicis provides motor innervation to the adductor pollicis muscle in the hand.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Terminal branch of ulnar nerve below the flexor retinaculum.

Course: Passes deep through the hypothenar muscles and curves laterally to end at the adductor pollicis muscle.

Branches: Muscular and articular branches.

Supply: Hypothenar muscles, medial two lumbricals, and interosseous muscles, adductor pollicis muscle, radiocarpal joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep branch of ulnar nerve arises below the flexor retinaculum as one of the terminal branches of ulnar nerve in the palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
At the radiocarpal joint (wrist), the ulnar nerve lies between the flexor carpi ulnaris and the flexor digitorum superficialis muscles. The nerve enters the palm by passing superficial to the flexor retinaculum and lateral to pisiform bone, while being covered by a superficial slip of the retinaculum (volar carpal ligament). At the distal border of retinaculum, the nerve terminates by dividing into its superficial and deep branches.

The deep branch accompanies the deep branch of the ulnar artery. It passes backwards between the abductor and flexor digiti minimi, and then between the opponens digiti minimi and the fifth metacarpal bone, lying on the hook of the hamate. Finally, it turns laterally within the concavity of the deep palmar arch. It ends by supplying the adductor pollicis muscle.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve provides muscular branches to the intrinsic muscles of the hand and articular branches to the radiocarpal joint.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles (abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi, opponens digiti minimi), medial two lumbricals, palmar and dorsal interosseous muscles, adductor pollicis, and deep head of flexor pollicis brevis muscles. It also supplies the radiocarpal joint.

24782.name: Common Palmar Digital Branches of Median Nerve
24782.latin: Rami digitales palmares communes nervi mediani

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Median nerve (C6—C8).

Course: Median nerve enters the palm underneath the flexor retinaculum and divides into medial and lateral division. The medial division gives off common palmar digital branches for second and third interdigital clefts, which further give off proper palmar digital branches. 

Branches: Proper palmar (or volar) digital of median nerve.

Supply: Adjoining sides of index, middle, and ring fingers in the second and third interdigital clefts.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The common palmar digital branches of median nerve arise from the median nerve below the flexor retinaculum (C6—C8).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The median nerve enters the palm by passing deep to the flexor retinaculum, where it lies in the narrow space of the carpel tunnel in front of the ulnar bursa enclosing the long flexor tendons of the forearm. Immediately below the retinaculum, the nerve divides into lateral and medial divisions.

The medial division divides into common palmar digital branches for the second and third interdigital clefts, supplying the adjoining sides of the index, middle, and ring fingers. The common palmar digital branches for the medial one and half digits come from the ulnar nerve. The lateral division gives off a muscular branch to thenar muscles and three digital branches for the lateral one and half digits (including thumb).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Proper palmar (or volar) digital nerves arise from the common digital branches of the median nerve inside the palmar aspect of the hand.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The common palmar digital branches of the median nerve supply the second and third interdigital clefts, and adjoining sides of the index, middle, and ring fingers. It also innervates the second lumbrical.

24030.name: Muscular Branch of Median Nerve to Lumbricals 1-2
24030.latin: Ramus musculorum lumbricalium primi et secundi nervi mediani

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve (C8, T1). 

Course: As the median nerve splits into common palmar digital branches, a branch to the lateral side of the index finger also innervates the first lumbrical. The common palmar digital branch for the medial side of the index finger also innervates the second lumbrical. 

Branches: None.

Supply: First and second lumbricals.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The median nerve enters the hand by passing through the carpal tunnel (i.e., deep to the flexor retinaculum) along with the long flexor tendons. After emerging from carpal tunnel, it divides into the common palmar digital branches. These innervate the first and second lumbricals.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The common palmar digital branches can be divided into lateral and medial divisions. The lateral division supplies a muscular branch to the thenar muscles and three proper palmar digital branches. Out of the three digital branches, two supply the thumb and one lateral side of the index finger. The common palmar digital branch to the index finger also innervates the first lumbrical.

The medial division divides into two common digital branches for the second and third interdigital clefts, supplying the adjoining sides of the index, middle, and ring fingers. The common digital branch for the second interdigital cleft also innervates the second lumbrical.

Occasionally the first and second lumbricals could receive their innervation from the ulnar nerve.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of median nerve to lumbricals 1–2 provides motor innervation to the first and second lumbrical muscles.

18196.name: Recurrent Branch of Median Nerve
alternate: Thenar Muscular Branch of Median Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Median nerve (C8-T1).

Course: Travels laterally, curving slightly around the flexor retinaculum to the thenar muscles.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis muscles).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The recurrent branch of the median nerve arises from the lateral side of median nerve, just distal to the flexor retinaculum (C8-T1).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The median nerve enters the palm by passing deep to the flexor retinaculum where it lies in the narrow space of the carpal tunnel. Immediately below the retinaculum the nerve gives off a lateral branch, namely the recurrent branch. 

The recurrent branch curves slightly upwards around the distal border of the flexor retinaculum to lie superficial to the flexor pollicis brevis muscle. 

The recurrent branch of the median nerve may vary in origin and can arise from the median nerve within the carpal tunnel. In this instance, it pierces the flexor retinaculum to reach the thenar muscles.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: No named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies motor innervation to the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis muscles).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ulnar nerve above the wrist (C8-T1).

Course: Descends with the main trunk of ulnar nerve and divides into three dorsal digital nerves.

Branches: None.

Supply: Medial half of the dorsum of hand and medial two and half fingers.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal branch arises from the main trunk of the ulnar nerve about 5 cm above the radiocarpal (wrist) joint. It contains sensory nerve fibers for the C8-T1 spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The dorsal branch of ulnar nerve descends with the main trunk of ulnar nerve almost to the pisiform bone. Here it passes backwards to divide into three (and sometimes two) dorsal digital nerves.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The dorsal branch of ulnar nerve gives rise to three dorsal digital nerves.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The dorsal digital nerves (from the dorsal branch) provide cutaneous innervation to the skin of the medial half of the back of hand and the skin of the dorsal aspect of the medial two and half fingers. Note that the terminal parts of the dorsal aspect of the digits are supplied by the median nerve.

21516.name: Dorsal Digital Branches of Radial Nerve
alternate: Radial Dorsal Digital Nerves of Hand

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial branch of radial nerve.

Course: Descend as four dorsal digital nerves.

Branches: None.

Supply: Cutaneous innervation to the dorsal surface of the proximal and middle phalanges of the lateral three digits.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial terminal branch of the radial nerve divides into four dorsal digital branches upon reaching the dorsum of the hand (C6—C8 spinal segments).

sections.title: Course
sections.text: In the lower one third of the forearm, the superficial terminal branch of the radial nerve passes backwards underneath the tendon of brachioradialis muscle. As it winds around the radial bone, it pierces the deep fascia to reach the dorsum of the hand. It provides cutaneous innervation to the skin of the dorsum of the hand and divides into four dorsal digital branches to further supply the skin of the digits.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Sensory nerve fibers from the skin of the dorsum of the hand and digits ascend through the superficial terminal branch and the dorsal digital branches of the radial nerve to eventually convey the information into the C6—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial nerve (C6—C8).

Course: Descends in the posterior forearm. Passes underneath the brachioradialis tendon to reach the dorsum of hand. 

Branches: Four dorsal digital branches.

Supply: Skin of dorsum of hand and proximal parts of the dorsal surfaces of the thumb, index finger, and lateral half of the middle finger.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The radial nerve terminally divides into its two superficial and deep branches in the cubital fossa at the level of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. The superficial branch contains sensory nerve fibers from the C6—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial terminal branch runs inferiorly on the anterior aspect of the forearm. It is closely related to the radial artery at the middle one third of the forearm. In the upper one third, it is widely separated from the artery, while in the lower one third it passes backwards underneath the tendon of brachioradialis muscle and winds around the radial bone to reach the dorsum of the hand.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Upon reaching the dorsum of the hand, the superficial branch of the radial nerve divides into four dorsal digital branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The superficial terminal branch is purely cutaneous and is distributed to the lateral half of the dorsum of the hand and to the proximal parts of the dorsal surfaces of the thumb, index finger, and lateral half of the middle finger.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve (C7-C8).

Course: Descends between the two heads of the supinator muscle, along the interosseous membrane of the forearm to innervate the muscles of the dorsal forearm.

Branches: Muscular and articular branches.

Supply: Most of the muscles on the dorsal surface of the forearm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior interosseous nerve of the forearm is a continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve as it passes between the two heads of supinator muscle. The nerve changes its name to posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve after it has crossed the supinator muscle. It contains motor fibers which originate from the anterior horns of the C7-C8 cervical segments of the spinal cord.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep branch of the radial nerve is one of the two terminal branches of the radial nerve given off inside the cubital fossa. The deep branch enters the back of the forearm by passing through the supinator muscle. It emerges through the muscle and descends further as the posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve between the superficial and deep layers of the extensor muscles of the forearm. At the lower border of extensor pollicis brevis muscle, it passes deep to extensor pollicis longus. It then runs on the posterior surface of the interosseous membrane to the wrist, where it enlarges into a pseudoganglion in the fourth compartment of the extensor retinaculum. It ends by innervating the radiocarpal (wrist) and intercarpal joints.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Muscular branches are given off the posterior interosseous nerve of the forearm to the deep muscles in the posterior compartment of the forearm. In addition, it also gives off articular and sensory branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
The posterior interosseous nerve of the forearm supplies muscles on the dorsal aspect of the forearm, including extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris, supinator muscle, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus, and extensor indicis.

The posterior interosseous nerve of the forearm provides articular branches to the wrist, the distal radioulnar, and intercarpal joints. Sensory branches are given to the interosseous membrane, radius, and ulna.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Supinator syndrome (Bonfiglioli, Mattioli and Violante, 2015)

sections.title: References
sections.text: Bonfiglioli, R., Mattioli, S. and Violante, F. S. (2015) 'Occupational mononeuropathies in industry', Handb Clin Neurol, 131, pp. 411-26.

18793.name: Anterior Branch of Medial Antebrachial Cutaneous Nerve
18793.latin: Ramus anterior nervi cutanei medialis antebrachii
alternate: Anterior Branch of Medial Cutaneous Nerve of Forearm
Ramus anterior nervi cutanei antebrachii medialis
Ramus volaris nervi cutanei antebrachii medialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm (C8—T1).

Course: Descends on the anteromedial aspect of the forearm.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Skin of the anteromedial aspects of the forearm as far as the wrist.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve arises from the medial cord of brachial plexus and divides into anterior and posterior terminal branches (C8—T1 spinal segments).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve is a large nerve that arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus. It descends in the anterior compartment of the arm along with the ulnar nerve and medial to the axillary and brachial artery. The nerve then pierces the deep fascia at approximately the mid-arm, alongside the basilic vein to enter the subcutaneous tissues of the forearm. The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve divides into anterior and posterior (or volar and ulnar) terminal branches.

The anterior branch (volar branch) of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve is typically larger than the posterior branch and usually passes anteriorly to the basilic vein. The nerve then descends on the anteromedial aspect of the forearm distributing small cutaneous branches to the ulnar side of the forearm as far as the wrist.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Distally the anterior branch communicates with the palmar cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve. The nerve fibers from the anterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve eventually end up relaying sensory information to the C8 and T1 segments of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior branch of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve provides cutaneous sensory innervation to the skin of the ulnar side of the forearm and wrist.

16930.name: Posterior Branch of Medial Antebrachial Cutaneous Nerve
16930.latin: Ramus posterior nervi cutanei medialis antebrachii
alternate: Posterior Branch of Medial Cutaneous Nerve of Forearm
Ramus posterior nervi cutanei antebrachii medialis
Ramus ulnaris nervi cutanei antebrachii medialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve (C8—T1).

Course: Descends along the posterior aspect of the forearm.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Skin of the medial portion of the proximal two thirds of the dorsal side of the forearm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve arises from the medial cord of brachial plexus and divides into anterior and posterior terminal branches (C8—T1 spinal segments).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve is a large nerve that arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus. It descends in the anterior compartment of the arm along with the ulnar nerve and medial to the axillary and brachial artery. The nerve then pierces the deep fascia at approximately the mid-arm, alongside the basilic vein to enter the subcutaneous tissues of the forearm. The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve divides into anterior and posterior (or volar and ulnar) terminal branches.

The posterior branch (ulnar branch) passes obliquely down along the medial side of the basilic vein to the posterior aspect of the forearm and descends on its ulnar side giving off small cutaneous terminal branches along its course.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The posterior branch communicates with the medial brachial cutaneous nerve and the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve, a branch of the radial nerve.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior branch of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve provides cutaneous sensory innervation to the skin of the medial portion of the proximal two thirds of the dorsal side of the forearm.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C6).

Course: Emerges from the lateral intermuscular septum between the biceps and brachialis muscles.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Skin of lateral forearm.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve (or lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm) is a continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve in the distal arm. It contains sensory nerve fibers for the C5—C7 spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve emerges from the lateral intermuscular septum between the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles, traveling from medial to lateral. It pierces the deep fascia in the roof of the cubital fossa, lateral to the biceps tendon and deep to the cephalic vein, about 2–3 cm above the bend of the elbow. The nerve further descends along the radial border of forearm down to the wrist where it lies anterior to the radial artery.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve gives off filaments that extend to the thenar eminence as cutaneous rami.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve provides cutaneous sensory innervation to skin of lateral forearm.

23139.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus
23139.latin: Ramus musculi radialis longi extensoris carpi nervi radialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep branch of radial nerve (C6—C7).

Course: Arises from the radial nerve as it reaches the cubital fossa.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Extensor carpi radialis longus muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A motor nerve branch to extensor carpi radialis longus muscle originates from the deep branch of the radial nerve and contains motor nerve fibers from the C6—C7 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep branch is a terminal branch of radial nerve given off in the cubital fossa, at the level of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. The nerve leaves the cubital fossa and enters the back of the forearm by passing between the two planes of fibers of the supinator muscle. Before piercing the supinator, branches are given to the brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, and the supinator.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of the radial nerve to extensor carpi radialis longus provides motor innervation to the extensor carpi radialis longus muscle.

17540.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Extensor Indicis
17540.latin: Ramus musculi extensoris indicis nervi radialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve (C7-C8).

Course: Arises from the posterior interosseous nerve as it descends and emerges distally from the supinator muscle.

Branches: None.

Supply: Extensor indicis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A motor nerve branch to extensor indicis muscle originates from the posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve (distal continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve). It contains motor nerve fibers from the C7—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve is a continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve as it passes between the two heads of supinator muscle. The nerve changes its name to posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve after it has crossed the supinator muscle. It contains motor fibers which originate from the anterior horns of the C7-C8 cervical segments of the spinal cord. As it descends in the forearm, it gives of muscular branches to the extensor muscles of the forearm including extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris, supinator muscle, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus, and extensor indicis.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscle branch of radial nerve to extensor indicis provides motor innervation to extensor indicis muscle.

16996.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Supinator

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve (C7-C8).

Course: Arises from the posterior interosseous nerve as it descends and emerges distally from the supinator muscle.

Branches: None.

Supply: Supinator muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A motor nerve branch to supinator muscle originates from the posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve (distal continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve). It contains motor nerve fibers from the C7—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve is a continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve as it passes between the two heads of supinator muscle. The nerve changes its name to posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve after it has crossed the supinator muscle. It contains motor fibers which originate from the anterior horns of the C7-C8 cervical segments of the spinal cord. As it descends in the forearm, it gives of muscular branches to the extensor muscles of the forearm including extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris, supinator muscle, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus, and extensor indicis.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscle branch of radial nerve to supinator provides motor innervation to the supinator muscle.

24360.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Extensor Pollicis Brevis
24360.latin: Ramus musculi extensoris pollicis brevis nervi radialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve (C7-C8).

Course: Arises from the posterior interosseous nerve as it descends and emerges distally from the supinator muscle.

Branches: None.

Supply: Extensor pollicis brevis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A motor nerve branch to extensor pollicis brevis muscle originates from the posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve (distal continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve). It contains motor nerve fibers from the C7—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve is a continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve as it passes between the two heads of supinator muscle. The nerve changes its name to posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve after it has crossed the supinator muscle. It contains motor fibers which originate from the anterior horns of the C7-C8 cervical segments of the spinal cord. As it descends in the forearm, it gives of muscular branches to the extensor muscles of the forearm including extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris, supinator muscle, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus, and extensor indicis.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscle branch of radial nerve to extensor pollicis brevis provides motor innervation to extensor pollicis brevis muscle.

21894.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Brachioradialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Radial nerve (C5-C6).

Course: Arises from the radial nerve as it reaches the cubital fossa.

Branches: No named branches.

Supply: Brachioradialis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A motor nerve branch to brachioradialis muscle originates from the radial nerve and contains motor nerve fibers from the C5—C6 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
In the upper part of the arm, it descends posterolaterally (with the profunda brachii vessels) through the lower triangular space, between the shaft of the humerus, long head of triceps brachii, and teres major muscles. The nerve then enters the radial groove along with the profunda brachii vessels. It descends downwards and laterally between the lateral and medial heads of the triceps muscle, while in contact with the humerus.

In the lower part of the arm, it pierces the lateral intermuscular septum and passes into the anterior compartment of the arm to reach the cubital fossa where it lies between the brachialis muscle medially and brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus muscles laterally. The radial nerve then passes deep to the brachioradialis muscle in the posterior compartment of the forearm and gives off a branch to the muscle before splitting into its superficial and deep terminal branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscular branch of the radial nerve to brachioradialis provides motor innervation to the brachioradialis muscle.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Inverted brachioradialis (inverted supinator) reflex (McGee, 2016)

sections.title: References
sections.text: McGee, S. (2016) Evidence-Based Physical Diagnosis E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences.

17709.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis
17709.latin: Ramus musculi radialis brevi extensoris carpi nervi radialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep branch of radial nerve (C7—C8).

Course: Descends and emerges distally from the supinator muscle.

Branches: None.

Supply: Extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A motor nerve branch to extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle originates from the deep branch of radial nerve. It contains motor nerve fibers from the C7—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep branch is a terminal branch of radial nerve given off in the cubital fossa, at the level of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. The nerve leaves the cubital fossa and enters the back of the forearm by passing between the two planes of fibers of the supinator muscle. Before piercing the supinator, branches are given to the brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, and the supinator.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscle branch of radial nerve to extensor carpi radialis brevis provides motor innervation to the extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle.

21439.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Extensor Carpi Ulnaris
21439.latin: Ramus musculi extensoris carpi ulnaris nervi radialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve (C7-C8). 

Course: Arises from the posterior interosseous nerve as it descends and emerges distally from the supinator muscle. 

Branches: None. 

Supply: Extensor carpi ulnaris muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A motor nerve branch to extensor carpi ulnaris muscle originates from the posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve (distal continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve). It contains motor nerve fibers from the C7—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve is a continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve as it passes between the two heads of supinator muscle. The nerve changes its name to posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve after it has crossed the supinator muscle. It contains motor fibers which originate from the anterior horns of the C7-C8 cervical segments of the spinal cord. As it descends in the forearm, it gives of muscular branches to the extensor muscles of the forearm including extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris, supinator muscle, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus, and extensor indicis.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The muscle branch of radial nerve to extensor carpi ulnaris provides motor innervation to extensor carpi ulnaris muscle.

17644.name: Muscular Branch of Radial Nerve to Abductor Pollicis Longus
17644.latin: Ramus musculi abductor pollicis longi nervi radialis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve (C7-C8).

Course: Arises from the posterior interosseous nerve as it descends and emerges distally from the supinator muscle.

Branches: None.

Supply: Abductor pollicis longus muscle.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: A motor nerve branch to abductor pollicis longus muscle originates from the posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve (distal continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve). It contains motor nerve fibers from the C7—C8 cervical spinal segments.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve is a continuation of the deep branch of radial nerve as it passes between the two heads of supinator muscle. The nerve changes its name to posterior antebrachial interosseous nerve after it has crossed the supinator muscle. It contains motor fibers which originate from the anterior horns of the C7-C8 cervical segments of the spinal cord. As it descends in the forearm, it gives of muscular branches to the extensor muscles of the forearm including extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris, supinator muscle, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus, and extensor indicis.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
