It then enters the space between the internal intercostal and innermost intercostal muscles to course through the tenth intercostal space. It is also accompanied by an intercostal artery and vein, where the vein sits closest to the rib above, followed by the artery and nerve.

As the anterior rami of the seventh to eleventh thoracic nerves leave the intercostal space, they continue anteriorly into the abdominal wall. They course between the transversus abdominis and internal abdominal oblique muscles. They then enter the lateral margin of the rectus sheath, passing posterior to the rectus abdominis muscle. They pierce the rectus abdominis muscle and the anterior rectus sheath to pass anteriorly to the overlying skin.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
Near its origin, the anterior ramus of the tenth thoracic nerve gives off a collateral branch that descends in the intercostal space and courses along the inferior border of the space, in the same plane as the anterior ramus itself.

The lateral cutaneous branch of the anterior ramus of tenth thoracic nerve branches from the anterior ramus around the mid-axillary line. It briefly accompanies the nerve before piercing through the chest wall. The lateral branch further subdivides into anterior and posterior branches that supplying the overlying skin.

The anterior cutaneous branch arises as the anterior ramus of tenth thoracic nerve pierces the anterior rectus sheath.

sections.title: Supplied Structures & Function
sections.text: The anterior ramus of the tenth thoracic nerve supplies the intercostal muscles of the tenth intercostal space (external intercostal, internal intercostal, innermost intercostal). It also supplies motor innervation to most of the abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, external abdominal oblique, internal abdominal oblique, transversus abdominis) and sensory innervation from the anterolateral abdominal wall. Sensory fibers also extend to the costal parts of diaphragm and parietal peritoneum.

18461.name: Meningeal Branch of Spinal Nerve (Thoracic; Right)
alternate: Recurrent Branch of Spinal Nerve (Thoracic; Right)

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior ramus of spinal nerves.

Course: Passes backwards into the vertebral canal.

Branches: Ascending, descending, and transverse branches.

Supply: Posterior longitudinal ligament, vertebral bodies, intervertebral discs, ventral surface of the dural sac, dura mater along the clivus, and the atlantoaxial joint.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The meningeal branches occur at all vertebral levels and originate directly from the anterior rami of the spinal nerves, with contributions from the gray communicating branches (gray rami communicantes), except at cervical levels C1-C5. Therefore, most of the meningeal branches contain sensory and sympathetic fibers. The meningeal branches at C6 and C7 spinal levels receive contributions from the vertebral nerve.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Each meningeal branch passes backwards (recurrent pathway) from their origin through the intervertebral foramen to enter the vertebral canal. These branches will form a plexus on the ventral surface of the dural sac as well as provide innervation to the vertebral column ventral to the dural sac.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Each meningeal branch has ascending, descending, and transverse branches, each of which communicates with the corresponding branches above, below, and from the opposite side of the body.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The meningeal branches supply the ventral surface of the dural sac, periosteum of the vertebral bodies, posterior aspect of intervertebral discs, posterior longitudinal ligament, dura mater along the clivus, and atlantoaxial joint.

18482.name: Posterior Ramus of Sixth Thoracic Nerve
alternate: Dorsal Ramus of Sixth Thoracic Nerve
Posterior Ramus of Spinal Nerve T6

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Thoracic nerve.

Course: Posteriorly to the epaxial muscles.

Branches: Medial and lateral branches.

Supply: Motor innervation to the epaxial muscles. Sensory innervation to the zygapophyseal joints and skin overlying the dorsal thoracic region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior ramus is one of two branches of the thoracic nerve, the other being the anterior ramus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior ramus runs posteriorly and inferiorly from its origin just lateral to the intervertebral foramen between its corresponding numerical vertebra and the one below. The ramus passes inferior to the transverse process of its corresponding numerical vertebra, lateral to the zygapophyseal joint, and medial to the intertransverse ligament. Here, the posterior ramus divides into medial and lateral branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The specific targets and branching patterns of the posterior rami of thoracic nerves exhibit variability depending on vertebral level and individual. In general, the posterior rami of the thoracic nerves split into two major branches, one lateral and one medial. Both branches run posteriorly and inferiorly towards their targets.

sections.title: Supplied Structures & Function
sections.text:
The posterior rami of the thoracic nerves supply the epaxial musculature and skin dorsal to the thoracic vertebrae.

The lateral branches of the posterior rami of the thoracic nerves supply motor innervation to the iliocostalis and longissimus muscles, as well as sensory information from its targeted epaxial muscles. The lower lateral branches of the posterior rami (T7-T12) continue dorsally and inferiorly to pierce the superficial back muscles to reach the skin, in order to receive sensory information from the skin of the back (see our dermatome map for cutaneous innervation).

The medial branches of the dorsal rami of the thoracic nerves supply motor innervation to the intrinsic muscles of the back, including multifidus, semispinalis thoracis, spinalis thoracis, interspinales thoracis, and rotatores muscles. All medial branches provide an articular branch to the zygapophyseal joint. The upper medial branches of the posterior rami (T1-T6) continue dorsally and inferiorly to pierce the superficial back muscles to reach the skin, in order to receive sensory information from the skin of the back (see our dermatome map for cutaneous innervation).

17573.name: Lateral Branch of Posterior Ramus of Eighth Thoracic Nerve
17573.latin: Ramus posterior lateralis nervi thoracici octavi
alternate: Lateral Branch of Dorsal Ramus of Eighth Thoracic Nerve
Lateral Branch of Posterior Ramus of Spinal Nerve T8

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior ramus of the thoracic nerve.

Course: Crosses laterally to the costotransverse joint and then dorsally and inferiorly.

Branches: None.

Supply: Motor innervation to levator costarum, longissimus, and iliocostalis muscles; Lower lateral branches (T7-T12) provide sensory innervation to skin of back.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral branch is one of two branches that arise from of the posterior ramus of the thoracic nerves, the other being the medial branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Near the zygapophyseal joint, the posterior ramus of the thoracic nerve divides into medial and lateral branches. The lateral branch continues laterally, coursing between the superior costotransverse and intertransverse ligaments. As it reaches the medial border of levator costarum, the lateral branch travels inferoposteriorly. The upper lateral branches (T1-T6) remain intramuscular, while the lower lateral branches (T7-T12) continue to descend, piercing the serratus posterior inferior and latissimus dorsi muscles in line with the costal angles. These lower branches can descend a distance of four ribs to become cutaneous.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no branches of the upper lateral branches; however, the lower lateral branches become cutaneous nerves as they pierce the latissimus dorsi muscle to reach the skin of the lower back and anterior gluteal region.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The lateral branches of the posterior rami of thoracic nerves primarily supply motor innervation to the iliocostalis and longissimus muscles. The upper lateral branches of the posterior rami (T1-T6) convey sensory innervation from its target epaxial muscles, while the lower lateral branches (T7-T12) provide sensory innervation from the skin of the back and anterior gluteal region. See our dermatome map for cutaneous innervation.

16901.name: Lateral Branch of Posterior Ramus of Fourth Thoracic Nerve

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior ramus of the thoracic nerve.

Course: Crosses laterally to the costotransverse joint and then dorsally and inferiorly.

Branches: None.

Supply: Motor innervation to levator costarum, longissimus, and iliocostalis muscles; Lower lateral branches (T7-T12) provide sensory innervation to skin of back.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral branch is one of two branches that arise from of the posterior ramus of the thoracic nerves, the other being the medial branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Near the zygapophyseal joint, the posterior ramus of the thoracic nerve divides into medial and lateral branches. The lateral branch continues laterally, coursing between the superior costotransverse and intertransverse ligaments. As it reaches the medial border of levator costarum, the lateral branch travels inferoposteriorly. The upper lateral branches (T1-T6) remain intramuscular, while the lower lateral branches (T7-T12) continue to descend, piercing the serratus posterior inferior and latissimus dorsi muscles in line with the costal angles. These lower branches can descend a distance of four ribs to become cutaneous.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no branches of the upper lateral branches; however, the lower lateral branches become cutaneous nerves as they pierce the latissimus dorsi muscle to reach the skin of the lower back and anterior gluteal region.

18916.name: Posterior Ramus of Third Thoracic Nerve
alternate: Dorsal Ramus of Third Thoracic Nerve
Posterior Ramus of Spinal Nerve T3

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Thoracic nerve.

Course: Posteriorly to the epaxial muscles.

Branches: Medial and lateral branches.

Supply: Motor innervation to the epaxial muscles. Sensory innervation to the zygapophyseal joints and skin overlying the dorsal thoracic region.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior ramus is one of two branches of the thoracic nerve, the other being the anterior ramus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The posterior ramus runs posteriorly and inferiorly from its origin just lateral to the intervertebral foramen between its corresponding numerical vertebra and the one below. The ramus passes inferior to the transverse process of its corresponding numerical vertebra, lateral to the zygapophyseal joint, and medial to the intertransverse ligament. Here, the posterior ramus divides into medial and lateral branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The specific targets and branching patterns of the posterior rami of thoracic nerves exhibit variability depending on vertebral level and individual. In general, the posterior rami of the thoracic nerves split into two major branches, one lateral and one medial. Both branches run posteriorly and inferiorly towards their targets.

sections.title: Supplied Structures & Function
sections.text:
The posterior rami of the thoracic nerves supply the epaxial musculature and skin dorsal to the thoracic vertebrae.

The lateral branches of the posterior rami of the thoracic nerves supply motor innervation to the iliocostalis and longissimus muscles, as well as sensory information from its targeted epaxial muscles. The lower lateral branches of the posterior rami (T7-T12) continue dorsally and inferiorly to pierce the superficial back muscles to reach the skin, in order to receive sensory information from the skin of the back (see our dermatome map for cutaneous innervation).

The medial branches of the dorsal rami of the thoracic nerves supply motor innervation to the intrinsic muscles of the back, including multifidus, semispinalis thoracis, spinalis thoracis, interspinales thoracis, and rotatores muscles. All medial branches provide an articular branch to the zygapophyseal joint. The upper medial branches of the posterior rami (T1-T6) continue dorsally and inferiorly to pierce the superficial back muscles to reach the skin, in order to receive sensory information from the skin of the back (see our dermatome map for cutaneous innervation).

The ramus passes inferior to the transverse process of its corresponding numerical vertebra, lateral to the zygapophyseal joint, and medial to the intertransverse ligament. Here, the posterior ramus divides into medial and lateral branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The specific targets and branching patterns of the posterior rami of thoracic nerves exhibit variability depending on vertebral level and individual. In general, the posterior rami of the thoracic nerves split into two major branches, one lateral and one medial. Both branches run posteriorly and inferiorly towards their targets.

sections.title: Supplied Structures & Function
sections.text:
The posterior rami of the thoracic nerves supply the epaxial musculature and skin dorsal to the thoracic vertebrae.

The lateral branches of the posterior rami of the thoracic nerves supply motor innervation to the iliocostalis and longissimus muscles, as well as sensory information from its targeted epaxial muscles. The lower lateral branches of the posterior rami (T7-T12) continue dorsally and inferiorly to pierce the superficial back muscles to reach the skin, in order to receive sensory information from the skin of the back (see our dermatome map for cutaneous innervation).

The medial branches of the dorsal rami of the thoracic nerves supply motor innervation to the intrinsic muscles of the back, including multifidus, semispinalis thoracis, spinalis thoracis, interspinales thoracis, and rotatores muscles. All medial branches provide an articular branch to the zygapophyseal joint. The upper medial branches of the posterior rami (T1-T6) continue dorsally and inferiorly to pierce the superficial back muscles to reach the skin, in order to receive sensory information from the skin of the back (see our dermatome map for cutaneous innervation).

sections.title: Quick Facts

Course: Posteriorly to the epaxial muscles.

Branches: Medial and lateral branches.

Medial Branch of Posterior Ramus of Spinal Nerve T8

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior ramus of the thoracic nerve.

Course: Extends laterally over the transverse process of underlying vertebra, then passes medially between semispinalis thoracis and multifidus muscles.

Branches: Articular and cutaneous branches.

Supply: Motor innervation to intrinsic muscles of the back. Sensory innervation to zygapophyseal joints and to skin of the back (T1-T6).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial branch is one of two branches that arise from of the posterior ramus of the thoracic nerves, the other being the lateral branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
Near the zygapophyseal joint, the posterior ramus of the thoracic nerve divides into medial and lateral branches. The medial branches continue laterally, briefly, to extend over the transverse process of the underlying vertebra. They then turn inferiorly and medially, coursing between the multifidus and semispinalis muscles.

The upper medial branches (T1-T6) continue to travel inferomedially, piercing through the rhomboid and trapezius muscles to reach the skin, adjacent to the spinous processes of the vertebrae. The lower medial branches (T7-T12) remain intramuscular, however, occasionally supply filaments to the skin.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The medial branches give rise to articular branches. The upper medial branches (T1-T6) also give rise to cutaneous branches as they pierce through the rhomboid and trapezius muscles to access the skin.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The medial branches of the posterior rami of thoracic nerves primarily supply motor innervation to the intrinsic muscles of the back, including multifidus, semispinalis thoracis, spinalis thoracis, interspinales thoracis, and rotatores muscles. Course: Laterally a short distance to the bifurcation of anterior and posterior rami.

Supply: The posterior ramus supplies motor innervation to the epaxial muscles. It conveys sensory innervation from the skin over the mid-dorsal trunk. The anterior ramus supplies motor innervation to the muscles of the sixth intercostal space and superior abdomen. It conveys sensory innervation from the skin of the anterolateral thoracic and anterior abdominal walls.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The sixth thoracic nerve is formed when the posterior and anterior roots of the sixth thoracic nerve merge, roughly in the intervertebral foramen between the T6 and T7 vertebrae.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The sixth thoracic nerve runs only a very short distance laterally, from its origin at the merger of posterior and anterior roots, to its bifurcation into posterior and anterior rami. This all occurs in or lateral to the intervertebral foramen between the T6 and T7 vertebrae.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The sixth thoracic nerve gives rise to two branches or rami: the anterior and posterior. The anterior and posterior rami carry all somatic motor and sensory innervation from the sixth thoracic spinal level as well as the sympathetic fibers associated with tissue targeted by this nerve.

The posterior ramus runs posteriorly to the epaxial musculature overlying the T6-T7 vertebrae, where it gives off both lateral and medial branches.

The anterior ramus (or sixth intercostal nerve) remains in the sixth intercostal space, running between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles.

sections.title: Supplied Structures & Function
sections.text:
The sixth thoracic spinal nerve splits into two branches: the posterior and anterior rami.

The posterior ramus conveys motor innervation to the epaxial muscles epaxial muscle, including the erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis), transversospinal (rotatores, multifidus, semispinalis), and deep segmental back muscles (interspinales, levatores costarum). The posterior ramus conveys sensory innervation from the skin of the back. See dermatome map for cutaneous distribution.

The anterior ramus (or sixth intercostal nerve) supplies the intercostal muscles of the sixth intercostal space (external, internal, and innermost intercostal muscles), and transversus thoracis muscle. In addition, it provides motor innervation to the most superior fibers of the rectus abdominis and external abdominal oblique muscles. Sensory innervation is received from the skin of the anterolateral thoracic and abdominal walls.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The second thoracic nerve is formed when the posterior and anterior roots of the second thoracic nerve merge, roughly in the intervertebral foramen between the T2 and T3 vertebrae.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The second thoracic nerve runs only a very short distance laterally, from its origin at the merger of posterior and anterior roots, to its bifurcation into posterior and anterior rami. This all occurs in or lateral to the intervertebral foramen between the T2 and T3 vertebrae.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The second thoracic nerve gives rise to two branches or rami: the anterior and posterior rami. The anterior and posterior rami carry all somatic motor and sensory innervation from the second thoracic spinal level as well as the sympathetic fibers associated with tissue targeted by this nerve.

The posterior ramus runs posteriorly to the epaxial musculature overlying the T2-T3 vertebrae, where it gives off both lateral and medial branches.

The anterior ramus forms the second intercostal nerve. This nerve remains in the second intercostal space, running between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles.

The second intercostal nerve gives off a lateral cutaneous branch that pierces the musculature of the second thoracic space. Unlike the lateral cutaneous branches of most other intercostal nerves, the lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve runs through the axilla to supply sensory innervation from the skin of the medial and posterior arm. This branch is called the intercostobrachial nerve.

sections.title: Supplied Structures & Function
sections.text:
The second thoracic nerve splits into two branches: the posterior and anterior rami.

The posterior ramus conveys motor innervation to the epaxial muscles epaxial muscle, including the erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis), transversospinal (rotatores, multifidus, semispinalis), and deep segmental back muscles (interspinales, levatores costarum). The posterior ramus conveys sensory innervation from the skin of the back. See dermatome map for cutaneous distribution.

The anterior ramus (or second intercostal nerve) supplies the intercostal muscles of the second intercostal space (external, internal, and innermost intercostal muscles), transversus thoracis, and serratus posterior superior, and the skin of the anterolateral thoracic wall.

The lateral cutaneous branch of the anterior ramus continues laterally, piercing the external and internal intercostal and serratus anterior muscles, to enter the axilla. Known as the intercostobrachial nerve, it conveys sensory information from the skin of the medial arm and axilla.

The anterior ramus (or subcostal nerve) runs inferior to the twelfth rib, coursing anterior to the quadratus lumborum muscle before passing between the transversus abdominis and internal abdominal oblique muscles. An early branch of the subcostal nerve merges with the iliohypogastric nerve to contribute to the sensory and motor innervation of that nerve.

The posterior ramus conveys sensory innervation from the skin of the back and anterior gluteal region. See dermatome map for cutaneous distribution.

The anterior ramus (or subcostal nerve) supplies motor innervation to the serratus posterior inferior muscle, abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, external abdominal oblique, internal abdominal oblique, transversus abdominis, pyramidalis), and hip flexors (psoas major, quadratus lumborum, iliacus). The communicating branch of the subcostal nerve that joins with the iliohypogastric nerve and can carry some of the sensation from the lateral gluteal region. sections.text: The first thoracic nerve is formed when the posterior and anterior roots of the first thoracic nerve merge, roughly in the intervertebral foramen between the T1 and T2 vertebrae.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The first thoracic nerve gives rise to two branches or rami: the anterior and posterior rami. The anterior and posterior rami carry all somatic motor and sensory innervation from the first thoracic spinal level as well as the sympathetic fibers associated with tissue targeted by this nerve.

The posterior ramus runs posteriorly to the epaxial musculature overlying the T1-T2 vertebrae, where it gives off both lateral and medial branches.

The anterior ramus forms two nerves. The bulkier nerve forms the inferior root of inferior trunk of the branchial plexus. It runs laterally out of the thorax to merge with fibers of the eighth cervical anterior ramus, thus forming the inferior trunk of the brachial plexus. These fibers contribute to the median, radial, ulnar, and medial pectoral nerves, as well as the medial brachial and antebrachial cutaneous nerves.

The smaller branch of the anterior ramus forms the first intercostal nerve, which remains in the first intercostal space. It courses between the internal intercostal and the innermost intercostal muscles.

The first intercostal nerve, which arises from the anterior ramus, supplies the intercostal muscles of the first intercostal space (external intercostal, internal intercostal, innermost intercostal), and the skin of the anterolateral thoracic wall.

The larger inferior root of the inferior trunk of the branchial plexus, which arises from the anterior ramus of first thoracic nerve contributes both motor and sensory innervation to the upper limb.

20200.name: Lateral Basal Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung
20200.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis lateralis pulmonis sinistri
alternate: Lateral Basal Tertiary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The lateral basal segmental bronchus (B9) is one of four segmental bronchi that arise from the inferior lobar bronchus. The others include the superior, posterior basal, and anteromedial basal segmental bronchi. It descends laterally and provides an airway to the lateral basal bronchopulmonary segment (S9) of the inferior lobe of the left lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lateral basal segmental bronchus is accompanied by the lateral basal segmental artery of the left lung.

18078.name: Left Inferior Lobar Bronchus
alternate: Inferior Lobar Bronchus of Left Lung
Inferior Secondary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The left inferior lobar bronchus arises as a branch of the left main bronchus. It descends posterolaterally to enter the inferior lobe of the left lung. Initially, the left inferior lobar bronchus gives off the superior segmental bronchus posteriorly. The left inferior lobar bronchus continues inferiorly, giving off an anteromedial basal segmental bronchus and finally the posterior and lateral basal segmental bronchi. These bronchial branches ensure each bronchopulmonary segment of the inferior lobe of the left lung is supplied with an airway.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The left inferior lobar bronchus is accompanied by the inferior lobar artery and its continuation as the basal part of the inferior lobar artery. The left inferior lobar bronchus may give rise to a subsuperior (or subapical) segmental bronchus, just below the origin of the superior segmental bronchus. The anterior basal segmental branch may arise from the left inferior lobar bronchus, independent from the medial basal segmental bronchus (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

18625.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis posterior pulmonis sinistri
alternate: Posterior Basal Tertiary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The posterior basal segmental bronchus (B10) is one of four segmental bronchi that arise from the inferior lobar bronchus. The others include the superior, anteromedial basal, and lateral basal segmental bronchi. It descends posteriorly and provides an airway to the posterior basal bronchopulmonary segment (S10) of the inferior lobe of the left lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The posterior basal segmental bronchus is accompanied by the posterior basal segmental artery of the left lung.

23332.name: Anteromedial Basal Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung
23332.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis anteromedialis pulmonis sinistri
alternate: Anteromedial Tertiary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The anteromedial basal segmental bronchus (B7+8) is one of four segmental bronchi that arise from the inferior lobar bronchus. The others include the superior, posterior basal, and lateral basal segmental bronchi. It descends anteriorly and divides into medial and anterior segmental bronchi. The medial and anterior segmental bronchi provide airways to the medial (S7) and anterior (S8) bronchopulmonary segments of the inferior lobe of the left lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anteromedial basal segmental bronchus is accompanied by the anteromedial basal segmental artery of the left lung.

22460.name: Superior Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung
alternate: Superior Tertiary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The superior segmental bronchus (B6) is one of four segmental bronchi that arise from the inferior lobar bronchus. The others include the anteromedial, lateral, and posterior basal segmental bronchi. It passes posteriorly to provides an airway to the superior bronchopulmonary segment (S6) of the inferior lobe of the left lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The superior segmental bronchus is accompanied by the superior segmental artery of the left lung.

19897.name: Medial Basal Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung
19897.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis medialis pulmonis sinistri
alternate: Medial Basal Tertiary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The medial basal segmental bronchus (B8) arises from the anteromedial basal segmental bronchus of the inferior lobar bronchus. It descends anteromedially and provides an airway to the medial basal bronchopulmonary segment (S7) of the inferior lobe of the left lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The medial basal segmental bronchus is accompanied by the medial basal segmental artery of the left lung.

17795.name: Anterior Basal Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung
17795.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis anterior pulmonis sinistri
alternate: Anterior Basal Tertiary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The anterior basal segmental bronchus (B8) arises from the anteromedial basal segmental bronchus of the inferior lobar bronchus. It descends anterolaterally and provides an airway to the anterior basal bronchopulmonary segment (S8) of the inferior lobe of the left lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anterior basal segmental bronchus is accompanied by the anterior basal segmental artery of the left lung.

17055.name: Left Superior Lobar Bronchus
alternate: Superior Lobar Bronchus of Left Lung
Superior Secondary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The left superior lobar bronchus arises as a branch of the left main bronchus. It passes anterolaterally to enter the hilum of the left lung, and consequently, the superior lobe of the left lung. The left superior lobar bronchus divides into superior and inferior divisions, both of which supply the superior lobe of the left lung. The superior division supplies most of the superior lobe, while the inferior division, the lingular bronchus, supplies the ligula of the left lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The left superior lobar bronchus is accompanied by the left superior lobar artery of the left lung.

22372.name: Anterior Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung
alternate: Anterior Tertiary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The anterior segmental bronchus (B3) is one of two segmental bronchi that arise from the superior division bronchus. The other branch is the apicoposterior segmental bronchus. The anterior segmental bronchus passes anteriorly to provide an airway to the anterior (S3) bronchopulmonary segment of the superior lobe of the left lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anterior segmental bronchus is accompanied by the anterior segmental artery of the left lung.

17387.name: Apicoposterior Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung
alternate: Apicoposterior Tertiary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The apicoposterior segmental bronchus (B1+2) is one of two segmental bronchi that arise from the superior division bronchus. The other branch is the anterior segmental bronchus. The apicoposterior segmental bronchus passes superiorly and divides into apical and posterior segmental bronchi. These provide airways to the apical (S1) and posterior (S2) bronchopulmonary segment of the superior lobe of the left lung, respectively.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The apicoposterior segmental bronchus is accompanied by the apicoposterior segmental artery of the left lung.

21090.name: Inferior Lingular Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung
21090.latin: Bronchus segmentalis lingularis inferior pulmonis sinistri
alternate: Inferior Lingular Tertiary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The inferior lingular segmental bronchus (B5) is one of two segmental bronchi that arise from the common lingular bronchus. The other branch is the superior lingular segmental bronchus. The inferior lingular segmental bronchus passes anteroinferiorly to provide an airway to the inferior lingular bronchopulmonary segment (S5) of the superior lobe of the left lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The inferior lingular segmental bronchus is accompanied by the inferior lingular segmental artery of the left lung.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The lingular bronchus is one of the two terminal branches of the left superior lobar bronchus, the other being the superior division bronchus. It descends anterolaterally to enter the lingula of the left lung. The lingular bronchus bifurcates into superior and inferior lingular segmental bronchi.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lingular bronchus is accompanied by the lingular artery of the left lung.

19748.name: Superior Division Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The superior division bronchus is one of the two terminal branches of the left superior lobar bronchus, the other being the lingular bronchus. It ascends laterally, giving off the apicoposterior and anterior segmental bronchi.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The superior division bronchus is accompanied by the superior lobar artery of the left lung.

23564.name: Superior Lingular Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung
23564.latin: Bronchus segmentalis lingularis superior pulmonis sinistri
alternate: Superior Lingular Tertiary Bronchus of Left Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The superior lingular segmental bronchus (B4) is one of two segmental bronchi that arise from the common lingular bronchus. The other branch is the inferior lingular segmental bronchus. The superior lingular segmental bronchus passes anteriorly and slightly superiorly to provide an airway to the superior lingular bronchopulmonary segment (S4) of the superior lobe of the left lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The superior lingular segmental bronchus is accompanied by the superior lingular segmental artery of the left lung.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The left main bronchus is formed at the bifurcation of the trachea into right and left main bronchi around the level of the sternal angle. It passes inferolaterally to reach the hilum of the left lung at the level of the sixth thoracic vertebra. Here, it divides into two lobar (or secondary) bronchi, the superior and inferior lobar bronchi.

The left main bronchus is narrower and twice as long as the right main bronchus. Additionally, it travels more horizontally than the right main bronchus; thus, inhaled objects are more likely to become lodged in the right main bronchus.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
As the left main bronchus courses from its origin at the distal end of the trachea to the hilum of the left lung, it passes under the aortic arch. Additionally, the left main bronchus passes anterior to the descending thoracic aorta and thoracic duct and is accompanied by the pulmonary artery and veins.

The left main bronchus forms part of the root of the lung. As it enters the hilum of the left lung, it lies inferior to the left pulmonary artery, posterior to the left superior pulmonary vein, and superior to the left inferior pulmonary vein.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The bronchus intermedius is simply a continuation of the right main bronchus, distal to the origin of the superior lobar bronchus. It quickly gives rise to the middle and inferior lobar bronchi, which supply middle and inferior lobes of the right lung, respectively. Additionally, a subsuperior (or subapical) segmental bronchus may arise from the bronchus intermedius or the right inferior lobar bronchus, just below the origin of the superior segmental bronchus. This bronchus is distributed between the superior and posterior basal bronchopulmonary segments (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

18473.name: Right Inferior Lobar Bronchus
alternate: Inferior Lobar Bronchus of Right Lung
Inferior Secondary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The right inferior lobar bronchus arises as a continuation of the bronchus intermedius, past the origin of the middle lobar bronchus. The right inferior lobar bronchus passes inferolaterally and slightly posterior to enter the inferior lobe of the right lung. Initially, a large superior segmental bronchus arises from the right inferior lobar bronchus posteriorly. The right inferior lobar bronchus continues inferiorly, giving off several basal segmental branches, including the medial, anterior, lateral, and posterior basal segmental bronchi. These bronchial branches ensure each bronchopulmonary segment of the inferior lobe of the right lung is supplied with an airway.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The right inferior lobar bronchus is accompanied by the inferior lobar artery and its continuation as the basal part of the inferior lobar artery. A subsuperior (or subapical) segmental bronchus may arise from the right inferior lobar bronchus or the bronchus intermedius, just below the origin of the superior segmental bronchus. This bronchus is distributed between the superior and posterior basal bronchopulmonary segments (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

24771.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis anterior pulmonis dextri
alternate: Anterior Basal Tertiary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The anterior basal segmental bronchus (B8) is one of five segmental bronchi that arise from the inferior lobar bronchus. The others include the superior, posterior basal, medial basal, and lateral basal segmental bronchi. It descends anteriorly and provides an airway to the anterior basal bronchopulmonary segment (S8) of the inferior lobe of the right lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anterior basal segmental bronchus is accompanied by the anterior basal segmental artery of the right lung.

16736.name: Superior Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
alternate: Apical Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
Superior Tertiary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The superior segmental bronchus (B6) is one of five segmental bronchi that arise from the inferior lobar bronchus. The others include the medial, anterior, lateral, and posterior basal segmental bronchi. It passes posteriorly and divides into medial, superior, and lateral branches. The superior segmental bronchus provides an airway to the superior bronchopulmonary segment (S6) of the inferior lobe of the right lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The superior segmental bronchus is accompanied by the superior segmental artery of the right lung.

22344.name: Medial Basal Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
22344.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis medialis pulmonis dextri

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The medial basal segmental bronchus (B7) is one of five segmental bronchi that arise from the inferior lobar bronchus. The others include the superior, posterior basal, anterior basal, and lateral basal segmental bronchi. It descends medially and provides an airway to the medial basal bronchopulmonary segment (S7) of the inferior lobe of the right lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The medial basal segmental bronchus is accompanied by the medial basal segmental artery of the right lung.

24914.name: Posterior Basal Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
24914.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis posterior pulmonis dextri
alternate: Posterior Basal Tertiary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The posterior basal segmental bronchus (B10) is one of five segmental bronchi that arise from the inferior lobar bronchus. The others include the superior, medial basal, anterior basal, and lateral basal segmental bronchi. It descends posteriorly and provides an airway to the posterior basal bronchopulmonary segment (S10) of the inferior lobe of the right lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The posterior basal segmental bronchus is accompanied by the posterior basal segmental artery of the right lung.

22881.name: Lateral Basal Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
22881.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis lateralis pulmonis dextri
alternate: Lateral Basal Tertiary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The lateral basal segmental bronchus (B9) is one of five segmental bronchi that arise from the inferior lobar bronchus. The others include the superior, posterior basal, anterior basal, and medial basal segmental bronchi. It descends laterally and provides an airway to the lateral basal bronchopulmonary segment (S9) of the inferior lobe of the right lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lateral basal segmental bronchus is accompanied by the lateral basal segmental artery of the right lung.

16997.name: Medial Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
alternate: Medial Tertiary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The medial segmental bronchus (B5) is one of two segmental bronchi that arise from the middle lobar bronchus, the other being the lateral segmental bronchus. It passes anteromedially to provide an airway to the medial bronchopulmonary segment (S5) of the middle lobe of the right lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anterior segmental bronchus is accompanied by the medial segmental artery of the right lung.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The middle lobar bronchus arises as a branch of the bronchus intermedius, a continuation of the right main bronchus. It passes anterolaterally to enter the middle lobe of the right lung. The middle lobar bronchus divides into the medial and lateral segmental bronchi, thus, providing each bronchopulmonary segment of the middle lobe of the right lung with an airway.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The middle lobar bronchus is accompanied by the middle lobar artery.

22096.name: Lateral Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
alternate: Lateral Tertiary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The lateral segmental bronchus (B4) is one of two segmental bronchi that arise from the middle lobar bronchus, the other being the medial segmental bronchus. It passes anterolaterally to provide an airway to the lateral bronchopulmonary segment (S4) of the middle lobe of the right lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anterior segmental bronchus is accompanied by the lateral segmental artery of the right lung.

20270.name: Posterior Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
alternate: Posterior Tertiary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The posterior segmental bronchus (B2) is one of three segmental bronchi that arise from the right superior lobar bronchus. The others include the apical and anterior segmental bronchi. It passes posterolaterally and slightly superiorly and terminated by dividing into lateral and posterior branches. The posterior segmental bronchus provides an airway to the posterior bronchopulmonary segment (S2) of the superior lobe of the right lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The posterior segmental bronchus is accompanied by the posterior segmental artery of the right lung.

24838.name: Anterior Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
alternate: Anterior Tertiary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The anterior segmental bronchus (B3) is one of three segmental bronchi that arise from the right superior lobar bronchus. The others include the posterior and apical segmental bronchi. It passes anteroinferiorly and terminates by dividing into lateral and anterior branches. The anterior segmental bronchus provides an airway to the anterior bronchopulmonary segment (S3) of the superior lobe of the right lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anterior segmental bronchus is accompanied by the anterior segmental artery of the right lung.

22773.name: Right Superior Lobar Bronchus
alternate: Superior Lobar Bronchus of Right Lung
Superior Secondary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The right superior lobar bronchus arises as a branch of the right main bronchus. It passes superolaterally and enters the hilum of the right lung, and consequently, the superior lobe of the right lung. The right superior lobar bronchus divides into three segmental bronchi, including the apical, anterior, and posterior segmental bronchi, thus, providing each bronchopulmonary segment of the superior lobe of the right lung with an airway.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The right superior lobar bronchus is accompanied by the right superior lobar artery.

17801.name: Apical Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
alternate: Apical Tertiary Bronchus of Right Lung

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The apical segmental bronchus (B1) is one of three segmental bronchi that arise from the right superior lobar bronchus. The others include the posterior and anterior segmental bronchi. It passes superolaterally towards the apex of the right lung and terminates by dividing into apical and anterior branches. The apical segmental bronchus provides an airway to the apical bronchopulmonary segment (S1) of the superior lobe of the right lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The apical segmental bronchus is accompanied by the apical segmental artery of the right lung.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The right main bronchus is formed at the bifurcation of the trachea into right and left main bronchi around the level of the sternal angle. It passes inferolaterally to reach the hilum of the right lung at the fifth thoracic vertebra level. Here, it gives off the superior lobar (or secondary) bronchus and continues as the bronchus intermedius.

The right main bronchus is wider and much shorter than the left main bronchus. Additionally, it travels more vertically than the left main bronchus; thus, inhaled objects are more likely to become lodged in the right main bronchus.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
As the right main bronchus courses from its origin at the distal end of the trachea to the hilum of the left lung, the azygos vein arches over it. Additionally, the right main bronchus is accompanied by the pulmonary artery and veins.

The right main bronchus forms part of the root of the right lung. As it enters the hilum of the right lung, it lies posterior to the right pulmonary artery and right superior pulmonary vein, and superior to the right inferior pulmonary vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Left side of the thoracic cavity.

Arterial Supply: Left bronchial arteries.

Venous Drainage: Left bronchial veins.

Innervation: Pulmonary plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: Superficial and deep lymphatic plexuses, intrapulmonary and bronchopulmonary lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The left lung has two lobes, the superior and inferior lobes, which are separated by the oblique fissure. The inferior lobe forms the base of the left lung and a portion of the costal and mediastinal surfaces. The superior lobe is anterosuperior to the inferior lobe and makes up the apex and the majority of the mediastinal and costal surfaces.

Like the inferior lobe of the right lung, the inferior lobe of the left lung is subdivided into five bronchopulmonary segments; the superior, medial basal, lateral basal, anterior basal, and posterior basal bronchopulmonary segments. Each of these bronchopulmonary segments has its own segmental bronchus and segmental artery.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The inferior lobe of the left lung sits inferior to the oblique fissure. This fissure begins on the mediastinal surface, at the posterosuperior margin of the hilum. It courses in a superoposterior direction to the posterior border of the lung, 6 cm inferior to the apex. It descends anteriorly along the costal surface as far as the anterior portion of the inferior border. It then continues onto the mediastinal surface and extends as far as the inferior border of the hilum.

The inferior lobe of the left lung sits over the left hemidiaphragm. Therefore, the inferior lobe on the left is in close proximity to the fundus of the stomach and the spleen.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The lungs are involved in respiration, which is the process of gas exchange between the atmospheric air and the blood. The lungs consist of lung parenchyma and supportive connective tissue. The lung parenchyma is the functional tissue of the lungs, where gas exchange occurs with pulmonary capillaries; it is composed of alveolar ducts and alveoli.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The right and left bronchial arteries are distal branches of the thoracic aorta. They supply oxygenated blood to the tissues of the tracheobronchial tree and the visceral pleura.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The bronchial veins that drain the more proximal regions of the tracheobronchial tree drain into the heart via azygos and accessory hemiazygos veins (i.e., via the systemic circulation). The bronchial veins that drain the more distal regions of the tracheobronchial tree form anastomoses with pulmonary veins and drain back to the heart via these veins (i.e., via the pulmonary circulation).

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text:
The nerve supply to the lungs and visceral pleurae is via the pulmonary plexus. The pulmonary plexus provides autonomic (i.e., visceral) innervation to these structures, and it consists of both parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers.

- Parasympathetic stimulation within the respiratory system promotes bronchoconstriction, vasodilation of pulmonary blood vessels, and secretion from glands within the walls of the tracheobronchial tree.

- Sympathetic stimulation promotes bronchodilation, and vasoconstriction of pulmonary blood vessels.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text:
The lymphatic drainage system within the lungs can be divided into two plexuses; the superficial plexus and the deep plexus.

- The superficial lymphatic plexus (or subpleural plexus) is located within the lung parenchyma adjacent to the visceral pleura. This plexus provides lymphatic drainage to the superficial regions of the lungs and the distal ends of the tracheobronchial tree. It drains into the bronchopulmonary lymph nodes.

- The deep lymphatic plexus is located within the walls of the proximal tracheobronchial tree and the lung parenchyma adjacent to it. This plexus drains these areas, and, in turn, drains into the intrapulmonary lymph nodes.

sections.text:
- Lung cancer

- Pulmonary collapse (atelectasis)

- Lung resection

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The right lung is divided into three lobes, which are separated by the oblique and horizontal fissures. These are the superior, middle, and inferior lobes. The middle lobe is the smallest of the three lobes and sits between the superior and inferior lobes. It forms a portion of the costal, diaphragmatic, and mediastinal surfaces, and the inferior part of the anterior border of the right lung.

The middle lobe of the right lung is subdivided into two bronchopulmonary segments, the medial and lateral bronchopulmonary segments. Each of these bronchopulmonary segments has its own segmental bronchus and segmental artery.

sections.text:

It courses in a superoposterior direction, to the posterior border of the lung, 6 cm inferior to the apex. It descends anteriorly along the costal surface as far as the anterior portion of the inferior border. It then continues onto the mediastinal surface and extends as far as the inferior border of the hilum. It is similar to the oblique fissure of the left lung, but it is not as vertically orientated.

The horizontal fissure is shorter and extends from the oblique fissure approximately at the mid-axillary line. It passes horizontally in an anterior direction at the level of the fourth costal cartilage, then on to the mediastinal aspect of the lung, where it extends as far as the hilum of the right lung.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The pulmonary ligament is a roughly triangular extension of parietal and visceral pleura inferiorly from the hilum of the lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The parietal and visceral layers envelope the hilar structures where they form the pleural sleeve. This continues inferiorly as the pleural ligament.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The mediastinal pleura sits on the lateral aspect of the mediastinum and has different anatomical relations on the left and the right.

At the hilum the mediastinal pleura reflects in a lateral direction and is continuous with the visceral pleura. This forms the pleural sleeve which extends inferiorly from the hilum as the pulmonary ligament

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The mediastinal parietal pleura is continuous with the cervical parietal pleura superiorly, the costal pleura laterally, and the diaphragmatic pleura inferiorly.

The right mediastinal pleura lines the right brachiocephalic vein, upper superior vena cava, azygos vein, right phrenic and vagus nerves, esophagus, and trachea.

The left mediastinal pleura lines the aortic arch, left vagus and phrenic nerves, left brachiocephalic and superior intercostal veins, left common carotid and subclavian arteries, thoracic duct, and esophagus.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The diaphragmatic pleura is molded into the domed shape of the diaphragm and lines the majority of the superior aspect of the respiratory diaphragm.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Laterally, the diaphragmatic pleura is continuous with the costal pleura at the costodiaphragmatic pleural reflection, while medially, it is continuous with the mediastinal pleura. It is tethered to the central dome of the diaphragm along with the outer, parietal layer of pericardium.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The costal pleura covers the internal aspect of the sternum, the ribs, and the vertebral bodies, as well as the innermost intercostal muscles and costal cartilages. It begins along the posterior aspect of the sternum, where it is a continuation of the mediastinal pleura. On the right, it reaches the xiphisternal joint, while on the left it diverges laterally due to the presence of the left ventricle and creates the cardiac notch of the left lung.

On both sides, the costal pleura continues laterally, following the curvature of the ribs and covers the sympathetic trunk and splanchnic nerves. When it reaches the lateral aspect of the vertebral bodies, it becomes continuous with the mediastinal pleura again.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The costal pleura continues inferiorly along the rib cage to the inferior border where it is continuous with the diaphragmatic pleura. Above the first rib, the costal pleura continues superiorly as the cervical pleura. External to the costal pleural is an additional fascial layer called the endothoracic fascia. This layer is akin to the endoabdominal fascia lining the abdominal wall.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The cervical pleura covers the superior aspect of the lung, namely the apex. The cervical pleura extends into the neck, 2.5 cm above the medial one third of the clavicle.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The cervical pleura ascends from the internal surface of the first rib to the tip of the apex of the lung. It then courses inferiorly along the lateral aspect of the trachea and is continuous with the mediastinal pleura.

The suprapleural membrane supplements the cervical pleura and is a fibrous extension of the endothoracic fascia lining the thoracic wall.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Surrounds the left lung.

Arterial Supply: Bronchial arteries.

Venous Drainage: Bronchial veins.

Innervation: Pulmonary plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: Superficial pulmonary lymphatic plexus.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The pleura consists of two layers, an inner visceral and an outer parietal layer. The inner visceral pleura closely invests the surface of the lungs and sits within the fissures of the lung. In cadaveric dissection, it is not possible to separate the visceral pleura from the lung tissue. The visceral and parietal pleura are continuous at the hilum where they form the pulmonary ligament.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Since the visceral and parietal pleurae are continuous at the hilum, they form a closed sac called the pleural cavity, which contains serous fluid. Due to the position of the heart, the left pleural cavity is smaller than the right.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Within the pleural cavity, a thin layer of fluid is produced by the serous epithelial membrane lining the visceral and parietal pleurae. In addition, the visceral pleura invests all surfaces of the lung and gives the lung a shiny appearance. This smooth surface and fluid layer allow friction-free movement during respiration.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The visceral pleura is supplied, along with the lungs, via the bronchial arteries. At the hilum of each lung, the bronchial arteries branch around the primary bronchus and pleural branches arise from here. They supply the mediastinal visceral pleura, the interlobar surfaces, the apex, and a portion of the diaphragmatic visceral pleura.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The visceral pleura receives afferents from the pulmonary plexus that course with the bronchial vessels (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The visceral pleural afferents from the pulmonary plexus course with the bronchial vessels (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: Lymph from visceral pleura is drained via the superficial pulmonary lymphatic plexus.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Pneumothorax

- Hydrothorax

- Hemothorax

- Chylothorax

- Pleurectomy

- Pleurisy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The cervical pleura covers the superior aspect of the lung, namely the apex. The cervical pleura extends into the neck, 2.5 cm above the medial one third of the clavicle.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The cervical pleura ascends from the internal surface of the first rib to the tip of the apex of the lung. It then courses inferiorly along the lateral aspect of the trachea and is continuous with the mediastinal pleura.

The suprapleural membrane supplements the cervical pleura and is a fibrous extension of the endothoracic fascia lining the thoracic wall.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The mediastinal pleura sits on the lateral aspect of the mediastinum and has different anatomical relations on the left and the right.

At the hilum the mediastinal pleura reflects in a lateral direction and is continuous with the visceral pleura. This forms the pleural sleeve which extends inferiorly from the hilum as the pulmonary ligament.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The mediastinal parietal pleura is continuous with the cervical parietal pleura superiorly, the costal pleura laterally, and the diaphragmatic pleura inferiorly.

The right mediastinal pleura lines the right brachiocephalic vein, upper superior vena cava, azygos vein, right phrenic and vagus nerves, esophagus, and trachea.

The left mediastinal pleura lines the aortic arch, left vagus and phrenic nerves, left brachiocephalic and superior intercostal veins, left common carotid and subclavian arteries, thoracic duct, and esophagus.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The costal pleura covers the internal aspect of the sternum, the ribs, and the vertebral bodies, as well as the innermost intercostal muscles and costal cartilages. It begins along the posterior aspect of the sternum, where it is a continuation of the mediastinal pleura. On the right, it reaches the xiphisternal joint, while on the left it diverges laterally due to the presence of the left ventricle and creates the cardiac notch of the left lung.

On both sides, the costal pleura continues laterally, following the curvature of the ribs and covers the sympathetic trunk and splanchnic nerves. When it reaches the lateral aspect of the vertebral bodies, it becomes continuous with the mediastinal pleura again.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The costal pleura continues inferiorly along the rib cage to the inferior border where it is continuous with the diaphragmatic pleura. Above the first rib, the costal pleura continues superiorly as the cervical pleura. External to the costal pleural is an additional fascial layer called the endothoracic fascia. This layer is akin to the endoabdominal fascia lining the abdominal wall.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The diaphragmatic pleura is molded into the domed shape of the diaphragm and lines the majority of the superior aspect of the respiratory diaphragm.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Laterally, the diaphragmatic pleura is continuous with the costal pleura at the costodiaphragmatic pleural reflection, while medially, it is continuous with the mediastinal pleura. It is tethered to the central dome of the diaphragm along with the outer, parietal layer of pericardium.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The pulmonary ligament is a roughly triangular extension of parietal and visceral pleura inferiorly from the hilum of the lung.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The parietal and visceral layers envelope the hilar structures where they form the pleural sleeve. This continues inferiorly as the pleural ligament.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Surrounds the right lung.

Arterial Supply: Bronchial arteries.

Venous Drainage: Bronchial veins.

Innervation: Pulmonary plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: Superficial pulmonary lymphatic plexus.
