sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Posterior surface of the thyroid gland.

Arterial Supply: Inferior thyroid artery.

Venous Drainage: Venous plexus along the anterior surface of the thyroid gland.

Innervation: Sympathetic innervation from the superior or middle cervical ganglion.

Lymphatic Drainage: Along the thyroid and thymus glands.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The parathyroid glands are paired ovoid structures lying on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland. There are two superior and two inferior glands that typically measure 6 mm long, 3 mm wide, and 1 mm from anterior to posterior. These glands are principally responsible for the production and release of parathyroid hormone (PTH) (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The paired parathyroid glands reside along the posterior surface of the thyroid gland.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The parathyroid glands are principally responsible with synthesizing and secreting parathyroid hormone (PTH), which directly relates to the levels of calcium and phosphorus in the blood. When blood calcium levels are decreasing, the production and release of PTH increases.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: Both the superior and inferior parathyroid glands are supplied by the inferior thyroid artery. The superior glands are occasionally supplied by the superior thyroid arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The parathyroid glands are drained by a venous plexus on the anterior thyroid surface.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The parathyroid glands receive sympathetic innervation from the superior or middle cervical ganglia (via thyroid branches).

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The cervical paratracheal lymph nodes receive afferent vessels from the thyroid and parathyroid glands. The efferent vessels of the cervical paratracheal lymph nodes pass to the internal jugular nodes of the deep lateral cervical lymph nodes (Földi et al., 2012).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Thyroidectomy

- Parathyroidectomy

- Hypoparathyroidism,

- Hyperparathyroidism

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Földi, M., Földi, E., Strößenreuther, R. and Kubik, S. (2012) Földi's Textbook of Lymphology: for Physicians and Lymphedema Therapists. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Anterior to the larynx and trachea.

Arterial Supply: Superior and inferior thyroid arteries.

Venous Drainage: Superior, middle, and inferior thyroid veins.

Innervation: Superior, middle, and inferior cervical ganglia.

Lymphatic Drainage: Prelaryngeal or deep cervical nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The thyroid gland is a large gland residing in the anterior neck along the inferior larynx and superior trachea. The gland is one of the largest endocrine glands. 

The thyroid gland can be divided into left and right lobes that are separated by the trachea. The lobes are joined by a very thin isthmus. In about 40% of individuals, a pyramidal-shaped lobe sometimes extends superiorly from the isthmus. Each lobe is approximately 5 cm long (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). 

The thyroid is surrounded by a thin connective tissue capsule which penetrates the parenchyma of the thyroid gland, dividing the tissue into small irregular units or lobules. 

The thyroid follicles are the functional units of the gland and the parenchyma consist of two cell types, follicular cells and parafollicular cells.

The thyroid gland has a rich blood supply and innervation and responsible for synthesizing and releasing two thyroid hormones. These hormones directly regulate important processes like metabolism and protein synthesis.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The thyroid gland is covered by the sternothyroid, sternohyoid, and omohyoid muscles anteriorly and the sternocleidomastoid muscle inferiorly. The superior pole of the gland contacts the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle and the side of the cricoid cartilage.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The thyroid gland synthesizes the thyroid hormones (triiodothyronine [T3] and thyroxine [T4]). These hormones are important for cell differentiation, growth, oxygen consumption in cells, and control of basal metabolic rate. These hormones also affect protein, lipid, and carbohydrate metabolism. 

Calcitonin is also synthesized and secreted by the thyroid gland and is responsible for lowering calcium levels in the blood.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The superior and inferior thyroid arteries (and occasionally the thyroid ima artery) supplies the thyroid gland. These arteries anastomose with one another on the same side and on the contralateral side. The superior thyroid artery divides into anterior and posterior branches, which supply the anterior surface, and lateral and medial surfaces, of the gland, respectively. The inferior thyroid artery gives rise to superior (ascending) and inferior branches, which supply the inferior and posterior surfaces of the gland. The superior branch also supplies the parathyroid glands.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Superior, middle, and inferior thyroid veins drain the thyroid gland. The superior thyroid vein drains the upper part of the gland and drains into the internal jugular vein. The middle thyroid vein drains the inferior part of the gland and empties into the internal jugular vein. The inferior thyroid veins arise from the thyroid venous plexus which also connects to the superior and middle thyroid veins. The left and right inferior thyroid veins drain into the left and right brachiocephalic veins respectively.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The thyroid gland is innervated by the superior, middle, and inferior cervical ganglia of the sympathetic trunk. Postganglionic fibers from the inferior cervical ganglion form a plexus on the inferior thyroid artery and accompany it to the thyroid gland. Some parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve, via the recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves, communicate with this plexus (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: Lymph from the thyroid gland is drained by the prelaryngeal and thyroid nodes located above and below the isthmus. Their efferents carry lymph to the pre- and paratracheal nodes. Laterally, the gland is drained by the deep anterior cervical nodes. Some lymph vessels may also drain directly into the thoracic duct (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Thyroidectomy
—Parathyroidectomy
—A Goiter is an enlargement of the thyroid gland due to either hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The epididymis is a highly convoluted structure, measuring up to seven meters long (Standring, 2016). Anatomically, it is divided into a head, body, and tail region. The head is connected to the efferent ducts of the testes, through which primitive spermatozoa (immature sperm cells) travel to enter the epididymis. Distally, the tail is continuous with the ductus deferens.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The epididymis is attached to the posterior aspect of the testis and is covered in tunica vaginalis. The sinus epididymis separates the epididymis from the testis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The epididymis serves to store and facilitate the maturation of spermatozoa (immature sperm cells). During ejaculation, sperm is transported from the epididymis by peristalsis, via the ductus deferens, towards the prostatic urethra. Here, seminal fluid produced in the seminal gland, travels to the prostatic urethra, via the ejaculatory duct. Sperm and seminal fluid mix to form semen, which leaves the body via the external urethral orifice.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The straight, terminal portion of the seminiferous tubules unite to form the rete testis. The rete testis is thin, flat tubes lined with an epithelial layer.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The rete testis is thin interconnected network of tubules within the mediastinum testis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The rete testis coalesces to form seven to fifteen efferent ductules, which carry immature sperm into the head of the epididymis (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: There are approximately up to 20 efferent ductules of the testis, which are dispersed throughout the hilum of the testis (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The efferent ductules are surrounded by a thin circular coat of smooth muscle. They are lined by ciliated columnar epithelial and non-ciliated endocytic cells (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The efferent ductules of testis connects the rete testis to the head of the epididymis, allowing immature sperm to enter the epididymis.

sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

25200.name: Tunica Albuginea of Testis (Lateral Part; Left)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The tunica albuginea is the intermediate layer of three layers that surround the testis. It is composed of bundles of dense white collagen fibers.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The tunica albuginea becomes slightly thickened posteriorly as the mediastinum of the testis. Blood vessels, lymphatics, and genital ducts enter and leave the testis at the mediastinum.

sections.title: Function
References
sections.text: Middendorff R, Muller D, Mewe M, Mukhopadhyay AK, Holstein AF, Davidoff MS. The tunica albuginea of the human testis is characterized by complex contraction and relaxation activities regulated by cyclic GMP. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2002;87(7):3486-99.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Each testis has approximately 250 lobules separated by septa (Standring, 2016). The lobules are conical in shape, with the base oriented near the circumference of the testis and the apex directed towards the mediastinum.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lobules consist of one to four seminiferous tubules and interstitial tissue (consisting of blood vessels, nerves, Leydig cells, and macrophages).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The lobules serve as the location for seminiferous tubules (which are responsible for the production of sperm) and Leydig cells (which are responsible for the production of testosterone).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The fundiform ligament of the penis is a thickened extension of the lower aspect of the superficial fascia of the abdomen. It is a semicircular ligament that surrounds the base of the penis.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The fundiform ligament of the penis is located superior to the suspensory ligament of the penis. It adheres to, and blends with, fibers of the linea alba, pubic symphysis, and the aponeurosis of the external abdominal oblique muscle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The fundiform ligament of the penis supports the structure for the shaft of the penis.

25130.name: Tunica Albuginea of Corpora Cavernosa Penis (Left Half)
alternate: Tunica albuginea corporis cavernosi penis (Left Half)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum comprises an elastic layer of fibrous tissue that is primarily made of collagen and elastin.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The thick layer of tunica albuginea envelops the corpora cavernosa of the penis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The elastic nature of the tunica albuginea allows blood to flow easily through the dorsal arteries of the penis to initiate an erection. The deep fascia of the penis is less elastic and puts pressure on the dorsal vein of the penis nearer the root to prevent blood from leaving the penis.

25023.name: Tunica Albuginea of Corpus Spongiosum Penis (Left Half)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The tunica albuginea comprises an elastic layer of fibrous tissue that is primarily made of collagen and elastin.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Due to the smaller density of erectile tissue in the corpus spongiosum, the tunica albuginea is thinner in comparison to the thick tunica albuginea covering the corpus cavernosum.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The elastic nature of the tunica albuginea allows blood to flow easily through the dorsal arteries of the penis to initiate an erection. The deep fascia of the penis is less elastic and puts pressure on the dorsal vein of the penis nearer the root to prevent blood from leaving the penis.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The fascia of the penis consists of a deep layer of fibrous tissue, which surrounds the corpus cavernosum, and splits to surround the corpus spongiosum. Distally, it blends with the tunica albuginea of all corporal bodies. Proximally, the deep fascia of the penis is continuous with the deep perineal fascia. It is also anchored to the suspensory ligament of the penis.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The fascia of the penis surrounds the three corpora erectile bodies, as well as the deep dorsal vein, the dorsal arteries of the penis, and the dorsal nerves of the penis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The fascia of the penis is responsible for the structural integrity of the three erectile bodies of the penis.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Penis shaft.

Arterial Supply: Deep artery of Penis.

Venous Drainage: Deep Dorsal Vein.

Innervation: Parasympathetic: Cavernous nerve.

Lymphatic Drainage: Internal iliac nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: A common misconception is that the corpus cavernosum is two distinct structures. It is actually a singular structure that is separated in the midline by a fibrous septum. The septum is incomplete distally to allow for the communication of blood flow. There are dilatable spaces within the corpus cavernosum of the penis, which fill with blood and become distended during erection.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The corpus cavernosum is located along the dorsal side of the penis. A wide median grove of the corpus cavernosum contains the singular corpus spongiosum of the penis. The major neurovascular bundle of the penis is located dorsally on the corpus cavernosa.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The corpus cavernosum helps to maintain erections by preventing blood return from the penis through the deep dorsal vein of the penis.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The corpus cavernosum is supplied by the deep artery of the penis, which is a terminal branch of the internal pudendal artery. It pierces the inferior fascia of the urogenital diaphragm and runs in the corpus cavernous penis.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The cavernous veins from the deep dorsal vein drain the corpus cavernosum. These veins ultimately drain into the internal pudendal veins.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: Innervation of the corpus cavernosum is supplied by the cavernous nerves, which are derived from the prostatic plexus of nerves. The cavernous nerves are postganglionic parasympathetic nerves that facilitate penile erection.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The lymph of the corpus cavernosum is drained by the internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Erectile dysfunction

25035.name: Corpus Spongiosum of Penis (Left Half)
alternate: Spongy Body of Male Urethra (Left Half)

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Shaft of penis.

Arterial Supply: Artery of bulb of penis.

Venous Drainage: Deep dorsal vein of penis.

Innervation: Cavernous nerve.

Lymphatic Drainage: Internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The corpus spongiosum of the penis is an erectile tissue that surrounds the spongy part of the male urethra within the penile shaft. The proximal part of the corpus spongiosum is enlarged to form the bulb of penis. Cavernous spaces in the corpus spongiosum are dilatable spaces that fill with blood during erection.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The corpus spongiosum is located on the ventral surface of the penile shaft, whereas the corpus cavernosum is located on the dorsal surface. The spongy (penile) urethra travels throughout the length of the corpus spongiosum.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Cavernous spaces in the corpus spongiosum fill with blood during erection to prevent the urethra from closing to allow for ejaculation.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The corpus spongiosum is supplied by the artery of bulb of penis, which is a branch of the perineal artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The corpus spongiosum of the penis is drained by the deep dorsal vein of the penis. These veins ultimately drain into the internal pudendal veins.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The cavernous nerve on the dorsum of the penis runs from the prostatic plexus to supply the erectile tissue of the corpus cavernous and corpus spongiosum.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The lymph of the corpus spongiosum drains into the internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Urethral catheterization

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Distal end of the penis.

Arterial Supply: Dorsal artery of penis and artery of bulb of penis.

Venous Drainage: Deep dorsal vein of the penis.

Innervation: Visceral afferent: Dorsal nerve of the penis.

Lymphatic Drainage: Deep inguinal and external iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The glans penis is an enlarged bulbous shaped erectile tissue, which is composed of the terminal portion of the corpus spongiosum.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The glans penis is covered by a fold of skin called the prepuce. The external urethral meatus is an opening is the distal tip of the glans penis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The high concentration of sensory nerves in the glans penis indicates that stimulation of the glans penis contributes to maintaining an erection and initiating ejaculation.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The glans penis is supplied by the dorsal artery of the penis and the artery to the bulb of the penis. Both are branches from the perineal artery, which is a branch of the internal pudendal arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The glans penis is drained by the deep dorsal vein of the penis, which drains into the prostatic venous plexus.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The glans penis is very sensitive due to the high concentration of nerve endings in the glans penis. It is innervated by the dorsal nerve of the penis.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The lymph of the glans penis is drained into the deep inguinal and external iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The suspensory ligament of the penis is a strong fibrous ligament, which extends from the pubic symphysis to the dorsal aspect of the penis. It forms a sling around the lateral aspect of the base of the penis.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The suspensory ligament of the penis extends from the pubic symphysis to the dorsal surface of the penis. It is deep to the fundiform ligament.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The suspensory ligament secures the base of the penis to the pubis during erection.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The septum penis is a fibrous structure that divides the corpus cavernosum. The septum is complete proximally, but distally it is incomplete to allow for the communication and blood flow between the two sides of the corpus cavernosum.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The septum penis is located within the corpus cavernosum. It lies in the midline of the penile shaft and is continuous with the tunica albuginea.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The septum penis divides the corpus cavernosum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: At the base of the prostate, between the bladder and rectum.

Arterial Supply: Artery to ductus deferens and inferior vesical artery.

Venous Drainage: Inferior vesical plexus.

Innervation: Sympathetic: Inferior hypogastric nerve; Parasympathetic: Pelvic and inferior hypogastric nerves.

Lymphatic Drainage: Internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The seminal gland is an out pouching of the terminal ductus deferens. It is a coiled tube measuring approximately 3–5 cm in adults, with a volume capacity of approximately 13 ml (Standring, 2016). The right seminal vesical is often larger than the left. However, they both decrease in size with age. 

The seminal gland consists of a highly convoluted duct, which is surrounded by a capsule of connective tissue.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The seminal glands are posterior to the urinary bladder and prostate, and lateral to the ampulla of the ductus deferens. 

The inferior hypogastric plexus lies posterolaterally on either side on the seminal glands.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The seminal glands secrete a thick alkaline seminal fluid with fructose, via the ejaculatory duct, into the prostatic urethra. This seminal fluid mixes with sperm from the ductus deferens, to form semen, which is expelled during ejaculation.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The seminal glands are supplied by branches from the Inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The seminal glands are drained by the vesical venous plexus into the internal iliac vein.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The pelvic and inferior hypogastric nerves supply sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation to the seminal gland. Parasympathetic supply is also supplied by the pelvic nerve.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The lymph of the seminal glands is drained into the internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: References:
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Deep perineal pouch.

Arterial Supply: Artery of bulb of penis.

Venous Drainage: Internal pudendal vein.

Innervation: Hypogastric nerve.

Lymphatic Drainage: Deep inguinal nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The bulbourethral glands are pea sized, paired exocrine glands. They are lobulated structures measuring approximately 1 cm in diameter. They are drained by excretory ducts of approximately 3 cm long. They penetrate the perineal membrane and open into the urethra.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The bulbourethral glands are in the deep pouch of the perineum, at the base of the penis, posterior and lateral to the membranous urethra, just below the prostate gland.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The bulbourethral glands are responsible for the production and release of pre-ejaculate fluid that aids in the passage of sperm and neutralization of the pH in the vagina.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The bulbourethral glands are supplied by the artery to the bulb of the penis, which is a branch of the internal pudendal artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The Internal pudendal veins drain the bulbourethral gland.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: Autonomic nerve supply to the bulbourethral glands is by the hypogastric nerve.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The lymphatic drainage of the bulbourethral gland is through the deep inguinal lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The ampulla of the ductus deferens is the enlarged, tortuous terminal portion of the ductus deferens.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The ampulla of ductus deferens is located posterior to the fundus of the bladder and medial to the seminal vesicle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The ampulla of the ductus deferens joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, which enters the prostatic urethra.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Posterior to the bladder and superior portion of the prostate gland.

Arterial Supply: Inferior vesical artery.

Venous Drainage: Prostatic and vesical venous plexuses.

Innervation: Sympathetic: Hypogastric nerve.

Lymphatic Drainage: Internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The ejaculatory duct is a muscular tube, approximately 2 cm long, that is formed by the union of the duct of the seminal vesicle and the ampulla of the ductus deferens. Small openings of the ejaculatory duct open on both sides, or within, the prostatic utricle, to open into the prostatic urethra.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The ejaculatory duct is located posterior to the bladder and superior portion of the prostate gland.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: During ejaculation, the ejaculatory duct dilates and propels sperm and seminal fluid into the prostatic urethra, and subsequently out of the body via the external urethral orifice.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The ejaculatory duct is supplied by the inferior vesical artery, which is a branch of the internal iliac artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The ejaculatory duct is drained by the prostatic and vesical venous plexus, which drain into the internal iliac vein.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: During ejaculation, the hypogastric nerve controls rapid contraction of the ejaculatory duct, by way of the sympathetic nervous system.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The lymph of the ejaculatory duct is drained into the internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The wall of the prostatic utricle consists of fibrous tissue, smooth muscle fibers, and a mucus membrane. This “cul-de-sac” opening is approximately 6 mm long within the medial portion of the prostate (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The prostatic utricle is the embryological remnant of the fused caudal ends of the paramesonephric ducts and is considered the homologue to the vagina or the uterus. The urethral (prostatic) sinuses open into the prostatic urethra on either side of the utricle.

sections.text:
—Benign prostatic hyperplasia
—Prostate cancer

Location: Directly inferior to the bladder. 

Arterial Supply: Inferior vesical, internal pudendal, and middle anorectal arteries. 

Venous Drainage: Prostatic venous plexus.

Innervation: Somatic visceral afferent: pudendal nerve; Autonomic: Inferior hypogastric and prostatic plexuses.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The prostate is a walnut-sized, globular fibromuscular gland. It is fixed superiorly to the base of the urinary bladder and sits superior to the pelvic floor.

The prostate is traditionally divided into ill-defined lobes.
—The isthmus of the prostate lies anterior to the urethra and contains little to no glandular tissue.
—The right and left lobes are separated anteriorly by the isthmus. 

Each lobe can be further subdivided into four distinct lobules:
—Inferoposterior lobule lies posterior to the urethra and inferior to the ejaculatory ducts. Readily palpable during a digital rectal examination.
—Inferolateral lobule lies lateral to the urethra, forming the bulk of each lobe.
—Superomedial lobule lies deep to the inferoposterior lobule and directly surround the ejaculatory duct on each side.
—Anteromedial lobule deep to the inferolateral lobular and directly lateral to the urethra.

In addition to the lobe classifications, the prostate can be divided into four different zones: 
—the central zone surrounding the ejaculatory ducts;
—the transitional zone surrounding the proximal urethra;
—the peripheral zone surrounding the distal urethra;
—the stromal zone (also known as the anterior fibromuscular zone) that is comprised of muscles and connective tissue.

The superior aspect of the prostate is termed the base and the inferior aspect is termed the apex. There are two posterolateral surfaces, and an anterior and posterior surface of the prostate.

The prostatic urethra passes directly through the substance of the prostate on its way to the penis.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The superior aspect of the prostate is termed the base and is continuous with the neck of the bladder. The inferior aspect is termed the apex and marks the junction of the membranous and prostatic urethra. The anterior surface of the prostate lies directly posterior to the pubic arch. It is connected to the pubic bone by the puboprostatic ligament. The inferolateral surfaces of the prostate are related to the anterior muscle fibers of levator ani. They surround the prostate in a sling termed the pubourethral sling or pubourethalis. The posterior surface of the bladder lies anterior to the rectum and the rectourethralis muscle. The superior surface of the prostate is penetrated by two ejaculatory ducts.

The prostate is surrounded by an anatomically variable prostatic capsule which is formed from the surrounding fascia. The prostatic plexus of veins and nerves reside within the capsule.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The prostate provides passage for urine and sperm to pass out of the body. During ejaculation the prostate secretes a slightly alkaline fluid into the prostatic urethra. Fluid from the prostate, together with seminal fluid from the seminal gland, and sperm from the ductus deferens combine to form semen.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The prostate revives blood from various sources. Prostatic branches from the inferior vesical artery communicate across the midline of the prostate. The inferior gluteal, internal pudendal, and middle anorectal arteries supply branches to the prostate.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The prostatic venous plexus surrounds the anterolateral aspect of the prostate. It receives tributaries from the deep dorsal vein of the penis and the vesical venous plexus to drain into the internal iliac veins.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The prostate receives both autonomic and somatic visceral innervation. The inferior hypogastric plexus supplies the prostate. Nerves traveling to the prostate form a periprostatic nerve plexus within the prostatic capsule. The prostatic plexus supplies the smooth muscle of the prostate and prostatic urethra. The skeletal muscle is supplied by the pudendal nerve. This skeletal muscle contracts and dilates the prostatic urethra.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The lymph of the prostate is drained by the medial group of external iliac nodes, in which the efferent nodes pass to the internal iliac nodes.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Prostate cancer
—Benign prostatic hyperplasia

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The fascia of the prostate consists of dense connective tissue that surrounds the prostate and houses prostatic neurovascular structures.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: This layer of fascia fuses with endopelvic fascia anterolaterally and is continuous with the obturator fascia laterally. The lateral surface of the fascia encloses the neurovascular bundle and is the most important surgically. The posterior surface of the fascia attaches to the anterior portion of the rectoprostatic (Denonvilliers’) fascia.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The fascia of the prostate provides a rigid structure for the prostate and keep a close relationship between the prostatic neurovasculature and the prostate (MacLennan, 2012).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Prostatectomy
—Benign prostatic hyperplasia
—Prostate cancer

sections.title: References
sections.text: MacLennan, G. T. (2012) Hinman's Atlas of Urosurgical Anatomy. Elsevier/Saunders.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: In young adult males, the capsule of the prostate consists of smooth muscle internally and connective tissue externally. The capsule typically increases in thickness with age and with increased signs of benign prostatic hyperplasia (Holder et al., 2021).

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The prostatic capsule forms the outer surface of the prostate. In some instances, the capsule is fused with the outer connective tissue covering, the fascia of prostate.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The capsule of the prostate provides a smooth muscle and connective tissue enclosure for the prostate.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Prostatectomy
—Benign prostatic hyperplasia
—Prostate cancer

sections.text: Holder, K. G., Galvan, B., Knight, A. S., Ha, F., Collins, R., Weaver, P. E., Brandi, L. and de Riese, W. T. (2021) 'Possible clinical implications of prostate capsule thickness and glandular epithelial cell density in benign prostate hyperplasia', Investig Clin Urol, 62(4), pp. 423–429.

26620.name: Parietal Layer of Tunica Vaginalis Testis (Medial Part; Left)
alternate: Parietal Layer of Tunica Vaginalis of Testis (Medial Part; Left)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis testis is a mesothelial lined tissue producing lubricating fluid.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis testis is a continuation of the processus vaginalis, formed as a part of the descension of the testes. Following the descent, a small sac remains and is referred to as the tunica vaginalis. The parietal and visceral layers of the tunica vaginalis are continuous at the poles of the testes. Between the two layers is the cavity of the tunica vaginalis (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis testis provides lubrication for the testes to decrease the risk of friction caused by movement.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Indirect inguinal hernia
—Hydroceles

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

26617.name: Parietal Layer of Tunica Vaginalis Testis (Lateral Part; Right)
alternate: Parietal Layer of Tunica Vaginalis of Testis (Lateral Part; Right)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis testis is a mesothelial lined tissue producing lubricating fluid.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis testis is a continuation of the processus vaginalis, formed as a part of the descension of the testes. Following the descent, a small sac remains and is referred to as the tunica vaginalis. The parietal and visceral layers of the tunica vaginalis are continuous at the poles of the testes. Between the two layers is the cavity of the tunica vaginalis (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis testis provides lubrication for the testes to decrease the risk of friction caused by movement.

—Hydroceles

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The detrusor apron is an inferior extension of the detrusor muscle. It expands over the anterior surface of the prostate. Distally and anteriorly, the detrusor apron condenses to form the puboprostatic ligaments.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Scrotum, spermatic cord, and pelvis.

Arterial Supply: Artery to ductus deferens.

Venous Drainage: Pelvic venous plexus.

Innervation: Autonomic: Autonomic: Inferior hypogastric plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: External and internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The ductus deferens is a tube-like structure derived from the mesonephric duct. It is approximately 30 cm long and is lined by multiple layers of smooth muscle (Standring, 2016). There are four parts of the ductus deferens, including the scrotal, funicular, inguinal, and pelvic part.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Within the spermatic cord, the ductus deferens lies posteriorly and parallel to the vessels. It runs through the superficial inguinal ring, inguinal canal, and deep inguinal ring to enter the pelvis. Within the pelvis, the ductus deferens passes superolaterally over the bladder to merge with the seminal vesicles, posterior to the bladder, culminating at the ejaculatory duct.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The ductus deferens transports sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory ducts, which opens into the prostatic urethra in males.

During ejaculation, the smooth muscle lining the ductus deferens contracts and sperm is transported via peristalsis towards the urethra. Along the way, seminal fluid from the seminal vesicles, and fluid from the prostate and bulbourethral glands join the sperm. Collectively, these fluids are known as semen.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The ductus deferens is supplied by the artery to ductus deferens, a branch of the umbilical artery. Additionally, it may be supplied by the inferior vesical artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The ductus deferens is drained by veins from the ductus deferens and seminal vesicles into the inferior vesicle plexus.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The ductus deferens is supplied by mostly preganglionic sympathetic fibers derived from the inferior hypogastric plexus.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: Lymphatic drainage of the ductus deferens is via the external and internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Vasectomy

sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Abdominal and pelvic cavity.

Arterial Supply: Ureteric branches of the renal, gonadal, abdominal aorta, common iliac, internal iliac, inferior vesicle, and uterine arteries (females).

Venous Drainage: Same pattern as arterial supply.

Innervation: Through ureteric plexus; Sympathetic: lesser and least thoracic splanchnic nerves, renal, aortic, superior hypogastric, and inferior hypogastric plexuses; Parasympathetic: vagus and pelvic splanchnic; Sensory afferent.

Lymphatic Drainage: Left and right lumbar lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The ureters are bilateral muscular tubes that are 25–30 cm long and 0.3 cm wide (Standring, 2016). They extend from the renal pelvis, at the hilum of the kidney, to the ureteric orifices on the internal aspect of the bladder.

The ureters are slightly narrower in three regions: just inferior to the renal pelvis, where it crosses the pelvic brim, and where it enters the urinary bladder. Thus, these are the most likely sites for renal calculi.

The ureters are composed of an inner mucosa lined with urothelium, a submucosal layer, a smooth muscle coat, and an outer adventitial layer.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
Superiorly, the ureters are a continuation of the renal pelvis as they emerge from the kidneys. They are retroperitoneal and descend within the abdominal cavity. As they travel inferiorly, they sit anterior to the medial edge of the psoas major muscle. This corresponds to the lateral tips of the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae. Upon their descent, they pass over the genitofemoral nerves but pass beneath the gonadal vessels. 

They cross anterior to the common iliac vessels as they cross the pelvic brim. Firstly, they course in a posterolateral direction and run along the anterior edge of the greater sciatic notch. At the ischial spine, they turn in an anteromedial direction and they approach the bladder.

In males, the ureters pass inferior to the vas deferens and anterior to the superior portion of the seminal vesicle before they then enter the bladder. In females, they sit posterior to the ovary, and then run adjacent to the cervix and lateral fornices of the vagina before entering the bladder.

Finally, the ureters pass through the bladder wall in an oblique manner and end at the ureteric orifices.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The ureters provide a conduit for the passage of urine from the kidney to the bladder. They actively assist in the passage of urine via the peristaltic action of the smooth muscle layer. This is particularly evident in the distal ureter where it has an extra muscular coat. Additionally, the ureters prevent urine reflux due to the oblique passage of the ureters through the bladder wall.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The abdominal portion of the ureters is supplied by the ureteric branches of the renal, gonadal, abdominal aorta and common iliac arteries.

The pelvic portion is supplied by branches of the internal iliac and inferior vesicle arteries. In the female the uterine artery also contributes to its vascularization. In the abdomen the branches arise medial to the ureter and in the pelvis, the branches arise on the lateral side of the ureter (Standring, 2016). 

There is large variation in the branches that supply the ureters, but longitudinal anastomoses ensure it has adequate vascularization.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The ureteric veins that drain the ureters follow the same branching pattern as the arterial supply.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text:
Nerves supplying the ureter are located in the ureteric plexus, within the outer adventitial layer, and extend into the muscular layer. 

Sympathetic innervation to the ureter arises from the lesser and least thoracic and the splanchnic nerves. The nerves travel to the renal and aortic plexuses (its upper part), from the superior hypogastric plexus and hypogastric nerve (its intermediate part), and from the hypogastric nerve and inferior hypogastric plexus (its lower part) (Standring, 2016).

If present, parasympathetic nerve fibers to superior ureter travel in the vagus nerve, and to the inferior ureter via pelvic splanchnic nerves. The axonal density increases distally, and waves of muscular contraction travel away from the kidney towards the bladder to aid in the passage of urine from the kidneys into the bladder. In addition, nerve endings on the ureteric muscle and on the smooth muscle cells in the walls of blood vessels have been observed and are presumed to be efferent in function (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: Lymph drainage of the superior abdominal portion of the ureter collects in the retrocaval, lateral caval, precaval, and lateral aortic lymph nodes. The inferior portion of the ureter is drained into the common, external, and internal iliac lymph nodes (Földi et al., 2012).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Referred pain

—Renal and ureteric calculi

—Duplex ureters

—Ectopic ureters

—Ureteroceles

—Retrocaval ureters

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Wall of the bladder.

Insertion: Posterior wall of the pubic bone and prostate (if present). 

Action: Assist in micturition by increasing the pressure in the bladder and forcing urine into the urethra.

Nerve Supply: Inferior hypogastric plexus, with parasympathetic fibers originating from S2-S4, and sympathetic fibers originating in the lateral horn of gray matter of T10-L2. 

Arterial Supply: Superior vesical, inferior vesical (if present), vaginal (if present), obturator, and inferior gluteal arteries.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The detrusor vesicae is composed of smooth muscle fibers organized into three layers in the bladder, inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The detrusor vesicae forms the internal urethral sphincter at the neck of the bladder. It forms a circular loop around the opening of the ureters into the posterior surface of the bladder, preventing reflux of urine from the bladder into the ureters. It is continuous as the detrusor apron over the prostate (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: This smooth muscle layer of the bladder is responsible relaxing the bladder while it fills with urine and contracting during micturition to aid in forcing urine into the urethra.

sections.text:
—Catheter placement 
—Bladder cancer

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Base of the pelvis.

Arterial Supply: Superior and inferior vesical arteries.

Venous Drainage: Superior (and inferior) vesical veins.

Innervation: Via the vesical and hypogastric plexus: Sympathetic: sacral splanchnic nerves; Parasympathetic: pelvic splanchnic nerves; visceral afferent fibers.

Lymphatic Drainage: Paravesical lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The urinary bladder is essentially a hollow, muscular reservoir. The morphology changes as it becomes filled with urine, moving a portion of the bladder into the greater pelvis.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The urinary bladder is directly posterior to the pubic symphysis and superior to the pelvic diaphragm. In females, the uterus, cervix, and vagina are posterior to the bladder. In males, the rectum is posterior to the bladder.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The urinary bladder stores urine that has passed from the kidneys through the ureters. Urination occurs when the internal urethral sphincter (distal portion of the bladder) relaxes and the detrusor (smooth muscle) of the bladder contracts, expelling urine into the urethra.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The urinary bladder receives a dual blood supply that supplies the superior and inferior parts of the organ. Superior vesical arteries are branches off the umbilical artery. In males, the inferior vesical arteries branch directly from the internal iliac arteries. In females, the vaginal branch of the uterine artery serves the function of the inferior vesical and supplies the inferior bladder (Tubbs et al., 2016).

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The bladder is drained by the vesical venous plexus, where blood is returned to the internal iliac vein via the superior (and in the male, the inferior) vesical veins.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text:
The nerves supplying the bladder arise from the pelvic plexuses. Sympathetic ﬁbers are derived from the sacral splanchnic nerve and synapse with the postganglionic neuronal cell bodies inside the celiac and mesenteric plexuses. From here the hypogastric plexuses descend into the pelvis and connect with the vesical plexus surrounding the bladder. 

Parasympathetic ﬁbers arise from the neuronal cell bodies in the pelvic splanchnic nerve.

Vesical afferent nerves are concerned with pain and awareness of distension of the bladder (Burnstock, 1990).

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The paravesical lymph nodes are found in the subperitoneal tissue surrounding the urinary bladder. These nodes drain to the external (mostly) and internal (minimally) iliac lymph nodes, returning lymph to the lateral aortic and caval lymph nodes and the left and right lumbar lymph trunks (Földi et al., 2012).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Bladder cancer

sections.title: References
sections.text:

Földi, M., Földi, E., Strößenreuther, R. and Kubik, S. (2012) Földi's Textbook of Lymphology: for Physicians and Lymphedema Therapists. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Urothelium (transitional epithelium) and the lamina propria (connective tissue) form the mucosa of the bladder. The urothelium is approximately 4–7 cells thick and can change shape with increased fluid volume in the bladder. The urothelium is separated from the lamina propria by a basal lamina. The lamina propria contains capillaries, lymphatics, nerve endings, elastic fibers, and small amounts of smooth muscle fibers (Standring, 2020).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The mucosa forms the internal surface of the bladder, deep to the detrusor muscle (muscularis propria) and adventitial layers.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The mucosa lines the internal surface of the bladder, which forms a nearly impermeable layer, aiding in the storage of urine. The epithelial layer is classified as urothelium, or transitional epithelium, due to the cells’ unique ability to adapt their shape with an increase in fluid volume.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The trigone of the bladder is a smooth triangular shaped segment of the urinary bladder wall.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The trigone of the bladder is located along the posterior surface of the bladder and marks the point of opening for the two ureters.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The trigone of the bladder is particularly sensitive to stretch and expansion, which signals the brain to become aware of the “need” to urinate.

22382.name: Fat Body of Renal Sinus (Anterior Part; Left)

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The hilum of the kidney is filled by the renal sinus, renal artery, and renal vein. The remainder of the space is filled with adipose tissue often referred to as the fat body of the renal sinus. The amount of fat in this region normally increases with age (Rha et al., 2004).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Renal sinus lipomatosis

sections.title: References
sections.text: Rha, S. E., Byun, J. Y., Jung, S. E., Oh, S. N., Choi, Y.-J., Lee, A. and Lee, J. M. (2004) 'The Renal Sinus: Pathologic Spectrum and Multimodality Imaging Approach', RadioGraphics, 24(suppl_1), pp. S117-S131.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The renal pelvis is the funnel shaped, dilated proximal portion of the ureter.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The renal pelvis is within the renal hilum, consists of a transitional epithelium (urothelium), and smooth muscle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Urine from the major calices drains into the renal pelvis before continuing distally into the ureter via peristaltic waves of smooth muscle contraction.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Kidney stones

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Each minor calix is funnel shaped and lined with smooth muscle for peristaltic motion of urine distally.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The minor calices directly surround each renal papilla (the apex of each renal pyramid) in order to collect the urine excreted from the pyramids. Two or more minor calices continue as a single major calix.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The minor calices serve as funnel shaped urine collectors due to their close approximation to renal papilla.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Kidney stones

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The major calices are tubular chambers formed by the merging of two or more minor calices. The major calices are lined with smooth muscles, which helps to propel urine distally.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: There are usually two or three major calices per kidney (Standring, 2016). The major calices are located closer to the renal hilum in comparison to the minor calices.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The major calices drain the excreted urine into the large singular renal pelvis.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Kidney stones

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.text: The renal cortex is made up predominately of the renal corpuscles (glomeruli & Bowman’s capsules), the majority of renal tubules, blood vessels, and the portion of collecting ducts within the cortex.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The renal cortex is superficial to the deeper renal medulla. It is a semicircular mass of tissue, which spans from the base of the renal pyramids to the renal capsule.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: This portion of the kidney is responsible for the “ultrafiltration” function of the kidney, which includes filtering of liquid waste, reabsorption of useful substances (ions, vitamins, and small proteins), and regulation of water in the body. This is also the location in which erythropoietin is produced and released into the blood stream, which controls the production of red blood cells.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Polycystic Kidney

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: A thin fibrous capsule composed of collagen rich tissue with some elastic and smooth muscle fibers encloses each kidney. Each fibrous capsule is surrounded by renal fascia and a layer of perirenal fat, known as the adipose capsule of the kidney.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The tough fibrous capsule of the kidney helps to protect the kidney from injury and supports the kidney mass. Additionally, it plays a role in restricting volume changes of the kidney in response to increases in blood pressure (Pocock, Richards and Richards, 2013).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. & Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology, 4 edition. OUP Oxford.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The renal columns are segments of the renal cortex that contain blood vessels (interlobar) and fibrous connective tissue.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The renal columns are extensions of the renal cortex that separate adjacent renal pyramids.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The renal columns provide passage for blood vessels to extend throughout the renal cortex as they continue towards the renal pyramids. The columns also contain fibrous connective tissue contributing to the stroma of the renal cortex.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The renal papillae are described as the apex or pointed end of each renal pyramid. Each papilla projects into a minor calix, which lies in the central space of the renal pelvis. 

A distinct feature of papillae is their sieve-like appearance, which can be attributed to the presence of many small openings on their surface. Each opening represents a small tubule called the papillary duct, into which the collecting tubules within the renal pyramid converge.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Renal papillae are located at the apex of the renal pyramids at the junction of the renal medulla and renal pelvis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Renal papillae carry renal filtrate from the papillary ducts to the minor calices of the renal pelvis via papillary ducts.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Renal papillary necrosis

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The renal pyramids are triangular and consist of numerous collecting ducts that condense at the apex of each pyramid called the renal papilla.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The renal pyramids make up a majority of the renal medulla. A renal column separates adjacent pyramids.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The collecting ducts within the renal pyramids direct urine towards the renal papilla where each pyramid is surrounded by single minor calix. Urine is then transported to a major calix, the renal pelvis and out of the kidney.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The renal pelvis is the funnel shaped, dilated proximal portion of the ureter.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The renal pelvis is within the renal hilum, consists of a transitional epithelium (urothelium), and smooth muscle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Urine from the major calices drains into the renal pelvis before continuing distally into the ureter via peristaltic waves of smooth muscle contraction.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Kidney stones

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The major calices are tubular chambers formed by the merging of two or more minor calices. The major calices are lined with smooth muscles, which helps to propel urine distally.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: There are usually two or three major calices per kidney (Standring, 2016). The major calices are located closer to the renal hilum in comparison to the minor calices.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The major calices drain the excreted urine into the large singular renal pelvis.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Kidney stones

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Each minor calix is funnel shaped and lined with smooth muscle for peristaltic motion of urine distally.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The minor calices directly surround each renal papilla (the apex of each renal pyramid) in order to collect the urine excreted from the pyramids. Two or more minor calices continue as a single major calix.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The minor calices serve as funnel shaped urine collectors due to their close approximation to renal papilla.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Kidney stones

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The renal pelvis is within the renal hilum, consists of a transitional epithelium (urothelium), and smooth muscle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Urine from the major calices drains into the renal pelvis before continuing distally into the ureter via peristaltic waves of smooth muscle contraction.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Kidney stones

17066.name: Fat Body of Renal Sinus (Posterior Part; Right)

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The hilum of the kidney is filled by the renal sinus, renal artery, and renal vein. The remainder of the space is filled with adipose tissue often referred to as the fat body of the renal sinus. The amount of fat in this region normally increases with age (Rha et al., 2004).

sections.text: —Renal sinus lipomatosis

sections.title: Structure/Morphology

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The minor calices directly surround each renal papilla (the apex of each renal pyramid) in order to collect the urine excreted from the pyramids. Two or more minor calices continue as a single major calix.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The minor calices serve as funnel shaped urine collectors due to their close approximation to renal papilla.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Kidney stones

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Distal to membranous urethra extending to external urethral orifice within the corpus spongiosum.

Arterial Supply: Urethral artery and dorsal artery of penis.

Venous Drainage: Dorsal veins of penis and internal pudendal veins.

Innervation: Visceral afferent: Dorsal nerve of penis; Parasympathetic: Pelvic splanchnic nerves; Sympathetic: Lumbar splanchnic nerves.

Lymphatic Drainage: Deep inguinal lymph and external iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: In a flaccid penis, the spongy urethra is approximately 15 cm long and extends from the membranous urethra to the external urethral orifice (Standring, 2016). The proximal part of the spongy urethra is termed the bulbar urethra. This because the bulbourethral glands open into the urethra here. The distal part of the spongy urethra curves downwards and is termed the penile urethra. The penile urethra dilates at its terminal portion within the glans penis as the navicular fossa.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The spongy urethra lies within the corpus spongiosum of the penis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The spongy urethra provides passage for urine and semen out of the body by way of the male external urethral orifice.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The urethral artery, a branch of the internal pudendal artery, enters the penis, just inferior to the perineal membrane. It supplies the spongy urethra and surrounding erectile tissue. Circumflex branches of the dorsal artery of the penis also supply the spongy urethra.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The venous drainage of the spongy urethral is mainly through dorsal veins of the penis and internal pudendal veins, which drain into the prostatic plexus.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: Autonomic fibers arrive at the spongy urethra by way of the prostatic plexus, an inferior extension of the inferior hypogastric plexus. Lumbar splanchnic nerves supply sympathetic innervation, whereas the pelvic splanchnic nerves supply parasympathetic innervation to the spongy urethra. Somatic innervation is supplied by dorsal nerve of the penis, a branch of the pudendal nerve.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: Lymphatic drainage of the spongy urethra drains mainly into the deep inguinal and external iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Kidney stones

—Hypospadias

—Urethritis

—Catheterization

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The navicular fossa is the enlarged distal portion of the spongy urethra.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The navicular fossa is at the distal end of the penis within the glans penis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The navicular fossa is the final portion of the urethra. Urine and semen pass through here, prior to being expelled from the body through the external urethral orifice.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Kidney stones

—Hypospadias

—Urethritis

—Catheterization

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Within the substance of the prostate.

Arterial Supply: Urethral artery.

Venous Drainage: Internal pudendal vein.

Innervation: Visceral Afferent: Second to fourth sacral nerves; Parasympathetic: Pelvic splanchnic nerves; Sympathetic: Inferior hypogastric plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: External and internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The prostatic urethra is the widest and longest portion of the urethra, at 3–4 cm long (Standring, 2016). The urethral crest is a raised ridge that lies between two prostatic sinuses within the prostatic urethra. Prostatic ducts open into the prostatic sinuses. The seminal colliculus is a rounded eminence of the urethral crest with a slit that opens into the prostatic utricle (vestigial remnant of the embryonic uterovaginal canal). The ejaculatory ducts open into the prostatic utricle.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The prostatic urethra passes through the central region of the prostate and continues inferiorly as the membranous urethra.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The prostatic urethra provides passage for urine to travel through the prostate. In addition, it contains the opening of the ejaculatory ducts (sperm and seminal fluid) and several prostatic ducts.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The prostatic urethra is supplied by prostatic branches of the inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The venous plexus surrounding the urethra drains into the vesical plexus surrounding the bladder. The vesical plexus then drains into the internal pudendal veins.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The prostatic urethra has both somatic and autonomic innervation. The somatic innervation is supplied by the second to fourth sacral nerves. The pelvic splanchnic nerve supplies parasympathetic innervation to the prostatic urethra. The inferior hypogastric plexus is extended inferiorly as the prostatic plexus, which supplies mixed sympathetic, parasympathetic, and visceral afferent fibers to the intramural part of the urethra.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: Lymphatic drainage of the intramural part of urethra drains into the internal and external iliac nodes.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Prostate cancer

—Benign prostatic hyperplasia

—Kidney stones

—Hypospadias

—Urethritis

—Catheterization

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The external orifice of the male urethra is the slightly narrower portion of the urethra compared to the other subsections.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The external orifice of the male urethra is located at the terminal end of the glans penis (expansion of the corpus spongiosum).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The external orifice of the male urethra is the opening of the urethra that allows for passage of urine or semen.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Catheter placement
—Hypospadias

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Inferior to the prostate, in the deep perineal pouch.

Arterial Supply: Branches from the dorsal artery of the penis.

Venous Drainage: Internal pudendal vein.

Innervation: Visceral afferent: Second to fourth sacral nerves; Parasympathetic: Pelvic splanchnic nerves; Sympathetic: Lumbar splanchnic nerves.

Lymphatic Drainage: External and internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The membranous urethra is the shortest portion of the male urethra at 2-2.5 cm long (Standring, 2016). It passes through the external urethral sphincter.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The membranous urethra begins at the apex of the prostate and descends inferiorly within the deep perineal pouch. The bulbourethral (Cowper’s) glands are directly posterior to it. The membranous urethra passes through the perineal membrane in order to reach the bulb of the penis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The membranous urethra provides passage for urine and semen to travel to the spongy urethra and to pass out of the body.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The membranous urethra is supplied by the branches of the dorsal artery of the penis, which drains into the internal pudendal vein.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The venous plexus surrounding the urethra drains into the vesical plexus surrounding the bladder. The vesical plexus then drains into the internal pudendal veins.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: Autonomic fibers arrive at the membranous urethra by way of the prostatic plexus, an inferior extension of the inferior hypogastric plexus. Lumbar splanchnic nerves supply sympathetic innervation, whereas pelvic splanchnic nerves supply parasympathetic innervation to the membranous urethra. Somatic innervation is supplied by the second to fourth sacral nerves.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: Lymphatic drainage of the intramural part of urethra drains into the internal and external iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Kidney stones

—Hypospadias

—Urethritis

—Catheterization

sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

25209.name: Male Internal Urethral Sphincter (Right Part)
alternate: Internal Sphincter of Male Urethra (Right Part)
Musculus sphincter internus urethrae masculinae (Right Part)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The male internal urethral sphincter is a circular sphincter muscle consisting entirely of smooth muscle.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The internal urethral sphincter represents the junction between the urinary bladder (superiorly) and the urethra (inferiorly).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: This sphincter is under involuntary control and is tonically contracted due to sympathetic innervation from the lumbar plexus. During urination, the pelvic splanchnic nerves (parasympathetic) cause the internal urethral sphincter to relax allowing urine to pass from the bladder to the urethra.

25030.name: Male Internal Urethral Sphincter (Posterior Part)
alternate: Internal Sphincter of Male Urethra (Posterior Part)
Musculus sphincter internus urethrae masculinae (Posterior Part)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The male internal urethral sphincter is a circular sphincter muscle consisting entirely of smooth muscle.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The internal urethral sphincter represents the junction between the urinary bladder (superiorly) and the urethra (inferiorly).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: This sphincter is under involuntary control and is tonically contracted due to sympathetic innervation from the lumbar plexus. During urination, the pelvic splanchnic nerves (parasympathetic) cause the internal urethral sphincter to relax allowing urine to pass from the bladder to the urethra.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Immediately inferior to bladder. 

Arterial Supply: Inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries. 

Venous Drainage: Internal pudendal vein.

Innervation: Visceral Afferent: second to fourth sacral nerves; Parasympathetic: Pelvic splanchnic nerves; Sympathetic: Inferior hypogastric plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: External and internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The intramural part of the urethra is approximately 1 cm long and consists of a transitional epithelium (Standring, 2016). Depending on the fullness of the bladder the size of the intramural part of the urethra can vary.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The intramural part of the urethra is located between the bladder superiorly and prostate inferiorly. It marks the location of the internal urethral sphincter.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The intramural part is the first portion of the urethra and serves as a transition between the bladder and prostate.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The intramural part of the urethra is supplied by the urethral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Small veins surrounding the intramural part of the urethra drain into the inferior vesical plexuses surrounding the bladder. The vesical plexus drains into the internal pudendal veins.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The intramural part of the urethral has both somatic and autonomic innervation. The somatic innervation is supplied by the second to fourth sacral nerves. The pelvic splanchnic nerves supply parasympathetic innervation to the intramural urethra. The inferior hypogastric plexus is extended inferiorly as the prostatic plexus, which supplies mixed sympathetic, parasympathetic, and visceral afferent fibers to the intramural part of the urethra.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: Lymph of the intramural part of urethra drains into the internal and external iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Kidney stones

—Hypospadias

—Urethritis

—Catheterization

25307.name: Male Internal Urethral Sphincter (Left Part)
alternate: Internal Sphincter of Male Urethra (Left Part)
Musculus sphincter internus urethrae masculinae (Left Part)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The male internal urethral sphincter is a circular sphincter muscle consisting entirely of smooth muscle.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The internal urethral sphincter represents the junction between the urinary bladder (superiorly) and the urethra (inferiorly).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: This sphincter is under involuntary control and is tonically contracted due to sympathetic innervation from the lumbar plexus. During urination, the pelvic splanchnic nerves (parasympathetic) cause the internal urethral sphincter to relax allowing urine to pass from the bladder to the urethra.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The median umbilical ligament is composed of smooth muscle fibers close to the bladder and becomes more fibrous as it approaches the umbilicus. It typically maintains a small lumen that is lined by epithelium.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The median umbilical ligament attaches to the apex of the bladder and travels superiorly to the umbilicus. This structure is also known as the urachus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The median umbilical ligament is a remnant of the allantois, a canal that ran from the apex of the bladder to the umbilical cord in the developing fetus. Its function was to allow for the exchange of gases and removal of liquid waste (Dorland, 2011). The allantois largely closes and is referred to as the urachus or median umbilical ligament after birth. As an adult this structure serves no function.

sections.text:
—Urachal cyst

—Urachal sinus

—Urachal fistula

—Adenocarcinoma
