sections.text:
The skin is the largest organ in the human body accounting for almost 15% of its weight. It covers the entire external surface of the body and is continuous with the mucosae of the digestive, respiratory, and urogenital tracts. The thickness of the skin varies greatly from 1.5-5 mm, depending on its location (Standring, 2016).

The skin consists of three layers including the superficial epidermis, the dermis in the middle and the deep subcutaneous tissue.

- The epidermis is an epithelial tissue layer that undergoes constant renewal throughout life, mediated by a stem cell population within it. It mainly consists of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

- The dermis lies beneath the epidermis. It’s a dense connective tissue that provides strength to the skin through a diffuse interwoven orientation of collagen and elastic fibers throughout it. It’s in the dermis where the skin receives its neurovascular supplies. The dermis has two sublayers, namely a superficial papillary layer and a deeper reticular layer.

- The subcutaneous tissue is the deepest layer and is composed of a loose connective tissue with variable amounts of adipose cells interspersed (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

There are two main types of skin:

- thick, hairless (glabrous) skin, which is found on the soles of feet, palms of the hands, and flexor surfaces of the digits;

- thin, hairy skin that covers the largest area of the body.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The skin functions as a barrier against the external environment, such as harmful microbial organisms and damage from mechanical, chemical, thermal, and UV stimuli. The skin also performs an important endocrine function, such as Vitamin D formation and synthesis of cytokines and growth factors. The skin also plays a role in excretion, through the secretion of sweat and sebum. Also, the skin is important in maintaining homeostasis by controlling the body's temperature and water loss. The various sensory receptors inside the skin make it an important organ for receiving sensory information from the external environment.

sections.title: Dermatomes
sections.text:
Nerves transmit sensory information from the skin to designated spinal nerves through its anterior and posterior rami. The defined area of skin corresponding to each nerve fiber is known as a dermatome. There are 3 trigeminal, 5 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, and 5 sacral spinal nerves supplying the dermatomes. Various models for the distribution of dermatomes, or dermatome maps, now exist. However, because different experimental procedures were used to establish these maps, significant variation exists throughout the literature (Keegan and Garrett, 1948; Foerster, 1933; Lee, McPhee and Stringer, 2008; Head, Campbell and Kennedy, 1997). Generally, dermatome maps are inconsistent and there is significant overlap between adjacent spinal nerves. The commonly used Keegan and Garrett map is a widely accepted dermatome map and is portrayed in this model (Keegan and Garrett, 1948). Dermatome maps still remain a fundamental concept in human anatomy relevant to clinical practice, e.g., differential diagnosis of referred pain from visceral disease, to determine sensory limits of region anesthesia, determining the level of spinal cord injury, or insult caused by prolapsed intervertebral discs.

The L1 dermatome (from the first lumbar spinal nerve) covers the upper part of the lower limb, around the hip girdle and the groin area. L2 dermatome covers the anterior and medial aspect of the thigh, while L3 dermatome includes the anterolateral part of the thigh, down to the medial part of the knee and covers a portion of the medial leg. L4 covers the anterolateral aspect of the thigh, traveling across the knee joint and the anterior tibial aspect of the leg to the medial part of the ankle, foot, and great toe. The distribution of the L5 dermatome can be traced just inferior to the L4 dermatome on the lateral aspect of the thigh, lateral to the knee joint. It wraps around to the anterolateral surface of the leg and dorsum of the foot. It also includes the plantar aspect of the foot and the second, third, and fourth toes. The S1 dermatome includes the posterolateral thigh, most of the posterolateral leg to lateral part of the ankle and foot. The S2 dermatome can be traced medial to the distribution of S1 on most of the posterior thigh and covers a small area of the posterior leg on its medial aspect. All the above dermatomes have distributions to the skin of the gluteal region.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The lacrimal caruncle is a small, pink, globular nodule situated in the medial canthal region (or in the inner corner of the eye). It is embryologically derived from the lower eyelid and hence contains sebaceous and sweat glands, hair, and other skin appendages.

The lacrimal caruncle is mounted on the plica semilunaris, which is a fold of the conjunctiva, considered by some as a vestigial remnant of the nictitating membrane in the lower animals.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lacrimal caruncle is situated medial to the lacrimal punctum and lacrimal canaliculi. The caruncle is a component of the medial rectus capsulopalpebral fascia. The latter originates from the fascia of the medial rectus muscle and contains several structures, including the medial rectus muscle pulley, the medial check ligament, and the lacrimal caruncle, before finally reaching the medial aspect of the tarsal plate.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The lacrimal caruncle has a potential role in the normal lacrimal drainage. Additionally, the tissue around the lacrimal caruncle contains smooth muscle, and its contraction or relaxation may change the size of the lacrimal lake. The sympathetic stimulation of the smooth muscle fibers in the medial rectus capsulopalpebral fascia may pull the caruncle posteromedially. The contraction of smooth muscle fibers of the lower eyelid retractors (the inferior rectus muscle and its capsulopalpebral fascia) pulls the caruncle inferolaterally. Consequently, the area of the lake becomes larger, which may allow increased pooling of lacrimal fluid and more effective suction into the lacrimal punctum (Kakizaki et al., 2010).

sections.text: - Lesions of the lacrimal caruncle

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The upper eyelid is 2–3 mm thick, comprising of skin and a delicate subcutaneous connective tissue in its anterior two thirds and a conjunctival mucosa in its posterior third. The palpebral part of orbicularis oculi muscle lies in between. Externally, it separates the eyelashes in front from the yellowish tarsal (meibomian) glands posteriorly. A loose fibrous layer of submuscular connective tissue lies deep to the muscle, which is extremely rich in its innervation (Standring, 2016).

The firm, dense fibrous tarsal plates provide support to the eyelids, with superior tarsal plate being larger than the inferior one. The tarsal plate is attached superiorly to the orbital septum and on the sides to the medial and lateral canthal ligaments. The deeper fibers of levator palpebrae superioris muscle are attached to the anterior surface of superior tarsus and helps eyelid elevation on sympathetic stimulation.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The upper eyelid is separated from the inferior eyelid by a palpebral fissure but joins it at its extremities, thus, forming the medial and lateral canthi. A small elevation called the lacrimal papilla can be seen on the medial end of the palpebral margin of the eyelid. The papilla possesses an opening called the lacrimal punctum, which serves as the site of drainage of lacrimal fluid into the lacrimal canaliculi.

The arterial supply to the upper eyelid comes from medial and lateral palpebral branches of the ophthalmic artery. The veins correspond with the arteries. The lymph vessels eventually drain into superficial and deep parotid lymph nodes laterally and submandibular lymph nodes inferiorly and medially.

The cutaneous innervation of the eyelids comes from the ophthalmic (CN V1) and maxillary (CN V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve. The upper eyelid is mainly innervated by supraorbital and supratrochlear branches of frontal nerve, lacrimal nerve, and infratrochlear branch of nasociliary nerve.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The eyelids protect the eye from mechanical trauma and serve as a shield from excessive light. Periodic blinking helps prevent corneal dryness (and ulceration) by maintaining a homogenous distribution of tear film over the cornea.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The auricle is the part of the external ear which resides outside the skull. It possesses a cartilaginous framework, which is covered by the skin. Like the skin in all other body regions, the auricular skin comprises epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
Function
sections.text: The auricle collects sound waves from the external environment and funnels them to the external auditory canal. It also helps in the amplification of sound.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The lips are the soft, visible part of the humans’ mouth and comprise the upper and the lower lips. Together these serve as the gatekeepers of the oral cavity.

Embryologically, the lower lip is derived from the first pharyngeal arch and covers the body of the mandible anteriorly. It is lowered by the facial muscles, such as depressor labii inferioris, depressor anguli inferioris, and mentalis, which help to open the oral orifice. The orbicularis oris helps in closing the mouth.

The lips are richly innervated structures. The lower lip receives its cutaneous sensory innervation from the mental nerve (branch of inferior alveolar nerve).

Arterial supply to the lower lip comes from the inferior labial branch of the facial artery (a branch of the external carotid artery).

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The surface of the lips is covered by a thin skin comprising of stratified squamous epithelium. It is non-hairy and lacks sweat glands.

Externally, the lips’ skin forms a junction with the surrounding facial skin, which is marked by the vermilion border (also called the cupid’s bow in the case of the upper lip). Internally, it forms a junction with the mucous membrane inside the oral cavity.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Serving as the gatekeepers of the oral cavity, the lips help in food intake and in articulation of speech. Moreover, being tactile sensory organs and due to their rich sensory innervation, they also serve as erogenous zones in acts of intimacy. Additionally, lips also contribute to the facial expressions.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Cleft lip (and palate)

- Cheilitis

It is raised by facial muscles, such as levator labii superioris, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, levator anguli oris, and zygomaticus major and minor, which help open the oral orifice. sections.text:
The skin is the largest organ in the human body accounting for almost 15% of its weight. It covers the entire external surface of the body and is continuous with the mucosae of the digestive, respiratory, and urogenital tracts. The thickness of the skin varies greatly from 1.5-5 mm, depending on its location (Standring, 2016).

The skin consists of three layers including the superficial epidermis, the dermis in the middle and the deep subcutaneous tissue.

- The epidermis is an epithelial tissue layer that undergoes constant renewal throughout life, mediated by a stem cell population within it. It mainly consists of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

- The dermis lies beneath the epidermis. It’s a dense connective tissue that provides strength to the skin through a diffuse interwoven orientation of collagen and elastic fibers throughout it. It’s in the dermis where the skin receives its neurovascular supplies. The dermis has two sublayers, namely a superficial papillary layer and a deeper reticular layer.

- The subcutaneous tissue is the deepest layer and is composed of a loose connective tissue with variable amounts of adipose cells interspersed (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

There are two main types of skin:

- thick, hairless (glabrous) skin, which is found on the soles of feet, palms of the hands, and flexor surfaces of the digits;

- thin, hairy skin that covers the largest area of the body.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The skin functions as a barrier against the external environment, such as harmful microbial organisms and damage from mechanical, chemical, thermal, and UV stimuli. The skin also performs an important endocrine function, such as Vitamin D formation and synthesis of cytokines and growth factors. The skin also plays a role in excretion, through the secretion of sweat and sebum. Also, the skin is important in maintaining homeostasis by controlling the body's temperature and water loss. The various sensory receptors inside the skin make it an important organ for receiving sensory information from the external environment.

sections.title: Dermatomes
sections.text:
Nerves transmit sensory information from the skin to designated spinal nerves through its anterior and posterior rami. The defined area of skin corresponding to each nerve fiber is known as a dermatome. There are 3 trigeminal, 5 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, and 5 sacral spinal nerves supplying the dermatomes. Various models for the distribution of dermatomes, or dermatome maps, now exist. However, because different experimental procedures were used to establish these maps, significant variation exists throughout the literature (Keegan and Garrett, 1948, Foerster, 1933, Lee et al., 2008, Head et al., 1997). Generally, dermatome maps are inconsistent and there is significant overlap between adjacent spinal nerves. The commonly used Keegan and Garrett map is a widely accepted dermatome map and is portrayed in this model (Keegan and Garrett, 1948). Dermatome maps still remain a fundamental concept in human anatomy relevant to clinical practice, e.g., differential diagnosis of referred pain from visceral disease, to determine sensory limits of region anesthesia, determining the level of spinal cord injury, or insult caused by prolapsed intervertebral discs.

The S2 and S3 dermatomes cover the skin of the penis and scrotum, S3 and S4 dermatomes cover the perianal region, while S5 covers the skin adjacent to the anus.

L2 dermatome covers the anterior and medial aspect of the thigh, while L3 dermatome includes the anterolateral part of the thigh, down to the medial part of the knee and covers a portion of the medial leg. The S1 dermatome includes the posterolateral thigh, most of the posterolateral leg to lateral part of the ankle and foot. The S2 dermatome can be traced medial to the distribution of S1 on most of the posterior thigh and covers a small area of the posterior leg on its medial aspect. All the above dermatomes have distributions to the skin of the gluteal region.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Perineum.

Arterial Supply: Inferior rectal artery.

Venous Drainage: Inferior rectal vein.

Innervation: Pudendal nerve.

Lymphatic Drainage: Superomedial superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The anus is the distal and external opening of the gastrointestinal tract. At its distal end, the epithelium becomes continuous with the skin of the perineum.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anus is encircled by an area of pigmented skin which roughly matches the area of the external anal sphincter.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The anus provides an opening for the elimination of fecal matter from the gastrointestinal tract.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: It is supplied by the inferior rectal arteries which are branches of the internal pudendal arteries.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The inferior rectal veins accompany the arterial supply and drain into the internal pudendal veins.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text: The inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerves (S2-4) provides sensory innervation to the anus. Visceral sensation from the perineum and anus travels back to the CNS via the ganglion impar (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The superomedial superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain lymph surrounding the anus (Földi et al., 2012).

sections.text: - Hemorrhoids

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The subcutaneous tissue is composed of loose connective tissue containing adipose tissue. It is found just underneath the dermis, as opposed to the visceral fat which lies within the peritoneal cavity. The amount of adipose tissue depends on various aspects, such as the location in the body, sex of the individual, and the nutrition of the individual. There is no adipose tissue in the subcutaneous portions of the eyelids, clitoris, or penis. The subcutaneous tissue contains an extensive network of blood vessels. These are important for the rapid uptake of drugs delivered by hypodermal injections, such as insulin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

The subcutaneous tissue acts as a thermal insulator, as a storage of energy, and as a shock absorber. It loosely attaches to underlying deep fascia, aponeurosis and periosteum, thus allowing skin to glide over these underlying structures.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The subcutaneous tissue is composed of loose connective tissue containing adipose tissue. It is found just underneath the dermis, as opposed to the visceral fat which lies within the peritoneal cavity. The amount of adipose tissue depends on various aspects, such as the location in the body, sex of the individual, and the nutrition of the individual. There is no adipose tissue in the subcutaneous portions of the eyelids, clitoris, or penis. The subcutaneous tissue contains an extensive network of blood vessels. These are important for the rapid uptake of drugs delivered by hypodermal injections, such as insulin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

The subcutaneous tissue acts as a thermal insulator, as a storage of energy, and as a shock absorber. It loosely attaches to underlying deep fascia, aponeurosis and periosteum, thus allowing skin to glide over these underlying structures.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The inferior vertebral end plate forms the inferior part of the intervertebral symphysis between two adjacent vertebrae. It lies on the superior surface of the vertebral body that sits inferiorly in an intervertebral joint and is surrounded by smooth, bony epiphyseal rims, the anular epiphyses.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: As a part of the intervertebral symphysis, the intervertebral end plates contribute to maintaining the stability of the vertebral column and resisting various forces in movement. They also help to maintain a fluid pressure of the water content of the nucleus pulposus, by preventing the loss of water to the vertebral body.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The inferior vertebral end-plates are bi-layered cartilages; they are flat and lie obliquely. End plates are relatively dense as they contain both hyaline cartilage and fibrocartilage. The fibrocartilage component lies nearer to the disc and is formed by the collagen fibers of the inner two-thirds of the annulus fibrosus. The cartilage end plates are typically between 0.1 and 2.0 mm thick; however, this varies depending on vertebral region and position (Lotz, Fields and Liebenberg, 2013). In the Lumbar region the end-plates are thinner centrally then peripherally.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Disc Herniation

sections.title: References
sections.text: Lotz, J. C., Fields, A. J. and Liebenberg, E. C. (2013) 'The role of the vertebral end plate in low back pain', Global Spine J, 3(3), pp. 153-64.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The cardinal ligament is the middle condensation of fibrous tissue within the endopelvic fascia that attaches from the lateral pelvic wall to the cervix and vagina. Within the cardinal ligament is an important clinical relationship between the uterine vessels and the ureter (Standring, 2016). The uterine vessels pass superior to the ureter in order to reach the uterus. The common saying used to remember this relationship is “water under the bridge,” with the ureter equaling the water, and the uterine vessels equaling the bridge.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Support to the uterus and passage for the uterine vessels and the ureter towards the urinary bladder.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Hysterectomy

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The rectovaginal septum is formed through a merging of rectovaginal fascia (endopelvic fascia along the lateral walls of the vagina) and the anterior portion of mesorectal fascia. This septum is the equivalent to the rectovesical septum in males (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Vaginal prolapse

—Rectal prolapse

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The arcus tendineus rectovaginalis, similar to the tendinous arch of pelvic fascia, is a condensation of the pelvic fascia lining the levator ani muscles. It projects posteroinferiorly from the lateral aspect of the vagina to the perineal body. Additionally, it attaches the lateral wall of the vagina to the parietal pelvic fascia lining the levator ani muscles posterolaterally. The arcus tendineus rectovaginalis intersects near the midpoint of the tendinous arch of pelvic fascia.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Similar to other condensations of endopelvic fascia, the arcus tendineus rectovaginalis aids in supporting pelvic viscera, specifically the vagina. This structure also creates the vertical axis orientation of the distal vagina (Albright et al., 2005).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Albright, T. S., Gehrich, A. P., Davis, G. D., Sabi, F. L. and Buller, J. L. (2005) 'Arcus tendineus fascia pelvis: a further understanding', Am J Obstet Gynecol, 193(3 Pt 1), pp. 677-81.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The vesicocervical ligament is a thickened portion of endopelvic fascia that is also referred to as the Vesicocervical pillar. This condensation of connective tissue attached the posterolateral surface of the bladder to the cervix. This ligament also blends with a portion of the anteromedial aspect of the cardinal ligaments near the connection to the cervix (Baggish and Karram, 2011).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Baggish, M. S. and Karram, M. M. (2011) Atlas of Pelvic Anatomy and Gynecologic Surgery - E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The rectovaginal fascia is a thin fascia located within the endopelvic fascia separating the vagina (anteriorly) from the rectum (posteriorly). This fascia is equivalent to the rectoprostatic fascia in males. The rectovaginal fascia fuses the mesorectal fascia, forming a rectovaginal septum (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Rectocele

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The uterosacral ligaments are condensations of the endopelvic fascia that span from the sacrum (posteriorly) to the cervix and body of the uterus (anteriorly). They form the lateral boundary of the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The uterosacral ligaments provide support to the uterus and cervix.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The pubovesical ligaments extend from the neck of the bladder to the pubic bones anteriorly. These ligaments consist of both dense connective tissue and smooth muscle tissue from the detrusor muscle of the bladder. In females, this ligament is divided into medial and lateral parts (Dorland, 2011). The lateral part of the ligament extends from the neck of the bladder to the tendinous arch of pelvic fascia, while the medial part is an anterior continuation of the tendinous arch of pelvic fascia to attach to the pubis. In the male, the pubovesical ligament runs parallel and medial to the puboprostatic ligament, and for that reason it is also known as the medial puboprostatic ligament.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The pubocervical ligament attaches from the inferior portion of the pubic bone, passes along and part of the fascia blends with the bladder before terminating near the cervix and upper vagina (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: This small fascia acts like a supportive "hammock" for the bladder and prevents the bladder from herniating into the anterior wall of the vagina.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Cystocele

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The paired pubourethral ligaments attach from the posterior surface of the pubic bone to the dorsal aspect of the proximal urethra and the neck of the bladder (Standring, 2016). These ligaments are thought to aid in the suspension of the urethra in both active and passive phases.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

20020.name: Membranous layer of Perineal Subcutaneous Tissue
alternate: Membranous Layer of Subcutaneous Tissue of Perineum
Membranous layer of Superficial Fascia of Perineum

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The membranous layer of the superficial fascia of the perineum sits in a plane deep to the skin of the anterior perineum along the limits of the urogenital triangle.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: In males, the membranous layer of superficial fascia of the perineum is continuous with the Dartos fascia of scrotum. In females, it has the same boundaries but is not as far-reaching in the labia majora and is continuous with the lower abdominal wall fascia, namely Scarpa’s fascia (or membranous layer of superficial fascia of abdomen) (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: It supports the superficial structures of the perineum.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Fibers of compressor urethrae muscle.

Insertion: Fibrous septum on posterior aspect of urethra.

Action: Constricts urethra.

Innervation: Perineal nerve (S2-S4).

Arterial Supply: Perineal artery.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The fibers of the sphincter urethrae muscle are continuous inferiorly with those of the compressor urethrae muscle.

sections.title: Insertion
sections.text: The fibers of the sphincter urethrae muscle travel posteriorly, encircle the urethra, and insert onto the fibrous septum found along the posterior aspect of the urethra (Jung, Ahn and Huh, 2012).

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Actions
sections.text: The female external urethral sphincter muscle constricts the urethra, keeping it closed and contributing to urinary continence. Its fibers relax during micturition (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Urinary incontinence

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Jung, J., Ahn, H. K. and Huh, Y. (2012) 'Clinical and functional anatomy of the urethral sphincter', Int Neurourol J, 16(3), pp. 102-6.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Rami of both left and right ischial bones.

Insertion: Fibers surround anterior aspect of urethra.

Action: Constricts urethra.

Innervation: Perineal nerve (S2-S4).

Arterial Supply: Perineal artery.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The compressor urethrae muscle originates from the rami of both the left and right ischial bones.

sections.title: Insertion
sections.text: The fibers of the compressor urethrae muscle travel medially, from both its left and right origin sites, to the anterior aspect of the urethra. Its left- and right-sided fibers are continuous with each other as they arch over the anterior aspect of the urethra (Jung, Ahn and Huh, 2012).

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Actions
sections.text: The female external urethral sphincter muscle constricts the urethra, keeping it closed and contributing to urinary continence. Its fibers relax during micturition (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Urinary incontinence

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Jung, J., Ahn, H. K. and Huh, Y. (2012) 'Clinical and functional anatomy of the urethral sphincter', Int Neurourol J, 16(3), pp. 102-6.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Perineal body.

Insertion: Fibers encircle urethra and vagina.

Action: Constricts urethra and vagina.

Innervation: Perineal nerve (S2-S4).

Arterial Supply: Perineal artery.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The sphincter urethrovaginalis muscle originates from anterior aspect of the perineal body.

sections.title: Insertion
sections.text: The fibers of the sphincter urethrovaginalis muscle travel anteriorly, encircle the lower part of the vagina, and continue anteriorly to encircle the urethra. The fibers that encircle the urethra are continuous with those of the compressor urethrae muscle.

sections.title: Key Features & Anatomical Relations
Actions
sections.text: The female external urethral sphincter muscle constricts the urethra, keeping it closed and contributing to urinary continence. Its fibers relax during micturition (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Urinary incontinence

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Jung, J., Ahn, H. K. and Huh, Y. (2012) 'Clinical and functional anatomy of the urethral sphincter', Int Neurourol J, 16(3), pp. 102-6.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

19938.name: Medial Mammary Branches of Internal Thoracic Artery
19938.latin: Rami mammarii mediales arteriae thoracicae internae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Second, third, and fourth perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery.

Course: Extend from the second, third, and fourth intercostal spaces to the anteromedial aspect of the breast.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Anteromedial side of breast.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial mammary branches arise from the internal thoracic artery via the second, third, and fourth perforating branches.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The internal thoracic artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery on the right and left side. As it descends posterior and lateral to the sternum, it gives off perforating branches to the skin corresponding to the upper six intercostal spaces. The second, third, and fourth perforating branches provide medial mammary branches to the supply the anteromedial aspect of the breast. These branches become enlarged during lactation.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The medial mammary branches supply the anteromedial aspect of the breast. The second medial mammary artery is usually the largest and supplies the nipple, areola, and adjacent tissue.

20852.name: Lateral Mammary Branches of Lateral Thoracic Artery
20852.latin: Rami mammarii laterales arteriae thoracicae lateralis
alternate: Lateral Mammary Branches of External Mammary Artery
Rami mammarii externi arteriae thoracicae lateralis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Axillary artery.

Course: Curves around the lateral border of the pectoralis major muscle to the lateral aspect of the breast.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Lateral aspect of the breast.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral mammary branches arise from the lateral thoracic artery, an artery that arises from the second part of the axillary artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: After the lateral thoracic artery arises from the second part of the axillary artery, it descends along the lateral border of pectoralis minor. In females, it gives off lateral mammary branches that curve around the lateral border of pectoralis major muscle. It enters the breast from the lateral side.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The lateral mammary branches of the lateral thoracic artery supply the lateral aspect of the breast.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Median sacral artery.

Course: Travels via the anococcygeal ligament.

Branches: Small unnamed branches.

Supplied Structures: Anus and rectum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The arteriae lumbales imae originates at the level of L5 vertebra.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The arteriae lumbales imae travels anteriorly via the anococcygeal ligament.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Small unnamed branches from the arteriae lumbales imae traverse the rectal and anal fascia.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The arteriae lumbales imae gives a small contribution to the vasculature of the rectum and anal canal near the anorectal junction.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ovarian artery.

Course: Medially towards uterus.

Branches: Small unnamed branches.

Supplied Structures: Distal portion of the uterine tube.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ovarian artery divides into tubal and ovarian branches within the broad ligament as it approaches the lateral aspect of the ovary.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The tubal branches travel medially within the mesosalpinx and forms an anastomosis with the tubal branch of the uterine artery.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The tubal branches give several small unnamed branches as it travels along the distal portion of the uterine tube.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The tubal branches supply the distal one third of the uterine tube. The tubal branches of the ovarian artery form an anastomosis with the tubal branch of the uterine artery.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: The ascending uterine artery.

Course: Laterally towards the ovary.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Ovary and uterine tube.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: As the ascending uterine artery approaches the ovarian ligament and the uterotubal junction, it gives off an ovarian branch of the uterine artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ovarian branch of the uterine artery travels laterally towards the ovary, where it forms an anastomosis with the ovarian branch of the ovarian artery.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: Several small unnamed branches enter the tissue of the ovary.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ovarian branch of the uterine artery contributes to the ovarian arterial supply. The proportion of the ovary supplied via the uterine artery, compared to the ovarian artery varies between individuals.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Abdominal aorta.

Course: Descends into the pelvic cavity.

Branches: Ovarian and tubal branch.

Supplied Structures: Ovary, uterine tube, uterus, and ureter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The ovarian arteries originate as paired branches from the abdominal aorta at the level of L2 vertebra, just inferior to the emerging renal arteries.

During fetal life, the ovarian arteries are short due to the position of the ovaries within the abdomen. Postnatally, the ovaries descend into the pelvic cavity and, therefore, the vessels are identifiable by their long, slender appearance in adults.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The ovarian artery is retroperitoneal and descends within the abdominal cavity. At its origin, it lies medial to the ureters. It continues in an inferolateral direction and passes anterior to the ureters. The ovarian artery then extends over the external iliac vessels and crosses the pelvic brim.

The artery continues within the pelvic cavity and descends medially within the suspensory ligament of the ovary. As it approaches the lateral aspect of the ovary, it divides into tubal and ovarian branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
Upon its descent, the artery lies in close proximity with the ureter and gives small ureteric branches to the ureter.

The ovarian branch travels in the mesovarium to supply the ovary and the tubal branch travels in the mesosalpinx to supply the distal portion of the uterine tube. Both branches anastomose with the corresponding tubal and ovarian branches of the ascending uterine artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
Upon its descent, the ovarian artery supplies a portion of the ipsilateral ureter.

The ovarian branch supplies the ovary and anastomoses with the ovarian branch of the ascending uterine artery.

The tubal branch supplies the distal portion of the uterine tube and anastomoses with the tubal branch of the ascending uterine artery.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Abdominal aorta.

Course: Descends into the pelvic cavity.

Branches: Ovarian and tubal branch.

Supplied Structures: Ovary, uterine tube, uterus, and ureter.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text:
The ovarian arteries originate as paired branches from the abdominal aorta at the level of L2 vertebra, just inferior to the emerging renal arteries.

During fetal life, the ovarian arteries are short due to the position of the ovaries within the abdomen. Postnatally, the ovaries descend into the pelvic cavity and, therefore, the vessels are identifiable by their long, slender appearance in adults.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The ovarian artery is retroperitoneal and descends within the abdominal cavity. At its origin, it lies medial to the ureters. It continues in an inferolateral direction and passes anterior to the ureters. The ovarian artery then extends over the external iliac vessels and crosses the pelvic brim.

The artery continues within the pelvic cavity and descends medially within the suspensory ligament of the ovary. As it approaches the lateral aspect of the ovary, it divides into tubal and ovarian branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
Upon its descent, the artery lies in close proximity with the ureter and gives small ureteric branches to the ureter.

The ovarian branch travels in the mesovarium to supply the ovary and the tubal branch travels in the mesosalpinx to supply the distal portion of the uterine tube. Both branches anastomose with the corresponding tubal and ovarian branches of the ascending uterine artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text:
Upon its descent, the ovarian artery supplies a portion of the ipsilateral ureter.

The ovarian branch supplies the ovary and anastomoses with the ovarian branch of the ascending uterine artery.

The tubal branch supplies the distal portion of the uterine tube and anastomoses with the tubal branch of the ascending uterine artery.

21514.name: Artery of Round Ligament of Uterus

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior epigastric artery.

Course: Follows the course of the round ligament.

Branches: No named branches.

Supplied Structures: The round ligament of the uterus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The artery of the round ligament of the uterus originates from the inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: It follows the round ligament through the inguinal canal as it courses towards the labia majora.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: No named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: It supplies the round ligament of the uterus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Uterine artery.

Course: Ascends on the lateral aspect of the uterine body.

Branches: Arcuate arteries, ovarian branch of the uterine artery, and tubal branch of the uterine artery.

Supplied Structures: Uterus, uterine tube, and ovary.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: It originates at junction of the cervix and uterus as the uterine artery bifurcates into an ascending and a descending branch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
It ascends along the lateral aspect of the uterine body within the broad ligament and is characterized by a highly tortuous appearance.

At the level of the ovarian ligament (near the uterotubal junction), the ascending artery divides into its two terminal ovarian and tubal branches.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
As the artery ascends along the lateral aspect of the uterine body, it gives off the arcuate arteries.

It divides into terminal branches before it reaches the uterotubal junction. These are the ovarian branch of the uterine artery and tubal branch of the uterine artery.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The arcuate arteries supply the uterus while the ovarian branch and the tubal branch contribute to ovarian and tubal vasculature, respectively.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Uterine artery.

Course: Laterally towards ovary.

Branches: Small unnamed branches.

Supplied Structures: Proximal portion of the uterine tube.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The uterine artery divides into tubal and ovarian branches within the broad ligament as it approaches the ligament of the ovary and the uterotubal junction.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: It travels laterally within the mesosalpinx and forms an anastomosis with the tubal branch of the ovarian artery.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: It gives several small unnamed branches as it travels along the proximal portion of the uterine tube.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The tubal branch of the uterine artery supplies the proximal two thirds of the uterine tube. The tubal branch of the uterine artery forms an anastomosis with the tubal branch of the ovarian artery.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ascending branch of the uterine artery.

Course: Towards midline on anterior and posterior aspects of the uterus.

Branches: Helicine arterioles.

Supplied Structures: Uterus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The tortuous ascending uterine artery gives off several arcuate branches that run along the anterior and posterior aspects of the uterus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The arcuate branches divide several times before they reach the midline. Here they form anastomoses between the right and left sides.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The terminal branches of the arcuate arteries are the helicine arterioles.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The arcuate arteries supply all layers of the uterus. The helicine arterioles form a dense network within the myometrium and endometrium.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anterior division of internal iliac artery.

Course: Descends in an anteromedial direction and travels towards the lateral aspect of the uterus.

Branches: Ascending and vaginal branch of uterine artery, arcuate arteries.

Supplied Structures: Vagina, cervix, uterus, uterine tube, and ovary.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The uterine artery originates as a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The artery descends, then travels in an anteromedial direction. It crosses anterior to the ureter as it travels medially within the broad ligament.

It approaches the uterus at the junction between the cervix and the uterus. Here it divides into an ascending and descending branch known as the vaginal branch of the uterine artery.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
The ascending uterine artery is the major branch of the uterine artery and has a tortuous appearance as it ascends to the uterine body.

The uterine artery also gives a branch that descends along the cervix. This branch is known as the vaginal branch of the uterine artery. It travels inferiorly from the cervicouterine junction along the vagina.

Terminal arcuate branches of the uterine artery sit within the endometrium and are named helicine arterioles because of their torturous appearance. These arteries undergo changes throughout the menstrual cycle.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The uterine artery supplies the uterus, cervix, and a portion of the vagina. In addition, it also supplies a portion of the uterine tube and the ovary.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From the uterine artery at the uterocervical junction.

Course: Descends along the cervix and the vagina.

Branches: Azygos arteries.

Supplied Structures: Cervix and upper vagina.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vaginal branch of uterine artery originates at the uterocervical junction, where the uterine artery bifurcates into an ascending and descending branch. The descending branch is also known as the vaginal branch of uterine artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: It descends along the lateral aspect of the cervical and vaginal walls.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The vaginal branches of the uterine artery give a series of azygos arteries which form anterior and posterior median longitudinal arteries along the external vaginal wall.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The vaginal branches of the uterine artery supply the upper vagina. However, the contribution of the vaginal branch of the uterine artery to the vasculature of the vagina is highly variable.

16975.name: Vaginal Branches of Middle Anorectal Artery
alternate: Vaginal Branches of Middle Haemorrhoidal Artery
Vaginal Branches of Middle Hemorrhoidal Artery
Vaginal Branches of Middle Rectal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Middle anorectal artery.

Course: Medially towards the vagina.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: The vagina.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vaginal branches originate from the middle anorectal artery as it travels inferiorly towards the rectum. It is the equivalent to the prostatic branch of the middle anorectal artery in males.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The vaginal branch continues towards the lateral aspect of the vagina.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The contribution of the middle anorectal artery to the vasculature of the vagina is highly variable.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Uterine artery.

Course: Medially towards the lateral aspect of the vagina.

Branches: Azygos arteries and inferior vesical artery.

Supplied Structures: Lower vagina and fundus of the bladder.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vaginal artery originates from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery or it may originate directly from the uterine artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The vaginal artery travels towards the midline. As it approaches the lateral aspect of the vagina, it gives off a series of smaller vessels call the azygos arteries.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text:
Azygos arteries arise from the vaginal artery and form anterior and posterior median longitudinal arteries along the external vaginal wall.

The inferior vesical branch extends anteriorly towards the bladder.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The vaginal artery supplies the inferior aspect of the vagina. However, the contribution of the vaginal artery to the vasculature of the vagina is highly variable.

18139.name: Inguinal Branches of Deep External Pudendal Artery
18139.latin: Rami inguinales arteriae pudendalis externae profundae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep external pudendal artery, a branch of the femoral artery.

Course: Short course in the inguinal region.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Skin of perineum.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inguinal branch originates from the deep external pudendal artery, a branch of the femoral artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: After the deep pudendal artery pierces the fascia lata, it divides into inguinal and anterior labial branches (female), or scrotal branches (male).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The inguinal branch of the deep external pudendal artery supplies the skin of the perineum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Perineal artery.

Course: Travels into superficial perineal pouch.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Vestibule of the vagina.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The artery to the bulb of the vestibule originates from the perineal artery in the superficial perineal pouch.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The artery pierces the perineal membrane and travels towards the vestibule of the vagina within the superficial perineal pouch.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches of the artery of the bulb of the vestibule. However, small unnamed branches extend through the vestibular region of the vagina.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The artery supplies the bulb of the vestibule and the vestibular glands.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Internal pudendal artery.

Course: Anteriorly and traverses the perineal membrane.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Corpora cavernosa of the clitoris.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep artery of clitoris originates as one of the two terminal branches of the internal pudendal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: It travels in an anteromedial direction and must traverse the perineal membrane before it enters the crura of the clitoris.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches of the deep artery of clitoris; however, small unnamed branches extend throughout the erectile tissue of the clitoris.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The deep artery of clitoris supplies the corpora cavernosa of the clitoris.

22451.name: Posterior Labial Arteries
alternate: Posterior Labial Branches of Perineal Artery

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Perineal artery.

Course: Within superficial fascia of labia majora.

Branches: No named branches.

Supplied Structures: Skin of the labia majora and minora.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior labial arteries arise from the perineal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: They run anteriorly within the fascia of the labia majora.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The posterior labial arteries supply the skin of the labia majora and minora, along with the ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles.

18310.name: Anterior Labial Arteries
alternate: Anterior Labial Branches of Deep External Pudendal Artery
Labial Branches of Deep External Pudendal Artery
Rami labiales anteriores arteriae pudendalis externae profundae
Rami labiales arteriae pudendalis externae profundae

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep external pudendal artery, a branch of the femoral artery.

Course: Short course in the inguinal region.

Branches: No branches.

Supplied Structures: Labium majus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior labial arteries originate from the deep external pudendal artery, a branch of the femoral artery. They are synonymous with the anterior scrotal arteries in males.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: After the deep external pudendal artery pierces the fascia lata, it divides into inguinal and anterior labial branches (female), or scrotal branches (male). The anterior labial branches of deep external pudendal artery may anastomose with the posterior labial arteries arising from the internal pudendal artery.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: As the anterior labial branches are terminal arteries, they undergo no further division.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anterior labial arteries supply the labia majora.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Inferior pudendal artery.

Course: Traverses perineal membrane and runs on dorsal aspect of clitoris.

Branches: No named branches.

Supplied Structures: The clitoris.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The dorsal artery of clitoris originates as one of two terminal branches of the internal pudendal artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The artery courses anteromedially in the deep perineal pouch and traverses the perineal membrane and the suspensory ligament of the clitoris. It then continues on the dorsal aspect of the clitoris.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches from the dorsal artery of clitoris.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The artery supplies fascia, glans, and prepuce of the clitoris.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: The ovarian artery.

Course: Towards the ureters.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Portion of the abdominal ureters.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The ureteric branch originates from the ovarian artery as it descends adjacent to the ureters within the abdominal cavity.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ureteric branch travels a short distance to the ureter.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The ureteric branch supplies the ureter in the region where the ovarian artery and the ureter lie in close proximity to each other within the abdominal cavity.

19203.name: Pubic Vein
alternate: Pubic Branch of Inferior Epigastric Vein

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Posterior to the pecten pubis.

Course: Descends posterior to the pubis bone.

Tributaries: No tributaries.

Drainage: Pubis and Pubic symphysis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The pubic vein originates posterior to the pecten pubis.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the pubic vein runs adjacent to the femoral vein and descends posterior to the pubis bone adjacent to the femoral ring. The pubic vein drains into the inferior epigastric or obturator vein. Anatomical variation of the pubic vein is common. It may replace the obturator vein or join the obturator vein as an accessory obturator vein (Moore et al., 2013).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The pubic vein does not receive any tributaries but forms an anastomosis with the pubic branch from the obturator vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The pubic vein drains the pubis and the pubic symphysis.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Strangulated femoral hernia during correction of inguinal or femoral hernia

sections.title: References
sections.text: Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

18232.name: Medial Mammary Branches of Internal Thoracic Vein
18232.latin: Rami mammarii mediales venae thoracicae internae
alternate: Medial Mammary Branches of Internal Mammary Vein

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anteromedial side of breast.

Course: Empties into the internal thoracic vein, which ascends posterolateral to the sternum and empties into the brachiocephalic vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Anteromedial aspect of breast.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The medial mammary branches originate in the anteromedial aspect of the breast.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: As they leave the breast, they perforate the anterior thoracic wall to drain into the internal thoracic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries of the medial mammary branches.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The medial mammary branches drain blood from the anteromedial aspect of the breast and from the areolar venous plexus (of Haller) (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

18209.name: Lateral Mammary Branches of Lateral Thoracic Vein
18209.latin: Rami mammarii laterales venae thoracicae lateralis
alternate: Lateral Mammary Branches of External Mammary Vein

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Lateral side of breast.

Course: Empties into the lateral thoracic vein, which follows the lateral border of pectoralis minor muscle to drain into the axillary vein.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Lateral aspect of breast.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The lateral mammary branches originate in the lateral aspect of the breast.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: As they leave the breast, they curve around the lateral border of pectoralis major to drain into the lateral thoracic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries of the lateral mammary branches.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The lateral mammary branches drain blood from the lateral aspect of the breast and from the areolar venous plexus (of Haller) (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of vessels from pampiniform plexus in the broad ligament.

Course: Ascend to the abdomen to drain into the left renal vein (left ovarian vein) and inferior vena cava (right ovarian vein).

Tributaries: Pampiniform plexus and ureteric veins.

Drainage: Ovaries and lateral part of the uterine tubes.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The veins of the pampiniform plexus are located within the mesovarium of the broad ligament and the suspensory ligament of the ovary. These unite to form the left and right ovarian veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ovarian veins exit the lesser pelvis alongside the ovarian arteries, within the suspensory ligament of the ovary, and ascend into the abdomen. The veins travel lateral to the ureters, and eventually run across them in the abdomen, to run medial to them. The left ovarian vein drains into the horizontal left renal vein, whereas the right ovarian vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The ovarian veins receive venous drainage from the pampiniform plexus and veins draining the abdominal ureter.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The ovarian veins drain the ovaries, the lateral two thirds of the uterine tubes, and the ureter.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of vessels from pampiniform plexus in the broad ligament.

Course: Ascend to the abdomen to drain into the left renal vein (left ovarian vein) and inferior vena cava (right ovarian vein).

Tributaries: Pampiniform plexus and ureteric veins.

Drainage: Ovaries and lateral part of the uterine tubes.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The veins of the pampiniform plexus are located within the mesovarium of the broad ligament and the suspensory ligament of the ovary. These unite to form the left and right ovarian veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The ovarian veins exit the lesser pelvis alongside the ovarian arteries, within the suspensory ligament of the ovary, and ascend into the abdomen. The veins travel lateral to the ureters, and eventually run across them in the abdomen, to run medial to them. The left ovarian vein drains into the horizontal left renal vein, whereas the right ovarian vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The ovarian veins receive venous drainage from the pampiniform plexus and veins draining the abdominal ureter.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The ovarian veins drain the ovaries, the lateral two thirds of the uterine tubes, and the ureter.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of veins from the uterine venous plexus.

Course: Laterally and superiorly within the broad ligament to drain into the internal iliac vein.

Tributaries: Uterine and vaginal venous plexus.

Drainage: Uterus and vagina.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The uterine veins originate from the union of veins from the uterine plexus on either side of the cervix.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the uterine vein travels through the broad ligament. It then travels laterally and superiorly within the pelvis to drain directly into the internal iliac vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Veins from the uterine venous plexus unite to form the uterine vein. Indirectly, the veins from the vagina venous plexus also drain into the uterine veins via the uterovaginal venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The uterine vein drains the lateral sides of the uterus and the vagina.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Pregnancy

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Network of veins that surround the uterus.

Course: Surround the uterus and drains into the uterine vein.

Tributaries: Uterovaginal plexus.

Drainage: Uterus and vagina.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The uterine venous plexus surrounds the uterus on both sides of the cervix.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Small tributaries of the uterine venous plexus unite to form the single uterine vein. The uterine vein enters the broad ligament and travel laterally and superiorly, within the pelvis to drain into the internal iliac vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Veins from the uterine venous plexus unite to form the uterine vein. Indirectly, the veins from the vaginal venous plexus also drain into the uterine veins, via the uterovaginal venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The uterine vein drains the lateral sides of the uterus and the vagina.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Pregnancy

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Plexus of veins within the vaginal mucosa.

Course: Travel around the sides of the vagina to form anastomoses with the uterine venous plexus.

Tributaries: No tributaries.

Drainage: Vagina.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vaginal venous plexus is formed as a continuation of the uterine venous plexus.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The vaginal venous plexus surrounds the vaginal walls and unites with the uterine venous plexus (Schünke et al., 2006; Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013). The uterine venous plexus connects superiorly with the uterine venous plexus and drains into the uterine vein. However, the vaginal venous plexus may drain directly into a left and right vaginal vein (not modeled). If present, the vaginal veins travel superiorly within the pelvis to drain into the uterine vein or take a longer course to drain directly into the internal iliac vein (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The vaginal venous plexus does not receive any tributaries, but it does connect superiorly with the uterine venous plexus.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The vaginal venous plexus drains the walls of the vagina. It may also provide venous drainage to the lower limb (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Schünke, M., Schulte, E., Ross, L. M., Lamperti, E. D. and Schumacher, U. (2006) Atlas of Anatomy: Neck and Internal Organs. Thieme Atlas of Anatomy: Thieme.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of smaller veins in the crus of the clitoris.

Course: Leaves the clitoris, passing under the pubic ligament and in front of the anterior border of the pubic membrane, to drain into the deep dorsal vein of the clitoris or the vesical venous plexus.

Tributaries: Small tributaries.

Drainage: Clitoris.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep veins of the clitoris are small, variable veins that originate in the prepuce of the clitoris.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep vein of the clitoris travels through the substance of the clitoris. In order to drain into the deep dorsal vein of the clitoris or directly into the vesical venous plexus, it travels between the inferior pubic and transverse perineal ligaments to enter the true pelvis (Netter, 2011).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The deep veins of the clitoris receive small perpendicular tributaries, in a ladder-like configuration, from the substance of the clitoris (Di Marino and Lepidi, 2014).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep veins of the clitoris drain the erectile tissue of the clitoris (Di Marino and Lepidi, 2014).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Di Marino, V. and Lepidi, H. (2014) Anatomic Study of the Clitoris and the Bulbo-Clitoral Organ. Springer International Publishing.

Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Netter Basic Science Series: Saunders/Elsevier.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of venules in the posterior labia majora.

Course: Travels in the posterior aspect of the labia and enters the superficial pouch to drain into internal pudendal vein.

Tributaries: Small tributaries.

Drainage: Posterior aspect of labia majora.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The posterior labial vein originates from the union of small venules in the posterior aspect of the labia majora.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From their origin, the posterior labial veins enter the superficial pouch, and travel posteriorly, below the perineal membrane to drain into the internal pudendal vein (Netter, 2011). The posterior labial veins may also drain into the perineal vein or vesical venous plexus or the (not modeled) (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Small tributaries of the posterior labial vein unite to drain into the internal pudendal vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The small tributaries of the posterior labial vein drain the posterior aspect of the female external genitalia.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Netter Basic Science Series: Saunders/Elsevier.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of venules in the anterior aspect of labia majora.

Course: Travels in the anterior aspect of the labia majora and drains into the deep external pudendal vein.

Tributaries: Small venules.

Drainage: Anterior labia, bulb of vestibule, and clitoris.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The anterior labial veins originate in the anterior aspect in this tissue of the labia majora.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The anterior labial veins receive venous blood from the anterior aspect of the labia. From its origin, the veins run laterally, within the superficial fascia of the labia majora, to drain into the deep external pudendal vein. In some instances the anterior labial veins may drain into the internal pudendal vein (not modeled) (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The anterior labial vein is formed by the union of small venules in the anterior aspect of the vagina.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The anterior labial veins drain the anterior aspect of the labia majora, bulb of the vestibule, and clitoris. During the excitement phase of sexual response, the labial veins engorge, increasing the size and consistency of the clitoris and the bulbs of the vestibule of the vagina.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Small tributaries from the scrotum (males) or labia majora (females).

Course: Travels medially to drain into the long saphenous vein.

Tributaries: Superficial dorsal vein of penis (males) or clitoris (females).

Drainage: Skin of medial thigh, external genital, and pubic symphysis.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial external pudendal veins originate as small branches that surround the skin of the scrotum in males, or the labia majora in females.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial external pudendal veins travel medially from its origin, in front of the spermatic cord in males, or the round ligament of the uterus in females, to drain into the great saphenous vein at the saphenous opening.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The veins receive blood from the superficial dorsal veins of the penis in males or the superficial dorsal vein of clitoris in females.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The veins drain the skin of the medial thigh, skin of the external genitalia, and the pubic symphysis.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Superficial perineal space.

Course: Pierces perineal membrane to drain into the internal pudendal vein.

Tributaries: No tributaries.

Drainage: Bulb of vestibule and greater vestibular gland (female).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The vein originates around the vestibule of vagina in the superficial perineal space.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From its origin, the vein of the bulb of the vestibule runs laterally in the superficial perineal space. It pierces the perineal membrane to drain into the internal pudendal vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The vein of the bulb of the vestibule receives no tributaries as it is a terminal branch of the internal pudendal vein.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The vein drains the bulb of the vestibule and greater vestibular gland which lie in the superficial perineal space.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Substance of the clitoris.

Course: Crosses the transverse ligament of the clitoris and pierces perineal membrane to drain into the vesical venous plexus.

Tributaries: Deep veins of clitoris.

Drainage: Clitoris.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep dorsal vein of clitoris originates in the substance of the clitoris.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: Along its course, the deep dorsal vein traverses the suspensory ligament of the clitoris and pierces the perineal membrane, close to the pubic symphysis, to drain into the vesical venous plexus.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: Deep dorsal vein of the clitoris may receive tributaries from the deep vein of the clitoris.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep dorsal vein of the clitoris drains venous blood from the clitoris. During sexual arousal, the deep dorsal vein of the clitoris is compressed by the bulbospongiosus muscles. This aids in the erection of the clitoris.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Urogenital injuries

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Deep to the clitoral fascia.

Course: Travels laterally to medial thigh and drains into the external pudendal or long saphenous vein.

Tributaries: Small tributaries.

Drainage: Clitoris and clitoral hood.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superficial dorsal veins of clitoris originate under the clitoral fascia.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superficial dorsal veins cross the base of the suspensory ligament of the clitoris (Di Marino and Lepidi, 2014). It travels laterally from its origin to the medial thigh where it drains into the superficial external pudendal or long saphenous vein (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superficial dorsal veins of the clitoris are small venous tributaries from the glans and body of the clitoris (Di Marino and Lepidi, 2014).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superficial dorsal veins drain the clitoris and clitoral hood.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Di Marino, V. and Lepidi, H. (2014) Anatomic Study of the Clitoris and the Bulbo-Clitoral Organ. Springer International Publishing.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: A continuation of the anterior labial (females) or anterior scrotal (males) veins.

Course: Travels laterally to drain into the great saphenous vein.

Tributaries: Anterior labial (females) or anterior scrotal (males) veins.

Drainage: Medial thigh, labia majora (females), or scrotum (males).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The deep external pudendal vein originates within the labia majora in females or the scrotum in males.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The deep external pudendal veins take a lateral horizontal course from its origin, deep and parallel to the superficial external pudendal vein. As it traverses the thigh, it becomes more superficial and drains into the great saphenous vein or directly into the femoral vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The deep external pudendal vein receives the anterior labial veins in females or the anterior scrotal veins in males.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The deep external pudendal vein drains the medial aspect of the thigh and the external genitalia.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Multiple branches drain the superior aspect of the bladder and unite to form the superior vesical vein.

Course: Ascends from the bladder, through the lateral ligament of the bladder, to drain to the internal iliac vein.

Tributaries: No tributaries.

Drainage: Superior portion of the bladder.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: Multiple branches on the superior aspect of the bladder unite to form the superior vesical vein.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior vesical vein ascends in the pelvis, with the superior vesical artery to unite with the internal iliac vein. Along their course, both artery and vein pass through the lateral ligament of the bladder.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superior vesical vein forms multiple anastomoses with the paraumbilical veins and inferior epigastric vein in the region of the umbilicus. These veins play an important role in the collateral circulation of the portal vein in the event of hepatic obstruction (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The superior vesical veins drain the superior portion of the bladder.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Arise in the cortex of the ovary and accompanies the ovarian arteries.

Drainage: Paranchyma of ovaries and fallopian tubes.

Direction of Flow:

Right side: Precaval & lateral caval nodes > right lumbar trunk > cisterna chyli > thoracic duct.

Left side: Preaortic and lateral aortic nodes > intestinal trunk and left lumbar trunk > cisterna chyli > thoracic duct.

sections.title: Description:Description: (Location & Drainage)
sections.text:
The lymphatic vessels of the ovary arise as a dense network around the follicles and corpus luteum in the cortex of the ovary. As the vessels pass through the medulla, and towards the hilum of the ovary, the network transitions into 6–8 collector vessels that exit the ovary accompanied by the blood vessels (Földi et al., 2012).

The collecting vessels ascend with the ovarian artery. The ovarian lymph vessels on the right side drain into the precaval and lateral caval nodes that are located near the renal vein. On the left side, the lymph vessels terminate in the preaortic and lateral aortic nodes near the left renal vein (Földi et al., 2012).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Földi, M., Földi, E., Strößenreuther, R. and Kubik, S. (2012) Földi's Textbook of Lymphology: for Physicians and Lymphedema Therapists. Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.title: Description:Description: (Location & Drainage)
sections.text:
The lymphatic vessels of the ovary arise as a dense network around the follicles and corpus luteum in the cortex of the ovary. As the vessels pass through the medulla, and towards the hilum of the ovary, the network transitions into 6–8 collector vessels that exit the ovary accompanied by the blood vessels (Földi et al., 2012).

The collecting vessels ascend with the ovarian artery. The ovarian lymph vessels on the right side drain into the precaval and lateral caval nodes that are located near the renal vein. On the left side, the lymph vessels terminate in the preaortic and lateral aortic nodes near the left renal vein (Földi et al., 2012).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Situated around the uterus.

Drainage: Uterus and peritoneum.

Direction of Flow: External and Internal iliac lymph nodes (also superficial inguinal lymph nodes) > Common iliac lymph nodes > Lateral aortic lymph nodes (left) and lateral caval lymph nodes (right) > left and right lumbar lymph trunk > cisterna chyli > thoracic duct.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The parauterine lymph vessels are situated around the uterus, beneath the peritoneum in the broad ligament.
