18768.name: Suspensory Ligaments of Breast (Inferior Medial Quadrant; Right)
alternate: Ligamenta suspensoria mammae (Inferior Medial Quadrant; Right)
Retinaculum cutis mammae (Inferior Medial Quadrant; Right)
Suspensory Retinacula of breast (Inferior Medial Quadrant; Right)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The breast is composed of glandular tissue surrounded by adipose and ligamentous tissue derived from the superficial fascia of the anterior thoracic wall.

The suspensory ligament of the breast is composed of fibrous strands of connective tissue that extends from the dermis of the skin covering the breast to the deep fascia forming the bed of the breast (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The suspensory ligaments of the breast help to support the breast. It is usually well developed in the upper half of the breast, thus preventing ptosis (or sagging).

sections.title: References

17359.name: Adipose Tissue of Breast (Inferior Lateral Quadrant; Right)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The breast is composed of glandular tissue surrounded by adipose and ligamentous tissue derived from the superficial fascia of the anterior thoracic wall.

The adipose tissue sits between the lobes of the mammary glands of the breast and not between the lobules. In non-lactating breasts, the amount of adipose tissue (fat) surrounding the glandular elements of the breast determines their size.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The distribution and amount of adipose tissue within the breasts give rise to the difference of breast shape and size between individuals.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Largest and most lateral of the three pairs of cerebellar peduncles; dense fascicles of myelinated axons

– Arise from the contralateral pontine nuclei and project to the pontocerebellar cortex of the lateral hemispheres

– Form part of the lateral wall of the fourth ventricle; the lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka) pass at their posterior aspect

– Function: principal input pathway from the cerebral cortex via corticopontocerebellar fibers; coordination of skilled voluntary movement and cognitive and emotional function

– Arterial supply: anterior inferior cerebellar artery

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The middle cerebellar peduncles are the largest and most lateral of the three pairs of cerebellar peduncles, consisting of dense fascicles of myelinated axons arising from the contralateral pontine nuclei and projecting to the pontocerebellar cortex of the lateral cerebellar hemispheres. 

Viewed from the ventral brainstem surface, they are easily identified as large bundles of fibers emerging from the body of the pons and running posterolaterally into the cerebellum. 

They form part of the lateral wall of the fourth ventricle near its widest extent, and the lateral apertures of the fourth ventricle (foramina of Luschka) pass between the posterior aspect of the middle cerebellar peduncle and the dorsolateral medulla oblongata.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The middle cerebellar peduncle carries the axons of the pontine nuclei, forming the principal input pathway from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum—all corticopontocerebellar fibers enter the cerebellum via this peduncle. 

This circuit is fundamental to the coordination of skilled, precise voluntary movement, and to the cerebellar contributions to cognitive and emotional function.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The middle cerebellar peduncle is supplied by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The middle cerebellar peduncle is drained by an anterior cerebellar surface veins. These drain into the superior petrosal sinus. It is also drained by lateral pontine veins which empty into the veins of the medulla.DR

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Forms the caudal portion of the roof of the fourth ventricle

– Bilaminar structure with inner ependymal layer and outer pial layer

– Carries the choroid plexus, which produces cerebrospinal fluid

– Arterial supply: choroidal branches of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery

– Venous drainage: inferior vermian veins and adjacent cerebellar veins

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The inferior medullary velum forms the caudal portion of the roof of the fourth ventricle, extending from the nodule of the cerebellum to the lateral recesses of fourth ventricle.
 
Unlike the superior medullary velum, it has a bilaminar structure, consisting of an inner ependymal layer and an outer pial layer, which fuse to form the choroid membrane carrying the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle. 

The median aperture of the fourth ventricle (foramen of Magendie) is a midline opening within the inferior medullary velum through which the ventricular system communicates with the subarachnoid space.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The inferior medullary velum lies caudal to the superior medullary velum. Its superior surface is related to the nodule and uvula of the cerebellar vermis. 

The cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) lies posterior and inferior to the velum. Ventral to the superior medullary velum is the caudal lumen of the fourth ventricle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The inferior medullary velum serves two roles: forming the caudal roof of the fourth ventricle, and carrying the choroid plexus, which produces cerebrospinal fluid within the fourth ventricle. 

Cerebrospinal fluid exits the ventricular system through the median aperture (foramen of Magendie) in the inferior medullary velum and the paired lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka) at the lateral recesses of the fourth ventricle.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The inferior medullary velum and its choroid plexus are supplied primarily by choroidal branches of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA).

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage occurs via the inferior vermian veins and adjacent cerebellar veins, draining into the straight, sigmoid, or occipital sinuses.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Rostralmost division of the brainstem

– Divided into the tectum, tegmentum, and cerebral peduncles

– Lies between the diencephalon superiorly and the pons inferiorly

– Function: processes visual and auditory information in the superior and inferior colliculi

– Arterial supply: posterior cerebral artery and superior cerebellar artery

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The midbrain (mesencephalon), is the rostralmost portion of the brainstem, composed of numerous axon tracts and nuclei; it is often divided into four parts:

– The roof of the midbrain, also known as the tectum, consists primarily of the quadrigeminal plate (tectal plate) which bears the superior and inferior colliculi. It sits posterior to the mesencephalic aqueduct (aqueduct of the midbrain).

– The tegmentum is the middle portion of the midbrain, lying between the mesencephalic aqueduct posteriorly and the substantia nigra anteriorly. It contains the red nucleus, periaqueductal grey, and the nuclei of the oculomotor and trochlear nerves (CN III–IV).

– The substantia nigra is a distinct nuclear mass lying between the tegmentum and the cerebral peduncles, separating the two.

– The cerebral peduncles comprise the anterior-/ventralmost portion of the midbrain, which primarily carry descending corticospinal/-bulbar fibers. Some resources will include the substantia nigra as part of the cerebral peduncles rather than the tegmentum.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The midbrain is the most rostral division of the brainstem, lying between the diencephalon superiorly and the pons inferiorly. It passes through the tentorial notch of the tentorium cerebelli, which marks the boundary between the posterior cranial fossa and the middle cranial fossa. 

The interpeduncular cistern lies anterior to the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles, the ambient cisterns flank it laterally, and the quadrigeminal cistern lies posterior to the tectum.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The midbrain serves as the link between the cerebral cortex and diencephalon above, and the brainstem and spinal cord below. It transmits axons from the cerebral cortex to the pons, cerebellum, medulla oblongata, and spinal cord and is essential for movements. Fibers running from the cerebellum to the cerebral cortex emerge from the superior cerebellar peduncle into the midbrain as they ascend to the thalamus. All sensory fibers from the body travel through the midbrain to reach the thalamus. Visual and auditory information are processed and integrated with other stimuli in the superior and inferior colliculi. Additionally, cranial nerves III and IV and their respective functions are associated with the midbrain.

The midbrain connects the cerebral cortex and diencephalon superiorly to the pons and spinal cord inferiorly, transmitting descending axons from the cerebral cortex to the pons, medulla oblongata, and spinal cord, and ascending somatosensory fibers to the thalamus.

Fibers from the cerebellum emerge from the superior cerebellar peduncles and decussate within the midbrain tegmentum as they ascend to the thalamus. Visual and auditory information are processed in the superior and inferior colliculi respectively. 

The nucleus of oculomotor nerve, accessory nucleus of oculomotor nerve (Edinger-Westphal), and nucleus of trochlear nerve are located within the midbrain, mediating extraocular movements, pupillary constriction, and accommodation.

The substantia nigra projects dopaminergic fibers to the dorsal striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen) and is integral to the basal nuclei circuitry regulating voluntary movement.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The midbrain is supplied primarily by branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and the superior cerebellar artery (SCA), supplemented by direct branches of the basilar artery. 

The posteromedial central arteries supply the medial tegmentum and cerebral peduncles, the posterolateral central arteries supply the lateral tegmentum, and the collicular artery supplies the tectum.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
Venous drainage of the midbrain follows three routes:

– Anterior drainage from the interpeduncular and anteromedian and anterolateral pontomesencephalic veins drains into the basal vein (of Rosenthal) and subsequently into the great cerebral vein (of Galen). 

– Lateral drainage is carried by the lateral mesencephalic vein, which also drains into the basal vein (of Rosenthal). 

– Posterior drainage passes via the posterior mesencephalic veins into the great cerebral vein (of Galen) before emptying into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Weber syndrome: ipsilateral oculomotor palsy and contralateral hemiplegia resulting from infarction of the medial midbrain, involving the fascicles of cranial nerve III and the adjacent cerebral peduncle.

– Parinaud syndrome: upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and light-near dissociation resulting from compression or infarction of the dorsal midbrain at the level of the superior colliculi.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Paired dense fascicles of myelinated axons; run from the base of the arbor vitae to the midbrain

– Form the dorsolateral wall of the rostral fourth ventricle

– Function: principal efferent pathway; fibers from the dentate nucleus project to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus, forming the cerebellothalamocortical circuit

– Also carries afferents of the anterior spinocerebellar tract

– Arterial supply: superior cerebellar artery

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The superior cerebellar peduncles are a pair of dense fascicles of myelinated axons conveying neural circuits into and out of the cerebellum. 

They run from the base of the arbor vitae to the midbrain, lying on either side of the rostral fourth ventricle where they form its dorsolateral wall.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The superior cerebellar peduncle is the principal efferent pathway of the cerebellum.

The majority of its fibers originate from the dentate nucleus and project to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamic nuclei, and on to the cerebral cortex, forming the cerebellothalamocortical circuit. This circuit contributes to the smoothing and coordination of intentional movements, with additional modulatory effects on behavior and emotion.

The superior cerebellar peduncle also carries afferent fibers of the anterior spinocerebellar tract, conveying information about muscle contraction and limb position to the cerebellum. These fibers cross at spinal cord level and cross again within the superior cerebellar peduncle, projecting to the ipsilateral cerebellar cortex.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The superior cerebellar artery supplies blood to the superior cerebellar peduncle.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Blood is drained from the superior cerebellar peduncles via superior cerebellar peduncle veins. These small variable veins drain into the superior petrosal sinus.DR

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Thin trilaminar membrane spanning the right and left superior cerebellar peduncles

– Forms the roof of the rostral portion of the fourth ventricle

– Layers: ependyma, white matter, and pia mater

– Arterial supply: largely avascular; within the vascular territory of the superior cerebellar artery

– Venous drainage: superior vermian veins and superior cerebellar veins

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The superior medullary velum is a thin membrane that spans the gap between the right and left superior cerebellar peduncles, forming the roof of the rostral portion of the fourth ventricle. 

It is a trilaminar structure: the innermost layer is ependyma, continuous with the ependymal lining of the fourth ventricle; the middle layer is a thin sheet of white matter containing decussating efferent axons from the deep cerebellar nuclei, primarily the dentate nucleus, and fibers of the anterior spinocerebellar tracts; and the outermost layer is pia mater.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
As the roof of the rostral fourth ventricle, the lateral relations of the superior medullary velum are the superior cerebellar peduncles. Rostrally it is attached to the rim of the pontine portion of the fourth ventricle (pontine triangle), and caudally to the most rostral part of the cerebellar vermis and paravermal cortex. The lingula (lobule I), the most rostral vermal lobule, extends over the superior pial surface of the velum and becomes tightly fused to it, forming its dorsal relation. 

Immediately dorsal to the lingula lies the quadrigeminal cistern. Ventral to the superior medullary velum is the rostral lumen of the fourth ventricle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The superior medullary velum's primary function is structural, forming the roof of the rostral fourth ventricle and creating a closed space filled with cerebrospinal fluid. Within the fourth ventricle are three apertures — two lateral and one median (foramina of Luschka and foramen of Magendie respectively) — through which cerebrospinal fluid exits the ventricular system and enters the subarachnoid space, including the superior cistern. 

The white matter core of the velum also contains decussating cerebellar efferent fibers, primarily from the dentate nucleus, preceding the complete decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle in the caudal midbrain tegmentum.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The superior medullary velum is considered largely avascular. It lies within the vascular territory of the superior cerebellar artery (SCA) and its branches, including the medial branch, which supplies primarily the cerebellum, and the collicular artery, which supplies primarily the midbrain tectum.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The superior medullary velum is considered primarily avascular, although related to nearby veins.  The primary venous drainage occurs by the superior vermian veins.  These drain midline structures such as the rostral lobules of the vermis and most of the superior medullary velum.  More lateral regions of the superior medullary velum may flow into superior cerebellar veins that also drains rostral paravermal and lateral hemispheric cerebellar cortex.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Dense fascicles of myelinated axons; run from the posterolateral medulla into the cerebellar white matter, medial to the middle cerebellar peduncle

– Function: transmits multiple afferent pathways to the cerebellum

– Carries the posterior spinocerebellar, cuneocerebellar, and trigeminocerebellar tracts (proprioception) and vestibulocerebellar input to the flocculus and nodule

– Also carries efferent fibers projecting back to the vestibular nuclei

– Arterial supply: posterior inferior cerebellar artery

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The inferior cerebellar peduncles are dense fascicles of myelinated axons carrying information into and out of the cerebellum. They run from the posterolateral wall of the medulla oblongata into the cerebellar white matter, passing medial to the middle cerebellar peduncle. 

Although they appear to merge with the caudal portion of the middle cerebellar peduncle, the axons travelling in each peduncle do not intermix and project to entirely different targets.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The inferior cerebellar peduncle transmits multiple afferent pathways to the cerebellum. 

The posterior (dorsal) spinocerebellar, cuneocerebellar and trigeminocerebellar tracts carry proprioceptive information from the trunk, limbs, and head and neck respectively to the spinocerebellar cortex. Vestibular information from the medial and inferior vestibular nuclei is conveyed via the vestibulocerebellar tract to the vestibulocerebellar cortex of the flocculus and nodule. 

Efferent fibers from the cerebellum project back to the vestibular nuclei via the same peduncle.

Together these pathways make the inferior cerebellar peduncle a critical component of the system for integrating vestibular, proprioceptive and oculomotor information to maintain awareness of body position in space and the relative position of body parts.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The primary arterial supply for the inferior cerebellar peduncle is the posterior inferior cerebellar artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The venous plexus of the brainstem and an inferior cerebellar peduncle vein will drain the inferior cerebellar peduncle into the inferior petrosal sinus and the sigmoid sinus.DR

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Two lateral regions of the cerebellar cortex, flanking the midline vermis; central white matter core covered by cortex

– Cortex folds into tight, uniform, parallel folia

– Lie lateral to the vermis, filling most of the posterior cranial fossa; superior surface beneath the tentorium cerebelli, inferior surface against the occipital and temporal bones

– Function: lateral portions form the pontocerebellum (motor planning, cognition); medial portions the spinocerebellum; flocculus the vestibulocerebellum

– Arterial supply: superior cerebellar arteries (SCA) and the inferior group (PICA and AICA)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The cerebellar hemispheres are the two lateral regions of the cerebellar cortex, flanking the midline vermis. 

Like the vermis, each hemisphere consists of a central core of white matter covered by a cortex, with a total hemispheric surface area of approximately 2400–3200 cm².
To accommodate this area, the cortex folds into tight, uniform, parallel ridges called folia — distinct from the gyri of the cerebral cortex in their small size, regularity, and common parallel orientation.

sections.title: Anatomical Location and Relations
sections.text:
The cerebellar hemispheres lie lateral to the midline vermis, filling most of the posterior cranial fossa. They are posterior to the medulla and pons, connected to them by the three pairs of cerebellar peduncles — inferior, middle and superior.

The superior surface lies directly beneath the tentorium cerebelli, while the inferior surface rests against the squamous part of the occipital bone posteriorly and medially, and the petrous part of the temporal bone anteriorly and laterally, where they are closely related to the transverse and sigmoid dural venous sinuses.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The cerebellar hemispheres contribute to all three functional zones of the cerebellum. 

Their lateral portions form the pontocerebellum, the most phylogenetically recent subdivision, extensively interconnected with the cerebral cortex via corticopontocerebellar loops and contributing to motor planning, action observation, and higher cognitive functions including working memory, language, executive function and visuospatial processing. 

Their medial (paravermian) portions contribute to the spinocerebellum, regulating limb coordination and fine motor control. 

The flocculus forms the hemispheric component of the vestibulocerebellum, contributing to balance and gaze stabilisation.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The cerebellar hemispheres are supplied by two vascular groups, superior and inferior. 

The superior group of arteries comprise the superior cerebellar arteries (SCA), which are branches of the distal end of the basilar artery. 

The inferior group arise from the vertebral arteries and the proximal region of the basilar artery and comprise the posterior inferior and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries, respectively. They supply the inferior surface of the cerebellar hemispheres, roughly from the horizontal fissure to the posterolateral fissure. 

These two vascular territories anastomose near their distal extents.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
Venous drainage largely follows the arterial territories. The superior cerebellar veins drain the anterior lobe and superior vermis, while the posterior and anterior inferior cerebellar veins drain the inferior vermis. 

All veins ultimately drain into the great cerebral vein and the dural venous sinuses of the posterior cranial fossa i.e., straight sinus, superior petrosal sinuses, transverse sinuses, and sigmoid sinuses.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Cerebellar ataxia: lesions of the cerebellar hemispheres produce ipsilateral limb ataxia, characterised by dysmetria and decomposition of movement.

– Intention tremor: an oscillating tremor of the limb that increases as the target is approached, resulting from disruption of cerebellar error correction circuits.

– Dysdiadochokinesia: inability to perform rapid, alternating repetitive movements e.g., pronation and supination of the forearm, reflecting impaired coordination of agonist and antagonist muscle groups.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Paired eminences on the base of the brain, composed of medial and lateral mammillary nuclei

– Located caudal to the tuber cinereum and rostral to the posterior perforated substance; forms part of the floor of the third ventricle

– Receives hippocampal input via the fornix; project to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus via the mammillothalamic tract

– Function: relay in the medial limbic circuit (of Papez), contributing to episodic memory consolidation and spatial navigation

– Arterial supply: perforating branches of posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries

– Venous drainage: basal vein (of Rosenthal) and/or cavernous sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The mammillary bodies are two small, paired eminences on the base of the brain, which are composed primarily of neuronal cell bodies, organized into the medial and lateral mammillary nuclei. The medial mammillary nucleus constitutes the majority of the mammillary body volume and is the principal relay in the medial limbic circuit (of Papez).

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The mammillary bodies lie immediately posterior/caudal to the tuber cinereum and anterior/rostral to the posterior perforated substance. 

They form part of the floor of the third ventricle superiorly and are flanked by the cerebral peduncles. The fornix, carrying the principal afferent input to the mammillary bodies, enters their superior surface.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The mammillary bodies form a key relay in the medial limbic circuit (of Papez), receiving input from the hippocampus via the fornix and projecting to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus via the mammillothalamic tract. This circuit is involved in episodic memory consolidation and spatial navigation.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The mammillary bodies are supplied by small perforating branches of the posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries. The tuberothalamic (premammillary) and mammillary branches, arising from the posterior communicating artery, are principal contributors.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The mammillary bodies are drained by small veins into the basal vein (of Rosenthal) and/or the cavernous sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most commonly from chronic alcohol misuse, causing hemorrhagic necrosis of the mammillary bodies. The acute Wernicke encephalopathy phase presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion; the chronic Korsakoff syndrome is characterized by severe anterograde amnesia and confabulation.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Origin: formed by the merging of fibers from the optic nerves

– Location: sits superior and anterior to the pituitary gland

– Continuations: optic tracts

– Function: partial decussation of optic fibers

sections.title: Location
sections.text:
The optic chiasm is located at the base of the brain within the suprasellar region, anterior to the pituitary stalk and superior to the lobes of the pituitary gland. 

It represents the partial decussation of retinal ganglion cell axons (optic nerve fibers), specifically the crossing of fibers from the nasal halves of each retina into the contralateral optic tract.

sections.title: Continuations
sections.text: Anteriorly, the optic chiasm is continuous with the right and left optic nerves. Posteriorly, it divides into the right and left optic tracts, which course posterolaterally around the cerebral peduncles toward the lateral geniculate nuclei of the thalamus. Some fibers also project to the pretectal area and superior colliculus for reflex visual pathways.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The optic chiasm transmits visual information from the retina toward the thalamus. By allowing nasal retinal fibers to cross while temporal retinal fibers remain ipsilateral, it ensures that visual information from the right visual field is conveyed to the left cerebral hemisphere and information from the left visual field to the right hemisphere. These fibers continue in the optic tracts to synapse primarily in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus before being relayed to the visual cortex.

sections.text: Standring, S. (2021). Gray’s Anatomy: the Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd ed. Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Subdivision of the diencephalon occupying its dorsal and caudal aspect, superior to the midbrain

– Comprises the pineal gland, habenular nuclei and habenular commissure, stria medullaris thalami, and posterior commissure

– Ventricular surface lined by ependyma, forming the roof of the posterior third ventricle

– Function: pineal gland secretes melatonin, regulating circadian rhythms; habenular nuclei link limbic forebrain with brainstem monoaminergic systems

– Arterial supply: posterior choroidal artery (PCA)

– Venous drainage: internal cerebral veins and basal veins (of Rosenthal) into the great cerebral vein (of Galen)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The epithalamus is a subdivision of the diencephalon and comprises the pineal gland (described separately), the habenular nuclei and habenular commissure, the stria medullaris thalami, and the posterior commissure. 

Its ventricular surface is lined by ependyma, which forms the roof of the posterior portion of the third ventricle.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The epithalamus occupies the dorsal and caudal aspect of the diencephalon, superior to the midbrain and immediately rostral to the superior colliculi. The stria medullaris thalami runs along the superomedial border of each thalamus to reach the habenular nuclei. The pineal gland projects posteriorly between the superior colliculi, and the great cerebral vein (of Galen) lies in close relation to it superiorly.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The pineal gland is an endocrine organ which synthesizes the hormone melatonin. The habenula and stria medullaris have limbic connections.

The pineal gland is an endocrine organ, which synthesizes melatonin and is involved in the regulation of circadian rhythms (described in detail under its own entry). The habenular nuclei receive limbic and basal forebrain input via the stria medullaris thalami and project to the interpeduncular nucleus and brainstem raphe nuclei via the habenulointerpeduncular tract (fasciculus retroflexus), forming part of a circuit linking the limbic forebrain with brainstem monoaminergic systems.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The epithalamus is supplied by the posterior choroidal artery, a branch of the posterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The epithalamus drains into the internal cerebral veins, which converge with the basal veins (of Rosenthal) to form the great cerebral vein (of Galen), lying immediately superior to the pineal gland.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Parinaud syndrome: Compression of the dorsal midbrain by pineal region tumors causes impaired upward gaze and abnormal pupillary responses.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Curved sheet of myelinated nerve fibers covering the lateral surface of the thalamus

– Contains thalamocortical and corticothalamic projection fibers

– Separates the main thalamic nuclei medially from the thalamic reticular nucleus laterally

– Function: route through which afferent and efferent projection fibers enter and exit the thalamus

– Arterial supply: thalamoperforating and thalamogeniculate arteries

– Venous drainage: superior and/or inferior thalamostriate veins

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The external medullary lamina is a curved sheet of myelinated nerve fibers covering the lateral surface of the thalamus. It contains thalamocortical and corticothalamic projection fibers, which sort themselves as they pass into and out of the thalamic nuclei.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The external medullary lamina lies on the lateral surface of the thalamus, separating the main thalamic nuclei medially from the thalamic reticular nucleus laterally. The thalamic reticular nucleus in turn separates it from the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The external medullary lamina serves as the route through which afferent and efferent projection fibers enter and exit the thalamus, including thalamocortical fibers projecting to the cerebral cortex and reciprocal corticothalamic feedback fibers.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: Arterial supply to the external medullary lamina is primarily provided by the thalamoperforating and thalamogeniculate arteries, as per the thalamus.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage of the external medullary lamina is facilitated via the superior thalamostriate vein and/or inferior thalamostriate veins, as per the thalamus.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Curved, sheet-like shell of GABAergic neurons partially surrounding the lateral and anterior surfaces of the thalamus

– Classified as prethalamus, distinct from the thalamus proper

– Lies lateral to the external medullary lamina and medial to the posterior limb of the internal capsule

– Function: regulates thalamic output by projecting inhibitory (GABAergic) fibers to other thalamic nuclei; implicated in generation of sleep spindles

– Arterial supply: thalamoperforating and thalamogeniculate arteries

– Venous drainage: superior and/or inferior thalamostriate veins

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The reticular nucleus of the thalamus forms a curved, sheet-like shell of neurons partially surrounding the lateral and anterior surfaces of the thalamus. Its neurons are GABAergic and inhibitory, distinguishing it from all other thalamic nuclei, which use glutamate as their primary neurotransmitter. 

The reticular nucleus, although conventionally described as part of the thalamus, is classified within the prethalamus—the ventral subdivision of the diencephalon comprising the reticular nucleus, zona incerta, and related nuclei—in Terminologia Neuroanatomica, reflecting its distinct embryological origin and connectivity from the thalamus proper.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The reticular nucleus lies lateral to the external medullary lamina of the thalamus and medial to the posterior limb of the internal capsule, forming a curved shell partially surrounding the lateral and anterior surfaces of the thalamus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The reticular nucleus receives collateral branches from both thalamocortical and corticothalamic projection fibers as they pass through it, and projects inhibitory (GABAergic) fibers back to other thalamic nuclei. In this way it acts as a regulator of thalamic output, modulating the flow of information between the thalamus and cerebral cortex. 

It has also been implicated in the generation of sleep spindles.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: Arterial supply of the reticular nucleus of the thalamus is via the thalamoperforating and thalamogeniculate arteries, as per the thalamus.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage of the reticular nucleus is facilitated via the superior thalamostriate vein and/or inferior thalamostriate veins, as per the thalamus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Hallucinations: Dysfunction of the reticular nucleus, through impaired sensory gating and disruption of thalamocortical oscillations, has been implicated in hallucinatory phenomena in schizophrenia and sleep-wake boundary states.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Paired ovoid mass of gray matter; largest component of the diencephalon

– Connected across the midline by the interthalamic adhesion (massa intermedia)

– Internal medullary lamina divides each thalamus into anterior, medial, and lateral regions, containing seven nuclear groups; the pulvinar nuclei form its posterior pole

– Forms part of the floor of the lateral ventricle and the lateral wall of the third ventricle; separated from the lentiform nucleus by the internal capsule

– Function: principal relay and integrative center between subcortical structures and the cerebral cortex; processes all sensory modalities except olfaction

– Arterial supply: thalamoperforating, thalamogeniculate, anterior choroidal, and posterior choroidal arteries

– Venous drainage: superior thalamostriate vein into the internal cerebral vein and great cerebral vein (of Galen)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The thalamus is a paired ovoid mass of gray matter and the largest component of the diencephalon. The two thalami are connected across the midline by the interthalamic adhesion (massa intermedia), a band of gray matter present in the majority of individuals. The lateral surface is covered by the external medullary lamina, a sheet of myelinated fibers through which thalamic afferents and efferents are routed. The pulvinar nuclei form the large posterior pole of the thalamus, overhanging the midbrain.

Internally, a "Y-shaped" internal medullary lamina of white matter divides each thalamus into anterior, medial, and lateral regions, within which are seven nuclear groups: anterior, medial, lateral, posterior, intralaminar, periventricular, and geniculate.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The thalamus lies inferior to the body of the lateral ventricle, the floor of which it forms, and its medial surface forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle. 

The thalamus is separated from the lentiform nucleus laterally by the posterior limb of the internal capsule, and from the hypothalamus inferiorly by the hypothalamic sulcus. The thalamostriate sulcus marks its superior boundary with the caudate nucleus. Caudally, the pulvinar nuclei overlap the superior colliculus of the midbrain, and anteriorly the column of the fornix bounds it at the interventricular foramen.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The thalamus acts as the principal relay and integrative center between subcortical structures and the cerebral cortex, processing all sensory modalities except olfaction before they reach cortical awareness. Beyond simple relay, it regulates which information reaches the cortex and participates in motor control, memory, and emotional processing through its diverse nuclear groups.

sections.title: Connections
sections.text:
The thalamic nuclei project to and receive reciprocal input from the cerebral cortex. 

Sensory relay nuclei transmit somatosensory, visual, and auditory information to primary cortical areas while the ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei relay cerebellar and basal nuclei output to motor cortex. The anterior nucleus relays limbic input via the mammillothalamic tract to the cingulate gyrus, while the dorsomedial nucleus and pulvinar nuclei connect with prefrontal and parietotemporooccipital association cortex, respectively.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The thalamus is supplied by branches of the posterior cerebral artery and posterior communicating artery. 

The thalamoperforating arteries, arising from the posteromedial group of central branches of the posterior communicating artery and proximal posterior cerebral artery, supply the anterior and medial thalamus. The thalamogeniculate artery, arising from the posterior cerebral artery distal to its junction with the posterior communicating artery, supply the posterior thalamus and medial geniculate body.

Additionally, the posterior choroidal artery, the anterior choroidal artery, and several other minor branches of the posterior cerebral artery or posterior communicating artery can also provide arterial supply to the thalamus.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text:
Venous drainage of the thalamus occurs primarily via the superior thalamostriate vein, which unites with the superior choroidal vein near the interventricular foramen to form the internal cerebral vein. The paired internal cerebral veins converge to form the great cerebral vein (of Galen), which drains into the straight sinus.

Additional drainage occurs variably via inferior thalamostriate veins into the basal vein (of Rosenthal, via the anterior perforated substance).

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome): Contralateral pain and allodynia following thalamic infarction.

– Deep brain stimulation: Stereotactic stimulation of thalamic nuclei is used in the surgical management of essential tremor and other movement disorders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Ovoid elevation on the posteroinferior surface of the thalamus; part of the metathalamus

– Lies inferior to the pulvinar nuclei and medial to the lateral geniculate body

– Receives ascending auditory fibers from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus

– Function: thalamic relay of the central auditory pathway; projects to the primary auditory cortex via the auditory radiation

– Arterial supply: thalamogeniculate branches and posterolateral central branches of the posterior cerebral artery

– Venous drainage: superior and/or inferior thalamostriate veins

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The medial geniculate body is an ovoid elevation on the posteroinferior surface of the thalamus, forming part of the metathalamus alongside the lateral geniculate body. It contains the medial geniculate nucleus, through which ascending thalamocortical auditory fibers are relayed to the cerebral cortex.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The medial geniculate body lies on the posterior inferior surface of the thalamus, inferior to the pulvinar nuclei and medial to the lateral geniculate body. 

The brachium of the inferior colliculus approaches it from the posterolateral aspect, carrying ascending auditory fibers from the inferior colliculus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The medial geniculate body serves as the thalamic relay of the central auditory pathway. It receives ascending auditory fibers from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects to the primary auditory cortex via the auditory radiation.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The medial geniculate body is supplied by thalamogeniculate branches and posterolateral central branches of the posterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous drainage of the medial geniculate body is facilitated via the superior thalamostriate vein and/or inferior thalamostriate veins, as per the thalamus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlate
sections.text: – Auditory processing deficits: Unilateral lesions of the medial geniculate body impair frequency discrimination and sound localization contralaterally but do not cause complete deafness, due to the bilateral representation of auditory input at the thalamic level.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Structure: small, ovoid gland; anterior (adenohypophysis) and posterior (neurohypophysis) parts

– Location/Relations: sella turcica; inferior to hypothalamus; superior to sphenoid sinus; close to optic chiasm

– Function: master endocrine regulator; adenohypophysis secretes trophic (ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH) and nontrophic hormones (GH and PRL); neurohypophysis releases ADH & oxytocin

– Arterial Supply: superior and inferior hypophyseal arteries (branches of ICA)

– Hypophyseal Portal System: primary network (median eminence) → portal veins → secondary network (pars distalis)

– Venous Drainage: hypophyseal veins → cavernous sinus → inferior petrosal sinus → internal jugular vein

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The pituitary gland is a small, ovoid structure approximately the size of a chickpea. It consists of two distinct tissue types.
The gland has two primary divisions:

– Anterior part (adenohypophysis): derived from oral ectoderm; glandular in nature (adenohypophyseal (Rathke's) pouch). It comprises three parts, namely the pars distalis, pars intermedia, and pars tuberalis.

– Posterior part (neurohypophysis): derived from neural tissue (diencephalon); primarily composed of axons originating from the hypothalamus. It comprises two parts, namely the infundibulum and pars nervosa.

sections.title: Location/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The pituitary gland is located ventral to the hypothalamus and is continuous with it via the infundibulum, which extends from the median eminence at the base of the hypothalamus. It resides within the sella turcica, a saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone.

Superiorly, the pituitary gland is in close proximity to the optic chiasm, which lies just above it. This proximity is clinically significant, as enlargements of the gland can impinge upon the optic apparatus, potentially affecting vision.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The pituitary gland serves as a major endocrine conduit between the brain and the rest of the body.

The neurohypophysis (i.e., posterior part) acts as a storage and release site for antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) and oxytocin produced in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus.

The adenohypophysis (i.e., anterior part) secretes hormones in response to releasing or inhibiting signals from the hypothalamus. These include:

– four trophic hormones (adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH))

– two nontrophic hormones (growth hormone (GH) and prolactin)

The hormones released by the pituitary gland regulate a wide range of homeostatic functions such as metabolism, growth, reproductive processes (e.g., ovulation, production of testosterone), cardiovascular regulation, osmolarity, and temperature control.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The pituitary gland is supplied by two branches of the internal carotid artery: the superior hypophyseal artery (which primarily supplies the median eminence, infundibulum, and adenohypophysis) and the inferior hypophyseal artery (which mainly supplies the neurohypophysis).

sections.title: Hypophyseal Portal System
sections.text: Branches of the superior hypophyseal artery form a primary capillary network in the median eminence of the hypothalamus, into which hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones are secreted. These hormones are conveyed to the adenohypophysis via the hypophyseal portal system (long and short portal veins), which descends from the median eminence through the infundibulum/pars tuberalis into the pars distalis, where a secondary capillary network is formed. The hypothalamic hormones are then released from the secondary capillary network and diffuse to act on adenohypophyseal endocrine cells, thereby regulating the secretion of most anterior pituitary hormones.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: Venous blood draining the pituitary gland, enriched with hormones secreted by adenohypophyseal glandular cells and neurohypophyseal axon terminals, passes via small hypophyseal veins to the cavernous sinus. From here, blood primarily drains via the inferior petrosal sinus to the internal jugular vein. This venous drainage system enables rapid transport of hormones from the pituitary to target organs (e.g., suprarenal (adrenal) glands, thyroid gland, gonads). (Sav et al., 2025)

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Most caudal component of ventricular system, continuous with fourth ventricle at obex

– Originates from lumen of embryonic neural tube

– Extends length of spinal cord and terminates within conus medullaris

– Lined by a single layer of ependymal cells

– Carries cerebrospinal fluid in early life; partial or complete obliteration in adults

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The central canal is the most caudal component of the ventricular system, continuous with the fourth ventricle at the obex. It originates from the lumen of the embryonic neural tube and extends the length of the spinal cord, terminating within the conus medullaris. In cross-section it is generally oval, with the longer axis oriented dorsoventally. It is lined by a single layer of ependymal cells. The canal carries cerebrospinal fluid in early life but undergoes partial or complete obliteration in adults. Just before its termination, it expands to form the terminal ventricle (of Krause).

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Syringomyelia: Pathological fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord, which may communicate with or develop independently of the central canal; causes progressive loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape distribution and motor weakness

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Paired C-shaped cavities lying within the cerebral hemispheres

– Parts: frontal horn, central part, atrium, occipital horn, and temporal horn

– Medial walls separated by septum pellucidum; roof formed by corpus callosum

– Related laterally to corona radiata and internal capsule

– Caudate nucleus and thalamus contribute to the lateral walls

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The lateral ventricles are paired, C-shaped cavities lying within the cerebral hemispheres, one on each side of the midline. Their shape reflects the developmental expansion of the cerebral hemispheres, during which the temporal lobe is displaced inferiorly and anteriorly.

Each ventricle consists of five parts: the frontal horn, central part, atrium, occipital horn, and temporal horn. The two ventricles are separated in the midline by the septum pellucidum.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The medial walls of the lateral ventricles are separated by the septum pellucidum. The corpus callosum forms the roof of each ventricle throughout its extent. Laterally, the ventricles are related to the corona radiata and internal capsule. 

The head of the caudate nucleus bulges into the lateral wall of the frontal horn, and the body of the caudate nucleus and thalamus form the lateral wall of the central part. The temporal horn lies in close relation to the hippocampus inferiorly and the amygdala anteriorly.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Obstructive hydrocephalus: Dilation of the lateral and third ventricles resulting from stenosis or occlusion of the cerebral aqueduct, most commonly due to congenital stenosis, tumor, or hemorrhage

– Colloid cyst: Benign cyst arising at the interventricular foramen that may cause acute obstructive hydrocephalus by blocking CSF flow between the lateral and third ventricles.

27057.name: Choroid Plexus of Lateral and Third Ventricles
27057.latin: Plexus choroideus ventriculi lateralis et tertii

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Highly vascularized connective tissue core covered by cuboidal choroidal epithelial cells

– Tight junctions constitute blood–cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) barrier

– Lateral ventricular choroid plexus follows C-shaped course from temporal horn to interventricular foramen

– Third ventricular choroid plexus forms two narrow longitudinal strands in roof

– Arterial supply: internal carotid and posterior cerebral artery branches

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The choroid plexus consists of a highly vascularized connective tissue core covered by a single layer of cuboidal choroidal epithelial cells — modified ependymal cells joined by tight junctions that constitute the blood–cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) barrier. 

In the lateral ventricle, the choroid plexus follows a continuous C-shaped course from the temporal horn, through the atrium and body of the ventricle, to the interventricular foramen, where it is continuous with the choroid plexus of the third ventricle. It is absent from the frontal and occipital horns. 

Within the third ventricle, the plexus forms two narrow longitudinal strands in the roof, suspended within the tela choroidea.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The choroid plexus is the principal source of cerebrospinal fluid, producing approximately 500 mL per day through a process of active secretion across the choroidal epithelium. The tight junctions between choroidal epithelial cells restrict the passage of substances from blood to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), maintaining the ionic composition of the CSF and selectively excluding large molecules. 

The choroid plexus also contributes to homeostasis of the central nervous system by transporting metabolic waste products and potentially neurotoxic substances out of the CSF.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The choroid plexus of the lateral and third ventricles is supplied by branches of the internal carotid and posterior cerebral arteries. 

– The anterior choroidal artery (internal carotid artery) enters the temporal horn via the choroidal fissure and supplies the choroid plexus of the inferior horn.

– Posterior choroidal branches of the posterior cerebral artery supply the choroid plexus of the body of the lateral ventricle and the third ventricle, with the medial posterior choroidal arteries coursing within the tela choroidea of the third ventricle roof. 

The two arterial systems anastomose at the choroid enlargement (glomus choroideum) of the lateral ventricle.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– T-shaped choroid plexus carried within inferior medullary velum

– Invaginates into caudal half of fourth ventricle

– Vertical limbs flank midline and adhere to roof

– Horizontal limbs project laterally into lateral recesses; small tufts protrude through lateral apertures

– Contributes to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) production; supplied by inferior cerebellar arteries

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is T-shaped and is carried within the inferior medullary velum, invaginating into the caudal half of the ventricle. 

Its vertical limbs are paired, flanking the midline and adherent to the roof; these limbs fuse at the superior margin of the median aperture and may extend onto the ventral surface of the cerebellar vermis. The horizontal limbs project laterally into the lateral recesses, with small tufts protruding through the lateral apertures into the subarachnoid space of the cerebellopontine angle, where they remain covered by ependyma.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: As with the choroid plexus of the lateral and third ventricles, the fourth ventricular choroid plexus contributes to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) production through active secretion across its choroidal epithelium.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is supplied by the inferior cerebellar arteries.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– White matter tract along the medial border of the hippocampus

– Continuous posteriorly with the crus of the fornix; carries efferent and afferent fibers

– Functions: episodic memory; part of medial limbic circuit (of Papez)

– Arterial supply: anterior choroidal artery; posterior medial and lateral choroidal arteries (P2 segment of posterior cerebral artery)

– Venous drainage: inferior ventricular vein → basal vein (of Rosenthal)

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The fimbria (lit. 'fringe') is a white matter tract running along the medial border of the hippocampus. Although named for its attachment to the hippocampus, it is continuous posteriorly with the crus of the fornix and is considered the first segment of that pathway. It consists of both efferent and afferent fibers.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The fimbria runs along the medial border of the hippocampus, along the floor of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle. It continues posteriorly as the crus of the fornix beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The fimbria carries efferent fibers from the hippocampus through the fornix toward the mammillary bodies, septum, and thalamus, as well as septal and commissural afferent fibers entering the hippocampus. It plays a role in episodic memory and the medial limbic circuit (of Papez).

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The fimbria of the hippocampus is supplied by branches of the anterior choroidal artery. Additional contributions arise from the posterior medial choroidal branches and posterior lateral choroidal branches of the P2 segment of the posterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The main venous drainage of the fimbria is via tributaries of the inferior ventricular vein, which drains directly into the basal vein (of Rosenthal).

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
– Memory and amnesia: Damage to the fimbria disrupts hippocampal output via the fornix, producing deficits in episodic memory analogous to direct hippocampal injury.

– Epilepsy surgery: The fimbria may be involved or transected during selective amygdalohippocampectomy, with implications for postoperative memory function.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Major white matter tract connecting cerebral cortex with subcortical structures and brainstem

– Location: between caudate nucleus and thalamus (medially) and lentiform nucleus (laterally)

– Subdivisions: anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolentiform limb, sublentiform limb

– Contains corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine, and thalamocortical fibers

– Arterial supply: internal carotid artery (anterior choroidal artery); middle cerebral artery (lenticulostriate arteries)

– Venous drainage: thalamostriate veins → internal cerebral veins → great cerebral vein (of Galen) → straight sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text:
The internal capsule is a large, vertical, V-shaped band of white matter in each cerebral hemisphere, forming a dense sheet of projection nerve fibers that connect the cerebral cortex with subcortical structures including the thalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord. 

It is divided into five parts: the anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolentiformpart, and sublentiform part, each containing distinct functional fibre populations.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The internal capsule lies deep within the cerebral hemisphere, bounded medially by the thalamus and head of the caudate nucleus, and laterally by the lentiform nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The internal capsule carries virtually all of the major ascending and descending fibre pathways connecting the cerebral cortex with the rest of the central nervous system, including the corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine, thalamocortical, visual, and auditory pathways.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The internal capsule is supplied by three main arterial sources:

– Anterolateral central arteries (lenticulostriate arteries); branches of the middle cerebral artery, supplying the anterior limb, genu, and most of the posterior limb.

– Long striate artery (long central artery, recurrent artery (of Heubner)); a branch of the anterior cerebral artery, supplying the lower part of the anterior limb and adjacent genu.

– Anterior choroidal artery; a branch of the internal carotid artery, supplying the lower part of the posterior limb, the retrolenticular part, and parts of the sublenticular region.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The internal capsule is drained by deep cerebral veins, predominantly the thalamostriate veins, which empty into the internal cerebral veins and reach the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
–Pure motor stroke: Lacunar infarction of the posterior limb (typically from lenticulostriate occlusion) produces contralateral hemiparesis affecting face, arm, and leg, without sensory or cortical signs.

– Anterior choroidal artery syndrome: Occlusion produces contralateral hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, and homonymous hemianopia from involvement of the posterior limb and retrolenticular part.

– Long striate artery (Heubner's) stroke: Occlusion produces contralateral face and arm weakness with behavioral changes, reflecting involvement of the anterior limb and adjacent caudate.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Large mass of myelinated nerve fibers deep to the cerebral cortex within each cerebral hemisphere

– Contains projection fibers (corona radiata), association fibers (U-fibers and long fasciculi), and commissural fibers (corpus callosum)

– Continuous inferiorly with the internal capsule

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
– Curved white matter tract comprising approximately 2 million fibers

– Six parts: crus, hippocampal commissure, body, column, precommissural fornix, postcommissural fornix

– Principal efferent pathway of hippocampal formation; part of medial limbic circuit (of Papez)

– Functions: episodic memory, spatial cognition; lesions cause anterograde and retrograde amnesia

– Arterial supply: posterior cerebral artery; anterior cerebral artery; posterior choroidal arteries

– Venous drainage: veins of septum pellucidum; internal cerebral veins → great cerebral vein (of Galen) → straight sinus

sections.title: Morphology/Structure
sections.text: The fornix is a curved white matter tract comprising approximately 2 million fibers. It is divided into six parts: the crus, hippocampal commissure, body, column, precommissural fornix, and postcommissural fornix. It carries both efferent and afferent fibers, including commissural connections between the two hippocampal formations via the hippocampal commissure.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The fornix arises from the fimbria of the hippocampus and curves posterosuperiorly as the crus beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum. The two crura unite to form the body of the fornix, which runs anteriorly beneath the corpus callosum and above the third ventricle, separated from the thalamus by the choroidal fissure. At the anterior commissure, the fornix divides into pre- and postcommissural portions: the precommissural fornix passes to the septal area and preoptic hypothalamus, while the postcommissural fornix descends through the hypothalamus to terminate primarily in the medial mammillary nucleus.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The fornix is the principal efferent pathway of the hippocampal formation, connecting it to the hypothalamus, septal nuclei, and thalamus as part of the medial limbic circuit (of Papez). 

It is broadly associated with episodic memory and spatial cognition; lesions of the columns are associated with anterograde and retrograde amnesia. There is also evidence for functional lateralization, with the left fornix carrying information associated with verbal memory and the right with visuospatial memory. 

Along its medial-to-lateral axis, the medial fornix is associated with object recognition while the lateral fornix is involved in emotion and motivational aspects of memory.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text:
The fornix receives arterial supply from multiple sources according to segment. 

The fimbria and crus are supplied by the lateral posterior choroidal artery and the anterior choroidal artery; the body by the medial posterior choroidal artery; and the columns by anteromedial perforating branches of the anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries. 

The posterior choroidal arteries are branches of the P2 segment of the posterior cerebral artery.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The fornix is drained mainly by the veins of the septum pellucidum and the internal cerebral veins, which typically pass caudally to drain into the great cerebral vein and then the straight sinus.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: – Anterograde and retrograde amnesia: Bilateral fornix lesions disrupt hippocampal output to the mammillary bodies and thalamus, producing deficits in both the formation of new memories and recall of recent past events.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The external spermatic fascia is derived from the lower portion of the fibrous aponeurosis of the external abdominal oblique muscle as the testis descend in the embryo, from the abdomen to lie outside the pelvis. It is one of the layers that surrounds the testes and the spermatic cord, lying deep to the dartos fascia and superficial to the cremaster muscle.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The external spermatic fascia is the external layer of three spermatic coverings of the testis. The other being the internal spermatic fascia, which itself lies deep to the cremaster muscle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Areolar tissue separates the dartos fascia from the external spermatic fascia and permits a degree of motility between the facial coverings and the overlying skin. This movement is responsible for the control of the temperature of the testes.

25220.name: Tunica Vaginalis Testis (Lateral Part; Left)
alternate: Tunica vaginalis propria testis (Lateral Part; Left)

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The tunica vaginalis testis is superficial to the tunica albuginea. There is a cavity containing a small volume of fluid between the visceral and parietal layers of the tunica vaginalis testis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The tunica vaginalis testis produces a small volume of fluid to provide lubrication to reduce friction of testes within the scrotum.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
— Hydrocele

—Indirect hernia

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The septa testis are connective tissue structures that span from the mediastinum testis to the tunica albuginea.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The testes are divided into a number of separate lobules. The fibrous tissue structures that separate these lobules are known as the septa testis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The septa testis divides the testis into discrete lobules. Each lobule contains one to four seminiferous tubules which are responsible for sperm production.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The fibrous tissue of the tunica albuginea testis thickens posteriorly as the mediastinum testis.

sections.title: Key Features/ Anatomical Relations
sections.text: This internal aspect of the mediastinum of the testis consists of a fibrous connective tissue network that gives off numerous incomplete septa that attach to the tunica albuginea. The septa separate the testis into approximately 250 lobules. Each lobule contains one to four convoluted seminiferous tubules (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The mediastinum of the testis supports the rete testis and the testicular vessels as they enter and exit the testis.

sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

25395.name: Posterior Trunk of Internal Iliac Vein
alternate: Posterior Division of Internal Iliac Vein

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The posterior trunk of the anterior iliac vein closely follows the path of the corresponding artery and provides venous drainage to the gluteal region and pelvis.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Between the obturator vein and the external iliac or inferior epigastric veins.

Course: Passes behind the superior pubic ramus.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Anastomosis between two veins.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The venous corona mortis, or aberrant obturator vein, is an anastomosis formed between the obturator vein and the external iliac or inferior epigastric veins. Although considered an anatomical variant, one study noted its presence in 41.7% of specimens (Sanna et al, 2018).

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The corona mortis passes behind the superior pubic ramus, 40-96 mm away from the pubic ramus (Darmanis et al., 2007). 

The term “corona mortis” translates as "crown of death," indicating the importance of this structure in orthopedic surgery. Accidental damage to this structure can cause significant hemorrhaging which may be difficult to then achieve hemostasis. It must therefore be considered cautiously during surgery.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: There are no named tributaries.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: The corona mortis forms an anastomosis between two major veins draining the pelvis and the anterior abdominal wall.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Darmanis, S., Lewis, A., Mansoor, A. & Bircher, M. (2007) Corona mortis: an anatomical study with clinical implications in approaches to the pelvis and acetabulum. Clin Anat, 20(4), 433-9.

Sanna, B., Henry, B. M., Vikse, J., Skinningsrud, B., Pekala, J. R., Walocha, J. A., Cirocchi, R. & Tomaszewski, K. A. (2018) The prevalence and morphology of the corona mortis (Crown of death): A meta-analysis with implications in abdominal wall and pelvic surgery. Injury, 49(2), 302-308.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The vein of the ductus deferens runs with the ductus in the spermatic cord. It is a tributary of the vesical venous plexus and it anastomoses with the testicular vein.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The smaller veins inside the testis that converge forming the pampiniform plexus which drains blood from the testis.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The urethral vein is a tributary of the internal pudendal vein. It receives blood from the genitals, urethral bulb and perineum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Union of vessels from the vesical venous plexus.

Course: Ascends in the pelvis to drain into the internal iliac vein.

Tributaries: Ramifications of the vesical venous plexus enter the inferior surface of the bladder.

Drainage: Bladder and distal ureter; prostate, seminal vesicles, and ductus deferens (males).

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The inferior vesical vein is formed by the union of vessels from the vesical venous plexus. Some of these ramifications enter the surface of the bladder in order to drain it.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The inferior vesical vein ascends in the pelvis, with the inferior vesical artery, to drain into the internal iliac vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The inferior vesical vein branches into ramifications that enter the surface of the bladder as the vesical venous plexus. In males, small branches will also drain the prostate and seminal vesical (glands).

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Due to the ramifications of the inferior vesical vein into the vesical venous plexus, it drains multiple structures in the pelvic area. The inferior vesical vein drains mainly the inferior surface of the bladder. The superior surface is drained by the superior vesical vein. In males, the plexus ramifies and may drain part of the prostate, seminal vesical and ductus deferens (Moore et al., 2013).

sections.title: References
sections.text: Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

25259.name: Anterior Trunk of Internal Iliac Vein
alternate: Anterior Division of Internal Iliac Vein

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The majority of the veins in the pelvis follow the path of the arteries with the exception of the iliolumbar vein and the umbilical vein. The anterior trunk of the internal iliac vein drains a large portion of the pelvis region including many of the plexi surrounding the pelvic viscera.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Anastomosis between the obturator artery and the external iliac or inferior epigastric artery.

Course: Arches over the pubic bone between the lacunar ligament and the iliopubic eminence.

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Contributes to local supply and provides a potential collateral route for blood flow.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The corona mortis is an anatomical variation of the obturator artery, where it connects the obturator artery to the external iliac artery or the inferior epigastric artery. It is often confused with another common variation called the aberrant obturator artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
The corona mortis forms a small arch over the pecten pubis of the superior pubic ramus, between the lacunar ligament medially and the iliopubic eminence laterally.

The corona mortis connects the intrapelvic obturator artery with the extrapelvic external iliac artery or inferior epigastric artery. In fact, there are up to six variations of this anastomosis reported (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

The obturator artery itself typically arises from the internal iliac system (approximately 70%), but it may arise from the external iliac artery, the inferior epigastric artery, or, on rare occasions, from the femoral artery. The variation in the obturator artery itself complicates the accurate reporting of specific anatomical variations, namely the aberrant obturator artery (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016).

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: There are no named branches.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The anastomosis behind the superior pubic ramus is important clinically as a fracture of the superior pubic ramus may result in severe bleeding and hemorrhages. Additionally, these variant vessels lie near the femoral ring and are important clinically during surgery (e.g., laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair) (Standring, 2016). The “corona mortis” translates as the “crown of death.” This is reference to the risk of accidental injury during surgery (Cedra, 2016).

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Hernia repair

sections.title: References
sections.text:

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Location: Posterior to the prostatic urethra.

Arterial Supply: Inferior vesical, internal pudendal, and middle rectal arteries.

Venous Drainage: Prostatic venous plexus.

Innervation: Autonomic: Inferior hypogastric plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: External and internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The posterior lobe of the prostate is formed of prostatic glandular tissue.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The posterior lobe of the prostate is located posterior to the prostatic urethra.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The prostate provides passage for urine and sperm to pass out of the body. During ejaculation, the prostate secretes a slightly alkaline fluid into the prostatic urethra. Fluid from the prostate, together with seminal fluid from the seminal gland, and sperm from the ductus deferens combine to form semen.

sections.title: Arterial Supply
sections.text: The prostate receives blood from various sources. Prostatic branches from the inferior vesical artery communicate across the midline of the prostate. The inferior gluteal, internal pudendal, and middle rectal arteries supply branches to the prostate gland.

sections.title: Venous Drainage
sections.text: The prostatic venous plexus surrounds the anterolateral aspect of the prostate. It receives tributaries from the deep dorsal vein of the penis and the vesical venous plexus, which drain into the internal iliac veins.

sections.title: Innervation
sections.text:
The prostate gland receives both autonomic and somatic visceral innervation. The inferior hypogastric plexus supplies the prostate. The nerves traveling to the prostate form a peri-prostatic nerve plexus within the prostatic capsule. The prostatic plexus supplies the smooth muscle of the prostate and prostatic urethra.

The transversely crescent-shaped skeletal muscle is supplied by the pudendal nerve. This skeletal muscle contracts and dilates the prostatic urethra.

sections.title: Lymphatic Drainage
sections.text: The lymphatic drainage of the prostate is through the medial group of external iliac nodes, in which the efferent nodes pass to the internal iliac nodes.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Prostate cancer

—Benign prostatic hyperplasia

sections.text:

Arterial Supply: Inferior vesical, internal pudendal, and middle rectal arteries.

Venous Drainage: Prostatic venous plexus.

Innervation: Autonomic: Inferior hypogastric plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: External and internal iliac lymph nodes.

sections.title: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The embryonic middle lobe of the prostate is a cone-shaped portion of the prostate gland which gives rise to the superomedial and anteromedial lobule.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations

The middle lobe tends to undergo hormone induced hypertrophy with advancing age.

sections.text: Anterior to the prostatic urethra, there is a crescent-shaped mass of skeletal tissue that is completely devoid of glandular tissue.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The anterior lobe of the prostate corresponds to part of the transitional zone, anterior to the prostatic urethra. It is continuous inferiorly with the external urethral sphincter.

sections.title: Function
