sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The skin is the outer integument or covering of the body, consisting of the dermis and epidermis, and resting upon the subcutaneous tissue (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The skin forms the outermost layer of the scalp and is relatively thick, measuring approximately 3 mm (vertex) to 8 mm (occiput) in thickness (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2015).

The skin of the scalp resembles skin covering the rest of the body and is composed of an epidermis and dermis, with an underlying superficial fascia. The epidermis is the outermost layer of the skin and is composed of a stratified squamous keratinized epithelium. The dermis is the layer of skin found deep to the epidermis and contains the skin appendages, such as hair follicles, sweat glands, and sebaceous glands. 

The superficial fascia that lies beneath the dermis and forms the second layer of the scalp is often considered part of the skin, since they are difficult to separate during surgery.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The skin is the most superficial layer of the scalp. It is adjacent to the dense connective tissue of the superficial fascia.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
In general, the skin functions as a barrier against the external environment, such as harmful microbial organisms and damage from mechanical, chemical, thermal, and UV stimuli. The skin also performs an important endocrine function, such as Vitamin D formation and synthesis of cytokines and growth factors. The skin is also involved in excretion, through the secretion of sweat and sebum. 

The skin is important in maintaining homeostasis by controlling the body's temperature and water loss. During thermoregulation, sweating first occurs on the forehead and scalp (Pawlina, 2016).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cranium is the large round superior part of the skull; it encloses the brain, forms the skeleton of the midface, and is made up of the cranial bones held together by sutures, synchondroses, and bony unions (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The bones that make up the neurocranium, the portion of the cranium that houses the brain, are the frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, ethmoid, and sphenoid bones. The cranial bones are considered flat bones derived from the mesenchyme and develop by intramembranous and endochondral ossification. The bones contain a thin inner and outer layer of compact bone, separated by cancellous bone, known as diploë. The inner layer of compact bone is thinner and more brittle than its external layer (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013; Snell, 2011).

The frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital bones make up the calvaria, which is covered by the scalp. The scalp attaches to the calvaria via the pericranium. The outer surface of the pericranium is loosely fused with the epicranial aponeurosis of the scalp via a loose connective tissue. The inner surface of the pericranium firmly attaches to the calvaria. Due to its elasticity, the pericranium can be easily removed from the calvaria, except at the location of the suture lines where it is firmly attached.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The cranial bone is located deep to the scalp and superficial to the meninges and brain parenchyma.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The cranial bones protect the brain within the cranial vault.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The lateral lacunae are venous meshworks within the dura mater on either side of, and continuous with, the superior sagittal sinus; arachnoidal granulations project into them (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
There are usually three irregularly shaped venous spaces, or lacunae, present inside the dura mater, on either side of the superior sagittal sinus. They can be considered as the lateral extensions of the sinus. These include a small frontal, large parietal, and intermediate occipital lacunae. The venous lacunae could potentially become confluent with age and form large single spaces on either side of the superior sagittal sinus. 

Most of the cerebral veins open into the venous lacunae and numerous arachnoid granulations project into them from below. The venous lacunae also drain diploid, emissary, and meningeal veins.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by union of tiny meningeal veins at the crista galli.

Course: Runs backwards within the attached upper margin of the falx cerebrum, from crista galli (anteriorly) to the confluence of sinuses (posteriorly).

Tributaries: Communications with the veins of the frontal sinus, veins of the nose (via foramen cecum), the superior cerebral veins, parietal emissary veins, and venous lacunae. 

Drainage: Anterior cerebral hemispheres.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The superior sagittal sinus begins at the crista galli, formed by the union of small meningeal veins.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The superior sagittal sinus lies within the upper fixed convex margin of the falx cerebrum. It courses in the midline in a shallow groove on the inner aspect of the cranium and grows in caliber as it continues posteriorly. The sinus extends backwards from the crista galli to the confluence of sinuses where it usually turns to the right side to become continuous with the right transverse sinus (Pamir, Black and Fahlbusch, 2010).

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The superior sagittal sinus communicates anteriorly at the crista galli with the veins of the frontal sinus and nose (via foramen cecum). The sinus has additional connections with the superior cerebral veins, parietal emissary veins, and venous lacunae.

sections.title: Structures Drained
sections.text: Lying along the sagittal groove, the superior sagittal sinus drains lateral aspects of the anterior cerebrum into the confluence of the sinuses.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The diploic veins are veins of the skull, including the frontal, occipital, anterior temporal, and posterior temporal diploic veins, that form sinuses in the cancellous tissue between the laminae of the cranial bones. They send branches to the external and the internal lamina, the periosteum, and the dura mater, and empty in part inside and in part outside the skull, communicating with meningeal veins, dural sinuses, pericranial veins, and each other (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cerebral arteries are the arteries supplying the cerebral hemispheres, derived from the internal carotid artery (anterior choroid, anterior cerebral, middle cerebral, and posterior communicating arteries and the circle of Willis) or from the basilar artery (posterior cerebral artery) (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The anterior and middle cerebral arteries are terminal branches of the internal carotid arteries and supply more than 80% of the cerebrum. 

The anterior cerebral arteries anastomose via the anterior communicating artery and supply the superior and medial surfaces of the frontal and parietal lobes. 

The middle cerebral artery is the largest branch of the internal carotid artery. It passes through the lateral sulcus of each hemisphere to supply lateral parts of the parietal and temporal lobes. 

The basilar artery, formed by the union of the right and left vertebral arteries, divides into posterior cerebral arteries. They supply the occipital lobes and the inferomedial temporal lobes. They are connected to the middle cerebral arteries by two short posterior communicating arteries (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The cerebral arteries provide blood to the brain.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The arteries that supply the scalp are located in the subcutaneous tissue and form an anastomosing network.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The scalp has a particularly rich blood supply, with vessels located in the dense subcutaneous tissue. Branches of the external carotid artery supplying the scalp include the occipital, posterior auricular, and superficial temporal arteries. Branches of the internal carotid artery include the supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The arteries of the scalp course through the subcutaneous tissue. These arteries form an anastomosing network with adjacent and contralateral arteries. The arteries are attached to the fibrous connective tissue of the subcutaneous tissue, thus, if a vessel is cut, the ends become retracted between the fibrous septae which may lead to profuse bleeding (Ellis and Mahadevan, 2014).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The arteries of the scalp provide blood to the five layers of the scalp.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The emissary vein is one of the small, valveless veins that pass through foramina of the skull, connecting the dural venous sinuses with scalp veins or with deep veins below the base of the skull (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cerebral veins are veins that drain the surfaces or inner regions of the cerebral hemispheres; they are divided into superficial and deep groups (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
The cerebral veins that drain venous blood from the brain are classified into superficial and deep veins. They are valveless, possess thin walls, and lack muscular tissue. Cerebral veins and venules in the cerebral cortex or white matter have a larger lumen and thin walls compared to the cerebral arterioles which are surrounded by smooth muscle (Standring, 2016; Snell, 2010).

Cerebral veins pierce the arachnoid and meningeal layer of dura and terminate in the nearest dural venous sinus.

The superficial cerebral veins have thin walls and their external surface area is covered by a single layer of meningeal cells. They are divided into three groups which are the superior, middle, and inferior cerebral veins.

The superior cerebral veins drain the superolateral and medial surfaces of each hemisphere of the brain and eventually open into the superior sagittal sinus. The lateral portion of each hemisphere is drained by the middle cerebral vein which ends in the cavernous sinus.

The inferior cerebral veins on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe join the superior cerebral veins and drain into the superior sagittal sinus. The inferior cerebral veins on the temporal lobe anastomose with the middle cerebral veins and drain into the transverse, superior petrosal, and cavernous sinuses (Standring, 2016).

Deep structures of the brain, such as the thalamus, are drained by internal cerebral veins. These veins unite, forming the great cerebral vein, which drains into the straight sinus.

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Cerebral veins end in the nearest dural venous sinuses.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The cerebral veins drain the cerebrum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The veins of the scalp are located in the subcutaneous tissue and largely follow the course of the arteries.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text: The scalp has a particularly rich blood supply, with vessels located in the dense subcutaneous tissue. The venous drainage of the anterior scalp is via the supraorbital and supratrochlear veins. The scalp anterior to the auricles is drained by the superficial temporal veins, while the scalp posterior to the auricles is drained by the posterior auricular veins. The occipital region of the scalp is drained by the occipital veins. The deep parts of the scalp in the temporal region are drained by the deep temporal veins (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.title: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The veins that drain the scalp generally accompany the arteries. The supraorbital and supratrochlear veins terminate by forming the angular vein at the root of the nose. The superficial temporal veins terminate by joining the maxillary veins to form the retromandibular veins. The posterior auricular veins descend behind the auricle and unite with the posterior division of the retromandibular vein, thus forming the external jugular vein. The deep temporal veins are tributaries of the pterygoid venous plexus which is drained by the deep facial vein. Tributaries of the external jugular veins drain the scalp posteriorly and laterally.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The veins of the scalp drain blood from the scalp.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The clivus is the wide, sloping depression found along the midline on the occipital and sphenoid bones. It extends posteroinferiorly from the dorsum sellae of the sphenoid bone to the foramen magnum.

For descriptive purposes, the clivus can be arbitrarily divided into two portions:

- anterior portion, which is located on the superior aspect of the body of sphenoid bone;

- posterior portion, which is located on the internal surface of the basilar part of occipital bone.

The clivus accommodates the brainstem.

sections.text: The tubercles are the two expanded, posterior ends of the greater horns of hyoid bone. On its corresponding side, each tubercle of hyoid bone provides an attachment site for a lateral thyrohyoid ligament.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The body is the horizontal, quadrilateral, centrally located part of the hyoid bone. It is continuous:

—posterolaterally, with both the right and left greater horns of hyoid bone;

—superolaterally, with both the right and left lesser horns of hyoid bone.

The body of hyoid bone consists of anterior and posterior surfaces, and superior and inferior borders.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The spinous process is the single, posteriorly projecting process located at the posterior part of the vertebral arch of the axis (second cervical vertebra). It extends from the junction between the two laminae, which itself is found at the midline.

The spinous process of the axis is large, bifid and horizontally oriented. It provides attachment sites for both neck and intrinsic back muscles and the nuchal ligament.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The horizontal plate (horizontal part) is the horizontal, flat, bony plate of the palatine bone. It is one of the two bony plates of the palatine bone, the other being the perpendicular (vertical) plate, and it is continuous:

—superolaterally with the perpendicular plate;

—posterolaterally with the pyramidal process.

The horizontal plate consists of nasal and palatine surfaces, and anterior and posterior borders. It articulates with the maxilla, vomer and the opposite palatine bone.

The horizontal plates of the palatine bones combine to form the posterior one quarter of the bony hard palate, while the palatine processes of the maxilla combine to form its anterior three quarters. The bony hard palate contributes to the formation of both the floor of the nasal cavity and the roof of the oral cavity.

20207.name: Central Groove of Mandibular First Premolar Tooth
20207.latin: Sulcus centralis dentis premolaris primi mandibularis

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The central groove is the centrally located, horizontal depression found along the occlusal surface of the mandibular first premolar tooth. It travels mesiodistally and separates the buccal and lingual cusps.

23201.name: Lingual Cusp of Mandibular First Premolar Tooth
23201.latin: Cuspis lingualis dentis premolaris primi mandibularis

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lingual cusp is the superiorly located, pointed elevation found along the lingual aspect of the crown of mandibular first premolar tooth. It is one of the two cusps of this tooth, the other being the buccal cusp, and they are separated from each other by the central groove.

The lingual cusp consists of both mesiolingual and distolingual cusp ridges and a triangular ridge. The triangular ridges of both the lingual and buccal cusps combine to form the transverse ridge of this tooth.

23635.name: Buccal Cusp of Mandibular First Premolar Tooth
23635.latin: Cuspis buccalis dentis premolaris primi mandibularis

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The buccal cusp is the superiorly located, pointed elevation found along the buccal aspect of the crown of mandibular first premolar tooth. It is one of the two cusps of this tooth, the other being the lingual cusp, and they are separated from each other by the central groove.

The buccal cusp consists of both mesiobuccal and distobuccal cusp ridges and a triangular ridge. The triangular ridges of both the buccal and lingual cusps combine to form the transverse ridge of this tooth.

20912.name: Occlusal Surface of Mandibular First Premolar Tooth
20912.latin: Facies occlusalis dentis premolaris primi mandibularis
alternate: Masticatory Surface of Mandibular First Premolar Tooth

sections.title: Description

22083.latin: Facies lingualis dentis premolaris primi mandibularis

sections.title: Description

18430.name: Cervical Line of Mandibular First Premolar Tooth
18430.latin: Linea cervicalis dentis premolaris primi mandibularis
alternate: Cementoenamel Junction of Mandibular First Premolar Tooth

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The cervical line (cementoenamel junction) is a thin, irregular margin that forms the boundary between the enamel covering the crown and the cementum covering the root. Therefore, the cervical line separates the crown and root of the tooth.

21109.name: Crown of Mandibular First Premolar Tooth
alternate: Anatomical Crown of Mandibular First Premolar Tooth

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The crown (anatomical crown) is the superior portion of the mandibular first premolar tooth that is covered by enamel. It is separated from the root by the cervical line and consists of five surfaces (buccal, lingual, mesial, distal, and occlusal) and two cusps.

The clinical crown is a term used to describe the superior portion of a mandibular tooth that is not covered by gingiva when viewed in the oral cavity.

16766.name: Distal Surface of Maxillary First Premolar Tooth
16766.latin: Facies distalis dentis premolaris primi maxillaris

sections.title: Description

24005.name: Marginal Ridges of Mandibular First Premolar Tooth
24005.latin: Cristae marginalis dentis premolaris primi mandibularis

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The marginal ridges are the curved elevations found along the occlusal surface of the mandibular first premolar tooth. They consist of:

- A mesial marginal ridge, which extends lingually from the mesial end of the buccal cusp to the mesial end of the lingual cusp.

- A distal marginal ridge, which extends lingually from the distal end of the buccal cusp to the distal end of the lingual cusp.

23304.name: Buccal Surface of Maxillary First Premolar Tooth
23304.latin: Facies buccalis dentis premolaris primi maxillaris

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
sections.text: The sublingual fossae are the two shallow depressions found along the internal surface of the body of the mandible. On its corresponding side, each sublingual fossa is located superior to the anterior portion of a mylohyoid line and lodges a sublingual gland.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior mental spine (superior genial spine or superior genial tubercle) is a small, midline process found along the internal surface of the body of the mandible. It is the upper of the two mental spines that are found along the lower portion of the mandibular symphysis, the other being the inferior mental spine. 

The superior mental spine provides an origin site for the genioglossus muscle. In some individuals, the superior mental spine may be split and present as a pair of superior mental spines.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The infraorbital groove (infraorbital sulcus) is the shallow, posteriorly located depression found along the orbital surface of the maxilla. It travels anteriorly from the posterior border of the orbital surface to the infraorbital canal. The infraorbital nerve and vessels pass through this groove.

Description

16707.name: Posterior Ethmoidal Groove of Ethmoid Bone
alternate: Posterior Ethmoidal Sulcus of Ethmoid Bone

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The sphenoethmoidal suture is a fibrous joint of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the anterior surface of the body of sphenoid bone and the posterior aspect of the ethmoid bone.

The sphenoethmoidal suture is present in adults and replaces the sphenoethmoidal synchondrosis during development.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The ethmoidomaxillary suture (maxilloethmoidal suture) is a fibrous joint found along the orbit of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the orbital plate of the ethmoid bone and the orbital surface of the maxilla.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The ethmoidolacrimal suture (lacrimoethmoidal suture) is a fibrous joint found along the orbit of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the orbital plate of the ethmoid bone and the posterior border of the lacrimal bone.

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
sections.text: The uncinate processes are the two curved, hook-like projections found along the inferolateral aspects of each of the ethmoidal labyrinths. On its corresponding side, each uncinate process articulates with the ethmoidal process of an inferior nasal concha.

sections.title: Description
Description

24088.name: Anterior Ethmoidal Groove of Ethmoid Bone
alternate: Anterior Ethmoidal Sulcus of Ethmoid Bone

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The alae are the two wing-like, lateral projections that form the anterior aspect of the crista galli of ethmoid bone. They form the posterior margin of the foramen cecum and articulate with the inferomedial aspect of the frontal bone, contributing to the formation of the frontoethmoidal suture.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The frontoethmoidal suture is a fibrous joint of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the inferomedial aspect of the frontal bone and the superior aspect of the ethmoid bone.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The basilar part (basioccipital or clival part) is the quadrilateral portion of the occipital bone that is located anterosuperior to the foramen magnum. It is continuous posteriorly with both the right and left lateral parts of the occipital bone.

The basilar part consists of the pharyngeal tubercle, the medial portion of the groove for the inferior petrosal sinus, and the posterior portion of the clivus. It provides insertion sites for the longus capitis and rectus capitis anterior muscles, and an attachment site for the pharyngeal raphe and anterior atlantooccipital membrane.

The basilar part articulates:

—anteriorly, with the posterior surface of the body of sphenoid bone, forming the sphenooccipital synchondrosis;

—laterally, with the petrous part of temporal bone, contributing to the formation of the petrooccipital synchondrosis.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The ethmoidal process is the thin, irregularly shaped, posterosuperiorly located projection found along the superior border of the inferior nasal concha. It is one of three processes found along the superior border of inferior nasal concha, the other two being the lacrimal and maxillary processes.

The ethmoidal process of inferior nasal concha articulates with the uncinate process of the ethmoid bone.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The rami of mandible (mandibular rami) are the two vertical, quadrilateral, posterolaterally located parts of the mandible. Each ramus extends posterosuperiorly from the posterior ends of the body of the mandible and is continuous:

—anterosuperiorly with the coronoid process on its corresponding side;

—posterosuperiorly with the condylar process on its corresponding side.

Each ramus consists of medial and lateral surfaces, anterior and posterior borders, and an angle of the mandible. They are larger and wider in males than females.

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
sections.text: The mental tubercles are the two small prominences found along the external surface of the body of the mandible. Each mental tubercle contributes to the formation of the prominence of the chin and is continuous medially with the mental protuberance.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The submandibular fossae are the two shallow depressions found along the internal surface of the body of the mandible. On its corresponding side, each submandibular fossa is located inferior to a mylohyoid line and lodges a submandibular gland.

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
Description
sections.text: The body of mandible (mandibular body) is the horizontal, U-shaped, centrally located part of the bone. It is continuous superiorly with the alveolar process and continuous posterolaterally with both the right and left rami of the mandible. It consists of internal and external surfaces and a base.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The mandibular symphysis (mental symphysis or symphysis menti) is the vertical, sometimes indistinct, line found along the midline on the body of the mandible. It marks the site of fusion between the right and left halves of the mandible that unite during its development. 

On the external surface of the body of the mandible, the lower portion of the mandibular symphysis is continuous inferiorly with the mental protuberance. On the internal surface of the body of the mandible, the superior and inferior mental spines are found along the lower portion of the mandibular symphysis.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The mental protuberance is the triangular, midline elevation found along the external surface of the body of the mandible. It contributes to the formation of the prominence of the chin and is continuous:

—superiorly with the mandibular symphysis;

—laterally, with the mental tubercles.

The mental protuberance is more pronounced in males than females.

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
sections.text: The coronal suture (frontoparietal suture) is a fibrous joint found along the superior aspect of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the parietal margin of the frontal bone and the frontal borders of both the right and left parietal bones.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The sagittal suture (interparietal suture) is a fibrous joint found along the superior aspect of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the sagittal borders of both the right and left parietal bones.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The coronal suture (frontoparietal suture) is a fibrous joint found along the superior aspect of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the parietal margin of the frontal bone and the frontal borders of both the right and left parietal bones.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The glabella is a craniometric point found along the midline on the anterior aspect of the cranium. It is the most anterior midline portion of the frontal bone and is located between its right and left superciliary arches.

In some individuals, a remnant of the metopic suture may be present along the glabella. The metopic suture separates the right and left halves of the frontal bone before they fuse during development.

The glabella is more pronounced in males than females.

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
Description
sections.text: The nasion is a craniometric point found along the midline on the anterior aspect of the cranium. It is formed by the frontal bone and the right and left nasal bones and is located at the area where the internasal and frontonasal sutures meet.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The occipitomastoid suture is a fibrous joint found along the lateral aspect of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the mastoid border of the occipital bone and the occipital border of the mastoid part of temporal bone.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The coronal suture (frontoparietal suture) is a fibrous joint found along the superior aspect of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the parietal margin of the frontal bone and the frontal borders of both the right and left parietal bones.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The sphenosquamous suture (sphenosquamosal suture) is a fibrous joint found along the lateral aspect of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the squamosal margin of the greater wing of sphenoid bone and the sphenoidal border of the squamous part of temporal bone.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The pterion is a craniometric point found along the lateral aspect of the cranium. It is formed by the frontal, parietal, sphenoid and temporal bones and is located at the area of the temporal fossa where these four bones meet.

The pterion is the location site for the sphenoidal (anterolateral) fontanelle in infants.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lambdoid suture (lambdoidal suture) is a lambda-shaped, fibrous joint found along the posterior aspect of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the lambdoid border of the occipital bone and the occipital borders of both the right and left parietal bones.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The squamous suture (squamosal, squamoparietal, or parietosquamosal suture) is a fibrous joint found along the lateral aspect of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the squamosal border of the parietal bone and the parietal border of the squamous part of temporal bone.

The squamous suture is continuous, posteriorly, with the parietomastoid suture.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The asterion is a craniometric point found along the lateral aspect of the cranium. It is formed by the occipital, parietal and temporal bones and is located at the area where the lambdoid, occipitomastoid and parietomastoid sutures meet.

The asterion is the location site for the mastoid (posterolateral) fontanelle in infants.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The sagittal suture (interparietal suture) is a fibrous joint found along the superior aspect of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the sagittal borders of both the right and left parietal bones.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lambdoid suture (lambdoidal suture) is a lambda-shaped, fibrous joint found along the posterior aspect of the cranium. It is the articulation site located between the lambdoid border of the occipital bone and the occipital borders of both the right and left parietal bones.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The vertex is a craniometric point found along the midline on the superior aspect of the cranium. It is the most superior point of the cranium, formed by both the right and left parietal bones, and is usually located along the sagittal suture.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The bregma is a craniometric point found along the midline on the superior aspect of the cranium. It is formed by the frontal bone and the right and left parietal bones and is located at the area where the sagittal and coronal sutures meet.

The bregma is the location site for the anterior fontanelle in infants.

16638.name: Groove for Superior Sagittal Sinus (Right Parietal Part)
alternate: Sulcus for Superior Sagittal Sinus (Right Parietal Part)

sections.title: Description

20941.name: Groove for Superior Sagittal Sinus (Frontal Part)
alternate: Sulcus for Superior Sagittal Sinus (Frontal Part)

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The anterior clinoid processes are the two sharp, posteriorly projecting processes found along the medial ends of the posterior margins of both the right and left lesser wings of sphenoid bone. On its corresponding side, each anterior clinoid process provides attachment sites for the tentorium cerebelli and diaphragma sellae.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The grooves for transverse sinuses (sulci for transverse sinuses or transverse sulci) are the two wide, horizontal depressions found along the internal surface of the occipital bone. They extend laterally from the internal occipital protuberance and travel towards the mastoid angles of the parietal bones. They separate the cerebral fossae of occipital bone from its cerebellar fossae.

The right groove for transverse sinus is continuous superiorly with the groove for the superior sagittal sinus, while both the right and left grooves for transverse sinuses are continuous laterally with a groove for the sigmoid sinus. 

The grooves for transverse sinuses each lodge a transverse sinus and their margins provide attachment sites for the tentorium cerebelli.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The internal occipital crest is the ridge found along the internal aspect of the squamous part of occipital bone. It extends anteroinferiorly, along the midline, from the internal occipital protuberance towards the foramen magnum.

The internal occipital crest separates the right and left cerebellar fossae of occipital bone and provides attachment sites for the falx cerebelli.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The frontal crest is the ridge found along the internal surface of the squamous part of frontal bone. It extends superiorly, along the midline, from the foramen cecum and is continuous superiorly with the groove for the superior sagittal sinus. The frontal crest provides an attachment site for the falx cerebri.

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
Description
Description
sections.text: The pharyngeal tubercle is the small prominence found along the midline on the inferior aspect of the basilar part of occipital bone. It provides an attachment site for the pharyngeal raphe.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The mandibular fossa (glenoid fossa of temporal bone) is the smooth, deep depression found along the inferolateral aspect of the temporal bone. Within the mandibular fossa lies its articular and non-articular portions:

—the anteriorly located articular portion is formed by the inferior aspect of the squamous part of temporal bone and attaches to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint;

—the posteriorly located non-articular portion is formed by the tympanic part of temporal bone.

The mandibular fossa contributes to the formation of the temporomandibular joint, along with the condylar process of the mandible and an intervening articular disc of the temporomandibular joint.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The external occipital crest (median nuchal line) is the ridge found along the external aspect of the squamous part of occipital bone. It extends anteroinferiorly, along the midline, from the external occipital protuberance to the foramen magnum. The inferior nuchal lines extend laterally from the middle of the external occipital crest.

The external occipital crest divides the nuchal plane into right and left halves and provides an attachment site for the nuchal ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The inferior nuchal lines are the lower pair of curved ridges found along the external aspect of the squamous part of occipital bone. They extend laterally from the middle of the external occipital crest, curve across the nuchal plane, and travel towards the jugular processes of the occipital bone.

The inferior nuchal lines provide insertion sites for the rectus capitis posterior major and minor muscles. They are more pronounced in males than females.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior nuchal lines are the middle pair of curved ridges found along the external aspect of the squamous part of occipital bone. They extend laterally from the external occipital protuberance and travel towards the lateral angles of the occipital bone. 

The superior nuchal lines separate the occipital and nuchal planes of the squamous part of occipital bone and provide:

—origin sites for the descending part of trapezius muscle and the occipital belly of occipitofrontalis muscle;

—insertion sites for the sternocleidomastoid and splenius capitis muscles.

The superior nuchal lines are more pronounced in males than females.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The external occipital protuberance is the palpable prominence found along the external aspect of the squamous part of occipital bone. It is located at the point along the midline where the occipital and nuchal planes meet. It consists of the inion, which is a craniometric point located at the tip of the external occipital protuberance. The external occipital crest extends inferiorly from the external occipital protuberance, and the supreme and superior nuchal lines extend laterally from it.

The external occipital protuberance provides an origin site for the descending part of trapezius muscle and an attachment site for the nuchal ligament. It is more pronounced in males than females.

sections.title: Description
Quick Facts
sections.text: The meridional fibers of ciliary muscle are the most external fibers of the ciliary muscle that run meridionally or longitudinally from the reticulum trabeculae toward the ciliary processes (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The meridional fibers of the ciliary muscles form the external part of the ciliary muscle. The fibers pass longitudinally from the trabecular meshwork of the posterior wall of the scleral venous sinus towards the ciliary processes.

The oculomotor nerve (CN III) provides parasympathetic innervation to the ciliary muscle via the short ciliary nerves, with the superior cervical ganglion providing sympathetic contributions (Giampani & Giampani, 2013).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Found just internal to the ciliary stroma layer, the meridional fibers of the ciliary muscle form the external part of the ciliary muscle. Just internal are radial muscle fibers.

sections.title: Function
sections.text:
The ciliary body suspends the lens of the eyeball by fines suspensory ligaments. When the ciliary muscle contracts it varies tension on the lens, and this changes its shape and hence its refractive power. This process is called accommodation.

Additionally, since the meridional fibers insert into the trabecular meshwork of the scleral venous sinus, contraction and relaxation of the meridional fibers alters the pore size within the meshwork, thus, facilitating aqueous humor drainage into the scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm).

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation)

—Hyperopia-aging

sections.title: References
sections.text:

Giampani, A. S. B. and Giampani, J. (2013) Anatomy of Ciliary Body, Ciliary Processes, Anterior Chamber Angle and Collector Vessels. INTECH Open Access Publisher.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The circular fibers of ciliary muscle are the most internal fibers of the ciliary muscle that form a discrete portion of the ciliary muscle and extend around the apex of the ciliary body close to the root of the iris (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The circular fibers of the ciliary muscle form its internal part. They extend around the apex of the ciliary body forming a sphincter closely related to the root of the iris.

The oculomotor nerve (CN III) provides parasympathetic innervation to the ciliary muscle via the short ciliary nerves, with the superior cervical ganglion providing sympathetic contributions (Giampani & Giampani, 2013).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The circular fibers of the ciliary muscle are the internal-most part of the ciliary muscle.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The ciliary body suspends the lens of the eyeball by fines suspensory ligaments. When the ciliary muscle contracts it varies tension on the lens, and this changes its shape and hence its refractive power. This process is called accommodation.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation)

—Hyperopia-aging

sections.title: References

Giampani, A. S. B. and Giampani, J. (2013) Anatomy of Ciliary Body, Ciliary Processes, Anterior Chamber Angle and Collector Vessels. INTECH Open Access Publisher.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The choroid is the thin, pigmented, vascular coat of the eyeball extending from the ora serrata to the optic nerve; it furnishes blood supply to the retina and conducts arteries and nerves to the anterior structures (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Along with the ciliary body and iris, the choroid forms part of the vascular layer of the eyeball. It is approximately 200 µm thick at birth, but this thickness decreases with age (Nickla and Wallman, 2010).

The choroid contains dense vascular beds supported by collagen and elastic connective tissue. The finest of these vessels are on the innermost aspect of the choroid and is called the capillary lamina of the choroid or choriocapillaris. This layer is so vascularized, it is responsible for the “red-eye” that can be observed when using flash photography. External to the choriocapillaris, the choroid contains much larger blood vessels that supply these vascular beds. These are called Haller’s and Sattler’s layers. 

The anterior choriocapillaris receives its blood supply from the long posterior ciliary arteries and recurrent branches of the anterior ciliary arteries, while the posterior choroid receives blood from the short posterior ciliary arteries.

The outermost layer of the choroid is the suprachoroid, which forms the transition between the choroid and the fibrous capsule surrounding it, the sclera. Here, the choroid contains numerous melanocytes that gives it a dark reddish pigmentation.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The choroid sits between the outer sclera and the inner retina. It extends from the optic nerve posteriorly, where it’s continuous with the internal sheath of the optic nerve. Here, the choroid is firmly attached to the sclera, however, elsewhere it may only be loosely attached to the sclera.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The vascular beds of the choriocapillaris are vital for supplying the adjacent avascular retina with oxygen and nutrients. There is a strong oxygen/carbon dioxide diffusion gradient between the choroid and the outermost layers of the retina, where the outer segments and cell bodies of the rod and cone photoreceptors are located. As these cells are highly metabolically active, but the layers avascular to maintain clarity, oxygen diffusion from the choroid is essential for retinal function. Additionally, the choroid is likely involved in thermoregulation and modulates intraocular pressure via vasomotor control of blood flow, and drainage of aqueous humor from the anterior chamber via the ureoscleral pathway (Nickla and Wallman, 2010).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Nickla, D. L. and Wallman, J. (2010) 'The multifunctional choroid', Prog Retin Eye Res, 29(2), pp. 144-68.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: Vitreous humor is the clear gelatinous substance contained within the interstices of the stroma in the vitreous body of the camera postrema of the eyeball (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The vitreous humor is a colorless liquid (99% water) contained within the posterior aspect of the eyeball, filling the space between the posterior surface of the lens and iris and the inner surface of the retina. It occupies about four fifths of its overall volume. It is thick and gel-like peripherally and more liquid near its center, which gives it some structure.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The vitreous humor is loosely attached to the inner surface of the retina, the ciliary body, and the posterior surface of the lens, most especially to the pars plana of the ciliary body and the edge of the optic disc. Because of the lens, the anterior surface of the vitreous humor is hollowed into a deep concavity, the hyaloid fossa, in which the lens sits.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The vitreous humor helps maintain the shape of the eyeball and its attachment to the outer surface of the retina presses it against the choroid and sclera layers of the eyeball, preventing wrinkling and detachment. Its clarity allows faithful transmission of light from the lens to the retina.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

15597.name: Inner Sheath of Optic Nerve (Pial Sheath; Left)
alternate: Internal Sheath of Optic Nerve (Pial Sheath; Left)

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The inner sheath of optic nerve is the internal sheath of the optic nerve, continuous with the pia mater and arachnoid mater (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The eye and optic nerve are outgrowths of the brain and as such carry the three layers of meningeal coverings with them. They are called collectively, the optic sheath. Of these, the inner two layers, arachnoid and pia, are referred to collectively as the inner or internal sheath of the optic nerve. 

The innermost layer of the inner sheath of the optic nerve is continuous with the pia mater of the brain. It is referred to as the pial sheath of the inner sheath of the optic nerve. As the optic nerve enters the eyeball, the inner sheath becomes continuous with the choroid of the eyeball (Dorland, 2011). The pial sheath is vascular and penetrates the optic nerve, subdividing it into 300–400 fascicles (Hayreh, 1984). This organization gives access to the pial blood vessel to supply the optic nerve (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The pial sheath intimately invests the external surface of the optic nerve and sends extensions within its substance. Externally is the cerebrospinal fluid of the subarachnoid space that separates the pial sheath from the arachnoid sheath. These sheaths surround and accompany the optic nerve up to the eyeball where they become continuous with the choroid coat of the eyeball.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Similar to the brain, the pial sheath supports the axons of the optic nerve, providing a route for nutrients and oxygen.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Hayreh, S. S. (1984) 'The sheath of the optic nerve', Ophthalmologica, 189(1-2), pp. 54-63.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

15353.name: Inner Sheath of Optic Nerve (Arachnoid Sheath; Left)
alternate: Internal Sheath of Optic Nerve (Arachnoid Sheath; Left)

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The inner sheath of optic nerve is the internal sheath of the optic nerve, continuous with the pia mater and arachnoid mater (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The eye and optic nerve are outgrowths of the brain and as such carry the three layers of meningeal coverings with them. They are called collectively, the optic sheath. Of these, the inner two layers, arachnoid and pia, are referred to collectively as the inner or internal sheath of the optic nerve. 

The outermost layer of the inner sheath of the optic nerve is continuous with the arachnoid mater of the brain. It is referred to as the arachnoid sheath of the inner sheath of the optic nerve. As the optic nerve enters the eyeball, the arachnoid sheath becomes continuous with the choroid of the eyeball (Mukherjee, El-Dairi and Bhatti, 2013).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The arachnoid sheath is sandwiched between the external dural sheath, separated from it by a subdural space, and the internal pial sheath, separated from it by a subarachnoid space. The subarachnoid space is filled with cerebrospinal fluid continuous with that of the brain. The sheaths end as the optic nerve enters the eyeball to form the optic nerve head.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Contrary to popular notion, the optic nerve is not a peripheral nerve but a white matter tract of the central nervous system. As such it is covered, and partially supported by the same three meningeal sheaths and their fluid filled separating spaces as the brain. These perform the same support functions for the optic nerve (Mukherjee, El-Dairi and Bhatti, 2013).

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mukherjee, N., El-Dairi, M. A. and Bhatti, M. T. (2013) 'Optic Nerve Sheath Fenestration—Indications and Techniques', US Ophthal. Rev., 6(2), pp. 125-131.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The iris is the circular pigmented membrane, behind the cornea, that surrounds the pupil; the most anterior portion of the vascular tunic of the eye, it is made up of a flat bar of circular muscular fibers surrounding the pupil, a thin layer of smooth muscle fibers by which the pupil is dilated, thus regulating the amount of light entering the eye, and posteriorly two layers of pigmented epithelial cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The iris is an annular structure that lies in the anterior chamber of the eye, between the cornea anteriorly and the lens posteriorly. It acts as a contractile diaphragm to a centrally located aperture called the pupil. 

From an anterior view, the iris can be divided into zones, the large zone adjacent to the ciliary body (ciliary zone) and a smaller internal zone adjacent to the pupil (pupillary zone). These two zones meet at the collarette. Additionally, the iris may contain large depressions called crypts (crypts of Fuchs) (Standring, 2016).

The iris contains several cellular layers. From anterior to posterior these include the anterior border layer, the stroma, and two pigmented epithelial layers. 

The anterior border layer is modified from the stroma layer and contains an increased number of fibroblasts and underlying melanocytes. It blends with the double epithelial layer covering the posterior surface of the iris at the pupillary rim, and with the trabecular connective tissue of the iridocorneal angle (the angle formed by the iris and cornea allowing for aqueous humor to drain).

The stroma is simply composed of fibroblasts and melanocytes nested in a loose connective tissue. It contains blood vessels and nerves as well as smooth muscle cells that form the sphincter pupillae that encircles the pupil.

The posterior surface of the iris is covered by a double layer of pigmented epithelium, which gives rise to a person’s eye color. This double layer is continuous with the double-layered epithelium of the ciliary body. At the pupillary rim, the epithelium curves onto the anterior surface of the iris, forming a ruffled margin, the pupillary ruff. 

The anterior layer of the double-layered epithelium of the iris (confusingly called the anterior epithelium even though it lines the posterior surface of the stroma of the iris) is a sort of myoepithelium, giving rise to the radial, dilator pupillae muscle. It is continuous with the pigmented epithelial layer of the ciliary body. The posterior layer is more heavily pigmented and is continuous with the non-pigmented layer of ciliary epithelium. It lies in contact with the anterior surface of the lens.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The iris lies between the lens and the cornea and is bathed in aqueous humor. Anteriorly, the pupillary zone of the iris is in contact with the lens. However, because of the convex shape of the lens, the ciliary zone of the iris moves away from the lens forming a space called the posterior chamber of the eye. The space between the cornea and the iris is referred to as the anterior chamber. The posterior surface of the iris has numerous folds that channels the flow of aqueous humor from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Light entering the pupil and passing to the retina is regulated by the iris and is controlled by two involuntary muscles, the sphincter pupillae and the dilator pupillae muscle. Additionally, the double-layered pigmented epithelium of the iris restricts light reaching the retina.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The pupil is the opening at the center of the iris of the eye, through which light enters the eye (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The pupil is the central aperture or opening of the iris of the eye. It allows light to enter the eyeball, be focused by the lens, and eventually impinge on the retina. In normal illumination, the pupil appears black, since light entering the eyeball is absorbed by the retina and not reflected (except in the case of flash photography, when the pupil can be seen as red due to reflection from the vascular choroid). The diameter of the pupil is continuously variable so as to regulate the amount of light entering the eye, i.e., under different lighting conditions. This is an involuntary response known as the pupillary light reflex.

In humans, the pupil is round, however, in species such as cats and goats, the pupil is a vertical or horizontal slit, respectively.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The pupil is located at the center of the iris, with the lens of the eye directly posterior to it. The diameter of the pupil is regulated by the iris by way of two sets of involuntary muscles, the sphincter pupillae and dilator pupillae muscles. The sphincter pupillae is arranged circularly and decreases the diameter of the pupil i.e., constriction, while the dilator pupillae muscle, which is arranged radially around the pupil, increases the size of the pupil (dilation).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The pupil allows for the entry of light into the eye.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Mydriasis
—Fixed, dilated pupils

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The dilator pupillae muscle is a name given to fibers extending radially from the sphincter pupillae to the ciliary margin; it dilates the iris (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The dilator pupillae muscle is formed by the muscular processes of the anterior epithelial layer of the posterior surface of the iris. Non-myelinated axons pass between the muscular processes of the dilator papillae muscle supplying them with sympathetic innervation that originates from the superior cervical ganglion. Some of these fibers travel through the ciliary ganglion and reach the iris via the short ciliary nerves. Others travel in the long ciliary nerves, which arise from the nasociliary nerve (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The dilator pupillae receive sympathetic innervation. This results in contraction of the radially arranged muscle fibers increasing the dilator of the aperture formed by the iris and dilating the pupil.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cornea is the transparent structure forming the anterior part of the fibrous layer of the eyeball. It consists of five layers: (1) the anterior corneal epithelium, continuous with that of the conjunctiva; (2) the anterior limiting layer (Bowman membrane); (3) the substantia propria, or stroma; (4) the posterior limiting layer (Descemet membrane); and (5) the endothelium of the anterior chamber (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The cornea forms a small, anterior most, part of the tough outer fibrous layer of the eyeball. It constitutes about 7% of the external surface of the eyeball, the remainder being sclera. 

The cornea is convex anteriorly, projecting as a dome from the sclera and varies in thickness, from about 670 μm at the corneoscleral junction (where the cornea and sclera become continuous) to 520 μm at the center. The external surface of the cornea is covered by a tear film, lubricating and hydrating its surface.

The cornea consists of five layers including, from anterior to posterior, corneal epithelium, anterior limiting lamina, stroma, posterior limiting lamina, and endothelium.

The corneal epithelium is composed of 5–6 layers of cells and makes up 10% of the corneal thickness. Its role is to protect the surface of the eye from abrasion, preventing the entry of pathogens into the eyeball, while allowing passage of small molecules, such as water and certain ions. Directly behind the corneal epithelium lies the anterior limiting lamina or Bowman’s layer. It is thin, composed of dense collagen fibrils. The thickest layer of the cornea is the substantia propria (or stroma). It is composed of 200–250 layers of collagen fibrils with interposed fibroblasts. All collagen fibrils within a single layer are parallel with each other, and those between layers are orthogonal. This highly regular geometry allows the stroma to retain clarity.

The posterior limiting lamina, or Descemet’s layer, lines the stroma posteriorly and acts as a basement membrane from the underlying endothelium. The endothelium is a single cell layer of squamous cells lining the posterior aspect of the cornea (Standring, 2016).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The cornea is continuous with the sclera at the limbus. Here, the epithelial layer of the cornea merges with the epithelium of the conjunctiva. The anterior limiting lamina terminates, and the corneal stroma loses its collagen density and regular geometry. The posterior limiting lamina becomes continuous with the trabecular meshwork, while the endothelium of the cornea is continuous with the epithelium covering the trabeculae.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The cornea is the most powerful contributor to the optical power of the eye, accounting for 70% of its refractive power. Therefore, changes to the shape of the cornea have significant implications for vision.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Astigmatism

—Corneal cataracts

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The sphincter pupillae are circular fibers of the iris, innervated by the short ciliary nerves (parasympathetic), and acting to contract the pupil (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The sphincter pupillae muscle is formed by small bundles of smooth muscle cells in the stroma of the iris. The muscle fibers are arranged circumferentially around the pupil.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The sphincter pupillae muscle is approximately a 750 μm wide band at the central margin of the iris and the edge of the pupil. The muscle is covered anteriorly and posteriorly by the connective tissue of the stroma. It aids in binding the sphincter pupillae muscle to the dilator pupillae muscles in the pupillary zone and to the epithelial layers of the iris at the pupillary rim.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The sphincter pupillae muscle receives mostly unmyelinated parasympathetic innervation from the short ciliary nerves whose cell bodies are located in the ciliary ganglion. This results in contraction of the circularly arranged muscle fibers, closing the diaphragm formed by the iris. Thus, the sphincter pupillae muscle decreases the diameter of the iris aperture and constricts the pupil. The pupil dilates as the ambient illumination decreases allowing more light to pass through and maximize visual sensitivity. It does this at some cost to visual acuity lost by opening the aperture to maximum and decreasing the depth of focus.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The outer sheath of optic nerve is the thick external sheath of the optic nerve, continuous with the dura mater and connecting it with the sclera (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The eye and optic nerve are outgrowths of the brain and as such carry the three layers of meningeal coverings with them. They are called collectively, the optic sheath. Of these, the outer layer is the direct continuation of the dura mater. Upon emergence from the optic canal, the dura splits into an external sublayer, continuous with the periosteum of the orbit, and an internal sublayer, that continues as the external sheath of the optic nerve (Hayreh, 1984). It surrounds and accompanies the optic nerve to the posterior eyeball. As the optic nerve enters the eyeball, the external sheath becomes continuous with the sclera of the eyeball.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Within the optic canal, the external sheath of the optic nerve (dural sheath) externally lines the canal attached to the periosteum. Upon emergence it splits into a periosteal, outer sublayer and a meningeal, external sheath of the optic nerve (Hayreh, 1984). Internally is the subdural space and the arachnoid sheath.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The dural sheath is thick and fibrous and like its counterpart in the brain protects the optic nerve.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Hayreh, S. S. (1984) 'The sheath of the optic nerve', Ophthalmologica, 189(1-2), pp. 54-63.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: From the venules inside the retina.

Course: Accompanies central retinal artery in the optic nerve.

Tributaries: Superior and inferior nasal and temporal branches.

Drainage: Retina.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The central retinal vein arises from the union of the superior and inferior nasal and temporal venules in the retina.

sections.title: Course
sections.text:
Within the eyeball, the intraocular part of the central retina vein does not share a similar distribution with the arteries. Arteries, which lie more superficially, can often cross over the veins. In individuals with severe hypertension, the arteries press on the veins causing dilations of the veins.

The extraocular part of the central retinal vein accompanies the central retinal artery within the optic nerve. It is short and drains either directly into the cavernous sinus, or into the superior ophthalmic vein.

sections.title: Tributaries
sections.text: The central retinal vein receives the superior and inferior nasal and temporal venules, which each drain a quadrant of the retina.

sections.title: Structures drained
sections.text: The central retinal vein is responsible for draining the inner layers of the retina of the eyeball including the outer plexiform layer, the inner nuclear layer, the inner plexiform layer, and the ganglion cell layer.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —“Nicking” of central retinal veins as an indication of hypertension observable upon ophthalmoscopic examination

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nucleus of lens is the harder internal part of the lens of the eye (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
Function
sections.text: As a lens cell matures, it elongates, synthesizes crystallin, and loses its organelles and nuclei until it becomes a mature lens fiber (and no longer can be considered a “cell”). This developmental gradient is represented by the lens cells/fibers present from the peripheral to central zones of the nucleus.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Taylor, V. L., al-Ghoul, K. J., Lane, C. W., Davis, V. A., Kuszak, J. R. and Costello, M. J. (1996) 'Morphology of the normal human lens', Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci, 37(7), pp. 1396-410.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cortex of lens is the softer, external part of the lens of the eye (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The lens consists of three layers, from external to internal: capsule epithelium, and lens fibers. The lens fibers can be further subdivided into the external cortex and internal nucleus. The cortical cells are immature and less densely packed, which conveys to the cortex a disorganization and soft consistency. The cortex represents 16% of the total diameter of the lens (Taylor et al., 1996).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The cortex of the lens serves as the “nursery” for the new lens cells formed by the epithelium. A developmental gradient exists whereby newly formed lens cells are found most peripherally in the cortex. As they mature, they get “pushed” (by the formation of even younger cells) inwards, eventually losing organelles and nuclei while forming and organizing crystallins as they enter the nuclear region of the lens.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Cataracts

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Taylor, V. L., al-Ghoul, K. J., Lane, C. W., Davis, V. A., Kuszak, J. R. and Costello, M. J. (1996) 'Morphology of the normal human lens', Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci, 37(7), pp. 1396-410.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The corona ciliaris is the region on the anterior inner surface of the ciliary body of the eye from which radiate the ciliary processes (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The ciliary body can be divided into two parts, the distal (or anterior) corona ciliaris (or pars plicata) and the more proximal (posterior) orbiculus ciliaris (ciliary ring or pars plana).

The anterior, ridged corona ciliaris makes up about one third of the ciliary body and surrounds the base of the iris. The posterior orbiculus ciliaris is relatively thin. It extends from the corona ciliaris to the ora serrata (the junction between the retina and ciliary body). 

The corona ciliaris contains about 70–80 ridges, or ciliary processes, that radiate from the base of the iris. Between the ciliary processes are the ciliary folds. There is less pigmentation in the folds, therefore, giving it a striated appearance. The suspensory ligaments (zonular fibers) arising from the lens extend between these ciliary processes to fuse with the ciliary ring of the posterior part of the ciliary body.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The corona ciliaris is bounded externally by the sclera and internally by the posterior chamber of the eye. The vitreous chamber is posterior.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The corona ciliaris contains a dense plexus of ciliary blood vessels. These vessels concentrate in the ciliary processes and aid in the production of aqueous humor.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The sclera is the tough white outer coat of the eyeball, covering approximately five-sixths of its posterior surface, and continuous anteriorly with the cornea and posteriorly with the external sheath of the optic nerve; it and the cornea constitute the tunica fibrosa bulbi (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The sclera forms part of the tough white outer fibrous layer for most of the eyeball, covering more than 93% of the surface of the eyeball. Only a small portion of the sclera is visible when the eyeball sits in situ in the orbital cavity. The sclera is replaced by the transparent cornea in the anterior portion of the eyeball (Standring, 2016).

The sclera can vary in thickness, ranging from about 0.3-1 mm. It is composed of collagen fibers that are interlaced, providing the strength and flexibility of the eyeball. The organization of these fibers lends the sclera its opaque appearance.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The sclera is continuous anteriorly with the cornea at the corneoscleral junction and is attached to the ciliary body. Additionally, it is covered anteriorly by the conjunctiva. 

Posteriorly, the sclera is pierced by the optic nerve medial and slightly inferior to the midline of the eyeball. The outer surface of the sclera is continuous with the dura mater that covers the optic nerve, while the inner surface forms a plate with many perforations, the lamina cribrosa sclerae. Fibers from the optic nerve pass through these small perforations, along with the central retinal artery and vein. 

The internal surface of the sclera is lined by the choroid, thus, separating the sclera from the retina.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The fibrous layer of the eyeball provides the tensile strength for withstanding intraocular pressure and determines its overall shape. Its toughness helps protect the eye from damage from the external environment. Additionally, the sclera provides the attachment for extraocular (extrinsic) muscles of the eyeball.

sections.title: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Scleritis

—Jaundice

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The retina is the innermost of the three tunics of the eyeball, surrounding the vitreous body and continuous posteriorly with the optic nerve (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The retina forms the inner layer of the eyeball. It is a thin, delicate transparent sheet and contains two parts, the central optic part and the peripheral non-visual part.

The inner optic part of the retina contains neural and pigmented layers. The neural layer contains the photoreceptors, the light receptive cells of the eye, and a series of cells that modify and transmit the information transduced by the photoreceptors before sending it into the brain via the optic nerve. 

The outer pigmented layer, or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), consists of a monolayer of cuboidal cells containing melanosomes that give them their black pigment. The pigmentation aids the choroid, which is also darkly pigmented, in absorbing light that enters the eyeball and passes across the retina, thereby reducing scattered light. The optic part of the retina terminates at the ora serrata, the posterior border of the ciliary body. 

The non-visual part of the retina is an anterior continuation of the pigmented layer of the RPE. It extends over the ciliary body (ciliary part of retina) and posterior surface of the iris (iridial part of retina).

The inner layers of the retina receive its blood supply from the ophthalmic artery via the central retinal artery. The outer layers of the retina, including its photoreceptive rods and cones, are avascular and receives is blood supply by diffusion from the choriocapillaris layer of the choroid.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The retina is the innermost layer of the optic globe. Its outer surface is against the vitreous body, separated from the humor by the vitreous membrane. The outer surface of the retina, the RPE, abuts the choroid at Bruch’s membrane, which separates it from the choriocapillaris sublayer of the choroid. At the center of the retina is the optic nerve head or optic disc, where the axons forming the optic nerve leave the eyeball. The optic disc is functionally blind as there are no photoreceptors, or any of the other layers of the retina here.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The neural retina receives, modulates, and transmits visual stimuli from the external environment to the optic nerve and the visual cortex of the brain. The retinal pigment epithelium phagocytoses the shed outer segments of photoreceptors after the photopigment has been transformed by light. This is an essential function for the health of the neural part of the retina.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Retinal detachment

—Vitreous detachment

—Macular Edema

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The vascular circle of optic nerve is a circle of arteries in the sclera surrounding the site of entrance of the optic nerve (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The vascular circle of the optic nerve (circle of Zinn or Haller) is formed by numerous branches of the ophthalmic artery, via the posterior ciliary arteries, that giving rise to about 20 short posterior ciliary arteries. These follow the course of the optic nerve and are apparent around it. Where the nerve pierces the sclera, they form an anastomotic circle that supplies the optic nerve head.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The short posterior ciliary arteries that form the vascular circle of the optic nerve travel in the subarachnoid space between the intermediate (arachnoidal) and inner (pial) layers of the inner optic nerve sheath.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The vascular circle of the optic nerve gives off centripetal branches that supply the laminar region of the head of the optic nerve. Additionally, pial vessels arising from the vascular circle pass retrogradely supplying the postlaminar region of the optic nerve head. Other branches arising from the short posterior ciliary arteries pierce the sclera and contribute to the vascularity of the choroid coat of the eye.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Axons of retinal ganglion cells collect at the optic disc to form the optic nerve head.

Course: Runs posteriorly from the posterior margin of the eye, through the optic canal, and into the cranium.

Branches: Merges with the contralateral optic nerve at the optic chiasm.

Supply: Conveys visual information to the midbrain and thalamus.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The optic nerve forms when the axons of retinal ganglion cells converge at the optic disc at the back of the eyeball.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: From the optic nerve head, the nerve axons traverse fenestrations in the sclera, called the lamina cribrosa, to pass through it. Upon emerging from the eyeball, the axons become myelinated by oligodendroglia, approximately doubling the nerve’s diameter. It continues posteriorly across the orbit and exits through the optic canal. At the other end of the canal, it emerges intracranially in the middle cranial fossa, just anterior to the pituitary and flanked by the internal carotid arteries. The nerve has a short intracranial course before merging with its partner from the opposite side to form the optic chiasm.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The optic nerve does not branch. However, it merges with the contralateral optic nerve at the optic chiasm, where fibers, from temporal retina, decussate while those from nasal retina, remain ipsilateral.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The optic nerve is a sensory nerve. It conveys all visual information from the retina towards into the brain, primarily to the midbrain (superior colliculus, pretectum), thalamus (lateral geniculate nucleus) and hypothalamus (suprachiasmatic nucleus). Most of its axons will travel to the lateral geniculate nucleus and then on to primary visual cortex to serve conscious vision.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Ophthalmic artery.

Course: Runs inside the optic nerve to reach the eyeball.

Branches: Superior and inferior nasal and temporal branches.

Supplied Structures: Retina.

sections.title: Origin
sections.text: The central retinal artery is the small, first branch of the ophthalmic artery.

sections.title: Course
sections.text: The central retinal artery arises just below the optic nerve. For a short time, it lies inferiorly in the dural sheath surrounding the optic nerve, and then enters the optic nerve to course towards the retina (extraocular part). It enters the eyeball through the lamina cribrosa, where it gives off several branches (intraocular part). The intraocular part course over the innermost surface of the retina, superficial to the ganglion cell layer. It sends small branches into the retina that extend through and supply cells of the ganglion cell layer, the inner plexiform layer, the inner nuclear layer, and the outer plexiform layer. It does not supply the rod and cone photoreceptors of the outer nuclear layer which are served by diffusion from the choriocapillaris.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: The intraocular part of the central retinal artery divides into superior and inferior temporal, and superior and inferior nasal branches, each of which supply a quadrant of the retina. The superior and inferior temporal branches arc above and below the macula but do not supply structures at the depths of the fovea.

sections.title: Supplied Structures
sections.text: The central retinal artery supplies the inner layers of the retina of the eyeball.
