sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The head of fibula is the irregularly shaped, expanded, proximal end of the bone. It is the superior continuation of its neck and contains an apex and articular facet.

The head of fibula provides origin sites for the fibularis longus and soleus muscles, an insertion site for the biceps femoris muscle, and an attachment site for the fibular collateral ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral intercondylar tubercle (lateral intercondyloid tubercle or lateral intercondylar spine) is the small projection found on the lateral end of the intercondylar eminence of tibia.

It is the lower of the two intercondylar tubercles that are found on the intercondylar eminence, the other being the medial intercondylar tubercle. Overall, both the medial and lateral intercondylar tubercles are believed to play a role in stabilizing the knee joint, by fitting into the space created by the intercondylar fossa of femur.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral condyle of tibia (lateral tibial condyle or external condyle of tibia) is the laterally located, round, articular eminence found on the proximal end of the tibia. It is the smaller of the two articular condyles of the tibia, the other being the medial condyle.

It articulates with the lateral condyle of femur, via the lateral meniscus, forming the lateral femorotibial joint. Overall, the lateral femorotibial, medial femorotibial and patellofemoral joints collectively form the knee joint.

The lateral condyle of tibia contains the fibular articular facet and the tubercle of iliotibial tract. It provides an origin site for the extensor digitorum longus muscle and an attachment site for the lateral patellar retinaculum.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral (fibular) malleolus is the expanded, distal end of the fibula. It contains the malleolar groove of fibula, malleolar fossa, and the articular facet of lateral malleolus.

The lateral malleolus provides attachment sites for the anterior talofibular, posterior talofibular, posterior tibiofibular, and calcaneofibular ligaments, as well as the superior fibular retinaculum.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior border (anterior crest) of tibia is the sharp, subcutaneous margin found along the frontal aspect of the bone. It is one of the three borders of the tibia, the other two being the medial and interosseous (lateral) borders, and it separates the medial and lateral surfaces of the tibia.

The anterior border extends inferiorly from the tibial tuberosity, and its lower portion curves medially to end at the anterior aspect of the medial malleolus. It provides an attachment site for the crural fascia.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial (tibial) malleolus is the medially located, rounded projection found on the distal end of the tibia. It contains the malleolar groove of tibia and the articular facet of medial malleolus.

The medial malleolus provides attachment sites for the medial collateral ligament of ankle joint (deltoid ligament), and the flexor retinaculum of the foot.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral (fibular, or peroneal) surface of fibula is the area found along the lateral aspect of the bone. It is one of the three surfaces of fibula, the other two being the medial and posterior surfaces, and is an area that is bounded:

—anteriorly, by the anterior border of fibula;

—posteriorly, by the posterior border of fibula.

The lateral surface of fibula provides origin sites for the fibularis longus and fibularis brevis muscles. Because these muscles originate from this lateral surface, it is therefore also known as the fibular, or peroneal, surface of the fibula.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial condyle of tibia (medial tibial condyle or internal condyle of tibia) is the medially located, round, articular eminence found on the proximal end of the tibia. It is the larger of the two articular condyles of the tibia, the other being the lateral condyle.

It articulates with the medial condyle of femur, via the medial meniscus, forming the medial femorotibial joint. Overall, the medial femorotibial, lateral femorotibial and patellofemoral joints collectively form the knee joint.

The medial condyle of tibia provides an insertion site for the semimembranosus muscle, and an attachment site for the medial patellar retinaculum.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The tibial tuberosity is the large, oval, elevation found on the anterior aspect of the proximal part of tibia. Its upper half is smooth and provides an attachment site for the patellar ligament, while its lower half is rough and is covered by the infrapatellar bursa.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial condyle of femur (medial femoral condyle, internal condyle of femur, or tibial condyle of femur) is the medially located, round, articular eminence on the distal end of the femur. It is one of the two articular condyles of the femur, the other being the lateral condyle.

It contains the medial epicondyle of femur and adductor tubercle, and its lateral aspect contributes to the formation of the intercondylar fossa. It provides an insertion site for the adductor magnus muscle, and attachment sites for the tibial collateral and posterior cruciate ligaments.

The medial condyle of femur articulates with the medial condyle of tibia, via the medial meniscus, forming the medial femorotibial joint. Overall, the medial femorotibial, lateral femorotibial and patellofemoral joints collectively form the knee joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral condyle of femur (lateral femoral condyle, external condyle of femur, or fibular condyle of femur) is the laterally located, round, articular eminence on the distal end of the femur. It is one of the two articular condyles of the femur, the other being the medial condyle.

It contains the lateral epicondyle of femur and the groove for popliteus muscle, and its medial aspect contributes to the formation of the intercondylar fossa. It provides an origin site for the lateral head of gastrocnemius muscle, and attachment sites for the fibular collateral and anterior cruciate ligaments.

The lateral condyle of femur articulates with the lateral condyle of tibia, via the lateral meniscus, forming the lateral femorotibial joint. Overall, the lateral femorotibial, medial femorotibial and patellofemoral joints collectively form the knee joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial process of calcaneal tuberosity is the rough, medially located projection found along the plantar surface of the calcaneus. It is the larger of the two processes that make up the calcaneal tuberosity, the other being the lateral process, and is the weight-bearing part of the bone.

The medial process of calcaneal tuberosity provides origin sites for the abductor hallucis, abductor digiti minimi and flexor digitorum brevis muscles. It also provides an attachment site for the plantar aponeurosis.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The lateral process of calcaneal tuberosity is the rough, laterally located projection found along the plantar surface of the calcaneus. It is the smaller of the two processes that make up the calcaneal tuberosity, the other being the medial process.

The lateral process of calcaneal tuberosity provides an origin site for the abductor digiti minimi muscle.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The calcaneal tubercle (anterior tubercle of calcaneus) is the small prominence found along the plantar surface of the calcaneus. It provides an attachment site for the plantar calcaneocuboid and long plantar ligaments.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus muscle is the smooth depression found along the inferior aspect of the sustentacular tali of calcaneus. The tendon of the flexor hallucis longus muscle passes through this groove.

23810.name: Second Metatarsal Articular Facet of Lateral Cuneiform Bone
23810.latin: Facies articularis metatarsi secundi ossis cuneiformis lateralis

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The second metatarsal articular facet is the narrow, vertical, anteriorly located area on the medial surface of the lateral cuneiform bone. It is one of the two articular facets found on the medial surface of the lateral cuneiform bone, the other being the intermediate cuneiform articular facet.

It articulates with the lateral cuneiform articular facet of the second metatarsal bone, contributing to the formation of the tarsometatarsal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lateral cuneiform articular facet is the narrow, vertical area on the lateral surface of the intermediate cuneiform bone. It articulates with the intermediate cuneiform articular facet of the lateral cuneiform bone, contributing to the formation of the intercuneiform joints.

16605.name: Fifth Metatarsal Articular Facet of Cuboid Bone
16605.latin: Facies articularis metatarsi quinti ossis cuboidei

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The fifth metatarsal articular facet is the triangular, laterally located area found on the distal articular surface of the cuboid bone. It is one of the two facets found on the distal articular surface of the cuboid bone, the other being the fourth metatarsal articular facet.

The fifth metatarsal articular facet articulates with the proximal articular facet of the fifth metatarsal bone, contributing to the formation of the tarsometatarsal joints.

22836.name: Fourth Metatarsal Articular Facet of Cuboid Bone
22836.latin: Facies articularis metatarsi quarti ossis cuboidei

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The fourth metatarsal articular facet is the quadrilateral, medially located area found on the distal articular surface of the cuboid bone. It is one of the two facets found on the distal articular surface of the cuboid bone, the other being the fifth metatarsal articular facet.

The fourth metatarsal articular facet articulates with the proximal articular facet of the fourth metatarsal bone, contributing to the formation of the tarsometatarsal joints.

22126.name: Fourth Metatarsal Articular Facet of Lateral Cuneiform Bone
22126.latin: Facies articularis metatarsi quarti ossis cuneiformis lateralis
alternate: Fourth Metatarsal Articular Facet of Third Cuneiform Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The fourth metatarsal articular facet is the crescent-shaped, laterally located area on the distal articular surface of the lateral cuneiform bone. It is smaller of the two articular facets found on the distal articular surface of the lateral cuneiform bone, the other being the third metatarsal articular facet.

It articulates with the lateral cuneiform articular facet of the fourth metatarsal bone, contributing to the formation of the tarsometatarsal joints.

17537.name: Medial Cuneiform Articular Facet of Intermediate Cuneiform Bone
17537.latin: Facies articularis cuneiformia medialia ossis cuneiformis intermedii
alternate: First Cuneiform Articular Facet of Intermediate Cuneiform Bone
First Cuneiform Articular Facet of Second Cuneiform Bone
Medial Cuneiform Articular Facet of Second Cuneiform Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The medial cuneiform articular facet is the smooth, slanted, posterosuperiorly located area on the medial surface of the intermediate cuneiform bone. It articulates with the intermediate cuneiform articular facet of the medial cuneiform bone, contributing to the formation of the intercuneiform joints.

24341.name: Third Metatarsal Articular Facet of Lateral Cuneiform Bone
24341.latin: Facies articularis metatarsi tertii ossis cuneiformis lateralis
alternate: Third Metatarsal Articular Facet of Third Cuneiform Bone

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The third metatarsal articular facet is the oval, medially located area on the distal articular surface of the lateral cuneiform bone. It is larger of the two articular facets found on the distal articular surface of the lateral cuneiform bone, the other being the fourth metatarsal articular facet.

It articulates with the proximal articular facet of the third metatarsal bone, contributing to the formation of the tarsometatarsal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The tuberosity of fifth metatarsal bone is the large, blunt projection found on the lateral aspect of its base. It provides an insertion site for the fibularis brevis muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The navicular articular surface of talus is the oval, convex, anterior area of the head of talus. It is orientated in the anteromedial direction and articulates with the proximal articular surface of the navicular bone, contributing to the formation of the talocalcaneonavicular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The talar sulcus (talar groove, or sulcus of talus) is the shallow depression found on the plantar aspect of the neck of talus. It extends, anterolaterally, between the middle and posterior calcaneal articular facets.

The talar sulcus is converted into the talar sinus by the calcaneal sulcus, which contains ligaments.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior process of talus is the rough prominence found on the posterior aspect of the bone. It contains the medial and lateral tubercles of talus, with the groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus muscle located in between them.

The posterior process of talus provides attachment sites for the medial and posterior talocalcaneal ligaments and the posterior talofibular ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lateral process of talus is the prominence found on the lateral aspect of the bone. It provides an attachment site for the lateral talocalcaneal ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior facet for calcaneus (anterior calcaneal articular facet, or anterior calcaneal articular surface) is the small, flat area found along the inferolateral aspect of the head of talus. It is continuous anteriorly with the navicular surface of talus and is one of the three facets on the talus that articular with the calcaneus, the other two being the middle and posterior calcaneal articular facets.

The anterior facet for calcaneus articulates with the anterior talar articular facet of the calcaneus, contributing to the formation of the talocalcaneonavicular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral tubercle of talus is the laterally located prominence found on the posterior process of talus. It is the larger of the two tubercles that make up the posterior process of talus, the other being the medial tubercle of talus. These two tubercles are separated from each other by the groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus muscle.

The lateral tubercle of talus provides attachment sites for the posterior talocalcaneal and posterior talofibular ligaments.

17935.name: Groove for Tendon of Flexor Hallucis Longus of Talus
17935.latin: Sulcus tendinis musculi flexoris longi hallucis ossis tali
alternate: Groove for Tendon of Flexor Hallucis Longus Muscle of Talus
Sulcus tendinis flexoris hallucis longi ossis tali
Sulcus tendinis musculi flexoris hallucis longi

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus muscle is the smooth, oblique, short depression on the posterior process of talus. It located in between the medial and lateral tubercles that form the posterior process, with the tendon of the flexor hallucis longus muscle passing through this groove.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial tubercle of talus is the medially located prominence found on the posterior process of talus. It is the smaller of the two tubercles that make up the posterior process of talus, the other being the lateral tubercle of talus. These two tubercles are separated from each other by the groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus muscle.

The medial tubercle of talus provides an attachment site for the medial talocalcaneal ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The facet for plantar calcaneonavicular ligament is the area found along the inferomedial aspect of the head of talus. It is covered with articular cartilage and sits on the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lateral malleolar facet of talus is the concave, triangular area found along the lateral aspect of the body of talus. It is continuous medially with the trochlea of talus and articulates with the articular facet of lateral malleolus on the fibula, contributing to the formation of the ankle joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The superior facet of talus is the saddle-shaped, superiorly facing, articular area on the trochlea of talus. It articulates with the inferior articular surface of tibia, contributing to the formation of the ankle joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The medial malleolar facet of talus is the smooth, crescent-shaped area found along the medial aspect of the body of talus. It is continuous laterally with the trochlea of talus and articulates with the articular facet of medial malleolus on the tibia, contributing to the formation of the ankle joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The plantar (inferior) surface is the rough, concave area on the lower aspect of the calcaneus. It is one of the six surfaces of the calcaneus, the other five being the posterior, dorsal, medial and lateral surfaces, and the cuboid articular surface.

The plantar surface of calcaneus contains the calcaneal tubercle and the medial and lateral processes of calcaneal tuberosity. It provides origin sites for the abductor hallucis, abductor digiti minimi, flexor digitorum brevis and quadratus plantae muscles. It also provides attachment sites for the plantar aponeurosis and the plantar calcaneocuboid and long plantar ligaments.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral surface is the flat, subcutaneous area on the lateral aspect of the calcaneus. It is one of the six surfaces of the calcaneus, the other five being the posterior, plantar, dorsal and medial surfaces, and the cuboid articular surface.

The lateral surface of calcaneus contains the fibular trochlea and the groove for tendon of fibularis longus muscle. It provides an origin site for the extensor digitorum brevis muscle and attachment sites for the calcaneofibular ligament and the inferior fibular retinaculum.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior surface is the rounded, convex area on the posterior aspect of the calcaneus. It is one of the six surfaces of the calcaneus, the other five being the dorsal, plantar, medial and lateral surfaces, and the cuboid articular surface.

The posterior surface of calcaneus contains the calcaneal tuberosity. It provides insertion sites for the gastrocnemius, soleus and plantaris muscles, all via the calcaneal tendon.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The dorsal (superior) surface is the area on the upper aspect of the calcaneus. It is one of the six surfaces of the calcaneus, the other five being the posterior, plantar, medial and lateral surfaces, and the cuboid articular surface.

The dorsal surface of calcaneus contains the sustentaculum tali, calcaneal sulcus, and the anterior, middle, and posterior talar facets. It provides an origin site for the extensor digitorum brevis muscle, and attachment sites for the bifurcate, dorsal calcaneocuboid and talocalcaneal interosseous ligaments.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior process of calcaneus is the large, saddle-shaped, anterior end of the bone. It contains the cuboid articular surface and the anterior talar articular facet.

The anterior process of calcaneus provides an origin site for the extensor digitorum brevis muscle and attachment sites for the bifurcate, dorsal calcaneocuboid and plantar calcaneocuboid ligaments.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The calcaneal sulcus (calcaneal groove or sulcus of calcaneus) is the rough, deep depression found along the dorsal surface of the calcaneus. It extends, anterolaterally, between the middle and posterior talar articular facets.

The calcaneal sulcus is converted into the talar sinus by the talar sulcus, which contains ligaments.

17705.name: Groove for Tendon of Fibularis Longus Muscle of Calcaneus
17705.latin: Sulcus tendinis musculi fibularis longi calcanei
alternate: Groove for Tendon of Peroneus Longus Muscle of Calcaneus
Sulcus tendinis musculi peronaei longi calcanei
Sulcus tendinis musculi peronei longi calcanei

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The groove for tendon of fibularis longus muscle is the smooth, oblique depression found along the lateral surface of the calcaneus. It is located posteroinferior to the fibular trochlea, and the tendon of the fibularis longus muscle passes through this groove.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The fibular trochlea (peroneal trochlea, fibular tubercle, or peroneal tubercle) is the small, sometimes indistinct, prominence found along the lateral surface of the calcaneus. It is located between the tendons of the fibularis longus and brevis muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The middle talar articular surface (middle facet for talus, or middle talar articular facet) is the oval, concave area found along the dorsal surface of the sustentaculum tali of calcaneus. It’s one of the three facets on the calcaneus that articulates with the talus, the other two being the anterior and posterior talar articular facets.

The middle talar articular facet articulates with the middle calcaneal articular facet of the talus, contributing to the formation of the talocalcaneonavicular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The malleolar fossa is the small, rough depression found the medial aspect of the lateral malleolus of fibula. It is located posterior to the articular facet of lateral malleolus and provides attachment sites for the posterior tibiofibular and posterior talofibular ligaments.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lateral epicondyle (external epicondyle) of femur is the rough eminence found along the lateral aspect of the lateral condyle. It provides an origin site for the popliteus muscle and the lateral head of gastrocnemius muscle, and an attachment site for the fibular collateral ligament.

20728.name: Articular Facet of Lateral Condyle of Tibia

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The articular facet of lateral condyle of tibia is the smooth, circular area found on the superior aspect of the lateral condyle of tibia. It is the smaller of the two articular facets found on the superior surface of the proximal part of tibia, the other being the articular facet of medial condyle of tibia.

It articulates with the lateral condyle of femur, via the lateral meniscus, forming the lateral femorotibial joint. Overall, the lateral femorotibial, medial femorotibial and patellofemoral joints collectively form the knee joint.

22233.name: Articular Facet of Medial Condyle of Tibia

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The articular facet of medial condyle is the smooth, oval, slightly concave area found on the superior aspect of the medial condyle of tibia. It is the larger of the two articular facets found on the superior surface of the proximal part of tibia, the other being the articular facet of lateral condyle of tibia.

It articulates with the medial condyle of femur, via the medial meniscus, forming the medial femorotibial joint. Overall, the medial femorotibial, lateral femorotibial and patellofemoral joints collectively form the knee joint.

19021.name: Articular Facet of Medial Condyle of Femur

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The articular facet of medial condyle of femur is the smooth, convex area found on the anterior, inferior and posterior aspects of the medial condyle. It is continuous laterally with both the patellar surface and intercondylar fossa of femur.

The articular facet of medial condyle of femur articulates with the articular facet of medial condyle of tibia, via the medial meniscus, forming the medial femorotibial joint. Overall, the medial femorotibial, lateral femorotibial and patellofemoral joints collectively form the knee joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The adductor tubercle is the small prominence found on the superomedial aspect of the medial condyle of femur. It is found at the inferior end of the medial supracondylar line and lies superior to the medial epicondyle of femur. It provides an insertion site for the adductor magnus muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The medial epicondyle (internal epicondyle) of femur is the rough eminence found along the medial aspect of the medial condyle. It provides an attachment site for the tibial collateral ligament.

24571.name: Articular Facet of Lateral Condyle of Femur

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The articular facet of lateral condyle of femur is the smooth, convex area found on the anterior, inferior and posterior aspects of the lateral condyle. It is continuous medially with both the patellar surface and intercondylar fossa of femur.

The articular facet of lateral condyle of femur articulates with the articular facet of lateral condyle of tibia, via the lateral meniscus, forming the lateral femorotibial joint. Overall, the lateral femorotibial, medial femorotibial and patellofemoral joints collectively form the knee joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The groove for popliteus muscle (popliteal groove) is the smooth, curved depression found along the lateral aspect of the lateral condyle of femur. The tendon of the popliteus muscle passes through this groove and attaches to its anterior end.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial intercondylar tubercle (medial intercondyloid tubercle or medial intercondylar spine) is the small projection found on the medial end of the intercondylar eminence of tibia.

It is the higher of the two intercondylar tubercles that are found on the intercondylar eminence, the other being the lateral intercondylar tubercle. Overall, both the medial and lateral intercondylar tubercles are believed to play a role in stabilizing the knee joint, by fitting into the space created by the intercondylar fossa of femur.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The soleal (popliteal) line is the rough ridge found on the proximal half of the posterior surface of tibia. It extends inferomedially from the fibular articular facet to the medial border of tibia. It provides an origin site for the soleus muscle, and an attachment site for the transverse intermuscular septum of leg.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The tubercle of iliotibial tract (Gerdy’s tubercle) is the flat, triangular area found on the anterior aspect of the lateral condyle of tibia. It provides an attachment site for the iliotibial tract.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The apex (styloid process) of head of fibula is the upward projecting process found along the posterolateral aspect of the head of fibula. It provides an insertion site for the biceps femoris muscle, and attachment sites for the fibular collateral and arcuate popliteal ligaments.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The body (shaft) of tibia is the long, tubular part of the bone. It is located between the proximal and distal parts of the tibia. It is narrowest at the junction between its middle and distal thirds and expands both proximally and distally from this area. 

The body of tibia is triangular in cross-section, and consists of:

—three surfaces (medial, lateral and posterior);

—three borders (anterior, medial and interosseous).

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior intercondylar area (posterior intercondylar fossa or posterior intercondyloid fossa) is the posteriorly located, non-articular part of the region that is found between the articular facets of the medial and lateral condyles of the tibia. It is separated from the anterior intercondylar area by the intercondylar eminence.

The posterior intercondylar area provides attachment sites for the posterior cruciate ligament and the posterior horns of both the medial and lateral menisci.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial surface of tibia is the smooth, slightly convex, subcutaneous area found along the anteromedial aspect of the bone. It is one of the three surfaces of tibia, the other two being the lateral and posterior surfaces, and is an area that is bounded:

—anteriorly, by the anterior border of tibia;

—posteriorly, by the medial border of tibia.

The medial surface of tibia provides insertion sites for the gracilis, sartorius and semitendinosus muscles, as well an attachment site for the tibial collateral ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial border of tibia is the margin found along the posteromedial aspect of the bone. It is one of the three borders of the tibia, the other two being the anterior and interosseous (lateral) borders, and it separates the medial and posterior surfaces of the tibia.

The medial border extends inferiorly from the medial aspect of the medial condyle of tibia to the posterior aspect of the medial malleolus. It provides attachment sites for the crural fascia and the tibial collateral ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior surface of tibia is the area found along the posterior aspect of the bone. It is one of the three surfaces of tibia, the other two being the medial and lateral surfaces, and is an area that is bounded:

—medially, by the medial border of tibia;

—laterally, by the interosseous (lateral) border of tibia.

The posterior surface of tibia contains the soleal line and the nutrient foramen of tibia. It provides origin sites for the flexor digitorum longus, tibialis posterior and soleus muscles, and provides an insertion site for the popliteus muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The distal part (end) of tibia is the slightly broader, inferior portion of the bone. It is continuous superiorly with the body of tibia and contains the medial malleolus and its malleolar groove.

Both its inferior articular surface and articular facet of medial malleolus articulate with the talus, contributing to the formation of the ankle joint.

The distal part of tibia also contains the fibular notch, which articulates with the distal part of fibula, forming the inferior tibiofibular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The interosseous border (interosseous crest or lateral border) of tibia is the sharp margin found along the posterolateral aspect of the bone. It is one of the three borders of the tibia, the other two being the anterior and medial borders, and it separates the lateral and posterior surfaces of the tibia.

The interosseous border extends inferiorly from the lateral aspect of the lateral condyle of tibia to its fibular notch. It provides an attachment site for the interosseous membrane of leg.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral surface of tibia is the smooth area found along the anterolateral aspect of the bone. It is one of the three surfaces of tibia, the other two being the medial and posterior surfaces, and is an area that is bounded:

—anteriorly, by the anterior border of tibia;

—posteriorly, by the interosseous (lateral) border of tibia.

The lateral surface of tibia provides an origin site for the tibialis anterior muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The malleolar groove (sulcus) of tibia is the smooth, vertical depression found on the posterior aspect of the medial malleolus. The tendons of the tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus muscles pass through this groove.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The fibular notch is the triangular, articular indentation found along the lateral aspect of the distal part of tibia. It is continuous superiorly with the interosseous border of tibia and articulates with the distal part of the posterior surface of fibula, forming the inferior tibiofibular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular facet of medial malleolus is the smooth, crescent-shaped area found on the lateral aspect of the medial malleolus of the tibia. It is continuous laterally with the inferior surface of tibia and articulates with the medial malleolar facet of talus, contributing to the formation of the ankle joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior border (anterior crest) of fibula is the margin located along the anterolateral aspect of the bone. It is one of the three borders of the fibula, the other two being the posterior and interosseous borders, and it separates the medial and lateral surfaces of the fibula.

The anterior border extends inferiorly from the anterior aspect of the head of fibula to the anterior aspect of the lateral malleolus and it provides an attachment site for the anterior intermuscular septum of leg.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial (extensor) surface of fibula is the narrow area found along the anteromedial aspect of the bone. It is one of the three surfaces of fibula, the other two being the lateral and posterior surfaces, and is an area that is bounded:

—anteriorly, by the anterior border of fibula;

—posteriorly, by the interosseous border of fibula.

The medial surface of fibula provides origin sites for the extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus and fibularis tertius muscles. Because these muscles originate from this medial surface, it is therefore also known as the extensor surface of the fibula.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior border of fibula is the margin located along the posterolateral aspect of the bone. It is one of the three borders of the fibula, the other two being the anterior and interosseous borders, and it separates the lateral and posterior surfaces of the fibula.

The posterior border extends inferiorly from the posterior aspect of the head of fibula to the malleolar groove of fibula, with its proximal end being less distinct than its distal end. It provides an attachment site for the posterior intermuscular septum of leg.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior (flexor) surface of fibula is the area found along the posteromedial aspect of the bone. It is one of the three surfaces of fibula, the other two being the medial and lateral surfaces, and is an area that is bounded:

—medially, by the interosseous border of fibula;

—laterally, by the posterior border of fibula.

The posterior surface of fibula contains the medial crest and nutrient foramen of fibula. Its distal end articulates with the fibular notch of the tibia, forming the inferior tibiofibular joint. It provides origin sites for the tibialis posterior, soleus and flexor hallucis longus muscles. Because these muscles originate from this posterior surface, it is therefore also known as the flexor surface of the fibula.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The neck of fibula is the short, constricted section that extends from the head to the body of the bone. The common fibular nerve passes along the posterolateral aspect of the neck of fibula.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The interosseous border (interosseous crest) of fibula is the margin located along the medial aspect of the bone. It is one of the three borders of the fibula, the other two being the anterior and posterior borders, and it separates the anterior and posterior surfaces of the fibula.

The interosseous border extends inferiorly from the anteromedial aspect of the neck of fibula to the anteromedial aspect of the lateral malleolus and it provides an attachment site for the interosseous membrane of leg.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The inferior articular surface of tibia is the smooth, saddle-shaped, inferiorly facing articular area on the distal end of bone. It is continuous medially with the articular facet of medial malleolus and articulates with the superior facet of talus, contributing to the formation of the ankle joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The intercondylar eminence is the prominent elevation located in the middle of the region that is found between the articular facets of the medial and lateral condyles of the tibia. It separates the anterior and posterior intercondylar areas and contains medial and lateral intercondylar tubercles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The tuberosity of navicular bone is the blunt projection found along the inferomedial aspect of the bone. It provides an insertion site for the tibialis posterior muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The tuberosity is the blunt projection found on the inferolateral aspect of the cuboid bone. It is located posterior to the groove for tendon of fibularis longus muscle and provides an attachment site for the plantar calcaneocuboid ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial border of fibula is the sharp, longitudinal ridge found along the posterior surface of the bone. It extends inferiorly from the posteromedial aspect of the head of the fibula, and its lower portion curves medially to end at the distal half of the interosseous border of the fibula.

The medial border of fibula provides an attachment site for the deep fascia that separates the tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The malleolar groove (sulcus) of fibula is the smooth, vertical depression on the posterior aspect of the lateral malleolus. The tendons of the fibularis longus and fibularis brevis muscles pass through this groove.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The intertrochanteric line is the rough ridge on both the anterior and medial aspects of the proximal end of the femur. It forms the anterior and medial portions of the junction between the body and neck of femur. It spirals inferomedially from the greater trochanter to the lesser trochanter, where it becomes continuous with the spiral line.

The intertrochanteric line provides an origin site for the vastus medialis muscle, and an attachment site for the iliofemoral ligament.

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
Description
sections.text: The lesser trochanter is the blunt, conical projection on the proximal end of the femur. It projects medially from the posteroinferior aspect of the junction between the neck and body of femur. It provides an insertion site for the psoas major muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The gluteal tuberosity is the broad, rough margin located along the upper posterolateral aspect of the body of femur. It is the superior continuation of the lateral lip of linea aspera, extends in a superolateral direction to the greater trochanter, and separates the posterior and lateral surfaces of femur.

The gluteal tuberosity provides insertion sites for the gluteus maximus and adductor magnus muscles.

20132.name: Fovea for Ligament of Head of Femur

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The fovea (fossa) of head of femur is the small pit found on the medial aspect of the head of femur. It provides an attachment site for the ligament of head of femur.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral lip of linea aspera is the edge of the linea aspera that lies further from the midline of the body. It is one of two lips of the linea aspera, the other being the medial lip, both of which surround the intermediate zone of linea aspera. It is continuous:

—superiorly, with the gluteal tuberosity;

—inferiorly, with the lateral supracondylar line.

The lateral lip of linea aspera provides an origin site for the vastus lateralis muscle and the short head of biceps femoris muscle. It also provides an attachment site for the lateral femoral intermuscular septum.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The quadrate tubercle is the small prominence on the posterior aspect of the proximal end of the femur. It is found along the intertrochanteric crest, close to its mid-point, and provides an insertion site for the quadratus femoris muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial lip of linea aspera is the edge of the linea aspera that lies closer to the midline of the body. It is one of two lips of the linea aspera, the other being the lateral lip, both of which surround the intermediate zone of linea aspera. The medial lip is continuous:

—superiorly, with the spiral line;

—inferiorly, with the medial supracondylar line.

The medial lip of linea aspera provides an origin site for the vastus medialis muscle and an attachment site for the medial femoral intermuscular septum.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The pectineal line of femur is the ridge found along the posterior aspect of the proximal end of the body of femur. It is the superior continuation of the intermediate zone of linea aspera, extends up to the lesser trochanter, and provides an insertion site for the pectineus muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The trochanteric fossa is the rough, deep depression found along the posterosuperior aspect of the proximal end of femur. It is formed by the concave posteromedial aspect of the greater trochanter and provides an insertion site for the obturator externus muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The promontory (sacral promontory) is the prominent anterosuperior edge found on the body of the first sacral vertebra. It is located 1 cm posterior to the body’s center of gravity.

The promontory and linea terminalis combine to form the pelvic inlet, which is the distinct bony ridge that separates the greater pelvis from the lesser pelvis.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The transverse ridges (transverse lines) of the sacrum are the four horizontal linear elevations that cross the pelvic surface of the bone. Each transverse ridge extends from one anterior sacral foramen to its level corresponding foramen on the opposite side. 

The transverse ridges each mark the sites of fusion between the sacral vertebrae, representing the position of the intervertebral discs that were once found in between the five sacral vertebrae in the immature bone.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior articular processes are the two upwardly projecting processes located on the base of the sacrum. They are found in the area where the body of the first sacral vertebra meets the ala of the sacrum.

The superior articular processes of sacrum consist of posteromedially facing superior articular facets. They articulate with the inferior articular processes of the fifth lumbar vertebra, forming zygapophyseal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The sacral horn (cornu) is the horn-like projection found along the inferior end of the dorsal surface of the sacrum. The sacrum has two sacral horns, one on its right side and one on its left side, and the sacral hiatus is located in between these.

The sacral horn is formed by the inferior articular tubercle of the fifth sacral vertebra, which is a remnant of its inferior articular process. It articulates with the coccyx at its coccygeal horn and provides an attachment site for the intercornual ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The ala (wing) of sacrum is the fan-shaped, laterally located area on the base of the sacrum. It is the anterosuperior aspect of the lateral part of sacrum, lateral to the articular facet of the base, and its anterior boundary is defined by the anterior border of ala. 

The ala of sacrum provides an attachment site for the iliolumbar ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior inferior iliac spine (PIIS) is the sharp process found along the posterior border of ilium. It is located between the posterior superior iliac spine and the greater sciatic notch.

The posterior inferior iliac spine provides an attachment site for the sacrotuberous ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) is the blunt process that marks the posterior end of the iliac crest. It cannot be palpated but a small skin dimple often marks its location.

The posterior superior iliac spine provides an attachment site for the sacrotuberous and posterior sacroiliac ligaments.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The greater sciatic (ischiatic or ischiadic) notch is the larger of the two indentations found along the posterior border of the coxal bone. From the ischial spine, it extends superiorly along the posterior border of the body of ischium and then along the posterior border of ilium, before ending at the posterior inferior iliac spine.

The greater sciatic notch is wider in females than males and is converted into the greater sciatic foramen by the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments. This foramen allows for the passage of the piriformis muscle, sciatic nerve and other nerves and vessels of the lower limb.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The ischial spine (spine of ischium) is the pointed, triangular process found along the posterior border of body of ischium. It extends posteromedially and separates the greater sciatic notch from the lesser sciatic notch.

The ischial spine provides origin sites for the coccygeus and levator ani muscles, as well as an attachment site for the sacrospinous ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) is the blunt process that marks the anterior end of the iliac crest. It is subcutaneous and can be palpated at the lateral end of the inguinal fold.

The anterior superior iliac spine provides origin sites for the sartorius and tensor fasciae latae muscles, as well as an attachment site for the lateral end of the inguinal ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) is the thick, rough process found along the anterior border of ilium. It is located between the anterior superior iliac spine and the acetabulum.

The anterior inferior iliac spine provides origin sites for the rectus femoris muscle, as well as an attachment site for the iliofemoral ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The pubic tubercle (pubic spine) is the small, raised eminence found along the lateral end of the pubic crest. It can be palpated at the medial end of the inguinal fold.

The pubic tubercle provides insertion sites for the external abdominal oblique and cremaster muscles, as well as an attachment site for the medial end of the inguinal ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The intercondylar fossa (intercondylar notch or intercondyloid fossa) of femur is the depression found along the posteroinferior aspect of the distal end of the femur. It is located between the medial and lateral condyles of femur and is bounded:

—anteriorly, by the patellar surface of femur;

—posteriorly, by the intercondylar line.

Its lateral wall is formed by the medial aspect of the lateral condyle of femur, and this provides an attachment site for the anterior cruciate ligament. Its medial wall is formed by the lateral aspect of the medial condyle of femur, and this provides an attachment site for the posterior cruciate ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral supracondylar line (lateral supracondylar ridge, lateral supracondyloid line, or lateral epicondyloid line) is the margin located along the lower posterolateral aspect of the body of femur. It is the more distinct of the two supracondylar lines, the other being the medial supracondylar line. It is the inferior continuation of the lateral lip of linea aspera, extends to the lateral condyle of femur, and separates the popliteal and lateral surfaces of femur.

The lateral supracondylar line provides an origin site for the plantaris muscle and short head of biceps femoris muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial supracondylar line (medial supracondylar ridge, medial supracondyloid line, or medial epicondyloid line) is the margin located along the lower posteromedial aspect of the body of femur. It is the less distinct of the two supracondylar lines, the other being the lateral supracondylar line. It is the inferior continuation of the medial lip of linea aspera, extends to the adductor tubercle, and separates the popliteal and medial surfaces of femur.

The medial supracondylar line provides an origin site for the vastus medialis muscle, and an insertion site for the adductor magnus muscle.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The intercondylar line is the horizontal ridge on the posterior aspect of the distal end of the femur. It extends from the medial condyle of femur to the lateral condyle.

The intercondylar line provides an attachment site for the capsular ligaments of the knee joint and the oblique popliteal ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The patellar surface of femur is the groove-like area on the anterior aspect of the distal end of femur. It is located between the articular facets of the medial and lateral condyles of the femur.

The patellar surface of femur articulates with the vertical ridge of patella, contributing to the formation of the patellofemoral joint, and accommodates the gliding of the patella over the distal end of the femur during flexion and extension of the knee joint. Overall, the patellofemoral joint, medial femorotibial joint and lateral femorotibial joint collectively form the knee joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial border of the patella forms its medial margin. It separates, medially, the anterior and articular surfaces of the patella, is continuous superiorly with the base of the patella, and converges with the lateral border at the apex of the patella.

The medial border of the patella provides an insertion site for the vastus medialis muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral border of patella forms its lateral margin. It separates, laterally, the anterior and articular surfaces of the patella, is continuous superiorly with the base of patella, and converges with the medial border at the apex of patella.

The lateral border of patella provides an insertion site for the vastus lateralis muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The apex of the patella is the thin, tapered, distal edge of the bone. It provides an attachment site for the patellar ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior surface of patella is the rough, convex, subcutaneous area on the outer aspect of the bone. It is one of the two surfaces of the patella, the other being the articular (posterior) surface. It is an area that is bounded by the medial and lateral borders, base, and apex of the patella.

The anterior surface of patella consists of longitudinal striations and multiple nutrient foramina.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The base (superior border) of the patella is the thick, blunt, proximal edge of the bone. It provides an attachment site for the quadriceps tendon.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral articular facet of patella is the smooth, concave, laterally located area of the articular surface of patella. It is the larger of the two articular facets of patella, the other being the medial articular facet.

The lateral articular facet of patella articulates with the articular facet of lateral condyle of femur, contributing to the formation of the patellofemoral joint. Overall, the patellofemoral joint, medial femorotibial joint and lateral femorotibial joint collectively form the knee joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The vertical ridge of patella is the vertical, linear elevation that crosses the articular surface of the bone. It divides the articular surface of patella into unequal medial and lateral articular facets.

The vertical ridge of patella articulates with the groove of the patellar surface of femur, contributing to the formation of the patellofemoral joint. Overall, the patellofemoral joint, medial femorotibial joint and lateral femorotibial joint collectively form the knee joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial articular facet of patella is the smooth, concave, medially located area of the articular surface of patella. It is the smaller of the two articular facets of patella, the other being the lateral articular facet.

The medial articular facet of patella articulates with the articular facet of medial condyle of femur, contributing to the formation of the patellofemoral joint. Overall, the patellofemoral joint, medial femorotibial joint and lateral femorotibial joint collectively form the knee joint.

23190.name: Groove for Tendon of Fibularis Longus Muscle of Cuboid Bone
23190.latin: Sulcus tendinis musculi fibularis longi cuboidei
alternate: Groove for Tendon of Peroneus Longus Muscle of Cuboid Bone

Sulcus tendinis musculi peronei longi ossis cuboidei

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The groove for tendon of fibularis longus muscle is the smooth, oblique depression found on both the lateral and plantar surfaces of the cuboid bone. It is located anterior to the tuberosity, and the tendon of the fibularis longus muscle passes through this groove.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The posterior border is the thin, concave, nonarticular margin of both the alae and cuneiform part of the vomer. It is one of the four borders of the vomer, the other three being the anterior, superior and inferior borders.

The posterior border of vomer consists of the vomerine crest of choana, which separates the right and left choanae (posterior nasal apertures) of the nasal cavities.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The inferior border (inferior margin) is the thin, horizontal, lower margin of the cuneiform part of vomer. It is one of the four borders of the vomer, the other three being the anterior, posterior and superior borders.

The inferior border of vomer articulates:

—anteriorly, with the nasal crests of both the right and left maxillae;

—posteriorly, with the nasal crests of both the right and left palatine bones.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The superior border (superior margin) is the thick, grooved, upper margin of both the right and left alae of vomer. It is one of the four borders of the vomer, the other three being the anterior, posterior and inferior borders.

The superior border of vomer articulates with the inferior surface of the body of sphenoid bone, forming the sphenovomerine suture.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The alae are the two wing-like, lateral projections that form the posterosuperior part of the vomer. They are continuous anteroinferiorly with the cuneiform part of vomer and articulate with the inferior surface of the body of sphenoid bone, forming the sphenovomerine suture.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The nasopalatine grooves are the narrow, oblique depressions found along both the right and left lateral surfaces of the vomer. They each travel anteroinferiorly from the superior border towards the maxilla and each lodge a nasopalatine nerve and vessels.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The vomerine crest of choana is the concave ridge found along the posterior border of the vomer. It separates the right and left choanae (posterior nasal apertures) of the nasal cavities.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The conchal crest is the oblique, anteriorly located ridge found along the nasal surface of the maxilla. It extends posterosuperiorly from the nasal notch to the lacrimal groove of the maxilla and it articulates with the inferior nasal concha.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The maxillary tuberosity (maxillary eminence) is the rounded, inferiorly located projection found along the infratemporal surface of the maxilla. It provides an origin site for the medial pterygoid muscle.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The canine eminence is the prominence found along the anterior surface of the maxilla. It is located superficial to the socket of the canine tooth.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The nasal crest is the medially located ridge found along the superior aspect of the palatine process of maxilla. The nasal crests of both the right and left maxillae articulate with the inferior border of the vomer.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The greater palatine groove is the shallow, oblique, posteriorly located depression found along the nasal surface of the maxilla. It travels superomedially from the greater palatine foramen and is converted into the greater palatine canal by its combination with the greater palatine groove of the palatine bone. This canal allows for the passage of the greater palatine nerve and vessels.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior surface of radius is the concave area on the frontal aspect of the body of the radius. It is one of the three surfaces of the body of the radius, the other two being the posterior and lateral surfaces. It is an area that is bounded:

—anterolaterally, by the anterior border of radius;

—medially, by the interosseous border of radius.

The anterior surface of radius contains the nutrient foramen. It also provides origin sites for the flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum superficialis muscles, as well as an insertion site for the pronator quadratus muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior border of radius is the margin located along the anterolateral aspect of the body of the radius. It extends inferiorly from the anterior edge of the radial tuberosity to the radial styloid process.

The anterior border of radius separates the anterior and lateral surfaces of the radius and provides an origin site for the flexor digitorum superficialis muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral surface of radius is the convex area on the posterolateral aspect of the body of the radius. It is one of the three surfaces of the body of the radius, the other two being the anterior and posterior surfaces. It is an area that is bounded:

—anterolaterally, by the anterior border of radius;

—posteriorly, by the posterior border of radius.

The lateral surface of radius provides insertion sites for the supinator and pronator teres muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior border of radius is the margin located along the dorsal aspect of the body of the radius. It extends inferiorly from the posterior edge of the radial tuberosity to the dorsal radial tubercle.

The posterior border of radius separates the lateral and posterior surfaces of the radius.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior surface of radius is the flat area on the posteromedial aspect of the body of the radius. It is one of the three surfaces of the body of the radius, the other two being the anterior and lateral surfaces. It is an area that is bounded:

—anteromedially, by the interosseous border of radius;

—posteriorly, by the posterior border of radius.

The posterior surface of radius provides origin sites for the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The interosseous border (interosseous crest or medial border) of radius is the sharp margin located along the medial aspect of the body of the radius. It extends inferiorly from the inferomedial edge of the radial tuberosity to the ulnar notch.

The interosseous border of radius separates the anterior and posterior surfaces of the radius and provides an attachment site for the interosseous membrane of the forearm.

17018.name: Articular Circumference of Head of Radius

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The articular circumference of head of radius is the smooth, round perimeter of the head of the radius.

Its medial aspect articulates with the radial notch of ulna, forming the proximal radioulnar joint, contributing to the formation of the elbow joint. The rest of the articular circumference is surrounded by the annular ligament of the radius.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The grooves for extensor muscle tendons are the smooth, oblique and vertical depressions found on the posterior aspect of the distal part of radius. 

These grooves are divided, by the dorsal radial tubercle, into two groups:

—those that are found medial to the tubercle, the grooves for the tendons of the extensor digitorum, extensor pollicis longus, and extensor indicis muscles;

—those that are found lateral to the tubercle, the grooves for the tendons of the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The neck of radius is the short, constricted portion on the proximal part of the bone. It is the inferior continuation of the head of the radius. It is located superior to the radial tuberosity.

It is closely surrounded by the annular ligament of radius, and its medial aspect provides an attachment site for the quadrate ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The ulnar notch is the smooth, concave, articular indentation found along the medial aspect of the distal part of radius. Its inferior margin provides an attachment site for the articular disc of the distal radioulnar joint.

The ulnar notch articulates with the articular circumference of the head of the ulna, forming the distal radioulnar joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lunate articular facet of radius is the quadrangular, medially located area found on the inferior aspect of the distal part of the bone. It is one of two facets that make up the carpal articular surface of the radius, the other being the scaphoid articular facet of the radius.

The lunate articular facet of radius articulates with the radial articular facet of the lunate bone, forming the radiolunate joint. This joint contributes to the formation of the radiocarpal (wrist) joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The head of radius is the disc shaped, expanded portion on the proximal part of the bone. It is the superior continuation of the neck of the radius. It contains two articular areas:

—the articular circumference of head of radius, which articulates with the radial notch of ulna, forming the proximal radioulnar joint;

—the articular facet of head of radius, which articulates with the capitulum of humerus, forming the humeroradial joint.

Both of these joints contribute to the formation of the elbow joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The radial (bicipital) tuberosity is the oval, elevated area found on the anteromedial aspect of the proximal part of the radius. It is located inferior to the neck of the radius.

It provides an insertion site for the biceps brachii muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The dorsal radial tubercle (Lister’s tubercle) is the palpable, small prominence on the posterior aspect of the distal part of radius. It is found between the grooves for extensor muscle tendons.

It provides attachment sites for the extensor retinaculum of hand and the dorsal radiocarpal ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The radial styloid process is the blunt projection found on the inferolateral aspect of the distal part of radius. 

It provides an insertion site for the brachioradialis muscle, as well as attachment sites for the radial collateral ligament of the wrist joint and the radioscaphocapitate ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The scaphoid articular facet of radius is the triangular, laterally located area found on the inferior aspect of the distal part of the bone. It is one of two facets that make up the carpal articular surface of the radius, the other being the lunate articular facet of the radius.

The scaphoid articular facet of radius articulates with the radial articular facet of the scaphoid bone, forming the radioscaphoid joint. This joint contributes to the formation of the radiocarpal (wrist) joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral epicondyle (external epicondyle) of humerus is the projection found at the distal end of the lateral supracondylar ridge. It is less prominent than the medial epicondyle of the humerus.

The lateral epicondyle provides origin sites for the superficial group of muscles of the posterior compartment of forearm and the supinator and anconeus muscles. It also provides an attachment site for the radial collateral ligament.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The medial epicondyle (internal epicondyle) of humerus is the subcutaneous projection found at the distal end of the medial supracondylar ridge. It is more prominent than the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.

The medial epicondyle contains the groove for ulnar nerve. It provides origin sites for the superficial group of muscles of the anterior compartment of the forearm, as well as an attachment site for the ulnar collateral ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior surface (dorsal surface) of scapula is the convex area on the posterior aspect of the bone. It is one of two surfaces of the scapula, the other being the costal surface.

The dorsal surface of scapula consists of the spine of the scapula, which separates its supraspinous and infraspinous fossae. It provides origin sites for the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, teres major, and deltoid muscles, and an insertion site for the trapezius muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The medial border (vertebral border or vertebral margin) of scapula is the thin, medially located edge of the bone. It extends from the superior angle of the scapula to its inferior angle and is longest of three borders of the scapula, the other two being the lateral and superior borders.

The medial border of scapula provides insertion sites for the serratus anterior, levator scapulae, rhomboid major, and rhomboid minor muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The inferior angle of scapula is the blunt area of the bone where its medial and lateral borders meet. It is located superficial to the seventh rib or the seventh intercostal space and is one of the three angles of the scapula, the other two being the superior and lateral angles.

The inferior angle of scapula provides an insertion site for the serratus anterior muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral border (axillary margin or border) of scapula is the thick, laterally located edge of the bone. It extends from the lateral angle of the scapula to its inferior angle. It is one of three borders of the scapula, the other two being the superior and medial borders.

The lateral border of scapula provides origin sites for the teres major and teres minor muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior angle (medial angle) of scapula is the sharp area of the bone where its medial and superior borders meet. It is located superficial to the second rib and is one of the three angles of the scapula, the other two being the inferior and lateral angles.

The superior angle of scapula provides an insertion site for the levator scapulae muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior border (cranial border or cranial margin) of scapula is the thin, superiorly located edge of the bone. It extends from the superior angle of the scapula to its superior scapular notch and is the shortest of the three borders of the scapula, the other two being the medial and lateral borders.

The superior border of scapula provides an origin site for the inferior belly of omohyoid muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The costal surface (anterior or ventral surface) of scapula is the concave area on the anterior aspect of the bone. It is one of the two surfaces of the scapula, the other being the dorsal surface.

Most of the costal surface of scapula is occupied by the subscapular fossa, which provides an origin site for the subscapularis muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The scapular notch (superior scapular notch or suprascapular notch) is the indentation found along the lateral area of the superior edge of the scapula. It is continuous:

—medially, with the superior;

—laterally, with the base of the coracoid process. 

The scapular notch is converted into the suprascapular foramen by the superior transverse scapular ligament, which transmits the suprascapular nerve and vessels.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The spine of scapula is the triangular, shelf-like plate that projects from the superior area of the dorsal surface of the scapula. The apex of this triangle is located along the medial border of the scapula and extends laterally towards its base, which itself is continuous laterally with the acromion. It consists of two borders:

—a posterior border, which is formed by the posterior-most edge of the spine and is also known as its crest;

—a lateral border, which lies adjacent to the neck of the scapula, both of which contribute to the formation of the inferior scapular notch. 

The spine of scapula divides the dorsal surface into two parts:

—the superiorly located supraspinous fossa;

—the inferiorly located infraspinous fossa.

It provides attachment an origin site for the deltoid muscle and an insertion site for the trapezius muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The spinoglenoid notch (inferior scapular notch or notch of scapular spine) is the indentation formed between the neck of the scapula and the lateral border of its spine. It serves as a point of communication between the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae and provides a passage for the suprascapular nerve and vessels to travel between these two fossae.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The infraglenoid tubercle (infraglenoid tuberosity) is the rough prominence found along the inferior portion of the head of the scapula. It is located inferior to the glenoid fossa and provides an origin site for the long head of triceps brachii muscle.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The subscapular fossa is the concave area that occupies almost the entire costal surface of the scapula. It consists of ridges that travel in an inferomedial direction along the fossa. These ridges provide origin sites for the subscapularis muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The supraglenoid tubercle (supraglenoid tuberosity) is the small, rough prominence found along the superior portion of the head of the scapula. It is located superior to the glenoid fossa and provides an origin site for the long head of biceps brachii muscle.

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
sections.text: The coracoid process is the thick, curved, anterior projection that extends from the head and neck of the scapula. It provides origin sites for the coracobrachialis and short head of biceps brachii muscles, and an insertion site for the pectoralis minor muscle. It also provides attachment sites for the coracoacromial, coracohumeral and coracoclavicular ligaments.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anatomical neck of humerus is the short, constricted part of the bone that connects the head and body of the humerus. It is formed by a shallow groove, which encircles the head of the humerus. 

The anatomical neck of humerus separates the head from the greater and lesser tubercles. It provides an attachment site for the capsule of the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The lesser tubercle (lesser tuberosity, or tubercle of Weber) is the small eminence found on the anterior aspect of the proximal end of the humerus. It projects anteriorly from the junction between the anatomical neck and body of the humerus. It is located anteromedial to the greater tubercle, with these two tubercles being separated from each other by the intertubercular sulcus. 

The lesser tubercle contains a posterolaterally located crest. It provides an insertion site for the subscapularis muscle, and an attachment site for the transverse humeral ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The acromial facet (acromial articular surface) of the clavicle is the smooth, oval, articular area found on the lateral aspect of the acromial end of the bone. It articulates with the acromion of the scapula, forming the acromioclavicular joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The sternal facet (sternal articular surface) of the clavicle is the convex, quadrangular, articular area found on the medial aspect of the sternal end of the bone. It articulates with the clavicular notch of the manubrium of the sternum, forming the sternoclavicular joint, and provides an attachment site for the interclavicular ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The trapezoid line (trapezoid ridge) is the narrow ridge found on the lateral one third of the inferior surface of the clavicle. It extends anterolaterally from the conoid tubercle and provides an attachment site for the trapezoid ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The conoid tubercle is the prominent eminence found on the lateral one third of the inferior surface of the clavicle. It is located between the trapezoid line and the groove for subclavius muscle and provides an attachment site for the conoid ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The groove for subclavius muscle (subclavius groove) is the shallow depression found on the middle one third of the inferior surface of the clavicle. It extends anteromedially from the conoid tubercle and provides an insertion site for the subclavius muscle and an attachment site for the clavipectoral fascia. The groove for subclavius muscle is larger in males than females.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The impression for costoclavicular ligament (costal tuberosity, costal impression, or tuberosity of clavicle) is the rough, oval area found on the medial one third of the inferior surface of the clavicle. It provides the attachment site for the costoclavicular ligament.
