sections.title: Description
sections.text: The mesiobuccal cusp is the superiorly located, pointed elevation found along the mesiobuccal aspect of the crown of mandibular first molar tooth. It is one of the five cusps of this tooth, the other four being the mesiolingual, distobuccal, distolingual, and distal cusps. The mesiobuccal cusp consists of both cusp and triangular ridges.

19303.name: Buccal Surface of Maxillary First Molar Tooth
19303.latin: Facies buccalis dentis molaris primi maxillaris

sections.title: Description

24717.name: Mesial Surface of Maxillary First Molar Tooth
24717.latin: Facies mesialis dentis molaris primi maxillaris

sections.title: Description

20038.name: Distobuccal Cusp of Mandibular First Molar Tooth
20038.latin: Cuspis distobuccalis dentis molaris primi mandibularis

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The distobuccal cusp is the superiorly located, pointed elevation found along the distobuccal aspect of the crown of mandibular first molar tooth. It is one of the five cusps of this tooth, the other four being the mesiobuccal, mesiolingual, distolingual, and distal cusps. The distobuccal cusp consists of both cusp and triangular ridges.

22879.name: Crown of Mandibular First Molar Tooth
alternate: Anatomical Crown of Mandibular First Molar Tooth

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The crown (anatomical crown) is the superior portion of the mandibular first molar tooth that is covered by enamel. It is separated from the root by the cervical line and consists of five surfaces (buccal, lingual, mesial, distal, and occlusal) and five cusps.

The clinical crown is a term used to describe the superior portion of a mandibular tooth that is not covered by gingiva when viewed in the oral cavity.

23939.name: Cervical Line of Mandibular First Molar Tooth
23939.latin: Linea cervicalis dentis molaris primi mandibularis
alternate: Cementoenamel Junction of Mandibular First Molar Tooth

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The cervical line (cementoenamel junction) is a thin, irregular margin that forms the boundary between the enamel covering the crown and the cementum covering the root. Therefore, the cervical line separates the crown and root of the tooth.

22422.name: Root of Mandibular First Molar Tooth
alternate: Anatomical Root of Mandibular First Molar Tooth

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
Description
sections.text:
The pubic crest (crest of pubis) is the thick, rounded, superior border of the body of pubis. Its lateral end consists of a small raised eminence, known as the pubic tubercle. It contributes to the formation of the linea terminalis (pelvic brim), which is a distinct ridge that separates the greater pelvis from the lesser pelvis.

The pubic crest provides origin sites for the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis muscles, as well as an attachment site for the superior pubic ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The ramus of ischium (ischial ramus) is the flat, bony bar that projects from the inferior portion of the body of ischium. It is one of the two parts of the ischium, the other being the body of ischium. From the body, the ramus of ischium extends in anterosuperior and medial direction to fuse with the inferior pubic ramus. Collectively, the ramus of ischium and inferior pubic ramus are known as the ischiopubic ramus, which forms the inferior margin of the obturator foramen.

The ramus of ischium consists of:

- two surfaces (external and internal);

- two borders (superior and inferior).

It provides origin sites for the superficial and deep transverse perineal, ischiocavernosus and adductor magnus muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The inferior pubic ramus (inferior ramus of pubis) is the inferiorly located, flat bony bar that projects from the inferolateral aspect of the body of pubis. It is one of the two rami of the pubis, the other being the superior pubic ramus. From the body, it extends in a posteroinferior and lateral direction to fuse with the ischial ramus. Collectively, the inferior pubic ramus and ramus of ischium are known as the ischiopubic ramus, which forms the inferior margin of the obturator foramen. The right and left inferior pubic rami collectively form the pubic arch.

The inferior pubic ramus consists of:

—two surfaces (external and internal);

—two borders (medial and lateral).

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The body of pubis (pubic bone) is the medially located, quadrilateral-shaped part of the bone. The superior and inferior pubic rami extend from its superolateral and inferolateral aspects, respectively, while its medial aspect is the site of articulation with the fibrocartilaginous disc of the pubic symphysis joint.

The body of pubis consists of anterior, posterior and symphyseal surfaces, the pubic crest and pubic tubercle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior pubic ramus (superior ramus of pubis) is the superiorly located, bony bar that projects from the superolateral aspect of the body of pubis. It is one of the two rami of the pubis, the other being the inferior pubic ramus. From the body, it extends in a posterosuperior and lateral direction to the acetabulum, where it fuses with the bodies of the ilium and ischium. It forms the anterior one-fifth of the acetabulum and the superior margin of the obturator foramen.

The superior pubic ramus consists of:

—three surfaces (pectineal, obturator and pelvic);

—three borders (obturator crest, pecten pubis and inferior border).

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The pecten pubis (pectineal line of pubis) is the posterosuperiorly located ridge on the superior pubic ramus. It is one of the three borders of the superior pubic ramus, the other two being the obturator crest and the inferior border of superior pubic ramus, and it separates the pectineal and pelvic surfaces of the superior pubic ramus. It extends, laterally, from the pubic crest to the iliopubic eminence, at which point it becomes continuous with the arcuate line of ilium. The pecten pubis contributes to the formation of the linea terminalis (pelvic brim), which is a distinct ridge that separates the greater pelvis from the lesser pelvis.

The pecten pubis provides an origin site for the pectineus muscle, as well as attachments site for the transversalis fascia and pectineal ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The iliopubic (iliopectineal) eminence is the raised area on the coxal bone that marks the union between the body of ilium and the superior pubic ramus. It contributes to the formation of the linea terminalis (pelvic brim), which is a distinct ridge that separates the greater pelvis from the lesser pelvis.

The iliopubic eminence provides an insertion site for the psoas minor muscle, as well as attachment sites for the pubofemoral ligament and the iliopsoas fascia.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The arcuate line of ilium is the narrow ridge found along the internal surface of the bone. It extends anteromedially from the anterior margin of the auricular surface of ilium to the iliopubic eminence.

It contributes to the formation of the linea terminalis (pelvic brim), which is a distinct ridge that separates the greater pelvis from the lesser pelvis. The arcuate line of ilium also forms the lower part of the medial border of ilium.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lesser sciatic (ischiatic or ischiadic) notch is the smaller of the two indentations found along the posterior border of the coxal bone. From the ischial spine, it extends inferiorly along the posterior border of the body of ischium, to the upper margin of the ischial tuberosity.

The lesser sciatic notch is converted into the lesser sciatic foramen by the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments. This foramen allows for the passage of the tendon of the obturator internus muscle, the internal pudendal vessels and the pudendal nerve.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The body (shaft) of first rib is the long, curved part of the bone that extends from its neck to its chondral end. It is flattened in appearance, however, because of its orientation, it differs from the other ribs by having superior and inferior surfaces and external and internal borders.The body of first rib consists of a scalene tubercle and grooves for the subclavian artery and vein. Unlike the other ribs, the first rib does not have a costal groove and lacks a distinct angle of rib, although it does provide attachment sites for the intercostal muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: Anterior end of the groove for popliteus muscle

sections.title: Description
sections.text: Pectineal line of femur and the proximal one-third of linea aspera of femur

18190.name: Origin of Short Head of Biceps Femoris Muscle

sections.title: Description
sections.text: Lateral lip of linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of femur

sections.title: Description
sections.text: Ischial part of the internal aspect of the bony margin of obturator foramen and the pelvic surface of the body of ischium

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The gluteal surface of ilium is the large, rough, and curved outer aspect of the ilium. 

It is one of the three surfaces of the ilium, the other two being the sacropelvic surface and iliac fossa, and is an area that is bounded:

—anteriorly, by the anterior border of ilium;

—posteriorly, by the posterior border of ilium;

—superiorly, by the iliac crest;

—anteroinferiorly by the acetabulum.

Its posteroinferior end is continuous with the dorsal surface of body of ischium.

The gluteal surface of ilium contains anterior, posterior and inferior gluteal lines, which divide the gluteal surface into four regions:

—The region between the acetabulum and inferior gluteal line provides an origin site for the rectus femoris muscle.

—The region between the inferior and anterior gluteal lines provides an origin site for the gluteus minimus muscle.

—The region between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines provides an origin site for the gluteus medius muscle.

—The region behind the posterior gluteal line provides an origin site for the gluteus maximus muscle, and an attachment site for the sacrotuberous ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The intertrochanteric crest is the ridge on the posterior aspect of the proximal end of the femur. It forms the posterior portion of the junction between the body and neck of femur. It extends inferomedially from the greater trochanter to the lesser trochanter.

The prominent quadrate tubercle is located close to the mid-point of the intertrochanteric crest, and this tubercle provides an insertion site for the quadratus femoris muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The laminae are the two broad, flat, bony plates that project posteromedially from the posterior ends of the pedicles of a lumbar vertebra. They form the posterolateral parts of the vertebral arch, the posterolateral walls of the vertebral foramen, and their posterior ends unite at the midline.

The transverse and superior articular processes extend from the junctions between the pedicles and laminae, the spinous process extends from the junction between the two laminae, and the inferior articular processes extend inferiorly from the laminae.

Overall, the laminae of the vertebral column provide attachment sites for intrinsic back muscles and the ligamenta flava.

16483.name: Transverse Process of Fifth Lumbar Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The transverse processes are the two laterally projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a lumbar vertebra. They extend from the junction between the pedicles and laminae.

Overall, the transverse processes of lumbar vertebrae are generally long, thin, blunt and consist of accessory processes. They provide origin sites for the psoas major muscles, insertion sites for the quadratus lumborum muscles, and attachment sites for the intrinsic muscles of the back, thoracolumbar fascia and intertransverse ligaments.

In addition, the transverse processes of the fifth lumbar vertebra provide attachments sites for the iliofemoral ligaments.

19174.name: Vertebral Body of Fifth Lumbar Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The vertebral body is the anteriorly located cylindrical part of a lumbar vertebra. When viewed from above, it appears kidney-shaped. Its anterior aspect is concave, while its posterior aspect, which forms the anterior wall of the vertebral foramen, is flat. It is connected to the vertebral arch via two pedicles, which extend from the upper corners of its posterior aspect. It consists of:

—superior and inferior intervertebral surfaces;

—superior and inferior annular epiphyses;

—vascular foramina.

The vertebral body of the fifth lumbar vertebra provides attachment sites for the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments.

Overall, the sizes of the vertebral bodies gradually increase caudally along the vertebral column. Adjacent vertebral bodies articulate with each other via intervertebral discs, forming the intervertebral symphysis joints.

In terms of function, each vertebral body provides structural support to the body weight that lies superior to it.

16825.name: Superior Articular Process of Fifth Lumbar Vertebra
16825.latin: Processus articularis superior vertebrae lumbalis quintae
alternate: Superior Zygapophysis of Fifth Lumbar Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior articular processes (superior zygapophyses) are the two upwardly projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a lumbar vertebra. They extend from the junction between the pedicles and laminae.

Overall, the superior articular processes of lumbar vertebrae consist of mammillary processes and posteromedially facing superior articular facets. They articulate with the inferior articular processes of the vertebra above, forming zygapophyseal joints.

22146.name: Spinous Process of Fifth Lumbar Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The spinous process is the single, posteriorly projecting process located at the posterior part of the vertebral arch of a lumbar vertebra. It extends from the junction between the two laminae, which itself is found at the midline.

Overall, the spinous processes of lumbar vertebrae are generally short, thick, and blunt. They are more horizontally oriented than other vertebrae and provide attachment sites for intrinsic back muscles, thoracolumbar fascia, and the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The first coccygeal vertebra (Co1) is the largest and most superior of the four coccygeal vertebrae. It consists of the base of coccyx, two coccygeal cornua, and two transverse processes. However, it has no spinous process, pedicles or laminae.

The first coccygeal vertebra articulates with the sacrum superiorly, forming the sacrococcygeal joint, while it fuses with the second coccygeal vertebra inferiorly.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The second coccygeal vertebra (Co2) lies inferior to, and is smaller than, the first coccygeal vertebra. It sometimes presents traces of transverse processes. However, it has no spinous process, pedicles or laminae.

The second coccygeal vertebra fuses with the first coccygeal vertebra superiorly, and with the third coccygeal vertebra inferiorly.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The fourth coccygeal vertebra (Co4) is the oval-shaped bone that lies inferior to, and is smaller than, the third coccygeal vertebra. It has no transverse processes, spinous processes, pedicles or laminae.

The fourth coccygeal vertebra fuses with the third coccygeal vertebra superiorly.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The third coccygeal vertebra (Co3) is the oval-shaped bone that lies inferior to, and is smaller than, the second coccygeal vertebra. It has no transverse processes, spinous processes, pedicles or laminae.

The third coccygeal vertebra fuses with the second coccygeal vertebra superiorly, and with the fourth coccygeal vertebra inferiorly.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The acetabular fossa is the centrally located, non-articular, rough portion of the acetabulum. It forms the floor of the acetabulum and is bounded inferiorly by the lunate surface of acetabulum except inferiorly, where it is continuous with the acetabular notch.

The acetabular fossa is filled with fat and provides an attachment site for the ligament of head of femur.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior gluteal line is a curved ridge found along the gluteal surface of ilium. It is the shortest of the three gluteal lines, the other two being the anterior and inferior gluteal lines. It begins at the dorsal region of the iliac crest, and then travels in a posteroinferior direction, curving slightly to end at the greater sciatic notch.

The region between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines provides an origin site for the gluteus medius muscle, while the region behind the posterior gluteal line provides an origin site for the gluteus maximus muscle and an attachment site for the sacrotuberous ligament.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The iliac tubercle (tubercle of iliac crest or cristal tubercle) is the prominence found along the iliac crest. It is located along on the outer lip, 5–6 cm posterior to the anterior superior iliac spine, and provides an attachment site for the iliotibial tract.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior gluteal line is a curved ridge found along the gluteal surface of ilium. It is the longest of the three gluteal lines, the other two being the posterior and inferior gluteal lines. It begins at a point along the iliac crest that lies anterior to the iliac tubercle, and then travels in a posteroinferior direction, curving greatly to end at the greater sciatic notch.

The region between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines provides an origin site for the gluteus minimus muscle, while the region between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines provides an origin site for the gluteus medius muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The inferior gluteal line is a curved ridge found along the gluteal surface of ilium. It is the least distinct of the three gluteal lines, the other two being the anterior and posterior gluteal lines. It begins at the notch between the anterior superior and anterior inferior iliac spines, and then travels in a posteroinferior direction, curving slightly to end at the greater sciatic notch.

The region between the inferior gluteal line and acetabulum provides an origin site for the rectus femoris muscle, while the region between the inferior and anterior gluteal lines provides an origin site for the gluteus minimus muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The iliopubic (iliopectineal) eminence is the raised area on the coxal bone that marks the union between the body of ilium and the superior pubic ramus. It contributes to the formation of the linea terminalis (pelvic brim), which is a distinct ridge that separates the greater pelvis from the lesser pelvis.

The iliopubic eminence provides an insertion site for the psoas minor muscle, as well as attachment sites for the pubofemoral ligament and the iliopsoas fascia.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior intercondylar area (anterior intercondylar fossa or anterior intercondyloid fossa) is the anteriorly located, non-articular part of the region that is found between the articular facets of the medial and lateral condyles of the tibia. It is separated from the posterior intercondylar area by the intercondylar eminence.

The anterior intercondylar area provides attachment sites for the anterior cruciate ligament and the anterior horns of both the medial and lateral menisci.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The obturator groove (sulcus) is the wide, shallow depression found along the inferior aspect of the superior pubic ramus. It extends, anteromedially, across the pelvic surface, inferior border, and obturator surface of the superior pubic ramus.

The obturator groove is converted into the obturator canal by the upper margin of the obturator membrane. This canal allows for the passage of the obturator nerve and vessels.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text:
The right lateral part (lateral mass) of the sacrum is the large, longitudinal projection that extends from the right side of the median part of sacrum. It is formed by the transverse processes that extend from the right side of the sacral vertebrae as individual bony bars. These transverse processes fuse at their lateral ends, forming the anterior and posterior sacral foramina.

The right lateral part of sacrum is one of three parts of the sacrum, the other two being the left lateral part and the median part. Both the right and left lateral parts of sacrum consist of a lateral sacral crest, an ala, a sacral tuberosity, and an auricular surface.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lateral border of coccyx is the margin found along the lateral side of the bone. It separates the dorsal and pelvic surfaces of the coccyx and provides an insertion site for the levator ani muscle. It also provides attachment sites for the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The apex (tip) of coccyx is the narrow lower end of the bone. It is formed by the fourth coccygeal vertebra and provides an origin site for the external anal sphincter muscle and an insertion site for the levator ani muscle. It also provides an attachment site for the anococcygeal ligament.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The lateral surface of sacrum is the lateral aspect of the bone. Its superior end is wide and becomes progressively narrower inferiorly until it reaches its end at the inferolateral angle. It consists of the auricular surface and the sacral tuberosity.

The lateral surface of sacrum provides attachment sites for the sacrotuberous, sacrospinous, and interosseous sacroiliac ligaments.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The pelvic surface (anterior surface) of sacrum is the smooth, concave, anterior aspect of the bone. It consists of the anterior sacral foramina and four transverse ridges, and it contributes to the formation of the posterior wall of the pelvis.

The pelvic surface of sacrum provides an origin site for the piriformis muscles and an insertion site for the coccygeus muscles. It also provides an attachment site for the anterior sacrococcygeal and anterior longitudinal ligaments. The median and lateral sacral vessels and the caudal end of the sympathetic trunk travel along this surface.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The base of sacrum is the large, upper aspect of the bone. It is formed by the superior surface of the body and transverse processes of the first sacral vertebra. It consists of the ala, promontory, and superior articular processes of sacrum. 

Its medially located articular facet articulates with the fifth lumbar vertebra, forming the lumbosacral joint.

The base of sacrum provides attachment sites for the iliolumbar ligament. In some individuals, the fifth lumbar vertebra can be partially or completely fused to the base of the sacrum, which is known as sacralization of the fifth lumbar vertebra.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The pelvic surface (anterior surface) of coccyx is the smooth, concave, anterior aspect of the bone. It provides an insertion site for the coccygeus muscles, as well as attachment sites for the anterior sacrococcygeal ligaments. The median and lateral sacral vessels and the caudal ends of the sympathetic trunks travel along this surface.

21198.name: Anterior Border of Ala of Sacrum

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The anterior border of ala of sacrum is the margin found along the anterosuperior aspect of the sacrum. It separates the ala from the pelvic surface of the sacrum. 

The anterior border of ala of sacrum contributes to the formation of the linea terminalis (pelvic brim), which is a distinct ridge that separates the greater pelvis from the lesser pelvis.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The body of ischium is the posteriorly located, thick, irregularly shaped part of the bone. It is one of the two parts of the ischium, the other being the ramus of ischium. Its superior portion fuses with the body of ilium and the superior pubic ramus and forms the posteroinferior two fifths of the acetabulum. Its inferior portion consists of the ischial tuberosity and the ramus of ischium extends anteromedial from this portion.

The body of ischium consists of:

—three surfaces (femoral, pelvic, and dorsal);

—three borders (anterior, posterior, and lateral).

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The body of ilium is the inferiorly located, thick, irregularly shaped part of the bone. It is one of the two parts of the ilium, the other being the ala of ilium. It fuses with the body of ischium and the superior pubic ramus and forms the posterosuperior two fifths of the acetabulum.

Overall, the ilium consists of:

—three surfaces; gluteal, sacropelvic, and iliac fossa;

—three borders; anterior, posterior, and medial.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The ala (wing) of ilium is the superiorly located, thin, fan-shaped part of the bone. It is one of the two parts of the ilium, the other being the body of ilium, and consists of the iliac crest, four iliac spines, auricular surface, and iliac tuberosity. It provides attachment sites for muscles of the abdominal, thigh and gluteal regions.

Overall, the ilium consists of:

—three surfaces; gluteal, sacropelvic, and iliac fossa;

—three borders; anterior, posterior, and medial.

24256.name: Pectineal Surface of Superior Pubic Ramus
24256.latin: Facies pectinealis rami superioris ossis pubis

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The pectineal surface is the triangular area on the anterosuperior aspect of the superior pubic ramus. It extends from the pubic tubercle to the iliopubic eminence. It is one of the three surfaces of the superior pubic ramus, the other two being the obturator and pelvic surfaces, and it is an area that is bounded:

—anteriorly, by the obturator crest;

—posteriorly, by the pecten pubis.

Its medial end is continuous with the crest of pubis, and its lateral end is continuous with the iliac fossa.

The pectineal surface of superior pubic ramus provides an origin site for the pectineus muscle.

19445.name: Pelvic Surface of Superior Pubic Ramus
19445.latin: Facies pelvica rami superioris ossis pubis

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The pelvic surface of superior pubic ramus is the smooth, concave area on the posterior aspect of this part of the bone. It is one of the three surfaces of the superior pubic ramus, the other two being the obturator and pectineal surfaces, and it is an area that is bounded:

—superiorly, by the pecten pubis;

—inferiorly, by the inferior border of superior pubic ramus.

Its medial end is continuous with the posterior surface of body of pubis, and its lateral end is continuous with both the sacropelvic surface of ilium and pelvic surface of body of ischium.

The pelvic surface of superior pubic ramus consists of part of the obturator groove, which also extends along the inferior border and obturator surface of the superior pubic ramus.

18578.name: Posterior Surface of Body of Pubis

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The posterior surface is the smooth area on the posteromedial aspect of the body of pubis. It is one of the three surfaces of the body of pubis, the other two being the anterior and symphyseal surfaces, and it is an area that is bounded:

—superiorly, by the crest of pubis;

—anteromedially, by the symphyseal surface of body of pubis.

Its inferior end is continuous with the internal surface of inferior pubic ramus, and its posterolateral end is continuous with the pelvic surface of superior pubic ramus.

The posterior surface of body of pubis provides origin sites for the levator ani and obturator internus muscles, as well as an attachment site for the puboprostatic ligament in males. It lies immediately anterior to the urinary bladder.

21400.name: Symphyseal Surface of Body of Pubis
alternate: Medial Surface of Body of Pubis
Symphysial Surface of Body of Pubis

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The symphyseal surface (medial surface) of body of pubis is the rough, oval area on the medial aspect of the body of pubis. It is one of the three surfaces of the body of pubis, the other two being the anterior and posterior surfaces, and it is an area that is bounded superiorly by the crest of pubis. Its inferior end is continuous with the medial border of inferior pubic ramus.

The symphyseal surface of body of pubis is the site of articulation with the fibrocartilaginous disc of the pubic symphysis joint.

22755.name: Internal Surface of Inferior Pubic Ramus
22755.latin: Facies interna rami inferioris ossis pubis
alternate: Posteromedial Surface of Inferior Pubic Ramus

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The internal surface (posteromedial surface) is the area on the posteromedial aspect of the inferior pubic ramus. It is one of the two surfaces of the inferior pubic ramus, the other being the external surface, and it is an area that is bounded:

—anteromedially, by the medial border of inferior pubic ramus;

—posterolaterally, by the lateral border of inferior pubic ramus.

Its superior end is continuous with the posterior surface of body of pubis, while its inferior end is continuous with the internal surface of ramus of ischium.

The internal surface of inferior pubic ramus provides an origin site for the obturator internus muscle.

23187.name: Internal Surface of Ramus of Ischium
alternate: Posterior Surface of Ramus of Ischium

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The internal surface (posterior surface) of is the smooth area on the inner aspect of the ramus of ischium. It is one of the two surfaces of the ramus of ischium, the other being the external surface, and is an area that is bounded by the superior and inferior borders of ramus of ischium. Its anteromedial end is continuous with the internal surface of inferior pubic ramus, while its posterolateral end is continuous with the pelvic surface of body of ischium.

The internal surface of ramus of ischium provides attachment sites for the crus of penis in males, the crus of clitoris in females, and the external urethral sphincter muscle.

23331.name: Pelvic Surface of Body of Ischium

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The pelvic surface is the smooth area on the medial aspect of the body of ischium. It is one of the three surfaces of the body of ischium, the other two being the femoral and dorsal surfaces, and it is an area that is bounded:

—anteriorly, by the anterior border of body of ischium;

—posteriorly, by the posterior border of body of ischium.

Its superior end is continuous with the sacropelvic surface of ilium and the pelvic surface of superior pubic ramus. Its inferior end is continuous with the inferior internal surface of ramus of ischium.

The pelvic surface of body of ischium provides an origin site for the obturator internus muscle.

sections.title: Description

23613.name: Vertebral Body of Tenth Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description

24510.name: Inferior Articular Process of Tenth Thoracic Vertebra
24510.latin: Processus articularis inferior vertebrae thoracicae decimae
alternate: Inferior Zygapophysis of Tenth Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The inferior articular processes (inferior zygapophyses) are the two downwardly projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a thoracic vertebra. They extend inferiorly from the laminae.

Overall, the inferior articular processes of thoracic vertebrae generally consist of inferior articular facets that face anteriorly and slightly medially. They articulate with the superior articular processes of the vertebra below, forming zygapophyseal joints.

18000.name: Inferior Articular Facet of Tenth Thoracic Vertebra
18000.latin: Facies articularis inferior vertebrae thoracicae decimae

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The inferior articular facets are the smooth, anteriorly and slightly medially facing articular areas on the inferior articular processes of a thoracic vertebra. They articulate with the corresponding superior articular facets of the vertebra below, forming zygapophyseal joints.

22434.name: Spinous Process of Tenth Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The spinous process is the single, posteriorly projecting process located at the posterior part of the vertebral arch of a thoracic vertebra. It extends from the junction between the two laminae, which itself is found at the midline.

Overall, the spinous processes of thoracic vertebrae are generally long, thin, and tapered. They are obliquely oriented in the posteroinferior direction, resulting in adjacent spinous processes overlapping each other. They provide attachment sites for both intrinsic and extrinsic back muscles, thoracolumbar fascia, and the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments.

17914.name: Transverse Process of Tenth Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The transverse processes are the two laterally projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a thoracic vertebra. They extend from the junction between the pedicles and laminae.

Overall, the transverse processes of thoracic vertebrae are generally long, thick, and have expanded lateral ends. All thoracic transverse processes, except those of the eleventh and twelfth thoracic vertebrae, consist of transverse costal facets. Thoracic transverse processes provide attachment sites for the levatores costarum and intrinsic back muscles, as well as attachment sites for the intertransverse ligaments, superior costotransverse, and lateral costotransverse ligaments. The transverse processes of the first to tenth thoracic vertebrae also provide attachment sites for the costotransverse ligaments.

16472.name: Superior Articular Process of Tenth Thoracic Vertebra
16472.latin: Processus articularis superior vertebrae thoracicae decimae
alternate: Superior Zygapophysis of Tenth Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior articular processes (superior zygapophyses) are the two upwardly projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a thoracic vertebra. They extend from the junction between the pedicles and laminae.

Overall, the superior articular processes of thoracic vertebrae generally consist of superior articular facets that face posteriorly and slightly laterally. They articulate with the inferior articular processes of the vertebra above, forming zygapophyseal joints.

22758.name: Superior Articular Facet of Tenth Thoracic Vertebra
22758.latin: Facies articularis superior vertebrae thoracicae decimae

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The superior articular facets are the smooth, posteriorly and slightly laterally facing articular areas on the superior articular processes of a thoracic vertebra. They articulate with the corresponding inferior articular facets of the vertebra above, forming zygapophyseal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The tubercle of second rib is a small prominence on the external surface of the junction between its neck and its body. It consists of two parts:

—a smooth, medially located articular facet, which articulates with the transverse process of second thoracic vertebra;

—a rough, laterally located non-articular part, which provides the attachment site for the costotransverse ligament.

Overall, only the first to tenth ribs have a tubercle, while the eleventh and twelfth ribs lack this bony feature.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The chondral end (anterior end or sternal end) of second rib is located at the anterior end of the shaft. It has a small, rough, concave facet, which attaches to the second costal cartilage, forming the second costochondral joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The body (shaft) of second rib is the long, curved part of the bone that extends from its neck to its chondral end. It is flattened in appearance, where it has external and internal surfaces and superior and inferior borders.

The body of second rib consists of the costal groove and the angle, and provides attachment sites for the intercostal muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The neck of second rib is the short section that extends from the head to the body. It is located medial to the tubercle and anterior to the transverse process of second thoracic vertebra.The neck of second rib is somewhat flattened in appearance, where it has external and internal surfaces, and superior and inferior borders. Its superior border is sharp and is known as the crest, while its inferior border is blunt and round. It provides attachment sites for the internal intercostal membrane and the costotransverse ligament.Overall, only the first to tenth ribs have a neck, while the eleventh and twelfth ribs lack this bony feature.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: External surface of second rib

sections.title: Description
sections.text: External surface of second rib

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The head of second rib is the round, expanded, posterior part of the bone. It is the medial continuation of its neck.

It consists of superior and inferior articular facets, which are separated from each other by its crest. These articular facets articulate with the bodies of the adjacent thoracic vertebrae, forming the joint of the head of the second rib.

18262.name: Transverse Process of Second Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The transverse processes are the two laterally projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a thoracic vertebra. They extend from the junction between the pedicles and laminae.

Overall, the transverse processes of thoracic vertebrae are generally long, thick, and have expanded lateral ends. All thoracic transverse processes, except those of the eleventh and twelfth thoracic vertebrae, consist of transverse costal facets. Thoracic transverse processes provide attachment sites for the levatores costarum and intrinsic back muscles, as well as attachment sites for the intertransverse ligaments, superior costotransverse, and lateral costotransverse ligaments. The transverse processes of the first to tenth thoracic vertebrae also provide attachment sites for the costotransverse ligaments.

19454.name: Superior Articular Facet of Second Thoracic Vertebra
19454.latin: Facies articularis superior vertebrae thoracicae secundae

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The superior articular facets are the smooth, posteriorly and slightly laterally facing articular areas on the superior articular processes of a thoracic vertebra. They articulate with the corresponding inferior articular facets of the vertebra above, forming zygapophyseal joints.

16711.name: Inferior Articular Process of Second Thoracic Vertebra
16711.latin: Processus articularis inferior vertebrae thoracicae secundae
alternate: Inferior Zygapophysis of Second Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The inferior articular processes (inferior zygapophyses) are the two downwardly projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a thoracic vertebra. They extend inferiorly from the laminae.

Overall, the inferior articular processes of thoracic vertebrae generally consist of inferior articular facets that face anteriorly and slightly medially. They articulate with the superior articular processes of the vertebra below, forming zygapophyseal joints.

24801.name: Inferior Articular Facet of Second Thoracic Vertebra
24801.latin: Facies articularis inferior vertebrae thoracicae secundae

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The inferior articular facets are the smooth, anteriorly and slightly medially facing articular areas on the inferior articular processes of a thoracic vertebra. They articulate with the corresponding superior articular facets of the vertebra below, forming zygapophyseal joints.

22356.name: Superior Articular Process of Second Thoracic Vertebra
22356.latin: Processus articularis superior vertebrae thoracicae secundae
alternate: Superior Zygapophysis of Second Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior articular processes (superior zygapophyses) are the two upwardly projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a thoracic vertebra. They extend from the junction between the pedicles and laminae.

Overall, the superior articular processes of thoracic vertebrae generally consist of superior articular facets that face posteriorly and slightly laterally. They articulate with the inferior articular processes of the vertebra above, forming zygapophyseal joints.

sections.title: Description
Description
sections.text: The clavicular notches are the oval indentations found along the superior border of the manubrium of the sternum. They are superolaterally facing articular areas located on either side of the jugular notch of the sternum. Each clavicular notch articulates with the sternal facet of the clavicle on its respective side, forming the sternoclavicular joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The first costal notches are the superiorly located, laterally facing articular areas found along the lateral borders of the manubrium of the sternum. They are one of the seven pairs of articular facets that are found on the lateral borders of the entire sternum.

Each first costal notch articulates with the first costal cartilage on its respective side, forming the first costosternal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The second costal notches are the lateral facing articular areas found along the lateral borders of the sternum. They are one of the seven pairs of articular facets that are found on the lateral borders of the entire sternum.

Each second costal facet is formed by the combination of two demifacets:

—The upper demifacet is located at the inferior end of the lateral border of the manubrium of the sternum.

—The lower demifacet is located at the superior end of the lateral border of the body of the sternum.

Each second costal notch articulates with the second costal cartilage on its respective side, forming the second costosternal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The third costal notches are the lateral facing articular areas found along the lateral borders of the body of the sternum. They are one of the seven pairs of articular facets that are found on the lateral borders of the entire sternum.

Each third costal notch articulates with the third costal cartilage on its respective side, forming the third costosternal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The fourth costal notches are the lateral facing articular areas found along the lateral borders of the body of the sternum. They are one of the seven pairs of articular facets that are found on the lateral borders of the entire sternum.

Each fourth costal notch articulates with the fourth costal cartilage on its respective side, forming the fourth costosternal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The fifth costal notches are the lateral facing articular areas found along the lateral borders of the body of the sternum. They are one of the seven pairs of articular facets that are found on the lateral borders of the entire sternum.

Each fifth costal notch articulates with the fifth costal cartilage on its respective side, forming the fifth costosternal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The sixth costal notches are the lateral facing articular areas found along the lateral borders of the body of the sternum. They are one of the seven pairs of articular facets that are found on the lateral borders of the entire sternum.

Each sixth costal notch articulates with the sixth costal cartilage on its respective side, forming the sixth costosternal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The seventh costal notches are the lateral facing articular areas found along the lateral borders of the sternum. They are one of the seven pairs of articular facets that are found on the lateral borders of the entire sternum.

Each seventh costal facet is formed by the combination of two demifacets:

—The upper demifacet is located at the inferior end of the lateral border of the body of the sternum.

—The lower demifacet is located at the superior end of the lateral border of the xiphoid process.

Each seventh costal notch articulates with the seventh costal cartilage on its respective side, forming the seventh costosternal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The tubercle of first rib is a small prominence on the external surface of the junction between its neck and its body. It consists of two parts:

—a smooth, medially located articular facet, which articulates with the transverse process of first thoracic vertebra;

—a rough, laterally located non-articular part, which provides the attachment site for the costotransverse ligament.

The angle of first rib is obscure because it is located in the same area as its tubercle.

Overall, only the first to tenth ribs have a tubercle, while the eleventh and twelfth ribs lack this bony feature.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The chondral end (anterior end or sternal end) of first rib is located at the anterior end of the shaft. It has a small, rough, concave facet, which attaches to the first costal cartilage, forming the first costochondral joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: Superior surface of first rib

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The head of first rib is the round, expanded, posterior part of the bone. It is the medial continuation of its neck.

It consists of a single articular facet, which articulates with the body of the first thoracic vertebra, forming the joint of the head of the first rib.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The neck of first rib is the short section that extends from the head to the body. It is located medial to the tubercle and anterior to the transverse process of first thoracic vertebra. 

The neck of first rib is round in appearance, and therefore lacks the distinctive external and internal surfaces, and superior and inferior borders that are seen on the second to tenth ribs. It provides attachment sites for the internal intercostal membrane and the costotransverse ligament.

Overall, only the first to tenth ribs have a neck, while the eleventh and twelfth ribs lack this bony feature.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: Superior surface of first rib, posterior to the subclavian artery

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The groove (sulcus) for subclavian artery is a shallow depression located on the middle part of the superior surface of the first rib. It lies immediately posterior to the scalene tubercle, while the groove for the subclavian vein is located anterior to this tubercle.

This groove lodges the subclavian artery, as well as the lower trunk of brachial plexus.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The scalene tubercle (tubercle of anterior scalene muscle or Lisfranc’s Tubercle) is a small raised eminence located on the middle part of the superior surface of the first rib. It is lies between the grooves for the subclavian artery and vein.

The scalene tubercle provides the insertion site for the scalenus anterior muscle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The groove (sulcus) for subclavian vein is a shallow depression located on the middle part of the superior surface of the first rib. It lies immediately anterior to the scalene tubercle, while the groove for the subclavian artery is located posterior to this tubercle.

This groove lodges the subclavian vein.

18904.name: Crest of Head of Fifth Rib
alternate: Interarticular Crest of Head of Fifth Rib

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The crest (interarticular crest) is the horizontal ridge found along the medial aspect of the head of the fifth rib. It separates the superior and inferior articular facets and attaches to its adjacent intervertebral disc, via an intraarticular ligament.

Overall, only the heads of the second to ninth ribs consist of a crest, while the first, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth ribs do not.

21321.name: Superior Articular Facet of Head of Fifth Rib
21321.latin: Facies articularis superior capitis costae quintae

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior articular facet is the upper, smaller, smooth area located on the medial aspect of the head of the fifth rib. It is one of two articular facets on the head of the fifth rib, the other being the inferior articular facet, and these two facets are separated from each other by the crest of the head of the rib.

This superior articular facet articulates with the inferior costal facet of the fourth thoracic vertebra, forming the upper part of the joint of the head of the fifth rib. The lower part of this joint is formed by the articulation between the inferior articular facet on the head of the fifth rib and the superior costal facet of the fifth thoracic vertebra.

Overall, the first, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth ribs have a single articular facet on their heads, while the remaining ribs have two articular facets, known as the superior and inferior articular facets on heads of ribs.

21454.name: Inferior Articular Facet of Head of Fifth Rib
21454.latin: Facies articularis inferior capitis costae quintae

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The inferior articular facet is the lower, larger, smooth area located on the medial aspect of the head of the fifth rib. It is one of two articular facets on the head of the fifth rib, the other being the superior articular facet, and these two facets are separated from each other by the crest of the head of the rib.

This inferior articular facet articulates with the superior costal facet of the fifth thoracic vertebra, forming the lower part of the joint of the head of the fifth rib. The upper part of this joint is formed by the articulation between the superior articular facet on the head of the fifth rib and the inferior costal facet of the fourth thoracic vertebra.

Overall, the first, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth ribs have a single articular facet on their heads, while the remaining ribs have two articular facets, known as the superior and inferior articular facets on heads of ribs.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The neck of fifth rib is the short section that extends from the head to the shaft. It is located medial to the tubercle and anterior to the transverse process of fifth thoracic vertebra.The neck of fifth is somewhat flattened in appearance, where it has external and internal surfaces, and superior and inferior borders. Its superior border is sharp and is known as the crest, while its inferior border is blunt and round. It provides attachment sites for the internal intercostal membrane and the costotransverse ligament.Overall, only the first to tenth ribs have a neck, while the eleventh and twelfth ribs lack this bony feature.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The head of fifth rib is the round, expanded, posterior part of the bone. It is the medial continuation of its neck.

It consists of superior and inferior articular facets, which are separated from each other by its crest. These articular facets articulate with the bodies of the adjacent thoracic vertebrae, forming the joint of the head of the fifth rib.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The external surface (outer surface) of fifth rib is its smooth, convex, outer area. It is one of the two surfaces of the body of the fifth rib, the other being the internal surface.

The external surface of fifth rib consists of the angle, which is located on its posterolateral aspect. It provides:

—origin sites for the external abdominal oblique, iliocostalis cervicis, pectoralis minor and serratus anterior muscles;

—insertion sites for the serratus posterior superior, levatores costarum breves, iliocostalis thoracis, iliocostalis lumborum and longissimus thoracis muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The internal surface (inner surface) of fifth rib is its smooth, concave, inner area. It is one of the two surfaces of the body of the fifth rib, the other being the external surface.

The internal surface of fifth rib consists of the costal groove, which is located on its inferior edge, adjacent to the ribs inferior border. It provides an origin site for the insertion site for the transversus thoracis muscle, attachment sites for the innermost intercostal muscles, and is covered by endothoracic fascia.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The angle (costal angle) is an area of the body of fifth rib where its curvature changes sharply. It is located lateral to the tubercle and is marked by a prominent linear ridge on the ribs external surface, which itself provides attachment sites for muscles of the back.Overall, the first to eleventh ribs have an angle, while the twelfth ribs lack this bony feature. Furthermore, although the first rib has an angle, it occurs at the same site as its tubercle and is therefore indistinguishable. The distance between the angle and tubercle progressively increases from the second to tenth ribs.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The costal groove (costal sulcus) is the short, shallow depression found along the body of the fifth rib. It begins lateral to the tubercle and travels along the internal surface of the body, adjacent to the inferior border, and gradually becomes indistinguishable as it travels to the more anterior part of the body of the fifth rib.

The intercostal vein, artery and nerve travel along the costal groove, with the vein lying most superior and the nerve most inferior. The upper edge of the costal groove provides an attachment site for the innermost intercostal muscle.

Overall, only the second to eleventh ribs have a costal groove, while the first and twelfth ribs lack this bony feature.

21087.name: Crest of Neck of Fifth Rib
alternate: Ridge on Neck of Fifth Rib

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The crest (ridge) is the sharp, upper edge of the neck of the fifth rib. It is continuous laterally with the superior border of the body of fifth rib and provides an attachment site for the superior costotransverse ligament.

Overall, only the necks of the second to tenth ribs consist of a crest. It is absent from the neck of the first rib due to its round shape, while the eleventh and twelfth ribs have no neck at all.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The tubercle of fifth rib is a small prominence on the external surface of the junction between its neck and its body. It consists of two parts:

—a smooth, medially located articular facet, which articulates with the transverse process of fifth thoracic vertebra;

—a rough, laterally located non-articular part, which provides the attachment site for the costotransverse ligament.

Overall, only the first to tenth ribs have a tubercle, while the eleventh and twelfth ribs lack this bony feature.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The external surface (outer surface) of twelfth rib is its smooth, convex, outer area. It is one of the two surfaces of the body of the twelfth rib, the other being the internal surface.

The external surface of twelfth rib provides:

—origin sites for the external abdominal oblique, iliocostalis thoracis and latissimus dorsi muscles;

—insertion sites for the levatores costarum breves, levatores costarum longi, internal abdominal oblique, longissimus thoracis and serratus posterior inferior muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The superior border (upper border) of twelfth rib is its blunt, smooth upper edge. It is one of the two borders of the body of the twelfth rib, the other being the inferior border. It provides insertion sites for the external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The chondral end (anterior end or sternal end) of twelfth rib is located at the anterior end of the shaft. It tapers to a point, which is capped by the very short twelfth costal cartilage, forming the twelfth costochondral joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The body (shaft) of twelfth rib is the long, curved part of the bone that extends from its head to its chondral end. It is flattened in appearance, where it has external and internal surfaces and superior and inferior borders.

Unlike the other ribs, the twelfth rib does not have a costal groove or angle. It provides attachment sites for the intercostal muscles, along with muscles of the back and abdomen.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The head of twelfth rib is the round, expanded, posterior part of the bone. Due to the absence of a neck on the twelfth rib, its head is continuous laterally with its shaft.

It consists of a single articular facet, which articulates with the body of the twelfth thoracic vertebra, forming the joint of the head of the twelfth rib.

21063.name: Vertebral Body of Sixth Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description

18118.name: Inferior Articular Facet of Sixth Thoracic Vertebra
18118.latin: Facies articularis inferior vertebrae thoracicae sextae

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The inferior articular facets are the smooth, anteriorly and slightly medially facing articular areas on the inferior articular processes of a thoracic vertebra. They articulate with the corresponding superior articular facets of the vertebra below, forming zygapophyseal joints.

18697.name: Superior Articular Process of Fourth Thoracic Vertebra
18697.latin: Processus articularis superior vertebrae thoracicae quartae
alternate: Superior Zygapophysis of Fourth Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior articular processes (superior zygapophyses) are the two upwardly projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a thoracic vertebra. They extend from the junction between the pedicles and laminae.

Overall, the superior articular processes of thoracic vertebrae generally consist of superior articular facets that face posteriorly and slightly laterally. They articulate with the inferior articular processes of the vertebra above, forming zygapophyseal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The inferior surface (lower surface) of first rib is one of the two surfaces of its body, the other being the superior surface. Unlike the other eleven ribs, which have internal and external surfaces, the unique orientation of the first rib gives it superior and inferior surfaces.The inferior surface of first rib is a smooth area that is covered by endothoracic fascia.

16695.name: Superior Articular Process of Twelfth Thoracic Vertebra
16695.latin: Processus articularis superior vertebrae thoracicae duodecimae
alternate: Superior Zygapophysis of Twelfth Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The superior articular processes (superior zygapophyses) are the two upwardly projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a thoracic vertebra. They extend from the junction between the pedicles and laminae.

Overall, the superior articular processes of thoracic vertebrae generally consist of superior articular facets that face posteriorly and slightly laterally. They articulate with the inferior articular processes of the vertebra above, forming zygapophyseal joints.

17426.name: Inferior Articular Process of Twelfth Thoracic Vertebra
17426.latin: Processus articularis inferior vertebrae thoracicae duodecimae
alternate: Inferior Zygapophysis of Twelfth Thoracic Vertebra

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The inferior articular processes (inferior zygapophyses) are the two downwardly projecting processes located at the lateral parts of the vertebral arch of a thoracic vertebra. They extend inferiorly from the laminae.

Overall, the inferior articular processes of thoracic vertebrae generally consist of inferior articular facets that face anteriorly and slightly medially. They articulate with the superior articular processes of the vertebra below, forming zygapophyseal joints.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The radial fossa is the small, shallow depression found superior to the capitulum of the humerus. It is the lateral of the two fossae located on the anterior aspect of the condyle of the humerus, the other being the coronoid fossa. 

It accommodates the head of the radius during elbow flexion.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The supinator fossa is the depressed area found along the anterolateral aspect of the body of ulna. It is located inferior to the radial notch and is bounded posteriorly by the supinator crest.

It accommodates the radial tuberosity during pronation of the forearm and provides an origin site for the supinator muscle.

sections.title: Description
Description
Description
Description
Description
sections.text:
The suprameatal triangle (suprameatal fovea, suprameatal pit, or Macewen’s triangle) is the shallow, triangular depression found along the temporal surface of the squamous part of temporal bone. It is located posterosuperior to the external acoustic meatus and its superior boundary is defined by the supramastoid crest.

In some individuals, a suprameatal spine may be present at the inferior angle of this triangle.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The postglenoid tubercle (postglenoid or retroarticular process) is the projection found along the inferior aspect of the squamous part of temporal bone. It is located anterosuperior to the external acoustic meatus and its anterior aspect contributes to the formation of the mandibular fossa. It provides an attachment site for the cartilaginous part of the external acoustic meatus.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The zygomatic arch is the curved, horizontal, bony bar found along the lateral aspect of the cranium. It is formed:

- anteriorly, by the temporal process of the zygomatic bone;

- posteriorly, by the zygomatic process of the temporal bone.

The zygomatic arch contributes to the formation of the cheek and the anteroinferior boundary of the temporal fossa. It provides an origin site for the masseter muscle and an attachment site for the temporal fascia.

sections.title: Description
sections.text:
The acetabulum is the cup-shaped cavity on the outer aspect of the coxal bone. It is formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis, where:

—its anterior one fifth is formed by the superior ramus of pubis;

—its posterosuperior two fifths is formed by the body of ilium;

—its posteroinferior two fifths is formed by the body of ischium.

It is circumscribed by a prominent edge, the acetabular margin, which is absent inferiorly, leaving a gap that is known as the acetabular notch. Within the acetabulum lies its articular and non-articular portions:

—The articular portion is formed by the peripherally located lunate articular surface, which articulates with the head of femur, forming the hip joint.

—The non-articular portion is formed by the centrally located acetabular fossa, which forms the floor of the acetabulum.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The skin of penis the skin covering the body and root of the penis.

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The skin overlying the body of the penis is thin, highly elastic, and devoid of skin appendages, such as hair and glands. It’s relatively mobile as it is loosely attached to the underlying subcutaneous tissue and fascia of the penis. The skin overlying the glans penis is immobile due to the fact it is directly attached to the underlying tunica albuginea (Standring, 2016). A narrow dark streak or ridge runs along the midline of the urethral surface of the penis. This is known as the raphe of the penis and is continuous posteriorly with the raphe of the scrotum.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The fascia of penis is the firm inner fascial layer that surrounds the corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum of the shaft of the penis collectively. It’s continuous with the fascia of the ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The fascia of the penis consists of a deep layer of fibrous tissue, which surrounds the corpora cavernosa, and splits to surround the corpus spongiosum. Distally, it blends with the tunica albuginea of all corporal bodies. Proximally, the fascia of the penis is continuous with the perineal fascia that invests the muscles of the superficial perineal space (i.e., bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, and superficial transverse perineal muscles). It is also anchored to the suspensory ligament of the penis.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The fascia of the penis surrounds the three corpora erectile bodies, as well as the deep dorsal vein, the dorsal arteries of the penis, and the dorsal nerves of the penis.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The fascia of the penis is responsible for the structural integrity of the three erectile bodies of the penis.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

15489.name: Tunica Albuginea of Corpora Cavernosa Penis

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The tunica albuginea of corpora cavernosa penis is the dense, white, fibroelastic sheath that encloses the corpora cavernosa penis. Its superficial, longitudinal fibers form a tunic surrounding both corpora, and the deep circularly coursing fibers surround them separately, uniting medially to form the septum of the penis (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: A dense fibroelastic coat, the tunica albuginea, surrounds each corpus cavernosum. It has an outer longitudinal layer and an inner circular layer although they are somewhat indistinct and difficult to discern in transverse sections.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The tunica albuginea envelops the corpora cavernosa of the penis. A thin septum of fibrous connective tissue extending from the tunica albuginea, dividing this erectile tissue into two columns. A rich venous plexus of the subalbugineal space is present.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The elastic nature of the tunica albuginea allows blood to flow easily through the dorsal arteries of the penis to initiate an erection. The deep fascia of the penis, which is less elastic, puts pressure on the dorsal vein of the penis near the root to prevent blood from leaving the penis.

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The subcutaneous tissue of penis is the loose external layer of fascial tissue of the penis, continuous with the dartos fascia and the subcutaneous perineal fascia (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The subcutaneous tissue of the penis is a motile sheath of loose areolar connective tissue that surrounds the penis. Penile skin is loosely attached to this underlying loose connective tissue but at the glans penis it is extremely thin and tightly attached. There is no adipose tissue (fat) in the subcutaneous tissue of the penis (Quartey, 2006).

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The subcutaneous tissue of the penis is located superficial to the fascia of the penis and deep to the skin of the penis. It is continuous with Dartos fascia of the scrotum, the membranous layer of abdominal subcutaneous tissue (Scarpa’s fascia) and the membranous layer of subcutaneous tissue of the perineum (Colles’ fascia) (Quartey, 2006).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The subcutaneous tissue of the penis permits a significant amount of movement of the skin of the penis over the underlying structures. This tissue region also transmits the passage of the superficial dorsal vein of the penis and its anastomoses.

sections.title: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Quartey, J. K. M. (2006) 'Anatomy and Blood Supply of the Urethra and Penis', in Schreiter, F. and Jordan, G.H. (eds.) Urethral Reconstructive Surgery. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg, pp. 11-17.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The corpus spongiosum penis is the column of erectile tissue surrounding the urethra in the penis; its distal expansion forms the glans penis (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The corpus spongiosum penis is an erectile tissue that surrounds the spongy part of the male urethra within the penis. The proximal and distal parts of the corpus spongiosum are enlarged to form the bulb and glans of the penis. 

Cavernous spaces in the corpus spongiosum are dilatable spaces that fill with blood during erection. However, the corpus spongiosum never becomes as firmly erect as the corpora cavernosa. While it does become engorged with blood, it does not become rigid, which is essential; since it would pinch shut the urethra and prevent ejaculation.

The tunica albuginea is thinner than that of the corpora cavernosa and the cavernous sinuses are smaller in the corpus spongiosum. For these reasons, it's incapable of complete erection.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The corpus spongiosum is located on the ventral surface of the penile body, whereas the corpus cavernosum is located on the dorsal surface. The spongy (penile) urethra travels throughout the length of the corpus spongiosum.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Cavernous spaces in the corpus spongiosum fill with blood during erection but not sufficiently to prevent the urethra from closing to allow for ejaculation.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Urethral catheterization

sections.title: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: The corpus cavernosum penis is one of two columns of erectile tissue forming the dorsum and sides of the penis (Dorland, 2011).

sections.title: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The penis is mainly composed of two corpora cavernosa that extend from the root of the penis to the glans. Within this erectile tissue, there are dilatable cavernous spaces lined with epithelium. These spaces, the cavernous sinuses, fill with blood and become distended during erection. The cavernous sinuses are separated by trabeculae of connective tissue and contain bands of smooth muscle. The smooth muscle relaxes upon parasympathetic stimulation allowing blood to fill the sinuses. The sinuses receive blood from the deep arteries.

sections.title: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The corpora cavernosa are located along the dorsal side of the penis. The major neurovascular bundle of the penis is located dorsally on the corpus cavernosa.

The corpora cavernosa are separated by a septal extension of the tunica albuginea. However the septum is incomplete and a communication remains between the corpora cavernosa (Quartey, 2006).

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The corpora cavernosa help maintain erections by preventing blood return from the penis through the deep dorsal vein of the penis.

sections.title: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Erectile dysfunction

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The long limb (long process or long crus) of incus is the small, inferomedial projection of the bone. It is continuous superolaterally with the body of incus, consists of a lenticular process and articulates with the head of stapes, forming the incudostapedial joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The body of incus is the expanded, quadrilateral, lateral part of the bone. It is continuous superomedially with the short limb of incus and continuous inferomedially with the long limb of incus. The body of incus consists of an articular facet for malleus, provides an attachment site for the superior ligament of incus and articulates with the head of the malleus, forming the incudomallear joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The short limb (short process or short crus) of incus is the small, superomedial projection of the bone. It is continuous inferolaterally with the body of incus and provides an attachment site for the posterior ligament of incus.

18876.name: Articular Facet for Malleus
alternate: Articular Facet of Body of Incus

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The articular facet for malleus is the smooth, concave, articular area found along the anterolateral aspect of the body of incus. It articulates with the articular facet of the head of the malleus, forming the incudomallear joint.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: The lenticular process (lentiform process or lentiform nodule) of incus is the small, bulb-like projection found on the inferomedial end of the long limb of incus. It articulates with the articular facet of the head of stapes, forming the incudostapedial joint.
